Student@SC: A Hands-On Introduction to HPC & AI
events.description:
Start your SC26 experience with a full-day, hands-on introduction to high performance computing and artificial intelligence.
This workshop will help students build practical familiarity with the tools, concepts, and workflows used in modern HPC and AI development. Through guided exercises, students will explore how to work in advanced computing environments, run computational workloads, and understand how AI applications connect with large-scale computing systems.
The workshop is designed for students with a range of backgrounds. Whether you are encountering HPC for the first time or looking to strengthen your foundation, this session will help you build confidence using technical computing resources.
Lunch will be provided to full-day participants.
Please see the SC26 Student Programming page for a detailed schedule.

events.title: Student@SC: A Hands-On Introduction to HPC & AI
events.description: Hands-on introduction to HPC and AI.

events.title: Using Containers To Accelerate HPC
events.description: The use of containers has revolutionized the way in which industries and enterprises have developed and deployed computational software and distributed systems. This containerization model has gained traction within the HPC community as well with the promise of improved reliability, reproducibility, portability, and levels of customization that were not previously possible on supercomputers. This adoption has been enabled by a number of HPC container runtimes that have emerged including Apptainer, Shifter, Sarus, Podman, and others. This hands-on tutorial looks to train users on the use of containers for HPC use cases. We will provide a detailed background on Linux containers, along with an introductory hands-on experience building a container image, sharing the container and running it on an HPC cluster. Furthermore, the tutorial will provide more advanced information on how to run MPI-based and GPU-enabled HPC applications, how to optimize I/O intensive workflows, how to set up GUI-enabled interactive sessions, and how to use containers for agentic AI and MCP servers. Users will leave the tutorial with a solid foundational understanding of how to utilize containers on HPC resources using Podman, Docker, and Apptainer, and in-depth knowledge to deploy custom containers for HPC and AI on their own resources.

events.title: Flux: Workload Management for HPC and AI/ML Simulation in Cloud
events.description: Modern scientific workloads require automation and elasticity beyond the reach of traditional HPC schedulers. Developed over a decade at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Flux is the next-generation workload manager powering El Capitan, the world's #1 exascale system. Flux is unique for its graph-based, hierarchical resource management, enabling seamless portability and performance for complex workflows. Recently, the project joined the High Performance Software Foundation (HPSF) and was integrated with the Kubernetes Kubeflow Trainer for AI/ML. Participants will explore Flux foundations before diving into advanced capabilities for on-premises, cloud, and Kubernetes environments. We will cover the orchestration of heterogeneous workloads that require interplay between simulation, analysis, and services. Through lectures and hands-on, energetic tutorials that include interactive questions and terrible jokes, attendees will have fun and learn the ins and outs of scheduling in the exascale era. Tutorial content will range from getting started with job submission to running Flux with the Kubeflow Trainer in Kubernetes, and orchestrating a workflow under the scope of agentic science. Importantly, Flux Framework has never had the opportunity to give a pure Flux tutorial at the SC conference, and an influx of interest and questions make this year a unique opportunity to address this gap.

events.title: Compression for AI and Scientific Data
events.description: Large-scale numerical simulations, experimental instruments, observational platforms, and modern AI workloads generate and consume unprecedented volumes of data, creating critical challenges for storage, I/O, communication, and analysis. Data compression—particularly error-bounded lossy compression—is a key enabling technology to address these challenges. This half-day tutorial reviews the motivations, fundamental principles, and algorithmic foundations of lossy compression for scientific and AI data workflows. It introduces core compression stages (decorrelation, approximation, and encoding) and examines their realizations in state-of-the-art compressors. It emphasizes trustworthiness through error control, uncertainty quantification, and application-specific quality metrics. New this year, we consistently incorporate compression for AI and data-driven workflows, including training data, model states (e.g., embeddings and activations), and communication buffers in distributed and federated learning. The 70-minute hands-on session covers generic compressors and demonstrates a novel generation of lossy compression framework for building practical, customized compression pipelines using real-world datasets, including ones from participants if available. Leading researchers in AI and compression researchers and developers present the tutorial targeted at beginners and practitioners seeking to understand and apply lossy compression in modern HPC and AI environments. It builds upon and significantly extends the highly rated SC17–SC25 tutorial series with new content on AI integration, trustworthiness, and next-generation workflows.

events.title: Accelerated Quantum Supercomputing: A Hands-On Tutorial on Quantum-Classical Hybrid Workflows Executed on QPUs and GPUs
events.description: Accelerated quantum supercomputing (AQSC) requires engineers to consider the hardware, software, and infrastructure challenges that arise when integrating quantum processing units (QPUs) into an HPC environment. This tutorial will provide attendees with hands-on experience to learn about AQSC infrastructure being deployed at supercomputing centers around the world. Participants will gain hands-on experience with the Python API of CUDA-Q. Attendees will have access to GPUs and IQM QPUs hosted at Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ). Live demonstrations and hands-on exercises include how to scale workflows, from a simple pip install to deploying multi-GPU, multi-node, and QPU jobs. This will all be tied under two quantum algorithms: sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD: quantum and HPC) and generative quantum eigensolver (GQE: AI and quantum), emphasizing the need for HPC and AI in quantum computing workflows. Attendees will learn about challenges in scaling quantum hardware and advancements in quantum error mitigation (QEM) and quantum error correction (QEC) which address them. They will learn about and execute commonly used QEM and QEC techniques in superconducting devices and perform GPU-accelerated decoding of quantum measurements. Participants will leave with practical skills in building hybrid applications locally and experience in scaling them on AQSC infrastructure.

events.title: A Tutorial for Kokkos: Performance Portability for C++ Applications and Libraries
events.description: This SC26 tutorial on Kokkos — an HPC, performance portability, open source, C++ library — targets a beginner audience who wants to write efficient code for CPU and GPU hardware, while maintaining only one code base. The course consists of lectures and hands-on exercises, covering the fundamental aspects of the Kokkos library, including parallel construct functions and memory management classes. The materials come from the official, open source Kokkos tutorial, which is freely accessible online. This is a full-day tutorial.

events.title: Core-Level Performance Engineering
events.description: While many developers put a lot of effort into optimizing large-scale parallelism, they often neglect the importance of an efficient serial code. Even worse, slow serial code tends to scale very well, hiding the fact that resources are wasted because no definite hardware performance limit (“bottleneck”) is exhausted. This tutorial conveys the required knowledge to develop a thorough understanding of the interactions between software and hardware on the level of a single CPU core and the lowest memory hierarchy level (the L1 cache). We introduce general out-of-order core architectures and their typical performance bottlenecks using modern x86-64 (Intel Sapphire Rapids) and ARM (NVIDIA Vera) processors as examples. We then go into detail about x86 and AArch64 assembly code, specifically including vectorization (SIMD), pipeline utilization, critical paths, and loop-carried dependencies. We also demonstrate performance analysis and performance engineering using the Open-Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) in combination with a dedicated instance of the well-known Compiler Explorer. Various hands-on exercises will allow attendees to make their own experiments and measurements and identify in-core performance bottlenecks. Furthermore, we show real-life use cases from computational science (sparse solvers, molecular dynamics) to emphasize how profitable in-core performance engineering can be.

events.title: Deep Learning at Scale: Engineering High-Resolution Scientific AI Models
events.description: Deep learning is increasingly used in scientific applications involving high-dimensional, high-resolution data. As models, datasets, and data resolutions scale, so does the need for efficient, distributed training on high performance computing (HPC) systems. This tutorial addresses practical challenges in training scientific AI models on high-resolution data, including data throughput, memory pressure, and communication overhead in distributed HPC workflows. Participants will learn to profile and build efficient data pipelines, optimize single-GPU performance, and scale training across GPUs and nodes using data, tensor, and spatial (domain) parallelism. Through hands-on examples drawn from scientific use cases, we will show how different model families, such as transformers, convolutional neural networks, and neural operators, benefit from these parallelization strategies. We will emphasize the performance trade-offs among computation, memory, and communication that determine scalability for high-resolution scientific workloads. Attendees will gain experience running optimized workloads on GPU-based supercomputers and learn strategies they can apply to train scientific AI models that exceed single-device memory limits while scaling efficiently.

events.title: Efficient Distributed GPU Programming for Exascale
events.description: Over the past decade, GPUs became ubiquitous in HPC installations around the world, delivering the majority of performance of some of the largest supercomputers, steadily increasing the available compute capacity. Four exascale systems (Frontier, Aurora, El Capitan, JUPITER) use GPUs as the core computing devices. To take advantage of these GPU-accelerated systems with tens of thousands of devices, application developers need to have the proper skills and tools to understand, manage, and optimize distributed GPU applications. In this tutorial, participants will learn techniques to efficiently program large-scale multi-GPU systems. While programming multiple GPUs with MPI is explained, also advanced tuning techniques and complementing programming models like NCCL and NVSHMEM are presented. Tools for analysis are shown and used to motivate and implement performance optimizations. The tutorial teaches fundamental concepts that apply to GPU-accelerated systems of any vendor in general, taking the NVIDIA platform as an example. It is a combination of lectures and hands-on exercises, using the JUPITER system for interactive learning and discovery.

events.title: High-Performance and Smart-Networking Technologies for HPC and AI
events.description: High-performance networking technologies are generating a lot of excitement towards building next-generation high-end computing (HEC) systems for HPC and AI with hundreds of thousands of servers with the latest CPU and GPU technologies, and a variety of application workloads. This tutorial provides an overview of these emerging technologies, their architectural features, current market standing, and suitability for designing HEC systems while delivering scale-up and scale-out principles. We present a holistic view of the major scale-out interconnects that power today’s supercomputers, such as IB, HSE, RoCE, Omni-Path, AWS-EFA, Slingshot, Tofu-D, and Ultra-Ethernet Consortium, followed by scale-up interconnects like NVLink/NVSwitch, AMD Infinity Fabric, CXL, and ESUN. We also highlight how the features of these networking technologies are integrated into libraries such as UCX, Libfabrics, and how these libraries are utilized in upper-level libraries such as MPI. The more advanced topics include discussions on DPU/IPUs and AI hardware such as Cerebras, Microsoft's Maia accelerator, and Meta's MTIA inference engine. Throughout the tutorial, we introduce four hands-on exercises to help attendees learn from the ground up (network-level concepts to MPI library integration) and how the network forms the foundation for designing HEC systems with scalable performance for HPC and AI workloads.

events.title: In-Network Computing with SmartNICs for HPC Applications
events.description: The past few years have witnessed an increased level of support for and deployment of programmable network adapters, known as "SmartNICs." These enhanced network devices offer standard packet processing capabilities as well as advanced "in-network" computing features built around programmable lightweight processing cores, FPGAs, and even CPU- and GPU-based platforms capable of running separate operating systems. SmartNICs have gained rapid adoption for data center tasks, including infrastructure management, packet filtering, and I/O acceleration. Increasingly these devices are also being explored for high-performance computing (HPC) and AI application acceleration. This tutorial provides an in-depth exploration of the state of the art in SmartNICs and the emerging software ecosystems that support them. Attendees will participate in hands-on exercises designed to demonstrate how SmartNICs can be leveraged to accelerate HPC and AI applications. Topics include packet processing frameworks such as P4, I/O acceleration techniques, MPI offloading, and algorithmic adaptations for utilizing SmartNIC processors. Participants will have the opportunity to run these exercises on cutting-edge platforms, including NVIDIA BlueField-3 Data Processing Units (DPUs), using cloud-based environments such as USC’s NETLAB and the FABRIC testbed. The tutorial will also highlight additional strategies for optimizing applications to effectively use SmartNICs as communication accelerators in HPC systems.

events.title: Introduction to MLIR
events.description:
MLIR is rapidly becoming the infrastructure of choice for building domain-specific languages (DSLs) and compilers for high performance computing — examples include OpenAI’s Triton, NVIDIA’s cuTile, and AMD’s AIR/AIE. Dialects are a core concept in MLIR, enabling data types and operations to be defined at different levels of abstraction, along with passes to systematically transform the programs through a hierarchy of dialects for optimized execution on target platforms. In-tree dialects like Linalg define operations that can represent common computation paradigms like tensor contractions and convolutions.
This tutorial will introduce MLIR and provide an understanding of the steps to build a DSL compiler to target CPUs and GPUs. Starting with an overview of core MLIR concepts, like dialects, operations, types and interfaces, the tutorial will give participants hands-on experience in building an optimizing compiler using MLIR. At the end of this tutorial participants should have a good understanding of the power of transformations in MLIR and how to use them.

events.title: Parallel Computing 101
events.description: This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of parallel computing, emphasizing those aspects most relevant to the user. It is suitable for new users, students, managers, and anyone seeking an overview of parallel computing. It discusses software and hardware/software interaction, with an emphasis on standards, portability, and systems that are widely available. The tutorial surveys basic parallel computing concepts, using examples from multiple engineering, scientific, machine learning, and data analysis problems. These examples illustrate using MPI on distributed memory systems; OpenMP on shared memory systems; MPI+OpenMP on hybrid systems; and CUDA or compiler directives on GPUs and accelerators. It discusses numerous parallelization and load balancing approaches; performance improvement tools; and an overview of recent developments such as machine learning on accelerators and data analysis via parallel versions of Python. The tutorial helps attendees make intelligent decisions by covering the primary options that are available, explaining how the different components work together and what they are most suitable for. Extensive pointers to web-based resources are provided to facilitate follow-up studies.

events.title: Programming Your GPU with OpenMP: A “Hands-On” Introduction
events.description: If you are an HPC programmer, you know the OpenMP® API. Alongside MPI, the OpenMP API is the open, cross-vendor foundation of HPC. As hardware complexity has grown, the OpenMP programming model has grown as well, adding GPU support in OpenMP 4.0 (2013). With over a decade of evolution since then, OpenMP GPU technology is a mature option for programming any GPU you are likely to find on the market. While there are many ways to program a GPU, the best way is through the OpenMP API. Why? Because the GPU does not exist in isolation. There are always one or more CPUs on a node. Programmers need portable code that fully exploits all available processors. In other words, programmers need a programming model, such as OpenMP, that fully embraces heterogeneity. In this tutorial, we explore GPU programming with the OpenMP programming model. We assume attendees are familiar with multithreading, so we will focus on the directives that define how to map loops onto GPUs and optimize data movement between the CPU and GPU. Students will use their own laptops (with Windows, Linux, or macOS) to connect to remote servers with GPUs and all the software needed for the tutorial.

events.title: 13th Annual International Workshop on Innovating the Network for Data Intensive Science — INDIS
events.description: Data networks are the circulatory system for science, discovery, society, and industry. But scientific data networking is not a solved problem, and significant challenges remain. These challenges reflect scientists' persistent needs from data networks: the needs for ever increasing capacity, flexibility, consistency, and collaboration. The theme for the 13th INDIS workshop is "Connected Science: Bridging Research and Industry" — reflecting not only the role of networking in connecting scientific infrastructure, but also our community's collaborations across different types of organizations to advance data-intensive science. This year INDIS plans to continue its tradition of having a discussion- and interaction-oriented schedule; based on past feedback, this is always well received. INDIS 2026 delivers an essential complement to the HPC-focused SC26 Technical Program, providing a dedicated platform for HPC researchers to explore data-intensive computing, interconnects, and networking.

events.title: 15th International Workshop on Runtime and Operating Systems for Supercomputers (ROSS 2026)
events.description:
With increasing levels of parallelism, increased heterogeneity, energy and memory constraints coupled with emerging post-Moore computing architectures like quantum and neuromorphic, a reevaluation of current approaches for extreme-scale operating systems and runtime environments is needed.

ROSS is a workshop aimed at identifying looming problems and discussing promising research solutions in the area of runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers. Specifically, ROSS focuses on principles and techniques to design, implement, optimize, or operate runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers and cloud environments. In addition to typical workshop publications, we encourage novel and possibly immature ideas, provided that they are interesting and on-topic. Well argued position papers are also welcome.

events.title: IA^3 2026 — 16th Workshop on Irregular Applications: Architectures and Algorithms
events.description: Data-intensive applications process heterogeneously, employing diverse methods and data structures that exhibit irregular data accesses, control flows, and communication patterns. Modern data analytics applications additionally require supporting dynamic data structures, asynchronous control flows, and mixed parallel programming models. Supercomputing systems are organized around software and hardware optimized for data locality and bulk synchronous computations. Managing irregular behaviors requires a substantial programming effort and lacks integration, leading to poor performance. Holistic solutions to these challenges emerge only by considering the problem from multiple perspectives: from micro- to system architectures, from compilers to languages, from libraries to runtimes, and from algorithm design to data characteristics. Only collaborative efforts among researchers with different expertise, including domain experts and end users, can lead to significant breakthroughs. This workshop brings together scientists from different backgrounds to discuss methods and technologies for efficiently supporting irregular applications in current and future architectures.

events.title: 21st Workshop on Workflows in Support of Large-Scale Science (WORKS26)
events.description:
Scientific workflows have underpinned some of the most significant discoveries of the past several decades. Workflow management systems (WMS) provide abstraction and automation that enable researchers to easily define sophisticated computational processes, and to then execute them efficiently on parallel and distributed computing systems. As workflows have been adopted by multiple scientific communities, they are becoming more complex and require more sophisticated workflow management capabilities.

This workshop focuses on the many facets of scientific workflow composition, management, sustainability, and application to domain sciences in an increasingly diverse landscape. The workshop covers a broad range of topics in the scientific workflow lifecycle that include: reproducible research with workflows; workflow execution in distributed and heterogeneous environments; application of AI/ML in workflow management; workflow provenance; serverless workflows; exascale computing with workflows; stream-processing, interactive, adaptive and data-driven workflows; workflow scheduling and resource management; workflow fault-tolerance, debugging, performance analysis/modeling; big data and AI workflows, etc.

events.title: The 9th Annual Parallel Applications Workshop, Alternatives to MPI+X (PAW-ATM)
events.description:
Supercomputers get faster and more complex every year. MPI, long the dominant model for distributed computation, has adapted by combining with models for intra-node parallelism (e.g., OpenMP, CUDA). These MPI+X hybrids offer performance but demand significant programmer effort to write, debug, and tune applications.

Alternatives to MPI+X are worth exploring as programmer productivity becomes a major component of the time to science. Alternatives include parallel programming languages (e.g., Chapel, Regent, Fortran), general purpose libraries (e.g., Charm++, COMPSs, HPX, Legion, UPC++), and domain-specific libraries (e.g., Arkouda, Dask, Spark). With many options to choose from, it is hard for programmers to know which alternative models are appropriate for their application and for programming model developers to understand the opportunities for improvement.

PAW-ATM brings together both application experts and programming model developers to disseminate knowledge about available applications and models, as well as advance their design.

events.title: HUST Welcome
HUST-26: 13th International Workshop on HPC User Support Tools
events.description: Supercomputing centers exist to drive scientific discovery by supporting researchers in computational science fields. To make users more productive in the complex HPC environment, HPC centers employ user support teams. These teams serve many roles, from setting up accounts, to consulting on math libraries and code optimization, to managing HPC software stacks. Often, support teams struggle to adequately support scientists. HPC environments are extremely complex, and combined with the complexity of multi-user installations, exotic hardware, and maintaining research software, supporting HPC users can be extremely demanding. With the 13th HPC User Support Tools (HUST) workshop, we continue to provide a necessary forum for system administrators, user support team members, tool developers, policy makers, and end users. We provide a forum to discuss support issues, and we provide a publication venue for current support developments. Scope includes best practices, user support tools, and ideas to streamline user support at supercomputing centers.

events.title: RISE 2026: 1st International Workshop on Rising Innovators in Sustainable Exacomputing
events.description:
RISE 2026: Rising Innovators in Sustainable Exacomputing is a half-day, symposium-style workshop dedicated to strengthening the global talent pipeline in high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI). The workshop spans hardware and system architectures, software environments, algorithms, applications, machine learning, quantum and cloud computing, energy efficiency, and sustainability, while integrating leadership and career development. RISE combines technical excellence with mentorship through a keynote on global collaboration, a cross-sector career panel, mentorship roundtables, and lightning talks highlighting women-led research project spotlights. Interactive elements, including the RISE Research Expertise Map, Global RISE Exhibit, and a community-built Pathways in Computing timeline, foster visibility, networking, and interdisciplinary exchange. By connecting students, researchers, and senior leaders across academia, labs, and industry, RISE establishes an inclusive, recurring platform that advances innovation, collaboration, and sustainable professional growth in exascale computing.

events.title: EduHPC-26: Workshop on Education for High Performance Computing
events.description: The EduHPC workshop is devoted to the development and assessment of educational innovations and resources in high performance computing (HPC) and parallel and distributed computing (PDC), with a particular focus on undergraduate and graduate education. We encourage contributions at the intersection of HPC/PDC education and other areas, including artificial intelligence, data science, and internet-of-things and edge (IoT/Edge) computing. Given the increasing relevance of ML/deep learning workloads on HPC systems, we especially encourage pedagogical papers on this topic. Historically, the workshop has accepted contributions from fields such as CS, CSE, DS, and computational courses across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. The workshop aims to foster collaboration among stakeholders within the SC context and provides a platform for discussing pedagogical challenges, solutions, and opportunities for HPC/PDC/DS/AI/ML/IoT education. Activities at EduHPC'26 include a featured speaker, presentations of our peer-reviewed papers, and a special session focusing on innovative HPC/PDC assignments.

events.title: XLOOP 2026: The 8th Annual Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing
events.description: Advancement in computational power and high-speed networking is enabling a new model of scientific experiment, experiment-in-the-loop computing (EILC). In this model, simulation and/or learning modules are run as data is collected from observational and experimental sources. Presently, the amount and complexity of data generated by simulations and by observational and experimental sources, such as sensor networks and large-scale scientific facilities, continues to increase. Several research challenges exist, many of which are independent of the scientific application domain. New algorithms, including artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, to merge simulation ensembles and experimental data sets must be developed. Data transfer techniques and workflows must be constructed to control the ensembles and integrate simulated and observed data sets. The Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing (XLOOP 2026) will be a unique opportunity to promote this interdisciplinary topic area. We invite papers, presentations, and participants from the physical and computer sciences.

events.title: PMBS26: The 17th International Workshop on Performance Modeling, Benchmarking, and Simulation of High Performance Computer Systems
events.description:
The PMBS26 workshop is concerned with the comparison of high performance computing systems through performance modeling, benchmarking, or through the use of tools such as simulators. We are particularly interested in research that reports the ability to measure and make trade-offs in software/hardware co-design to improve sustained application performance. We are also keen to capture the assessment of future systems.

The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers, from industry and academia, concerned with the qualitative and quantitative evaluation and modeling of high performance computing systems. Authors are invited to submit novel research in all areas of performance modeling, benchmarking, and simulation, and we welcome research that brings together current theory and practice. We recognize that the term "performance" has broadened to include power consumption and reliability, and that performance modeling is practiced through analytical methods and approaches based on software tools and simulators.

events.title: The 2nd International Workshop for Software Frameworks and Workload Management on Quantum-HPC Ecosystems
events.description: The integration of quantum computing (QC) with high performance computing (HPC) is emerging as a transformative paradigm for addressing complex scientific and engineering challenges. Given current quantum hardware limitations, such as noise, limited qubit counts, and constrained circuit depth, hybrid quantum–HPC (Q-HPC) ecosystems provide a practical path forward by combining complementary strengths. This workshop focuses on software frameworks, AI-enabled orchestration, and workload management strategies essential for scalable Q-HPC integration. Topics include architecture co-design, heterogeneous resource management, networking, fault tolerance, error mitigation, programming models, middleware, benchmarking, and large-scale distributed Q-HPC systems. Emphasis will be placed on open, interoperable ecosystems such as openQSE and on ML/AI techniques for adaptive workflow orchestration, topology-aware scheduling, performance prediction, and autonomous runtime control. Through invited talks, technical presentations, panels, and special sessions, the workshop will foster collaboration across academia, industry, national laboratories, and funding agencies to define research priorities and accelerate AI-driven Q-HPC ecosystems.

events.title: 2026 International Workshop on Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC
events.description: The Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC workshop aims to bring together developers and researchers with an interest in practical solutions, technologies, tools, and methodologies that enable the development of performance-portable applications across a diverse set of current and future high‑performance computers. The topic of Performance, Portability, and Productivity focuses on enabling applications and libraries to run across multiple architectures without significant impact on achieved performance and with the goal of maintaining developer productivity. This workshop provides a forum for discussions of successes and failures in tackling the compelling problems that lie at the intersection of performance, portability, and productivity in high performance computing. This area touches on many aspects of HPC/AI software development and the workshop program is expected to reflect a wide range of experiences and perspectives, including those of compiler, language and runtime experts; applications developers and performance engineers; and domain scientists. events.title: AI4S: 8th Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Scientific Applications
events.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a game-changing technology that has shown tremendous advantages and improvements in algorithms, implementations, and applications. We have seen many successful stories of AI-enhanced scientific applications. Recently, advances in generative AI have revolutionized not just science but the entire society. However, there are a number of problems remaining to be studied to sustain AI in scientific applications in the long term, bridge the gap between AI and scientific applications, and enable wider employment of AI in HPC. The purpose of this workshop is to bring together computer and domain scientists from academia, government, and industry to share recent advances in the use of AI in scientific applications, introduce new scientific problems to the community, and stimulate tools and infrastructures to support AI-enhanced science. events.title: Invited Talk 1
AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC
events.description: Recent progress in agentic AI—AI systems capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, adaptation, and tool use—opens transformative opportunities across the HPC research landscape. Beyond system-level optimization, agentic AI can play a pivotal role in code modernization, automated code translation across programming models, performance tuning for diverse hardware platforms, and the long-term sustainability of large scientific software stacks. As HPC systems continue to evolve toward exascale and beyond, developers face increasing challenges in maintaining legacy codes, porting applications to emerging architectures, and achieving performance portability across changing programming models and runtime environments. Agentic approaches offer the potential to autonomously refactor legacy codes, translate between models, recommend architecture-aware optimizations, and iteratively tune applications. AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC will bring together researchers and practitioners to explore methodologies, systems, and real-world applications that leverage agentic AI to accelerate HPC software development, enhance productivity, and enable sustainable performance at scale.

ROSS'26 Invited Opening Talk: Challenges in Integrating Quantum and HPC
events.description: As quantum computing transitions from experimental to practical, integrating it into the High-Performance Computing (HPC) ecosystem alongside CPUs and GPUs is essential. However, managing this heterogeneous, often geographically distributed infrastructure introduces significant systems challenges in resource scheduling, workflow orchestration, security, and interoperability. This talk examines these hurdles from a runtime and systems software perspective. Drawing on experiences building quantum-centric platforms, we will explore how operating systems and resource managers must evolve to make quantum resources first-class citizens in future HPC environments.

events.title: Distinguished Talk: Scaling Autonomy: Federated Agentic Middleware and Serverless Systems for Scientific Computing
events.description: Scientific discovery increasingly relies on integrating large-scale experiments, simulations, and AI models across diverse computing environments. However, existing workflows and middleware often struggle with the complexity of scaling across federated resources and lack the autonomy needed to overcome human bottlenecks. In this talk, I will present a vision for autonomous, agent-driven science enabled by federated serverless systems. I will show how agentic middleware can orchestrate stateful, collaborative agents across heterogeneous resources, relying on serverless computing to provide elastic, on-demand execution at extreme scale. Drawing on our prior work with Parsl, funcX, Globus, and Academy, I will present examples that demonstrate how federated agentic systems can deliver high-throughput, resilient, and scalable scientific computing, enabling more autonomous and efficient discovery.

events.title: Distinguished Speaker Talk: "Developing a task-based compressible Navier-Stokes solver - lessons learned and future developments"
events.description:
Leveraging task-based programming to efficiently execute scientific computing necessitates substantial adaptation of algorithms and software architectures in comparison to standard and established MPI implementations. In this context, the Hypersonic Task-based Research (HTR) solver is one of the examples of software for scientific computing that has adopted a task-based architecture. HTR is a compressible Navier-Stokes solver, and it is specifically designed for the study of reacting multiphysics flows at high Mach numbers. It employs finite-difference algorithms for discretizing the transport equations on curvilinear structured grids. The entire solver operates within the environment provided by the Legion runtime and is routinely utilized on hundreds of GPUs for scientific discoveries related to hypersonic turbulence, electrified combustion, and rocket burner ignition.
Over the years, the HTR solver has undergone significant updates and refactorings to enhance its capabilities and achieve improved performance while maintaining portability and maintainability. This talk aims to delve into some of the design decisions and trade-offs made during this development process. The primary objective is to shed light on the strengths and potential areas for improvement of this type of runtime from the perspective of an end user.

events.title: Supporting a Fast-Paced National AI Resource: Portal, Identity, and Federated Access at Scale
events.description: The UK AI Research Resource (AIRR) has grown in two years to over 5,000 users and over 800 awarded projects, reached through a single front door onto autonomous sites. Supporting a resource this large and heterogeneous rests on three foundations: a shared gateway (AIRRPortal), in production; a shared identity layer (AIRR ConnectID), live for the gateway with site brokering in development; and federated user support, discussed as future work. Support is easy to mismeasure: a user whose sign-in is broken cannot raise a ticket through an authenticated helpdesk, so the failures that matter most go unseen. From 25 months of production data, identity proves a large, hidden source of support load whose cost tracks account-lifecycle ownership more closely than a user's sector: self-managed identities are 13% of accounts but generate 70% of identity-related support, a 15.3x per-user difference. We draw lessons for scaling federated user support.

events.title: Featured Speech: From Vision to Impact: Lessons in National-Scale Collaboration and Research Impact from the Exascale Era
events.description: The delivery of the nation’s first generation of exascale supercomputers was one of the largest and most consequential collaborative efforts in the history of high-performance computing, spanning national laboratories, universities, and industry partners across the country. Lori Diachin helped lead this effort as Deputy Director and then Director of the U.S. Department of Energy's Exascale Computing Project (ECP) from 2018 through 2024. In this keynote, she will reflect on the technical, organizational, and human leadership lessons drawn from that journey: what it takes to align a multi-institutional team around a shared mission, how to sustain momentum through a decade-long research and engineering effort, and why mentorship and inclusive leadership are essential to building the next generation of computing talent. Drawing on her career across national laboratories and DOE programs, she will offer practical guidance for early- and mid-career researchers navigating their own paths in HPC and AI, and a candid look at what national-scale collaboration in science really requires.

events.title: Featured Talk: BURGS: Breaking the Perception Barrier in Undergraduate HPC Systems Research
events.description: Systems research can look intimidating from the outside: technically demanding, hard to enter, and disconnected from the things students care about. In this talk, I’ll share how the Broadening Undergraduate Research Group for Systems (BURGS) breaks that perception barrier by creating a welcoming community where undergraduates can engage directly in hands-on HPC systems research -- and what we learned from more than 200 graduates along the way.

events.title: Real-time Optimization of Simulation and Data Processing Pipelines for Experiments on Exascale Computing Platforms
events.description: Current and next-generation large-scale experiments, especially in high-energy physics and cosmology, involve increasing volumes of data that require exascale computing power to analyze and model. Exascale machines present challenges for workflow scaling and efficient resource usage. We propose a multi-stage task scheduling approach for optimizing resource usage and task scheduling for these workflows. We demonstrate task scheduling for an example Monte Carlo Simulation pipeline from the Short Baseline Near Detector (SBND), and present theoretical and numerical tools for modeling task scheduling in these workflows that can be used to identify optimal scheduling strategies and choose resources for a given problem size.

events.title: Invited Talk #1 - The Future of Q-HPC Software Tools and Frameworks
A Study In High Performance Portability Through Layered Abstractions
events.description:
In the past year NVIDA's CUDA programming model has grown to include several language extensions and DSLs, most notably with the addition of CUDA Tile, a tile-based parallel programming abstraction. We implemented CUDA Tile not just as a set of language features but as a series of compiler stages based around MLIR, allowing for much richer and more sophisticated code generation.

The effectiveness of this deeper compiler stack and the interaction between thread-level and tile-level parallelism quite honestly took us by surprise, and has provided remarkable insights into the mechanisms by which retargetable parallel abstractions provide excellent performance with a fraction the amount of code, requiring only auto-tuning with no code modification. NVIDIA's accelerated maths libraries are being converted to use CUDA Tile as a result.

We will share these insights and our analysis in this talk, along with additional conclusions from an investigation into how AI coding agents both benefit from and are impeded by Tile- and Thread-level abstractions when optimizing code.

events.title: Invited Talk: How to Beat CPU/GPUs on both Performance and Programmability: The UpDown Graph Supercomputer
events.description: Making graph algorithms fast and scalable on traditional architectures and GPUs often involves breaking them into large, coarse-grained computational blocks that access similar regions of memory. We show that graph algorithms, which have tremendous vertex- and edge-level parallelism, can be scaled as fine-grained programs on suitable architectures. Specifically, we investigate graph algorithms on the UpDown architecture and show how this many-threaded, cache-less architecture enables simple, fine-grained parallel graph algorithms to be both fast and scalable. Single-node UpDown performance is 28x (geomean) over an H200 GPU, and that same program scales to 1000’s of nodes. We evaluate the system three ways: simulation, analytical projection models, and selected validation studies at scale (simulation of 16,384 UpDown nodes, using 256 supercomputer nodes). These results show the UpDown system can achieve 680K giga-traversed edges per second (GTEPS) for PageRank and 989K GTEPS BFS, exceeding prior results significantly. The realism of UpDown models has been validated by commercial activity at Chicago UpDown Computing (www.chupdown.com).Beyond performance, the insights for programming are significant. Our measurements suggest that not only is programming difficult – for distributed memory and GPU-SIMT – it is unproductive. That is, the resulting programs are not performant. for example, we have measured up to 5x higher total memory traffic for GPU implementations compared with UpDown. And the trend is for increasing UpDown advantage as algorithms grow in complexity suggest that kernel and linear algebra library based approaches face significant challenges.

events.title: NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids
events.description:
The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA’s latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes.

We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture’s predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA’s GPU focus for such workloads.

events.title: Skip the SuperPOD - The User-Driven Case for Throughput-Optimized GPU Clusters
events.description: AI compute architectures are optimized for theneeds of the market, which today is hyperscaler AI training. It is critical for academic cyberinfrastructure leaders to understand the workload profiles in higher education and compare these to peer institutions to account for any local factors. This study seeks to compare and contrast the workload profiles across a set of university HPC centers to identify whether usage patterns are consistent across institutions and build out a data-driven model to capacity plan for GPU compute demand.

events.title: DART: ML-Accelerated Surrogate for Real-Time CFD Digital Twins
events.description:
Experimental aerodynamics facilities stream
surface-pressure measurements continuously, but the CFD
models used to interpret those measurements require minutes
to hours per evaluation. This multi-order-of-magnitude gap
prevents deploying the model inside the experiment’s control
loop. We present DART, a workflow engine that represents
a CFD digital-twin pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of
typed computational steps and makes surrogate substitution a
first-class operation: a machine-learned model replaces a node’s
implementation while preserving its declared input/output
contract, so adjacent stages remain unchanged. DART then
monitors the substituted loop by comparing prediction residuals
to incoming measurements and raises an alarm when the
surrogate leaves its fitted regime. On a steady aerodynamic
pipeline, a substituted surrogate answers in 4.1 ms what the
solver answers in 220s while reproducing 99.5% of held-out
lift variation. On an unsteady cylinder benchmark, an alarm
calibrated only on trusted-regime data detects out-of-envelope
deployment within six shedding cycles.

events.title: Exhibitor Lounge
Fabrica: Agentic CUDA-to-CSL Translation and Optimization for Wafer-Scale Systems
events.description: Porting GPU kernels across architectures requires more than syntax translation. CUDA embeds work decomposition through threads, blocks, and memory accesses; the Cerebras Software Language (CSL) demands explicit data movement across a processing-element mesh with distributed SRAM, fabric communication, event-driven tasks, and host/device coordination. We present Fabrica-Bench, 54 paired CUDA-to-CSL tasks, and Fabrica, an agentic framework combining target knowledge, execution, failure-directed repair, and correctness-gated optimization. With Claude Opus 4.8, Fabrica raises success from 6/28 (single attempt) to 26/28; 22 match or beat CSL references (16 speedups). In a Sonnet 4.6 ablation with repair loop and budget fixed, retrieved Cerebras knowledge raises success from 1/15 to 7/15, while structured design records improve neither 40-run comparison. Across 46 tasks, Fabrica passes 35, with a 3.42x geometric-mean speedup among passing held-out programs and up to 83x on ReLU. Target-specific knowledge and staged feedback, not prompt structure alone, drive cross-architecture kernel generation.

events.title: CAPIO: Safe Kernel-Bypass of Commodity Devices using Capabilities
events.description:
Securing low-latency I/O in commodity systems forces a fundamental trade-off: rely on the kernel’s high overhead mediated interface, or bypass it entirely, exposing sensitive hardware resources to userspace and creating new vulnerabilities. This dilemma stems from a hardware granularity mismatch: standard MMUs operate at page boundaries, making it impossible to selectively expose safe device registers without also exposing the sensitive control registers colocated on the same page. Existing solutions, enforce an isolation model that cannot protect sub-page device resources.

We present CAPIO, the first architecture to leverage hardware capabilities to enforce fine-grained access control on MMIO. Unlike prior page-based protections, CAPIO utilizes unforgeable capabilities to create precise, sub-page “slices” of device memory. This enables the kernel to delegate latency-critical hardware access to userspace applications while strictly preventing interaction with co-located privileged registers. We demonstrate that CAPIO achieves the latency improvements of kernel bypass while enforcing byte-level access control of resources.

events.title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
events.description:
AI question-answering assistants increasingly serve user support at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities, but they offer no systematic way to judge answer quality in production or attribute a bad answer to the component at fault, and they stay static after deployment apart from knowledge-base updates.

We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline that scores each production interaction, identifies whether a failure lies in missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes it to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core pairs answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test separating information absent from the corpus from information present but never retrieved. Controlled harness training, supervised by expert references and null-edit controls, improves the pipeline itself.

Across 2,174 support turns AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, and harness training raised agreement with expert labels from 108/150 to 123/150 turns, a governed self-evolution driven by production evidence.

events.title: Fine-Tuning Foundation Models for Micro-CT Image Segmentation Using HPC Platforms
events.description: Foundation models have demonstrated exceptional performance in computer vision, but adapting them to scientific imaging requires domain-specific datasets, scalable training methodologies, and high-performance computing (HPC) resources. This work presents methodologies for fine-tuning and deploying foundation models for synchrotron X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) image segmentation. We describe the adaptation of SAM3 for instance segmentation and DINOv3-Seg for semantic segmentation. We present strategies for data preprocessing, model configuration, loss design, and hyperparameter optimization for fine-tuning these models. We further describe scalable fine-tuning on local GPU servers through a web-based training interface and on the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) through Slurm-based job submission. Finally, we present distributed inference strategies on NERSC and the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), enabling near real-time segmentation of large synchrotron datasets across hundreds of GPUs. Together, these methods provide guidance for adapting, training, and deploying foundation models for large-scale scientific image segmentation at synchrotron facilities.

events.title: Automated Design Space Exploration of ARM CMN-Based HPC Architectures: A Case Study for the European Rhea Family Processors
events.description: The Network-on-Chip (NoC) is a major determinant of memory-system performance in modern high-performance computing (HPC) processors. Configurable coherent interconnects such as Arm Coherent Mesh Networks (CMNs) represent large design spaces involving request and home nodes, memory interfaces, queue resources, and node placement. This paper presents an automated multi-objective design-space exploration methodology combining automated Design Space Exploration (DSE) framework, Arm Performance Models, and industrial architecture-generation tools. The methodology is evaluated on a representative CMN-S3 subsystem defined in the context of future processors of the European Rhea family, exploring the organization of the coherent interconnect and memory subsystem while keeping the compute architecture fixed. Results highlight the importance of balancing request and home/cache resources to sustain DDR bandwidth while controlling implementation cost. The automated exploration identifies the same Pareto optimal configurations as exhaustive evaluation using only $26$ of $343$ valid configurations, reducing total exploration time from approximately $140$~h to $2$~h.

events.title: 14 GPU Programming Paradigms Put to the Test: Performance Portability and Halstead Difficulty in Scientific Computing
Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
events.description: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 5-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD. On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

events.title: CURATE: Leveraging LLM Agents to Compose, Catalog, and Deploy Reproducible Workflows
events.description: Agentic code generation has the potential to accelerate the development of computational workflows while also reducing barriers to entry. However, a key gap remains: existing coding agents focus on code generation and do not address the entire workflow lifecycle, including deployment and sharing. As a result, users develop and stitch modules independently while managing deployment on their own. To address this gap, we propose CURATE (Composition, User-in-the-loop, Reuse, and Automated Task Execution), a novel human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that uses LLM agents to manage and develop composable workflows across their entire lifecycle. A key feature of the system is a catalog that allows for the storage and reuse of modules across workflows. Module catalogs provide a foundation that can be expanded to support FAIR principles by facilitating the sharing and reuse of curated modules and subgraphs. We demonstrate the feasibility of our system with an initial prototype and 6 experiments.

events.title: RISE Research Expertise Map & Innovation Exhibit
events.description: An introduction to the interactive RISE map and the Curated HPC & AI Innovation Exhibit. Participants can explore who is in the room by expertise, career stage and country, and find collaborators, mentors and projects.

events.title: Quantum-HPC Workflows Across Multiple Quantum Computing Platforms: Two Case Studies
events.description:
We describe the Quantum-HPC hybrid system comprising the supercomputer Fugaku, the QPUs Quantinuum Reimei and ibm\_kobe, and the Tierkreis hybrid workflow software.
We present two demonstrations of the system at work.
In the first we compute the excited states of a biomolecular system using Fugaku and Reimei to
handle classical and quantum parts of the workflow respectively.
In the second, Fugaku coordinates Reimei and ibm\_kobe working together in a combined VQE + QPE workflow to compute the ground state energy of a simple system.

events.title: HUST Survey
Short Talk: When Should Quantum and HPC Systems Be Co-Located? Lessons from Real-World Workflows
Descriptive Execution of HPC Applications and Workflows
events.description: The means to execute and orchestrate software in high performance computing (HPC) has changed from human-written code to descriptive prose. We assess the extent to which an agentic framework can optimize and run an HPC scaling study with a low-latency network in Amazon Web Services, translate job specifications between workload managers, and design and run workflows. In job translation experiments, agents convert 982 of 1,000 specifications between Slurm and Flux, all validated by production Flux, matching human-written performance in all but one case. In the scaling experiments, agents deploy and optimize applications, demonstrating scaling through the largest size of nodes. In the bioscience workflow, the agent reproduces an expert-written variant-calling pipeline almost exactly -agreeing with the reference call set in 18 of 19 evaluable runs - through many distinct yet functionally equivalent implementations. This information is invaluable for enabling multi-cluster application deployment, with scheduling and transformation handled by agents.

Mosaic: Ephemeral, Capability-Aware Scheduling Across Heterogeneous Rack-Scale Systems
events.description:
Heterogeneous HPC racks combine CPU, GPU, and FPGA resources with workloads that need different hardware and software stacks. Hardware-compatible placement alone fails when persistent workers diverge in operating-system images, libraries, drivers, or runtime versions. Separate provisioning, container, and accelerator recovery paths further fragment admission and failure handling.
We present Mosaic, a Slurm-complementary lifecycle controller combining version-aware admission, capability-based dispatch, and explicit reset boundaries. Workers register capabilities and observed versions; Mosaic admits compatible workers and dispatches tasks through set inclusion and profile compatibility. It supports fast per-job userspace replacement, broader diskless PXE-to-RAM worker replacement, quarantine, and requeue.
On a heterogeneous rack-scale testbed, Mosaic reaches all-workers-ready for 32 concurrent workers under one controller in about 17s. Per-job images reproduce the expected package environment in 100% of runs, versus 45.83±14.55% with periodic Ansible and 24.17±10.17% with periodic reimaging. After failure, Mosaic restores a verified configuration in about 1.5s.

events.title: GPU-Accelerated de Bruijn Graph Traversal for Genome and Metagenome Assembly
events.description:
De novo genome and metagenome assembly often relies on De Bruijn graph traversals to reconstruct microbial genomes. Effective GPU implementation of this phase of the assembly is complicated by the presence of highly variable and unpredictable walk lengths, leading to severe warp divergence and memory requirements that are not known a priori.

We present a GPU-accelerated de Bruijn graph traversal adapted from MetaHipMer2 that uses a three-pass walk design to address these challenges. First, bounded walks enable more uniform work distribution and reduce warp divergence while bounding memory requirements in the first traversal phase. Second, symbolic walks determine the memory required to store generated sequences without requiring dynamic memory allocation. Finally, connection walks link subsequences generated in the first stage. Compared to the parallel CPU implementation in MetaHipMer2, our GPU implementation achieves a 45.84× speedup on a 440-million-k-mer dataset, substantially reducing single-node assembly time without affecting assembly quality.

events.title: nFlows: Enabling Efficient Data Movement in Data-Intensive Scientific Workflows on Non-Uniform Memory Access Architectures
events.description: Data movement across the memory subsystems of modern supercomputers is a major performance bottleneck for data-intensive scientific workflows. Preserving locality and minimizing data movement are key strategies to address this, yet support in workflow scheduling remains limited. nFlows is a runtime system for studying data movement in scientific workflows and prototyping memory-topology-aware scheduling algorithms. This version targets the main memory subsystem, focusing on Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architectures, which dominate modern compute-node design. We use nFlows to execute workflows under a traditional FIFO scheduler and a NUMA-aware FIFO scheduler from prior work, collecting traces for both. Our analysis shows some workflows are negatively affected when execution spreads across NUMA nodes, and NUMA-aware scheduling mitigates this: executions reading at least 60% of their data locally rise from 27.64% to 68.33%, executions with a makespan improvement rise from 3.07% to 11.71%, and best-case makespan reduction increases from 10.22% to 44.28%.

events.title: Invited talk: "Distributed HPC in Julia without MPI"
events.description:
MPI has long been the default substrate for distributed scientific computing, but it is not the only path to scalable performance—and in Julia, it is often not the most productive one. This talk surveys the landscape of MPI-free distributed computing in Julia, centered on the standard-library Distributed package and its surprisingly performant primitives for remote execution, data movement, and cluster management. I will review which widely-used Julia packages already run on top of Distributed, and how their capabilities compare to their MPI-based counterparts.
The core of the talk focuses on Dagger.jl, a task-based parallel runtime that provides unified support for both Distributed and MPI: every algorithm expressed in Dagger runs unchanged across either backend, as well as across multi-CPU and multi-GPU configurations. I will highlight Dagger's Datadeps API, which lets users express data dependencies declaratively and have the scheduler automatically handle communication, synchronization, and placement—whether the underlying transport is Distributed or MPI. Through concrete examples, I will show how this abstraction delivers portability without sacrificing performance, and close with an overview of the current state of distributed computing across the broader Julia package ecosystem.

events.title: hpcGPT: A Flexible Framework for Agentic User Support in HPC
events.description: High-performance computing centers spend significant staff time addressing recurring user questions about account management, software environments, job scheduling, and system architectures. Analyses of historical support tickets show that a small number of topics account for a disproportionate share of user requests, yet much of this knowledge remains buried in closed tickets and dispersed documentation. We present hpcGPT, an agentic command-line support assistant that combines OpenCode, a provider-independent terminal interface, with Model Context Protocol tools. The system delivers contextualized responses by integrating site documentation, historical ticket knowledge, and live cluster information, while preserving the ability to escalate unresolved issues through existing ticketing workflows. We describe the system architecture, MCP tool ecosystem, and ticket knowledge pipeline, including data ingestion, PII scrubbing, and retrieval mechanisms. Finally, we report on a pilot deployment in a production HPC environment and discuss its potential to improve user support, accelerate access to expertise, and reduce staff workload.

events.title: Panel: Career Pathways Across Academia, Labs, & Industry: A Global View
events.description: How do careers in HPC and AI really unfold, and how do you move between academia, national labs and industry? Panelists share candid perspectives on career-defining decisions, and building expertise. The panel includes open Q&A, so participants can bring their own career questions.

events.title: Validation of a Parallel and Distributed Computing Instrument for Early Computing Research
events.description:
Parallel and distributed computing (PDC) has become the dominant
computing model. Substantial research and advocacy efforts have been
made to introduce PDC early in computing curricula. However, much
of this research has relied on informal, ad-hoc measures of
intervention efficacy. We address this gap by developing and
validating an instrument designed to assess PDC knowledge of
introductory computing students. This instrument is intended for
use by researchers as a pre/post intervention assessment. We
validate our instrument using Item Response Theory under the Rasch
(1PL) model using data from multiple institutions. The
instrument demonstrated a broad range of item difficulties,
acceptable fit statistics, and evidence of unidimensionality.
After recalibration, the improved instrument demonstrates strong
reliability as a measure of foundational PDC knowledge. This
instrument will help improve the rigor and quality of future PDC
education research.

events.title: Drava: An Event-Driven Runtime for Scientific Pipelines with Agentic Configuration Optimization
events.description: Across scientific domains, detectors increasingly produce data faster than it can be transmitted, forcing analysis to run near the instrument. The analysis uses multi-stage pipelines that may include reconstruction and inference under latency and throughput constraints. Current solutions leave key performance choices such as batch size, inter-stage data transport, and resource placement to manual tuning that is brittle and time consuming. We introduce Drava, an event-driven runtime for edge scientific streaming pipelines. Developers express stages as reusable callbacks, while Drava manages scheduling, batching, data movement, and transport-aware execution across heterogeneous resources. On ptychography and tomography pipelines, Drava sustains 31 kHz on the runtime path and runs up to 2.36× faster than a PvaPy baseline that drops frames beyond 2 kHz. Drava remains ~2.6× faster than hand-tuned loss-free PvaPy, while its observability enables agentic optimization that finds a configuration 2.24× faster than the best manual one and exposes energy–throughput trade-offs.

events.title: Repository-Scale Performance Characterization of the IO500 Benchmark
events.description: The IO500 benchmark provides a common basis for evaluating high-performance computing (HPC) storage systems, while its growing submission repository also offers an opportunity to study performance behavior across systems and time. This work presents a repository-scale characterization of 294 post-reset IO500 submissions from 116 sites spanning 2019–2025. We combine descriptive and temporal analysis with phase-level correlation, scale-sensitivity analysis, and benchmark-log examination to investigate how performance characteristics represented by individual benchmark phases relate to composite rankings. The results show strong relationships among phases measuring similar I/O behavior, but weaker and scale-sensitive relationships between bandwidth and metadata performance. Temporal and log-level analyses further reveal information that is not apparent from aggregate scores alone. These findings demonstrate the value of analyzing IO500 results beyond leaderboard rankings and identify important considerations concerning system scale, benchmark execution, and repository provenance when using community benchmark data for comparative and longitudinal HPC performance analysis.

events.title: Examining QRMI as a Unified Interface for Quantum-HPC Integration
events.description: The efficient and scalable integration of quantum resources into HPC environments requires standardized mechanisms for resource management, scheduling, and workflow orchestration across diverse and heterogeneous infrastructures. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) addresses this challenge through a thin, vendor-agnostic middleware layer that provides standardized APIs for scheduling, executing, and monitoring quantum workloads while exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs. Previous work demonstrated QRMI integration with the Slurm workload manager. This paper extends the validation of QRMI to a broad range of workload managers, encompassing traditional batch schedulers, a cloud-native orchestration platform, and a graph-based scheduler. We examine the integration patterns, implementation requirements, and scheduler-specific considerations associated with each environment and compare QRMI with alternative approaches to quantum resource integration. We demonstrate that QRMI provides an abstraction layer that minimizes scheduler-specific modifications while enabling consistent access to heterogeneous quantum resources across both on-premises and cloud environments.

events.title: Achieving Performance Portability for Semi-Lagrangian Simulations via Automated Layout and Loop Tuning
events.description:
Hardware heterogeneity defines the exascale era, and scientific
application performance is increasingly dominated by memory access patterns
rather than operation count.

We analyze the performance profile of a portable semi-Lagrangian
mini-application extracted from the Gysela-X++ tokamak plasma simulation code.
While single-source portability guarantees correctness across architectures, we
show that per- formance portability remains elusive, even when a code is not
intentionally tied to specific hardware features (e.g., tensor cores, cache
size, etc.).

By embedding judiciously placed layout and loop nest tuning points into this
single-source C++ mini-application, simple automatic tuning of its main operator
sequence recovers lost performance at minimal productivity cost. This automated
approach achieves speedups of up to ×1.47 on GPUs and ×1.53 on CPUs over expert
manual optimization, while requiring a fraction of the development time.

events.title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
events.description:
Environment configuration remains a fundamental yet overlooked challenge in software engineering, requiring precise management of operating systems, dependencies, and hardware constraints. Existing LLM-based software engineering workflows often rely on predefined Dockerfiles or manual scripts, or exclude repositories with difficult environments, limiting generalization.

We present ENVAGENT, a multi-LLM-agent workflow that automatically synthesizes, builds, and verifies hardware-aware Dockerfiles from repositories. We further introduce ENVAGENT+, a resource-provisioning agent that infers computational requirements and allocates compatible resources, and ENVBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating environment reconstruction fidelity.

We evaluate ENVAGENT on 54 repositories from Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench across seven programming languages. Results show that ENVAGENT improves runnable counts by 16.2% and FCS scores by 33.91% over baselines, enabling reliable evaluation of repositories that existing approaches fail to configure.

events.title: Bridging Reasoning and Verification: A Generative AI Approach to Chemistry
events.description: While modern language models can perform high-level chemical reasoning, they often struggle to propose solutions to chemical design tasks that adhere to known principles of chemical validity or synthesizability. Here, we introduce CHARGE, a Chemistry-tool Augmented Reasoning-based Generative framework that combines large-scale reasoning models with automated tool calling to tackle molecular discovery and design challenges. We integrate cheminformatics utilities and neural-network property predictors into the reasoning loop, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation, verification, and refinement without user intervention. Across 10 molecule design tasks, CHARGE consistently designs molecules with improved properties compared to the unaugmented LLM baseline. For the task of predicting chemical synthesis outcomes, we show that the tool-assisted reasoning of CHARGE increases synthesis prediction accuracy from 12% to 40%. Together, these results point towards an agentic AI chemistry workflow, whereby LLMs provide flexible scientific reasoning and orchestration, while robust cheminformatics tools verify and guide the molecular design.

events.title: Towards Efficient HPC Systems for Agents: Challenges and Opportunities
events.description:
Coding agents have become real users of high-performance computing (HPC) systems, yet today's HPC abstractions, interfaces, and policies remain designed for humans. We observed 19.5% of users running coding agent, which account for 55.8% of job submissions, 29.1% of CPU core-hours, and 42.7% of GPU-hours. Agents are not simply faster humans. They issue commands at 20.8x the human rate, decompose work into fine-grained explore-modify-execute loops.
These behaviors strain abstractions built for human timescales, surfacing as control-plane pressure on the scheduler, metadata-intensive I/O on bandwidth-provisioned filesystems, repeated rediscovery of what earlier sessions already learned, and new prompt-injection and policy-enforcement surfaces. Neither banning agents nor treating them as ordinary users is sustainable. We instead argue for co-design, that facilities should treat agents as first-class principals where agents become facility-aware tenants. We outline the resulting challenges and opportunities in compute, storage, agent memory, and safety.

events.title: Accelerating Graph Neural Networks with Decoupled Access-Execute Architectures
events.description: Graph neural networks address critical problems in content recommendation, fraud detection, and drug discovery. Unlike dense machine-learning models, graph models are often memory bound rather than compute bound, making HBM-based processors a promising alternative to GPUs. This paper first characterizes how graph input locality shapes the architectural requirements of these workloads. It then evaluates locality-aware architectural optimizations, including decoupled memory access and near-memory processing, that enable HBM-based processors to outperform GPUs by up to 7x.

events.title: Consumption-Aware Memory Prediction for Scientific Workflows
events.description:
Distributed scientific workflow tasks exhibit signif-
icant variation in memory consumption, making accurate peak
memory estimation critical for resource management and avoid-
ing out-of-memory (OOM) failures. Existing workload schedulers
rely on static features like file sizes or tool names, which fail to
capture non-linear memory scaling. We present Consumption-
Aware Memory Prediction (CAMP), a closed-loop framework that
utilizes fine-grained, consumption-level provenance—the exact
number of bytes a task reads—measured dynamically via eBPF
kernel probes. To minimize tracing overhead across parallel task
executions at scale, we develop an active-learning-based, multi-
gate selective auditing policy that samples only the most informa-
tive workflow tasks for model retraining. We evaluate CAMP on
thousands of production-scale bioinformatics workflow records
executed under Slurm. Compared to size-based scheduling base-
lines, incorporating dynamic data-consumption features reduces
prediction median absolute percentage error by up to 40.31%.

events.title: From Answering to Acting: An AI Agent for Research Computing User Support
events.description: RCD/HPC centers increasingly run support chatbots, but these answer from static documentation and cannot handle information that changes or act when a user needs something done. We describe our experience building an agent for a national cyberinfrastructure program that both answers questions from live infrastructure data and takes actions on the researcher’s behalf, such as registering them for events, posting announcements, and filing tickets, under their own federated identity, with user data kept inside institutional infrastructure and a confirmation step before consequential writes. Because help is only useful if it stays good, we evaluate answers with a judge validated against human reviewers, which separates the agent from plain retrieval (0.97 vs. 0.47), and we run that evaluation two ways: a release gate that catches our own regressions, and a drift detector that catches when the underlying information has gone stale.

events.title: A Portuguese-Language Ecosystem for HPC Education: Design, Formative Development, and Evidence of Adoption
events.description: This paper presents a Portuguese-language educational ecosystem designed to support the progressive teaching of high-performance computing (HPC). Developed through an independent, author-led initiative, the ecosystem combines two textbooks with reproducible C programs using MPI, OpenMP, and OpenACC, exercises, instructor slides, Colab-compatible laboratory notebooks, interactive learning tools, and training and outreach activities. Its development followed an incremental process in which materials initially used in courses, bootcamps, and programming competitions were reorganized, tested on real systems, and refined through observations and feedback from authentic educational contexts.
