A preliminary analytical evaluation examines the ecosystem in terms of conceptual alignment, progressive complexity, reproducibility, adoptability, and authentic use. The results indicate that its components form a coherent and reproducible educational pathway covering distributed-memory, shared-memory, and accelerator programming. Although the available evidence supports claims of adoption and sustained use, controlled studies are still required to determine the ecosystem's effects on student learning.

events.title: Building Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories with the INTERSECT Federated Ecosystem
events.description: Failure resilience in federated ecosystems for instrument science presents a critical challenge. Failures disrupt experiments and make them potentially useless, wasting valuable resources and creating setbacks. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Self-driven Experiments for Science / Interconnected Science Ecosystem (INTERSECT) offers a federated ecosystem for instrument science, enabling autonomous experiments, self-driving laboratories, smart manufacturing, and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven design, discovery, and evaluation. This paper documents the recent advances in creating a resilient INTERSECT ecosystem. The proposed solution includes a resilient architecture with resilience design patterns, a resilient system of systems (SoS) architecture, and a resilient microservices architecture; and a resilient software development kit with reliable service communication and asynchronous and synchronous failure detection and notification. The resilience capabilities are demonstrated for an autonomous additive manufacturing process with a real-time feedback loop.

events.title: Orrery: Modeling and Simulation of GPU-direct MPI Communication with SimGrid
events.description: Simulation of HPC applications is an essential tool for analyzing system design trade-offs and enabling effective hardware–software co-design. As modern supercomputers increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, MPI implementations have evolved to support GPU-aware communication, enabling direct GPU data transfers. Modeling these mechanisms is therefore critical for simulating HPC applications on current systems. In this paper, we introduce Orrery, an interposition layer built on SimGrid’s SMPI to model GPU-aware MPI communication using existing collective implementations and flow-based simulation. Orrery intercepts GPU memory allocations, kernel launches, data transfers, and MPI operations, and models their execution in SimGrid according to target system specifications, enabling simulation without requiring physical GPUs. We validate Orrery using CUDA-aware MPI microbenchmarks and a Jacobi solver on up to 32 nodes of the MUSICA supercomputer and demonstrate that it reproduces key GPU-aware MPI mechanisms

events.title: PauLIB: HPC Strategies for Pauli-Arithmetic-Based Quantum Computing Workloads and Simulations
events.description:
As quantum devices become accelerators within classical HPC deployments, the efficiency of the classical partition becomes critical. Workloads such as Hamiltonian manipulation, observable backpropagation, and Pauli-based compilation reduce to bulk arithmetic on Pauli strings and sums.

We present HPC strategies for this arithmetic, demonstrated in PauLIB, a header-only C++20 library: a bit-packed binary symplectic representation reducing Pauli multiplication to a bitwise XOR and population count; a sorted, struct-of-arrays layout replacing hash maps and exposing contiguous word arrays to SIMD units and GPU warps; and deterministic OpenMP parallelism with race-free output partitioning.

These strategies deliver orders-of-magnitude higher throughput and smaller memory footprint than Qiskit and PauliEngine, plus a speedup from a CUDA outer-product kernel on an H100. Two case studies, g-sim and truncated Pauli propagation, inherit these gains and scale unchanged from a laptop Arm CPU to a 72-core HPC Arm server. PauLIB is open source with C++ and Python interfaces.

events.title: Invited talk: "From MPI+X to Domain-Specific Abstractions: Building Sustainable Weather and Climate Software"
events.description:
Weather and climate models are large and complex collections of mathematical modelling software. They can take more than a decade to develop and can be in use for a quarter of century or more. They also typically undergo constant revisions and improvements from teams of developers. The proliferation of programming models in the MPI+X paradigm is therefore particularly problematic as cost of developing and maintaining multiple X implementations for different architectures in such a code base becomes prohibitive. The rapid evolution of the programming models has exacerbated the problem. Fortran has been the de facto standard programming language for weather and climate applications and can considered a low-level domain specific language for numerical computation. The ability to write code that in some sense looks likes the maths is part of its appeal and enables developers to be productive. The invasive level of parallel code additions required for performance degrades the sustainability of the code base.
One approach to solving these problems has been to raise the level of abstraction from a general-purpose language to a domain specific language (DSL). Here domain specific information is encoded in and exploited by the programming model for optimisation purposes. Key to this approach is a strong separation of concerns between the science/maths code and the parallel and optimisation code. This approach enables developers to write code which looks like maths whilst allowing the portability and performance by having different routes to optimised codes for different architectures. This comes with the cost of designing and maintaining the DSL.
The Met Office is part of the Momentum partnership and is developing the Momentum modelling software system. The atmosphere model, LFRic, is developed and co-designed in a its own DSL, embedded in Fortran. Part of the DSL is the python domain specific compiler, PSyclone. The advantages and limitations of the this approach are discussed, including the consequences of design choices such as embedding the DSL in Fortran. Some performance results from LFRic are presented as evidence to support the arguments. Finally, how emerging agentic programming techniques may complement DSL-based approaches and what this implies for future weather and climate software development is considered.

events.title: Limitations of Generative Inverse Design for Scientific Simulations
events.description: Generative inverse design for scientific simulations addresses a many-to-one problem: generating distinct inputs whose forward simulations approximate a target output. Our prior work generated image-based initial conditions directly, but simulations often construct initial conditions at runtime from configuration variables. We shift the task upstream by generating variables whose effects propagate through intermediate representations before producing the final output. We use a deterministic heat-diffusion proxy with Cosine Phase and Perlin Noise geometry functions that create diverse material-layout patterns. Conditional normalizing flows generate input variables conditioned only on observed final states, and the resulting simulated outputs are evaluated against the corresponding targets. Variable-inclusion ablations isolate geometry and thermal variables, while posterior-factorization ablations compare full-joint, chained-joint, and disjoint decompositions. Results show error arises primarily when modeling geometry variables, whereas posterior factorization provides little improvement over baselines. These findings suggest the final outputs may not retain enough information about upstream variables and intermediate representations.

events.title: Diamond Agent: Agentic Control of Federated HPC Resources as a Service
events.description: Efficiently aggregating and orchestrating computing power across heterogeneous clusters for HPC workflows faces four practical challenges: preserving workflow context across independently administered clusters, moving large datasets between sites, reasoning about site-specific environments and scheduler policies, and exploiting live queue and resource states for efficient task scheduling. To this end, we design Diamond Agent, an agentic system that enables intelligent execution of HPC workflows across heterogeneous clusters. Diamond Agent provides an agent-facing workspace and skills that unify cross-site resource discovery, resource specification, data movement, task execution, and result retrieval. Diamond Agent translates high-level agent actions into valid site-specific executions, moves data through Globus Transfer, and uses live system capability and queue information to select feasible placements. Its event-driven continuation mechanism decouples agent actions from long-running batch jobs: persistent services monitor remote execution and resume the agent only when a result or decision-relevant event is available.

events.title: Performance Portability of Multi-GPU Hydrodynamics: SCALSALE with MPI+OpenMP Target Offload
events.description:
Directive-based offload enables portable GPU execution from one source, yet evaluations usually use microbenchmarks or compact kernels. We extend SCALSALE, a Modern Fortran full multi-material Lagrangian--Eulerian hydrodynamics proxy application, to multi-node GPU execution using MPI+OpenMP without vendor-specific paths. This required restructuring branch-heavy Eulerian advection and replacing host-staged halo exchange with GPU-aware MPI over device-resident buffers.
Tests on NVIDIA A100 and Intel Max 1550 GPUs and an Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ CPU yield weak-scaling efficiencies of 84%-91% within a GPU node, 88%-91% acrosss three GPU nodes, and higher 95%-96% across CPU nodes because longer computation amortizes communication.
Using Pennycook's metric with hierarchical-Roofline efficiencies, performance-portability scores are 34.9% (Eulerian) and 37.9% (Lagrangian) over all platforms, and 44.1% and 42.2% over the GPUs, respectively. Streaming kernels attain 63%-83% of their ceilings across architectures, whereas the dominant advection sweep ranges from 84% to 13%, identifying the optimization target.

events.title: Resolving Placement–Residency Conflicts in Multi-GPU Task-Graph Runtimes
events.description:
In multi-GPU task-graph runtimes, task placement affects both execution time and data locality. Earliest-finish-time (EFT) placement accounts for communication required by the current task but not how placement changes data residency for later tasks, potentially increasing subsequent communication. We observe that some placement-residency conflicts expose model-level slack, allowing lower-copy alternatives without extending the modeled completion of committed work.

We propose a communication-aware task placement scheduler that evaluates lower-copy alternatives and admits them only when they preserve modeled completion relative to the EFT choice. We implement the scheduler in CUDASTF and evaluate it on five task-graph workloads on an eight-GPU NVIDIA L4 platform. On the two workloads where placement changes, the scheduler reduces modeled input-copy volume by 39-81% and improves performance by 1.18-1.31x over the EFT baseline, while retaining EFT placement when no admissible alternative exists.

events.title: Parallel Shortest Hyperpath Update in Large Dynamic Hypergraphs
events.description: Finding shortest paths is a well-studied graph problem, with parallel approaches for both static and dynamic settings. However, most existing methods target dyadic networks, where each edge represents an interaction between only two vertices. Many real-world systems involve group interactions, which are modeled more naturally by hypergraphs, where a hyperedge may connect any number of vertices. Moreover, these interactions are often time-dependent, leading to frequent topological changes in the underlying hypergraphs. Yet no scalable approach exists to efficiently update shortest paths, or hyperpaths, in large dynamic hypergraphs. To address this gap, we propose a parallel shortest hyperpath update method that uses a dynamic data structure to maintain the hypergraph, identifies the subgraphs affected by temporal changes, and efficiently updates previously computed shortest hyperpaths. Experiments show that our GPU-based implementation outperforms the recomputation-based baseline by an average speedup of 28.6x and up to 178.3x on large real-world hypergraphs.

events.title: Interoperable Performance Prediction through Standardized Metadata Capture and Analysis
events.description: Accurately estimating execution times is essential in HPC, where users must request resources and wall-clock limits before execution. However, execution information relevant to prediction is typically scattered across profilers, schedulers, and workflow engines using incompatible representations. We argue that execution data should instead be treated as a standardized, reusable artifact of workflow execution rather than a disposable input to a single predictor. We present an architecture that captures distributed resource usage, packages it as Workflow Run RO-Crates, and persists it in a queryable hybrid storage architecture (ProvStor), enabling any execution environment producing compatible metadata to contribute to and reuse a shared knowledge base. We showcase an enactment of this architecture using the COMPSs workflow management system, introducing a SLURM-aware profiler, and show its value through a hybrid prediction methodology that combines the analytical Universal Scalability Law with Machine Learning models.

events.title: HPCMosaic: Adaptive Dashboard for an Evolving HPC User Base
events.description:
High-performance computing (HPC) resources are increasingly accessed by researchers outside of computational disciplines, yet HPC interfaces have not kept pace with this shift. Dashboards remain organized around system components rather than modern user goals, exposing complexity that generates extraneous cognitive load and drives incomplete, unresolvable support tickets to overburdened help staff.

This paper presents HPCMosaic, an HPC dashboard framework built on three design principles: adaptability, where the interface adapts to each user's workflow rather than imposing a fixed layout; progressive disclosure, surfacing common workflows clearly while keeping advanced options accessible; and closing the support loop, embedding guided request forms within relevant widgets to automatically capture technical context and route submissions to support staff. A composable widget architecture underpins all three principles, allowing contributors to extend the dashboard without modifying core framework code.

HPCMosaic is deployed in production at a large research university's HPC center and is available as open-source software.

events.title: A Free Online Textbook and Interactive Exercises for Introducing Parallel Computing
events.description:
We present the parallel and distributed computing
(PDC) content of Dive into Systems, a free, online textbook
that covers a broad range of computer systems topics. Dive
into Systems introduces many topics in the TCPP curriculum
including two chapters devoted to parallel computing. Our
textbook is written assuming only a CS1 background of the
reader, and it is designed to be used as a primary textbook for a
range of courses. As a supplement to our textbook, we developed
online interactive learning resources that provide practice to
students learning its content. These resources include interactive
end-of-chapter exercises and novel Ask me Another components,
including four specific to PDC. Ask me Another components
generate new instances of their question type, allowing a user
to generate a virtually infinite number of practice questions. We
also present results of a multi-institutional study that piloted one
of our PDC Ask me Another components.

events.title: Navigating the Spectrum of Science Workloads with ESnet JLab FPGA Accelerated Transport (EJFAT)
events.description:
Cross-facility workflows are no longer optional but a requirement for the success of current and future science campaigns. From remote labs to multi-institutional science campaigns, advances in instrumentation and technological innovation are enabling experimental and observational scientific user facilities to generate data faster than processing and storage can handle.

Our work explores EJFAT as a potential solution to these challenges. While EJFAT has been shown to be performant and scalable, this paper explores considerations for integrating EJFAT into real-world scientific experiments. We explore two applications: one highly integrated, the other highly generalizable. The first is a highly tuned and optimized workflow for pushing data as fast as possible to meet the goals of scientific experiments, while the second is a general ecosystem lowering the barrier for scientists to leverage HPC resources with minimal effort representing two common classes of applications typical found in scientific user facilities.

events.title: CXDVirt: Low Latency Kernel Module Based CXL-SSD Emulation
events.description: CXL-SSDs promise memory-semantic access to NAND-scale capacity through a small in-device DRAM cache, but scarce hardware makes emulation central to CXL-SSD research. Cylon, a state-of-the-art emulator, runs workloads in a VM, intercepting DRAM misses to inject NAND latency. We show this VM machinery adds over 3μs per miss, exceeding high-performance NAND read latency, while repeated VM exits inflate tail miss latencies several-fold. We present CXDVirt, a kernel-module-based CXL-SSD emulator that removes the VM entirely: the device is exposed through host devdax, hits run natively via the MMU, and a custom page-fault path models NAND latency on misses. CXDVirt preserves CXL-SSDs’ bimodal latency profile while reducing per-miss latency 1.4–1.6× (4.1× at P99.9); with eight threads its miss latency only doubles, against 8–9× for Cylon behind QEMU’s global lock. CXDVirt stays within 5% of remote DRAM without NAND traffic, where Cylon is 3.1–3.6× slower, and enables configurable eviction and prefetch policy studies.

events.title: Rethinking QDMI: Expanding the Quantum Device Abstraction to the Software Stack
events.description:
The increasing number of quantum devices being installed on-site in High Performance Computing (HPC) and data centres is creating a need for standardised interfaces to enable tighter integration. Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) is an emerging interface that address this challenge by providing low-level abstractions to enable seamless integration into HPC environment. It is designed to support multiple quantum modalities behind a unified interface, and it evolves in line with requirements. However, QDMI is versatile enough to be adapted as an interface for quantum software stacks.

In this work, we introduce the concept of stack-as-a-device and implement a proof of concept QDMI device for Munich Software Stack that is deployment at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre. We detail our implementation and know-how regarding the life cycle management of the software stacks and quantum jobs.

events.title: Comfort Dogs
The Agentic Memory Hierarchy: Cross-State I/O Characterization for a Unified Substrate
events.description:
LLM agents now run long, multi-agent, multi-user workloads whose state does not fit
a single store. An agent produces four kinds of state on one memory-storage hierarchy: the model context (KV cache), execution state of tool calls and checkpoints, cognitive memory of facts and skills, and bulk artifacts and embeddings. Each sits behind a separate, uncoordinated substrate, so lifetimes are uncorrelated, repeated content is unrecognized, evictions collide over one memory budget, and provenance is lost. We present the first cross-state I/O characterization, via an extract-normalize-replay method over real agent, serving, memory, and HPC I/O traces and the static footprint of four scientific agents. The states occupy distinct size regimes, span two stress axes, and contend in most windows; over half of KV prefix blocks are reusable, yet recency eviction captures only a third. Each finding maps to a unified-substrate requirement; we release the schema, extractors, and replay benchmark.

events.title: Reconverse: A new scheduling library for multithreaded task-based runtime systems
events.description: Task-based runtime systems, including Charm++, provide benefits not available with MPI, such as dynamic load balancing and automatic computation-communication overlap. Charm++ is currently built on top of an old scheduling layer called Converse. However, Converse lacks many features that are essential for distributed multithreaded performance, and other programming models cannot directly use the Converse scheduler. To solve these problems, we present Reconverse, a new scheduling layer for task-based runtime systems. Reconverse is a separately-compiled library that can be linked to Charm++ or other runtime systems. Compared to Converse, Reconverse contains experimental features for optimizing fine-grained applications such as lottery queue scheduling. Reconverse also supports new machine layers such as LCI, a new communication layer for multithreaded runtime systems. We show that Reconverse improves performance compared to Converse on multiple benchmarks and also demonstrated speedups of up to 2x on large-scale applications, showing the benefits of Reconverse for multithreaded distributed workloads.

events.title: "Meet Your Mentor / Senior Peer" Speed Networking
events.description: Four invited senior peers deliver 5-min lightning talks sharing their technical journeys, expertise development, career transitions, and leadership experiences. The fast-paced session offers opportunities for follow-up conversations and mentoring connections.

events.title: Coconut: An HPC-Native Inference Framework for Neural Surrogates in MPI Simulations
events.description: Neural surrogates can accelerate hybrid PDE solvers, but whether a surrogate delivers a speedup can only be determined in situ, because deployment configuration strongly affects its performance, and current HPC infrastructures support this exploration poorly. We present Coconut, an HPC-native inference framework that fits the MPI programming model and exposes deployment options at two levels: batch size, numerical precision, device placement, and inference backend at the model level, and process topology at the architecture level. A microbenchmark quantifies the cost of the embedded Python interpreter required by the PyTorch Inductor backend, showing when this model-safe execution path becomes efficient. In an industrial thermal multiphase-flow simulator, a thermodynamic surrogate moves from a 2.4× kernel-level slowdown to a 34.12× speedup over the original kernel and 2.51× over a multithreaded batched baseline, carrying through to application-level throughput gains. Deployment choices decide whether a surrogate pays off; Coconut enables their in situ evaluation.

events.title: Building a Trusted Agentic AI system for HPC Systems Management
events.description: High-performance computing (HPC) systems are large, complex environments comprising thousands of compute nodes, high-speed networks, storage systems, and dedicated management infrastructure. Despite the availability of advanced monitoring and management tools, users and administrators often face challenges due to the volume of operational data, the complexity of system interactions, and the expertise required to effectively interpret and act on available information. Recent advances in agentic AI (artificial intelligence) offer new opportunities for more autonomous, context-aware, and collaborative system management. In this work, we present an HPC Systems Management Copilot that integrates a collection of intelligent agents capable of interacting with job schedulers, monitoring frameworks, system databases, and other HPC management services. The copilot provides real-time assistance to users and administrators through a unified natural-language interface. We also present an experimental evaluation assessing the capabilities, effectiveness, and safety of the proposed system across representative HPC management scenarios.

events.title: Triple Overlap in Pipelined Krylov Methods on Multi-GPU Systems
events.description:
We introduce a novel triple-overlap implementation for the pipelined preconditioned conjugate gradient (Pipe-PCG) and pipelined stabilized biconjugate gradient (Pipe-BiCGStab) solvers. Our approach extends conventional computation-communication overlap to concurrently execute collective operations, point-to-point communication, and compute kernels. This enables true computation-communication-communication overlap across multiple GPUs.

We evaluate on the MareNostrum 5 (H100) and Leonardo (A100) supercomputers, comparing against PETSc and the state-of-the-art two-stream NCCL implementation using SuiteSparse matrices and three massive instances scaled up to 512 GPUs. The three-stream design consistently outperforms the two-stream baseline, with the margin widening from 2–6% at 4 GPUs to 18–47% at 64 GPUs.

At 64 GPUs, the geometric-mean speedup over the two-stream baseline is 1.33× on MareNostrum 5 and 1.23× on Leonardo for Pipe-PCG, reaching 1.30× for Pipe-BiCGStab. In large-scale experiments, we observed speedups of up to 35% (Pipe-PCG) and 33% (Pipe-BiCGStab) over the two-stream design, and up to 3.27× over PETSc for both solvers.

events.title: Offset-Aware Coalescing for Fine-Grained Scattered Reads in HPC Reproducibility Analytics
events.description: Data-intensive workloads in scientific computing, e.g., in-situ and ad-hoc data processing for numerical reproducibility analysis, exhibit I/O patterns dominated by small, non-contiguous reads from large files. Although many HPC frameworks overlap I/O with computation, existing interfaces, e.g., POSIX and io_uring, are primarily optimized for sequential or large-block access. Workloads issuing many random reads therefore incur high system-call overhead, inefficient batching, and underutilized bandwidth. We present SCISSOR, an I/O runtime for workloads dominated by fine-grained random access. SCISSOR applies gap-aware offset coalescing to merge nearby requests into contiguous segments, reducing kernel interactions and increasing effective I/O size. A regression-based performance model selects batching and coalescing parameters that balance I/O and computation throughput. Finally, SCISSOR leverages io_uring to issue large asynchronous batches with minimal context-switch overhead. On HPC reproducibility analytics over large-scale cosmology simulations (HACC), SCISSOR achieves 3.6× and 42× higher end-to-end throughput on average over io_uring and POSIX memory-mapped baselines, respectively.

events.title: Pelicanvil: A Web Platform for Discovering, Browsing, and Accessing Federated Datasets on HPC
events.description: Pelican is a data-federation platform, and the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF) is a national federation built on it, letting researchers pull external datasets into HPC workflows without maintaining a local copy. Whether this is viable in practice remains unclear. A feasibility study benchmarking Pelican/OSDF against local and object storage on a production HPC cluster found performance workable but surfaced two barriers: no federation-wide catalog surfaces dataset metadata, search, and streamability up front, and whether a dataset streams per file or downloads depends on how it's packaged at the origin. In response, we built Pelicanvil, an infrastructure-agnostic web platform running inside a production cluster's Open OnDemand portal that gives researchers a single interface for discovering, browsing, and accessing federated datasets, through generated code snippets or direct download. This work offers HPC support teams a measured answer on Pelican's production readiness and a concrete response to the barriers found.

events.title: An AI-Anchored Pathway into HPC Practice: Design and Initial Evaluation of a Three-Day Summer School in Vietnam
events.description: High Performance Computing (HPC) education increasingly serves students entering through artificial intelligence and data-intensive applications, despite uneven preparation in parallel programming and shared computing environments. This paper presents the design and initial evaluation of a three-day, practice-oriented HPC summer school for 36 selected students, of whom 34 attended at least one session, using a real Slurm cluster. The curriculum connected AI workloads with cluster access, resource management, OpenMP and MPI, GPU execution, reproducible environments, and an AI/HPC workflow challenge. We analyzed participation and assessment records, 25 post-school survey responses, and operational observations. Slurm and data-intensive AI workflows received the highest perceived-practicality ratings (4.12/5 and 4.08/5), while parallel programming presented the greatest knowledge load (3.36/5). The findings highlight the importance of teaching-assistant support, explicit instructional scaffolding, and reliable infrastructure, providing practical design lessons for institutions developing short, hands-on HPC training programs.

events.title: Short Talk: Extending Advanced Photon Source Data Management System Workflows with Globus Streaming
Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
events.description:
We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes.
The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO.
We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP.
Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost.
Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build.
We give per-workload procurement guidance.

events.title: System Level Energy and Cost Characterization of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Cloud Workloads
events.description: Near-term quantum workloads depend on hybrid quantum-classical cloud architectures, yet their power and performance dynamics remain difficult to characterize. To address this, we present a high-level simulation framework to evaluate power, energy, and cost across heterogeneous QPU and CPU clouds. By modeling macro level interactions such as job arrivals, workflow iterations, and device power states, the framework orchestrates administrative-level evaluation without requiring detailed quantum properties. To demonstrate the framework with selected configurations and workload, we sweep the variational iteration count over a fixed fleet, holding circuit width, depth, shots, and arrival patterns constant, so that loop length serves as the sole independent variable. While computation and per-job energy scale linearly, QPU occupancy and turnaround depart abruptly from linearity beyond a critical iteration count: past it, nearly all quantum phase time is spent blocked on qubit connectivity rather than computing, and turnaround per job becomes heavily tailed.

events.title: Meganeura: Vulkan and Metal as a Performance-Portability Layer for GPU Training and Inference
events.description: Meganeura explores Vulkan and Metal as a common foundation for GPU inference and training. Implemented in Rust, it combines computational graph compilation with bounded, automatic kernel tuning, aiming to keep the engine small and general while adapting to different hardware. We examine this approach across NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs, using PyTorch as a reference. Our evaluation considers not only steady-state performance, but also preparation time, numerical validation, memory use, and practical deployment barriers. We discuss how graphics APIs can support machine learning alongside rendering, where their execution model helps or limits performance, and what observability is needed to understand those trade-offs. The work asks how much performance portability a compact engine can achieve without maintaining separate implementations for each vendor.

events.title: DECARD: A Runtime for Distributed and Heterogeneous Architectures Based on Dataflow
events.description:
Distributed heterogeneous architectures improve performance by mapping application components to specialized resources, but exposing architectural details increases programming and runtime complexity. Program Execution Models (PXMs) abstract application dependencies from scheduling and data-movement mechanisms. The Codelet Model is a dataflow-inspired PXM based on explicit dependencies among codelets grouped into Threaded Procedures.

This paper presents DECARD (Distributed Execution Codelet Accelerated Runtime for Dataflow), an extension of the Codelet Model for distributed heterogeneous systems. DECARD defines hierarchical components for node-level scheduling, communication, codelet scheduling, and execution, implemented using C++, OpenMP, and MPI. Evaluation shows a stable runtime cost of 1.14--1.23~$\mu$s per codelet, 10.55$\times$ shared-node speedup from 4 to 48 cores with 87.95% efficiency, and 96.67% distributed scaling efficiency across five 48-core nodes. Communication and 2D stencil experiments further characterize token transfers and application-level execution, establishing DECARD as a platform for studying distributed dataflow execution.

events.title: LLMs as Packagers of HPC Software
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) software ecosystems are heterogeneous, with applications depending on hundreds of external packages across diverse build systems and configuration options. Package managers such as Spack automate dependency resolution, but rely on manually authored recipes encoding intricate build knowledge that becomes increasingly labor-intensive to maintain. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for software engineering tasks, but synthesizing HPC package recipes remains challenging: the output must capture dependency, configuration, and platform constraints that are often fragmented across repositories and prior packaging practice.

We present a systematic study of what context and feedback LLMs need to synthesize valid Spack recipes, isolating the effects of repository metadata extraction, reference retrieval, and iterative repair. Structured build information improves installation success from approximately 43% in minimal-context settings to 100% in the best configuration, showing that metadata distillation, reference packages, and diagnostic feedback are essential for HPC package synthesis.

events.title: Every State, Every Loop, All at Once: Reaching the Outer Loop of an Autonomous Laboratory
events.description:
An autonomous laboratory's inner loops are already closed, but the loop
spanning synthesis, measurement, and simulation closes through a person, where
a result changes the next decision. An agent placed there is blind, because the
state it needs lives in someone's head, in tools that disagree, and in files
that cannot be queried. We present \texttt{reach}, an intelligent state layer
holding knowledge, execution, and operational state as one navigable graph,
kept consistent across its many writers. With that state addressable, an agent plans
a campaign and decides each next step while the scientist supervises along a
trust gradient. We contribute (i)~the state layer architecture; (ii)~the seam
contract, implementable by any long-running external system; and (iii)~an
integration study at the Autonomous Chemistry Lab, where the deployed layer
drove an agent-planned vial-transfer chain and carried a measured diffraction
pattern through a vendor application into agentic Rietveld refinement.

events.title: National Data Platform, National Research Platform and Open Science Data Federation: How they collectively enable data-intensive science
events.description:
Data sharing is a critical challenge in modern scientific research, where progress depends on efficiently managing and processing massive volumes of data. To tackle these storage and performance demands, the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF) was created to establish a global research data distribution network. Originally built on the Open Science Grid’s StashCache, OSDF now runs on the Pelican Platform to strengthen its infrastructure.
The Pelican Platform adds several major upgrades to the OSDF, including precise GeoIP routing, origin and cache web interfaces, centralized registration, director services, host advertising systems, and detailed status telemetry. Together, these tools provide a precise, highly controllable, and stable global data-sharing framework. Benchmarking tests confirm that Pelican offers a robust, distributed infrastructure, allowing key initiatives—including the National Data Platform (NDP), National Research Platform (NRP), and Open Science Pool (OSPool)—to effectively simplify data orchestration for complex scientific workflows.

events.title: Topology-Aware Sparse Factorization for Multi-Socket NUMA Architectures
events.description: The numerical factorization of sparse symmetric matrices is an irregular, memory-bound kernel. State-of-the-art solvers leave the placement of the factor implicit on multi-socket NUMA architectures, binding it to a domain by first touch. This work instead binds the factor during the analysis phase, partitioning it along the elimination tree so that each supernode is placed close to those updating it. Each thread then factors the supernodes bound to its own memory and steals from the nearest domain. Furthermore, no thread binding or memory policy has to be chosen since every decision is derived from the discovered compute node topology. The method is implemented in a production-level LDL solver and evaluated on Intel Ice Lake, AMD Genoa, and NVIDIA Grace over 34 SuiteSparse matrices. It outperforms MKL PARDISO, Panua PARDISO, CHOLMOD, and PaStiX, achieving geometric-mean speedups from 1.3 to 9.5 and, at flop parity, 2.7 less cross-socket traffic than Panua PARDISO.

events.title: Decentralized Scheduling of Scientific Workflows
events.description:
Modern scientific workflows are evolving with the emergence of the Compute Continuum, which integrates geographically distributed, heterogeneous, and dynamic computing resources across HPC systems, cloud platforms, edge devices, and scientific facilities. In this context, traditional centralized Workflow Management Systems (WMSs) face scalability and fault-tolerance limitations, motivating the exploration of decentralized scheduling mechanisms.

In this paper, we present a general approach for implementing decentralized scheduling in WMSs, enabling distributed task submission, collaborative task allocation, and remote task execution. Using this approach, we implement a fully decentralized consensus-based scheduler in which agents collectively agree on task assignments without relying on a central coordinator or shared global state. The scheduler is integrated into the COMPSs WMS and evaluated on the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer using a distributed GridSearch application.

The results demonstrate improvements in workflow execution time and load balancing across agents. Our general approach provides a foundation for implementing decentralized scheduling mechanisms.

events.title: Efficient and Portable Support for Overdecomposition on Distributed GPU Platforms
events.description: Overdecomposition enables asynchronous many-task runtimes such as Charm++ to overlap communication with computation and to balance load dynamically. Its benefits are well established on CPUs, but GPUs favor large kernels and bulk transfers, so fine-grained execution risks prohibitive launch, synchronization, and communication overheads. We investigate whether overdecomposition can be sustained efficiently on GPUs and portably across vendors. We find that the dominant costs arise not on the device but from host-side serialization, in vendor-specific ways, and can be mitigated transparently by the runtime: by parallelizing kernel submission and completion detection across processes and threads sharing each GPU, and by routing every message through device-to-device paths. In a single-source Charm++/Kokkos environment running unchanged on NVIDIA and AMD systems, these techniques reduce the minimum effective task granularity on Task Bench from 26-37μs to 4μs, and overdecomposed Jacobi2D, MiniMD, and LULESH match MPI performance on up to 64 A40 and 32 MI250X GPUs.

events.title: Compliance, ColdFront, and Chaos: Tooling to Align HPCC User Life Cycles and Research Impacts with Changing Regulatory Landscapes
events.description:
As federal research funding in the United States becomes subject to additional compliance regulations, better understanding the research being done at high-performance computing centers (HPCCs) takes on new importance in HPCC system management. However, aggressive compliance regulations can often be at odds with the flexibility required to serve large user bases performing cutting-edge research, resulting in ad hoc measures, inconsistent applications, and disorganized communication.

This paper presents a case study of implementing new tooling and user life cycle management workflows to standardize user and project relationships at a large R1 university's HPCC. These relationships are structured to provide insight into compliance needs, while integrating with the popular HPCC management system ColdFront for research output tracking. The development and deployment process is provided in detail, including specification development, technical discussion of tooling, collaboration across the university, and user-facing considerations during a 30-month roll out process affecting over 11,000 user accounts.

events.title: Women-Led Technical Project Spotlights
events.description:
Three women technical leaders give 5-minute lightning talks on innovative projects, from open-source CFD and AI infrastructure scalability to AI for cancer surveillance:
→ One Code, Two Worlds: Building an Open-Source CFD Code in Collaboration with Industry — Michele Weiland (EPCC, UK)
→ Scalability Issues on AI Infrastructures — Isabel Schwerdtfeger (IBM, Germany)
→ Cancer Surveillance in the Age of AI — Sally R. Ellingson (University of Kentucky, USA)

events.title: From a Last-Week Add-On to First-Day Practice: Three Years of Integrating MPI Performance Analysis into HPC Education with EduMPI Suite
events.description: Performance analysis is essential for scalable MPI programs, yet tool and workflow complexity often relegates it to the end of Parallel Programming courses. EduMPI Suite lowers this entry barrier by automating cluster execution, measurement, and near-real-time analysis while visualizing MPI communication from the first program. This paper presents a three-year experience report on its integration into HPC education. We trace the transition of performance analysis from a last-week add-on to a recurring element of MPI development, using unpublished historical survey evidence and individual 2025 questionnaire data. Earlier cohorts perceived performance analysis as unnecessary, difficult, or unintuitive. In the final study, all students recommended introducing EduMPI Suite early in the course. Of 33 students, 29-33 rated it higher than conventional tools for understanding program behavior, interpreting communication, identifying bottlenecks, obtaining visual feedback, and navigating the tool. These findings support embedding performance analysis throughout MPI education before transitioning learners to professional environments.

events.title: HPL and HPL-MxP at Exascale on Aurora: Performance Engineering and Characterization
events.description: Running HPL and HPL-MxP at exascale requires more than optimized numerical kernels; it requires coordinated performance engineering across communication, resource mapping, runtime configuration, CPU--GPU interaction, and mixed-precision execution. This paper reports experience from large-scale benchmarking campaigns on Aurora, the Intel-based exascale supercomputer at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Aurora progressed from 0.585 EF/s on 5,439 nodes to 1.01 EF/s on 9,234 nodes in FP64 HPL, while HPL-MxP reached 11.64 EF/s on 9,500 nodes. We describe the system-level choices behind these results, including locality-aware rank, GPU, memory, and NIC placement; explicit CPU--GPU pipelining; host-buffer MPI and transport configuration; phase-specific NIC assignment; AMX-accelerated mixed precision; and a hybrid point-to-point/collective path introduced after synchronization stalls at scale. This experience-based study concludes with practitioner guidance separating Aurora-specific findings from broader principles for tightly coupled heterogeneous systems.

events.title: Special Session - The open Quantum-HPC Software Ecosystem (openQSE)
events.description:
Amir Shehata - Introduction
Doug Oucharek - openQSE: the future of the reference implementation
Sebastian Stern - Building the Quantum-Enabled HPC Center
Michael Ferguson - openQSE: Designing the FTQC compiler stack

events.title: LightshowAI-Agent: An MCP-Based Agentic Framework for Real-Time and Reproducible X-Ray Absorption Spectral Analysis at Scientific User Facilities
events.description: Identifying an unknown phase from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data requires a multi-step pipeline spanning candidate retrieval, surrogate inference, spectral alignment, expert-informed ranking, and provenance tracking across independent databases, models, and services that scientists coordinate manually. We present LightshowAI-Agent, a framework that automates and orchestrates this pipeline. Scientific capabilities are exposed as typed tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), providing access to the Materials Project database, XAS prediction surrogates, and American Science Cloud (AmSC) model services. Versioned skill files carry domain-specific analysis procedures that experts can inspect and revise independently of prompts. Reproducibility is supported by logging agent and model activity through MLflow and analysis metadata through Tiled. We demonstrate a workflow identifying a TiO2 polymorph from Ti K-edge spectra streamed from the NSLS-II Quick X-ray Absorption and Scattering (QAS) beamline.

events.title: PILOT: Parallel Implementation via LLM-Oriented Translation
events.description:
This paper presents PILOT, a Python-based workflow that automates the translation of serial C/C++ source code into parallel implementations targeting selected backends using Large Language Models (LLMs). The workflow implements an iterative compilation-error correction cycle that maintains multi-turn conversational context with the LLM, enabling automatic recovery from synthesis errors in successive rounds. Functional correctness is verified automatically by comparing the outputs of the original serial
program and the translated parallel version. PILOT further quantifies the achieved parallelization quality by measuring the execution speedup relative to the serial code. The system is evaluated across five state-of-the-art LLMs spanning diverse architectures. Tests were conducted on fifteen computational benchmarks and four parallel models. Results show that compilation success rates range from 88% to 100% depending on the backend, with MPI and Go achieving perfect compilation across all models. Kernel-level speedups reach up to 48.75× for Go and 31.84× for OpenMP on favorable benchmarks.

events.title: SciNet: Science-Aware Network Operations for Research Networks
events.description:
Emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is fundamentally changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed. However, research networks
remain passive communication infrastructures that seek to optimize packet delivery while being agnostic of the scientific workflows they support. This disconnect creates bottlenecks
in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making. In this paper, we propose Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a new networking paradigm where artificial intelligence (AI) is integrated into the
network control plane to continuously observe scientific workflows, predict network demands, reason about workflow dependencies, and optimize network behavior, done autonomously. Unlike conventional AIOps systems that optimize utilization or reliability, SciNet is focused on optimizing for scientific productivity through workflow-aware routing, predictive resource allocation, and autonomous mitigation of failures. We present the architecture, mathematical formulation, learning framework, and evaluation methodology, and discuss how the proposed system aligns with the Department of Energy’s vision for AI-driven autonomous laboratories.

events.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
events.description: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4\% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

events.title: Measured WAN Traffic Reduction from Federated Edge AI in a Distributed Cosmic-Ray Sensor Network
events.description:
Scientific instruments are increasingly built from large numbers of small, heterogeneous edge devices that operators cannot inspect or trust. Citizen-science cosmic-ray networks, in which commodity smartphones act as particle detectors, are an extreme example. Centralizing raw observations from such networks is the default architecture, but its wide-area traffic grows with every observation, and it requires participants to surrender raw data. We present an end-to-end federated alternative and attempt to measure its network behavior on smart-phone
data. Our system trains a compact artifact-rejection classifier for smartphone cosmic-ray detections entirely in the browser. Hits never leave the phone; clients exchange small weight payloads with a FedAvg coordinator on the National Research Platform. At matched accuracy, federation cuts WAN traffic 3.2–11.4 x, governed by per-client data volume, not client count, locating the crossover. We also address aggregator hardening and validation against a low-cost calibrated muon telescope.

events.title: Peachy Parallel Assignments (EduHPC 2026)
events.description:
Peachy Parallel Assignments are tested and ready-to-adopt assignments to teach parallel and distributed computing concepts. They are selected competitively for being "cool and inspirational" so that students spend time working on them. After selection, they are presented at the Edu* series of workshops.

This article describes three assignments presented at the EduHPC 2026 workshop. The first is an unplugged assignment that introduces MapReduce concepts by having students count word occurrences in a popular children's book. In the second assignment, students parallelize a power grid simulation using multiple parallel programming abstractions (OpenMP for shared memory systems, MPI for distributed memory systems, and CUDA/HIP/OpenCL for GPUs). For the third assignment, they perform distributed fine tuning of a Large Language Model (LLM), a popular but extremely resource-intensive application.

events.title: Emblase: Using Tiled as an AI-Ready Data Access Service for Live Scientific Workflows
events.description: Scientific user facilities such as the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II) need reliable paths from beamline acquisition to machine-learning analysis and scientist-facing interaction. We present a Tiled-centered architecture that publishes scientific data and inference results through one interface while keeping compute, model-registry, and language-model services replaceable. As an institutional partner in the American Science Cloud (AmSC), we developed Emblase to demonstrate an application that uses AmSC-provided compute, model-hosting, and LLM inference services in a live NSLS-II Soft Matter Interfaces (SMI) scattering workflow. Data acquisition creates Bluesky runs that Tiled exposes to an event-driven inference service. The service resolves a versioned physics-informed machine-learning model, processes incoming frames, and writes embeddings and associated products to Tiled for dashboard inspection. Authenticated Tiled tools support grounded natural-language interaction. The architecture keeps live experimental state behind one scientific interface while allowing deployment-specific choices for compute and AI services.

events.title: A Performance-Portable GPU-Accelerated Solution for Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh Method using Cabana and FFTX
events.description: One approach to the development of high-performance computing applications is based on libraries that implement algorithmic motifs in a portable, performant and concise fashion. We develop a GPU-accelerated algorithm for Method of Local Corrections, a particle-particle particle-mesh method for simulating incompressible flow in 3D, using such motif libraries. The algorithm comprises of structured grid calculations, local particle interactions, and free-space convolution. We use two motif libraries: Cabana, a motif library for particles, built on top of Kokkos; and FFTX for fast Fourier Transform, that uses the SPIRAL code generation system. By using motif libraries, we obtain a concise and portable implementation (2K lines of code). We compare the measured performance to that predicted by the roofline model and obtain 52\%-86\% on NVIDIA A100, 42\%-61\% on NVIDIA H100, 22\%-42\% on AMD MI100, and 17\%-38\% on AMD MI300A.

events.title: An Agentic Workflow for Legacy HPC Modernization: Converting the Two-Electron-Integral Core of GAMESS
events.description:
Modernizing legacy Fortran is a problem of volume: the transformations are individually routine, but the codebases are enormous, and the work goes undone. We propose an agentic workflow operating at production scale. Three prompt-specialized agent roles operate under a version-controlled specification the agents themselves authored, while humans hold a small number of gates. Safety is anchored to an exact verification oracle inherited from the domain.

We apply the workflow to the two-electron-integral routines of GAMESS (General Atomic and Molecular Electronic Structure System), converting twelve source files (56,448 lines, 225 subroutines) from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008. The agents ran as Claude Code roles in isolated worktrees. Because GAMESS's user community treats its printed test energies as canonical, we adopt bit-for-bit reproduction as the merge criterion. All twelve files pass the 51 standard tests with zero chemistry-relevant differences and the Jenkins continuous-integration test suite.

events.title: Network-Aware Caching in Distributed CMS XRootD Systems via Data-Driven Forecasting
events.description: High-Energy Physics experiments such as the Compact Muon Solenoid distribute petabyte-scale datasets across geographically dispersed sites, imposing sustained load on wide-area research networks. Although in-network caching mitigates repeated transfers, deployed policies remain reactive rather than anticipatory. In this work, we propose a two-stage predictive caching framework trained on 8.4 million XRootD session records from 25 cache nodes across four domains. In Stage-1, a gated recurrent unit model forecasts near-future dataset accesses. In Stage-2, directories and files within predicted datasets are identified through non-parametric resolution. Simulation results show that an architecturally decoupled side-cache preserves baseline performance. Over 23 days at a single cache node, it displaces 115 GB of wide-area traffic, reducing wide-area volume by 1.6% and improving the hit rate by 1.4–1.6 percentage points. This study demonstrates that predictive caching depends not only on prediction accuracy, but also on selecting prediction granularity and integrating predictions with cache operation.

events.title: Cross-Stack Resilience for Extreme Scale AI: Coordinated Recovery for Training and Inference
events.description:
Resilience has become significantly more complex for AI workloads. AI models distribute parameters, communication state, and inference caches across thousands of devices. Collective communication has moved onto the critical path of application execution, with large-scale training synchronizing at every step and parallel inference invoking collectives very often. In these environments, a single device or rank failure can affect training progress, model quality, and inference latency. Also, large-scale training and latency-sensitive inference now run on mixed CPU, GPU, and accelerator systems with multiple fabrics and tiers of storage. Large-scale scale-up, scale-out and heterogeneous systems all exacerbate the problem by spreading state across tightly coupled nodes and distributed domains.

Checkpoint/restart remains essential, but it is no longer sufficient as a stand-alone strategy for AI workloads. This paper treats resilience as an optimization problem and proposes a cross-stack resilience architecture that coordinates recovery across applications, framework, communication, storage, orchestration and system telemetry.

events.title: Exploring Sparse Matrix Multiplication Operations on Cerebras CS-3 Platforms
events.description:
In recent years, novel AI accelerators have emerged as promising alternatives to GPUs for AI model training and inference. The Cerebras CS-3 has demonstrated strong performance on machine learning and some scientific applications. While the benefits of Cerebras systems for dense workloads are well demonstrated, their potential for sparse workloads, particularly for large matrices with substantial memory requirements, is not yet understood.

In this work, we study two sparse linear algebra kernels, sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) and sampled dense-dense matrix multiplication (SDDMM), on the CS-3. We propose low-level CS-3 designs and optimize them for I/O performance, memory footprint, and scalability. Our evaluation shows that the CS-3 kernels can outperform the CPU by up to 100x for SpMM and 20x for SDDMM on 90% sparse matrices, with SpMM performance improving as matrix dimensionality increases. However, beyond 99% sparsity, our kernels suffer performance degradation and approach or underperform state-of-the-art CPU libraries.

events.title: How far can network congestion awareness improve scientific workflow scheduling?
events.description:
Scientific workflows execute on shared HPC infrastructures, where network congestion remains a persistent phenomenon. Congestion arises
from communication contention among tasks within the same workflow or across concurrent workflows, often increasing makespan. We show that the impact of congestion can be mitigated by delaying task execution; however, only when two conditions are satisfied: (i) a shared communication bottleneck exists, and (ii) there is available slack outside the workflow critical path. We propose the Valley-Filling Admission (VFA) mechanism, which holds off-critical-path transfers out of the congestion crest and releases them into the idle-bandwidth valley. Using realistic network telemetry, VFA reduces workflow makespan by up to 9.2% for SoyKB and 11.2% for the 771 GB Chip-Seq workflows. We evaluated VFA with simulations across three network topologies, driving eight workflows and a real execution trace against a congestion-free baseline, and systematically sweeping the slack margin, contention factor, workflow concurrency, and telemetry staleness.

events.title: What Your Job Queue Isn’t Telling You: Workflow Monitoring with Drona
events.description: Scientific workloads on high performance computing (HPC) systems often involve multi-stage workflows beyond simple job submission. Existing tools provide limited monitoring, exposing primarily scheduler-level metadata and forcing users to piece together workflow progress, performance behavior, and domain-specific results through fragmented interfaces. A new and improved version of the Drona Workflow Engine addresses this gap by providing a schema-driven framework combined with a support library for constructing integrated job monitoring artifacts throughout the workflow lifecycle. This paper presents Drona’s monitoring architecture, based on dynamic elements, retriever functions, workflow abstractions, and a support library, enabling real-time observability and interactive job management during execution within a unified interface. We demonstrate Drona monitoring dashboards for various domain-specific workflows.

events.title: Icebreaker and networking
events.description: An interactive session to help participants find shared research interests and make lasting connections.

events.title: ParslBox: Computational Materials Workflow Executor for AI-Agents on High-Performance Computing Systems
events.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can autonomously construct large computational materials workflows, but executing these adaptive, fine-grained workloads efficiently across diverse high-performance computing (HPC) systems remains challenging. We present ParslBox, a lightweight workflow execution toolkit for computational materials applications on HPC systems. ParslBox provides a local job database, fine-grained CPU/GPU resource management, portable execution across heterogeneous HPC systems, and command-line, Python, and Model Context Protocol interfaces. Scalability was demonstrated on up to 2,000 nodes and 24,000 concurrent workers while maintaining low orchestration overhead. Strong-scaling studies using LAMMPS with MACE, and VASP demonstrated transparent execution of scientific applications. Agentic benchmarks showed reliable, repeatable job registration at scale across multiple closed-weight and open-weight language models. End-to-end agent-driven generation of machine-learned interatomic potentials for molten LiCl-NaCl and LiCl-KCl systems further demonstrated autonomous orchestration of complex multi-stage HPC workflows. Overall, ParslBox provides a portable, low-overhead execution layer for computational campaigns on leadership-class systems.

events.title: Characterizing Network Behavior of Distributed LLM Inference on a Four Node Edge Cluster
events.description: Desk-side AI accelerator clusters enable local LLM execution, yet their networked system behavior remains uncharacterized. We evaluate a four-node NVIDIA GB10 (Grace Blackwell Architecture) cluster connected via a commodity Ethernet switch across twenty distributed inference configurations spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. Four key findings emerge. First, decode is memory-bandwidth bound: single-node and pipeline-parallel setups achieve 0.69–0.86 of the memory-bandwidth roofline, while tensor parallelism divides per-node weight reads to accelerate decoding by up to 2.5x over RDMA, inverting standard datacenter trade-offs. Second, link bandwidth is not a bottleneck; per-node traffic consumes under 4% of the 200 Gb/s link without congestion. Third, communication latency remains critical, as RDMA over Converged Ethernet lowers end-to-end token latency by 2.0x to 7.1x compared to TCP. Finally, enabling expert parallelism alters inter-node traffic by less than 0.5%, reflecting vLLM’s default all-reduce backend rather than an intrinsic property of expert parallelism.

events.title: End-to-end GPU-native communication in GROMACS simulations with PME task specialization
events.description:
Strong scaling of molecular dynamics simulations is increasingly limited by communication latency as per-step execution time becomes shorter. In task-specialized GROMACS runs, particle-particle (PP) tasks exchange coordinates and forces with particle-mesh Ewald (PME) tasks every time step through CPU-mediated MPI communication, exposing host synchronization on the critical path of a step that is otherwise entirely GPU-resident. We present an NVSHMEM-based GPU-native redesign of these pipelined producer-consumer communication phases. Our design combines stream-triggered and kernel-initiated communication, fuses PME force communication with receiver signaling, and is tuned for NVLink and RDMA interconnects to reduce
control-path overhead and increase overlap, improving end-to-end performance by up to 15%. This work extends GPU-native communication beyond halo exchange toward end-to-end
GPU-resident GROMACS execution, while highlighting the challenges that symmetric allocation without team-based support poses for task-specialized applications.

events.title: Performance comparison and analysis of macroscopic cross section lookup kernel on Cerebras CS-3 and NVIDIA GPUs
events.description: The Cerebras CS-3 integrates approximately 900,000 processing elements in a two-dimensional mesh and provides high memory bandwidth and an exceptionally high B/F ratio, making it attractive for memory-bound scientific workloads. We evaluate a computational kernel that abstracts the macroscopic cross section lookup in XSBench, a Monte Carlo particle transport mini-app, characterized by low arithmetic intensity and irregular random memory accesses. We measure maximum performance, strong scaling, and weak scaling on CS-3, analyze the factors contributing to its improvement over CS-2, and compare it with optimized implementations on NVIDIA GH200 and A100 GPUs. Without additional optimization, the CS-3 implementation achieves 9.44E+09 lookups/s and an 11% higher geometric-mean performance than CS-2. Under identical experimental conditions, it delivers 6.34× and 11.90× higher throughput than GH200 and A100, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of CS-3 for irregular, memory-intensive lookup workloads. Our analysis also highlights how wafer-scale architecture benefits this challenging class of kernels.

events.title: An Agentic Evaluation Framework for AI-Generated Scientific Code in PETSc
events.description:
While LLMs have accelerated scientific code gen-
eration, comprehensively evaluating generated code remains
challenging. Many benchmarks emphasize functional correctness
or task completion, which is insufficient for code built on pro-
duction HPC libraries, where solver selection, API conventions,
memory management, parallel awareness, and performance also
matter. We introduce PETSCAGENT-BENCH, a multidimensional
benchmark and agent-based framework for assessing whether
AI-generated scientific code uses a production HPC library as
an expert would. A tool-augmented evaluator compiles, executes,
and measures code and combines deterministic checks with
LLM-based assessments in a 14-evaluator pipeline spanning five
categories: correctness, performance, code quality, algorithmic
appropriateness, and library-specific conventions. A2A and MCP
enable black-box evaluation of compatible coding agents. Across
realistic PETSc problems, frontier models generate readable,
well-structured code but struggle with correctness on challeng-
ing problems and with library-specific conventions even when
code compiles and runs—limitations that conventional pass/fail
evaluation does not capture.

events.title: Security Mediation and Adversarial Evaluation for Agentic AI at HPC Facilities
events.description: For LLM agents at DOE facilities, prompt injection and unsupported citations share one shape: a value reaches a consequential action, a sink, from a forbidden origin. PALISADE, a sidecar gating six boundaries of the VISTA platform, labels values by origin outside the model, propagates labels by text matching, and admits a sink value only if its label permits. SIEGE, our 205-attack benchmark, enforces HPC job submission as a security boundary and scores detector evasion separately from sink access. The deterministic tier stops 19 of 32 sink-capable attacks and, with egress blocking, all 5 forged citations, at 0.28 ms/turn and 3.3% benign blocking. Adaptive attacks (PAIR, TAP) raise credited sink admissions to means of 28–31 of 32, but about 14 still carry the attack, none bearing an untrusted label at the check. Closing this propagation gap requires tracking dataflow or keeping untrusted values out of the planner.

events.title: Cross-Fabric Policy Reasoning for Hybrid InfiniBand/Ethernet HPC Systems
Exploring the Genesis Platform Capabilities to Accelerate Scientific Discovery in OPAL
events.description: Autonomous, cross-facility science requires capabilities that no individual project should have to build for itself: managed execution for long-lived services, versioned distribution of models to remote compute systems, governed access to large language models, a shared substrate for experimental data, and end-to-end provenance. The U.S. Department of Energy Genesis Mission platform, delivered through the American Science Cloud, provides these as reusable services. This paper reports how the Genesis platform enables cross-facility experiments and accelerates scientific discovery. We explore the plant phenotyping workflow of the Orchestrated Platform for Autonomous Laboratories as the exemplar: it couples Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Advanced Plant Phenotyping Laboratory with the Frontier supercomputer. In a 40-day nickel-treatment campaign, the resulting workflow replaced roughly twelve hours of manual analysis with interactive queries returning in seconds to minutes.

events.title: Fine-Grained Application-Aware Congestion Mitigation with Telemetry-Tuned Weighted SRv6 Policies
events.description:
Modern wide-area and research networks support
many different types of applications, each with its own perfor-
mance requirements. Because of this diversity, no single routing
strategy such as shortest path, least-utilized path, or Equal-
Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) can consistently deliver the best results
for every application. Existing telemetry mechanisms such as
IOAM and gNMI are fundamentally class-agnostic and operate
at 10–500ms timescales, while current SRv6-TE systems rely on
controller-driven path switching based on out-of-band statistics.
In this paper, we present a class-aware, in-header congestion
feedback mechanism for SRv6 that (i) encodes traffic engineering
(TE) class identity in the SRH Tag field, (ii) appends per-hop,
per-class congestion evidence in a Telemetry Tuned Weight -SRv6
(TTW-SRv6) record carried in-band with the SRv6 tunnel, and
(iii) uses load balancing algorithms per class within a distributed
architecture. A new architecture is presented where a trusted edge classifier
analyzes flow behavior.

events.title: Accelerating GPU Datalog with Kernel Fusion
events.description: Recursive Datalog queries such as transitive closure, connected components, and same generation iterate a rule to a fixpoint and express many graph analytics. GPU Datalog engines run each round as a chain of separate relational operators driven by a host loop, paying for repeated sorting, per-round allocation, and a CPU-GPU round-trip. Instead, we run each round as single CUDA kernel over GPU-resident data structure, so a single atomic operation per derived fact deduplicates, tests novelty, and inserts it together. Because the state stays on the device, the whole loop runs on the GPU via a replayed CUDA graph and a conditional graph node, and results are updated in place as edges arrive. On an NVIDIA A100, this cuts end-to-end time by up to 24x for transitive closure and 136x for connected components over MNMGDatalog, beats GPUlog by up to 29x in compute, and updates connected components up to 40x faster.

events.title: Dynamic and Static Workflow Orchestration for Large-Scale Uncertainty Quantification Campaigns
events.description:
Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is an essential component of computational science workflows. As the size of UQ campaigns continues to grow, efficiently orchestrating large ensembles of parallel simulations on High Performance Computing (HPC) systems becomes increasingly challenging. While workflow management frameworks simplify campaign execution, the choice of an orchestration strategy can significantly influence resource utilization, execution efficiency, and overall time to solution.

This paper evaluates two paradigms for large-scale campaigns on a parallel hemodynamics application use-case. The first approach employs dynamic task scheduling using EasyVVUQ and Dask Distributed, where simulations are executed through a pool of dynamically managed workers. The second approach relies on scheduler-native job arrays, where simulation instances are submitted as independent batch jobs.

The methodology combines strong scaling experiments with UQ campaigns executed under both orchestration strategies. The results provide practical guidance for selecting workflow execution strategies and highlight the trade-offs between dynamic and static workflow orchestration models.

events.title: Analyzing User Logs as a First Diagnostic Step in Open OnDemand
events.description: Open OnDemand (OOD) session failures generate developer-centric logs that may confuse researchers and burden HPC support staff with routine tickets. While large language models (LLMs) provide readable failure explanations, unconstrained models can hallucinate non-existent root causes. We present \textit{LogLight}, an asynchronous diagnostic panel running inside the OOD session card under the invoking user's Linux privileges without elevated service state. LogLight enforces a four-source trust hierarchy that prioritizes deterministic extraction from logs and scheduler accounting, incorporates an advisory site playbook, and restricts the LLM strictly to narrative synthesis. In a blind evaluation across 30 production sessions, binding deterministic findings into prompts significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and attribution over log-only inputs. Grounding enabled a lightweight Mistral-7B model to match the diagnostic performance of a GPT-OSS-20B model, offering an efficient, user-scoped architecture for failure analysis.

events.title: Rising Innovators Research Showcases
events.description:
Five invited rising innovators deliver 5-min lightning talks showcasing their research, technical ideas, projects, discoveries, or emerging directions in HPC and AI:
→ Algorithms as if Architecture Mattered: Moving Less, Computing Faster — Rabab Alomairy (KAUST, Saudi Arabia)
→ Sparse by Nature, Parallel by Design: HPC for the Life Sciences — Giulia Guidi (Cornell University, USA)
→ SwarmLoRA: Serverless Shared-Computation Disaggregation for Isolated, High-Throughput Multi-LoRA Serving — Tong Shu (University of North Texas, USA)
→ Abstract, Portable, Performant: Realizing Sustainable HPC — Floris-Jan Willemsen (Leiden University, Netherlands)
→ The Meaning of Compute: formal approaches to exascale AI development — Rubén Coll Sánchez (Huawei, Sorbonne University, France)

events.title: The LLM Writes Only the Algorithm: Bit-Identical Fortran-to-C++ Substitution, and What It Certifies
events.description: LLM Fortran-to-C++ translation is usually evaluated by compilation success, similarity metrics, or tests on isolated functions. However, none of these establishes substitutability: whether a translated function can replace the original in production without changing results. Reported here are two migration campaigns held to that standard by VIT (Verified Incremental Translator). VIT generates the interoperability code, and the LLM writes only the algorithmic function body. Each body passes two bit-identical gates, replay against captured production state and whole-simulation baselines. ROSCO, a wind-turbine controller, was fully translated to C++; 2.56 million nontrivial outputs match exactly across 27 scenarios. In OpenFAST’s AeroDyn, ten times ROSCO’s size, 33 of 507 procedures are translated under the same gates and tool. Of fourteen injected defects, three pass both gates. Thus, bit-identity certifies agreement on exercised inputs, not equivalence of two implementations, and as translation becomes inexpensive, the verification oracle becomes the limiting factor in migration.

events.title: Tutorial Lunch
A Multi-Layer Workflow for Diagnosing Performance Portability in RAJA Applications
events.description: Performance-portable frameworks like RAJA enable a single source to run on diverse HPC architectures, but productivity relies on the compiler removing abstraction overhead. When it does not, runtime data show where performance diverges, but not why. We present a multi-layer workflow that diagnoses abstraction-induced divergence by combining runtime measurements with compiler-visible evidence, including GPU resource usage, optimization remarks, and LLVM IR metrics. We apply this workflow to 55 RAJA Performance Suite kernels using HIP and OpenMP backends, three optimization levels, and three problem sizes (1,980 configurations). For selected kernels, the workflow distinguishes optimization-agnostic from optimization-sensitive behavior and links performance losses to the compiler's excessive loop unrolling, register pressure, reduced occupancy, scratch spills, and control-flow complexity. These diagnostics guide source changes that restore native-level performance for four kernels and an optimization-specific transformation that eliminates compiler-induced register pressure in a fifth, providing guidance for understanding and improving performance portability beyond runtime analysis.

events.title: ScaleTether: Graph Rewriting and Selective Timing Prediction for Megatron Parallelism
events.description: Automated planners for distributed training must evaluate configurations that have not yet run. ScaleTether transforms version-pinned Megatron executions into workload graphs for tensor, data, and pipeline parallelism.
