It exports graphs as Chakra traces for ASTRA-sim, while graph support and measured H100 timings determine whether it returns an estimate, requests measurements, or rejects an unsupported configuration. Six graphs created before their target runs matched later captures on every checked field, and all 72 injected corruptions were rejected. Across cases, median timing error ranged from 0.73% to 3.59%. In 80 four-GPU searches, all 35 estimates chose the measured optimum, while measurement intercepted all 19 ungated choices above 1% regret. Selective measurement cut acquisition by 30.3% to 7.58 H100 GPU-hours including calibration and by 44.0% to 6.09 with calibration reuse. Agents followed guidance in 120/120 offline sessions versus 52/120 with configuration numbers alone.

events.title: ROSS'26: Wrap-up discussion
Squid: Distributed-Memory k-mer Counting for Rack-Scale GPU Clusters
events.description: The problem of k-mer counting (KC) is to quantify the frequency of length-k substrings in a biological sequence. It is an essential and often limiting step in bioinformatics workloads. Despite the recent popularity of GPUs, the fastest distributed-memory KC solutions remain CPU-based. Existing GPU implementations have poor memory-bandwidth utilization and weak communication-computation overlap. To address these issues, we present Squid, a GPU-native distributed-memory, bulk-synchronous parallel k-mer counter. Squid introduces a transpose-based k-mer generation kernel that reaches up to 71% of peak high-bandwidth memory bandwidth and is 6× faster than prior approaches. On identical hardware, Squid runs 22× faster end-to-end than the previous state-of-the-art GPU counter, and scales to 256 GPUs on a modern GB200-NVL72 cluster at ≥85% intra-rack parallel efficiency. Squid is also the first GPU k-mer counter to outperform the CPU-based DAKC and HySortK, running on 1024 CPUs of Perlmutter, by up to 2× and 6.6×, respectively.

events.title: CUDA-Enabled Actors: Rekindling GPU Execution in the C++ Actor Framework
events.description: The C++ Actor Framework (CAF) once provided OpenCL-based GPU acceleration within the actor model, but this capability is no longer supported. This paper presents CUDA-Enabled Actors, a CUDA-based extension that re-establishes a practical path to GPU execution in CAF while preserving an actor-oriented programming interface. CUDA support is implemented through a thread-safe command runner that serves as the execution interface for launching CUDA kernels through an actor-oriented API and gives users finer control over host--device memory transfers. The resulting design hides much of the complexity of GPU programming while retaining the modularity and abstraction of the actor model. Experiments demonstrate that CUDA-Enabled Actors provides actor-oriented GPU execution with modest overhead relative to native CUDA, supports execution across multiple GPUs, enables recovery from worker failures, and improves resource use for irregular workloads, establishing it as a practical foundation for GPU-enabled applications in CAF.

events.title: Short Talk: Portable AI Workflows and Federated Agents for Experiment-in-the-Loop Synchrotron Science
FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
events.description:
A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates those claims and the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads across common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations.

These results indicate that emulation should not be evaluated as a replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-like: this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Even in this favorable regime, GEMM speedup is not sufficient: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale.

events.title: When Agents Break the Memory Hierarchy: Understanding Data Stalls in Agentic HPC Workflows
events.description: Scientific workflows use storage-memory hierarchies to manipulate exascale data without data loading stalls at feasible resource costs. These systems exploit the fact that traditional HPC workflows have deterministic access patterns. Agentic HPC workflows break this assumption, allowing AI agents to decide what will run next. We find that on a representative workflow, a state-of-the-art DMSH system increases wall time by 3.18x because data needs are learned too late for staging. We also find that 93% of artifact-loading time is representation transformation rather than byte transfer. The cost of transformation makes some representations nearly 65x more valuable to keep than others in terms of end-to-end workflow stall avoided. Models and transformed data also compete for host memory, making capacity value dependent on correctly predicting reuse timing through agent framework signals, and tuning memory management based on representation needs and hardware availability. These findings motivate memory management designed for agentic HPC workflows.

events.title: PROV-AGENT-LOOP: Provenance Data Management for Agentic Loop Engineering
events.description: AI agents governed by Large Language Models modify code, inspect logs, revise plans, invoke tools, spend tokens, and decide whether objectives have been satisfied, affecting computational outcomes in ways that require accountable provenance. This paper introduces PROV-AGENT-LOOP, a W3C PROV-compatible model that represents objective-plan-act-evaluate cycles as queryable provenance. The model builds on PROV-AGENT, aligns with MAS, BDI, ReAct, Reflexion, and MAPE-K concepts, and captures loop structure, communication, evaluation, authorization, delegation, and invocation evidence. We implement PROV-AGENT-LOOP in Flowcept, integrating agentic, workflow, machine-learning, scheduler, and telemetry records in one Provenance Database. We validate the model on Frontier, where an AI agent adapts a Dask-based training campaign. The database answers eight cross-domain queries with 100% structural evidence completeness under OPL+DPL, more than double the workflow-only baseline, while Codex token usage and database footprint are reported as observed values rather than controlled overhead.

events.title: LLM–Driven Root Cause Analysis of BGP and BFD Flap Events
events.description:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) flaps are key indicators of network instability. Frequent up/down transitions can increase latency, cause packet loss, and lead to Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations by repeatedly disrupting traffic forwarding and routing convergence. Root causes of the flaps can range from physical link failures to protocol misconfigurations and policy violations, making diagnosis costly and time-consuming, as operators must correlate evidence across devices, interfaces, protocols, logs, and performance metrics. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative, as they can integrate and reason across heterogeneous operational evidence to accelerate root cause identification and reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR). However, their effectiveness depends on explicit diagnostic reasoning, structured explanations, and validation of inferred causes against operational evidence. API-based LLMs also raise privacy concerns, while locally deployed open source alternatives require careful evaluation of their diagnostic accuracy and operational
performance. In this paper, we present an LLM-based prototype for automated root cause analysis of BGP and BFD flap events. The prototype uses locally deployed open-source LLMs to correlate protocol logs with topology, service state, and forwarding information, identifying likely root causes and affected network entities. We evaluate the approach through controlled failure
experiments in a Mininet-based testbed and through operational analysis of events from a production BGP/BFD testbed. The results show that prompt design substantially affects root-cause accuracy, with structured, domain-specific prompts enabling several medium-sized models to achieve perfect accuracy. Entity-extraction performance varies more widely across prompts and models, while model selection also affects inference latency. These findings suggest that locally deployed LLMs can support accurate, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving analysis of BGP and BFD flap events.

events.title: Adapting Classic List-Scheduling Heuristics for Conditional Task Graphs
events.description: Many scientific and machine-learning workflows are modeled as conditional task graphs (CTGs), in which some branches are chosen at runtime so only one of several alternative sub-graphs executes. Tasks on different branches are mutually exclusive, so a scheduler can overlap them on the same processor. We show that classic list-scheduling heuristics such as HEFT and CPoP can be adapted to CTGs with two small changes: a schedule representation that lets mutually exclusive tasks share a processor, and a priority function that weights each task by its probability of executing. Both are components of the open-source SAGA parametric list scheduler. Exploiting mutual exclusion is the dominant benefit, bringing expected makespan within a few percent of a clairvoyant scheduler. Probability reweighting does not help on generic conditional graphs, but helps decisively when a rare branch contains a heavy task competing with always-executed work for a fast processor, the structure of surrogate-model workflows.

events.title: uv-manager: A Transparent Wrapper for Safe, Architecture-Aware Python Environments on Heterogeneous HPC Clusters
events.description: uv suits high-performance computing unusually well, but a cluster violates three of its assumptions: that $HOME has room for a package cache, that a shell profile is available, and that every node shares one CPU architecture. uv-manager, a transparent wrapper deployed as a site module, resolves all three. Users invoke uv and uvx unchanged while it relocates per-user state onto capacity storage and partitions that state by an architecture key resolved on the executing node, with architecture-neutral trampolines so one PATH entry works everywhere. Relocation is half a solution: capacity storage is purged file by file, and uv performs no integrity check on an environment it believes installed, so it executes what a purge leaves behind. uv-manager protects against this failure mode by detecting and repairing on the executing node, which is what makes the placement safe.

events.title: Recall Is Not Honesty: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures for Trustworthy HPC Operational Analytics
events.description: Agentic systems answer operational queries over HPC telemetry for domain scientists who cannot verify the responses. Trustworthiness requires recovering the facts telemetry supports and refusing the questions it does not, since no facility instruments everything it runs. Existing architectures are built for capability on the assumption that reliability follows, and inference remains untested. We compare five configurations, one tool-using agent and four multi-agent designs varying only in inter-agent communication and shared-state structure, on EPIQ, a new benchmark of 55 multi-intent queries over Fugaku job telemetry with 119 verifiable facts and 25 unanswerable sub-questions. The single agent recovers the most facts (84.9%) but refuses least. Pairing peer messaging with typed dialogue-act fields refuses most (92.0%) while matching single-agent recall within noise, at 2.5 times the tokens. Refusal follows whether agents exchange results at all; typing those exchanges recovers recall. Agent count explains neither. Recall and refusal must be designed for separately.

events.title: BFS-FAR: Fragment-Local Asynchronous Relaxation with Host Reconciliation for Breadth-First Search on UPMEM
events.description: Breadth-first search (BFS) is difficult to accelerate because of irregular memory accesses, limited computation per edge, and frequent synchronization. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) offers high memory-level parallelism, but level-synchronous BFS is ill-suited to UPMEM because DRAM Processing Units (DPUs) cannot communicate directly and must coordinate through the host. To address this, we present BFS-FAR, an execution model that replaces strict level-by-level synchronization with fragment-local progress and update-aware reconciliation. BFS-FAR partitions graphs into per-DPU CSR fragments, performs in-place local relaxation, and reconciles replicated levels through a parallel host-side minimum reduction. Experiments on R-MAT and synthetic graphs using up to 2,540 DPUs show 18.0-86.5 algorithm-only speedups over PrIM-BFS, although CPU_64T remains faster because host-mediated coordination still limits complete BFS performance. These results highlight execution model and communication granularity as key design considerations for irregular PIM workloads.

Building Scalable Agentic Systems for Science: Concepts, Architectures, and Hands-On with Academy
events.description: Agentic systems, in which autonomous agents collaborate to solve complex problems, are emerging as a transformative methodology in AI. However, adapting agentic architectures to scientific cyberinfrastructure—spanning HPC systems, experimental facilities, and federated data repositories—introduces new technical challenges. In this half-day tutorial, we introduce participants to the design, deployment, and management of scalable agentic systems for scientific discovery. We will present Academy, a Python-based middleware platform built to support agentic workflows across heterogeneous research environments. Participants will learn core agentic system concepts, including asynchronous execution models, stateful agent orchestration, and dynamic resource management. A guided hands-on session will help attendees build and launch their own agentic workflows. It will include case studies in materials discovery, biology, and chemistry. This tutorial is designed for researchers, developers, and cyberinfrastructure professionals interested in advancing AI-driven science with next-generation autonomous systems.

events.title: Connecting the Quantum and HPC Communities: A Tutorial on High-Performance Software for Quantum Computing
events.description: Quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize many fields in the 21st century. Over the past decade, numerous quantum computers have been made publicly available. However, the effectiveness of the hardware is heavily reliant on the software ecosystem—a lesson drawn from classical computing's evolution. Unlike classical systems, which benefit from mature electronic design automation (EDA) and high performance computing (HPC) tools for handling complexity and optimizing performance, quantum software is still in its infancy. One of the goals of this tutorial is to educate the HPC community on quantum computing and to bring these two communities closer together. To this end, the tutorial covers two key topics at the intersection of classical and quantum software: quantum program compilation and the integration of quantum devices into HPC environments. Furthermore, the tutorial showcases how expertise in classical HPC can address key challenges in the quantum software stack. All of the above is accompanied by hands-on demonstrations based on the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT)—an open-source collection of high-performance software tools for quantum computing developed by the Chair for Design Automation at the Technical University of Munich, and the Munich Quantum Software Company.

events.title: Reproducible Benchmarking for High Performance Computing Applications
events.description: Benchmarking is integral to overall practices of HPC, AI and ML. A hierarchy of benchmarks allows comparison of machines to each other, vendors to respond to new procurements, and compute facilities to evaluate offers when selecting new platforms. Within a developer community, benchmarks allow an application’s performance to be evaluated and improved over time. Despite the importance of benchmarking, the process of performing a benchmark is challenging and requires many manual steps, such as researching the appropriate workloads, determining how to compile the software, acquiring execution steps, and extracting the correct metric for comparison. Collectively, these steps pose a high barrier for new users to perform a benchmark and an even higher barrier to executing these benchmarks across a wide set of compute facilities. This hands-on half-day tutorial provides a detailed introduction to a suite of open-source tools and their capabilities (Benchpark and Ramble) to enable reproducible benchmarking of HPC systems. The tutorial is structured to address reproducibility aspects including encoding of the run and build instructions for a given application and hardware system. Attendees of this tutorial will leave with foundational skills in conducting reproducible benchmarking using these tools for defining build and run instructions.

events.title: Towards Efficient Vertical Federated Learning on Distributed Scientific Infrastructure
events.description:
Modern scientific collaborations rely on combining data from multiple organizations while preserving data privacy according to regulations and policies. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables collaborative model training without requiring participants to share raw data. However, deploying VFL across geographically distributed infrastructure introduces significant execution overhead, and requires balancing computational cost and privacy requirements.

To address the communication overhead introduced by distributed VFL execution, we investigate the deployment of multiple VFL execution strategies within DYNAMOS, a policy-aware middleware for privacy-preserving data exchange. We evaluate the baseline VFL protocol alongside two communication-efficient variants, including a novel adaptation of an asynchronous optimization technique from Horizontal Federated Learning. The strategies are deployed in both a local environment and on a distributed research testbed, enabling a comparative evaluation under realistic scientific networking conditions. These experiments support execution time, model utility, and privacy analysis, demonstrating that the optimized strategies substantially reduce runtime while preserving predictive performance.

events.title: EESP 2026: 3rd International Workshop on Energy Efficiency with Sustainable Performance: Techniques, Tools, and Best Practices
events.description:
The Energy Efficiency and Sustainable Performance (EESP) workshop fosters the exchange of innovative strategies, tools, and best practices to enhance energy efficiency in modern computing environments. As energy costs rise and CO₂ emissions increase, sustainable operation has become critical for HPC, AI, and data center infrastructures. EESP addresses the challenge of balancing performance, power, and sustainability, focusing on actionable, cost-effective solutions for Tier-0/1 and Tier-2 systems. The workshop promotes cross-layer innovation by integrating hardware, software, runtime systems, and data-driven analytics to achieve end-to-end visibility and adaptive energy management. It advances transparency in energy use and carbon emissions, supports hardware innovations (e.g., new architectures and liquid cooling), and enables dynamic adaptation, predictive analytics, and intelligent workload scheduling for real-time optimization. By fostering collaboration between HPC and AI communities, EESP advances reproducible practices and operational insights that empower computing centers, researchers, and industry to implement scalable solutions for long-term sustainable performance.

events.title: EESP Welcome Remarks
Invited Talk: Billions of Edges per Hour: Generating and Partitioning Dynamic Contact Networks on Heterogeneous Exascale Systems
events.description: Agent-based simulations of population health model each individual's movement and contacts over time. At national scale this produces a dynamic, highly irregular graph: hourly contact networks whose size swings from millions of edges at night to tens of billions during the day, with heavy skew toward dense urban locations. Storing these networks explicitly is impractical and partitioning them by agent or location count leaves severe load imbalance. This talk presents ENABLE, a hybrid CPU-GPU framework developed to address these problems. GPUs generate each hour's contact network directly from activity schedules, and a GPU implementation of Uniform Cost Partitioning balances contact edges across ranks, while CPUs run the disease dynamics in an asynchronous pipeline. For a 350-million-agent population, generating edges on the GPU instead of storing them reduces memory per simulated hour from about 250 GB to 1.3 GB. On the Frontier supercomputer, ENABLE reaches 82% strong-scaling efficiency at 1,120 ranks and holds weak-scaling efficiency above 75% on up to 1,200 GPUs. Roofline analysis shows both partitioning kernels are memory-bandwidth bound, each using about 78% of peak HBM bandwidth on the MI250X. The talk closes with open problems in streaming mobility data, keeping results deterministic across rank counts and scaling dynamic-graph simulations toward virtual population health twins.

events.title: RLSA: Adaptive LLM Gating for Multi-Agent HPC Scheduling Agents
events.description: In decentralized scheduling of scientific workflows, multiple LLM-based agents reason over heterogeneous resources to bid for jobs. However, LLM reasoning incurs substantial latency and compute cost, limiting scalability in high-throughput environments. We therefore ask whether an LLM is necessary for every decision, and study adaptive LLM gating, where an RL-trained policy learns to choose between an LLM and a fast surrogate from downstream scheduling reward. We propose RLSA (Reinforcement Learning-enhanced Scheduling Agents), trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) under a reward balancing makespan, resource balance, and inference cost. In a controlled auction, RLSA halves LLM calls per job (4.00 to 2.06) while preserving makespan relative to always-LLM bidding (7686 vs. 7285 seconds). We further validate it with a real LLM bidder and a 17-VM FABRIC deployment where LLM calls grow sub-linearly with the number of bidders, positioning RL-based adaptive gating as a cost-control layer for LLM-based scheduling agents.

events.title: Parallel and Accelerated Dependent Partitioning
events.description: Dependent partitioning is a flexible framework for compactly describing and efficiently computing partitions of distributed data structures that contain indirections and interconnected references. These data structures are commonly found in scientific applications, which operate over meshes, graphs, and sparse tensors. However, existing implementations of dependent partitioning process the individual elements of their input data sequentially on CPUs. This limitation makes dependent partitioning an expensive component of application initialization, and hinders its use in dynamic or on-line contexts. In this work, we present parallel algorithms for computing dependent partitions, and show that these algorithms perform well on accelerators like GPUs. Across a series of microbenchmarks and existing applications that use dependent partitioning, we show that our work achieves speedups of 9.4–9,807× for computing dependent partitions. We then show that our algorithms enable dynamic and on-line partitioning during steady-state execution.

events.title: High Performance Python for Science at Scale
events.description: This symposium-style workshop aims to connect researchers, developers, and Python practitioners to share their experiences scaling Python-based applications and workflows on supercomputers. The goal is to provide a platform for topical discussion of best practices, hands-on demonstrations, and community engagement via open-source contributions to new libraries, runtimes, and frameworks. Based on talks and demos that survey and summarize the best practices and recent success stories and developments, the workshop provides attendees a forum for expanding their knowledge of tools and techniques as well as opportunities to engage with representatives from the broader Python community.

events.title: ISAV26: In Situ AI, Analysis and Visualization
events.description: HPC platforms and applications have reached such large scale, complexity, and heterogeneity, that a major challenge has become the wide gap between our ability to compute extreme-scale data and our ability to gain insight from it to make timely, data-driven decisions. A well known, yet challenging, approach to visual analysis, learning, and processing is performing the tasks in situ, i.e., while the data is still in memory, potentially in lieu of saving the raw data out. Since 2015, ISAV has fostered a community of in situ developers, practitioners, researchers, and users of in situ methods and infrastructure, connecting industry, government laboratories, and academia across all career levels. Through presentations, discussions, and peer-reviewed proceedings of research findings, lessons learned, and early ideas, ISAV illuminates new requirements and gaps driven by science and engineering applications and fosters the application of in situ methods.

events.title: Opening Remarks by ISAV OC
17th Workshop on Latest Advances in Scalable Algorithms for Large-Scale Heterogeneous Systems (ScalAH'26)
events.description:
Novel hybrid scalable scientific algorithms are needed with the advent of a variety of novel accelerators, including GPUs, FPGAs, etc., as well as with the growth in size of quantum computing devices, neuromorphic chips, and various AI-specific processors. This myriad of devices requires a unified approach that allows efficient and scalable hybrid approaches combining classical and novel computing paradigms to be implemented at scale.

These extreme-scale heterogeneous systems require these novel scientific algorithms to hide the complexity, hide network and memory latency, have advanced communication, and have no synchronization points where possible. With the advent of AI in the past few years, the need for such scalable mathematical methods and algorithms for such hybrid architectures that are able to handle data and compute-intensive applications at scale becomes even more important.

events.title: Benchmarking Physical GCD Placement Effects on Performance, Energy, and Co-Execution
events.description: GPU-accelerated supercomputers expose large populations of nominally identical resources that are often treated as interchangeable, even though physical device variability can affect performance and energy efficiency. This is particularly relevant for multi-die accelerators and workload co-execution, where outcomes depend on both workload compatibility and physical placement. We characterize these effects on Frontier using six synthetic workload classes. A solo campaign covers 600 node allocations and 4,800 AMD Instinct MI250X Graphics Compute Die (GCD) observations, while co-execution evaluates all workload pairs across 72 representative physical placements using matched solo baselines. Across the sampled population, best-to-worst GCD differences reach 18.7% in performance, 32.3% in average GPU-package power, and 36.9% in energy. Complementary co-executions approach ideal overlap and reduce energy by approximately 40%. Workload compatibility determines whether sharing is beneficial, while physical GCD placement determines its magnitude and stability, motivating GCD-aware scheduling to improve science per watt.

5th International Workshop on Cyber Security in High Performance Computing
events.description: The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers and practitioners in cybersecurity and HPC. Security in high performance computing (HPC) has traditionally been an “operational” challenge (i.e., restrict access and usage to certified users). Thus, despite significant advances in our understanding and mitigations of vulnerabilities, the cybersecurity research community has been somewhat disconnected from the HPC community. Recent increases in the heterogeneity of both the underlying platforms of HPC and the community of HPC-level users and applications point to an important and growing need for connection and synergy between these two communities.

events.title: Featured Speech: Holistic Power Efficiency: Squeezing Computing out of Every Watt
A Threat Model for Sensitive-Data Workloads on Multi-Tenant AI Supercomputers
events.description: Sensitive-data research increasingly requires the GPU scale of national AI supercomputers, yet the governed multi-tenant handling routine in cloud environments has not been established in supercomputing. Extending a Trusted Research Environment (TRE), or Secure Data Environment (SDE), onto such a system distributes security responsibility across three parties---a capacity owner, an infrastructure provider, and a TRE/SDE operator that governs data on infrastructure it neither owns nor operates. We present a threat model for this setting, expressed as attack trees and grounded in FRIDGE, a satellite-TRE architecture deployed as multi-tenant Kubernetes on two bare-metal national systems. It covers three adversaries---a privileged host operator, a malicious co-tenant, and a rogue researcher---and the supercomputing-specific attack surfaces conventional TRE work omits, mapping each attack path to a mitigation and its owning party. Underpinning the design is portable governance across independently-operated TRE/SDE platforms. This is work in progress.

events.title: HPPSS Featured Speaker
AI for Science: Building the future engines of scientific discovery
events.description: The U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is a national initiative to accelerate scientific discovery through artificial intelligence, with the ambitious goal of doubling research productivity and impact within a decade. This collaborative effort brings together DOE's 17 national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to build an integrated AI-powered discovery engine that addresses critical challenges in energy systems, materials manufacturing, biotechnology, fundamental science, and strategic technologies. The mission has selected 278 projects spanning 13 science themes and secured over $800 million in partner commitments, including a landmark $1 billion U.S.-Japan partnership. At its core, the initiative aims to create a coordinated scientific discovery system that integrates supercomputing resources, curated scientific data, AI models and agents, and experimental facilities into reusable workflows that close the loop from hypothesis generation to experimental validation. The ultimate vision is to develop AI systems that can propose falsifiable theories, design and execute their own experiments, provide calibrated uncertainty, and serve as public infrastructure accessible to researchers worldwide. However, the presentation emphasizes that success requires addressing AI for science not merely as a model problem, but as a comprehensive scientific-system problem encompassing data, theory, experiments, compute, incentives, governance, and human judgment working in concert.

events.title: This Data Will Self-Destruct in One Microsecond: Live Data Reduction and Steering at LCLS-II
events.description: The LCLS-II X-ray free electron laser at SLAC fires at repetition rates up to 1 MHz, generating raw data rates that start at 280 GB/s and will approach 1,120 GB/s by the end of the decade. At this scale, the traditional “write everything, analyze later” approach to science breaks down. Most raw data must be reduced, characterized, or discarded within moments of acquisition. At LCLS-II in situ processing is built into the architecture. This talk presents the overall design of the LCLS-II Data System, from detector readout through a distributed data reduction pipeline to fast feedback describing how LCLS measures, analyzes, and decides to steer experiments on the timescales of seconds, minutes, or hours. It also covers how the ILLUMINE project extends that pipeline with ML models that analyze high-rate data streams and steer experiments in near real time. I will discuss where AI/ML delivers today including event vetoing, rapid feature extraction and digital-twin aided reconstruction, and where it’s a work in progress. There are engineering realities that need to be reckoned with: latency budgets measured in microseconds, model deployment on heterogeneous edge hardware, coupling to remote HPC facilities, and earning scientists’ trust in decisions that are made before a human ever sees the data.

events.title: FAB-Cache: A Programmable Multi-Site Caching Service for Remote Dataset Retrieval Using FABRIC
events.description:
Scientific datasets, which often range from gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes, are frequently accessed within research institutions and shared among collaborators distributed globally. Thus, efficiently distributing these large-scale datasets to researchers has become a growing challenge.
We present FAB-Cache, a programmable, multi-site caching service deployed on NSF FABRIC testbed to accelerate access to remote scientific data. FAB-Cache chains NGINX proxies across geographically distributed FABRIC nodes and caches requested data on demand. It uses perfSONAR throughput measurements to select proxy paths. This design combines distributed storage and network measurements to support a stateful service within the network. We evaluate FAB-Cache using real-world scientific datasets retrieved across multiple FABRIC sites. Cache hits substantially outperform direct downloads over the public Internet, while cache misses achieve comparable or higher throughput in several scenarios. These results demonstrate the potential of FABRIC infrastructure to support flexible data distribution services for scientific workflows.

events.title: Guarded, State-Aware Orchestration for Schema-Constrained Scientific Model Execution
events.description: Trained scientific prediction models are often released as code, notebooks, or command-line tools requiring programming and exact schema knowledge, limiting access for domain researchers. Natural-language front ends can reduce this barrier, but standard LLM function calling provides a tool interface rather than workflow semantics for accumulating, validating, executing, and revising scientific inputs. We present guarded, state-aware orchestration for schema-constrained scientific model execution: the workflow collects inputs over multiple turns, constrains tool arguments with a typed schema, blocks incomplete execution, narrates results, and defines correction, what-if steering, and reset semantics. We instantiate the workflow for protein-corona prediction with a backend of 178 per-protein classifiers achieving 87.13% AUC-ROC. Evaluation using a cloud-hosted LLM produced 98.5% feature-extraction accuracy over 300 cases; a separate reliability evaluation of six interaction scenarios over 50 nanoparticle configurations passed all 300 scenario evaluations. These results demonstrate a testable extension of LLM function calling to scientific workflow orchestration.

events.title: Resource Contention in Point-to-Point Overlapping GPU Communication with NVSHMEM
events.description: Overlapping communication with computation is necessary at scale, and the communication library sets how cheaply that overlap can be had. We study point-to-point halo exchange overlapped with compute on a GH200 Grace Hopper platform with InfiniBand, comparing host-initiated GPU-aware MPI against device-initiated NVSHMEM and NCCL. Using a synthetic benchmark, we determine for which shared resource each backend competes. We then apply the communication models to a memory-bound workload, the SU(3) staplesum implemented with the hila framework. We find that in the memory-bound regime the constraint is HBM utilization rather than SM occupancy with an added L2 cost consistent with evicting the compute kernel's reused working set. Device-initiated NVSHMEM is fastest wherever communication is exposed, reaching 99% overlap efficiency in weak scaling at 128 GPUs and extending usable strong scaling 4X from 16 to 64 GPUs over non-overlapped execution. Every optimization reduces either L2 pressure or latency overhead in point-to-point communication.

events.title: Enhancing Data Center Efficiency and Throughput by Co-Scheduling
events.description:
Many HPC data centers have supercomputers with separate CPU-only and GPU compute nodes to support different workloads.
One approach to increase system throughput is to run CPU-only jobs on unused CPU resources on the GPU nodes.
Analysis of the workload running on NERSC's supercomputer showed that approximately 60% of Perlmutter's GPU node-hours employed fewer than 12 CPU cores and less than 128GB host memory.
The remaining 52 CPU cores and 128GB host memory could be used by co-scheduled CPU-only jobs.
However, it is critical that the co-scheduled CPU-only jobs and GPU jobs have controlled/bounded interference.
This preliminary study assesses the feasibility of co-scheduling in production.
Testing of the NERSC-10 benchmark applications on NVIDIA Grace-Hopper nodes using Memory System Resource Partitioning and Monitoring (MPAM) and network/InfiniBand quality of service for performance isolation measured a 70% throughput increase from co-scheduling compared with no co-scheduling, while maintaining an acceptable level of performance
isolation.

events.title: Privacy Foundations for Multi-Institutional Scientific Artificial Intelligence
events.description: Scientific AI, from foundation models to federated analysis pipelines, is becoming shared infrastructure across national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industry. Its privacy risks often concern an institution’s participation, strategy, or capability rather than single records. Differential privacy, federated learning, secure computation, trusted execution, and provenance each protect parts of the stack, but their guarantees rarely compose across mixed-trust institutions, access tiers, and autonomous agents. This perspective recasts privacy as an assurance problem defined by six elements: protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence. A lifecycle claim register for a composite cross-institutional scenario reveals two gaps specific to leadership-class facilities: scheduler metadata exposes institutional participation, and instrument-attached control loops leak research strategy through timing and accelerator contention. Six priorities emerge: institution-level guarantees, agent-communication privacy, cross-tier information flow, privacy-compatible reproducibility, leadership-scale accounting, and instrument side channels. We offer a common form for stating, comparing, and auditing otherwise fragmented privacy claims.

events.title: ORBIT: An AI-Powered Assistant for NOC Operations in a Data-Intensive Science Network
events.description: High-performance networks are critical infrastructure for data-intensive science, and their effective management relies on efficient incident response in Network Operations Centers (NOCs). This paper introduces the Operations Response \& Business Intelligence Toolkit (ORBIT), an AI-powered assistant that enhances incident response by consolidating information from disparate, siloed systems. ORBIT delivers synthesized results directly into the operator's primary work interface, applying agentic AI principles through a centralized reasoning service and a common model-access gateway. The system ensures transparency by logging all AI-generated outputs for operator review and rigorously controls access to sensitive data. In this paper, we describe the ORBIT architecture, present a selection of initial results from operational testing within ESnet’s NOC, and share lessons learned during its development and deployment; the complete findings are available in a companion technical report. Our findings highlight the importance of prompt engineering and a human-in-the-loop design for building trust and facilitating adoption.

events.title: Agents at Your Service: Reuse-First Workflow Composition with Laminar 3.0
events.description: Large language models show promise as software development assistants, but their tendency to hallucinate makes them unreliable for directly generating workflow implementations in specialized coordination languages. This paper presents Laminar 3.0, an evolution of the Laminar serverless framework that integrates a bounded, prompt-chained pipeline of role-specialized LLM agents to support workflow discovery and composition. It introduces an LLM-driven metadata generation mechanism to enrich the workflow registry, a hybrid retrieval mechanism combining semantic search, lexical search, and LLM-based re-ranking, and a retrieval-first, constraint-guided generation pipeline that proposes workflow skeletons only when no suitable artifacts exist. Laminar 3.0 prioritizes reuse and synthesizes only the coordination layer, leaving host semantics under developer control. Experiments show semantic retrieval remains robust even for compressed queries, achieving 79% top-1 and 81% top-3 retrieval, while the generation pipeline produces skeletons with a CodeBLEU score of 0.946, substantially outperforming direct generation with vanilla prompting.

events.title: Sub-Cycle Power Measurement of AI Workloads on Production GPU Racks
events.description: Different instruments report different power for the same AI workload. We show this on production H100 racks by recording the same events at three concurrent tiers: one-minute breakers, 100 ms per-GPU telemetry, and 10 kHz voltage and current on every rack feed. Disagreement between tiers shows what each instrument resolves. Coarse tiers return wrong numbers with no sign they are wrong: a training job pulses 5.75 times per second, and device telemetry, sampling ten times per second, reports 4.18. Only the feed record shows that a resumed job’s first pulse lands at full amplitude, and that an inference-serving instance under burst admission swings its whole rack from idle to peak twelve times per second. A resolution ladder states which tier resolves each phenomenon and how the others fail. For this load, ramp rates, transient magnitudes, and the coherence of aggregated units are sub-cycle quantities.

events.title: Distributed SpMV with HClib-Actor: A Case Study in Alternatives to MPI-Based PETSc
events.description: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) exhibits irregular computation and communication patterns that challenge distributed-memory execution. This paper presents a case study of distributed SpMV using HClib-Actor, an actor-based programming and runtime system implementing the Fine-grained Asynchronous Bulk-Synchronous Parallel (FA-BSP) model. We explore four HClib-Actor-based implementations as alternatives to MPI, varying matrix partitioning and sparse storage format, which together determine the communication direction and local traversal order. We evaluate their weak and strong scalability on synthetic and real-world graph matrices using up to 1,536 CPU cores, with PETSc as a highly optimized MPI baseline, on the Georgia Tech PACE Phoenix cluster. Our results show that HClib-Actor achieves good scalability on relatively well-balanced workloads and outperforms PETSc in several configurations, although performance remains sensitive to workload distribution. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of HClib-Actor for distributed SpMV and motivates further exploration of partitioning, scheduling, storage, and communication strategies.

events.title: Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines : From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
events.description: In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum J\"ulich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

events.title: Workflow-Level Scheduling of Hybrid Quantum-Classical Applications on Heterogeneous Resources
events.description: Hybrid quantum--classical applications involve coordinated execution of quantum and classical tasks across heterogeneous resources. We model such applications as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and formulate workflow scheduling as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that captures task dependencies, heterogeneous resource assignment, communication costs, makespan, and tardiness. To account for the the stochastic nature of QPU execution times, we additionally develop a robust counterpart based on budgeted uncertainty. The proposed framework enables workflow-level optimization beyond the performance of individual quantum or classical components. We evaluate the approach using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), illustrating how optimized scheduling can improve resource utilization and reduce end-to-end execution time in hybrid quantum--classical environments.

events.title: Custodian: Enabling Automatic Performance Engineering Agents on the NERSC HPC System
events.description: The advancement of Large Language Models and the rapid evolution of AI assistants and agents create an opportunity for the development of highly specialized HPC agents to enable automatic performance analysis. In this paper, we present Custodian, an HPC performance analysis agent that analyzes previously collected job telemetry and application-output data to characterize application behavior, identify potential performance bottlenecks, and transform performance metrics into natural language descriptions and figures that suggest optimizations or highlight computing inefficiencies. We validate Custodian’s telemetry-derived application states and roofline analyses against NVIDIA Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute across four representative applications executed on NERSC Perlmutter. Finally, we discuss the tradeoffs, cost, productivity and systems applicability of HPC agents on the NERSC HPC system.

events.title: Fidelity-Aware Scheduling of Quantum Circuits on Multi-QPU Systems
events.description:
High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) platforms expose multiple Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) that may differ in size, topology, native gates, and noise characteristics. For current noisy devices, errors compound along the compiled circuits quickly, and minimizing them, that is, maximizing the circuits' execution fidelity, is essential for reliable results.
Fidelity depends on the compilation to a specific target device: the same high-level circuit may produce different executables and, therefore, different expected fidelities across QPUs.
We present a low-overhead fidelity-aware scheduling framework for multi-QPU systems based on a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that estimates, before compilation, the expected fidelity of each circuit on each available QPU. Then, a tunable scheduler uses these estimates to control the trade-off between execution fidelity and parallelism. Results show that this framework allows for approximating an exhaustive fidelity-based assignment, saving computational resources compared to a brute-force approach that compiles each circuit on every device.

events.title: A First Look at Conventional Attacks on Scientific Applications
events.description: How vulnerable are scientific applications to conventional attacks mounted by intentionally manipulating their input? Prior work largely leaves this question unanswered. We begin to answer it by carefully adapting fuzzing and security-focused bug triage to characterize vulnerabilities in scientific codebases. Our process discovers almost 1000 unique crashes (likely distinct bugs) across Enzo, GROMACS, Laghos, and LAMMPS (about 3 million lines of code). Per application, an average of 7.3% of them represent easily exploitable vulnerabilities according to heuristic security analysis. Additionally, 26% of all bugs (51% for GROMACS) are exploitable heap memory safety issues. Cumulatively, we find over 110 distinct vulnerabilities that may permit arbitrary code execution (ACE). Manual inspection confirms the existence of exploitable bugs. Using a coding agent, we generate 59 reproducible proof-of-concept ACE exploits. Our results suggest untrusted data could have catastrophic effects on artifact integrity, creating real risk as computational scientific results drive increasingly consequential societal decisions.

events.title: A Next Generation Multi-Terabit/sec Campus and Global Network System for Data Intensive Sciences: The Global Network Advancement Group Data Intensive Science and AutoGOLE/SENSE Working Groups
events.description:
The Global Network Advancement Group (GNA‑G), through its Data‑Intensive Sciences (DIS) and SENSE/AutoGOLE Working Groups, is developing a next‑generation, multi‑terabit/sec global system to support the rapidly escalating demands of data‑intensive science. Scientific programs such as the LHC, Rubin Observatory LSST, SKA, Cryo‑EM, genomics, and distributed AI/ML workflows now generate unprecedented data volumes, requiring coordinated global infrastructure capable of predictable, high‑throughput, multi‑domain operation.
This system integrates programmable networks (P4, SRv6, PolKA, BGP‑CT), multi‑domain orchestration (SENSE/AutoGOLE), real‑time telemetry (INT, perfSONAR, ALTO, GradientGraph), ML‑driven intelligence (NetPredict, Hecate, GradientGraph), high‑throughput end systems (400G–800G DTNs, GPU nodes), and regional caches/data lakes into a unified, composable architecture. It is validated through global testbeds such as GP4L, FABRIC, NRP, and GRP, and deployed across multi‑Tbps optical infrastructures including APOnet, AmLight, Rednesp/RNP, ESnet, Internet2, GEANT, and StarLight.
At SC25, NRE‑125 and 16 partner NREs demo nstrated this architecture at scale, showcasing multi‑domain orchestration, programmable data planes, AI‑driven optimization, Digital Twin simulation, and multi‑Tbps global data movement. The system supports a progressive deployment model spanning R&D → advanced production → full production, ensuring coexistence with general R&E traffic while enabling the next decade of scientific discovery.
This has been enabled by strong industry support and collaboration, most notably from Ciena, Supermicro, Arista, Dell and Juniper.
This paper presents an overview of the architecture, mechanisms, development trajectory, operational model, and SC25 demonstration results of the GNA-G next‑generation global system, many of the development threads supporting its progressive implementation, and use cases in several disciplines of data intensive science.

events.title: Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling
events.description:
Test-time scaling can improve large language model reasoning by generating and combining multiple candidate responses. The inference budget is described by the number of generated candidates, N, but N tells us how many candidates are generated, not how they are executed. The same budget can come from one batched call or several sequential calls. Using Phi3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts, increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4 and 18.4 points, but accuracy alone does not show its system cost. Fixing N = 8, we compare
four generation schedules, 1×8, 2×4, 4×2, and 8×1, measuring latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy. On A100 GPUs, eight serial calls use 4.64–4.86× as much energy
and have 5.77–6.12× the P95 latency of one batched call, confirmed across A100 nodes and SciQ/V100 experiments. Candidate count alone cannot describe system cost; evaluations should also report generation schedule and GPU-level metrics.

events.title: SpSYRK: Half the Work in Distributed Sparse Matrix Multiplication
events.description:
The symmetric rank-k update (SYRK), C = AA^⊤,
computes the dot product between each pair of rows of A. Its sparse variant is central to
similarity-based approaches in machine learning, graph analytics,
and genomics. Existing distributed sparse
matrix multiplication algorithms, such as Sparse SUMMA, treat
sparse SYRK as a generic multiplication, leaving performance
untapped.

In this paper, we present a distributed sparse SYRK algorithm that leverages symmetry. The approach reduces per-process computation compared with state-of-the-art distributed SpGEMM. A second variant reorders
communication to avoid materializing A^⊤ and reduce communication volume.

The algorithm achieves a 2× speedup over an optimized Sparse
SUMMA on matrices. Our variant achieves
superior scaling at high process counts. The approach is a drop-
in replacement for any application computing C = AA^⊤ via
a distributed SpGEMM routine, and its triangular output can
be consumed directly by subsequent operations with reduced
compute and memory footprint.

events.title: Complexity and Scale in AI-Assisted Workflow Management: A Federated Learning Case Study
events.description: Federated learning over medical images is a demanding workflow application. Each round fans out across parallel client jobs and converges on an aggregation step that feeds the next round. At scale this yields 101 sub-workflows and 2,679 jobs on GPUs at four sites, which takes an expert months to build, mostly on workflow mechanics rather than science. We ask how far AI assistance can automate such workflows. An LLM agent, grounded in a released plugin of Pegasus-specific skills, first produces a reviewable specification of checkable constraints and acceptance criteria, then generates the executable workflow. A validation loop repairs runtime failures, checks code against those constraints, and regenerates the implementation from the specification alone. We evaluate three LLM agents, report end-to-end runs on the FABRIC testbed, and show how conformance checking against the specification caught three silent errors that failure-driven debugging missed, including one that trained 1,700 jobs on random tensors.

events.title: AI for Science with Python on AMD Supercomputers
events.description: Running Python workloads at scale is becoming increasingly important in the scientific landscape of today, especially given the rise of AI as a partner in scientific development and discovery. We will show various ways of deploying AI workloads (including AI agents) at scale running on AMD GPUs: our focus will be on AI for science on heterogeneous types of systems with variety of deployments (i.e. wheels and containers) and job schedulers (Slurm and Kubernetes). We will provide a walkthrough of AMD Inference Microservices (AIM) and how this inference engine can be used by scientists to deploy their Python AI workloads.

events.title: Heterogeneous Energy Characterization of GPU-Powered Datalog Engines
events.description: Datalog’s declarative rules support recursive analytics in databases, program analysis, and machine learning, yet the energy behavior of GPU-powered Datalog engines remains largely unexplored. We present the first heterogeneous CPU–GPU energy characterization of these systems, evaluating five engines across hash-based, index-nested-loop, sorted/hash-indexed, and DataFrame-based designs on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We measure total CPU–GPU energy, hardware-counter-based instructions per joule, and energy–delay product using Powerlog, a lightweight harness that samples GPU power through NVML and CPU-package power through RAPL while running unmodified engines. Results show that the fastest configuration is not always the most energy-efficient. Engine choice changes total energy by up to 3×, while CPUs account for 32–55% of total energy. Scaling from one to four GPUs reduces runtime by up to 2.9× but increases energy by 24–42%. Our reproducible methodology and artifacts support energy-aware Datalog system design and fair cross-engine comparison.

events.title: The MQSS Benchmarking Framework: Extensible Orchestration Layer for Quantum Benchmarking in HPC-Integrated Ecosystems
events.description: HPCQC systems are emerging as the practical path toward quantum computation, given current constraints on quantum noise, qubit count, and circuit depth. Benchmarking orchestrators can help pave the way by providing a unified framework for executing and evaluating workloads across het- erogeneous quantum hardware, simulators, and circuit libraries, while remaining extensible as the quantum computing ecosystem evolves. In light of this, we present the MBF, an open-source orchestration layer that unifies several components, such as benchmark definition, device abstraction, and execution strategies. MBF achieves these via its abstract benchmark, adapter and provider interfaces while supporting profiling at various stages to capture performance metrics across both the HPC and QC components of quantum computation. Together, these capabilities enable consistent and extensible benchmarking throughout diverse HPCQC environments, enabling the evaluation and performance analysis of quantum workloads across the full computational stack.

events.title: LASSI-EE: LLM-based Automated Refactoring of Parallel Scientific Codes for Energy Efficiency
events.description: Energy efficiency is a critical objective for high-performance computing, yet optimizing scientific applications for energy has traditionally required deep expertise and substantial manual effort. This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can generate energy-efficient parallel codes when guided by empirical execution feedback, and whether their optimizations adapt to the target application and architecture. We propose LASSI-EE, an automated refactoring framework integrating runtime power profiling, energy-aware prompting, self-correcting feedback loops, and an LLM-as-a-Judge for screening generated code. To quantify expected savings under LLM non-determinism, we introduce energy-reduction@k, a metric that accounts for all generation attempts, including failures. Across twenty-two scientific benchmarks and applications on NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI100 GPUs, compiled at full optimization, LASSI-EE achieves expected energy savings of 29% for a single attempt and 48% when selecting the best of three. Average reductions reach 34%-36% among passing energy-reducing refactorings, largely preserving or improving runtime without precision-reducing transformations.
