A Deployment-Aware Multi-Objective Hyper-Parameter Optimization Framework for Machine Learning
events.description: State-of-the-art ML models deliver unprecedented performance across computer vision, natural language processing, and multi-modal tasks. These improvements have been driven by significantly growing computational costs, memory footprint, and consequently, energy consumption. Several model compression techniques and hyperparameter optimization strategies have been proposed to address these increases. Most of these approaches, however, target the training phase and often overlook the deployment context and the model usage. We propose a general-purpose framework for ML model optimization, focused on deployment and inference, to assist practitioners by quantifying trade-offs between model accuracy, power consumption, and other deployment-relevant metrics such as latency and memory usage. The proposed system is validated in three use cases: deploying a computer vision model on a resource-constrained edge device, optimizing LLM serving on data center-grade hardware, and running a large-scale benchmark on the Frontier HPC system. The system successfully identifies optimal configurations, demonstrating its versatility and applicability to practical scenarios.

events.title: Optimizing Bloom Filters on Modern GPUs
events.description: Bloom filters are a fundamental data structure for approximate membership queries in applications ranging from analytics and databases to genomics. Deployed as prefilters, they eliminate irrelevant data before expensive downstream processing. As data-processing pipelines move onto GPUs, filtering must remain GPU-resident and keep pace with other stages. Although Bloom filters have been extensively optimized for CPUs, few implementations target GPUs, where fixed SIMD layouts map poorly to SIMT hardware and leave performance potential on the table. We present an architecture-aware GPU Bloom filter with tunable vectorization for performance portability across workloads, memory regimes, and GPU architectures. On NVIDIA B200, it sustains over $92\%$ of the measured random-access bound. At comparable false-positive rates, it outperforms the state-of-the-art GPU baseline by $15.4\times$ for lookup and $11.35\times$ for construction. These gains bring accurate Bloom filters to GPU-scale throughput previously reserved for high-error variants. The implementation is openly available in NVIDIA's cuCollections library.

events.title: The Other Half of Workflow Portability: Evidence-Backed HPC Site Profiles with Agentic Discovery
events.description: Moving a workflow developed at one HPC site to another rarely succeeds without trial and error. Package managers, containers, and workflow specifications such as backpacks all describe what a workflow needs, but none describes how a given site must be used, so even a portable workflow requires manual adjustment at each site. That missing half includes the site's resource shape, storage, network permissions, and operating policies, scattered across the batch system, prose documentation, and undocumented behavior. We propose the HPC site profile, a structured, evidence-backed description whose every field traces to the measurement, documentation, or pilot job that established it. A bounded language-model agent extracts documented fields with citations, each verified deterministically or discarded, while login measurements and pilot jobs supply the rest. The profile then preflights a workflow into an execution plan or an early, explainable failure. We build and evaluate profiles at three production sites.

events.title: Distributed Shared Timestamped Memory
events.description:
Parallel discrete-event simulation (PDES) and agent-based modeling and simulation (ABMS) are two important modeling and simulation paradigms used in domains such as network simulation, epidemiology, and transportation. Both must coordinate distributed state as simulation time advances, yet common approaches in each paradigm sacrifice either performance through blocking synchronization or scalability and simplicity through rollback mechanisms to do so. Moreover research in each field has largely progressed in isolation.

We present a partitioned distributed versioned array that can serve as a common global distributed memory layer in both PDES and ABMS for more flexible synchronization schemes. By allowing each rank to maintain multiple versions of a shared datastructure available at the same time, our approach enables unbalanced workloads to drift out of lockstep without rollbacks or neighborhood barriers. We demonstrated increased performance using this scheme on common benchmarks from both PDES and ABMS paradigms, against state of the art runtimes.

events.title: sundials4py: state-of-the-art time integrators for high-performance Python
events.description: We discuss sundials4py, a Python interface to the SUNDIALS suite of high-performance numerical time integrators, on AMD and NVIDIA GPU-based supercomputers. We show how sundials4py provides portable access to SUNDIALS’ accelerator-enabled solvers and zero-copy interoperability with numpy, PyTorch, and JAX. We also demonstrate how nanobind and litgen are used to generate much of the Python interface binding code, reducing the effort required to expose a large, evolving HPC library while integrating it naturally with the Python GPU ecosystem. Prepared by LLNL under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-ABS-2023376.

events.title: Ensemble PBVR: Interactive In Situ Visualization of Ensemble Statistics on Rendering Particles
events.description: Ensemble statistics are classically computed after every member has been written to storage. Forming them during the run instead requires gathering field data on the compute nodes, at the cost of global communication and memory copies. We present ensemble PBVR, which forms them from visualization particles instead: one set of particles circulates through the members by a ring exchange, and the mean, variance and coefficient of variation accumulate at the particle positions during batch execution. Gradients used as volume-rendering normals follow analytically from a chain-rule expansion that closes with four accumulated quantities per particle, and the target field is defined at run time by a user-supplied algebraic expression. We apply it to a 72-member CityLBM urban plume dispersion ensemble on a GPU supercomputer. Against a post hoc ParaView workflow it reaches the first image 4 to 30 times faster and transfers 60 times less data.

events.title: Scalable and Multi-NIC Parallel Trees Collective Algorithms for MPI Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast
events.description: Broadcast, Scatter, and Gather are MPI collectives critical to HPC and DL application scalability. As GPU clusters rely on multiple NICs per node for inter-node bandwidth, traditional single-tree algorithms fail to exploit this bandwidth for large messages. We propose a GPU-based, multi-NIC-aware design for large-message MPI Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast that partitions each collective across multiple independent binomial trees, each mapped to a distinct NIC, enabling communication to proceed concurrently across all rails. We implement and evaluate our design in Open MPI on two GPU platforms, full-mesh NVLink and NVSwitch, at 16, 32, and 64 GPUs. Compared to Open MPI, our design achieves latency reductions of 52.5%, 82.8%, and 74.6% for Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast on full-mesh, and 57.0%, 79.8%, and 74.3% on NVSwitch. A step-complexity analysis shows our design reduces critical-path communication rounds from ⌈log2 p⌉ to ⌈log2(p/g)⌉, where g is rails per node, yielding better scalability at scale.

events.title: PortWarp: A Cycle-Accurate GPU-Accelerated HPC Network Simulator Using Port-per-Thread Model
events.description: The cycle-accurate modeling methodology, used by popular tools such as BookSim2, Gem5, and SST, has become a de facto standard for modeling HPC networks and systems. However, single-threaded cycle loops limit the system size and time scales that can be explored. In this work, we developed PortWarp, a new cycle-accurate approach that efficiently models exascale-class HPC network designs by leveraging GPU accelerators. Because the thread-per-port mapping is hardware-agnostic, the identical validated build achieves 445x speedup on an NVIDIA H100 and 513x speedup on a B100 GPU, with the additional gain coming entirely from newer hardware. Per-port-occupancy instrumentation confirms that in the saturation regime where those speedups are realized, nearly every port-thread performs useful work each cycle. Overall, we are encouraged by PortWarp's performance gains and believe this modeling approach could be applied to other HPC computer systems modeling domains.

events.title: QSPredictor: Runtime Prediction for Tensor-Network based Quantum Circuit Simulation on GPUs
events.description: Tensor networks enable the simulation of large quantum circuits with limited entanglement, potentially reaching hundreds of qubits. For circuits with higher entanglement, predicting runtime before execution is important for assessing simulation feasibility, wait times, and resource utilization in quantum-centric computing systems. Metrics that allow runtime estimation, such as treewidth, are NP-hard to calculate and change with each specific circuit, complicating usability in HPC schedulers. Circuits belonging to different families or algorithms present a similar structure that allows grouping through cheap characterization, providing information relevant to total runtime. We present QSPredictor, a Transformer-based predictor of tensor network planning, contraction, and total runtime using structural circuit properties and OpenQASM text, and compare it against a family-aware baseline. To improve data efficiency, QSPredictor selects representative training circuits followed by conditioned k-means++ selection. Under the complete proposed pipeline, QSPredictor achieves a total-runtime MAPE of 7.09% and a log-space R² of 0.9906.

events.title: Extending the Performance Portability of Julia to Long-Vector Architectures
events.description:
The architecture of computing infrastructures is becoming increasingly diverse, making performance portability critical.
In the Julia language, JACC (Julia for Accelerators) provides performance portability across CPUs and GPUs.
However, JACC was not designed with long-vector architectures in mind, which effectively hide memory latency and deliver high sustained performance in memory-bound applications.
In this paper, we extend the performance portability of Julia to long-vector architectures by developing an execution backend for the NEC Vector Engine within JACC.
We compare JACC applications against native implementations on three GPU models and two VE models, with little or no architecture-specific code depending on the benchmark.
Our results show that the relative performance exceeds 90% on all architectures in most cases, and demonstrate that our backend extends the performance portability of JACC from CPUs and GPUs to long-vector architectures.

events.title: Distributed Volumetric Generation of Neuronal Morphology at Scale
events.description: Large-scale electron microscopy connectomes enable the study of neuronal morphology, but annotating and proofreading these datasets remains effort-intensive. Generative models offer a complementary approach, learning from manual reconstructions to synthesize neuronal structures. Dense volumetric occupancy grids are directly compatible with connectomics workflows, but cost grows cubically with linear resolution which is unfavorable for sparse objects like neurons. We present a distributed generative pipeline with this representation and characterize its cost–fidelity tradeoff. We extract 46,582 axonal and dendritic fragments under a fixed 20 µm field of view and train a compartment-conditioned 3D convolutional variational autoencoder at different resolutions. Generated fragments are evaluated using geometric and topological descriptors calibrated against natural variation in the data. Across up to 256 NVIDIA A100 GPUs on Polaris, our pipeline retain 74–85% strong-scaling efficiency for training and generation is sharded to produce one million fragments in 3.1 s at 64³ and 5.25 min at 256³.

events.title: Distinguished Address: Rethinking Security for AI: Enforcing Boundaries for AI Agents
events.description: As organizations adopt AI agents that execute code, access data, and coordinate across shared HPC infrastructure, every allowed action becomes a security decision. This talk explores how NVIDIA OpenShell brings isolation, deterministic policy enforcement, and controlled network access, unlocking actual enforceable agent runtime boundaries. Safe adoption requires extending zero trust to agent behavior, making continuous monitoring and governance foundational to how organizations grant, oversee, and govern agent autonomy.

events.title: Adaptive Control with Offline Reinforcement Learning for HPC Power Management
events.description: Power-capping policies for high-performance computing must reduce energy use without imposing unacceptable delays across heterogeneous applications. PowerSched, deployed on CPU nodes of the Hunter supercomputer at HLRS, identifies per-job operating points through iterative Golden-Section Search (GSS), which requires multiple measurement intervals and can respond slowly to workload changes. We replace this search with an Implicit Q-Learning controller trained offline on approximately 13 million telemetry transitions from 15,000 historical jobs. Using only telemetry already available to PowerSched, the controller requires no application instrumentation and predicts a bounded per-socket power cap every 15 seconds. We integrate it as a prototype behind PowerSched's predictor interface and conduct preliminary single-node experiments on HPL, HPCG, and eight NAS Parallel Benchmarks. Relative to a 400 W/socket maximum-cap baseline, the controller reduces measured node energy by 7.1% across all ten benchmarks with a 1.0% average performance reduction. The results use three independent runs per benchmark.

events.title: Energy and Cost-Aware Control at Scale: Multi-Dimensional Frequency Steering on AMD MI300A
events.description:
Energy and Power have become a first-order concern for large HPC and AI installations.
The optimization targets are no longer limited to production peak throughput, but include
stable output under electrical limits, carbon constraints, and infrastructure cost pressure.
This paper presents an extension to an operational control approach (PowerSched) that mitigates some of these concerns. The work reports on a PowerSched extension towards multi-dimensional frequency steering of GPU architectures that targets CPU boost frequencies, GPU clocks and memory/interposer-related controls, The control plane supports policy shaping through a configurable objective term, so operation can be shifted at runtime along an energy--performance--cost trade-off axis. Challenges and solutions for multi-dimensional steering algorithms are discussed, including mutual constraints, discrete-valued tunables, and noisy telemetry. First results for AMD mi300a architecture are presented. The results indicate performance gains up to 10% relative to the uncapped system and energy-efficiency gains up to 30%.

events.title: Cheaper by the Batch: Shared Traversal for Genotype Graph Editing
events.description:
Adding nodes in a graph while reusing existing structure is a recurring computational problem.
In population genetics, this problem arises in genotype representation graph (GRG), a DAG that losslessly encodes genetic variation across thousands of samples by sharing subgraph structure.
In GRG, mutation’s carrier is encoded as leaf nodes reachable from the node it is assigned to.
Current approaches update mutations individually.

This paper introduces a batched mutation-remapping algorithm that replaces independent traversals with a shared reverse-topological pass, identifying reuse candidates for a batch at once.
The pass propagates compact bit-parallel per-mutation state and uses an adaptive sparse/dense carrier set representation spanning rare-to-common variant densities.
Batching adds memory-scalablility to split-based parallelism, which replicates graph and traversal state per worker.
Our remapping approach is evaluated on standalone scenarios and end-to-end allele polarization workload.
It is up to 10.5$\times$ faster than independent remapping while preserving exact carrier-set semantics.

events.title: Enabling Radio Astronomy to Use French Supercomputers
events.description:
Next-generation radio telescopes, such as the SKA, will generate exascale data volumes requiring national supercomputing resources. However, the radio astronomy community faces systemic barriers in accessing French HPC centers due to the Zone à Régime Restrictif (ZRR), a cybersecurity regime enforcing individual accountability that conflicts with the community's shared-account model.
To reconcile these requirements, we leverage a "Scientific Application as a Service" framework using Ephemeral Buffers and Application Microservices, extending it with a proposed named service account model. We validate this approach by deploying the DDF Pipeline—a calibration imaging pipeline for the LOFAR telescope (an SKA pathfinder)—on the Jean Zay supercomputer. Our results show data transfer throughputs up to 137.9 MB/s download and 28.73 MB/s upload , and a reduction in execution time from 68.8 to 8.7 hours on 24 nodes (~7.9x speedup). Finally, validated cross-center executions between Jean Zay and Adastra demonstrate the feasibility of future cross-facility workflow integration.

events.title: Python as the Connective Tissue of the Genesis Mission: From Exascale Workflows to Federated Scientific Agents
events.description: The DOE Genesis Mission aims to couple AI, exascale computing, experimental facilities, and autonomous laboratories into an integrated discovery platform, and much of what holds that platform together is written in Python. Large-scale simulation campaigns, AI training and inference pipelines, workflow orchestration, provenance capture, and multi-agent systems all converge on a shared Python layer that lets scientists compose resources across institutional and facility boundaries. Drawing on experience designing agentic systems for scientific resource discovery and workflow composition, performance studies of workflow execution on leadership-class machines, and a decade of community building around scientific workflows, this talk examines where Python succeeds as the orchestration fabric for AI-coupled science and where it strains, from startup and coordination overheads at scale to environment portability across facilities, concurrency, and the cost of provenance and governance in autonomous loops.

events.title: Deciding whether a generative quantum eigensolver can work before running it
events.description: Generative quantum eigensolvers map naturally onto hybrid quantum-classical HPC systems. Configuring one means choosing an operator pool, a reference state, a circuit depth, and a simulator. With the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model as our testbed, we find that a symmetry calculation constrains all four choices. The pool and reference state fix how much of the state space a circuit can explore. That dimension names the cheapest exact simulator and the shortest circuit expressing a generic target. Exploiting the symmetry, a permutation-symmetric simulator reaches 1000 spins on one GH200 superchip. A companion test, one energy evaluation per pool token, asks whether any token improves on the reference state. Neither the calculation nor the test needs a run or the ground state, and together they explain three campaigns. A third and costlier scan fixes the working depth. Of its two pre-registered predictions, one held and one failed.

events.title: A Locality-Aware Execution Model for Distributed Graph Algorithms using NWGraph and HPX
events.description:
Graph processing at scale presents many challenges, including the irregular structure of graphs, the latency-bound nature of graph algorithms, and the overhead associated with distributed execution. While existing frameworks such as Spark GraphX and the Parallel Boost Graph Library (PBGL) have introduced abstractions for distributed graph processing, they continue to struggle with inherent issues like load imbalance and synchronization overhead.
In this work, we present a distributed library prototype and a distributed implementation of three key graph algorithms-Breadth-First Search (BFS), PageRank, and Triangle Counting, using C++ mechanisms from the NWGraph library and leveraging HPX's distributed containers and asynchronous constructs.
We evaluate our HPX-based implementations against GraphX and PBGL, showing that a high-performance runtime such as HPX enables the construction of algorithms that significantly outperform conventional frameworks by exploiting asynchronous execution, latency hiding, and fine-grained parallelism in shared memory.

events.title: PULSE: Parallel Uncertainty-guided Landscape Sampling Engine for In-Situ Molecular Dynamics
events.description: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations generate massive streams of high-dimensional data. However, biologically significant events are rare, transient, and not known ahead of time. Modern MD workflows execute many trajectories concurrently, but most adaptive sampling methods analyze trajectories in offline batches, delaying feedback and wasting computational resources on redundant exploration. We present PULSE, a scalable in-situ framework that closes the feedback loop between simulation and analysis through a synchronized producer-consumer runtime. PULSE performs online conformational state identification, detects previously unexplained regions of the conformational landscape, and adaptively redirects computational effort toward these regions during execution. We evaluate PULSE on two protein systems, Villin Headpiece and beta-lactoglobulin. Compared to conventional adaptive sampling, PULSE drives 70.77% and 37.17% of newly sampled conformations, respectively, into regions that the baseline never explored. We demonstrate end-to-end execution on eight GPUs and show that PULSE maintains nearly constant coordination overhead across concurrency levels up to 32 trajectories.

events.title: BlueField Assisted Resiliency Framework
events.description:
Efficient checkpoint/restart mechanisms are critical for high-performance computing systems, where long-running applications must quickly recover from failures to maintain productivity and resource efficiency. However, all current checkpoint/restart mechanisms rely on the host CPU, introducing cache contention and operating-system jitter. To address this issue, we present a BlueField-Assisted Resiliency Framework, AURORA: Accelerated User-space Remote Offload for Resilient Applications.
Unlike traditional methods that consume significant CPU resources, SmartNIC-assisted checkpoint/restart offloads IO-bound processes to the SmartNIC, allowing truly parallel operation between the host and its recovery mechanism. Through experimental microbenchmarks, we show that AURORA dramatically reduces host overhead, unlocking up to 10% faster runtimes for CPU-bound HPC workloads when compared to traditional host-based mechanisms.

events.title: DMSim: Configurable Data Management Simulation Framework for Scientific Computing Grid
events.description: Modern computing-grid simulators often emphasize system configuration and job allocation while simplifying data-management behavior, despite its stateful impact on performance. In data-centric infrastructures such as the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG), replica placement and transfer policies influence network contention, staging delay, storage utilization, and resiliency, yet production-scale evaluation is difficult. We present DMSim, a configurable data-management simulation framework for scientific computing grids. DMSim extends CGSim with a lightweight global file-system manager and SimGrid-based communication modeling to track replicas, simulate contention-aware transfers, and support configurable policies. It models reactive transfers triggered by job inputs, proactive background replication and rebalancing, and explicit drop-in transfers for irregular behaviors. We validate DMSim using historical PanDA and Rucio records, reconstructing initial file locations and comparing simulated transfer-queue times with production observations. Simulated staging times fall above bandwidth-based lower bounds and below observed job queuing times, supporting reproducible policy evaluation at scale in controlled experimental settings.

events.title: Stabilizing Autoregressive PDE Foundation Model Rollouts with Event-Triggered Context Healing
events.description: Autoregressive PDE foundation models enable fast full-field forecasting but accumulate errors as predicted states are recursively reused. We introduce Event-Triggered Context Healing (ETCH), which compares forecasts with measurements from 12 cylinder-surface pressure taps. When their discrepancy exceeds a threshold, pressure-conditioned hourglass diffusion transformers reconstruct the velocity--pressure context for subsequent predictions. On 43 RealPDEBench Cylinder trajectories, ETCH reduces velocity and pressure errors from 48.05 and 63.71% to 6.29 and 7.25% for DPOT, and from 74.97 and 76.91% to 5.16 and 6.84% for Poseidon-T, using the same reconstructors and threshold. For DPOT, correcting 14.56% of windows maintains errors close to reconstructing every window and supports average real-time forecasting and correction on an A100 GPU. These results show that sparse physical feedback stabilizes long autoregressive rollouts across PDE foundation models while reducing reconstruction cost.

events.title: Variation-Aware Non-Uniform Node Power Capping for Exascale HPC Systems
events.description:
Exascale systems such as Aurora operate under stringent power and thermal constraints, yet their nominally identical nodes exhibit substantial performance-per-watt variation due to manufacturing, aging, and thermal differences. Under uniform node power caps, this variation slows the critical-path node in tightly coupled applications and reduces the effectiveness
of a fixed job-level power budget. We present a variation-aware, non-uniform node power allocation method for Aurora that (i) characterizes the power–performance response of individual nodes using a large-scale RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) power sweep, (ii) represents the characterization using either a quadratic or a piecewise-linear model, and (iii) uses the selected model to compute non-uniform per-node power caps under a fixed job-level power budget. Using measured Nekbone experiments at approximately 512 nodes and 8,210 nodes, non-uniform allocation improves normalized application performance by up to 7.5% at moderate scale and 6.8% at 8,210 nodes compared with matched uniform node power capping.

events.title: The Price of a Single Source: Performance Portability of Chapel and Julia across CPUs and GPUs
events.description: Developing high-performance computing codes is challenging: exploiting modern hardware requires reasoning about architectural detail, and heterogeneity makes this harder still. Even portability frameworks leave much of a code specialised: across five C++ implementations of the same mini-application, only 16% of the source is shared by all backends. Languages such as Chapel/Julia promise a single-source approach, targeting CPUs and GPUs from multiple vendors while trading some control for productivity and portability. We implement BabelStream, CloverLeaf and TeaLeaf in Chapel and Julia, and compare them against CUDA, HIP and OpenMP C++ baselines across diverse hardware using the Pennycook performance-portability metric. Across three GPU platforms, CloverLeaf achieves P=89% (Julia) and 86% (Chapel); on TeaLeaf the ordering inverts, falling to 77% (Chapel) and 62% (Julia). Both languages need 45-64\% fewer lines of code, and where the C++ backends diverge by 0.63 on average, Chapel and Julia share almost all source between CPU and GPU.

events.title: MailRail: Mitigating Incast Congestion with User-space, Node-based Flow Control
events.description: Irregular workloads, such as those stemming from Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, frequently induce severe incast congestion in large-scale parallel environments. Existing fabric-level congestion control mechanisms rely on reactive, link-level rate limiting that degrades overall throughput. While receiver-driven, credit-based flow control offers a proactive alternative, scaling process counts reduces memory slots per rank below usable thresholds, rendering traditional rank-based accounting untenable. To address this challenge, we introduce MailRail, an out-of-order, asynchronous messaging framework, along with a novel user-space, node-based credit flow control system. By shifting credit accounting from individual processes to shared per-node pools, our proactive, fabric-agnostic approach maintains sufficient credit availability even as process density grows, enabling processes to dynamically utilize freed credits without waiting for receiver-side redistribution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that node-based flow control achieves an 1132× speedup over unconstrained execution at an adversarial incast ratio of 4096:1 while adding minimal overhead on uniform workloads.

events.title: Risk-Oriented Contracts for Non-Functional Requirements in Computing-Continuum Workflows
events.description: Continuum workflows move artifacts across edge-cloud heterogeneous resources, exposing them to disclosure, corruption, unauthorized modification, unavailability, and excessive-volume risks. Enforcing the corresponding non-functional requirements (NFRs) introduces energy and execution-time overheads. Here, we present a risk-oriented contract-realization layer (CRL) that represents risk mitigations as mandatory and optional contract clauses, translating them into pipelines of NFR mechanisms. The CRL profiles candidate realizations using empirical execution-time profiles and utilization-based power models. It admits only candidates that satisfy all mandatory clauses and whose estimated energy and makespan remain within the active admission thresholds while maximizing optional-clause coverage. The selected realization provides workflow management systems with artifact-level NFR pipelines, which are materialized as tasks. We evaluate the CRL across four workflow directed acyclic graphs, multiple deployment plans, contract profiles, and heterogeneous continuum resources. For a balanced contract profile, the CRL achieves 84% admitted optional-clause coverage, compared with 67% for a global-uniform policy.

events.title: First-Timers Orientation
events.description:
Feeling overwhelmed by SC? Don't worry, you're not alone. This conference is a massive, incredible experience, and we want to help you make the most of it.

Join our First-Timers Orientation for a stress-free session where you'll hear directly from our General Chair and seasoned conference volunteers. They'll walk you through everything you need to know, including:

- Navigating the conference schedule and finding your way around the venue.
- Understanding the different event types and what they mean.
- Understanding the various registration options.
- Learning valuable tips and tricks to maximize your conference experience.

Bring your questions. Let's get you ready to dive into SC26.
