events.title: Dispatch Granularity in Quantum-HPC ADMM Optimization: Implications for Near-Real-Time Computing
events.description:
Iterative-consensus decomposition enables combinatorial optimization problems exceeding a single quantum processing unit (QPU) by solving coupled block subproblems and
reconciling them at a consensus barrier. We evaluate whether sub-solver quality or execution mode governs performance. Across 880 byte-identical sub-QUBOs of widths 6–13, non-variational digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization (DCQO) and variational QAOA match exact enumeration at widths ≤ 7 under equal per-circuit shot budgets, whereas classical simulated annealing produces materially larger gaps. When routed onto the measured coupling map of the 54-qubit IQM Emerald, DCQO and QAOA circuit depths differ by at most 9% at supported widths. Their principal distinction is dispatch granularity: DCQO requires one circuit per block and permits round-level batching, whereas QAOA requires 25 sequential circuit evaluations per block in our execution model. Thus, for near-real-time hybrid optimization, execution-mode selection matters more than sub-solver choice.

events.title: TMD - A Label-Free, Misalignment-Robust Distance for HPC Attack Detection
events.description: In this paper, we present the Temporal Mahalanobis Distance (TMD), a distortion-robust, label-free distance for attack detection in HPC networks. The telemetry from the distributed facility components in HPC ecosystem is temporally misaligned, since the components differ in sampling rate, in when an attack reaches them, and in sample ordering. Additionally, the operational monitoring is label-scarce. TMD makes the Mahalanobis distance separation-aware by scaling spatial deviations against the timestamp separation. TMD is a general distortion-robust distance, and we found it most valuable in the HPC regime, where the discriminative signal is the cross-node structure. TMD sustains the attack-normal separability under the offset and the ordering distortion, where Euclidean and DTW perform near chance. We lift TMD into a Sinkhorn distance, namely, TMSD, which helps under severe misalignment. As another contribution, we build a just-in-time streaming detector on a calibrated, semi-supervised TMD head that scores each window in sub-millisecond time.

events.title: Decay-Driven Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Preference-Aware Power Control in HPC
events.description: Energy efficiency is a fundamental constraint in HPC systems, where electricity costs rival hardware costs and power budgets limit deployable performance. RL suits runtime power control, but online training is impractical in production, and offline RL needs a separate agent per operating point since preference weights are fixed beforehand. We present DDMORL, a Decay-Driven Multi-Objective RL framework for single-node energy management that exposes one application- and hardware-agnostic control: a user-specified scalar acceptable performance decay δ ∈ [0,1]. A lightweight, application-specific progress-to-power-cap model generates preference-aligned signals from this target, removing the need for learned interpolators or per-point agents, while letting the offline-trained policy control power live via Intel's RAPL. We evaluate DDMORL on compute- and memory-bound HPC benchmarks, showing decay levels map reliably to power caps delivering substantial energy savings within the requested degradation limit; the approach is application- and hardware-agnostic and generalizes to other nodes for production deployment.

events.title: Toward OpenSHMEM 2.0: Separating Memory from Execution in PGAS
events.description: OpenSHMEM and the wider Partitioned Global Address Space (PGAS) family were built for homogeneous, CPU-centric machines, and they rest on one design choice that modern hardware has outgrown. The agent that issues, orders, and completes communication, which we call the \term{executor}, is bound to the process (the PE) that owns symmetric memory, so that by default one PE is one executor. On a CPU node this costs nothing. On a heterogeneous node, where one process drives many CPU threads, GPU streams, and thousands of GPU blocks, it becomes the central obstacle. We argue that OpenSHMEM 2.0 turns on one decision: \term{split the executor from the process}. Within each executor the model attempts to stay OpenSHMEM 1.x, so a single-executor process is exactly a classic PE and existing programs keep working. This position paper makes the case; it offers no API and no measurements.

events.title: Utilizing Deep Learning-Based Video Frame Interpolation for Scientific Visualization
events.description: Scientific visualization workflows must balance visual fidelity against the storage and I/O costs of large image databases. We investigate deep learning-based Video Frame Interpolation (VFI) to reduce these costs by reconstructing omitted visualization images from stored keyframes. We evaluate the FILM and RIFE models on scientific visualization images using perceptual quality metrics and integrate them into the PyCinema analysis framework. Based on these results, we develop a greedy keyframe selection algorithm that stores an image only when it cannot be reconstructed from neighboring keyframes within a user-defined error tolerance. Its reliance on local information enables integration into an in situ ParaView Catalyst workflow. Experiments show that VFI can accurately reconstruct omitted images while substantially reducing the number of frames written to disk, improving the storage efficiency of scientific visualization pipelines.

events.title: A GPU-Accelerated Blocked Adaptive Randomized Range Finder Based on an Implicit Householder QR Decomposition
events.description: Low-rank methods can reduce the memory and computational requirements of deep neural network training in approaches such as GaLore. Randomized range finders offer an attractive alternative to singular value decompositions, particularly when the required rank is determined adaptively from a prescribed approximation tolerance. We introduce a blocked adaptive randomized range finder based on an implicit Householder QR decomposition and an optimized hybrid CPU--GPU implementation. The proposed method avoids explicit reorthogonalization. Numerical experiments show that it preserves orthogonality and approximation accuracy in regimes where block Gram--Schmidt without reorthogonalization becomes unstable. The blocked formulation exposes matrix--matrix operations and enables overlap of CPU panel factorization with GPU updates. On an NVIDIA GH200, the overlapped implementation reduces the runtime for the largest tested matrix from 9.91s on the CPU to 0.407s. The method provides a stable and efficient building block for low-rank approximation on heterogeneous systems with applications in computational science and engineering.

events.title: AMAI: Algebraic Modelling of Distributed AI Computations for Symbolic Performance Analysis
events.description: Developing large-scale AI systems requires extensive on-machine tuning: engineers evaluate hundreds of parallel configurations by trial and error, at considerable cost in accelerator rental and compute time. Existing performance models are either tied to specific frameworks or too coarse for modern distributed workloads. We present AMAI, a performance analysis framework featuring (i) a declarative domain-specific language for describing distributed deep-learning computations, and (ii) compositional cost semantics that map programs into symbolic models of time and per-device memory. Models are parameterized by hardware constants and structural variables that define the parallelism configuration. As a result, descriptions can be analyzed at any scale and reused across machines. Predictions stay within 3 percent of measured step time and peak memory across batch-size and data-parallel scaling when analyzing the training of Qwen3.5 0.8B on a multi-node NPU cluster.

events.title: ShardTensor: Democratizing Domain Parallelism for Scientific Machine Learning
events.description:
Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) faces unique challenges for extreme-resolution
data, with mitigations that often fail to scale or degrade the accuracy of
trained models. Some specialized methods have achieved remarkable
results in training models or performing inference on massive spatial datasets
with bespoke techniques, but each is a model-specific effort; there is no general
framework that makes domain parallelism accessible to SciML practitioners at large.
We introduce
\texttt{ShardTensor}, a PyTorch-native abstraction that brings domain
parallelism into the standard training and inference workloads the way DDP brought
data parallelism: non-invasively, without model changes, and composable with
existing data- and model-parallel techniques.
We describe the dispatch design that makes this possible, and show on
benchmarks and production applications that unmodified models train beyond
single-GPU memory, scale near-linearly at large input sizes, and run faster
inference on high-resolution data.

events.title: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models on R&E Backbone Telemetry
events.description: Research and Education (R&E) backbone networks support the transfer of petabyte-scale scientific data under stringent timing constraints. However, their operational monitoring remains predominantly reactive, relying on threshold-based alerts and visualization dashboards that provide. limited predictive capabilities and cannot anticipate congestion or anomalous events hours in advance. Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), large neural networks pre-trained on billions of diverse time series, offer a promising route to predictive monitoring, but their adaptation behavior on live R&E backbone telemetry remains poorly characterized. We present a systematic multi-task benchmark of five TSFMs (TimesFM, Moirai, Chronos, PatchTST, and TTM/Granite) across four adaptation strategies and four auto-labeled operational tasks (48-hour utilization trajectory, threshold exceedance detection, peak-timing estimation, and traffic asymmetry forecasting), using 26 months of SNMP telemetry from the AmLight backbone with no human annotation. Our results show that TSFM performance is task-structured: zero-shot models outperform classical baselines on trajectory and timing tasks, where broad pre-training captures diurnal patterns, but do not surpass classical methods on tasks that reward high autocorrelation exploitation. Standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting in some architectures. Linear-probe fine-tuning avoids forgetting but introduces a subtler failure: auto-labels designed for one task do not transfer to others, so performance improves only where the label aligns with the target. This label-task mismatch is the central failure mode we identify and characterize. The unifying solution is a frozen backbone with a small, task-specific MLP head trained on the correct auto-label for each objective. With at most 500 auto-labeled windows, this approach surpasses all fine-tuned models on exceedance detection and matches fine-tuning on peak-timing estimation. These results establish that pre-trained TSFM backbones already encode operationally relevant network representations, and that a frozen backbone with a lightweight task head can be a viable foundation for predictive operations on R&E networks.

events.title: Efficient cosmological friends-of-friends computation with fine-grained optimizations
events.description: One computationally intensive part of cosmological simulations is identifying clusters. One method to do this is via the friends-of-friends (FoF) algorithm, which is functionally equivalent to finding incremental connected components. Optimizing FoF for large, imbalanced datasets is challenging due to load and communication imbalance. In this paper, we present a parallel approach that integrates a tree traversal library with a union-find library. While this combination provided a foundational framework, we discovered that it fell short of meeting the rigorous performance demands of complex cosmological data. To overcome this, we designed and implemented a series of fine-grained optimizations tailored to the unique memory and processing patterns of the algorithm. We demonstrate that our approach achieves significant performance gains for highly imbalanced outputs without compromising cluster accuracy or quality. Finally, we analyze these results and identify remaining opportunities for further improvement in scalable cluster finding.

events.title: HPC-CARLA: Closed-Loop Evaluation of Autonomous Driving Agents as a Resilient, Schedulable HPC Workload
events.description: Closed-loop evaluation of autonomous-driving policies spans many conditions, but CARLA servers on shared GPU clusters often fail after producing valid episodes. We present HPC-CARLA, which runs these campaigns through a multi-node queue and reuses one simulator service per GPU. It restarts failed services and harvests episode checkpoints independently of job state. Its declarative pipeline framework brings six policies under one audited execution model. Across five agents on A100, HPC-CARLA retained 13,059 valid route evaluations; 94.3% came from jobs that ultimately failed. Three L40S campaigns tested another GPU and driver stack, although score agreement depended on the agent. As A100 coverage expanded, the relationship between an offline difficulty score and driving performance reversed, so the revised dispatcher gives per-agent coverage requirements precedence over that scalar. Together, the campaigns show why workflow state must include simulator health, episode progress, and condition coverage.

events.title: A Distributed HPC/AI Services Ecosystem for the Genesis Mission Platform
events.description: Modern HPC and AI applications require capabilities deployed, composed, and accessed on demand. However, reusable services must coordinate heterogeneous resources, lifecycles, and low-latency data exchange. We present a distributed service ecosystem for the American Science Cloud (AmSC) of the Genesis Mission, providing mechanisms for deploying, composing, and accessing HPC/AI capabilities. Our contribution is a service-building ecosystem for HPC/AI workflows that separates service management, workflow execution, and data exchange, enabling capabilities to be composed without application-specific integration. We demonstrate the approach through an asynchronous OpenFOAM optimization workflow, showing how HPC/AI capabilities become reusable services across AmSC resources.

events.title: Hardware-Aware Compilation of LLM-Generated, QEC-Encoded Quantum Circuits via Constraint-Aware Graph Retrieval
events.description: This paper presents an end-to-end workflow combining a locally hosted LLM for circuit generation, a deterministic stabilizer-code module for QEC encoding, and Constraint-Aware Hardware Graph Retrieval for identifying suitable connected hardware regions. We evaluate six compilation strategies across 720 method–configuration combinations, covering six IBM calibration snapshots, five three-qubit circuit families, and four optimization objectives. Compared with unoptimized raw mapping, the multi-candidate hardware_aware strategy reduces mean circuit depth from 956 to 468 and two-qubit gate count from 657 to 268. Compared with full-device Sabre, improvements are smaller, reducing depth from 488 to 468 and two-qubit gates from 281 to 268. Greedy CAHGR alone underperforms conventional baselines, demonstrating that calibration-aware region selection must be combined with effective placement and routing. Conclusions are limited to compilation efficiency because execution quality uses a no-fault proxy rather than logical fidelity or hardware execution.

events.title: Domain-Aware Power Rebalancing under Node-Level Power Caps on Aurora
events.description:
Node-level power capping is a scalable mechanism for enforcing electrical, thermal, and scheduling constraints on exascale systems. On a heterogeneous node, however, a single
cap hides a second decision: how platform firmware distributes the constrained budget among GPUs, CPU cores, memory, and the CPU uncore. This paper characterizes the hidden allocation
on the Aurora supercomputer. More importantly, under constrained node caps, firmware can keep the CPU uncore near its minimum even when application progress depends on data movement, increasing runtime enough to raise total board energy. We introduce U-PullUp, a lightweight GEOPM agent that uses recent GPU copy-engine activity as a data-movement signal and requests a higher uncore frequency while leaving the node cap active. Across the nine SPEChpc workloads, U-PullUp reduces board energy by up to 34.2% relative to default power control at the same cap, while the best configuration for each workload reduces energy by 19.6% on average.

events.title: Performance Improvement of Multi-Dimensional Parallel Loops in Kokkos
events.description: This paper presents performance improvements for tightly nested multi-dimensional parallelism in the Kokkos library. We show how this can be implemented for GPU and CPU backends, which leads to improved performance and code maintainability. A widely used library like Kokkos needs to be updated in a manner that is friendly to the users and the developers. Using various benchmarks, we show how our work enables Kokkos users to write performance-portable code in a productive manner.

events.title: Quantifying Workload Exposure in HPC Power Telemetry at Operational Sampling Rates
events.description: HPC centers publish power telemetry to support monitoring, scheduling, and optimization. While this telemetry is published for operational use, it can also reveal information about the workloads on a system. Prior work shows workloads leave signatures in high-frequency telemetry. How much of that signature survives at the coarse rates used in production is unknown. We study workloads using CPU power telemetry from Intel RAPL at approximately 1 kHz, downsampled to intervals as coarse as 60 s, measuring recoverability for resource classes and for individual workloads on unseen problem sizes. Recoverability declines as sampling coarsens, from 0.87 to 0.71 for resource class and 0.74 to 0.54 for workload identity. In short jobs, temporal information distinguishing individual workloads disappears under coarse sampling, while the steady power composition remains. At coarse rates, distinct workloads remain identifiable while similar ones become indistinguishable. Thus, coarsening the sampling rate is a practical but incomplete privacy control.

events.title: An In Situ Computational-learning Framework for the Simulation of the Cardiac Electrical System of a Patient-specific Human Heart
events.description:
Cardiac arrhythmias are associated with abnormal
propagation of electrical activity through the heart. High-
resolution simulations can capture these dynamics but generate
large data volumes that are expensive to store and transfer. Fixed
output intervals may save redundant states while undersampling
periods of rapid electrical propagation. We propose an adaptive
in situ workflow that learns when simulation states should be
retained. An offline teacher identifies informative voltage states,
and a lightweight causal neural network is embedded directly in
the parallel simulation to make runtime output decisions. The
selected nonuniform data are then used to train a continuous-time
neural operator. Compared with uniform temporal sampling, the
adaptive strategy stores fewer states while improving prediction
accuracy on unseen simulations. The results demonstrate an in
situ connection between high-performance cardiac simulation and
neural operator learning.

events.title: Saving Energy Costs and Time on Supercomputers: Scheduler-Integrated Recurring Node Shutdown Exploiting Malleable Jobs
events.description: Supercomputers consume electricity around the clock, yet photovoltaic generation can make power cheaper and cleaner by day than at night. Thus, shutting down idle nodes overnight could reduce energy cost but risks longer job waiting times. This paper studies scheduler-integrated shutdown policies that proactively power down a share of the nodes during recurring off periods, such as nights. To compensate, we exploit malleable jobs, which the scheduler shrinks before shutdowns to release nodes and expands afterward. In 270 simulations on job sets from three production supercomputers, we evaluate shutdown shares up to 30% under rigid and malleable scheduling with varying fractions of malleable jobs. Shutting down 30% of the nodes benefits both operators and users once 25% of the jobs are malleable. Compared with rigid scheduling without shutdown, operators save up to 12.5% of the daily electricity cost and users up to 56.2% of their job turnaround time.

events.title: Who Benefits from Federation? Heterogeneous Gains in Cross-Operator Network Traffic Representation Learning
events.description: Research and education networks, regional ISPs, and campus networks hold telemetry worth modeling jointly, but non-disclosure agreements and privacy policy prevent pooling it. We evaluate federated representation learning on real telemetry from ten Internet2 backbone routers and ten CESNET3 academic institutions, with a commercial ISP held out as an unseen-network probe, comparing centralized, federated, and local-only training at equal budget across five seeds. Federation is statistically equivalent to centralized pooling (5% equivalence bound, p = 0.020), so the data-custody constraint costs nothing in representation quality. Its benefit is not uniform: backbone clients gain a median 9.2% reduction in reconstruction error, campus clients 1.9% (p = 0.0003), an effect robust to outlier removal and training-set size that tracks a difference in traffic regularity we characterize but do not isolate. Two manipulations of local optimization selectively suppress the backbone benefit, identifying local adaptation as the mechanism.

events.title: Distributed Sparse P-bit Ising Machines for CPU Clusters
events.description:
Ising computing is a novel paradigm for combi-
natorial optimizations. Ising machines built from probabilistic
bits (p-bits) update each vertex from a weighted sum over
its graph neighbors forming an inherently irregular workload.
Distributing the sampler across Message Passing Interface (MPI)
processes or ranks lets each rank update its own p-bits while
restricting communication to halo p-bits. We characterize this
trade-off on 12 MAX-CUT instances using the GPI-2 one-
sided communication at 2-8 processes, sweeping synchronization
frequency and comparing two primary samplers for the first
time: Stochastic Simulated Annealing (SSA) and Probabilistic bit
Simulated Annealing (PSA). Poorly partitioned graphs can see
a speedup upto 53x from relaxed synchronization. The quality
cost, however, is set by density rather than halo/owned ratio.
Sparse graphs lose under 1% even at high halo ratios, while
dense instances lose 8.6%. PSA yields better solutions in 83% of
configurations whereas SSA runs up to 3.4× faster.

events.title: Scaling a Heterogeneous Metagenomics Workflow to 100,000 Samples with Nextflow on HPC
events.description: Running large-scale and heterogeneous metagenomics workflows is challenging not only because of CPU resources needed but also because of high requirements for storage and memory. We present GutMap, a thirteen-step Nextflow workflow that processes over 100{,}000 human gut metagenomes with a total size of 189~TB. We report the results of running GutMap on the Helios supercomputer using almost 1.5~million CPU-hours, describe memory-related optimisations and solutions to storage limitations and provide a detailed account of the resource profile of the workflow.

events.title: Panel: "Is Explicit Communication Obsolete? Compilers, Runtimes and On What Matters Next"
events.description:
As domain-specific accelerators gain importance and workloads increasingly exhibit structured, predictable communication patterns—particularly in machine learning, scientific computing, and tensor operations—the role of explicit communication primitives deserves renewed scrutiny. This panel examines whether the compiler and runtime stack should bear greater responsibility for inferring and optimizing communication, potentially relegating explicit APIs to legacy status.

The rise of Tile IRs and polyhedral compilation frameworks suggests a future where communication becomes an emergent property of program structure rather than a programmer directive. When tiling strategies, data dependencies, and memory hierarchies can be analyzed statically or just-in-time, do we still need developers to manually orchestrate point-to-point sends, broadcasts, and reductions? Or does the irregularity and dynamism of real applications—adaptive meshes, sparse data, load imbalance—ensure that explicit control remains essential?

This discussion will explore the tension between programmer productivity and performance portability, examining where today's compilation technology succeeds in hiding communication complexity and where it fails.

Panelists will debate whether the next decade belongs to smarter runtimes that auto-parallelize and auto-communicate, or whether the most demanding applications will always require the fine-grained control that only explicit communication provides.

events.title: Python-Based Distributed Training on AMD GPU Supercomputers: Lessons from Data, Pipeline, and Tensor Parallelism on LUMI
events.description: The growing computational demands of foundation AI models have made distributed training essential on modern supercomputers. This work presents an empirical study of data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism for Vision Transformer training on the LUMI supercomputer, an AMD GPU-based leadership-class HPC system. Using Python-based frameworks including PyTorch, FairScale, TensorFlow DTensor, and Colossal-AI within containerized ROCm environments, we evaluate framework compatibility, portability, implementation complexity, and reproducibility. Our findings show that software ecosystem readiness significantly impacts scalable AI training. PyTorch DDP and TensorFlow DTensor demonstrate reliable execution, while several CUDA-dependent approaches face deployment challenges on AMD architectures.

events.title: Gradient-Free Optimization of Quantum Circuits Parameters for Hybrid Machine Learning
events.description: Quantum Machine Learning generally aims to build more accurate models by using quantum mechanical principles to better capture complex correlation across data features. Existing methods scale poorly with the number of both data samples and features, making them very challenging to train on real quantum devices beyond trivial datasets. We introduce a new hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for supervised classification, which uses gradient-free optimization to learn the quantum circuit parameters and builds the final classical model from the quantum circuits measurements. We experiment over a variety of datasets and show that this algorithm performs better than standard Quantum ML algorithms in most cases, while being more scalable to larger datasets and fully trainable on current quantum devices.

events.title: Scalable AMG Preconditioning for DG Neutron Diffusion Solvers on Manycore CPUs
events.description: Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretizations of diffusion-type operators, including neutron transport, produce sparse systems that bottleneck simulation throughput. Standard incomplete LU (ILU) preconditioners exhibit O(h−1 ) iteration growth and prohibitive fill-in. This work presents a Smoothed Aggregation Algebraic Multigrid (SA-AMG) preconditioner for 3D DG systems, implemented via Trilinos/MueLu and Kokkos, demonstrating O(1) mesh-independent convergence on the Takeda Benchmark Model 1 up to 7.1e6 unknowns, yielding a 158× speedup over ILU. A strong scaling and roofline analysis across three manycore topologies — Intel Sapphire Rapids, AMD Genoa, and NVIDIA Grace — shows all solver phases memory-bound. On both dual-socket nodes, scalability regresses or halts at the socket boundary due to inter-NUMA traffic in the fine-grid solve, while the single-socket Grace platform sustains its efficiency and achieves the lowest time-to-solution despite fewer cores. These results identify memory topology, rather than core count, as the dominant scalability factor for heterogeneous reactor transport calculations.

events.title: SemQBench: Benchmarking Decomposition-Aware Runtime Policies for Quantum-HPC Search
events.description: Quantum processors increasingly act as accelerators in HPC workflows, where the runtime schedules the work. Many search problems split into independent parts, but the runtime can exploit this only if the workflow exposes those parts and a per-part validity check. SemQBench compares seven execution policies on the 20-qubit IQM Garnet processor, varying one choice at a time: whether to amplify, whether partial results combine across runs, and what a retry keeps. Amplifying the whole problem gives no clear gain over random sampling at 6.7-104x more device time. Collecting valid partial results across a batch cuts executions for 95% confidence by 2.20-4.00x and wins in 99/108 overhead settings. Fewer executions need not mean less device time: one workload drops from thirteen executions to four as device time rises from 7.44-9.81 μs. Exposed structure gives the runtime a strong default and the evidence to drop it when it does not pay.

events.title: A Distribution-Function GNN Surrogate for Lattice Boltzmann Flows: Adaptive Coarsening Is Where the Speedup Comes From
events.description: We evaluate a graph-network surrogate for two-dimensional lattice Boltzmann(LBM) flows on both accuracy and wall-clock time per case. The model predicts the increment of the velocity distribution function and reconstructs velocity and density from the LBM definitions; a 49-step rollout (9800 solver steps) completes without diverging. Adding the distribution function to the inputs cuts the velocity error by 20-46%. Static coarsening by variable-radius Poisson-disk selection from geometry alone cuts the node count 22.6-fold while accuracy on the evaluation grid stays on par with the uniform mesh, and cuts the time per case tenfold to 8.9 times faster than the reference solver. On the uniform mesh it is only on par, so the advantage appears solely under coarsening. Against a coarse-grid solver at the same obstacle Reynolds number the surrogate offers robustness, not speed: it returns a solution on all 48 cases, the solver on 42.

events.title: The Self-Driving Fusion Workflow: A Vision for Automated Scientific Discovery
events.description: Simulation-driven fusion research requires scientists to coordinate a complex sequence of activities, including application configuration, workflow composition, execution, data movement, and analysis. Although tools exist for individual stages, integrating them into a portable and automated end-to-end workflow remains difficult, particularly across heterogeneous leadership computing facilities. We present a vision for an AI agent-driven workflow framework that enables scientists to describe research objectives and constraints through a natural-language interface rather than manually orchestrating individual tasks. A composition layer translates this intent into an executable workflow assembled from a registry of containerized fusion applications and machine-readable application descriptions. Agent decisions are grounded in a curated knowledge vault of verified configurations and gated by declarative correctness hooks evaluated before, during, and after execution. The framework combines adaptive execution, application coupling, scientific data management, compression and reduction, in situ analysis and visualization, and campaign management into a cohesive ecosystem for executing end-to-end science workflows.

events.title: Agentic-ready data management workflow for material science
events.description:
Material science increasingly integrates experimental,
computational, and literature-derived evidence resulting in data
that are potentially incomplete or inconsistent; and that are
fragmented across instruments, notebooks, file systems, simulations,
and publications. This data fragmentation hinders the
promise of using large language model (LLM)-driven agentic
workflows to reason across natural-language, tabular, textual,
and image-based data with limited human intervention. To
close this gap, we present a methodology spanning domain
characterization and schematization, data inventory, integrated
data management via a lakehouse architecture, and automated
dataset enhancement for agentic interpretation. Our solution
enables an automated data workflow pipeline that can leverage
specific agentic data skills, semantically find correspondence
in the domain schema (generated), generated relevant queries
(with validation mechanism) for entries into data-lakehouse and
aggregate relevant data for a specific task/analysis We demonstrate
its value by comparing the potential of an agentic-ready dataset
vs. a “vanilla” baseline.

events.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Scientific Workflow Maintenance
events.description: AI coding agents could help maintain scientific workflows, but a repair that executes successfully may still duplicate calculations, compromise provenance, or change the scientific meaning of a result. We propose evaluating such repairs through the scientific and operational properties they must preserve. A pilot implementation explores this idea through twelve compact software maintenance tasks, with examples spanning safe recovery, portable analysis records, and scientific post-processing. Separate exploratory experiments provide preliminary motivation: some repairs passed all functional-component checks while failing scientific or robustness checks, and agents sometimes claimed completion despite failing independent assessment. These observations support distinguishing basic functionality from evidence of reliable workflow maintenance. They do not establish comprehensive task coverage or readiness for production use. We invite discussion of which properties should underpin such evaluations, whether component-level performance predicts reliability in integrated workflows, and how human oversight and computational cost should shape decisions about agent autonomy.

events.title: Collecting Infrastructure-Level Measures for Energy Analysis in Modern Computing Infrastructures
events.description:
Modern HPC facilities are complex environments in which all components are tightly coupled; consequently, precisely modeling and accounting for energy consumption requires approaches that go beyond instrumenting individual compute nodes.
Aiming for a cluster-wide vision, we designed a scalable data collection pipeline that aggregates fine-grained measurements from multiple subsystems—spanning component loads, software and hardware counters, sensors and energy—ensuring consistent sampling frequencies and synchronized data acquisition across the infrastructure.
We present a dataset of comprehensive metrics collected at 1 Hz over one month from a production research data center supporting heterogeneous workloads, including HPC, Kubernetes services, and distributed storage.
To illustrate what this approach makes possible in practice, we analyze two case studies—distributed I/O and large-language-model inference—showing how cluster-wide measurement reveals system-level dynamics missed by localized instrumentation.
The proposed dataset and collection methodology provide a foundation for future work on predictive modeling, energy-aware resource management, and more efficient computing infrastructures.

events.title: Graph500 Announcement
Using Persistent Digital Twins as Spatial Environments for Robotics Simulation and Deployment
events.description:
Deploying autonomous robots into new industrial sites requires their simulation and control software to understand the environment in which they will operate. This can create duplicated engineering effort between environments prepared for robotics simulation and 3D representations of physical sites already maintained for operational applications.

In an ongoing industrial robotics project, we are exploring whether a persistent 3D digital twin can serve as a reusable spatial environment for an external robotics simulator, with the objective of reducing the time and engineering effort required to deploy autonomous robots on new customer sites.

The robotics company maintains its own simulation, perception, navigation, and control stack. Through a bidirectional interface, robot poses are sent to the 3D environment, virtual sensor viewpoints are updated, and depth information is returned to the robotics simulator. Users can simultaneously visualize the simulation within the customer site and issue commands back to the simulated robot.

Using an API-driven, web-based architecture, the two independent systems were integrated in only a few weeks. This Community Talk will share this early industrial implementation and discuss practical questions around real-time coupling, sensor feedback, latency, and the potential for persistent digital twins to become shared spatial infrastructure across simulation and operational applications.

events.title: Towards Distributed-Memory All-Pairs Reachability over Homomorphically Encrypted Graphs
events.description:
Transitive closure determines reachability between all pairs of vertices
in a directed graph. For encrypted graphs, this computation requires
many expensive ciphertext operations. This makes single-node execution
slow even for small matrices.

We implement transitive closure (all-pairs reachability) for BGV-encrypted graphs on distributed memory systems. The implementation stores matrix rows and columns in
separate ciphertexts. Each output entry is computed from one row
ciphertext and one column ciphertext. We distribute these computations
over a two-dimensional MPI process grid. The output remains distributed
and is reused in the next transitive-closure step.

We evaluate the implementation with up to 1,024 MPI ranks and compare
against a single-node baseline with 32 OpenMP threads. At N=16, the
distributed implementation achieves a 5.66 times speedup over the
single-node baseline.

events.title: Guest Panel Talk: From Facility Endpoints to Portable Experiments
Mojo-Driven Performance Portability for LBM
events.description:
Lattice-Boltzmann methods (LBM) have emerged as a prominent approach for simulating fluid dynamics, owing to their inherent parallelism and suitability for high-performance computing on both multicore CPUs and GPUs.
In this study, we investigate Mojo, a low-level framework designed to bridge Pythonic programming with high-performance computing, and compare its performance portability against established parallel programming frameworks such as CUDA, HIP, and SYCL using lid-driven cavity simulations.
Our results show that template metaprogramming in Mojo enables high-performance portability without requiring manual loop unrolling.
Compared with FluidX3D, Mojo achieves application efficiencies above 80% across GPUs, although its performance is lower on CPUs, resulting in a 0.59 performance portability score for D3Q19-fp32 across all evaluated architectures, programming models and optimisations.
These results highlight Mojo's potential as a productive and efficient programming model for heterogeneous computing, but also suggest room for improvement on CPU platforms.

events.title: Research Infrastructure as enabler of New Scientific Research
events.description: While much scientific research is possible using traditional mechanisms (such as paper and pencil), research infrastructures play an important role in enabling new scientific research that's not possible otherwise. This talk will cover this aspect, with a bend towards data-intensive science through networking and distributed systems research infrastructures.

events.title: Panel Discussion: Navigating the Future of Scientific Workflows
Beyond FLOPS and Kernels: Benchmarking Agentic Science and the Future Role of Python
events.description:
Python has become the dominant language for scientific computing, AI, and high-performance computing workflows. As supercomputing enters an era increasingly shaped by foundation models, autonomous agents, and AI-guided scientific discovery, the community faces a fundamental question: what should we benchmark next?

This panel brings together leaders from HPC, AI, and scientific software to discuss how benchmarks can continue to influence system architecture in the age of agentic workflows. Should future benchmarks measure isolated kernels and application performance, or end-to-end scientific outcomes? How do we evaluate systems that combine simulation, machine learning, retrieval, reasoning, and autonomous decision-making? And what role should Python play as the orchestration layer for increasingly heterogeneous and distributed computing environments? Panelists will explore whether Python can serve as the foundation for next-generation benchmarks and how benchmark design can guide the architecture of future AI-enabled supercomputers.

events.title: Special Session - Research priorities and opportunities on integration of Q-HPC
N-VEG: 3D Gaussian Encoding for Neural Volume Compression
events.description: Research in Implicit Neural Representations has led to new lines of compression methods for large 3D volumetric data, offering aggressive compression ratios and direct data lookup without decompression. While these methods perform well at compression, they struggle to learn high-frequency information; though this is addressable by a variety of encoding methods, they add significant memory overhead, hampering compression goals. Other methods inspired by novel view synthesis attempt to model volumes explicitly with primitives, e.g. 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. In this work, we present a hybrid approach to volume compression that learns in-tandem a 3D Gaussian reconstruction and Neural representation of the input scene. We treat the 3D gaussians as an encoder for a small neural network, with latent feature vectors attached to each primitive. When sampling the volume, spatial locations are weighted by overlapping gaussians; feature vectors are then interpolated, harmonically activated, summed, and decoded by an MLP. Here, the 3D Gaussian encoder is a lagrangian alternative to global encoding structures, like hash grids, allowing the INR to be detail-aware when learning its encoding. This strategy achieves greater reconstruction quality than primitive-only reconstruction methods, while retaining fast training times and aggressive compression ratios, making it a viable in-situ volume compression technique.

events.title: Exploiting Memory Contiguity in Stencil Applications for Extreme Scalability on Heterogeneous Supercomputers
events.description: Exascale computing requires the development and execution of applications with massive scalability capabilities. Iterative Stencil Loop (ISL) applications are an important class of scientific applications with high scalability potential. EPSILOD is a tool designed to simplify the development and execution of ISL applications in heterogeneous distributed environments. This work proposes and evaluates new techniques in EPSILOD to optimize data communication in distributed ISL applications running on multi-GPU, multi-node systems. Specifically, it explores multidimensional partitioning policies and techniques to optimize MPI communications, including both host-staging and GPU-aware MPI, by automatically creating data contiguity in memory based on the chosen partitioning policy. Experimental results are presented using up to 1,024 NVIDIA GPUs across 256 nodes and up to 8,192 AMD GPUs across 1,024 nodes, showing significant improvements in strong and weak scalability across various scenarios and ISL applications.

events.title: Exploiting the Interplay of Compute- and Memory-Bound kernels in MPI Applications
events.description:
Parallel applications are typically designed for synchronous, lock-step execution, treating communication stalls as performance hazards. Yet, in a communication-light application with infrequent synchronization that alternates between compute-bound and memory-bound phases, an MPI communication stall can unintentionally relieve memory-bandwidth contention.
We demonstrate this using a Parallel Optical Flow Solver combining a compute-bound Ray Tracing kernel with a memory-bound Optical Flow kernel and negligible inter-process communication. Natural desynchronization and overlap between the two phases yield substantial speedup, with peak performance when the number of processes concurrently executing the memory-bound phase per ccNUMA domain remains near the memory-bandwidth saturation point. We further show that MPI asynchronous progress can significantly degrade performance by increasing concurrent memory-bandwidth contention. To study the underlying mechanisms, we develop a tunable dual-kernel microbenchmark, showing that substantial application or system noise is required to achieve full desynchronization. Finally, we validate these findings with a bandwidth-aware, model-based simulator.

events.title: On Multimodal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture models for Tokamak Plasma Dynamics
events.description: Experimental tokamak diagnostics are multimodal, heterogeneous, and sparsely sampled across discharges, making reusable pretrained representations valuable for plasma modeling. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn predictive latent representations without reconstructing every modality. We adopt TokaMark, a 14-task benchmark built from 11,573 MAST discharges, and introduce Tokamak JEPA (T-JEPA), a multimodal adaptation of V-JEPA~2.1 coupling a spatial poloidal magnetic-flux representation with six diagnostic encoders through bidirectional cross-attention. Across frozen, partial, and full adaptation, T-JEPA shows selective transfer, with frozen representations competitive for flux-map and plasma-current prediction. Our task-specific end-to-end models reduce NRMSE by 11.8--22.5\% relative to matched TokaMind FT-Base warm-starts on Groups 1--2, while normalization, actuator conditioning, and effective batch size affect accuracy and stability. Controlled studies show limited warm-start benefits and greater reliability when explicit coefficient targets are retained. Overall, task-specific optimization remains strongest for peak accuracy, while T-JEPA provides a basis for reusable multimodal representations across tokamak diagnostics.

events.title: Energy-Aware Performance Characterization of Kokkos Kernels Across Precision Levels
events.description:
Kokkos is a performance-portable programming model used in GPU-accelerated HPC applications comprising kernels with diverse computational and memory behaviors. We characterize kernels from two applications to evaluate how FP32, FP64, and mixed FP32/FP64 affect arithmetic intensity, performance throughput, and GPU energy consumption. We introduce an Energy-Aware Roofline Model that incorporates energy into performance analysis and a Thermal-Aware Inter-Kernel Energy Model that visualizes energy consumption alongside duration, GPU temperature, and execution order.
We study both applications with: (1) fine-grained, application-level instrumentation through the Kokkos Performance Tools PAPI Connector and (2) coarse-grained PAPI instrumentation applied to a dedicated-kernel benchmark using vendor-specific power management components.
Our analysis shows that precision effects vary by application, kernel, and workload. Mixed FP32/FP64 kernels generally achieve arithmetic intensity comparable to FP32, with modestly lower throughput and, in most cases, a modest increase in energy consumption. FP64 kernels generally exhibit the highest energy consumption among the evaluated precisions.

events.title: IA^3 Debate
Panel Discussion and Q&A: Challenges in AI-enabled Q-HPC Integration
An Integrated In-Situ Visualization Framework for Interactive Analysis and Surrogate Modeling
events.description: Image-based in-situ visualization has become a mature approach that not only helps mitigate notorious I/O bottlenecks, but also facilitates exploratory visual analysis by enabling interactive exploration in the spatiotemporal domain. This approach generates a large collection of visual representations from different viewpoints, and in this work, we extend this approach to surrogate modeling, using the generated visualization images as a common representation that bridges human-centered interactive visual analysis and machine learning. During in-situ visualization, metadata required by existing information-entropy-based smart visualization techniques are also generated. Unlike previous smart in-situ visualization approaches, which try to output only the set of most information-rich rendering images, the proposed framework also outputs the complete set of rendered images for offline surrogate modeling. Our initial results demonstrate the feasibility of training surrogate models directly from the image-based representation generated for visual analysis, enabling learned approximation without requiring the original simulation data.

events.title: HPC Security in the AI Era: Standards, Compliance, and Governance
Towards Direct-to-Chip Liquid-Cooled Megawatt Racks: Characterization of a Multi-Kilowatt Chip-Scale Cooler & The Implications on Facility Energy Use
events.description: The power density of artificial-intelligence (AI) and high-performance-computing (HPC) accelerators continues to increase. Although the HPC community adopted liquid cooling years ago, the broader computing industry is now undergoing a similar transition. With 1, 3, and 5 kW accelerators appearing on technology roadmaps, removing multi-kilowatt chip-level heat loads without excessive facility-cooling energy or hydraulic demand remains a challenge. This study characterizes a liquid-cooled thermal stack and identifies the design parameters needed to support next-generation AI devices. Repeatable steady-state measurements yielded an inlet-referenced thermal resistance of 0.0383 K/W. A reduced-order model separated coolant warming, cold-plate convection, and flow-independent stack resistance. At a 100 °C average heater limit and 5 L/min, the baseline stack dissipated 3.04 kW, while a controlled thin liquid-metal interface increased the projected capacity to 6.41 kW. At 3 kW, this interface reduced the required flow from 4.61 to 0.92 L/min and increased allowable inlet-temperature margin by 40.5 °C.

events.title: Triton Attention Backend: Portable High-Performance Paged Attention for Production-Grade LLM Inference
events.description:
Attention kernels represent the backbone of modern LLMs and are usually the most performance-critical GPU kernels. Today, state-of-the-art LLM inference relies primarily on attention kernels painstakingly hand-optimized for each GPU architecture. This approach delivers strong performance, but it also fragments the software ecosystem and requires substantial, ongoing engineering effort for every new model and hardware platform.

In this work, we present a case study on the performance portability of the paged attention kernel. We describe our platform-agnostic Triton Attention implementation and demonstrate that open-source domain-specific languages can deliver efficient, portable LLM inference across GPU vendors.

Our experimental evaluation shows that our Triton kernel matches the performance of platform-specific kernels on the latest NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and is up to 7x faster than existing portable attention implementations. We further discuss how our kernel improves the flexibility, portability, and developer productivity of vLLM, and share the design principles behind our approach.

events.title: A Distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering Framework for Fugaku and Beyond
events.description: Modern flagship HPC systems increasingly rely on GPU-accelerated architectures. While GPUs accelerate simulations, CPU resources may remain available, providing an opportunity for in-situ processing and visualization. This community talk presents an ongoing effort to develop a distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering (PBVR) framework that exploits this CPU/GPU division. Volumetric fields are converted in situ into compact visualization particles using CPUs on the HPC system, while interactive rendering is performed on a GPU-equipped remote client. We evaluate the approach on Fugaku using OpenFOAM and demonstrate particle generation across up to 2,304 compute nodes (110,592 CPU cores). For a separate 432 x 432 x 432 grid measurement at 576 MPI ranks, PBVR particle files were 98.1% smaller than the uncompressed logical Ux payload over 11 steps. We discuss the implementation, initial performance results, and potential applicability to future heterogeneous HPC systems such as FugakuNEXT.

events.title: IRISX: Performance Portable Scientific Computing via Code Generation and Runtime Co-Design
events.description:
Contemporary HPC, cloud, and embedded systems combine heterogeneous processors, and using them effectively requires careful trade-offs among kernel implementation, multi-device orchestration, and data transfers. Domain scientists need a framework that dynamically discovers performance-portable solutions from the characteristics of the application and the
underlying multi-accelerator platform. We propose IRISX, which integrates the SPIRAL code generation system with the IRIS runtime to deploy architecture-optimized kernels together with a portable abstraction for multi-device heterogeneity. IRISX transforms computation at the kernel, task, and graph levels—through kernel, task, and DAG fusion—to fit each target ar-
chitecture, and a hybrid analytical and ML model selects near-optimal configurations in 96% of unseen cases. On a partial differential equation library evaluated across Frontier, Aurora,
and multiple ExCL systems, IRISX delivers up to 25.9× speedup over unoptimized execution, up to 10× over the Proto library, and up to 74× over a StarPU implementation.

events.title: FHE-STREAM: Characterizing Memory Access Behavior in Fully Homomorphic Encryption Workloads
events.description: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, but adoption is limited by high memory overheads. The Residue Number System makes FHE arithmetic practical on CPUs while expanding each polynomial into a fragmented, pointer-based collection of limb arrays. Standard HPC memory benchmarks use flat, contiguous arrays and cannot capture how these structures behave under irregular access. We present FHE-STREAM, a microbenchmark suite that reproduces the memory layout of production RNS-based FHE libraries and measures the gap between the bytes an algorithm intends to move and the bytes the memory system actually transfers. Validation against hardware DRAM counters shows this gap is driven by cache-line utilization rather than access irregularity alone: cache-line-granular or coarser access shows little amplification, while sub-cache-line random access substantially increases traffic. This ordering predicts real cost, with OpenFHE relinearization spending more than half its runtime waiting on memory, providing measured targets for accelerator and library designers.

events.title: Scaling Laws for Physics-Aware ACOPF Surrogate Learning
events.description: Learning-based surrogates for AC optimal power flow (ACOPF) promise large speedups over classical solvers, but their operational value depends on physical feasibility as much as predictive accuracy. Physics-aware objectives such as the augmented Lagrangian (AL) improve constraint satisfaction at additional per-step cost, yet how this trade-off behaves with scale is uncharacterized. We sweep model and dataset sizes under MSE and AL training, and measure how violation changes with network size. Both objectives improve as power laws: MSE prediction loss depends more on model size than on data, while the AL composite of prediction loss and violation improves comparably along both axes. Violation grows markedly more slowly with network size under AL. On matched hardware and equal training samples, AL reduces violation about 19x with 2.4x training time and negligible added memory. The training objective shapes not only where a surrogate lands but how its quality evolves with scale.

events.title: OBSERVE: An Observable, Sustainable, and Fault-Tolerant Runtime for Hyperparameter Optimization on Production HPC Systems
events.description: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) has become a fundamental component of deep learning (DL) workflows, yet executing long-running optimization campaigns on High Performance Computing (HPC) systems remains a challenge, due to sustainability, computational costs, interruptions, heterogeneous hardware, and limited runtime visibility. Existing HPO frameworks primarily optimize the search effectiveness, while operational aspects required by HPC environments are neglected. This work introduces OBSERVE, an HPC-native framework for Bayesian Optimization (BO) offering energy-aware multi-objective optimization, fault tolerant checkpointing, and runtime observability. The framework is validated on the ClimateBench and MLPerf-DeepCAM benchmarks across heterogeneous HPC platforms with different schedulers and GPU architectures, and execution is tested by parallelizing the DL training in multi-GPU environments and the HPO process itself. Results confirm that the framework preserves the optimization effectiveness of BO while enabling resilient execution and exposing energy-performance trade-offs. More broadly, this work lays the foundation for energy-aware HPO as a runtime service in HPC infrastructures.

2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
events.description: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

events.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
events.description:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman
Music Composition and Performance: Stephan Vankov

Produced at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, UIC, and Calit2, UCSD

events.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
events.description:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

events.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
events.description:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.
