events.title: Biological Interfaces
events.description:
Water at biological interfaces contributes substantially to the mechanical behavior of membranes, yet how it responds to mechanical stress is not well characterized. This artwork was developed from molecular simulations, which examined how lateral tension influences interfacial water in lipid model membranes representative of mammalian and bacterial composition under physiological conditions.

In the resting state, interfacial water organizes into hydrogen-bonded networks, with small ring-like arrangements linking adjacent lipid. In the video, these ring-like arrangements are highlighted by the glowing planes between golden spheres. When lateral stress is applied, these arrangements persist in one mammalian membrane type, while in the other, stress-induced flattening of the membrane surface causes interfacial water to become partially decoupled from the lipid interface. This differential behavior points to a close relationship between a membrane's mechanical properties and the structural organization of its associated water network, offering insight into the mechanisms by which interfacial water contributes to membrane resilience under mechanical load. Whilst the video is mostly for aesthetical purposes, the findings of the molecular simulations suggest that interfacial water is not merely a passive boundary layer but an active participant in membrane stability that responds dynamically to stress, with implications extending across biophysics, drug design, and the study of biological adaptation.

events.title: Boiling the Ocean ... Literally
events.description:
The video shows monthly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the North Atlantic since 1980. The colors represent warming and cooling up to 2026 compared to the monthly averages from 1980 to 1995. The visualization highlights the rapid speed at which our oceans have been warming in a period of just over 45 years.

The video was made as realistic as possible with satellite imagery, realistic atmosphere thickness and density, a topography map and the use of ray-traced renders to present the data as realistically and prominently as possible.

events.title: Colourful Wind Assistance
events.description:
The video shows the flow past two wing sails arranged in tandem, representative of wind-assisted propulsion devices. The simulation was performed with x3d2, a high-order finite-difference incompressible-flow solver developed within the Xcompact3d framework (https://www.incompact3d.com). The simulation uses the immersed-boundary method to represent the foil geometry, together with non-periodic streamwise inflow/outflow boundary conditions and periodic transverse boundaries.

The calculation uses a uniform Cartesian mesh of approximately 381 million grid points. Based on the wing-sail chord and imposed inflow velocity, the Reynolds number is approximately 28,000. The case is an illustrative demonstration of the numerical methodology rather than a full-scale wing-sail prediction. Simulations were run in double precision on an NVIDIA Grace Hopper GH200 GPU using x3d2’s CUDA backend.

events.title: Entropy on the Edge of Collapse
events.description: This is a dynamical rendering of a detailed three-dimensional simulation of the explosion of the very-rapidly rotating core of a massive star that is exploding as a supernova. Rapid rotation leads to a powerful jet-like explosion along the two poles, accompanied by the generation and tangling of strong magnetic fields. This movie depicts the earliest phases of the supernova explosion that is simultaneously giving birth to a rapidly rotating radio pulsar.

events.title: Fatal Attraction
events.description:
Supermassive black holes are among the largest objects in the Universe. Their masses range from at least one hundred thousand to many billions of times that of our Sun. In a tidal disruption event, a star is captured by the black hole’s gravitational field.

This artwork illustrates the different phases of destruction of a star by the tidal field of a supermassive black hole.

The right panel combines multiple instants of times highlighting the enormous stretch incurred by the star as it is pulled back toward the black hole.

The left panel shows the star after its first orbit around the black hole. The star is then subsequently destroyed when colliding with its own accretion stream.

events.title: Flow Through a Pebble-Bed Reactor in NekRS
events.description: The pb146 case in NekRS is a benchmark computational fluid dynamics problem that simulates flow through a packed bed of 146 spherical particles, representing a simplified pebble-bed reactor geometry. It features a densely packed arrangement of spheres inside a cylindrical domain, producing complex flow behavior with tight gaps, recirculation zones, and turbulent interactions that are challenging to resolve numerically. Using NekRS’s high-order spectral element method, the case captures detailed boundary-layer physics and serves as a realistic yet standardized workload, making it widely used for testing solver accuracy, scalability, and performance on GPU-based high performance computing systems.

events.title: Fulfillment: Artistic Encounters with the Hidden Labor and Environmental Footprint of High Performance Computing
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) has become one of the defining infrastructures of contemporary society. Beyond enabling scientific discovery, HPC increasingly powers artificial intelligence, climate modeling, logistics, digital commerce, autonomous systems, and large-scale simulation. Despite its transformative role, HPC largely remains invisible to the public, obscuring the vast networks of human labor, material extraction, energy consumption, and environmental impact required to sustain computational infrastructures.

This project argues that artistic practice can make HPC visible, not only by visualizing scientific data, but by revealing the social, ecological, and political systems in which computational infrastructures are embedded. Rather than treating HPC solely as a technological achievement, the work positions it as part of a cultural-material landscape whose hidden operations shape everyday life.

Fulfillment is an interdisciplinary virtual reality artwork developed at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL), University of Illinois Chicago, in collaboration with anthropologists, designers, and computer scientists from several research institutions spanning the U.S., Europe, and Asia with support from the National Science Foundation. This proposal is for a public exhibition of the Fulfillment project as part of the Art Gallery Program at the SC26 conference. While the original work investigates global logistics and supply chain capitalism, this exhibition reframes those systems through the computational infrastructures that increasingly govern them. Warehouses, AI-driven optimization, cloud computing, data centers, predictive algorithms, and real-time simulation are presented as interconnected expressions of contemporary HPC ecosystems.

events.title: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night
events.description: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night (IOAN) is a multi-player VR experience that brings the rhythms of the cosmos to life in an endless remix instrument. Created from 758,457,209 magnitude readings for 817‚373 astronomical objects captured by the AST3 robotic telescopes in Antarctica, the experience transports players inside of a field of objects at the heart of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Within a multiplayer VR arena, and floating inside a luminous field between the Earth and the Large Magellanic Cloud, multiple players explore and collaboratively create new visual and sound remixes to perform the AST3 dataset as a soundscape for external visitors to the VR arena. The collaborative experience is inspired by communal percussion and multiplayer instruments. Real-time database queries, selections, and filtering operations enable multiple players in VR to collaboratively interact with the objects in the field to create data remixes from astronomical data. Visitors to the arena see and hear the virtual world in correct spatial relation to their real-world positions through spatialized 4K portals and spatialized ambisonic audio that align the physical space of the arena installation with the inner space of the multiplayer virtual environment.

events.title: JASMIN in July (Per Day): Brownian Bouquet
events.description:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Brownian Bouquet, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one day in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Stochastic Sea (which instead plots one spindle for one hour), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case a bouquet of flowers. The flower-like nature is encouraged by coercing the spindle centers into a sunflower-inspired pattern.

Brownian Bouquet invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

events.title: JASMIN in July (Per Hour): Stochastic Sea
events.description:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Stochastic Sea, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one hour in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Brownian Bouquet (which instead plots one spindle for one day), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case suggestive of a filamentary superstructure such as galactic super-clusters or a network of synapses. The spindle centers are randomly distributed across the composition, reinforcing this impression of a complex, interconnected structure.

Stochastic Sea invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

events.title: Ligand Dynamics Control Structure, Elasticity, and High-Pressure Behavior of Nanoparticle Superlattices
events.description: The spherical clusters in this image are a molecular dynamics simulation of lead sulfide nanocrystals, each seven nanometers wide, coated with radiating oleic acid ligands that allow such particles to self-assemble into an ordered crystal called a nanoparticle superlattice. The underlying research found that below a critical ligand coverage density, nanoparticles collapse and fuse together, while above it, the ligand layer cushions the structure enough to withstand applied pressures up to nearly 56 gigapascals while largely retaining its ordered arrangement. The image renders this simulated nanoscale structure alongside additional micrographs of nanoparticle superlattice material from the same body of research.

events.title: Morphogenesis
events.description:
Long before computers, Alan Turing asked how a smooth egg becomes a spotted, striped, branching creature. His answer, reaction-diffusion, is the chemistry of pattern itself. Here that chemistry runs as living paint: two competing substances diffuse and react across a field, blooming into coral, fingerprints, dividing cells, and restless worms, cycling endlessly through nature's vocabulary of form.

But look closely, and the field is split into three vertical territories, each a separate GPU. The luminous seams between them are the secret of large-scale simulation: the halo exchange, where neighboring processors trade their edge values every timestep so the pattern can flow seamlessly across boundaries. Gold packets pulse along the seams and communication is made visible.

This is how we simulate weather, galaxies, and combustion: cut reality into pieces, solve each in parallel, and stitch the edges back together. The pattern is the phenomenon; the seams are the high performance computing. Turing's morphogenesis is computed the way modern science actually computes it.

events.title: Oil on Canvas: Galactic Center on Palette
events.description:
My painting (Oil on Canvas) translates a radio-astronomy observation of our galaxy's heart into a dusky, nebular atmosphere, its aubergine and violet field that surrounds the Milky Way's core.

The source of my interpretation of the galactic center stemmed from discussions with Prof. Florina Ciorba from the University of Basel (UniBas), Switzerland, who is the co-founder member and PI of the UniBas node of the SKACH project — The SKA (Square Kilometre Array) of Switzerland Consortium (SKACH, https://skach.org/about-skach/). The underlying data comes from the 1.28 GHz MeerKAT galactic center mosaic created by Heywood et al. (2022), released by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO). The image that inspired me and my painting is a re-rendered version by J.C. Muñoz-Mateos and branded by SKACH (the Swiss SKA Consortium) and SKAO (the Square Kilometre Array Observatory).

https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/milky-way-center-meerkat-and-webb/

events.title: One-Sided: A Portrait of the New OpenSHMEM Standard
events.description:
In MPI, every memory transfer requires negotiation. The sender announces. The receiver posts a matching receive. Both wait. This is the contract at the heart of parallel communication — and this visualization begins there, in the weight of it: 256 processing elements, bilateral arcs crossing in every direction, a single REQUEST suspended at its target with no response coming.

Then the model changes.

OpenSHMEM eliminates the contract. Any process can write directly into any other's memory. No handshake. No prior agreement. The target is simply — a destination.

This 90-second visualization is a portrait of that principle, built entirely from real benchmark data captured on an HPE internal research cluster: four nodes, 256 processing elements, HPE Slingshot fabric.

The visual language is built around directionality. 256 PEs are arranged in four organic galaxy clusters — Realms α, β, γ, δ, 64 PEs each — with arcs cycling through one source cluster at a time so the viewer can track individual operations to their specific destinations, not interpret a global blur. Periodic spotlights isolate single PE-to-PE operations. The contrast with the MPI opening is deliberate and exact.

The data behind the animation is 500,000 real GUPS operations — Giga Updates Per Second, a standard benchmark for irregular remote atomic writes — captured live on the HPE Slingshot fabric. Each arc is a real operation. The pattern it makes is not designed; it is measured.

The closing act shows the full system in motion, with the GUPS source code, an operation counter climbing to 500,000, and the key argument: this workload cannot be handled without a global synchronization barrier in MPI — a cost that scales with every PE added. In OpenSHMEM, it just runs.

events.title: Open Polarity
events.description: This image depicts the 3D structure of the Sun's open coronal magnetic field from a snapshot of the “Live Prediction” HPC simulation developed by Predictive Science Inc. as part of their research for the August 12, 2026, total solar eclipse. See eclipse.predsci.com for more details on the simulation, which was created using the Magnetohydrodynamic Algorithm outside a Sphere Fortran code (github.com/predsci/mas) at a resolution of over 50 million cells. It ran faster than real time using 24 128-core EPYC Turin 9745 CPUs (3,072 total cores) on NASA's Athena supercomputer.

events.title: Portrait of Data Center
events.description:
A supercomputer has vital signs: a temperature, a metabolism, and a heartbeat. This piece paints them. Streaming GPU telemetry (utilization, power draw, temperature, and interconnect traffic) drives a generative flow field: thousands of particles drift and glow, each colored by heat, brightened by power, their speed set by how hard the machine is thinking. Nothing is invented; every gesture is a reading of the machine's own body.

The work is deliberately multi-dimensional. One dimension is data, which is the honest mapping of live signals to light. Another is choreography, drawn from Martha Graham's foundational language of modern dance: contraction and release. Graham built movement from the body's core, a gathering inward that coils tension, then an expansive release outward. Here the machine's heartbeat performs exactly that: on each slow breath the particles are drawn toward the core, gathering; then, on the release, they are expelled outward in a bloom of light and sparks, timed to the pulse. As load climbs from idle to peak, the breath deepens and the release becomes a throw. A supercomputer that is moving through its own register, from rest to full, dramatic exertion.

The third dimension is metaphor: the data center as a living, feeling body, its telemetry the score to which it dances. By borrowing Graham's grammar of gather-and-expel, the piece asks the audience to read a machine not as cold infrastructure but as a performer; one whose choreography is authored not by a human hand but by the physics of computation itself. High performance computing, rendered as contemporary dance.

events.title: Radiation: When Steels Fall Apart
events.description:
This visualization uses a high performance computing-based workflow to reveal the atomic-scale structure of neutron-irradiated steel. Highlighted in the image are nanoscale defects and chemical features that formed or evolved as a result of irradiation.

The specimen examined in this study was prepared from an HT-9 alloy irradiated to 0.68 displacements per atom (dpa) at 478 degrees Celsius in Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor. The visualization combines two correlative datasets collected from the same specimen: a two-dimensional image acquired using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and a three-dimensional dataset acquired using atom probe tomography (APT).

The combined datasets reveal several complex microstructural features associated with radiation damage. These include spherical clusters enriched in nickel and silicon, dislocation lines decorated with solute clusters, and a grain boundary exhibiting radiation-induced solute segregation. The dataset also captures a pre-existing vanadium nitride precipitate. Characterizing these features is important because they can influence the physical and mechanical properties of the alloy.

Using high performance computing and advanced deep-learning methods, this image-based workflow improves feature identification and enables more accurate spatial correlation of the complementary TEM and APT datasets. The multimodal computational model under development uses structural information obtained from TEM to support further analysis of the APT dataset and improve the identification and characterization of solute clusters.

This visualization is composed entirely of experimental data obtained from TEM and APT measurements. Rendering the datasets in this form allows researchers to more effectively interpret correlative measurements, identify and analyze complex radiation-induced features, validate computational methods, and communicate scientific findings.

events.title: Simulation of Tungsten Transport in the ASDEX-U Tokamak Plasma
events.description: Simulation of tungsten transport in the ASDEX-U tokamak plasma reveals critical insights for fusion reactor design. Tungsten, used for its heat resistance, ionizes during operation and can penetrate the core, radiating energy and reducing efficiency. These simulations explore the interaction of tungsten ions with rotation and light impurities like boron and helium in the complex edge region near the wall. The study highlights the role of binary collisions and asymmetries in tungsten penetration. Confidence in the model is bolstered by recent validation on a separate physics problem.

events.title: Spiral Wave: The Heart's Chaotic Dance
events.description:
A spiral of crimson, gold, mocha, and magenta moves through the heart, tracing the electrical activity that coordinates every heartbeat. Here, that rhythm has broken down. The spiral is a rotor, a self-sustaining electrical wave that drives atrial fibrillation, one of the most common and dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

Every frame is generated directly from a high-performance cardiac electrophysiology simulation. The left atrium is modeled as a large network of electrically coupled tissue, simulated in near real time using custom CUDA code running on NVIDIA GPUs. This computational framework allows researchers to investigate how atrial fibrillation begins, evolves, and responds to targeted intervention.

The colors are not arbitrary; they are the language of physiology. Crimson marks tissue at rest, ready to activate. Gold follows the wave of depolarization as it propagates through the muscle. Mocha and magenta represent the refractory period, when the tissue is recovering before it can fire again. In this simulation, the refractory period is shortened, and a precisely timed electrical stimulus initiates the spiral wave.

Spiral Wave lives at the intersection of computation, medicine, and art. Every color, every curve, and every swirl emerges from the underlying physics of cardiac tissue. Nothing in this animation was designed to be beautiful. It simply is.

events.title: The Oracle at DKRZ
events.description:
This video is a visualization of the algorithm used to generate "prophecies" from machine code — that will form part of a sculptural installation to be exhibited at the German Climate Computing Centre (DKRZ).

The work situates climate modeling in the broader, non-scientific history of humanity's attempts to grapple with the future. By reinterpreting the binary of the ICON climate model into words, and searching for where those words combine into statements about the future, ICON is reimagined as a modern-day oracle. The algorithm's lexicon comes from English translations of classical Greek texts. In these fictions, prophecies are true, and are intertwined with the distinct tragedy of not being believed or acted upon — a startling parallel to humanity's lackluster response to the climate crisis.

Inspiration for the project came through conversations with scientists at DKRZ; about the computation and storage of data, as well as the Centre's role in scientific research and weather prediction. On the computational side, the ability to abstract almost anything into a string of zeros and ones highlights a wonderful symmetry: if anything can be binary, then binary can be anything. From this perspective, binary becomes an interface between seemingly disparate media and raises questions about how the systems we use to interpret data give rise to meaning.

The connection to a history of fortune telling was developed through understanding the role DKRZ plays within the scientific landscape. The vast array of resources spent in the construction and maintenance of its supercomputers is a testament to how far humanity will go to fulfill a specific need — to know what the future will be like. From this perspective, it represents an incredibly sophisticated approach to something humans have been doing throughout history and across civilizations. The rulers of city-states in Ancient Greece would climb the steps to the Oracle at Delphi seeking counsel. Now, various clients come to DKRZ, looking to use its computing power for projections on the weather and climate.

events.title: Vortex Bubbles in Anabatic Upslope Flow During Morning Transition
events.description: Sea of bubbling vortices arising in upslope (anabatic) flow at a slope angle of eight degrees after sudden imposition of surface heat flux against a constant ambient stratification. This serves as a simplified model for the morning transition from nighttime downslope (katabatic) drainage to daytime upslope flow occurring during sunrise in valleys or mountains when solar radiation starts to heat up the sloped terrain, reversing the buoyancy and pressure gradients established during the cooler nocturnal conditions. Flow shown here is in an intermediate regime between laminar and fully turbulent.

events.title: Where Data Becomes Light: The Beauty of Scientific Visualization
events.description:
Where Data Becomes Light is a digital light projection and immersive visual experience that celebrates the beauty of science through contemporary visualization. On view nightly, Thursday through Sunday, at THE MART (artonthemart.com) September through mid-November, the large-scale imagery transforms the 2.5-acre building façade into a luminous canvas, where sweeping animations and vivid imagery inspire curiosity and wonder, and invite audiences to witness the elegance and complexity of the natural world through modern scientific computing.

Scientific discovery often begins with numbers, signals, and equations, but its deepest insights emerge when those patterns become visible. Scientific visualization transforms complex data into images that reveal structure, motion, and meaning, allowing us to see phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden. In these images, turbulence becomes choreography, molecular interactions resemble intricate architecture, and the evolution of galaxies unfolds like a vast celestial landscape.

Like Art of HPC, Where Data Becomes Light celebrates creativity and beauty in computational science. The projection includes several works from past SC Art of HPC exhibits and Scientific Visualization and Data Analytics Showcases, bringing the SC community's work to the city's skyline.

The Collaboration

For decades, researchers have used visualization to transform massive datasets into images that reveal patterns hidden in raw numbers. As high-performance computing has grown in prominence to address the biggest challenges in science and engineering, Argonne National Laboratory has played a key role in this evolution, operating world-class supercomputers and producing visualizations that illuminate everything from the structure of materials and the behavior of turbulent flows to the formation of galaxies and the dynamics of climate systems.

At the same time, the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago helped define the modern field of visualization. EVL researchers’ work contributed to the landmark National Science Foundation report on scientific visualization, which helped establish visualization as a critical component of scientific discovery. EVL’s innovations in immersive visualization environments and collaborative visual computing have expanded the ways scientists and the public experience complex data.

7:30-8:00 pm

events.title: You Only Have Seven Seconds
events.description:
You Only Have Seven Seconds is a poetic, human–AI collaborative documentary that unfolds as both a visual archive of an internationally exhibited installation and a cinematic experiment in memory preservation. Against the backdrop of rising Alzheimer’s cases and the emergence of machine-generated false memories, the film reimagines remembrance through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Inspired by her grandmother’s cognitive decline, the artist developed a custom AI system that transforms fragmented spoken recollections into synthetic visual sequences. Presented as an interactive AI art installation, the project ReCollection has traveled worldwide, welcoming thousands of visitors to whisper their fading memories — each within seven seconds — into the artwork and generate visual memories in real time. These memories form the foundation of an evolving archive, constructed through speech recognition, text auto-completion, and text-to-image generation.

Drawing from this archive, the film incorporates emerging speech-to-video technology to weave a collective, culturally diverse montage of love and loss. The participatory datasets are curated to build dialogical relationships, forming patterns, counterpoints, and resonances that evoke a poetics of relation. Initially conceived as a personal reflection, the work has evolved into a living, breathing, shared world-building experience that reassembles the ephemeral past into a dynamic portrait of collective human selfhood.

Beyond the Terminal: Preparing for HPC and AI Careers
events.description:
Beyond the Terminal: Preparing for HPC and AI Careers

Technical skills are only part of building a career in HPC and AI. This half-day workshop helps students understand the career landscape, strengthen their professional presence, and prepare for conversations with employers, mentors, and graduate programs.

Students will explore the range of roles available across HPC and AI, including research, systems and infrastructure, GPU and performance engineering, research software engineering, applied machine learning, and developer relations. The workshop will also cover how to evaluate graduate school options, build strong résumés and portfolios, search for roles effectively, and prepare for interviews and offers.

events.title: Preparing for HPC & AI Careers
events.description: In the first part of the workshop, students will explore the range of roles available across HPC and AI, including research, systems and infrastructure, GPU and performance engineering, research software engineering, applied machine learning, and developer relations. The workshop will also cover how to evaluate graduate school options, build strong resumes and portfolios, search for roles effectively, and prepare for interviews and offers.

events.title: Understanding Communication Performance in Large-Scale Codes: A Practical Guide
events.description: Communication has become a primary performance limiter for large-scale applications, from sparse solvers to AI workloads. This full-day tutorial introduces attendees to the practical use and performance analysis of modern communication libraries, including MPI, RCCL, and rocSHMEM, with a focus on profiling communication behavior using TAU. The tutorial will provide students, early-career researchers, and application developers, who are not necessarily specialists in communication libraries, a bottom-up understanding of communication performance. Participants will learn how to compile and run representative communication benchmarks, interpret latency and bandwidth results, and connect benchmark behavior to application-level communication patterns. Using hands-on examples, attendees will explore how communication choices affect performance on GPU-based systems and how profiling tools can reveal bottlenecks that are otherwise hidden at the source-code level. The tutorial emphasizes practical workflows for cross-referencing benchmark data with profiling output to guide optimization decisions. Built around a collaboratively developed, thoroughly tested code base, the session will provide a reproducible and accessible environment for live exercises. By the end of the day, attendees will be equipped to diagnose communication performance inefficiencies and make informed library and design choices for their own codes.

events.title: Rigorous Evaluation of LLM Components in HPC Research
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as components inside HPC research workflows. They are used from code generation and translation, to agentic tool use for debugging, profiling, and experiment orchestration. While these systems can accelerate development, they also introduce new challenges for rigorous evaluation: outputs are stochastic, behavior is sensitive to prompts and configuration, commercial models change silently over time, and the true contribution of the LLM is often confounded with many other experimental factors. As a result, a growing number of papers report results using LLMs in their study without sufficient transparency, suitable baselines, or statistically sound measurements. This tutorial will teach participants a practical framework for rigorous evaluation and reporting of LLM components in HPC research. We cover what must be reported for reproducibility, how to design experiments around stochastic components, and when and how to incorporate human validation. We then focus on HPC-specific evaluation and the unique challenges that arise in using LLMs in HPC research. Throughout, we highlight common pitfalls and provide guidance and templates that participants can directly apply to their own projects and papers.

events.title: Taming AI Storage Systems
events.description: Training and inferencing AI models require massively distributed GPU-based compute clusters. These clusters consume large amounts of data, via distributed storage solutions and high-speed networks. The storage solutions are facing huge amounts of clients accessing storage simultaneously while demanding low latency and high throughput. This tutorial directly supports SC’s focus on scalable high‑performance systems and AI/HPC convergence by providing practical methods to diagnose and alleviate storage-related bottlenecks in large GPU-based clusters. It will give an overview of existing and emerging distributed storage solutions. The audience will get tips from industry experts for configuring these storage systems and optimizing workloads to fully utilize the potential of these highly distributed storage systems.

events.title: Accelerating and Scaling Python for HPC
events.description: Python is powering breakthrough exascale scientific discoveries - come learn how to program the world's largest supercomputers with it! In this interactive tutorial you’ll learn how to write, debug, profile, and optimize high-performance, multi-node GPU applications in Python. You'll learn and master: CuPy for drop-in GPU acceleration of NumPy workflows, Numba for writing custom kernels that match the performance of C++ and Fortran, mpi4py for scaling across thousands of nodes, DragonHPC for workflow acceleration, CppJIT for on-demand interoperability between Python/C++ and automatic bindings generation, leveraging it for compiler-based automatic differentiation of C++ with Clad. Everything is hands-on: short and interactive lectures by expert instructors will be paired with guided Jupyter notebooks that introduce each concept and have you immediately apply it in bite-sized exercises: a mini-app applying various programming models with JAX, CuPy and CppJIT on cosmic web data, and a CARTopiaX CAR T-cell therapy example). We'll use a web-based environment that requires no installs and setup - just a laptop and a browser. Whether you’re a domain scientist seeking faster turnaround or a software engineer evaluating portable acceleration strategies, you’ll leave with a roadmap, skills, and code for bringing scalable Python practices back to your own HPC facility.

events.title: Advanced MPI Programming
events.description: The vast majority of production parallel scientific applications today use MPI and run successfully on the largest systems in the world. Parallel system architectures are evolving to include complex, heterogeneous nodes comprising general-purpose CPUs as well as accelerators such as GPUs. At the same time, the MPI standard itself is evolving to address the needs and challenges of future extreme-scale platforms as well as applications. This tutorial will cover several advanced features of MPI that can help users program modern systems effectively. Using code examples based on scenarios found in real applications, we will cover several topics including efficient ways of doing 2D and 3D stencil computation, derived datatypes, one-sided communication, hybrid programming (MPI + threads, shared memory, GPUs), topologies and topology mapping, neighborhood and nonblocking collectives, some of the new performance-oriented features in MPI-4, and the new application binary interface (ABI) in MPI-5. Attendees will leave the tutorial with an understanding of how to use these advanced features of MPI and guidelines on how they might perform on different platforms and architectures.

events.title: Julia for High Performance Computing
events.description:
This full-day, six-hour hands-on tutorial introduces participants to using the Julia programming language effectively in high performance computing (HPC) environments, from first principles to end-to-end deployment on a leadership-class system. The first portion introduces fundamental aspects of the language and emphasizes Julia’s unique features for scientific computing: mathematical syntax, multiple dispatch, type inference, LLVM-IR code inspection, modern package management, and performance pitfalls. Participants will work through notebook-based exercises that highlight key language features and progressively introduce parallel programming models for CPU and GPU. Attendees will learn node-level performance-portable approaches with KernelAbstractions.jl and JACC.jl and an introduction to Dagger.jl and kernel auto-tuning using the KernelTuner.jl framework.
The last portion focuses on building, running, and analyzing a realistic HPC application — an open-source Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion PDE solver (GrayScott.jl) — then scaling the application across nodes with MPI.jl. We also cover parallel I/O (ADIOS2.jl), scaling measurements, and GPU profiling using vendor tools. For this portion, we invite participants to apply for access to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) Odo training system (32 nodes of the Frontier supercomputer) until November 5. Please find instructions to register for an Odo account (subject to approval) and materials in our tutorial repository: https://github.com/JuliaParallel/julia-hpc-tutorial-sc26.

events.title: Leveraging and Evaluating LLMs for Scientific Computing
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) are progressing at an impressive pace. They can solve complex problems while presenting the opportunity to leverage their capabilities for scientific computing. Despite their progress, even the most sophisticated models can struggle with simple reasoning tasks and make mistakes, necessitating careful verification of their outputs. This tutorial focuses on these two important aspects: (1) leveraging LLMs to assist scientific computing code translation and automatic parallelization, and (2) presenting best practices for evaluating and comparing LLMs within the scientific computing context. Designed specifically for students, researchers, and engineers at beginner and intermediate levels, the tutorial features four hours of presentation and two hours of hands-on experience. Attendees learn the fundamentals of LLM design, development, and use cases for scientific computing. The tutorial deep-dives into three key topics for scientific computing: automatic parallelization, sequential code translation (Fortran to C++), and parallel code translation (OpenMP to Cuda) with the CodeScribe, LASSI, and PARACODEX tools. Attendees also learn various complementary methods to test and evaluate LLM responses rigorously. At the end of the tutorial, attendees are equipped with solid foundations, knowledge, and practical experience to leverage and evaluate LLMs for scientific computing and to transform theoretical insights into actionable solutions.

events.title: Managing HPC Software Complexity with Spack
events.description: Modern scientific software stacks rely on thousands of packages, from low-level libraries in C, C++, and Fortran to higher-level tools in Python and R. Scientists must deploy these stacks across diverse environments, from personal laptops to supercomputers, while tailoring workflows to specific tasks. Development workflows often require frequent rebuilds, debugging, and small-scale testing for rapid iteration. In contrast, preparing applications for large-scale HPC production involves performance-critical libraries (e.g., MPI, BLAS, LAPACK) and machine-specific optimizations to maximize efficiency. Managing these varied requirements is challenging. Configuring software, resolving dependencies, and ensuring compatibility can hinder both development and deployment. Spack is an open-source package manager that simplifies building, installing, and customizing HPC software stacks. It offers a flexible dependency model, Python-based syntax for package recipes, and a repository of over 9,000 packages maintained by more than 1,600 contributors. Spack is widely adopted by researchers, developers, cloud platforms, and HPC centers worldwide. This tutorial introduces Spack’s core capabilities, including installing and authoring packages, configuring environments, and deploying optimized software on HPC systems. Attendees will gain foundational skills for automating routine tasks and acquire advanced knowledge to address complex use cases with Spack.

events.title: Early Career Program
events.description: The Early Career Program is a series of workshop-style sessions for people in the early stages of their careers. It is intended to help guide program participants in navigating a successful career path. Participation in the program requires an application prior to the conference. Admission is restricted to the individuals who were accepted.

events.title: Welcome and Introduction
events.description: Participation in the Early Career Program requires an application prior to the conference. Admission is restricted to the individuals who were accepted.

events.title: Mastering OpenMP Tasking: From Start to Free-Agent Tasks
events.description: OpenMP® is the leading, portable, and widely supported directive-based programming model. Already in 2008, the OpenMP API introduced tasking to support the creation of composable parallel software blocks and the parallelization of irregular algorithms. Developers usually find the OpenMP language easy to learn. However, mastering the tasking concept requires a change in the way developers reason about the structure of their code and how they expose its parallelism. Our "Mastering Tasking" tutorial has been designed for the SC audience to learn about the tasking concept in detail and to understand code patterns as solutions to many common problems. Throughout all topics, we showcase the additions brought with OpenMP versions 5.0 through 6.1 and explain how to adopt codes. For this tutorial, we assume attendees understand basic parallelization concepts and know the fundamentals of the OpenMP API. First, we introduce the OpenMP tasking language features in detail and then focus on performance aspects, such as introducing cut-off mechanisms, exploiting task dependencies, and preserving locality. The new free-agent tasks introduced with OpenMP version 6.0 are covered in detail. Extensive case studies accompany all topics. As a full-day tutorial, we will include hands-on sessions.

events.title: Modern High-Performance I/O: Leveraging Files and Objects
events.description: As more diverse applications move to high performance computing (HPC), the I/O workload has also become more varied. The community has spent three decades improving large-scale parallel file systems, but object stores provide new approaches and novel interfaces. At the same time, traditional parallel I/O approaches and abstractions have evolved under the covers to make use of both novel object stores and classic parallel file systems. In this full-day tutorial we will explore several object storage technologies and discuss both old and new approaches to getting maximum performance from them. With a mix of lectures and hands-on exercises, attendees will learn about object storage design and usage. We will also tackle how the classic I/O software stack has evolved to make use of object stores, as well as provide attendees with the knowledge to know when file systems and object stores are the most appropriate storage approach for their applications. By the end of the day, attendees will know a bit more about what these new storage systems are doing while at the same time learning how to use libraries and tools to hide the details.

events.title: Performance Tuning of HPC and ML/AI Applications with the Roofline Model on GPUs, APUs, and CPUs
events.description: The Roofline performance model offers an insightful and intuitive method for extracting the key execution characteristics of HPC and ML/AI applications and comparing them against the performance ­bounds of modern CPUs and GPUs. Its abilities to abstract the complexity of memory hierarchies and identify the most profitable optimization techniques have made Roofline­-based analysis increasingly popular in the HPC and ML/AI communities. Although different flavors of the Roofline model have been developed, there remains a need for a systematic methodology when applying them to analyze applications running on multicore and accelerated systems. The tutorial aims to bridge this gap on both CPUs and GPUs by both exposing the fundamental aspects behind different Roofline modeling principles as well as providing several practical use­ case scenarios that highlight their efficacy for performance and energy optimization as well as understanding performance portability. This tutorial presents a unique combination of instruction in Roofline by its creator, hands-on instruction in using Roofline within NVIDIA’s, AMD’s, and Intel’s production performance tools, and discussions of real-world Roofline use cases at NERSC, ALCF, and OLCF. The tutorial presenters have a long history of collaborating on the Roofline model and have presented several Roofline-­based tutorials.

events.title: Principles and Practice of High-Performance AI Training and Inference
events.description: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have led to significant growth in model scale, computational demands, and system complexity, creating both new challenges and opportunities. Modern AI frameworks and systems such as PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, and distributed middleware including torch.distributed, Megatron-LM, and DeepSpeed enable scalable training, fine-tuning, inference, and deployment across the full AI model lifecycle. This tutorial provides an overview of recent trends in AI and highlights the convergence of AI and high performance computing (HPC), emphasizing the role of advanced hardware architectures, memory systems, and high-speed interconnects in enabling scalable AI workloads. We present an end-to-end view of the AI lifecycle, including training, fine-tuning, hyperparameter optimization, and inference, with a focus on parallelization strategies for large-scale models such as GPT, LLaMA, DeepSeek, and ViT. We discuss key system challenges related to compute, memory, and communication, and examine how modern communication runtimes and software stacks can efficiently leverage heterogeneous CPU/GPU architectures. We also highlight co-design efforts utilizing NCCL and MPI communication backends to support large-scale distributed AI workloads on modern HPC systems. Throughout the tutorial, we include hands-on exercises to provide attendees with practical experience in distributed AI on modern GPU clusters.

events.title: Programming Novel AI Accelerators for Scientific Computing
events.description: Scientific applications are increasingly adopting artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to advance science. There are specialized hardware accelerators designed and built to run AI applications efficiently. With a wide diversity in the hardware architectures and software stacks of these systems, it is challenging to understand the differences between these accelerators, their capabilities, programming approaches, and how they perform, particularly for scientific applications. In this tutorial, we will cover an overview of the AI accelerators deployed at ALCF, focusing on SambaNova, Cerebras, and Tenstorrent systems along with architectural features and details of their software stacks. Through hands-on exercises, attendees will gain practical experience in refactoring code and running models on these systems, focusing on use cases of pre-training and fine-tuning open-source large language models (LLMs) and deploying AI inference solutions relevant to scientific contexts. The tutorial will provide the attendees with an understanding of the key capabilities of emerging AI accelerators and their performance implications for scientific applications.

events.title: Beyond the Terminal: Career Coaching
events.description: The afternoon career coaching sessions give students the opportunity to participate in focused career conversations with HPC and AI professionals. These 10-15 minute, one-on-one sessions are designed to give students personalized guidance on career questions, résumés, graduate school decisions, job searches, technical growth, and professional next steps. Students will select their preferred coach in advance and are encouraged to come prepared with specific questions and goals so they can make the most of each conversation.

events.title: 10th International Workshop on Software Correctness for HPC Applications (Correctness '26)
events.description: Ensuring correctness in HPC applications is one of the fundamental challenges that the HPC community faces today. While significant advances in verification, testing, and debugging have been made to isolate software defects in the context of non-HPC software, several factors make achieving correctness in HPC applications and systems much more challenging than in general systems software — growing heterogeneity (CPUs, GPUs, and special purpose accelerators), massive scale computations, use of combined parallel programming models (e.g., MPI+X), new scalable numerical algorithms (e.g., to leverage reduced precision in floating-point arithmetic), and aggressive compiler optimizations/transformations are some of the challenges that make correctness harder in HPC. As the complexity of future architectures, algorithms, and applications increases, the ability to fully exploit exascale systems will be limited without correctness. The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers and developers to present and discuss novel ideas to address the problem of correctness in HPC.

events.title: Welcome
Research Software Engineers in HPC (RSE-HPC-2026)
events.description:
Research software engineers (RSEs) are critical to the impact of HPC, data science, and the larger scientific community. They have existed for decades, though often not under that name. The past several years, however, have seen the development of the RSE concept, common job titles, and career paths; the creation of professional networks to connect RSEs; and the emergence of RSE groups at universities, national laboratories, and in industry.

This workshop will bring together RSEs and allies involved in HPC, from all over the world, to grow the RSE community by establishing and strengthening professional networks of current RSEs and RSE leaders. We'll hear about successes and challenges that RSEs and RSE groups have experienced, and discuss ways to increase awareness of RSE opportunities and improve support for RSEs.

The workshop will be highly interactive, featuring panels, an invited talk, and short submitted talks.

events.title: Twelfth International Workshop on Heterogeneous High-Performance Reconfigurable Computing (H2RC 2026)
events.description: As in the previous 11 years, this workshop will bring together application experts, software developers, and hardware engineers, both from industry and academia, to share experiences and best practices to leverage the practical application of reconfigurable logic to scientific computing, AI/ML, and “big data” applications. In particular, the workshop will focus on sharing experiences and techniques for accelerating applications and/or improving energy efficiency with FPGAs using high-level design flows, which enable and improve cross-platform functional and performance portability while also improving productivity. Particular emphasis is given to cross-platform comparisons and combinations that foster a better understanding within the industry and research community on what are the best mappings of applications to a diverse range of hardware architectures that are available today (e.g., FPGA, GPU, many-cores and hybrid devices, ASICs), and on how to most effectively achieve cross-platform compatibility.

events.title: 6th International Workshop on RESource DISaggregation in High Performance Computing (RESDIS)
events.description: Disaggregation is an emerging compute paradigm that splits existing monolithic servers into a number of consolidated single-resource pools that communicate over a fast interconnect. This model decouples individual hardware resources and enables the creation of logical compute platforms with flexible and dynamic hardware configurations. The concept of disaggregation is driven by various recent trends in computation. From an application perspective, the increasing importance of data analytics and machine learning workloads brings unprecedented need for memory capacity, which is in stark contrast with the growing imbalance in the peak compute-to-memory capacity ratio of traditional system board-based servers. At the hardware front, the proliferation of heterogeneous, special-purpose computing elements promotes the need for composable platforms, while the increasing maturity of optical interconnects elevates the prospects of distance independence in networking infrastructure. The workshop intends to explore various aspects of resource disaggregation, composability, and their implications for future HPC platforms.

events.title: 8th Workshop on Programming and Performance Visualization Tools (ProTools)
events.description:
Understanding program behavior is critical to overcome the expected architectural and programming complexities, such as limited power budgets, heterogeneity, hierarchical memories, shrinking I/O bandwidths, and performance variability, that arise on modern HPC platforms. To do so, HPC software developers need intuitive support tools for debugging, performance measurement, analysis, and tuning of large-scale HPC applications. Data collected from these tools can be far too large and too complex to be analyzed in a straightforward manner. We therefore need automatic analysis and visualization approaches to help application developers intuitively understand the effects that algorithmic choices have on application correctness or performance.

The ProTools workshop brings together HPC application developers, tool developers, vendors, and researchers from the visualization, performance, and program analysis fields for an exchange of new approaches to assist developers in analyzing, understanding, and optimizing programs for extreme-scale platforms.

events.title: E4S: An HPC-AI Software Ecosystem for Science
events.description:
E4S, an HPSF project, provides a broad HPC-AI software ecosystem for science [https://e4s.io]. E4S is a curated, Spack based software distribution of 100+ HPC, EDA, and AI/ML packages. It features AI tools such as PyTorch, OpenClaw, NVIDIA NemoClaw, NVIDIA NeMo, NVIDIA BioNeMo, vllm, Ollama, Huggingface CLI, JAX, OpenAI, Google's Gemini API based chatbot, and other supporting tools including langchain, pandas, and SciKit-Learn. E4S supports containerized, bare-metal installation, and deployment on commercial cloud platforms with support for AWS, Azure, OCI, IBM, and Google Cloud. It includes Codium, an IDE, Jupyter notebook, and visualization tools such as VisIt and ParaView all launched from a web browser without installing any additional software. These tools provide an
open platform for education and research in HPC-AI.

events.title: Sovereign AI Supercomputing Cloud Workshop
events.description: As the HPC landscape shifts toward massive-scale AI infrastructures, the pursuit of a sovereign supercomputing ecosystem has become paramount. However, recent industry consolidations — notably NVIDIA’s acquisition of SchedMD — have shattered the illusion that open-source software (OSS) is a guaranteed failsafe against vendor influence. This workshop explores the paradox of modern HPC sovereignty: How can sites build autonomous, transparent infrastructures when critical "open" components are increasingly controlled by hardware vendors? We will evaluate the transition from passive consumption toward active community governance, highlighting initiatives like OpenCHAMI and the High Performance Software Foundation (HPSF). Through technical talks and interactive panels, this symposium seeks to move beyond an idealized view of OSS toward a pragmatic, risk-aware strategy for the next generation of sovereign on-premises infrastructure, ensuring interoperability and resilience in an era of vertical integration.

events.title: LLVM-HPC2026: The Twelfth Workshop on the LLVM Compiler Infrastructure in HPC
events.description: LLVM, winner of the 2012 ACM Software System Award, has become an integral part of the software-development ecosystem for optimizing compilers, dynamic-language execution engines, source-code analysis and transformation tools, debuggers and linkers and a whole host of programming-language and toolchain-related components. Now heavily used in both academia and industry, where it allows for rapid development of production-quality tools, LLVM is increasingly used in work targeted at high performance computing. Research in, and implementation of, program analysis, compilation, execution and profiling have clearly benefited from the availability of a high-quality, freely-available infrastructure on which to build. This workshop will focus on recent developments, from both academia and industry, that build on LLVM to advance the state of the art in high performance computing.

events.title: 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing
events.description:
Quantum computing is advancing rapidly, and its integration with high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important for enabling practical hybrid computational workflows. In a growing number of domains, research is progressing toward quantum advantage — with quantum computation already addressing problems that strain exact classical methods and increasingly competing with state-of-the-art approximate approaches. These combined methods offer new opportunities for accelerating progress in scientific areas such as physics, chemistry, materials, and optimization by leveraging quantum computing together with established classical and AI-based techniques.

The 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing (LSQCC) brings together recent research on quantum algorithms, system integration techniques, and emerging hybrid workflows that incorporate HPC and AI components where beneficial. The workshop highlights technical challenges, recent developments, and near-term opportunities for effectively combining quantum computing with complementary approaches.

events.title: PDSW’26: The 11th International Parallel Data Systems Workshop
events.description: Efficient storage, movement, and management of data are crucial to application performance and scientific productivity in both traditional simulation-oriented HPC environments and cloud, AI/ML/big data analysis environments. This issue is further exacerbated by the growing volume of experimental and observational data, the widening gap between the performance of computational hardware and storage hardware, and the emergence of new data-driven algorithms in machine learning. The goal of this workshop is to facilitate in-depth discussions of research and development that address the most critical challenges in large-scale data storage and data processing. PDSW will continue to build on the successful tradition established by its predecessor workshops: the Petascale Data Storage Workshop (PDSW, 2006-2015) and the Data Intensive Scalable Computing Systems (DISCS, 2012-2015) workshop. These workshops were successfully combined in 2016, and the resulting joint workshop has attracted up to 45 full paper submissions and 195 attendees per year from 2016 to 2025.

events.title: High Performance Computing for Environmental and Earth Sciences (HPC4EES)
events.description: With the availability of large-scale weather, climate, and Earth data from multiple sources, including satellites and sensors, existing modeling techniques need further improvement to handle these data volumes. The high-performance computing (HPC) community can help. In the last decade, HPC has played an essential role in scaling existing weather modeling methods, enabling improved forecasting and proactive responses to severe weather conditions. However, this area warrants greater attention from HPC researchers to better understand the impact of climate change on future generations and to mitigate sudden disasters, including earthquakes and extreme weather events. Thus, we propose a dedicated workshop about coupling HPC with environmental and earth science. We chose SC as the venue for this workshop to reach a broad segment of the HPC community. The workshop will cover challenges around large-scale environmental modeling and possible solutions from the HPC community.

events.title: High Performance Computing for Environmental and Earth Sciences (HPC4EES)
events.description: With the availability of large-scale weather, climate, and Earth data from multiple sources, including satellites and sensors, existing modeling techniques need further improvement to handle these data volumes. The high performance computing (HPC) community can help. In the last decade, HPC has played an essential role in scaling existing weather modeling methods, enabling improved forecasting and proactive responses to severe weather conditions. However, this area warrants greater attention from HPC researchers to better understand the impact of climate change on future generations and to mitigate sudden disasters, including earthquakes and extreme weather events. Thus, we propose a dedicated workshop about coupling HPC with environmental and earth science. We chose SC as the venue for this workshop to reach a broad segment of the HPC community. The workshop will cover challenges around large-scale environmental modeling and possible solutions from the HPC community.

events.title: WHPC: Building Community, Building Careers
events.description:
The WHPC@SC26 workshop has a goal of fostering a diverse and inclusive HPC community. We welcome all attendees who align with our goals and want to support broader participation in the HPC workforce.

The WHPC workshop series has become the leading SC event focused on DEI topics. We aim to cultivate skills for valuing a diverse workforce and creating a welcoming environment for all. Following the workshop held at SC24, we have an increased emphasis on diversity and inclusion of all people from underrepresented groups.

WHPC@SC26 will focus on the following topics:
- Building community through real-time networking
- Improving diversity and inclusion for all in the HPC workforce
- Highlighting and supporting early-career researchers from underrepresented groups
- Building a deeper understanding of what diversity, equity, and inclusion means for different groups
- Learning from, and valuing, different experiences and career paths

events.title: 8th International Workshop on Containers and New Orchestration Paradigms for Isolated Environments in HPC (CANOPIE-HPC)
events.description: The ongoing revolution enabled via containerization, virtualization, and new orchestration models has dramatically changed how applications and services are delivered and managed across the computing industry. This revolution has established a new ecosystem of tools and techniques with new, flexible and agile approaches, and continues to gain traction in the HPC community. In addition to HPC-optimized container runtimes, technologies like Kubernetes create a new set of opportunities and challenges. While adoption is growing, questions regarding best practices, foundational concepts, tools, and standards remain. Our goal is to promote the adoption of these tools and introspect the impact of this new ecosystem on HPC/AI use cases. This workshop serves as a key venue for presenting late-breaking research, sharing experiences and best practices, and fostering collaboration in this field. Our eighth workshop iteration will continue to emphasize real-world experiences and challenges in adopting and optimizing these new approaches for HPC and AI.

events.title: HPC Systems Professionals Workshop (HPCSYSPROS26)
events.description:
The complexity of high performance computing (HPC) systems necessitates advanced techniques in system administration, configuration, and engineering and with staff who are well-versed on the best practices in this field. HPC systems professionals include system engineers, system administrators, network administrators, storage administrators, and operations staff who face problems unique to HPC systems. The ACM SIGHPC SYSPROS Virtual Chapter, the sponsor for this workshop, has been established to provide opportunities to develop and grow relationships focused specifically on the needs of HPC systems practitioners and to act as a support resource for them to help with the issues encountered in this specialized field.

This workshop is designed to share best practices for common HPC system deployment and maintenance, to provide a platform to discuss upcoming technologies, and to present the state-of-the-practice techniques that increase performance and reliability of systems, and in turn increase researcher and analyst productivity.

events.title: Workshop on High Performance Fabrics for AI and HPC
events.description: As computing demands surge for AI and HPC applications, networking becomes essential for performance and scaling. AI and HPC fabrics are used in scale-up and scale-out communications. This workshop will cover innovations in AI/HPC fabric architecture, network transport, load balancing, congestion control, network resilience, and network visibility. The workshop will further focus on Ethernet technologies for AI and HPC including Scale-Up Ethernet Transport (SUE-T), Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN), Ultra Ethernet, advanced congestion control, lossless transport mechanisms, telemetry, and fabric management.

events.title: Opening Invited Talk: Tightly Coupled and Customizable Heterogeneity
events.description:
The slowing of Moore’s Law and the rapid growth of AI are pushing systems toward greater specialization across compute, memory, networking, and storage. At the same time, AI for Science is bringing simulation, analytics, training, inference, and agentic execution into increasingly connected workflows that need to share and move data efficiently. No single architecture is well suited to every part of these workflows.

This talk looks at tightly coupled and customizable heterogeneity as a way to build systems around these changing needs. A key focus will be macroheterogeneity, where different computing architectures work together as part of a larger system and each part of a workflow can run where it fits best. We will also look at customizable scale-up hypernodes, bringing compute, memory, accelerators, and high-bandwidth fabrics together in configurations shaped by workload needs. The goal is not simply to add more forms of heterogeneity, but to make them easier to couple, customize, and use as part of an end-to-end AI-HPC system.

events.title: Super(comptuing) Heroes
events.description: Members of underrepresented groups often lack access to role models within their minority. The HPC community is still predominantly male, making it difficult for young women to find female “superheroes” to identify with. Such role models are crucial for career planning and guidance. This session aims to provide especially women with the opportunity to meet influential, well-recognized female HPC “superheroes” from academia, research labs, HPC centers and industry. Join us to be inspired and find relatable role models as we work together to build a more inclusive and connected HPC community.

events.title: Plenary Talk: Jerry Chow
Invited Talk: Genesis Mission and the Next Generation of Verified Scientific Workflows
RSE-HPC Invited Talk
