events.title: Porting Codes to the NextSilicon Maverick-2 Dataflow Architecture: Early Experience, Best Practice and Performance
events.description: Porting parallel code to accelerators such as GPUs, FPGAs, or AI Accelerators often requires major changes. In contrast, the new NextSilicon Maverick-2 dataflow architecture and framework transparently accelerate OpenMP code without explicit offloading statements, offering a practical energy-efficient high-performance computing (HPC) platform. We present preliminary best practice, porting experience, and early performance results for the Maverick-2 architecture, its programming models, and the OpenMP-based code-to-device development workflow. The in-house proxy apps used in the benchmark cover several application domains typical for the tier-2 HPC system at NHR@ZIB: computational fluid dynamics, large-eddy simulations, molecular dynamics, and electronic structure theory.

events.title: HPC means Heterogeneity, Performance and Complexity
events.description:
The variety of applications using or seeking to use high-performance computing (HPC) resources is growing, as is their demand for computing power and data management. Meanwhile, the physical limits of Moore's law are prompting the development of new computing solutions, including a growing range of custom-designed processing units and accelerators, as well as emerging techniques such as quantum and neuromorphic computing. Data centres and HPC hosting sites face the challenge of designing systems that can meet the needs of diverse applications, integrate different processing technologies and minimize energy consumption and operational costs. This is resulting in increasingly heterogeneous system designs comprising multiple partitions or modules with different node architectures. However, such diversity also increases the complexity on the side of system operation, parallel programming, performance analysis, and application optimization.
This talk reviews current trends in the HPC landscape, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for the HPC/AI community.

events.title: Evolution of Python Compiler for GPUs
events.description: The Python programming language is famous for being highly productive and newcomer friendly but suffers runtime performance. Over the last decade, one attempt to close this performance gap is to build compilers for domain specific languages (DSL) and compile to native code. The LLVM/MLIR ecosystem has played a pivotal role in creating easy pathways for developers to build DSLs and become the dominant methodology for doing so. As GPUs have grown in complexity, Python DSLs have also become more popular leading to a new programming model, Tile Programming. These two trends have led to an explosion of Python DSLs. Join us as we talk about the Past, Present, and Future of Python compilers for GPUs.

events.title: The Relationship Between AI and Research Data Management
events.description:
With the scientific world focused on becoming ‘AI Ready’, a new opportunity has emerged: revisiting long-standing challenges and unmet needs in research data management and computation-heavy science. This talk examines that opportunity from two angles and the relative value propositions of both:
1. As newer AI technologies become more ubiquitous in science, what new approaches to research data management do they require?
2. How can research data management practices be applied to mine computational artifacts (e.g., benchmarks) for insight?

events.title: The NSF Leadership Computing Facility and the Rising Importance of Interconnects in the (AI+)HPC World
events.description: This talk will begin with updates on the deployment and early operations of the NSF's newest Leadership Computing and AI Inference systems. It will then discuss how the rise of the AI industry has Impacted the diversity and investment in interconnects in new AI and HPC platforms. Finally the talk will attempt to cover the ramifications of interconnect changes on old and new workloads.

events.title: On Big Data, Big Simulations, and Big plans for AI in Climate Sciences
events.description: Climate science is being transformed by the convergence of AI, simulations, and high-performance computing. This talk explores how data compression and representation learning can extract knowledge from massive climate datasets, how Gordon Bell Award-winning simulations are pushing the frontiers of weather and climate modeling, and how DaCe enables automatic optimization and differentiation of legacy Fortran codes for modern heterogeneous systems. Building on these advances, I will outline a roadmap toward an AI climate scientist: a system that unifies observations, simulations, scientific reasoning, and machine learning to accelerate discovery, formulate hypotheses, and ultimately become a collaborative scientific partner in understanding and predicting Earth's changing climate.

events.title: Orchestrating QCSC Workflows in Containerized HPC Environments
events.description:
Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) is emerging as a model for scientific discovery in which quantum processors work alongside HPC resources as part of larger computational workflows. Realizing this model requires more than access to a quantum processor: applications must coordinate heterogeneous resources, manage different execution environments and support workflows that span HPC schedulers, workflow managers and quantum execution layers.

In this talk, we present our work integrating openQSE and QCSC-Prefect to develop and orchestrate QCSC workflows. openQSE provides a software stack for integrating quantum resources into HPC environments, while QCSC-Prefect uses Prefect to orchestrate quantum and classical workflow stages. We use these components within a containerized development environment that supports workflow development, debugging and integration testing before moving to larger HPC systems and quantum resources.

We demonstrate this approach using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), a hybrid quantum-classical chemistry workflow that combines quantum sampling with classical processing and HPC-based diagonalization. Through this example, we illustrate how containerized environments can simplify workflow integration and validation while preserving flexibility in the underlying execution resources. We conclude with practical lessons and challenges from developing and validating the SQD workflow across the heterogeneous quantum and HPC execution stack.

events.title: Enabling Performance Isolation for Co-scheduled Workflows
events.description: Heterogeneous systems such as NVIDIA GH200 and GB200 pair powerful GPUs with substantial CPU capacity, but GPU jobs targeting these systems frequently leave much of the CPU capacity idle, lowering CPU utilization and overall system throughput. Co-scheduling CPU workloads alongside GPU jobs improves resource utilization, but can introduce interference and undermine performance predictability. We present a proof of concept for co-scheduling CPU and GPU jobs on GH200 nodes with hardware-enforced resource isolation using Arm Memory System Resource Partitioning and Monitoring (MPAM) for CPU, L3-cache, and memory bandwidth and InfiniBand QoS for host network traffic. We augment existing resource isolation mechanisms in Slurm to allocate jobs to dedicated CPU and GPU "shards" with allocations for compute cores, L3-cache, memory bandwidth, and network bandwidth. This proof-of-concept implementation provides a practical framework for evaluating co-scheduled workloads with hardware-enforced resource isolation and establishes an operational model for multi-tenant co-scheduling on heterogeneous HPC/AI nodes.

events.title: Wafer Scale Acceleration of Unstructured Finite Element Methods
events.description: Finite element simulations on unstructured meshes require high performance and bandwidth to solve realistic problems. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) represents a paradigm shift in large-scale compute acceleration, integrating 900,000 processing elements (PEs) on a single device. While prior work has demonstrated strong performance for structured stencils on the WSE, FEM on unstructured meshes remains largely unexplored, owing to the dissonance between its irregular connectivity patterns and the WSE's structured dataflow model. We present an architectural mapping that reconciles the disparate mesh structures of the target architecture and application. For the heat equation, we demonstrate near-ideal weak scaling up to the wafer scale and sub-linear cost with increasing per-PE workload, showing the architecture's advantages for structured stencils extend to irregular connectivity. We establish unstructured FEM as a workload that wafer-scale architectures can serve, and identify per-PE capacity, rather than irregularity, as the constraint that governs how far the approach extends.

events.title: Future directions from NSF's Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure
events.description: In this talk Katie Antypas, Senior Science Advisor for Cyberinfrastructure at the US National Science foundation with provide an update and future directions for computing, data infrastructure, coordination services for HPC systems, software and workforce development infrastructure from the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure. She will also provide an update on the NAIRR: a Super Intelligence Infrastructure for Science and the newly awarded NAIRR Operations Center.

events.title: Exhibitor Lounge
To SIMD Or Not To SIMD: Comparing RVV vs. CGRA SoCs For Non-Linear Functions In AI
events.description:
Non-linear functions are an important class of operations in modern large language models, yet chip vendors have so far relied on traditional vector or
scalar units for them, whose performance has not kept pace with the matrix
multiplication units (MMUs) now found in high-performance and edge devices from
almost every vendor. Reconfigurable units such as FPGAs and CGRAs have been
proposed, but never systematically compared against traditional units backed by
MMUs. We build two SoCs, one with an RVV vector processor and one with a
elastic CGRA, each coupled with an MMU and driven by a
single-core CPU. For FFNs, we find
the CGRA shows maximum speedup in clock cycles of 7.12x over RVV for the activation of
simple point-wise functions like SiLU, whereas RVV shows up to
9.8x over the CGRA on complex functions such as softmax; over the
enclosing feed-forward block the corresponding maxima are 3.16x and 4.24x.

events.title: Plenary Talk: Tanner Crowder
A Tool Infrastructure for Runtime Correctness Checking of Device-Initiated Multi-GPU Communication
Operationalizing Workflow Support on Slurm: A Site Toolkit for Choosing Nextflow Deployment Strategie
events.description: Workflow-manager deployment choices determine which Slurm objects exist, how much controller load a workflow creates, and where accounting, policy, and failure isolation apply. We present an operator-run toolkit that freezes site and workload state, executes clean-start trials, attributes RPC demand to the benchmark identity, validates scientific completion, audits the campaign, and produces offline analyses. We apply it in three replicates to native Slurm, job arrays, HyperQueue, and Flux using a real 4,823-task Nextflow alignment workload on ASU’s Phoenix production cluster, with a private Dev cluster providing co-tenancy-free context. On Phoenix, arrays reduced both walltime and attributable RPC demand in every paired comparison while retaining per-element Slurm control. Flux reduced RPC demand further but ran longer than arrays; HyperQueue’s fastest median was not stable across replicates or clusters. We provide a constraint-first decision procedure, deployment configurations, and operational guidance for selecting a defensible site default.

events.title: Past the FLOPS Era: Memory-Bandwidth Disaggregation as a Design-Space Coordinate for LLM Accelerators
events.description: LLM accelerator design inherited FLOPS-era HPC assumptions that today’s production serving no longer satisfies, foremost one high-bandwidth pool sized for weights. Key/value cache bandwidth demand overtakes weights at deployment batch sizes. We characterize accelerators by two bandwidth scalars (βw ,βs) and workloads by state-to-weight ratio ρ(n) and weight reuse r. Per decode latency splits across the two pools, and a local-minimum theorem proves the shared-pool corner strictly dominated past b·ρ(n) = 1, with the penalty at most 2×. The two-tier gain at equal cost rises from 1.6% at the balance point to 34% at 512K context, while one compromise design recovers 3.9%. Only 0.11% of the feasible designs in a 1,270,129-point space come within 10% of optimal. The contribution is a coordinate system in which memory-centric codesign can be reasoned about in hardware terms, not only at the serving layer: how the optimum migrates with context, and the trade-offs induced.

events.title: Building a Kubernetes-first, sovereign HPC system: OpenCUBE
events.description: Based on the need to define a vendor-neutral deployment-ready platform for European hardware we set out develop a software stack for system and user management, promoting performance, energy efficiency, and programming efficacy in a heterogeneous computing system. We will report on how the OpenCUBE testbed system is now using OpenCHAMI, Talos, and the Slingshot network, together with classic storage as well as OpenFAM, to implement an ‘everything is a container’ k8s-based environment on SiPearl’s Rhea processor and Semidynamic’s RISC-V accelerator bitstream (EPAC2).

events.description:
Embedding ‘Green Skills’ in our Day-to-day Work - Weronika Filinger, Edinburgh Parallel Computing Centre
Supporting HPC Research Software Engineers Across the UK: The HPC RSE SIG - Tuomas Koskela, University College London (UCL)

events.title: A Highly Optimized Double-Word Arithmetic Implementation using Versal DSPs
events.description:
Scientific applications often require high-precision floating-point operations.
Modern FPGAs provide dedicated hardware for single-precision (FP32) multiply-accumulate operations, but double-precision (FP64) still requires costly implementations using lookup tables (LUTs).
As an alternative to FP64, double-word arithmetic can nearly double the precision of FP32 using only single-precision instructions.
In double-word arithmetic, a number is represented as a pair of FP32 values, which is carefully normalized so that its two components never overlap.

This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first implementation of double-word arithmetic on FPGAs. We develop both an HLS-based and a hand-optimized implementation.
Our hand-optimized implementation fully exploits the functionality available in the DSP blocks, requiring zero LUTs or flip-flops for multiplication and almost no LUTs or flip-flops for addition.

We evaluate our double-word implementation by comparing to HLS and vendor provided IP, then demonstrate it to be a viable alternative to FP64 on modern FPGA.

events.title: Slingshot as a First-Class Kubernetes Resource: Bare-Metal RDMA for Multi-Tenant AI
events.description:
AI and HPC increasingly demand interconnects that are simultaneously high-performance, open, and cloud-native. HPE’s Ethernet-based Slingshot fabric substantially shaped the
Ultra Ethernet Consortium’s 1.0 transport, establishing it as a proven foundation for open, standards-based RDMA. Exposing its kernel-bypass RDMA plane to multi-tenant, bare-metal
Kubernetes is non-trivial: the fabric lives outside conventional Linux networking, and NIC particularities such as resource pools must be accommodated. Prior approaches depend on brittle, loosely-coupled external device plugins, chained CNI plugins, controllers, and databases. Building on a deployment on Isambard-AI, the UK’s sovereign AI Research Resource, we present a Cray eXascale Interconnect (CXI) Dynamic Resource Allocation
(DRA) driver making Slingshot devices first-class, scheduler-visible Kubernetes resources. It enables declarative, topology-aware allocation and native multi-tenant isolation without privileged pods, and coordinates cluster-wide Virtual Network Identifier lifecycle
through namespace attachment. We evaluate distributed LLM-serving workloads, demonstrating bare-metal RDMA performance with secure isolation within a Trusted Research Environment.

events.title: Reducing Confusion and Broadcasting Understanding: An Empirical Study of the Semantics of NCCL
events.description: We present a foundation for formalising the semantics of NCCL, the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library. NCCL is a key component in distributed machine learning and HPC stacks that utilise NVIDIA GPUs. By combining analysis of the official documentation with empirical testing of the library, we present several key insights that characterise the concurrent programming model of NCCL. This includes the introduction of the concept of command matching, and novel explanations of the conditions under which undefined behaviour may be observed.

events.title: Benchmarking Agentic AI Workflows with Charliecloud
events.description:
Agentic AI workflows are an emerging paradigm in the AI space that enable autonomous agents
to drive the traditional prompt token response through multi-step reasoning, tool calling, and
planning phases. Recent advances to orchestrate production level frameworks such as these
are trending towards using LLM inference engines such as vLLM and model abstraction layers like LiteLLM. Charliecloud enhances this work by leveraging portability across diverse HPC
systems. In this talk, we address why such frameworks are leveraging these tools with
Charliecloud and how we can assess end-to-end performance of these workflows through
benchmarking.

Tighter error bounds using structural floating-point properties and tail bounds
events.description: Traditional deterministic error analysis provide worst case error bounds and prior work on probabilistic error analysis do not model structural floating-point properties, leading to looser bounds for cancellation heavy cases. In this work, we use hybrid error analysis to provide tighter error bounds for long summation and dot product numerical kernels. We extend the FPChecker tool to track global and local rounding error to compute key statistics related to structural floating-point properties, such as the Sterbenz lemma, which is used to compute modified Bernstein's tail bound. We then compare our derived error bound with Higham and Mary's probabilistic error bound and show that our bound faithfully models the structural floating-point behavior. Finally, we show the applicability of the derived bounds on a physical example of computing the magnitude of Fourier modes for density wave function used in compressible-flow simulations.
