events.title: Energy-Efficient Streaming FPGA Accelerator for DeepSeek Sparse Attention Decode
events.description: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces long-context inference cost by scoring all cached tokens and attending only to the top-$k$. At batch one, however, GPUs execute this operation inefficiently because its dependent scan, exact selection, and irregular gather provide insufficient parallelism. For exact per-query DSA, we show that the bottleneck is primarily architectural: after eliminating host-side kernel-launch overhead, the kernel reaches at most 1.19% of GPU INT8 peak across 4K--128K contexts. We present a streaming FPGA accelerator that fuses index generation and sparse attention while retaining intermediates on chip. It reduces per-head scores immediately, finds the exact top-$k$ threshold by counting rather than ranking, and fetches each selected key/value vector once for all heads. On AMD Alveo U55C, post-route power is \SI{11.324}{\watt}; against an RTX 6000 Ada running the quantized kernel, it achieves $8.0$--$10.2\times$ lower energy and $3.9$--$6.4\times$ lower energy--delay product.

events.title: CoDISAR: A Composable Disaggregated Infrastructure for SAR Backprojection
events.description: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is a remote sensing technology, used on moving platforms such as aircraft. Challenges arise when generating high-resolution images due to the computational complexity of image formation algorithms. Traditional approaches generate the images offline or deploy high-throughput hardware onboard the aircraft. Onboard compute is restricted by drone constraints including size, weight, and power. We propose CoDISAR, a solution where accelerators are distributed in the field, accessible via composable disaggregated infrastructure. This enables drone swarms to support high-resolution SAR imaging in near-real time, where drones can request GPUs from pools of resources. We examine the effects on time-to-image for the backprojection algorithm using distanced accelerators. Network latencies attributed to distances of up to 1000 km are inserted to evaluate the performance of CoDISAR against typical compute resources available on drones. Modeling indicates that our solution can generate high-resolution images up to 5x faster over classical methods.

events.title: Orion: Observability framework for hybrid workflow-centric I/O monitoring in HPC systems
events.description: Scientific workflows depend on efficient data exchange, making practical, low-overhead I/O performance visibility essential for HPC optimization. Existing I/O monitoring tools force extreme choices, such as tracing all I/O events or using only coarse profiling, which either inflates data volume or hides attribution context. We design ORION, a workflow-centric I/O monitoring framework that enables users to dynamically choose temporal and spatial monitoring granularity for different regions. ORION provides multi-faceted I/O profiling across time, processes, and files at low overhead; captures critical I/O events in high-interest regions while preserving aggregated views elsewhere; and reconciles traces with profiles at 0.35M–1.15M events/s for scalable analysis. On large-scale workloads, including Montage and Llama fine-tuning, ORION Selective Aggregation identifies critical bottlenecks with 6.8×–36× fewer trace events at 100% ordered top-k severe-bottleneck accuracy, and is portable across two heterogeneous LLNL systems. These results demonstrate that adaptive-granularity monitoring makes high-fidelity I/O analysis practical at HPC scale.

events.title: OpenCHAMI for Deployment of Inference Services
events.description:
AI workloads at HPC sites increasingly expect Kubernetes, while traditional workloads still run under batch schedulers such as Slurm. Both layers are now shaped by vendors, so sites have good reason to keep control of the layer beneath them: how nodes are discovered, booted, configured and reassigned. If that layer is open and site-controlled, a site can change what runs on top without rebuilding its infrastructure.
This talk describes our use of OpenCHAMI, a community-governed, open-source system management platform, as that layer. Building on earlier work presented at SC25, where nodes are moved between Slurm and Kubernetes using kexec-based fast booting, we combined OpenCHAMI's discovery, boot and metadata services with a small set of custom OpenShift artifacts. This lets us add bare-metal nodes to an OpenShift cluster as workers on demand. The immediate goal is to shorten the time from idle hardware to a serving model, often called "time to first token." We also want the provisioning path to be independent of any single workload manager or Kubernetes distribution.
We will share the architecture, where the integration was simple and where it depended on distribution-specific pieces, and what that tells us about portability. We will close with ongoing work: extending the approach to other Kubernetes management stacks, and the experimental OpenCHAMI Operator, which runs the OpenCHAMI control plane itself as a Kubernetes-native resource.

events.title: Zero-Overhead Polymorphism on GPGPUs with LLVM Just-in-Time Compilation
events.description: An ahead-of-time compiler's ability to optimize strongly affects the runtime performance of an application, yet limited knowledge of runtime parameters restricts which optimizations it can apply. Just-in-time compilers can make more informed optimization decisions, but have seen limited adoption in high-performance computing due to build toolchain requirements and programming language restrictions. In this work, we use LLVM as a just-in-time compiler that can be tightly integrated into any application. We automatically specialize compute kernels by inspecting LLVM's intermediate representation to find simple loop-invariant conditionals, which we remove, and virtual function calls, which we inline. This suits C++ lambda functions better than previous work, which requires explicit annotation. We apply this method to a multiphysics simulation package that runs on general-purpose graphics processing units. This reduces iteration time by up to 35% by significantly simplifying control flow complexity of the compiled kernels and improves developer productivity through lower build times.

events.title: Algorithms & Applications
events.description:
This session highlights how quantum algorithms are being applied to real scientific problems in combination with large-scale classical computing. Speakers will present recent progress on end-to-end applications in areas such as chemistry, biomedicine, and materials science, with a focus on the role HPC plays in making these workflows practical, from pre- and post-processing to error mitigation and verification at scale. Rather than treating quantum hardware in isolation, the talks emphasize how algorithm design is shaped by the surrounding classical infrastructure, and what this means for the path toward utility-scale quantum-classical computing.

The session brings together perspectives from clinical research, a national HPC center, and quantum hardware vendors, offering a view of how applications are being developed across different platforms and institutions.

events.title: GPU-Aware h5py: A Pure-Python Extension for HDF5--GPU Data Movement
events.description:
GPU-accelerated scientific computing in Python needs to move data from
on-disk HDF5 files into GPU memory. We present a pure-Python extension
to h5py adding GPU-aware reading, writing, and reduction without
modifying its C extension or the HDF5 library. It carries h5py's
index-based, NumPy-style slicing unchanged from disk through host memory
to GPU-resident CuPy or PyTorch arrays, addressing a selection
identically regardless of the result's location. Internally, every
read, write, and reduction path pins host memory once, reuses it across
calls, and overlaps host-to-device transfer with the next piece's
storage read, optionally fusing a caller-supplied transform or reduction
into the same stream at no extra cost until the computation outweighs
the transfer. Measurements on real hardware show index-addressed reads
costing only for what is selected, host memory staying flat as dataset
size grows over an order of magnitude, and fused compute staying hidden
behind I/O until per-piece compute cost overtakes it.

events.title: Toward GPU-Resident Climate Models: A Feasibility Study on Lossy Compression for the Spherical Harmonic Transform’s Communication Bottleneck
events.description:
Operational pseudospectral atmospheric models such
as the ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) run today
almost exclusively on CPUs; GPU ports are under active
development but not yet used in production. These models rely
on the Spherical Harmonic Transform (SHT) to compute spatial
derivatives and to alternate between spectral and grid-space
representations. Each time-step requires forward and inverse
SHTs, and both passes depend on global pencil transposition:
row-wise/column-wise all-to-all collectives that redistribute multi-
dimensional arrays across compute nodes. While GPU floating-
point throughput has grown rapidly, inter-node network band-
width has not kept pace, and at large node counts these global
collectives dominate wall-clock time.
As an alternative to float16 truncation during communication,
we investigate GPU-resident lossy compression, a capability not
yet available to any operational CPU-bound pseudospectral model.
Using representative fields from the DYAMOND high-resolution
operational dataset as input, and combining measured GPU
compression throughput with SimGrid network simulation, we
show that ZFP at 16 bits per value (rate-16), about the same
storage budget as float16, matches the communication-time
reduction of float16 truncation while delivering approximately
1600× lower mean relative error. ZFP at 8 bits per value
(rate-8) achieves approximately 1.93× the speedup of float16
while retaining 4× lower mean relative error. We additionally
corroborate the simulated communication-time trend with real
measurements on the CPU partition of the CRESCO8 cluster.

events.title: Welcome Remarks
events.description: Welcome remarks from the workshop chairs.

events.title: Agentic Orchestration of HPC Applications in Cloud
events.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) are serving as a catalyst of change for research practices, influencing the daily lives of staff scientists, software engineers, and system administrators. Adopting LLM-based agents promises new degrees of autonomy, where categories of human work and decision making are replaced by goal-oriented systems. This transition necessitates novel architectural paradigms and solid understanding of the strengths and limitations of LLMs. In this work, we design agents to conduct the entire life-cycle of an HPC application experimental run in cloud -- creation and build of a container, deployment in Kubernetes, optimization, and orchestration of a scaling study. We execute the study for five well-known HPC applications to build multi-platform container images and optimize figures of merit across 21 instance types in Kubernetes. We present a successful agentic scaling study, designs that improve work time to completion, and suggested best practices for agentic design and collaboration.

events.title: Obleth: Fair Multi-Tenant LLM Serving for Self-Hosted Campus Infrastructure
events.description: LLMs are becoming more popular, and costs are continuing to rise. Many universities are looking to host LLMs on local infrastructure to meet compliance, cost, and data-sovereignty requirements. Most AI gateways assume a cloud-provider backend, one that handles seemingly unlimited connections and natively supports capabilities that many self-hosted models lack. This is why I created Obleth, a source-available AI gateway designed for locally hosted infrastructure. Obleth's standout features include: a weighted fairshare admission scheduler dividing inference capacity proportionally across tenants; a Slurm cluster provisioner for opportunistic compute on preemptible partitions with automatic preemption recovery; an auto router that selects the best available model from a registered fleet based on capability, capacity, and cost; runtime-configurable capability extensions (boons) for things like on-premise content policy enforcement and MCP tool integration; and per-request pipeline tracing requiring no external telemetry. We evaluate fairness guarantees and gateway overhead with an included reproducible benchmark harness.

events.title: Evaluating In-Network Collectives for AI/ML Workloads with ATLAHS
events.description: In-network collectives (INC) can accelerate many collective network operations by moving computations away from the CPU, either into the NIC or into switches. The benefits are reductions in both traffic and latency, at the cost of higher system complexity. Designers of AI/ML training and inference systems have to balance network costs and the performance impact of network features on current and potentially future workloads. The ATLAHS toolchain allows us to study the impact of latency, bandwidth, and topology changes on workload performance, while supporting simulations of unprecedented scale. In this work, we add INC support to ATLAHS and report the impact on collective performance for groups of up to 1024 ranks, and on Llama-2-7B training performance at up to 64 GPUs.

events.title: Effective Communication
events.description: Every early-career professional will have to effectively communicate results, challenges, and ideas during their career. Effective communication can be very challenging, but is a necessary skill that, when perfected, will bolster any early-career professional. In this session, we will first focus on how to craft an effective written abstract that conveys the main message to the reader with a short paragraph. Then, we will dive into how to structure an oral presentation for maximum effect with an audience.

events.title: WHPC Distinguished Speaker: From Silent 700s to El Capitan: Mentors and Community Made All the Difference
Evaluating Function-Level Accuracy and Performance of SIMD Math Libraries with FP32 Inputs
events.description:
SIMD math libraries are important building blocks for high perfor-
mance computer arithmetic. We evaluate unary IEEE 754 binary32
(FP32) AVX2 functions implementations from AOCL-LibM, GNU
libmvec, SLEEF, and Intel SVML. We exhaustively test every fi-
nite FP32 encoding against a 256-bit MPFR oracle. Most of the
functions achieve smaller error than the library-level bounds, but
several AOCL and SLEEF functions exceed stated accuracy bounds.
For performance evaluation, we identify and test data-dependent
performance paths from cheap SIMD execution to expensive fall-
backs. Cheap SIMD paths outperform matched scalar calls, but
expensive corrections can make vector functions slower than scalar
routines. This work fills a gap by providing the community with a
per-function, per-input reference for the accuracy and performance
of FP32 AVX2 math libraries.

events.title: SOO, MOO, and FOO: Transformer-Layer Execution on Ryzen AI NPUs
events.description: Consumer neural processing units (NPUs) make local large language model inference attractive, but limited resources make mapping transformer layers to them challenging. This paper categorizes and evaluates three ways to offload transformer layers on Ryzen AI NPUs. Single-operator offload (SOO) configures the NPU to execute one operation within a transformer layer. Multi-operator offload (MOO) submits an ordered list of operators to be executed sequentially on the NPU. We introduce fused-operator offload (FOO), which groups graph operators into subgraphs, maps their dataflows through the NPU, and adjusts the loop order to preserve intermediate data on-chip. Across encoder and decoder layers, FOO improves effective GFLOP/s over MOO and SOO by up to 2.22× and 6.30×, respectively. We further introduce a FOO method to speed up attention and feed-forward computations by 7.80× and 6.83×, respectively. Compared to the integrated GPU (iGPU), FOO improves energy efficiency by up to 9.15× higher effective GFLOP/s/W.

events.title: LinkPass: Transparent RDMA Link Failover and Recovery for Collective Communication
events.description: Optical links in high-bandwidth AI clusters are prone to failures from temperature, vibration, dust, and other factors, causing temporary or permanent disconnections or intermittent packet loss. In tightly synchronized distributed training, a single flapping link between a network interface card (NIC) and top-of-rack switch can stall every participating rank. We present LinkPass, a shim beneath the network-plugin interface shared by NVIDIA NCCL and AMD RCCL that transparently masks such failures. LinkPass uses an RDMA probe mesh to detect stalling links, fails traffic over across healthy NUMA-proximate NICs to avoid backup bottlenecks, and reverts traffic when the original NIC recovers. Operating entirely over standard InfiniBand Verbs, LinkPass is transparent to collective libraries and training code and agnostic to GPU and NIC vendors. Evaluations show that LinkPass prevents link flaps from crashing jobs, significantly increasing mean time between failures and reducing required checkpointing frequency.

events.title: Adaptive Block Mixed-Precision Cholesky Factorization for Large-Scale Space-Time Gaussian Processes
events.description: Gaussian process models underpin many environmental applications but are limited by the dense Cholesky factorization of an $N \times N$ covariance matrix that costs $O(N^3)$ operations and $O(N^2)$ memory. Low-precision arithmetic can reduce these costs, yet naive \fp{8}, half-, or single-precision Cholesky may fail on ill-conditioned covariance matrices because rounding destroys positive definiteness. We develop an adaptive block mixed-precision Cholesky factorization that partitions the covariance into blocks and assigns each the lowest precision satisfying a prescribed accuracy budget. A condition-number safety factor guarantees completion by preserving positive definiteness after rounding. Applied to a space-time Gaussian process for forecasting storm wind gusts over the northeastern United States, an extreme-weather forecasting task critical to hazard warning, the method scales to 131,589 observations on a single GPU, performs most arithmetic in \fp{8}, preserves the log-likelihood, and makes maximum-likelihood estimation practical at a scale beyond double precision while producing calibrated forecasts with predictive uncertainty.

events.title: GPUH5: A GPU-first I/O Library for Scientific Data
events.description: \I/O is a bottleneck in GPU-accelerated science, yet scientific data-format libraries run only on the host. A kernel cannot write where its data lives: it must exit and copy its array before HDF5 can run, so the write point becomes a kernel boundary. Systems that let a GPU initiate I/O give up the data model, emitting flat, untyped byte ranges. We present GPUH5, a GPU-first I/O library for persistent kernels. It keeps HDF5's hierarchical paths and chunked arrays, replacing the container format with a key-value store, so the host precomputes every chunk's key and an in-kernel write reduces to enqueuing a pointer, light enough that the producer holds 98.8% achieved occupancy. On a single-GPU Gray-Scott simulation writing 380 snapshots to NVMe, GPUH5 hides 96% of the I/O its synchronous twin exposes, finishing 1.9× faster than default HDF5.

events.title: Congestion-Aware Collective Communication for Composable Disaggregated GPUs
events.description: Traditional server-centric data center design relies on a fixed ratio of compute and memory, limiting adaptability to evolving workloads, particularly in AI. Composable Disaggregated Infrastructure (CDI) addresses this by enabling on-demand composition of disaggregated devices. We focus on the intersection of GPU disaggregation and MPI collective communications, introducing an emulation methodology that uses available hardware to emulate PCIe-based disaggregated GPUs. While high-end servers run collectives over high-bandwidth intra-node interconnects, PCIe-based disaggregated systems introduce congestion, making it challenging to identify the best-performing algorithm for each collective. We propose a congestion-aware scoring model that estimates congestion at step granularity and, grounded in a Hockney-based bandwidth model, predicts the absolute communication latency of each algorithm on different PCIe topologies. Experimental results show the model predicts absolute latency within an average accuracy of 94.73%, 93.25%, and 93.94% for Allgather, ReduceScatter, and Alltoall, respectively, providing an effective, profiling-free tool for algorithm selection in GPU-disaggregated systems.

events.title: DataCrumbs: Efficient Cross-Layer Data Capture for Explainable I/O Performance in HPC Storage Stacks
events.description: Modern scientific workloads move large data volumes through deep, complex I/O stacks in high-performance computing (HPC) systems. State-of-the-art tools such as Darshan capture API-level statistics describing what happened, not why, so performance variation is often dismissed as jitter without direct evidence. Emerging approaches such as eBPF enable fine-grained, low-overhead collection, but naively applied they produce overwhelming data volumes. We present DataCrumbs, an I/O monitoring tool that uses function probing to collect selective, fine-grained performance data across the full I/O stack, from user-space runtimes to kernel-space file-system paths, enabling explainable I/O analysis. DataCrumbs instruments 8,723 functions at only 0.1% profiling and under 3% tracing overhead, while a time-windowed, parallel event-association algorithm scales cross-layer root-cause analysis. Across four workloads, DataCrumbs exposes cross-layer insights invisible to user-space-only tools, including a tuned read-ahead insight that cuts Montage's POSIX I/O time by 1.35x. DataCrumbs thus enables selective, fine-grained, explainable I/O analysis for real HPC workloads.

events.title: A Probability-Based Static Analysis to Lower Overhead in Floating-Point Exception Detection in NVIDIA GPUs
events.description: Floating-point exceptions, including NaN, infinity, and division by zero, present significant challenges to GPU-accelerated programs. These exceptions can silently propagate in the programs, leading to inaccurate results that might go unnoticed. Existing tools like FPChecker and GPU-FPX detect these exceptions dynamically but impose significant run-time overhead, making them impractical for large-scale GPU applications. We propose a static analysis framework that allows selective instrumentation of only high-risk floating-point instructions in GPU programs. We achieve this selective instrumentation in two ways: first, by analyzing SASS files on a per-instruction basis, comparing IEEE 754 bit pattern exception probabilities with thresholds; second, by comparing propagated exception probabilities within basic blocks while traversing the data flow graphs. We evaluate our framework by testing 19 programs across four CUDA benchmark suites and demonstrate that our approach can eliminate certain checks with at least 90% exception detection coverage.

events.title: Rapid Dataflow Buffer Sizing for DNNs via Parallel RTL Control-Flow Simulation for FINN
events.description:
In dataflow architectures, first-in-first-out (FIFO) buffers decouple pipeline stages
working at different rates. Appropriately sizing FIFOs prevents deadlocks and sustains throughput, yet remains a difficult problem for automated deep neural network (DNN)-to-accelerator compilers. As DNNs increase in size and complexity, existing techniques suffer from excessive runtime, inaccurate results, or unacceptable manual modeling effort.

We present a FIFO sizing approach based on iterative simulation of mixed RTL/HLS black-box
designs. Two innovations manage the cost of cycle-accurate simulation: a resource-aware search algorithm that operates at memory-primitive granularity rather than
raw depth, minimizing simulation rounds; and a scalable, MPI-capable, massively layer-parallel simulation of only the control path, greatly accelerating individual runs.

Integrated into the FINN DNN-to-accelerator compiler and evaluated on a range of DNNs
against three existing techniques, the approach delivers near-optimal FIFO depths with guaranteed performance at an average of 2.88x the speed of the best competing approach offering the
same guarantees.

events.title: Sovereignty above the scheduler: pluggable site policies and a federated view for AI/HPC with Waldur
events.description:
Sovereign AI and HPC infrastructure requires that sites can enforce their own policies and replace underlying components without breaking their participation in federations.

We present the architecture of Waldur, an MIT-licensed allocation and accounting platform that serves as the allocation component of the EuroHPC Federation Platform and runs in production at sites including CSCS, Isambard-AI, Cambridge Dawn and the Estonian Government Cloud. Waldur separates two concerns that are often entangled. At the site level, a pluggable agent model lets each site map federated allocations onto its own backends (Slurm, Kubernetes, OpenStack or others) and apply local policies for account provisioning, quota enforcement, usage reporting and access rules. Scheduler choice and local governance thus remain site decisions. At the federation level, a common data model for projects, allocations, users and usage gives funders, allocation committees and users a single view across heterogeneous sites, without requiring those sites to adopt the same stack.

We discuss the design of the plugin boundary: what must be standardised for federation to work, what should stay site-specific, and how this boundary limits the impact when any one component changes its license or stewardship. We close with open questions on shared allocation and accounting standards across sovereign federations.

events.title: Multilingual GPU Communication Libraries with LLVM Bitcode and CUDA LTOIR
events.description:
GPU applications combine kernels produced by multiple compiler frontends with
production device libraries implemented in CUDA C++. Reimplementing libraries
per frontend is costly, especially communication libraries whose code depends
on host-created transport state. We show linkable device IR can serve as an
interoperability boundary for stateful GPU libraries without sacrificing
baseline performance. We package \nvshmem{} and \nccl{} implementations as
LLVM bitcode and CUDA LTOIR and consume them from CUDA C++, CUTLASS Python, and
numba-cuda-mlir. Across RMA benchmarks, packaged IR preserves latency and
bandwidth relative to conventional CUDA C++ linkage, reaching 98~GB/s. Across
both libraries, CUTLASS Python stays within 3.7\% of CUDA C++ latency and
delivers at least 90.7\% of its bandwidth, reaching \nccl{} bandwidth parity.
Fused GEMM+AllGather experiments show packaged communication IR composes with
tensor-core computation, while LTOIR remains within 0.57\% of baseline across
every tested \nccl{} shape. Results establish linkable device IR as a
performant multi-frontend library boundary.

events.title: No-Restart Elasticity in an Adaptive Runtime System for Cloud-Native HPC
events.description: Exploiting discounted spot instances for HPC requires changing an application's resource allocation at runtime, shrinking ahead of an interruption and expanding onto replacement capacity. Existing mechanisms implement rescaling as a full teardown and cold restart, where restart accounts for up to 95\% of the overhead, growing with node count and, on GPUs, with CUDA context initialization. We present a no-restart rescaling mechanism for Charm++ in which surviving processes never exit: it negotiates membership with a lightweight external coordinator, reconciles UCX endpoints with the new cluster view, and returns to the top of runtime initialization while preserving live application state. A rescaling operation costs 8--15\,ms on CPUs and 7--11\,ms on GPUs at 4--32 instances, two orders of magnitude below restart-based implementations. GPU device state persists in place, eliminating the checkpointing daemons previously required. End to end, eight simultaneous interruptions cost 0.2\% of runtime on CPUs and 0.6\% on GPUs.

events.title: HPC Infrastructure Management at Scale
events.description: HPC infrastructure management at scale depends on more than golden images: operators must build, version, and deploy the right operating-system image to the right node role safely, repeatably, and without interrupting running jobs. The HPC OS project replaces a Satellite-driven provisioning model, where behavior depended on Web UI host parameters and Ansible overrides, with a central patching source for on-premises clusters. Layered RHEL, Rocky Linux, and Ubuntu CPU/GPU images are built with Packer and Ansible, stored as versioned artifacts, tracked with release metadata, and deployed through MAAS, orchestration, and post-deploy Ansible. In scale testing across 300 CPU/GPU nodes, the most stable operating point was 100 concurrent deployments, driven by AWS SSM and Shell-specific tradeoffs rather than MAAS; Satellite stabilized at about 60 nodes. We present lessons for replacing build-centered automation with a reproducible image build and deployment platform for large HPC environments.

events.title: Comfort Dogs
Enabling Topology-Awareness for Performance Improvement: A Case Study with Trinetra-A HPC Network
events.description:
As HPC systems scale, the physical connectivity of
the underlying network plays an increasingly significant role in
application performance. The effectiveness of a parallel
application is strongly influenced by how well process placement
reflects the network topology.

This paper presents a methodology designed to enable
topology-aware process placement on Trinetra-A, a high-speed
switchless 3D torus network developed by C-DAC, highlighting
the key considerations and challenges involved in the process. Our
approach involves application communication analysis and a
process mapping framework that leverages existing process
mapping tools to implement topology-aware process placement.

We evaluate the methodology using MPI benchmarks and a
real application, achieving peak latency improvements of 89% for
MPI_Alltoall, 68% for MPI_Alltoallv and 8% for MPI_Allgather,
along with a 68% improvement in heFFTe application
performance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of
optimized placement on Trinetra-A and provide a reference that
can be readily adopted by HPC network developers.

events.title: Efficient Bayesian Spatially Clustered Factor Analysis with Adaptive Parallel Gibbs Sampling
events.description: Multivariate spatial data exhibit both spatial heterogeneity and spatial contiguity. Classical exploratory factor analysis (EFA), which assumes a globally homogeneous structure, is ill suited to capture these features. This paper proposes Bayesian spatially clustered factor analysis (BSCFA), which embeds a Bayesian approach within the spatially clustered factor analysis (SCFA) framework. BSCFA retains the spatially adaptive grouping mechanism of SCFA and shifts it from point estimation to posterior inference conditional on the estimated partition, providing conditional uncertainty quantification for group specific factor models given the final partition. In addition, conjugate priors introduce Bayesian regularization, which stabilizes group specific parameter estimation and is particularly beneficial when individual spatial groups contain limited samples. To overcome the computational burden of running full MCMC chains at each outer iteration, we develop a suite of optimization strategies including state projection, warm-start Gibbs sampling, adaptive short chain lengths, and group wise parallel execution, which collectively yield an approximately 23.6-fold speedup. Simulation studies demonstrate that BSCFA outperforms both EFA and SCFA in terms of loading covariance estimation accuracy and model selection criterion. Applied to built environment data from 1,535 stations in the Tokyo metropolitan area, BSCFA identifies spatially contiguous clusters with clear functional differentiation. The factor structures reveal regional variations in urban functionality, achieving a BIC reduction of 25.9% compared to SCFA and 31.2% compared to EFA.

events.title: Dynamic Planning for Scalable Data Movement in Accelerated Query Engines
events.description:
At scale, structured-data processing is often a data-movement problem. Joins and aggregations must choose whether to shuffle, broadcast, or reduce intermediate results,
and the right choice can depend on data properties that are hard to predict prior to execution. In this paper, we introduce dynamic planning, a query-optimization method that lets operators choose data-movement strategies at runtime. We have implemented this approach in GPU Polars, where RapidsMPF actors observe table chunks and exchange metadata before selecting a strategy. Controlled microbenchmarks and a PDS-H Q9 case study confirm that dynamic planning makes sensible runtime decisions while preserving both stability and performance.

events.title: PaFEx: Cross-platform Floating-point Exception Detection using LLVM and PAPI
events.description: Detecting floating-point exceptions defined by IEEE 754 across GPU vendors remains a conundrum, owing to varying hardware support for exception reporting. Existing tools address this problem through vendor-specific detection, requiring developers to use different tools to examine exception behavior on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. As HPC applications are deployed across different GPU architectures, this fragmentation limits the portability of diagnosing exceptions in GPU kernels. We present PaFEx, a cross-vendor tool that inserts runtime exception checks into GPU programs at the LLVM intermediate representation(IR) level. PaFEx runs on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, through shared exception checking logic, with vendor specific handling of device intrinsics and runtime integration. Across several HPC benchmarks, PaFEx incurs a geometric-mean slowdown of $1.30\times$ on NVIDIA and $1.70\times$ on AMD, measured over end-to-end execution. We also compare PaFEx with baseline tools, GPU-FPX and FloatGuard, examining similarities and differences in exception detection coverage and reporting.

events.title: High Speed Network Processing for Scientific Computing in the Open Cloud Testbed
events.description:
This paper presents an FPGA-based SmartNIC
architecture designed to address critical network challenges
in data-intensive scientific computing. As scientific workflows
increasingly demand high-bandwidth data movement and realtime
monitoring across wide-area networks, the Open Cloud
Testbed (OCT) provides an ideal platform for investigating
in-network processing solutions at line rate.

Our approach focuses on implementing network visibility, optimization,
and orchestration capabilities through FPGA acceleration.
The proposed system leverages P4-programmable dataplane
functions to support packet parsing, marking, telemetry
extraction, traffic steering, and machine learning inference—all
without requiring host CPU intervention or modifications to application
servers.

Our framework integrates SciTags, which associates network traffic with
scientific context through packet marking. Our
high-performance network bridge counts packets by their
SciTag values, as identified in the IPv6 Flow Label.
Experiments on AMD U280 FPGAs in OCT
demonstrates the feasibility of this approach, showing imperceptible
processing latency and line-rate packet handling, while
accurately monitoring scientific data flows.

events.title: RDMA control over lossy Ethernet: A new approach using synchronized clocks
events.description: Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) underpins storage and increasingly AI systems, reducing transfer latency and host CPU overhead. Traditional deployments rely on lossless fabrics, using priority flow control, credit-based flow control, congestion notification, and substantial switch memory for skid buffers. Can RDMA operate over lossy Ethernet at a single priority without in-network enhancements? Rather than implementing sophisticated loss recovery on RDMA-capable NICs, we explore end-to-end congestion control driven by one-way delay measurements. Pervasive software clock synchronization enables senders and receivers to estimate path congestion by subtracting send timestamps from receive timestamps and use these estimates to pace transmissions. Evaluations demonstrate sub-microsecond delay measurement accuracy, enabling fine-grained RDMA control. RDMA achieves near-zero packet loss and queueing delay over lossy Ethernet while coexisting harmoniously with legacy TCP traffic. These results establish delay-based, end-to-end congestion detection and mitigation as a compelling alternative to conventional in-network mechanisms for supporting RDMA on shared Ethernet fabrics.

events.title: Impact of Overheads in Disaggregated Systems on Job Turnaround Times
events.description: Disaggregated systems dynamically attach accelerators to and detach them from compute nodes over a network. They can thus allocate the exact number of accelerators requested by each job, reducing idle accelerators. However, resource disaggregation incurs two overheads. The communication latency between compute nodes and accelerators increases the execution times of jobs, and the reconfiguration to attach and detach accelerators takes time. These overheads may make job turnaround times longer, but their effects remain unclear. We investigate their effects using a scheduling simulator, which we developed for disaggregated systems. The results show that an approximately 20% increase in execution times, reconfiguration times of 90 seconds or longer, and a shortage of accelerators make turnaround times longer than those in traditional systems. We also show that introducing fixed compute nodes, to which accelerators remain attached and require no reconfiguration, reduces turnaround times. We finally summarize considerations for administrators adopting disaggregated systems.

events.title: Probe Less, Learn More: Characterizing and Correcting eBPF Instrumentation Overhead
events.description: We demonstrate that although eBPF and bpftrace are widely used for low-overhead tracing, their overheads are large when considering microsecond-scale events. We decompose these overheads into two parts that were not considered separately by prior work: a fixed floor paid for every probe that fires, and per-operation work layered on top. We measure these overheads on a controlled single-syscall harness, then characterize how overheads scale as probes accumulate: overhead is driven by the number of distinct events that fire (~42 ns each), not by the number of probe definitions (~3 ns per additional probe on an already-traced event). For example, a bare probe costs ~50 ns while a single map update or timestamp adds 100–300 ns. From these measurements we derive an observability budget that predicts, before any probe is attached, how much a proposed trace will distort its target and therefore how faithfully the event can be observed.

events.title: Short Break
RSE-HPC Short Break
Parameterized Verification of Deterministic MPI Programs
events.description: We consider the problem of verifying a message passing program in which the number of processes is a parameter NP and each process knows its unique ID. Processes communicate using send and receive commands which specify a single destination or source. To verify the program, the user provides functions specifying the number of messages sent from process i to process j, the level of each communication event in the happens-before hierarchy, and a fact that holds for the k-th message sent from i to j. These are used to transform the program to a parameterized sequential program which can be verified using any techniques appropriate for such programs. We realize this approach in an extension to Frama-C/Wp to verify C/MPI programs.

events.title: RSE-HPC Panel: Meeting RSE Challenges
events.description:
Hannah Cohoon, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

Thomas Flynn, Durham University

Helen Kershaw, National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)

events.title: Profiling and Optimization Opportunities for SmartNIC-Assisted MoE Inference
events.description: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models improve capacity through sparse expert activation but introduce bursty all-to-all communication and rank-level imbalance during inference. We profile decode-stage Mixtral-8x7B inference on a 4-GPU vLLM data- and expert-parallel setup and observe up to 3.63 ms expert-compute rank skew. We propose a SmartNIC-assisted dispatch design with destination batching, expert-aware admission, blocked-chunk reordering, and credit-based dispatch. A deterministic C++ simulator shows that the full policy reduces average expert-flow-chunk latency by 17.1% and packet count by 74.9% on the profiled workload, with 8.6–18.9% latency reduction across nine routing and arrival workloads. We further implement a trace-driven FPGA/HLS prototype on an AMD/Xilinx U280. A 1,024-chunk board-level replay executes without runtime errors and exactly matches simulator chunk records, demonstrating implementability of the proposed scheduling kernel.

events.title: AI4S and Sovereign Supercomputing in Japan
events.description:
In December 2025, the Japanese government adopted its first AI Basic Plan under the AI Promotion Act, positioning AI research and development, including the computing infrastructure behind it, as a national priority. In line with this, MEXT is promoting AI for Science (AI4S) and strengthening Japan’s computing infrastructure for it through two major initiatives. First, the RIKEN Center for Computational Science (R-CCS) introduced RIKYU in 2026, a supercomputer for AI4S development with 1,600 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. RIKYU complements Fugaku in developing and applying scientific foundation models, and its resources are also available to MEXT’s AI4S research programs, including ARiSE and SPReAD1000.
Second, MEXT’s FY2025 supplementary budget supports four university centers that provide National Infrastructure Systems (NIS) in HPCI, the framework for sharing computing resources across Japanese universities and research institutes, to expand shared GPU resources and make their use more efficient for AI4S. The four centers at Hokkaido Univ., Univ. of Tsukuba, UTokyo, and Kyushu Univ. have agreed to share operational know-how and standardize practices, and UTokyo will serve as an HPCI hub that links jobs across resource-providing centers.
This talk presents both efforts and discusses how national infrastructure for AI4S can be operated and shared across institutions.

events.title: Bringing OpenACC to LLVM’s Offload Stack: Dialect Contracts, Lowering Boundaries, and a First-Class ACC Runtime
events.description: OpenACC support in LLVM spans Flang and Clang frontends, an MLIR acc dialect with in-dialect transforms, and an offload runtime. Frontends already lower directives into acc IR. This paper presents the dialect design and IR contracts that keep transforms frontend-agnostic via type and operation interfaces rather than source-language IR. The mid-level form lets the compiler discover OpenACC's implicit aspects, notably data attributes and parallelism. We describe the compiler-runtime boundary: what MLIR decides versus what the runtime ABI must understand, including non-contiguous values whose layout is deferred to the runtime. We then present libacctarget, an OpenACC runtime in LLVM Offload that shares infrastructure with libomptarget via libompaccsupport while owning ACC-specific mapping, reference counting, async queues, and map kinds. We evaluate a Fortran-first path: a derived-type field-section case study, SPECaccel measurements of implicit data and late privatization, and the OpenACC VV suite as a probe of contracts that execute end to end

events.title: QC-HPC Ecosystem
events.description:
This session explores how the quantum-HPC ecosystem is taking shape from the vendor and technology-provider side. Speakers will share how their platforms, runtimes, and system software are being designed to integrate quantum processors into existing HPC environments, from job scheduling and resource management to GPU-accelerated classical computing and hybrid programming models. The talks emphasize practical integration paths: what is already working in production, what interfaces and standards are emerging, and where the remaining gaps lie.
The session brings together perspectives from GPU and accelerator providers, HPC software developers, and quantum hardware vendors, offering a view of how the building blocks of a quantum-classical computing stack are coming together across the industry.

events.title: GDSight: Per-Operation Cross-Layer Attribution for GPUDirect Storage
events.description: GPUDirect Storage (GDS) copies NVMe data into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU data path and the identity linking an operation to the device work it causes. To our knowledge, no external GDS tool attributes a device command to its causing application operation: cuFile stops at the call, counters report only aggregates, and time-based matching fails once submission is asynchronous, even at one operation in flight. We present GDSight, which attributes each NVMe command to the operation that caused it, whether it entered cuFile or fell back to POSIX. Using eBPF, it matches commands by timing and by physical address, and only address survives asynchrony. On unmodified KvikIO, NIXL and HDF5 we pin pathologies to their cause: a silent bypass cuFile’s counters miss, 4× device amplification, and 22× tail inflation. We show that each diagnosis resolves to a measured intervention, worth up to 17× where throughput is the limit, or none.

events.title: Building a Local Chapter as Civic Infrastructure: Chicago Women in HPC and the Quantum × HPC Pathways Initiative
Characterizing LLM Inference Performance on a WebAssembly Runtime
events.description: WebAssembly (WASM) has drawn attention as a portable binary format and a promising substrate for AI workloads. Delegating computation to a native backend through wasi-nn promises portability with native speed, yet to our knowledge this approach has not been evaluated quantitatively for LLM inference. We compare LlamaEdge, a WASM-based LLM runtime, with native llama-cli on a multi-socket node, aligning backend, build settings, and prompts so that only the execution environment differs. Across 1B–8B models, thread counts, context lengths, and GPU offload ratios, performance is equivalent under full GPU offload, while CPU-only execution shows a gap of up to 1.38×. We attribute this gap primarily to the in-page offset of the work buffer, set by the host-side allocation path, rather than WASM overhead. Confining cores and memory to one node reduces the gap to 1.07–1.13×, and allocating the work buffer from the main heap narrows it further to 1.02–1.04×.

events.title: Ops Knowledge That Stops Evaporating: Building an Evergreen Documentation, Search, and Monitoring System on an Agent CLI
events.description: Operational knowledge in HPC has a half-life measured in shifts. Queries get re-derived, negative results re-litigated, and incident reports cannot be reproduced months later. We describe a small, vendor-neutral system deployed at a large GPU-cluster site, and how to build your own in four weeks. Six pieces, five most sites already have: a terminal-native agent CLI, Model Context Protocol servers exposing telemetry read-only, versioned markdown procedures, a git repository, a local search index, and a few hundred lines of generator code. The load-bearing idea is not the model; it is a write-back rule under which any agent reading the knowledge verifies and extends it in the same task. The same repository distributes it: stable procedures become versioned skills, shipped to the team as a plugin through pull requests. A second-order effect surprised us: when a monitoring page costs a minute, dashboards become disposable. We close with anti-patterns and limits.

events.title: Workload-Derived Requirements for Reconfigurable AI/HPC Fabrics
events.description: Rack scale AI and HPC systems combine accelerators with high bandwidth fabrics but often impose fixed resource ratios and communication domains. We evaluate eleven applications and two bounds across training, inference, molecular dynamics, linear algebra, and graph analytics while varying host resources, accelerator count, and connectivity. Fabric sensitivity differs sharply. Disabling peer to peer communication reduces all to all bandwidth by 36.1× and all reduce by 16.3×; HPL fails to initialize and training slows 2.23×, while GPU HPCG and DeepDriveMD are unaffected. These results motivate software composition for resource changes and live optical reconfiguration for connectivity changes without destroying state. Our prototype matches native bandwidth, but state reconstruction adds substantial delay. Dynamic composition surpasses static goodput near 72 second idle windows and reaches 1.34× at 160 seconds. Reconfigurable fabrics therefore require topology, opportunity duration, predictability, and state preservation.

events.title: Portable, High-Performance and Differentiable Ocean Simulations with Unstructured Grids in Julia
events.description:
Ocean models are increasingly required to be two things at once: performance-portable
across heterogeneous accelerators, and differentiable, so that adjoint sensitivities are available for state estimation, parameter calibration, and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we introduce a software package for simulating the ocean system with these attributes, implemented in Julia. Anonymized.jl is a shallow-water ocean dynamical core discretized with the TRiSK scheme on unstructured Voronoi meshes, following the MPAS-Ocean software written in Fortran. Anonymized.jl is designed to run on CPUs and GPUs with architecture-independent kernel implementations and supports differentiable programming. Here, we describe the implementation of two configurations within Anonymized.jl and benchmark their performance on different accelerator devices.

events.title: Towards Server-Grade Device Pooling over Routable PCIe with Improved and Scalable Systems Software
events.description: Routable PCIe enables composable infrastructures and device pooling with native drivers, yet little is known about its end-to-end performance in production systems, leaving a gap between microbenchmark research and marketing whitepapers. We show routable PCIe challenges assumptions made by traditional operating systems, particularly in how DMA buffers are managed when accessed by remote devices. We resolve a cache incoherence issue in the IOMMU's interrupt remapping subsystem and adapt IOMMU scalability optimizations from the OS kernel to routable PCIe software, reducing median DMA deallocation latency by 90% versus prior work and enabling full parallelism for pooled devices. We further optimize the deallocation critical path via a novel IOMMU sidecore-offloading scheme, reducing median unmapping latency by 26% and tail latency by up to 89% compared to the kernel. Finally, we evaluate on server-grade storage and GPUs, showing routable PCIe achieves native IOPS at lower latency and CPU utilization than scale-out alternatives.

events.title: PInsight: Enabling In-Situ Performance Analysis for Parallel Applications
events.description:
Performance analysis of parallel HPC applications is today a
post-mortem workflow: measurement data is collected during a
run, then moved and analyzed after the application terminates,
and each tuning hypothesis costs another full execution. In this
paper, we present PInsight (Performance Insight), a frame-
work that leverages this iterative structure to enable in-situ
performance analysis of applications spanning MPI, OpenMP,
CUDA, and HIP in a single time-aligned trace. PInsight combines
asynchronous tracing via LTTng with rate-controlled per-region
sampling measurement, under a four-mode domain architecture
with fine-grained filtering, tracing windows, node-level GPU
activity policies, and runtime reconfiguration without application
restart. Its analysis toolkit, both scripts and GUI, can consume
the traces both post-hoc and in situ: window-end actions rotate
the trace and launch analyses during execution with sub-second
pause, turning a long-running application into a sequence of
measure–analyze windows

events.title: Verification of PETSc with CIVL using LLM-generated ACSL contracts and deterministic driver generation
events.description:
PETSc is widely used in science and engineering applications where wrong results can have costly consequences. Despite this, numerical libraries are rarely formally verified. One challenge
is the need for an expert to hand-write a specification and verification driver, which can introduce additional bugs. With modern large language models (LLMs), it is tempting to generate
drivers and reference models automatically, but one-shot generation is brittle and produces unverified code that must be audited. We present an approach that uses LLMs in a limited setting
to generate a small, human-certifiable ACSL contract from a function’s documentation. A deterministic toolchain supporting a restricted ACSL profile then generates a driver that uses CIVL to check the implementation against the contract. We demonstrate the pipeline end-to-end on three PETSc functions and discover a bug in MatAYPX.

events.title: GarageWork: A Shared Testbench Abstraction for Software Simulation and FPGA Testing
events.description: GarageWork is a lightweight FPGA testing framework that enables the same cocotb testbench to be used for both software RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated hardware simulation. A shared abstraction hides backend-specific interfaces, while synthesizable Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) dispatchers provide design-under-test (DUT)-specific control and test operations on the FPGA. GarageWork is intended for rapid bare-metal testing of standalone designs and on-chip processing logic for scientific sensors, rather than full SoC-level prototyping. The framework has been validated on AMD Alveo V80 FPGAs with several internal designs and provides initial support for AI-assisted generation of DUT-specific test components.

events.title: WHPC Global Activities and Efforts
Predict Before Replay: Joint FEC and Flight Control for Reliable Scale-Up Links
events.description: Scale-up accelerator fabrics send latency-sensitive flits over serial links at hundreds of gigabits per second. Their reliability pipeline first relies on FEC, then detects residual failures and replays unacknowledged data. At these line rates, delayed feedback lets later flits enter the replay window before a residual failure is reported, so standard replay can amplify one corrupted flit into a suffix retransmission. This paper presents PREFACE, a pre-FEC controller for temporally correlated burst errors. A two-state Bayesian filter converts corrected-symbol observations into a next-flit burst posterior and jointly selects FEC strength with an outstanding-flit cap. We implement PREFACE in ns-3 with publicly verifiable UALink 200G 1.0 replay semantics. PREFACE improves goodput by 10.52%, lowers P99 latency by 50.75%, cuts replay by 47.52%, and improves modeled ring AllReduce by 13.1–27.0%.

events.title: Stress-Testing Exascale Scientific Data Output - ADIOS2 Configuration Strategies for WarpX under Extreme Load Imbalance
events.description: Spatially imbalanced, temporally irregular simulation output challenges I/O configurations tuned for balanced workloads. This work evaluates ADIOS2 BP5 configurations through openPMD-api using WarpX on Frontier at ORNL and Perlmutter at NERSC, contrasting balanced 3D Cartesian output with boosted-frame back-transformed diagnostics (BTD). BTD combines rank-level output skew with snapshot contributions spanning multiple simulation steps. Balanced output reaches 3.64~TB/s without compression on 2,048 Frontier nodes and over 1~TB/s on 512 Perlmutter nodes; lossless Blosc2 compression achieves approximately 7~TB/s application-level effective throughput on Frontier. In the tested BTD configurations, SPAN combined with asynchronous writing provides the highest throughput on Frontier, FlattenSteps supports assembly of complete lab-frame snapshots for checkpointing without reader modification and with negligible write-time overhead and no penalty on read performance, and DataSizeBased aggregation improves throughput when subfile counts are constrained. These results identify complementary mechanisms for handling irregular output and provide configuration guidance for these workloads and systems.

events.title: Rapid Earthquake-to-Tsunami Waveform Generation via Large-Scale Multi-GPU FFT Convolution Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
events.description:
Data-driven methods for earthquake and tsunami early warning rely on large
ensembles of rupture scenarios and their resulting waveforms, but generating
such datasets with repeated high-fidelity seismic and tsunami simulations is
prohibitively expensive. We exploit the linear time-invariant structure of both dynamics to precompute elastic Green's functions and acoustic–gravity adjoint responses, reducing the source-to-waveform map to two consecutive %block lower-triangular Toeplitz matvecs.
convolution operators.
We evaluate these convolutions with a distributed, FFT-accelerated GPU pipeline that partitions the large seafloor grid across GPUs and directly generates the final observation waveforms.
We demonstrate the scalability of this pipeline for the Cascadia Subduction Zone with 963 subfaults, 2,416,530 seafloor grid points, 64 observation locations, and 256 timesteps, requiring 9.45~TiB of aggregate GPU memory. On 64 GB200 GPUs within one NVL72 domain, the pipeline generates waveforms in 24 ms per rupture once the response operators are resident, enabling large rupture ensembles to be evaluated within minutes.

events.title: BASE: A Reusable Streaming Preprocessing Accelerator for Heterogeneous FPGA Systems
events.description:
Modern heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) systems increasingly rely on FPGA-based accelerators to improve throughput and energy efficiency for data-intensive applications. However, many streaming workloads remain constrained by byte-level preprocessing and data movement, which can dominate end-to-end execution time.
This paper presents BASE (Byte-level Analytics and Statistical Engine), a reusable streaming preprocessing accelerator that integrates statistical feature extraction directly into the FPGA communication path. BASE performs single-pass histogram generation, entropy estimation, variance computation, and byte-transition analysis while data is transferred through the AXI DMA interface, overlapping preprocessing with communication and reducing host-side computation.
Using deployment-time FPGA bitstream screening as a representative workload, experiments on the ZCU104 show that BASE reduces preprocessing latency by 5.04× and improves end-to-end execution time by 4.23×. On the U55C, BASE achieves 1.32× preprocessing and 1.78× end-to-end speedups. These results demonstrate BASE’s potential as a reusable building block for streaming analytics in reconfigurable HPC systems.

events.title: Developing a Numerical Algorithm with CIVL Model Checking in the Loop
events.description: Verifying a numerical algorithm in a large scientific simulation is challenging: the framework is too big to model-check, and the unit tests exercise only sampled inputs. We report a case study developing a new cloud-in-cell (CIC) deposition algorithm for Flash-X, a multiphysics simulation framework, keeping the CIVL model checker in the loop. Rather than verify the algorithm within Flash-X, we extract only the interfaces the algorithm needs into a small, self-contained C model, and check the algorithm there. Treating particle positions as symbolic values, CIVL proves two physical properties---mass conservation and the deposition location---over the continuum of admissible positions, and verifies memory safety and freedom from MPI deadlocks and data races across rank distributions within bounds. Writing the verifying properties first and rechecking them at each stage turned CIVL into a design guardrail. It also surfaced a defect that our random-seed tests missed. We report its benefits, cost, and tradeoffs.

events.title: EESSI as a Vendor-Neutral, Community-Driven Stack for Heterogeneous HPC and Cloud
events.description:
Managing workloads across rapidly diversifying hardware—spanning x86, Arm, and emerging RISC-V CPUs alongside competing NVIDIA and AMD GPU architectures—demands a software infrastructure that is genuinely independent, vendor-neutral, and resilient against ecosystem lock-in.
This talk introduces the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI), a community-governed software stack designed to provide an autonomous, transparent foundation for heterogeneous scientific computing. Supported through the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking via the MultiXscale Centre-of-Excellence, EESSI delivers an on-demand, streaming distribution architecture (powered by CernVM-FS) that decouples scientific applications from specific host operating systems and single-vendor software ecosystems. By dynamically serving microarchitecture-optimized binaries across diverse CPU targets and GPU acceleration platforms without compromising performance, EESSI eliminates single-site redundancy and prevents vendor-driven stack fragmentation.

Ultimately, we demonstrate how establishing a shared, institutionally neutral software ecosystem ensures long-term scientific reproducibility, and returns software governance to the open scientific community.

events.title: GPU Code Generation for OpenACC Kernels construct in a Modern MLIR-Based Compiler
events.description: The OpenACC kernels construct asks the compiler to discover and exploit parallelism inside a region that may mix parallel and sequential loops, intervening sequential code, reductions, and control flow that can guard those loops. Mapping such regions to GPUs is harder than compiling the more prescriptive parallel construct: the compiler must decide where synchronization and launch boundaries fall, not only how to schedule a single nest. We describe an MLIR-based Fortran OpenACC pipeline with three strategies for kernels: (1) splitting kernels into sequenced host-side device launches; (2) a single cooperative grid with grid-scoped barriers; and (3) CUDA Dynamic Parallelism (CDP), launching child grids from a device driver kernel. The strategies share most of the parallelism-lowering stack and diverge on how nests are ordered, synchronized, and bridged. We detail their CUDA mechanisms and mappings, and evaluate them on proxy applications and a synthetic suite that isolates the axes driving strategy choice.

events.title: Parallel Restore-Optimized Snapshot Compression for Cost-Efficient Inference Serving
events.description: Inference services incur cold-start costs from KV-cache profiling and CUDA-graph construction. Container checkpoints avoid repeated initialization, but large memory images consume storage and serial reconstruction delays restoration. We present PROCS, a parallel, restore-optimized compression method for CRIU snapshots. PROCS stores pages in VMA-bounded, page-addressable blocks, supports partial and incremental reads, and reconstructs bounded batches using reusable workers. It coordinates parallel restoration of private mappings, memory-backed files, and anonymous shared memory under restore-wide CPU and buffer limits. We implement PROCS in CRIUgpu and evaluate five SGLang inference models. With 256 KiB blocks and serial restoration, PROCS reduces snapshot size by 12.5–45.5% and restore-to-first-token latency by 7.2–44.7% relative to uncompressed CRIUgpu. At fixed parallelism, 1 MiB blocks reduce size by 6.2%, checkpoint time by 12.4%, and restore-to-first-token latency by 22.5% relative to 4 KiB encoding. For Qwen3.5 27B FP8, increasing decompression parallelism to 16 threads reduces CRIU’s restore latency by 25.8%.

events.title: Architecting Multi-Petabyte Data Migration in a Live HPC Environment: From Strategy to Execution
events.description: Large-scale storage migrations are among the most challenging operational activities in high-performance computing (HPC) environments due to the need to preserve workflow continuity while moving petabyte-scale datasets across storage platforms. This paper presents the planning and execution of a live migration of 900 research projects totaling 3.28 PB of data across 3.30 billion files from Lustre-based storage to a VAST Data filesystem. We implemented a technology-agnostic namespace using automount abstractions and dual datapaths to decouple workflow migration from data movement. Supported by a custom toolchain for metadata-preservation, our pipeline integrated project prioritization, pre-copy transfers, incremental synchronization, and automated validation. Despite being a fully-managed migration, this framework minimized administrative overhead, preserved filesystem integrity, and achieved zero user-reported tickets for workflow disruption.

events.title: AAFLOW+: Stateful Operator Abstraction with Distributed KV Cache Orchestration for Multi-Agent Workflows
events.description: Multi-agent LLM workflows are distributed GPU-cluster applications that interleave retrieval, planning, and reasoning. However, text-centric agent communication repeatedly rebuilds shared context through expensive prefill, while the resulting KV cache remains confined to local serving runtimes rather than being reused as transferable state. We present AAFLOW+, a stateful abstraction of agentic workflow operators that elevates KV cache to a first-class distributed memory object, with explicit operators for materialization, transfer, fork, composition, and eviction over zero-copy, communication-aware execution graphs. Its cost-based scheduler selects transfer/recomputation using measured bandwidth and prefill costs. Evaluation uses a trace-driven model parameterized by A100/InfiniBand microbenchmarks with Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B. Modeled results show up to $50.2\times$ TTFT reduction at long context, up to $7.63\times$ lower aggregate multi-agent compute cost at 16-agent scale, and $1.72-6.10\times$ lower peak KV memory. Transfer–recompute analysis shows KV transfer dominates recomputation at 25 Gbps and above, placing state sharing squarely within reach of HPC interconnects.

events.title: Lunch
Tutorial Lunch
ACM SIGHPC Fellows Lightning Talks
events.description: In partnership with ACM SIGHPC, this year WHPC invites the SIGHPC Computational and Data Science fellows to give a lightning talk about their work.

events.title: Green Shift: Resize the GPU, Not the Process
events.description:
GPUs are multiplexed across workloads using NVIDIA MPS, MIG, and CUDA Green-Contexts. Multiplexing maximizes utilization while isolation keeps tail latency predictable. But MPS and MIG are inefficient: resizing a partition requires restarting the bound processes and reloading model weights and state, incurring seconds of idle downtime that grows with model size. This poorly fits modern inference, where many models share a GPU and their compute demands shift constantly.

Green-Contexts instead change a process’s Streaming-Multiprocessors (SMs) budget on the fly, with no restart or reload, lowering reconfiguration time and GPU idle gaps. However, they target intra-application resource management, lack notion of multi-tenancy, and are not natively supported in PyTorch/vLLM. We introduce Green Shift, which repurposes Green Contexts for multi-tenant inference. On an NVIDIA H100, Green Shift cuts a large model’s reconfiguration downtime from roughly 30s to ~3s (>10× reduction), and uses ~1.5 to 2× less energy during the resize than MPS.

events.title: A Heuristic Based Cache Miss Classifier
events.description: Cache misses can limit HPC applications, yet conventional profilers only identify where misses occur and not their root cause. Capacity pressure and cache-set conflicts often produce similar hotspots but generally require different optimizations. Conventional classification uses a fully associative shadow cache but introduces additional state and lookup work. We present an explainable classifier that combines five complementary signals. The signals are computed over bounded counter periods and combined on a signed capacity-conflict scale. The method uses bounded counters and a compact address-history table while diagnosing root causes. Across 12 program configurations and 48 data-object scopes, the classifier agreed in every tested case with the more frequent capacity or conflict label among the independently generated ground-truth misses in that scope. On the Himeno benchmark, CMSA required 2.32 times the runtime of baseline Cachegrind. These results demonstrate the potential of bounded signals for explainable cache diagnoses without shadow-cache labels during prediction.

events.title: Machine Learning for a Gamma-Ray Telescope Using Stream-HLS
events.description:
Machine learning is becoming an important contributor to data acquisition for science, performing many tasks more efficiently than previously utilized techniques. Scientific instrumentation frequently is required to separate the actual signals of interest from background signals, and machine learning has often been applied to this task. However, manually designing and tuning the HLS implementation of onboard neural network inference is labor-intensive, and the resulting designs often have significant room for improvement.

Automated dataflow HLS tools could be used to implement inference on an instrument's onboard FPGA. We focus on a recent tool - Stream-HLS. Here, we assess the suitability of the Stream-HLS framework to implement a background rejection task for a gamma-ray telescope. The Stream-HLS design proves to be able to fit the flight part (XC7K325T), whereas the hand-tuned baseline does not. Moreover, the Stream-HLS design achieves ~1.9X higher throughput, while leaving 43% of the available DSPs idle.

events.title: Correctness Evidence for I/O Optimizations in VPIC-Kokkos: Preliminary Results
events.description: Scientific input/output (I/O) optimizations require clear correctness evidence that application developers can review. We study deterministic export tests and scientist-vetted end-to-end analyses within the Kokkos implementation of the Vector Particle-in-Cell (VPIC) application. These validations rely on different oracles and target different properties. This work in progress explores what kinds of correctness evidence should be provided alongside an application I/O optimization.

events.title: Modernizing Hercules for GPU-Accelerated Earthquake Ground Motion Simulation on NVIDIA GPUs
events.description: Physics-based earthquake ground motion simulations, in order to achieve a desirable maximum frequency for practical applications, require billions of finite elements and tens of thousands of explicit timesteps, making the element-local force operators, inter-rank exchange, and output path all important to end-to-end performance. We present a modern GPU-resident implementation of Hercules, an octree-based finite-element earthquake simulator. The implementation maps effective stiffness, BKT viscoelastic attenuation, and explicit displacement update to CUDA; retains the primary field histories on the accelerator; exchanges boundary data through CUDA-aware MPI; and limits host transfers to data required by non-accelerated paths and output. On early-access NVIDIA GB200 resources, a fixed 67.1-million-element problem attains a 25.02X speedup on 64 GPUs, while a weak-scaling sweep maintains 95.6% efficiency from one to 64 GPUs and grows to 4.29 billion elements. At equal scaling-unit count, one GPU is 5.4–7.8 times faster per timestep than one 144-core NVIDIA Grace--Grace node. A 2-Hz simulation of the 2013 Mw 6.4 Ruisui earthquake contains 1.584 billion elements and 40,000 timesteps. It completes the solver in 1007.05s on 32 GPUs and 558.06s on 64 GPUs, speedups of 5.86X and 10.58X over 32 CPU nodes. Unfiltered station histories agree with the CPU implementation to a relative L2 error of 1.215e-5 and a minimum component correlation above 0.9999. These results demonstrate that GPU residency and accelerator-aware communication make Hercules practical for high-resolution production ground motion simulations without changing its established numerical model.

events.title: LASSI-Verify: Adaptive Empirical Verification of LLM-Generated Parallel Scientific Code Transformations
events.description:
Large language models transform parallel scientific code faster than
humans can review. Existing pipelines accept transformations that
compile, run, and satisfy an LLM judge, none of which evidences behavior
preservation, while whole-program formal proof remains impractical for
kernels lacking formal specifications. We present LASSI-Verify, a
work-in-progress adaptive empirical verification framework treating the
source's observable behavior as its specification and grounding
acceptance in three tiers: invariant assertions, observational
equivalence, and metamorphic relations. A seeded witness chain, added
after observing LLMs delete timed work to fabricate speedups, supplies
iteration-integrity evidence toward operational equivalence, and every
failure doubles as a repair signal. Because a verifier must itself be
verified, we grade benchmark checks before trusting them as oracles. In
preliminary results, the framework rejected all 13 oracle-detected
defects across 350 self-corrected variants of 16 HeCBench CUDA kernels,
while an LLM judge, reasoning over code text and output rather than
executed state, accepted three.

events.title: Trigger-Gated Multimodal LLM Agents for In-situ Scientific Simulation Monitoring
events.description: Simulations routinely run to completion while computing the wrong answer. No production tool monitors whether a running simulation computes valid science; we call this blind spot dark waste. Multimodal LLM agents could supply the physics-aware judgment such monitoring needs, but no scientific field fits in a context window. A rendering does. Vigil is a trigger-render-reason pipeline built as an ADIOS2 plugin engine on the application's I/O path. Deterministic triggers run every timestep inline with the write. Only flagged states stream in-transit to a visualization node, where an agent drives ParaView through tool calls and returns a structured verdict. Across four codes, with zero per-application training, Vigil confirms every parameter-induced failure and dismisses a trigger deliberately fired on a healthy run. Halting at the alert saves 39--68\% of an under-resolved Taylor--Green run, and gating costs 0.05\% of run time at 256 processes.

events.title: Using ethtrace to debug AI networks
events.description:
We introduce ethtrace, a simple and lightweight on-demand network monitoring tool that generates probes from a source host at a specified frequency and relies on switch telemetry
extensions such as the in-band flow analyzer to collect per hop and interactively displays or logs it at the destination host. ethtrace usage is as simple as that of established
tools like ping and traceroute, but provides richer visibility and
finer grained insights than existing approaches. ethtrace can
be used to track the path of an existing queue-pair or TCP
connection, or to monitor one or all paths between two hosts.
We present several use-cases where ethtrace was used to
quickly debug RoCEv2 performance anomalies such as PFC is-
sues, DCQCN parameters settings, offering visibility into complex
network behaviour that today is very difficult to understand
and debug. ethtrace is deployable today, as a large fraction
of deployed datacenter switches have telemetry support.

events.title: Fair, Random IO Operations are Hard
events.description: The IO500 Committee continuously works to improve and expand what the IO500 benchmarks cover to keep them both current and relevant. The latest change we have been working on is a random 4 KiB read phase. Our first attempt yielded some unexpected results prompting a deep dive and re-implementation from scratch. Where we are now requires community feedback to ensure the best path forward.

events.title: Closing Remarks
One Bus Accident Away from Death: The Fragility of HPC I/O Tools
events.description:
HPC I/O tools are essential for understanding application performance, yet a small number of individuals often drive their development and maintenance.
This work investigates the maintainability of open-source HPC I/O tools using CHAOSS-inspired metrics, analyzing repository activity, contributor distributions, code ownership, and maintenance continuity.
We examine how development responsibilities are distributed across projects and identify potential dependencies on key maintainers.
The results highlight the human sustainability risks behind HPC I/O software and motivate greater consideration of maintenance resilience within the HPC community.
