events.title: Navigating Mixed-Precision: Tools and Techniques for Floating-Point Error Profiling
events.description: Floating-point arithmetic is the bedrock of scientific computing, yet it frequently introduces subtle errors and non-deterministic behavior in numerical software. As the HPC community shifts toward mixed-precision execution to unlock performance and energy-efficiency gains, developers require robust methodologies to rigorously analyze floating-point error accumulation. This tutorial provides a comprehensive introduction to two state-of-the-art tools designed to guide precision-tuning decisions in both CPU and GPU-accelerated applications. The first tool is FPChecker, which leverages the Clang/LLVM compiler infrastructure to perform static and dynamic analysis of C/C++ applications. The second is NixNaN, a high-performance profiler built on the NVIDIA NVBit dynamic instrumentation framework, engineered to detect floating-point exceptional values arising during CUDA kernel execution without requiring source modification or recompilation. Throughout this session, participants will learn (1) to assess the floating-point dynamic range of applications, (2) to visualize the propagation of rounding errors, and (3) to isolate performance-critical numerical issues, such as overflows, and NaNs. The tutorial emphasizes a hands-on approach: attendees will engage with accessible examples (e.g., simple linear solvers) configured to run locally on their laptops. In the advanced session, we transition to real-world impact, where participants will apply these tools to larger numerical libraries (e.g., Hypre).

events.title: Workload-Manager-Agnostic QPU Integration with QRMI
events.description: Integrating quantum resources into HPC workflows is complicated by two layers of fragmentation: quantum hardware vendors expose incompatible APIs, and HPC centers run diverse job schedulers. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI), an open-source project developed by a growing community of 15 national laboratories, institutions, and quantum vendors, resolves both problems by exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs, independent of vendor or scheduler. This hands-on, three-hour tutorial targets HPC engineers and administrators, and gives quantum vendors concrete motivation: implement QRMI once, and your backend becomes accessible from any scheduler. The tutorial spans three modules covering today's HPC scheduling landscape: traditional batch schedulers, where attendees choose one of Slurm, PBS, IBM LSF, or Open Cluster Scheduler for hands-on exercises; Kubernetes, increasingly adopted for AI workloads; and the Flux Framework, a graph-based scheduler for next-generation HPC systems. In each module, participants submit real QRMI-managed jobs targeting cloud quantum resources from providers such as IBM, Pasqal, and Alice & Bob. Attendees will leave having experienced firsthand how QRMI integrates with their own workload manager to deliver quantum workloads to HPC users, giving them a concrete starting point for building quantum-ready HPC infrastructure today.

events.title: Mentorship in Practice: Building Relationships for Early-Career Growth
events.description: Early-career professionals are often told to “find a mentor,” with little guidance on where to start or how to navigate the relationship once they have one. This panel brings together professionals with experience as both mentors and mentees to discuss how these relationships begin, what makes them useful, what to talk about, and how they can evolve over time. Panelists will also discuss the distinction between mentors and sponsors and share their thoughts on building a broader network of people who can offer guidance, perspective, and advocacy at different career stages. The moderated discussion will be followed by an open Q&A, where attendees are invited to bring their own questions and experiences into the conversation.

events.title: Regional Tech Hub Inauguration
The 12th Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop (CAFCW26)
events.description: Cancer touches everyone. Since being established in 2015, CAFCW continues to bring together the community interested in impacting cancer with HPC and the community with an interest in learning more about HPC impacting cancer challenges. The workshop continues to grow, inviting the cancer and HPC communities to converge at SC, interact, and share insights and advances. The workshop highlights the diversity of opportunities where HPC serves as an essential element for advances in cancer treatments, driving new approaches to understand cancer and enabling translation of insights and new treatments to reach clinical impact. This year, the workshop will emphasize the role of HPC in translating research to clinical application and reaching patients, uniting research, clinic and patient. For over a decade, this workshop has catalyzed new biomedical research by connecting industry, government research laboratories, and academia at the intersection of computation, biomedical science, cancer, and healthcare.

events.title: ExaMPI26: Workshop on Extreme-Scale MPI
events.description: MPI is currently the de facto standard for programming HPC systems and developing parallel applications. Development of the MPI standard continues in earnest, with version 5.0 being released within the past year, and features for version 5.1d under active discussion. The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers and developers to present and discuss innovative algorithms and concepts within the Message Passing programming model, and to create a forum for open discussions on the future of the Message Passing Interface (MPI) in the post-exascale era. Possible workshop topics include and are not limited to algorithms for collective operations, MPI optimization for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, data-centric models, scheduling, fault tolerance, MPI optimization in heterogeneous systems, interoperability of MPI with other programming models (e.g., PGAS), integration of task-parallel models in MPI, the role of MPI in "smart" networks, and the use of MPI in large-scale simulations.

events.title: Invited Talk: Torsten Hoefler: AI Infrastructure at Hyperscale - The Role of (Ultra) Ethernet
events.description: The rapid rise of generative AI is driving an unprecedented expansion of hyperscale infrastructure. Modern AI services generate trillions of tokens per day, requiring ever larger clusters and making efficiency a first-order challenge. While specialized accelerators such as Maia 200 are essential for delivering performant and cost-effective inference, their capabilities can only be fully realized through a scalable and efficient network fabric. This talk explores the co-design of next-generation AI infrastructure, from accelerator architecture and large-scale inference systems to the communication challenges posed by massive distributed workloads. I will argue that networking has become the defining system bottleneck and discuss the role of Ethernet in addressing it. Finally, I will present the vision behind Ultra Ethernet and its evolution into a high-performance, open networking platform capable of supporting the communication demands of future AI and HPC systems at hyperscale.

events.title: FTXS: Workshop for Faults, Trustworthiness, and eXplainability for AI Systems at Scale
events.description:
FTXS convenes researchers and practitioners to address trustworthy AI systems at scale under real-world variability. Modern AI/LLM pipelines (training, inference, RAG, and agentic systems) face “gray failures” such as distribution drift, prompt/tool/RAG variability, infrastructure noise, and limited-precision effects. Small perturbations can amplify into hallucinations, instability, miscalibration, irreproducibility, and silent regressions — wasting GPU-hours and undermining confidence in AI-assisted decisions.

FTXS organizes discussion around a practical closed loop: Disturb → Degrade → Detect → Diagnose → Defend → Validate. We emphasize explainability as a diagnostic tool for attribution across components (model, retrieval, tools, infrastructure, precision), and we aim to synthesize shared taxonomies, measurement practices, and seed artifacts (checklists, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols) that improve both research and operational practice.

events.title: Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers
events.description: The Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers, or SQCS'26, considers combining two methodologies — collaborative co-design and data-driven analysis — to realize the potential of supercomputing more fully. By narrowing in on these two proven methodologies with the broad-community attention of an SC26 audience, we will address a host of identified challenges impacting high performance computing (HPC). The 2026 workshop focus will focus on upcoming machines and emerging technologies. The state of HPC is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving beyond a sole focus on raw peak FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) to prioritizing time-to-solution, energy efficiency, and AI-simulation convergence. The landscape is defined by the rise of "post-exascale" machines, the integration of generative AI into scientific workflows, and the emergence of hybrid quantum-classical architectures. This symposium will bring together leaders in the field to review current efforts across centers and discuss areas that show potential.

events.title: Accelerating HPC Performance Analysis with AI Agents
events.description: Successful performance analysis typically involves a combination of established workflows, measurement tools, architectural knowledge, performance models, hardware counter analysis, parametric studies, and visualization. AI agents can integrate and automate many of these activities, significantly reducing the effort required to collect, organize, analyze, and interpret performance data. Agents are particularly effective at automating command-line data collection, managing results from parametric studies, applying performance models to known architectures, interpreting well understood hardware counter data, and performing static analysis of compiler reports and generated assembly code. In this talk, we will present several success stories that demonstrate how AI agents can be used to analyze HPC proxy applications and accelerate the performance engineering process. For example, analysis of the RAJAPerf suite on AMD MI300A GPUs identified optimization opportunities that produced a 34× speedup in one kernel. We will also discuss practical lessons learned, including common challenges and limitations encountered when working with AI agents. We will also discuss emerging opportunities for agent-assisted performance analysis, including the skills, interfaces, and rules that performance measurement and analysis tool developers should consider providing to maximize agent effectiveness. Finally, we will highlight AI agent capabilities being developed for current and future releases of the ROCm ecosystem.

events.title: High-Accuracy Computing on Low-Precision Hardware
events.description:
This workshop aims to bring together researchers, application scientists, system developers, and industry partners to explore algorithmic and implementation approaches enabling accurate scientific computing on low-precision hardware. As accelerators increasingly favor reduced-precision arithmetic for performance and energy efficiency, many scientific applications continue to require accuracy, stability, and reproducibility. Addressing this widening gap demands community-driven advances across algorithms and scientific software, spanning domain-informed and cross-cutting approaches while building toward reusable, precision-aware libraries and tooling infrastructure.

The workshop will feature invited talks and solicited works highlighting mixed-precision methods, error-aware and adaptive numerical algorithms, floating-point emulation libraries, and practical deployment on large-scale systems. The workshop emphasizes building community-driven software ecosystems for broad adoption across domains, reducing duplication, and accelerating impact. By fostering discussion among application developers, numerical experts, and hardware vendors, the workshop will establish best practices, share lessons, and strengthen academia–industry collaboration to make low-precision hardware a reliable component of scientific workflows.

events.title: Afternoon Session Introduction
Software for Large Scale Application
events.description: This session surveys the software layers that make large-scale quantum-classical applications possible. Speakers will present the open Quantum Software Ecosystem (openQSE), the interfaces that connect quantum resources to HPC systems, and the workflow tools and libraries built on top of them. The talks highlight how these components fit together and what it takes to run real applications on integrated quantum-HPC systems today.

events.title: Sharing a Fabric with Collective Communication: Two Storage Penalties in DL Training
events.description: Distributed DL training on HPC systems often shares one network fabric for collective communication and parallel-filesystem I/O. Using a real GNN workload on a Slingshot-11 system, we identify two costs. First, shared-fabric I/O causes heavy-tailed DataLoader stalls: typical waits are 15 ms but spike to seconds in 28% of Lustre iterations and 12% of VAST iterations. Second, traffic-class contention slows collective communication: Lustre stalls all-reduce by up to 145 times in isolation. The first effect affects any shared-fabric storage path, whereas the second occurs only when storage and collective traffic share a traffic class. A dedicated all-flash tier on a separate traffic class substantially reduces the secondary effect but leaves its DataLoader tail heavy. Nimbus, which stages data to node-local NVMe, eliminates both by removing storage I/O from the shared fabric. Nimbus achieves 7.4 times higher throughput than Lustre and 1.31 times higher throughput than VAST with a warm cache.

events.title: 7th Workshop on Heterogeneity and Memory Systems (HMEM)
events.description: Heterogeneity is ubiquitous, not only in terms of processing units but also memories and networks. As heterogeneity increases, memory subsystems play an even more important role to attain performance, from their technology to the system architecture to the software management and programming model. While CPU-only compute nodes are becoming rare instances, heterogeneous memory architectures have recently emerged and revolutionized the traditional memory hierarchy. Today’s and upcoming architectures may well comprise multiple memory technologies next to DRAM, accelerators with dedicated memories, or even specific expansion cards hosting memory alone, such as: 3D-stacked memory, high-bandwidth multi-channel RAM, unified/shared memory on accelerators, Compute Express Link (CXL)-based architectures, Huawei's Unified Bus, persistent memory, or MRDIMMs.

events.title: Featured Talk: Hotness tracking in CXL hardware
events.description: Growing application memory demands are motivating heterogeneous memory systems that combine local DRAM with CXL-attached capacity. Their performance depends on identifying which data should occupy the faster tier and adapting placement as access patterns change. M5 and ARC are two complementary approaches to hardware–software co-design for CXL memory management. M5 uses device-side page and subpage tracking to guide migration, while ARC adapts the counting organization to workload behavior using shared hardware storage. Through measurements on real CXL prototypes, we examine how the location, granularity, and organization of hotness tracking influence migration decisions and application performance, highlighting trade-offs and opportunities for coordinating memory monitoring and placement.

events.title: WHPC Rising Starts Lightning Talks
The case for unprivileged containerization in HPC, or: Does software simplicity still matter in 2026?
events.description:
Containerization is an increasingly popular way to encapsulate an application or workflow along with all of its dependencies (other than the Linux kernel). This has been effective for HPC applications, both old and new. However, the principles and practices of HPC collide with those of cloud computing, including in particular container standards such as OCI. Also, containerization is often presented as a complex technology, with many concepts entangled, but in fact it is pretty straightforward.
This talk revisits the motivation for Charliecloud, an HPC-focused container implementation that has prioritized simplicity and lack of privilege since the beginning, based on my decade of experience leading the project. I argue for a simplicity-first view of how containers work, explore how the assumptions of HPC and cloud computing clash (particularly in the era of ML/AI) and outline some possible solutions. These ideas are incomplete, and my hope is that discussion with the CANOPIE community will help build a more robust path forward.

events.title: Subsurface to Stellar: HPC Enablement with Open OnDemand and ColdFront at bp and NASA
events.description: High-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure continues to grow in capability and scale, yet user access models and support mechanisms often lag behind evolving user expectations. Through a collaboration under the NASA-bp Space Act Agreement, bp and NASA identified a common challenge: reducing friction between users and HPC resources through modern, web-based interfaces. This paper presents two independent but complementary approaches. At bp, Open OnDemand (OOD) was deployed and extended to provide a browser-first interface for HPC resources, integrating existing infrastructure while supporting application deployment, operational visibility, and governance of user-developed web applications. At NASA's Flight Sciences Laboratory, ColdFront was extended through a plugin-based architecture to provide self-service management of projects, storage, licenses, and access controls with integrated approval workflows and auditability. Together, these case studies demonstrate how web-based platforms can improve accessibility, accelerate onboarding, increase user autonomy, and reduce administrative burden without requiring fundamental changes to underlying HPC systems.

events.title: AI on HPC: Performance Engineering, Challenges and Opportunities
events.description: How can AI workloads be engineered for optimal performance in modern HPC environments? As AI models grow in scale and complexity, high performance computing (HPC) systems are becoming essential for training and deploying these workloads. However, traditional HPC architectures, designed for batch processing, present unique challenges for AI/ML applications — such as dynamic workloads, high I/O demands, and parallelization intricacies. This workshop explores the intersection of AI and HPC, focusing on performance optimization, scalability, and portability. Topics include AI workload characterization, hybrid AI/HPC workflows, efficient execution strategies, and infrastructure co-design. By fostering collaboration between researchers, practitioners, and system developers, this workshop aims to advance best practices and innovations in AI-enabled scientific computing, aligning with SC26’s themes of exascale readiness and performance portability.

events.title: AI on HPC: Performance Engineering, Challenges and Opportunities
events.description: How can AI workloads be engineered for optimal performance in modern HPC environments? As AI models grow in scale and complexity, high performance computing (HPC) systems are becoming essential for training and deploying these workloads. However, traditional HPC architectures, designed for batch processing, present unique challenges for AI/ML applications — such as dynamic workloads, high I/O demands, and parallelization intricacies. This workshop explores the intersection of AI and HPC, focusing on performance optimization, scalability, and portability. Topics include AI workload characterization, hybrid AI/HPC workflows, efficient execution strategies, and infrastructure co-design. By fostering collaboration between researchers, practitioners, and system developers, this workshop aims to advance best practices and innovations in AI-enabled scientific computing, aligning with SC26’s themes of exascale readiness and performance portability.

events.title: (Featured Speaker) From Recovery to Explanation: Deterministic Replay as Evidence for Fault Diagnosis at Scale
events.description: For two decades, fault tolerance has meant recovery: checkpointing and restart, rollback recovery, consistent cuts — mechanisms that assume the fault announces itself. Something crashes, hangs, or times out; recovery restores a good state and continues.A growing and expensive class of failures in large-scale AI training does not announce itself. The job runs to completion, the loss curve looks healthy, and the model is nonetheless wrong: a parameter declared trainable never receives a gradient; a resume restores weights but not optimizer state; a precision policy silently degrades. These faults waste thousands of GPU-hours and surface days later, discovered by working backwards from an evaluation metric. For this class, recovery is worse than insufficient — applied blindly, it faithfully carries the defect forward across every restart.Such failures require explanation, not just recovery, and explanation requires evidence rather than inference. Telemetry-based root-cause analysis reasons from surface signals about what probably happened; deterministic record-and-replay makes the execution itself available for interrogation.This talk argues that the fault-tolerance community's next primitive is a queryable evidence base. I ground the argument in two prior systems: iReplayer (PLDI 2018), which showed that deterministic replay of production multithreaded programs is affordable and can be performed in place, and an OOPSLA 2020 system that automated root-cause diagnosis over such recordings using replay, hardware watchpoints, and binary analysis. I then examine what large-scale AI workloads change — a semantic gap between bytes and the logical entities of a model; distribution across ranks, where each rank's evidence is self-consistent yet insufficient; and silence, which removes the trigger these mechanisms assume — and describe early work on a semantic attribution layer addressing the first. Throughout, I am explicit about what such evidence establishes and what it does not: provenance is not proof of value correctness.

events.title: Opening Remarks from Workshop Chair
OPSERVE: Opportunistic LLM Inference over Fragmented GPU Capacity in HPC Systems
events.description: Large language model (LLM) inference is an important GPU workload, while batch-scheduled HPC systems often leave nodes transiently idle because available resources cannot satisfy queued jobs. Our analysis of a year-long HPC trace finds that this unused capacity accounts for 9.81% of total node-hours and changes on timescales of seconds. Exploiting such transient capacity therefore requires serving decisions to adapt to resource availability and request demand. We present OpServe, a malleable LLM serving system that combines persistent and transient inference workers, adapts worker roles between prefill and decode, and reuses completed prefill state through shared KV storage. We evaluate three request traces with Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B. When both OpServe and a fixed prefill/decode baseline sustain the request arrival rate, OpServe reduces p95 end-to-end latency by 1.5–2.1×. Under overload, adaptive allocation reduces queue growth and yields up to 14.3× lower observed p95 end-to-end latency.

events.title: Learning When to Unroll-and-Unmerge on GPUs: Experiences with Reinforcement Learning in LLVM
events.description:
Branching hurts performance on GPU architectures, so unmerging control flow inside a loop looks like a poor optimization. Prior work showed otherwise: unmerging recovers information that a control-flow merge destroys, and pairing it with unrolling helps further.
The static heuristic developed in prior work performs poorly on many applications.
On an NVIDIA A100 across HeCBench, it loses to doing nothing: -4.9% mean improvement where +10% was available, and 23.9% of loops made slower. Its rule cannot express a quarter of the best decisions.

We port the transform to a newer LLVM and build a reinforcement learning pipeline that decides per loop whether to unmerge and which unroll factor to use, using measured kernel time as feedback. Two agents fit their training loops but neither transfers, because profitability follows the application rather than the loop. Adapting on two loops of the target cuts regressions to 9.5% and reaches +4.0% at best.

events.title: Building Research Computing Capacity Through Collaborative Visualization
events.description: Access to high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) does not ensure their effective use in research. Investigators also need workflows that fit their data, expertise, and research questions. This extended abstract describes a collaborative approach to research computing at the University of Chicago Research Computing Center. The approach combines scientific visualization, GPU-accelerated analysis, and hands-on support across research disciplines. Three examples illustrate its application: biomedical image segmentation using 3D Slicer and MONAI, a cultural heritage reconstruction deployed to a display wall and a VR headset, and Gaussian splat workflows for interactive digital twins. A browser-based viewer also supports remote exploration and the exchange of annotations. Beyond individual projects, five workshops have engaged more than 75 participants. These activities show how reusable workflows, consultation, and training can connect computing resources to research practice.

events.title: Welcome and Introduction
Invited Talk with Eric Nielsen, Senior Research Scientist with the Computational AeroSciences Branch at NASA Langley Research Center
Evolution in Scientific Deep Learning: A Data-centric Study
events.description: Deep learning over the past six years has shifted away from highly specific models in favor of a generic yet tunable paradigm, but the I/O and data movement implications of this shift remain uncharacterized. We address this gap by profiling modern deep learning applications at LLNL using DFTracer, combining function-level and application-level profiling to trace compute, communication, and I/O in a previously unexplored manner across the stack. We find that similarities to classical deep learning bottlenecks still exist; however, novel inefficiencies from customizable in-situ preprocessing - arising from a need for heterogeneous data access and tunable graph representations - are increased and unaccounted for in optimizations. We suggest optimizations such as utilizing more effective data structures and offloading graph representation/transformations to the GPU, and aim to continue the study by profiling additional scientific codes with broader stack tracing.

events.title: GPU Device Compilation in ClangIR: Lowering CUDA and HIP Kernels Through the CIR Pipeline
events.description: ClangIR (CIR) is a high-level, MLIR-based intermediate representation that preserves source-level semantics between the C/C++ AST and LLVM IR, but its support for heterogeneous programming models has been largely unexplored. We present a path for compiling CUDA and HIP code through CIR, and show that it requires almost no new IR surface: kernels and device functions reuse cir.func, CIR’s intrinsic-call mechanism, and a small set of carry-across attributes lets whole-module runtime registration be deferred until a later pass can synthesize it. A single principle organizes the design—each decision is made at the earliest pipeline stage that has the information it needs—so the language-parameterized pipeline serves NVPTX and AMDGPU. Across PolyBench/GPU, our implementation compiles all benchmarks for NVPTX and AMDGPU architectures and runs them at parity with original Clang on an NVIDIA H100 and an AMD MI300X, at a compile-time cost of roughly 3%.

events.title: Connecting Skills, Training and Community: Lessons from Building the HPC Workforce
events.description: Developing the High-Performance Computing (HPC) workforce requires more than technical infrastructure and expertise. People entering the HPC community arrive with different levels of experience, skills and career goals. This manuscript reflects on my experience as a Community Manager across SHAREing and CAKE, two initiatives within the UK Digital Research Infrastructure programme. Through SHAREing, I have contributed to approaches that help learners identify knowledge gaps, explore relationships between HPC concepts, navigate existing training resources and build personalised learning pathways. Through CAKE, I have worked to make the wider HPC landscape more visible, accessible and connected through community events, outreach and knowledge exchange. These experiences highlight the complementary roles of skills development and community building in creating an HPC ecosystem where individuals can access opportunities, develop their expertise, connect with others and thrive.

events.title: Opening Panel Discussion - Uniting Research, Clinic and Patient
events.description: This panel will explore the different ways in which HPC works to unite cancer research, clinical care, and the patient experience, both directly and indirectly.

events.title: Lead Invited Talk (Satoshi Matsuoka, Director of Riken Center for Computational Science)
Anchor: Delivering Consistent Performance on Noisy Cloud-Based Quantum Computers
events.description: Quantum computers are becoming an important part of high-performance computing (HPC), with hybrid quantum-classical algorithms combining quantum processors with classical HPC resources. However, unlike classical accelerators, near-term quantum computers do not provide consistent performance. The quality of a program's output can vary from day to day on the same machine and from machine to machine on the same day, making results difficult to reproduce and limiting the use of quantum computers in scientific workflows. We present Anchor, a technique that combines machine-learning-based fidelity prediction with linear programming to distribute program executions across multiple circuit mappings. Compared with state-of-the-art noise-adaptive compilation, Anchor reduces output performance variability by 73% on average.

events.title: Performance Characterization of GPU Sharing Strategies for LLM Inference
events.description: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs), demand has grown for LLM inference services that run continuously within High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments. Because inference requests vary over time, GPU resources dedicated to a single model may remain idle during periods of low demand. Sharing these resources among multiple inference workloads can improve GPU utilization. This paper compares two approaches for concurrently serving multiple models on a single NVIDIA H100 PCIe GPU: software-level GPU sharing using vLLM and hardware-level GPU partitioning using vLLM in combination with Multi-Instance GPU (MIG). We evaluate both approaches while varying the number of concurrently running models and the offered load. The results show that MIG-based GPU partitioning provides stable performance and slightly outperforms software-based GPU sharing when all GPU instances are fully utilized. In contrast, software-based GPU sharing exploits otherwise idle GPU resources, achieving higher throughput and lower latency when fewer models run concurrently.

events.title: Hardware Aware Evaluation for Statistical Estimators: A Selection Rule and Reproducible Benchmark
events.description: Statistical estimators are almost always compared on accuracy only. We compare them on accuracy and compute cost together, on the hardware they would run on, and measure how often the recommendation changes. A rule selects a deployment configuration: an estimator with its implementation, device and fidelity setting. Three rules, error only, a balanced score of normalised error and run time, and a compute budget, are evaluated on six runtimes (four NVIDIA GPUs, an AMD MI300A node and a CPU only runtime), a covariance family, a regression family and two downstream tasks on real data. Weighing run time against error changes the recommended covariance estimator on 37 to 44% of decision groups on every accelerator; in the regression family the configuration changes on 72 to 85% of cells, the estimator does not. An adequate compute budget keeps out of sample performance; a tight budget and the balanced score do not.

events.title: Code Generation with MLIR for the OPS Structured-Mesh DSL
events.description:
Structured-mesh applications underpin high-performance scientific simulations, yet performance portability across CPUs and GPUs demands substantial compiler and runtime support. We present an MLIR-based compiler
framework for OPS, a structured-mesh DSL, that captures OPS abstractions at runtime and JIT-lowers them to OpenMP and CUDA backends. A key contribution is adapting the predominantly value-semantic xDSL stencil compilation stack to OPS’s buffer-semantic model, where pre-allocated datasets have memory identity and update semantics. This demonstrates that shared MLIR stencil infrastructure can accommodate lower-level, production-oriented DSLs without redesigning their programming model. The framework introduces an OPS
dialect and staged lowerings for parallel loops, data accesses, stencils, and execution policies. Evaluation of representative structured-mesh applications, including the OpenSBLI research code on multicore CPUs and an NVIDIA H100 GPU, shows performance competitive with OPS’s mature source-to-source backends, substantial memory-bandwidth utilization, closely matched GPU kernel times, and amortized JIT overheads, providing a practical path for modernizing DSL compilers.

events.title: Predicting and Explaining Alzheimer's Disease Using UK Biobank: An Auditable, Cost-Sensitive HPC Pipeline for Feature Discovery
events.description:
Age is the strongest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, and when it is left in the feature set it dominates both prediction and explanation. This work presents an auditable pipeline over UK Biobank tabular data, built for SLURM job arrays on the Discoverer supercomputer. It removes direct age and event-timing fields, reduces 4,366 candidate features to 95 with every removal logged, and fits a sparse lasso logistic regression on a cohort of 10,550 participants.

Test AUC falls from 0.84 with age kept to 0.75 in the controlled model. The features that remain most important by SHAP are vascular, body-size, lipid and blood markers, led by systolic blood pressure, weight and small-LDL cholesterol. At an assumed 1% prevalence, only about 1 in 74 positive predictions would be a true case, so the pipeline is positioned for hypothesis generation, not screening.

events.title: Copy2: Data Sync Tool For High Performance Storages
events.description: The rapid growth of scientific and AI workloads challenges HPC centers to efficiently move large datasets across high-performance storage systems. Data movement at this scale is constrained by I/O bandwidth, metadata processing, filesystem semantics, and resource consumption, while existing open-source and commercial solutions may lack required performance, resource guarantees, or cost effectiveness. Motivated by a large-scale storage migration at our HPC facility, we developed copy2, a resource-aware transfer tool for parallel and distributed storage systems including Lustre and VAST Data. copy2 combines fine-grained parallel metadata traversal, inode-based hard-link preservation, highly concurrent asynchronous I/O, and bounded memory management. Component-level and end-to-end evaluations across diverse file sizes and counts show 2-4x higher transfer bandwidth and 3-5x lower energy consumption than rclone and fpsync, while adhering to user-defined memory bounds. Production deployments involving hundreds of millions of files further demonstrate its effectiveness for predictable, high-throughput scientific data movement at scale.

events.title: Wafer-Scale Unstructured Scientific Computing
Platform-Agnostic Kernel Fusion Pipeline for Linear Algebra Kernels in MLIR
events.description:
We present a platform-agnostic transformation pipeline that blends kernel fusion
and algebraic optimization. Our approach begins with tensor-form linear algebra
operations in a Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) module and
automatically discovers compatible producer-consumer regions. The operations in
each region are represented and composed in Einstein notation. We use exact
operand-subset dynamic programming to select a binary contraction order,
lexicographically minimizing scalar multiplication work followed by logical
intermediate volume. The selected contractions are reconstructed in MLIR, and an
automatic partitioner selects connected fusion groups according to removable
logical storage, parallel-domain compatibility, and reduction topology. After
bufferization, the selected groups are outlined, their concrete memory
dependences are checked, compatible parallel loops are fused, and eligible
intermediates are forwarded as scalars. We implement the complete transformation
in Linear Algebra Performance through Intermediate Subprograms (LAPIS), an
MLIR-to-Kokkos compiler framework, so one optimized module can target backends
supported by Kokkos execution spaces.

events.title: Toward Software-Defined Performance Optimization for Emerging Quantum Systems
events.description:
Abstract—Quantum computing provides a promising computing
paradigm, yet physical hardware remains constrained by short
qubit coherence times, gate operational errors, and scarce
quantum resources [1]. In near-term quantum execution, software
efficiency directly impacts program viability: every redundant
gate consumes precious coherence time, accumulates operational
noise, and lowers execution success probability. Our broader
research investigates how compiler, systems, and learning-guided
optimization can maximize the usable computational throughput
extracted from constrained quantum hardware.

events.title: LLBPE: Linked-List Based GPU-Parallel BPE Tokenizer
events.description: Every LLM inference begins with tokenization, which converts raw input bytes into the discrete token sequence the model consumes. For text, this step is often implemented using Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), an algorithm originally introduced for data compression. BPE has traditionally run on the CPU with extensive optimization, but recent work has moved it to the GPU for higher throughput. We show that these GPU implementations are bottlenecked not by computation but by data movement. We develop LLBPE that represents the token sequence as an array-based linked list so that each merge reduces to a constant-time pointer update. Furthermore, LLBPE fuses rank lookup, minimum selection, and merging into a single kernel to eliminate redundant hash map queries. LLBPE achieves up to 5.2× higher throughput than the best existing GPU implementation and 24.6× over optimized CPU implementations, at the cost of minor discrepancies in tokenized output.

events.title: Extending the Life of HPC Systems in Resource-Constrained Environments: A Path from a Student Cluster Competition to Sustainable Computing in Africa
events.description:
In resource-constrained environments, High Performance Computing (HPC) often runs on repurposed hardware, making energy, rather than acquisition, the main expense. Building on PEARC '26 work, this extended abstract assesses repurposed systems by their Productivity-to-Energy (PTE) ratio rather than raw performance. CPU frequency, set through Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), and the number of active cores were tuned jointly on a repurposed dual-socket node. Compared with a 16-core, 3.5 GHz baseline, the best configurations lowered energy consumption by 49.60% for HPCG and 30.62% for OpenFOAM.

The abstract also traces the path of the author from no prior HPC knowledge, through a national Student Cluster Competition, to international recognition in just over a year. It further considers how extending the life of hardware reduces both the operational and embodied emissions of HPC in Africa.

events.title: Mixed-Precision Cholesky Factorization for Semidefinite Programming Using Ozaki Scheme II
events.description: This paper explores the accuracy and performance of a mixed-precision Cholesky factorization based on the INT8 Ozaki scheme II. Within the tiled Cholesky algorithm, we apply an optimized Ozaki scheme II to the symmetric rank-k update (SYRK), while keeping the diagonal factorization (POTRF) and the triangular solve (TRSM) in double precision. We further introduce a look-ahead technique and a dynamic tile size scheduler. On a server whose GPU has limited FP64 throughput, our implementation attains a 3.04x speedup over the OpenBLAS dpotrf routine while retaining double-precision accuracy. We also examine how the number of slices affects the backward error and the relative forward error, and find that 15 slices are required to preserve double-precision accuracy within the range covered by our experiment. Finally, we integrate the proposed factorization into a double-precision semidefinite programming solver and obtain a 1.47x speedup on an SDP benchmark instance (1et.2048).

events.title: Who You Gonna CALL? Static Whole-Program Call Graphs for Fortran
events.description: Fortran retains continued relevance in high-performance and scientific computing, yet its tooling ecosystem lags behind that of C and C++. Call graphs are a common foundation for analysis tools, and constructing them for modern Fortran requires resolving language features that elude simple source analysis. We present a static call-graph generator for Fortran implemented as a Flang plugin. Building on LLVM Flang's parse tree and semantic information, it produces whole-program call graphs from source code and resolves type-bound procedures, polymorphic dispatch, finalizers, operator overloading, generic interfaces, and C interoperability. We evaluate it on the production codes ICON, NEKO, and CP2K, and on the Fortran benchmarks of SPEChpc 2021, comparing against static LLVM-IR and dynamic Score-P call graphs. Across all applications, our analysis produces a reliable and detailed representation of procedures and call relationships. A case study demonstrates that the resulting graphs are well suited to guide instrumentation for performance analysis.

events.title: Leveraging high performance computing for simulation of snowpack liquid water content using SnowModel
Experiences with and Best Practices around Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs)
events.description: Cooling distribution units (CDUs) are becoming necessary to meet the cooling demands of modern compute and network systems. We present the experiences NSF NCAR has had with the CDUs on our HPE Cray EX test and production systems. Along with various topics including finding leaks, expansion tank issues, replacing pumps, and properly torqueing components, we will give a list of best practices we have developed for dealing with these specialize HPC system components. Included in our presentation is an artifact for querying the Redfish endpoints of the CDU system and populating a timeseries database for plotting CDU values over time.

events.title: Prefetching in Disaggregated Memory Systems
events.description:
The growing prevalence of memory-intensive applications has exposed several limitations of traditional server architectures. Disaggregated memory systems address some of these limitations by enabling memory and compute resources to scale independently. However, disaggregation introduces new challenges, particularly the high latency of remote memory accesses. In this work, we present an approach for mitigating remote-access latency in multi-rack disaggregated memory systems. We also discuss broader open challenges and research
opportunities in memory-system design.

events.title: Accurate and Scalable Graph AI for Early and Explainable Health Risk Assessment
events.description:
Early and explainable health risk assessment can enable proactive and informed medical intervention. Comprehensive assessment, however, relies on intrinsically multimodal clinical data that are often irregular, sparse, and temporally misaligned, making accurate and scalable assessment challenging. We address these two connected challenges: (1) improving the accuracy of early and explainable health risk assessment through Graph AI and (2) scaling Graph AI training to reduce training time and support larger training data volumes.

To address (1), we develop M-GrEEnHeRA, a multimodal graph-based approach for early and explainable health risk assessment that represents multimodal clinical data as dynamic graph sequences and performs spatio-temporal learning over these graphs using Graph AI. To address (2), we develop a distributed producer-consumer (DPC) workflow that tackles key Graph AI training bottlenecks, including memory inefficiency, batch-construction-induced stalls, and GPU load imbalance.

events.title: Evaluation of LLVM Flang for Production HPC Applications and Modern Fortran Features
events.description: In 2025, LLVM released its first Flang Fortran compiler version considered ready for widespread evaluation. We know of no published assessment of Flang compiling a workload-derived portfolio of high-performance computing (HPC) applications. We address this gap using workload data from the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), which supports more than 10,000 scientists on approximately 1,000 projects. We selected ten Fortran packages heavily used at NERSC with available source code and compiled them using recent versions of Flang on NERSC’s Perlmutter system. Seven compiled without code modifications, though some required build-system changes. Three compiled after minor source edits, mostly to address Fortran standard violations. We evaluated seven additional packages selected for their use or enablement of standard Fortran parallel features: multi-image execution and do concurrent. Six such codes compiled with most or all unit tests passing.

events.title: Serving Masked Diffusion LLMs: Characterization and Design Principles from Real Hardware
events.description: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) promise faster generation than autoregressive (AR) models by denoising many tokens at once, but their behavior under concurrent serving load is unmeasured. We characterize dLLM serving using LLaDA-8B-Instruct with a D2F LoRA adapter on one NVIDIA H200 GPU, evaluated on GSM8K and HumanEval. First, request difficulty is discrete: denoising-step counts fall into 11 fixed levels, and no admission-time signal predicts the level (best R² = 0.150). Second, generation budgets below ~320 tokens understate serving variance through truncation. Third, 24% of single-request wall-clock time is GPU computation; the rest is CPU-side dispatch overhead. Sharing one forward pass per denoising step amortizes this overhead, reaching 16.0× single-request throughput at batch size 16. We also derive a batch-timeout stability rule for synchronized batching under Poisson arrivals. These results show that dLLM serving needs parallelism at the level of each denoising step. Code and data are available at https://github.com/flarebrienne/Serving-Masked-Diffusion-LLMS.

events.title: WHPC Networking Breakout
Measurement-Driven Contention-Aware, Herd-Safe Stripe Placement for Lustre
events.description:
Parallel file systems such as Lustre are shared by many concurrent jobs, so the write bandwidth observed by a single job fluctuates over time as other jobs place load on the same object storage targets (OSTs). Users can change how files are placed across OSTs, yet it remains unclear when doing so is beneficial. Based on measurements from three production Lustre systems, this paper finds that the contrast between busy and idle OSTs is a property of the moment rather than of the system, so the decision to tune has to be measured per job: always tuning costs 13% in the worst case, never tuning 43%.

Building on this observation, the paper presents CASTOR, a client-side tuner that operates without special privileges. It measures per-OST latency using a small write-probe, determines whether tuning is worthwhile, selects a layout with a simple model, and randomly distributes jobs across cool OSTs to prevent them from converging on the same targets. Across three file systems and six workloads, CASTOR demonstrates that an unprivileged write probe can detect contention and that randomly selecting among cool OSTs prevents concurrent tuners from colliding. Where a contrast exists, placement raises bandwidth by up to 1.85x and cuts its variance by up to 4.7x. The central lesson is that whether to tune is itself a measurement problem, and one that has to be solved before any layout is chosen.

events.title: Charliecloud: Image Build Optimization for AI Workloads
events.description:
Charliecloud is a lightweight, unprivileged container runtime for HPC. Its Git-based image build cache has structural advantages over standard layer-based caches and performs competitively, as we have previously shown. Because Git cannot track all file types or the metadata to rebuild images, Charliecloud supplements it with a complete image traversal per build instruction. Since this traversal time increases with image size, we sought to reduce it.
Our approach recursively watches for changes to the image with inotifywait, a commandline tool that reports file “events” via the Linux inotify interface. Because inotifywait can sometimes miss events, we add a verification step that walks new directories. Surprisingly, monitoring speeds up some instructions but slows down others. The major gains from monitor-informed updates shrink as more files change and eventually become slowdowns, because they must be added to Git individually. This motivates a hybrid strategy that captures monitoring’s benefit while minimizing its cost.

events.title: Linalg vs MDH: Why Reduction Semantics Matter
events.description:
Data-parallel computations are performance-critical building blocks in domains like scientific computing and machine learning. In the MLIR ecosystem, the Linalg dialect—in particular linalg.generic—is a central abstraction for such computations, yet it does not treat reduction operators as first-class, compiler-visible constructs.

To address this gap, we propose the mdh dialect: it makes reduction (combine) operators explicit—including user-defined operators beyond standard pointwise cases—thereby enabling reduction-aware code generation and richer expressivity for reduction-based computations. Our experiments on GPU and CPU—across linear algebra, deep learning, data mining, and quantum chemistry workloads—isolate the effect of explicit reduction operators, estimating the relative performance opportunity if linalg.generic exposed such operators.

events.title: No Bits Left Behind: A Precision-Preserving On-Wafer Reduction for FP64 GEMM
events.description:
Wafer-scale AI engines pack hundreds of thousands
of cores onto a single die, but their arithmetic is low-precision,
with no native double precision (FP64)—the workhorse of sci-
entific computing. We emulate FP64 matrix multiply (GEMM)
entirely on the wafer, to the accuracy of a true FP64 computation,
using the Ozaki scheme to split each operand into bfloat16
slices. On a grid with no shared memory, the Ozaki slices
must be reduced on the wafer itself in extended precision;
otherwise the reduction would discard the low-order bits the split
preserves. Accuracy is FP64-class at every size we measured, up
to 3360 × 3360, and we scale FP64 GEMM to span∼50% of
the wafer. The method extends to complex FP64 through a host-
side Karatsuba wrapper and drives a Newton–Schulz solver to
FP64-class residuals.

events.title: MiniLlama-Infra: Micro-Architecture Ablation of LLM Inference on Commodity GPU Accelerators
events.description: Quantizing LLM weights to INT8 can reduce storage yet still slow inference when GPU access patterns are poorly matched to the hardware. We present MiniLlama-Infra, a transparent from-scratch CUDA inference engine for Llama-3.2-1B and a six-stage micro-architecture study. Archived Nsight Compute measurements on an RTX 4060 Laptop show that naive INT8 GEMV reduces memory throughput from 58.1 to 19.2 GB/s and increases latency from 289.1 to 298.5 µs. A warp-cooperative mapping improves coalescing and available parallelism together, reducing kernel latency to 52.3 µs, a 5.7× speedup. Matched Stage 5/6 experiments further show that W8A8 improves decoding throughput by 15.8% on RTX 4060 Laptop and 12.8% on A100 SXM4, with estimated GPU energy-efficiency gains of 17.0% and 8.4%. Additional A100 kernel experiments, selected historical cross-generation and 3B results, and a compiled-engine perplexity pilot extend the evaluation while explicitly bounding the scope of the claims.

events.title: Secure integration and scaling for thousands of Jupyter sessions across hybrid cloud and HPC resources on Anvil
events.description: The Anvil Notebook Service is a highly scalable Kubernetes-based JupyterHub platform on Purdue University's NSF-funded Anvil supercomputer. We present technical solutions bridging Anvil's 1000-node Slurm HPC partition and its Kubernetes cloud resource to scale JupyterLab, VSCode and Linux Desktops for thousands of users. To scale beyond the capacity of the Kubernetes infrastructure, a locally developed, open-source software called Dynamic Node Manager converts idle HPC nodes to Kubernetes nodes on demand. To enable access to shared HPC filesystems from Jupyter pods, custom user identity integration allows containers to run as the logged-in user's UID. Users can access HPC Slurm queues for batch job submission. For efficient GPU utilization, users can dynamically slice GPUs based on vRAM requirements. Users can also run Apptainer containers and access AI agents and MCP tools. This talk shares the engineering insights for the hybrid HPC/cloud container orchestration of the service.

events.title: An LLVM Pass for Automatic Skeletonization of MPI Applications
events.description:
We present an LLVM pass that automatically skeletonizes MPI
applications: it statically identifies computations that do not affect
the arguments of MPI calls and removes them, producing a much faster
program that preserves the original's communication semantics. The
pass operates on the LLVM IR, propagating a communication
variable status backward from MPI call sites through the program's
data and control dependencies, and handles the non-trivial engineering
challenges (recursion, loops, dynamic libraries, memory allocation)
that arise when applying this analysis to real, non-trivial HPC codes
such as Lulesh and miniFE. We validate that the generated skeletons
reproduce the communication pattern of the original application, and
illustrate one concrete use of this technique: accelerating MPI
runtime tuning by running the parameter search on the skeleton rather
than on the full application.
