WHPC Career Pathways
events.description: Three women working in industry, national laboratories, and academia will share their career journeys and perspectives on navigating professional transitions, mentorship, challenges, and opportunities. This session offers practical insights for students and early-career professionals exploring diverse pathways in careers within HPC.

events.title: MPI-CCOB: Benchmarking MPI Overlap on CPU and GPU Systems
events.description: In this paper, we introduce the MPI Communication–Computation Overlap Benchmark, or MPI-CCOB, a configurable benchmark for evaluating overlap in MPI applications on CPU and GPU systems. Motivated by domain-decomposition applications, the benchmark organizes processing units into one-, two-, or three-dimensional Cartesian topologies, producing different numbers of concurrent neighbor-exchange requests. It supports both compute-bound and memory-bound workloads to examine how computational characteristics affect overlap. Since not all MPI implementations support asynchronous progress, MPI-CCOB also provides an optional user-level progress thread per processing unit. By controlling workload characteristics and communication-progress mechanisms, our benchmark reveals the conditions required for effective overlap. Experiments with MPICH and Open MPI show that active progress enables nearly complete overlap during compute-bound workloads. However, overlap decreases substantially under memory-bound workloads on both CPU and GPU systems, even when communication is continuously given the option to progress.

events.title: Characterizing Failure Types Across HPC and AI Clusters
events.description:
High-performance computing studies conclude that user error causes most job failures, while large-scale AI training reports attribute most interruptions to hardware. The two are rarely compared, because they publish failure evidence in incompatible forms: attributed causes, scheduler outcome labels, or bare event rates.

We survey 162 public datasets and reports, assign each an evidence verdict, and normalize the usable evidence into an eleven-class taxonomy tagging each failure type as a cause, a symptom, or an outcome label. The resulting denominator-disciplined maps cover 38 systems across 44 matrix columns, and include a GPU error-class characterization spanning five hardware generations.

Read on common footing the literatures agree: failure rates are similar but exposure is not, counting failures and weighting by compute give opposite priority orders, interconnect leads attributable GPU hardware failures, and the largest logged error class is application-induced. The survey table, taxonomy, and source quotations are released as a public artifact.

events.title: Deep codesign of advanced technology systems
Deriving Vendor-Agnostic GPU Metrics from AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 Hardware Counters
events.description:
Large-scale scientific applications increasingly run on GPUs from multiple vendors, and comparing performance across architectures is essential to porting and tuning codes. Such comparisons rely on hardware counters, but AMD and NVIDIA expose counter sets designed independently, with different names, granularities, and semantics, and no correspondence between them exists. We construct and validate a mapping between AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 hardware counters for FP64 compute and memory-hierarchy metrics, scoring each candidate pair across 12 kernels from the RAJA Performance Suite. Counters that appear comparable can measure different quantities: AMD reports FP64 instructions per wavefront without indicating how many of its 64 threads were active, which makes it report up to 3.19× more FP64 FLOPs than NVIDIA for the same kernel. We show how to correct this, and report every mapping we tested, including those that agree poorly and the metrics for which no
mapping exists.

events.title: Invited Talk with Pradeep Dubey, Intel Senior Fellow
A Production Compiler Implementation of Hardware Transactional Memory for OpenMP
events.description: Hardware Transactional Memory (HTM) has long been proposed as an alternative to lock-based synchronization, yet no production-quality compiler support for HTM exists in OpenMP. Several OpenMP extensions have been proposed to expose HTM to programmers, but setbacks in commercial hardware — most notably the security-related disabling of Intel TSX — led much of the community to abandon the effort. In this paper, we show that HTM support can be implemented with modest engineering effort in Clang/LLVM, a widely used production compiler. We adopt a previously proposed OpenMP transaction construct with a single max_retries clause and semantics mirroring the existing critical construct. We detail non-trivial challenges encountered during its implementation in LLVM 23, including two previously unreported correctness pitfalls: one in the transactional fallback mechanism and another in statement emission along transaction control-flow paths. Evaluation on an Intel Xeon shows that OpenHTM outperforms the standard critical construct by up to 1.97×.

events.title: Software for Large Scale Application (2)
events.description: This session surveys the software layers that make large-scale quantum-classical applications possible. Speakers will present the open Quantum Software Ecosystem (openQSE), the interfaces that connect quantum resources to HPC systems, and the workflow tools and libraries built on top of them. The talks highlight how these components fit together and what it takes to run real applications on integrated quantum-HPC systems today.

events.title: STARCH: RPC-Lifecycle Tracing of Margo-Based Distributed Systems for Performance Analysis
events.description: STARCH is a low-perturbation LTTng-based tracing system targeting RPC-Lifecycles, designed to instrument Margo-based applications without any code modification on the target. Per-node collectors aggregate events from clients and servers, while causal association of a client request to a server response is handled outside of the HPC job. The resulting trace database can be used to generate statistics and test many hypotheses without needing to run multiple manually instrumented experiments. In this paper we use STARCH to analyze a known CHFS performance degradation using IOR, and present the potential general applicability of STARCH on GekkoFS. STARCH typically incurs under 1.7\% overhead on our IOR+CHFS benchmark, and reliably collects and reconstructs tracing data in a manageable per-node data volume. STARCH was able to surface a nontrivial performance finding about CHFS, reducing the problem scope to a specific area of RPC handling.

events.title: Optimizing system memory bandwidth with micron CXL memory expansion modules on intel Xeon 6 processors
events.description: High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads typically demand substantial memory bandwidth and, to a degree, memory capacity. CXL memory expansion modules, also known as CXL "type-3" devices, enable enhancements in both memory capacity and bandwidth for server systems by utilizing the CXL protocol which runs over the PCIe interfaces of the processor. This paper discusses experimental findings on achieving increased memory bandwidth for HPC and AI workloads using Micron's CXL modules. Memory expansion via CXL boosts read-only bandwidth by 24% and mixed read/write bandwidth by up to 39%. Across HPC and AI workloads, the geometric mean of performance speedups is 24%.

events.title: CI for E4S: Build and Test Automation for a Containerized HPC-AI Software Stack
events.description: Modern HPC-AI software depends on complex webs of applications, libraries, and accelerator toolchains across many hardware platforms. E4S addresses dependency conflict resolution by distributing Spack-provisioned, containerized HPC-AI stacks across x86\_64, AArch64, and ppc64le, with CPU, CUDA, ROCm, and oneAPI variants. However, building, testing, and keeping stacks updated presents major challenges for small teams. We describe the GitLab CI pipeline and E4S Testsuite built to automate this: staged binary caching, Spack-driven environment builds, Docker/Singularity image generation, and per-package smoke tests. As of E4S 26.06, this approach drives about 200 CI jobs per pipeline, builds up to 127 CPU packages per architecture, and exercises 236 tests, with full x86\_64 CPU builds completing in 5 to 8 hours, and in minutes when cached. Automation has reduced maintainer workload, improved reproducibility, and lowered barriers to external contributions, demonstrating that CI automation is instrumental to sustaining community-maintained HPC-AI ecosystems at scale.

events.title: The Evolution of the Coaraci HPC Infrastructure: Operational Lessons from a Brazilian Research Computing Center
events.description:
High-performance computing (HPC) is a necessary tool for many research fields. However, the cluster is not the only component necessary to operate an HPC environment. This paper presents the evolution of the Coaraci High-Performance Computing infrastructureat the Gleb Wataghin Institute of Physics (IFGW), University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil; The project modernized an existing academic data center through upgrades to electrical power, backup generation, UPS systems, precision cooling, airflow management, high-speed networking, workload management, monitoring, user onboarding, and technical support. Thermal improvements included cold-aisle containment, high-flow floor panels, and high-airflow rack doors.
Average Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) decreased from 2.14 in April 2024 to 1.56 in June 2025, an observed reduction of about 27%. The optimized cooling strategy also enabled operation with two active cooling units and one standby unit. Since February 2024, Coaraci has operated 24/7 with 366 registered users, 284 of whom have executed workloads.

events.title: Career Pathways
events.description: Navigating your career is a challenge that all early-career professionals must face. Career pathways will vary depending on those in academia, government research lab, or industry. In this panel, we will hear from professionals in each of these sectors to hear about their unique experiences and challenges as they embarked upon their career roadmap.

events.title: T-CCL: Resource Efficient and Performant Collective Communication using Tensor Memory Accelerator
Addressing Challenges in Collaborative Computational Cancer Policy Research
events.description:
Two computational artifacts underpin personalized lung cancer screening: a natural history model (NHM) that reproduces disease progression (CHRONOS-Lung), and a decision-analytic framework that converts individual risk into a screening schedule. ENGAGE provides the latter as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), solved once per risk profile across a O(10^8) combinatorial space. Both are written in Julia and were developed at MD Anderson. Since 2020, successive ALCC allocations have let our team run large-scale calibration and analysis campaigns for multiple cancer modeling groups on leadership computing, which made the ENGAGE campaigns conceivable. We review four themes from moving these models onto HPC.

The first was dependency and portability. The POMDP solves relied on a commercial solver, so we moved to the open, JuMP-compatible HiGHS. Scale then exposed fragility local runs never showed, with 230 of 1,000 solves failing at default tolerances. Sweeping three tolerances across 64 combinations identified relaxed settings we adopted. Separately, the Julia projects pinned no manifests, so library drift triggered recompilation on compute nodes, a limited issue locally but a large one when many concurrent compilations fire at once. Pinning environments and amortizing JIT and library-load costs across node-local task batches removed that overhead.

The second was scale. The POMDP campaign produces an enormous number of small files in Julia-specific binary formats, a pattern parallel filesystems handle poorly and one aggravated by sharing an allocation and file systems with other cancer modeling groups. We ran in batches of two million POMDP solves, chaining an archival tar job that triggered the subsequent batch, staged through the scratch file system, and served the resulting archives through a Globus collection. Input handling had similar issues. The solves re-read the same jld2 files repeatedly, so at our scale 55,680 of them contended for the same files, causing I/O deadlock and sharply longer runtimes until we rewrote them to cache the reads.

The third was pluggability. CHRONOS-Lung, the sex-, histology-, and nodule-attenuation-specific NHM, comprises 12 Julia models sharing a 15-state monthly-cycle structure with Gompertz tumor growth and size-dependent stage transitions. Its original calibration was a bespoke extreme-elitist genetic algorithm in Julia, in which the two fittest of 100 individuals produced every child. Because the EMEWS model exploration framework treats both the NHM and the exploration algorithm as pluggable tasks, we could investigate alternatives efficiently, using EMEWS queues for Python to let the open-source Python DEAP library drive the Julia NHM over MPI. We finally adopted a (mu + lambda) scheme with tournament selection, which produced robust fits across the multiple calibration targets.

The fourth was statistical. Calibration had used 1,000-person cohorts for expediency. Scaling studies let us move to 100,000, spending concurrency on reduced uncertainty and better estimator quality rather than wall-clock alone. The calibrated models reproduced their SEER targets closely and validated against four independent external cohorts.

Throughout, the governing question was how much domain code must change to meet HPC constraints and how much the workflow layer can absorb on its behalf.

events.title: Analytical Resource Management for Fine-Grained MoE Computation-Communication Overlap
events.description:
Fine-grained computation-communication overlap lets distributed Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference start communication on partial results. Compute and communication cooperative thread arrays (CTAs), however, contend for finite streaming-multiprocessor (SM) residency and progress in discrete waves, and a fixed partition cannot adapt to workload or kernel changes.
We present a wave-quantized analytical model and launch-time resource manager that selects the communication-CTA count from routed-tile counts, kernel occupancy, residency constraints, and split-level readiness dependencies before launch, without profiling or recompilation.
We integrate it into the COMET A100 implementation and evaluate three MoE models on four A100 GPUs under three parallelism configurations at the GEMM2+GatherRS operator, complete post-router MoE layer, and complete-model prefill levels.
Speedups over COMET reach 4.218×, 2.584×, and 1.439× at these levels, respectively.
At every feasible TP=2/EP=2 sequence length of at least 4096, our implementation outperforms Megatron core-TE and FastMoE TP+NCCL.

events.title: PRISM: Lightweight Surrogation for Lossy Compression Quality Prediction
events.description:
Error-bounded lossy compression is indispensable for managing the data deluge in exascale
scientific workflows, yet selecting compressor configurations requires evaluating quality
metrics (CR, PSNR, SSIM) that are expensive to compute directly. Deep surrogate models
address this bottleneck but must be retrained from scratch whenever new data fields,
compressors, or metrics are introduced, creating a combinatorial scaling problem. We present
PRISM, a lightweight framework that trains a single foundation backbone and adapts to new tasks via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), removing the need
for full retraining. Evaluated on the Hurricane Isabel application across eight fields, four
compressors, and three metrics, PRISM achieves MAPE below 10% in 81 of 96 tasks using
rank-4 adaptation with under 1% trainable parameters (107x reduction), and is more
accurate than from-scratch training when samples are scarce. By amortizing one reusable
backbone across the task space, PRISM offers scalable compression quality prediction for
large-scale HPC workflows.

events.title: Extending MPI One-Sided Communication with Lightweight Notification-Based Synchronization
events.description:
As high-performance computing systems scale toward many-core architectures, hybrid programming models combining message passing and task-based execution require efficient communication and synchronization. However, integrating communication and synchronization into these models remains challenging.

We present two contributions to address these challenges. First, we introduce Task-Aware LPF (TALPF), a task-integrated implementation of the Lightweight Parallel Foundations library supporting asynchronous communication and relaxed synchronization while preserving the analyzable Bulk Synchronous Parallel model and enabling overlap of computation and communication. Second, we extend a notification-based MPI communication model to support multiple occurrences of the same notification identifier, enabling fine-grained synchronization without additional overhead. This mechanism is exported through Task-Aware MPI (TAMPI) and underpins Two-Sided RDMA (2SR), which emulates two-sided MPI semantics using one-sided operations with notifications.

We evaluate these contributions on the MareNostrum5 supercomputer and demonstrate competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art task-aware and MPI one-sided implementations while improving programmability, safety, and portability.

events.title: Domain Bounds as a Silent-Fault Detector for AI-Ready Scientific Data
events.description: We address an incipient type of data-based faults, driven by increasing data reuse in AI-enhanced computational science workflows. A dataset is created under specific conditions; its categories, measures, and labels depend on that context, but that context is usually unavailable downstream and abandoned when datasets are used to train models. We propose encoding this context, called domain bounds, with the data to which it applies. A domain bound flags apparently valid data proposed for reuse in an incompatible context, even when every value falls within its expected range. We present cases from computational science and biomedicine where missing domain bounds allow silent reuse errors, and show why description and provenance approaches miss them. Our detector uses standard data container technologies and catches faults from a taxonomy of published cases, at a cost independent of dataset size. It caught 17 of 18 injected domain-bound reuses that lineage and descriptive records accepted.

events.title: Fantastic Hardware Counters and How to Use Them for Noise-Resilient Performance Modeling
events.description: Performance models are a key instrument in HPC, exposing scalability bugs early and predicting scaling behavior. Most empirical models, however, rely on time measurements, which can be distorted by noise. Hardware counters offer a robust alternative, but not every counter is noise-resilient and reflects scaling behavior. We close the loop between noise-resilience analysis and performance modeling. Building on NORC, we introduce a selection stage combining a knee-based cutoff on noise-resilient counter rankings with a modeling-quality assessment that compares counter models from a benchmark suite against ground truth via lead-exponent deviation, then clusters redundant counters. The selected counters feed two strategies added to Extra-P that derive a model's term structure from the counters and fit only the coefficients from runtime. Evaluated using PolyBench, Kripke, and RELeARN, our approach reduces model error by up to 75% while keeping measurement effort at a standard Extra-P level.

events.title: PathLlama: Domain-Adapted Language Models for Cancer Surveillance at Scale
events.description:
Population-based cancer surveillance depends on converting narrative pathology reports into structured tumor characteristics. Automated coding must handle ambiguous reports and rare tumor categories while allowing difficult cases to remain under expert review [1]. We investigate whether domain-specific continual pre-training improves cancer registry coding by a general-purpose language model with tunable abstention.

We adapted Meta Llama 3 8B [2] on 16.1 million clinical and cancer-registry records containing approximately 7.0 billion words from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program, MIMIC-III [3], and MIMIC-CXR [4]. The supervised dataset comprised 4,054,951 pathology reports from six SEER registries, with case-level splits. Five classification heads predict site, subsite, laterality, histology, and behavior, each with an additional abstention output. Development and evaluation ran within the secure CITADEL environment on Frontier. Supervised fine-tuning used Fully Sharded Data Parallelism [5], bfloat16 precision, partial layer freezing, and 64 nodes with 256 AMD MI250X modules.

A Deep Abstaining Classifier-inspired objective [6] learns when to defer each task. During training, a validation controller adjusts each task’s abstention penalty toward a chosen accuracy target among accepted predictions. The DAC is a tunable parameter and we tested it at both the 95% and 97.5% target configurations. At inference, the highest-scoring output determines the label or abstention, without confidence thresholding.

We compared domain-adapted PathLlama-adap with PathLlama-base, the same backbone fine-tuned directly using identical supervised protocols, on 395,299 held-out reports from five registries. The 95% target configuration used random sampling; the 97.5% configuration used sequential sampling, intended to stabilize controller updates through deterministic record coverage. Target and sampler effects were not tested separately. Comparisons were made within each configuration; targets were not guarantees of test accuracy.

PathLlama-adap produced more correct automatic labels per test report in all ten task/configuration comparisons and deferred fewer reports in nine, while accuracy among accepted predictions differed by at most 0.4 percentage points. For histology at the 95% target, abstention fell from 55.8% with PathLlama-base to 53.4% with PathLlama-adap, and macro F1 over the same 566 test classes increased from 0.4541 to 0.4782. At the 97.5% target, abstention fell from 75.5% to 73.7%, and this F1 increased from 0.3145 to 0.3366. For rare histology classes (11–50 test reports each), the mean fraction correctly auto-coded per class was 22.4% with PathLlama-adap versus 3.8% with the Hierarchical Self-Attention Network (HiSAN) at the 95% target. This secondary benchmark does not isolate continual pre-training.

Domain adaptation was associated with more correct automated cancer labels while maintaining similar accuracy among accepted predictions. Tunable abstention provides a mechanism for balancing automated coding with expert review. Findings remain descriptive and internal: each arm had one run, all test registries contributed training data, corpus overlap was unquantified, and additional pre-training exposure was not controlled. External, replicated evaluation is needed before operational use.

events.title: Co-Designing the NIC and Transport: Simpler Hardware, Scalable Communication
Error-Explicit Low-Precision Factorizations for Iterative Refinement
events.description:
Recent NVIDIA GPUs prioritize low-precision throughput while native FP64 stagnates, falling from $37$ to $1.25$\,TFLOP/s between B200 and B300.
Mixed-precision iterative refinement factorizes in FP32 but retains the FP64 matrix $A$ for residual evaluation, requiring $12n^2$ bytes of persistent storage.
We present two refinement algorithms that remove this dependence.
Split-$A$ iterative refinement (SA-IR) represents $A$ as two FP32 words, while error-explicit iterative refinement (R-IR) stores the FP32 factorization residual $R=PA-LU$ and discards $A$, reducing storage to $8n^2$ bytes.
R-IR inherits refinement's convergence condition, and in our tests its accuracy is limited by residual evaluation rather than FP32 storage of $R$.
Across five GPUs the advantage tracks the FP32:FP64 ratio.
On B300 at $n=32{,}768$, SA-IR is $25\times$ faster than emulated FP64 and $1.4\times$ faster than vendor refinement, and R-IR is $24\times$ faster at $8192$ right-hand sides.
Streamed construction of $R$ peaks at $8.24$--$8.57n^2$ bytes, reaching $n=184{,}320$ where $12n^2$ will not fit.

events.title: Characterizing and Auto-Tuning 175B-Parameter LLM Training on Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 Accelerators
events.description: Training large language models on production HPC systems requires parallelism configurations tailored to accelerator memory, interconnect topology, and software maturity. We present an empirical study of GPT-style training on Intel Data Center Max 1550 GPUs in SuperMUC-NG Phase 2, using the upstream Megatron-DeepSpeed stack without custom kernels, evaluating 3.6B-, 20B-, and 175B-parameter models to quantify how tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, micro-batch size, and gradient accumulation affect throughput and feasibility. Results show a pronounced penalty when tensor-parallel collectives cross the eight-tile node boundary, while more micro-batches amortize pipeline bubbles until throughput saturates. Bayesian optimization of the 175B space yields a configuration reaching 58.91 TFLOP/s per tile; scaling to 128 nodes (1024 tiles) retains 91% weak-scaling and 82% strong-scaling efficiency. We derive an empirical cost decomposition from pipeline depth, micro-batch size, and gradient accumulation that bounds what further auto-tuning alone can deliver on this system.

events.title: Keeping up the Pace: Growing AMD Flang's OpenMP Offloading Ecosystem
events.description: Contemporary supercomputers are massively parallel, heterogeneous systems with accelerators---mostly graphics processing units (GPUs)---that provide additional compute and memory performance. Fortran continues to have a large developer base with new code written every day. The OpenMP Application Programming Interface (API) thus constitutes one of the key programming languages to support developers in their need to write portable, high-performance code for such heterogeneous systems. In this paper, we will highlight the evolution of the AMD Fortran Compiler (AMD Flang) in the past twelve months. As AMD Flang is based on LLVM Flang, much of the evolution is also relevant for the LLVM project via pull requests that have been contributed or will be contributed in the future.

events.title: National Lab Strategies
events.description: This session brings together representatives from national laboratories and supercomputing centers that are building or operating quantum computing capabilities alongside their HPC systems. Each speaker will give a short talk on their organization's strategy, covering plans, lessons learned, and priorities for integrating quantum computing into HPC environments. The talks will be followed by a panel discussion on common challenges and how institutions across regions can work together to move quantum-HPC integration forward.

events.title: One API, Five Memories: Measuring Unified Memory Across NVIDIA and AMD Architectures
events.description:
Managed memory promises one pointer that both the CPU and the GPU can dereference, with the system deciding where the pages live.
We measured what that promise means on five systems: NVIDIA H100 NVL, GH200, GB10, and AMD MI300A and MI300X, running one benchmark identically on all of them: a page-granular pointer chase bracketed by device- and host-resident anchor buffers, cross-checked by an operating-system residency probe, and probing placement, lifecycle costs, memory pressure, memAdvise hints, and concurrency.
The five systems follow four different placement rules.
The same managed access costs 244ns on an empty H100 and 40152ns when GPU memory is full; the GH200 degrades eightfold under the same pressure, the GB10 not at all.
Hints rescue the H100 by 40x, harm the GH200 by up to 44x and are inert on single-pool systems.
A routine operating-system update rewrote the MI300X's placement rule on unchanged hardware and ROCm.

events.title: Expanded Slurm container runtime support
events.description: Slurm 26.11 will add a new runtime plugin capability intended to replace the existing OCI container support as well as become the key integration point for all container runtime engines going forward. This capability will enable the community to build lua bindings to properly adapt Slurm to each container runtime, and will enable greater workflow composability with a diversity of emerging workloads. Runtime plugins will continue to enable command line interface flexibility while extending support to the Slurm REST interfaces. Further this capability will enable container runtimes to properly layer namespace usage with Slurm's administrative namespace plugins.

events.title: Faster Post-Outage Testing at Full Machine Scale
events.description: System testing after outages is a standard workflow across HPC centers. When returning from an unplanned outage, the main focus is identifying any degraded hardware and quickly returning the system to production. We have developed a post-outage testing tool called pray4us that checks the full machine with component-wise tests, provides a simple to interpret pass/fail answer, provides specific actions to take if failures are encountered, and runs end-to-end at full scale with all tests in a short wall-clock time. We cover the pray4us tool and discuss using it to investigate a Slingshot-11 bandwidth problem uncovered by the tool. Through the tool we have discovered the bandwidth problem is correlated with message size suggesting a stall event rather than a degraded network component. This may be related to enabling Prioirty Flow Control on our Slingshot-11 network, so next steps for our tool includes recording NIC level counters looking for pause frames.

events.title: Co-designing MoE Architectures and System Stacks for Scalable Training on Leadership Supercomputers
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) have shown exceptional promise as scientific foundation models. However, substantial pre-training costs pose a major bottleneck in training high-quality models. The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has emerged as an effective solution to this problem. Preceding MoE studies have been conducted on NVIDIA platforms, while many scientific foundation models are trained on supercomputers with diverse accelerators. By examining pretraining strategies on a dataset sourced from scientific texts and porting state-of-the-art MoE training techniques to the ROCM-stack on Frontier, we identify crucial factors to achieve high training throughput. For the first time, we show that it is possible to scale training of massive MoE models on clusters with thousands of GPUs. Leveraging these insights, we train a suite of MoE models for science, called SMOREs. Evaluations of these models against standard benchmarks such as SciQ and ARC-Challenge show that they outperform their dense counterparts in the early phases of training.

events.title: Optimizing Semiconductor Device Simulations through Low-Precision Arithmetic
events.description:
Architectural changes in GPUs, especially the boost in low-precision computational units, pose significant challenges to traditional, FP64-based high-performance computing (HPC) applications, while also presenting opportunities.
Adopting reduced-precision data formats is a promising avenue to exploit the increased throughput capabilities. However, straightforward data conversions may lead to degraded accuracy or even erroneous results. For a given application, only an in-depth analysis of its numerical stability can reveal the potential of low-precision arithmetic. In this work, we consider the open-source quatrex package, a quantum transport solver capable of breaking the sustained FP64 Eflop/s barrier, to illustrate trade-offs between accuracy losses and computational speed-ups when moving from high- to low-precision formats.
We use three representative benchmark structures to explore the application's numerical properties.
Applying the gained insights to a larger, more realistic system, we achieve up to 51% higher throughput while maintaining accurate results, on 40% fewer HPC resources than the FP64 reference.

events.title: Large Scale Sorting on UPMEM Processing-in-Memory Architectures
events.description: Sorting is fundamental in many data-intensive applications, and its memory-bound nature limits parallel efficiency on parallel processors. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architectures co-locate DIMM Processing Units (DPUs) with memory and are designed to mitigate the memory bottleneck, but their distributed memory model, lack of peer-to-peer communication between DPUs, and lightweight cores yield several challenges. We present PIM-Sort, a comparison-based sorting algorithm designed for large-scale execution on the UPMEM PIM platform, the first commercially produced PIM system. We design PIM-Sort to address the architectural challenges above, and evaluate it on a UPMEM system with 2546 operational DPUs across uniform and skewed inputs up to 155 GiB. PIM-Sort outperforms a parallel CPU baseline on a separate, higher-bandwidth platform by up to 1.24x on 79 GiB of uniformly distributed data (the largest input that fits in a single DPU wave), while the multi-core CPU remains faster on heavily duplicated inputs where cache reuse yields a performance advantage. We find that PIM-Sort is more energy efficient (up to 35%) than the parallel CPU algorithm even when the latter strongly benefits from cache reuse.

events.title: The Bipartible Architecture Pattern: Transparently Directing HTTP Requests over InfiniBand
events.description:
Large-scale compute (HPC) systems often deploy InfiniBand (IB) networks for high-bandwidth and low latency communication. In an HPC system, a TCP network is typically used for control-plane and general-purpose communication. The last decade has seen the rise of cloud-native software patterns which are characterized by container based software distribution and communication over TCP/IP.

This paper introduces the Bipartible Architecture Pattern that transparently redirects HTTP traffic onto IB without changing workload implementation or network configuration. This is achieved by introducing a service on the host(s) that intercepts HTTP requests and transforms them into global filesystem requests. This maintains the HTTP interface while leveraging the IB network for data transfer.

The feasibility of this pattern is demonstrated by implementing a prototype for Garage (S3) and Pulp (repository). We offer this pattern as one of many alternative approaches to address the performance challenges of deploying scientific software containers at scale on HPC environments.

events.title: Geometry-Routed Attention for Multi-Magnification Histopathology Fusion in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
events.description:
Multi-view histopathology provides multiple histopathological images (HI) at different magnifications and tissue regions for each patient. Existing methodology includes complex fusion based learning architecture. However, existing state-of-the-art deep fusion models fails to capture the acquisition geometry of the multi-view HI. On the recently released Multi-Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC) benchmark, a self-attention fusion module was reported to under-perform plain feature concatenation, suggesting that unstructured attention cannot recover the scale-and-region relationships from a small cohort of 925 training patients.

In this work, we proposed dot-product based Geometry-Routed Attention fusion model (GRA), that incorporates a low-parameter routing that considers the acquisition geometry along with tumor core/edge regions prior directly into the attention logits. We study two realizations, ALiBi-style bias (GRA-P) and a learned per-relation routing (GRA-R). We validate our proposed methodology on Multi-OSCC dataset comprising of six classes with HI captured under three magnification factors. GRA-R attains a mean test AUC of 77.97%, with the highest class specific AUC for recurrence of 91.27%. Our results surpass existing benchmark Concat by 2.97% on mean multi-class performance. In particular, GRA-R surpass existing state of the art by 4.89% for lymph node metastasis and 5.04% for tumor differentiation. Additionally, the data-scaling ablation demonstrates that the GRA-R largest performance yield in low-data regimes, highlighting the utility of the proposed model under limited training data. Component-wise ablations further demonstrate that both acquisition-geometry and region-aware routing terms contribute independently to the overall performance.

events.title: Scalable Hierarchical Multi-NIC GPU-Aware MPI Alltoall via Hamiltonian Decomposition
events.description: Alltoall is a communication-intensive collective, realizing a full-mesh exchange among all processes, which relies on RDMA's Reliable Connection (RC) transport for inter-node communication, requiring a dedicated Queue Pair (QP) per peer and exhausting on-NIC memory as peer count grows. We propose a GPU-aware MPI Alltoall that avoids vendor-specific transports, decomposing the full-mesh exchange graph into edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles so each process has a small, fixed number of direct peers, combined with a pipelined, multi-NIC exchange overlapping intra- and inter-node communication. Experimentally, at 36 and 72 GPUs, we reduce measured QPs per NIC by up to 98% and 93% versus Open MPI and NCCL, matching an analytical model projecting 66%-98% reductions up to 1152 GPUs. Our design achieves up to 34% and 36% lower Alltoall latency than Open MPI and MVAPICH-Plus, matches NCCL's latency using MPI, and delivers up to 1.2x and 1.66x higher heFFTe throughput than Open MPI and MVAPICH-Plus.

events.title: Asynchrony Promotes Scalable Recovery of Iterative Linear Solvers from Silent Errors
events.description: Distributed memory linear solvers are the workhorse of many scientific HPC applications and are also close counterparts to AI algorithms. The increasing scale and heterogeneity of HPC systems renders them susceptible to silent data corruption (SDC). Physics based checksums (PBCs) can detect SDC errors locally on each computing node. Detection can be followed by rollback to a checkpoint: however, this localized checkpointing does not scale optimally as fault rates increase. Increased asynchrony in Krylov solvers promotes scalability of fault recovery from SDC errors. We focus on the s-step communication-avoiding conjugate gradient (CACG), and describe the algorithmic changes needed to implement PBCs to protect all portions of the CACG algorithm. Our results show that local recovery incurs much lower overhead and remains scalable at much higher node counts and fault rates compared to global recovery and that as fault rates increase, the benefit of asynchrony increases.

events.title: An Omnistat-Guided Workflow for Energy-Efficiency Analysis
events.description: Large-scale accelerator applications can exhibit variation in device activity and completion times as workloads evolve. Allocation-wide averages may obscure whether reduced activity reflects improved energy efficiency or devices waiting for slower ranks. We present an Omnistat-guided workflow that aligns timestamped node- and accelerator-level telemetry with application timers and algorithmic steps. Omnistat operates in user mode and requires no modification or recompilation. We demonstrate the workflow using a 64-node CRK-HACC cosmological hydrodynamics simulation spanning 512 GCDs and 625 steps. Its evolving particle distribution illustrates how computational heterogeneity manifests in application timings and system telemetry. Dynamic load balancing is disabled to provide a controlled configuration. The analysis shows how cross-rank timing variability propagates to accelerator utilization, frequency, power, and energy. Relating step energy to cross-device power dispersion identifies intervals for load-distribution analysis and phases that may benefit from power management, making Omnistat a practical first-pass diagnostic layer for subsequent profiling and optimization.

events.title: Adopting Emerging AI Frameworks in HPC Environments
events.description: Computational scientists use HPC in two primary ways: to run simulations and to process data, iterating until a new observation emerges. As scientific computation becomes more sophisticated and resource-heavy, researchers increasingly turn to AI/MLtools to accelerate discovery. Yet before these tools can be used, scientists often spend undue time on tasks like environment setup, dependency management, model acquisition, and determining the correct way to run each framework on shared HPC systems. This demands a system that can streamline and standardize these setup tasks, so that scientists can focus on analysis rather than infrastructure. With a reproducible, well-defined workflow for deploying and running AI tools on HPC, we can accomplish this goal. In this work, we demonstrate such a workflow using four widely used AI tools: Stable Diffusion (text-to-image generation), vLLM (high-throughput large language model inference), Ollama (lightweight local LLM serving), and AlphaFold3 (protein-structure prediction).

events.title: Co-Design for new processor and system architectures at JSC
Optimizing Podman Storage Performance on Shared Filesystems
events.description:
By default, Podman assumes that container image storage resides on local disks, reflecting its heritage as a developer-friendly tool designed for single workstations or servers. Currently it stores individual container layers as extracted tarballs using OverlayFS to merge them into a container file system. While efficient locally, extracting each layer to disk triggers metadata-heavy operations that perform poorly on shared filesystems like NFS and Lustre.

This presentation explores alternatives being proposed within the Podman ecosystem to address these limitations. Specifically, we will examine the imagefs storage plugin, which implements two backends optimized for shared filesystems: EROFS and SquashFS. SquashFS is well-known in the HPC community and we will also the potential of EROFS. We will present the storage plugin implementation, analyze its performance implications, and discuss how direct enhancements to the Podman ecosystem can alleviate container image storage challenges in HPC environments.

events.title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
events.description: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth challenge efficient inference. Pruning often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity remains challenging due to irregular memory accesses and workload imbalance. In this work, we investigate standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance using roofline analysis, showing that a 3 × 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of ~10 FLOP/byte compared to ∼96 FLOP/byte for dense convolution. We propose techniques for efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results show that our approach achieves up to 1.65× speedup over dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and up to 1.52× on NVIDIA Tegra X1, demonstrating the potential of direct sparse convolution for efficient inference on modern GPUs and edge devices.

events.title: DGEMM with Ozaki Scheme I/II on FP4 Tensor Cores: A Base-13 E2M1 Limb Representation
events.description: This paper proposes a method and its implementation for emulating FP64 matrix multiplication (DGEMM) by constructing, on FP4 (E2M1) Tensor Cores, Ozaki schemes I and II. The key property is that every FP4 value becomes an integer when doubled, and that shifting this integer set by multiples of 13 covers all integers. Converting an arbitrary integer into base-13 FP4 limbs keeps intermediate sums error-free in FP32 accumulators. By the same principle, the integer GEMM of INT8 Tensor Cores can be emulated bit-exactly on FP4. When FP4 Tensor Cores have twice the throughput of FP8, Ozaki scheme II theoretically achieves slightly higher performance than its FP8 counterpart. This paper further proposes kernel optimizations raising the attained fraction of peak performance. We verify this on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, achieving performance competitive with an existing FP8-based implementation of Ozaki scheme II, and exceeding it at a large problem size (16384^3).

events.title: Security and Day-2 Resilience as First Class Control Plane Primitives for Heterogeneous Supercomputers
events.description: This experience report describes how reproducibility, security, and safe day-2 operations are handled in OpenCHAMI, an open, API-first, composable HPC control plane developed collaboratively under a Linux Foundation foundation and deployed in production across multiple sites. Modern centres run Slurm-scheduled HPC alongside Kubernetes-based AI, and maintenance windows test the management plane hardest. Rather than a controlled benchmarking study, we contribute a deployed open system, transferable operational practices, and an honest account of what is validated today versus roadmapped. We describe a composable microservices architecture with snapshot-based, predictably degrading state; a layered image-build pipeline with one-shot cloud-init convergence that removes configuration drift; and a WireGuard-based ephemeral bootstrapping model that keeps no long-lived credentials in images. We report author-reported outcomes, including a boot-to-scheduler-ready reduction from roughly eight minutes to ninety seconds, and evidence that the same control plane transfers across sites, architectures, and workload classes.

events.title: WHPC Closing Remarks
Evaluating OpenMP API Version 6.1 Target Kernel Language
events.description: The OpenMP API has steadily evolved into a comprehensive, highly portable alternative to vendor-specific APIs for GPU acceleration. The upcoming OpenMP 6.1 specification introduces two key features for code acceleration: access to dynamic shared memory and multidimensional, kernel-like programming. In this paper, we provide an overview of these newly standardized features for C++ and Fortran codebases. We implement a functional prototype based on the official LLVM infrastructure, extending both the Clang and Flang compilers to support these additions. We evaluate our implementation across several C++ and Fortran benchmarks, confirming that these new OpenMP capabilities effectively help close the performance and expressiveness gap with vendor-specific APIs. During the evaluation, we also observe a few remaining opportunities where OpenMP could become even more competitive for specific computational patterns.

events.title: DAOS Update: Version 2.8 and MLPerf Storage
events.description: The Distributed Asynchronous Object Storage (DAOS) is an open source software-defined high performance storage system that has redefined performance and scalability for a wide spectrum of AI and HPC workloads. This PDSW26 WiP session presents the new features in DAOS 2.8, as well as DAOS results for the MLPerf Storage v3.0 benchmarks.

events.title: Extending ecoHMEM to Arm: Automatic Data Placement Using Statistical Profiling Extension
events.description: The growing diversification of high-performance processor architectures and adoption of heterogeneous memory systems introduce new challenges for performance portability and efficient memory management. As Arm-based platforms gain relevance in HPC and technologies such as HBM and CXL memory expansion become widespread, mechanisms that automatically exploit memory heterogeneity are increasingly important. Precise sampled hardware events have proven valuable for characterizing memory behavior across processor families, but their use on Arm has only recently become feasible with the Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE). In this work, we extend the ecoHMEM automatic data-placement framework to Arm-based systems by leveraging SPE to obtain precise memory-access information. We design and implement the required profiling infrastructure and analyze its key tradeoffs. Experimental evaluation on an Arm system with emulated memory heterogeneity demonstrates the feasibility of integrating SPE into automatic data placement, achieving performance improvements of up to 22% over mainstream NUMA strategies.

events.title: Overlay Containers in Apptainer
events.description:
Apptainer recently added the concept of overlay containers. Unlike OCI which natively uses many layers, Apptainer has always been based on a container image of one layer, which has advantages especially for HPC environments. It has also always supported overlay images, but they were solely for runtime and were of limited use. Apptainer now has an overlay option at build time that creates a container image that has only the defined additions/changes along with information to identify the base image, not the base image itself. The intended use case is for a software project to produce a shared base image containing the bulk of the software of the project, and for individual project members to each add their much smaller modifications in their own overlay container image. This aids especially in distribution, since the larger images change less often and can be pre-distributed using a more appropriate method.
~

events.title: Stretch Break
Exploring DAOS as a Burst Buffer for Nx100 Gbps Scientific Streaming
events.description: Scientific experiments are shifting from batched-file acquisition to online streaming readout, where O(1) MB detector frames flow directly to HPC facilities for real-time processing. Each HPC node runs a multi-stage workflow, and the slowest stage determines the overall throughput. On a pair of 100 Gbps nodes, throughput drops from 35 Gbps to 6 Gbps once downstream processing is enabled. Based on a 2024 experiment, we estimate that streaming live data would require about 300 Perlmutter nodes. This work explores Distributed Asynchronous Object Storage (DAOS) as a burst buffer that decouples the counting-house upstream from HPC downstream processing, such that fewer nodes can absorb the same traffic. Writing raw 8.6 KB packets to DAOS through an asynchronous queue achieved 32 Gbps end-to-end, limited by a single DAOS connection. Ongoing Aurora experiments suggest near-linear client-side scaling. We outline open challenges: small-object read penalties, tail latency under continuous production, and the throughput–latency trade-off.

events.title: A Comparative Study of Energy Scaling Behavior for AI Training: Wafer or Die Scale
events.description:
Datacenter electricity consumption is projected to grow rapidly, driven primarily by AI. Meeting this demand sustainably requires understanding how training energy scales with model size, and whether this holds across increasingly diverse hardware, particularly for wafer-scale dataflow accelerators like the Cerebras WSE series, which integrate compute and memory on a single wafer, unlike die-scale GPUs.
We compare a Cerebras WSE-2 and an NVIDIA GH200 as representative wafer- and die-scale accelerators, using a matched sweep of seven CNN and Vision Transformer architectures with batch sizes from 2 to 512 to cross-validate energy models. We find distinct energy-scaling behavior between the two: the WSE-2's dataflow execution makes scaling more predictable, while its high baseline power and lack of workload-controlled power management increase sensitivity to model size and batch size.

events.title: Mixed Precision at Scale: From Peak FLOPs to Trusted Science
Move Metadata, Not Data: A Register-in-Place Lakehouse for Large Autonomous-Driving Datasets
events.description: Even when autonomous-driving data is available on shared storage, analysis pipelines often copy and reorganize it. To register sensor files without copying them, we built an Apache Iceberg lakehouse that records their locations and metadata. We registered about 647,000 lidar and radar Parquet files from a resident ∼13TB sample of NVIDIA’s 133 TB PhysicalAI Autonomous Vehicles dataset. Registering these Parquet files over NFS took approximately 2 h 8 min, based on log timestamps. In a separate four-scale experiment, registration time grew approximately linearly with file count. Timed after warm-up in that experiment, eleven queries over metadata or materialized tables had median latencies of 21–352 ms as total registered rows grew 36×; these timings do not characterize general sensor or media scans. Deployment also exposed an ownership hazard when DROP TABLE PURGE unintentionally deleted ∼11TB of source data. We describe safeguards and are developing a copy-based baseline.

events.title: The American Science Cloud and the Genesis Mission
events.description: The Genesis Mission is a U.S. Department of Energy initiative to accelerate AI-driven scientific discovery across the national research complex. At its core is the American Science Cloud (AmSC),a secure, federated, and science-optimized platform connecting DOE leadership computing facilities, national laboratories, and experimental user facilities into a unified environment for large-scale scientific workflows. This talk will provide an overview of AmSC and Genesis from a project-wide perspective, representing contributions from across the DOE laboratory community. It describes the platform architecture and the central role that cloud-native technologies such as containers, Kubernetes, and cloud infrastructure play in enabling AmSC's vision. The talk will also discuss some of the major challenges the AmSC platform is designed to address and its future goals.

events.title: Execution-Path- and Restriction-Aware Autotuning for MPI Collective Operations
events.description: Machine-learning autotuning selects MPI collective algorithms by benchmarking candidates and predicting the fastest for each execution configuration. Existing methods often assume that all candidates are valid throughout the configuration space and that measurements reflect their actual execution paths. These assumptions fail when restrictions cause silent fallback or compositional algorithms invoke nested collectives whose performance depends on the policy being trained. We present an execution-path- and restriction-aware framework for MPICH \texttt{MPI_Bcast}. It partitions the configuration space by algorithm restrictions, trains corresponding submodels, and combines them into a unified runtime policy. A multistage procedure first trains an intermediate policy using independent algorithms, then benchmarks compositional algorithms under that policy to build the final model. On Polaris, the intermediate policy improves \texttt{smp} performance by up to $2.275\times$; the final policy achieves speedups of up to $30.71\times$ over default MPICH and $2.76\times$ over ACCLAiM.

events.title: Studying Silent Data Corruption Sensitivity of Precision Reduction Techniques during Deep Neural Network Training
events.description: High Performance Computing platforms have nurtured the development of deep learning (DL) models, particularly providing the massive computing power needed for training those models. However, the alarming growth rate of DL models has made their optimization, to reduce memory size and energy consumption, a priority. In particular, precision reduction techniques have been developed to tackle those challenges. The available literature provides a good description of how precision reduction affects the performance deep learning models. However, there is a knowledge gap of how sensitive precision reduction techniques are to silent data (SDCs), that can lead to unsuspected errors. SDCs are becoming more prevalent, for that reason, we set out to investigate how deep learning models, optimized with precision reduction techniques, react to bit flips caused by silent data corruption. Our results show that those optimized models are, in most cases, surprisingly resilient to bit flips compared to original model.

events.title: A Unified Semantic Interface Specification for Parallel Programming Tools
events.description: The growing number of parallel programming models (PPMs) has led to an ecosystem of tools for performance analysis, optimization, and correctness checking. These tools typically embed PPM-specific semantics into their implementations, creating tight coupling that hinders extensibility, maintainability, and semantic consistency across tools. This paper introduces a Unified Semantic Interface Specification (USIS) that decouples PPM semantics from tool implementations and generalizes a proposed MPI interface format. USIS provides deeper semantic coverage, including GPU semantics and an operational data-flow and synchronization layer that enables reasoning about procedures without prior PPM-specific knowledge. USIS is instantiated for MPI, OpenSHMEM, NCCL, and NVSHMEM, with a workflow combining vendor artifacts and curated files to generate the specifications. The resulting descriptions are integrated into two independently developed tools, the SPMD IR project and MUST, replacing their separate PPM-specific semantic representations with a shared specification. The paper identifies aspects that remain inherently coupled to PPMs or tools.

events.title: PDO Drug Screening Studies for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
events.description:
Background: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Most DRP models are trained on drug screening data of immortalized cancer cell lines, which differ substantially from patient tumors in genomic and molecular characteristics and treatment response. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) better recapitulate patient tumors, but PDO drug screening data remain scarce.

Methods: We conducted four drug screening studies using PDOs from colorectal cancer, head and neck cancer, and sarcoma, generating matched treatment responses and omics data with multiple screening technologies. The four datasets contain: (1) 27 colorectal and 20 head and neck cancer PDO lines, 37 compounds, and 1,316 experiments (pairs of PDOs and compounds); (2) 4 colorectal PDO lines, 100 compounds, and 400 experiments; (3) 5 colorectal PDO lines, 40 compounds, and 200 experiments; and (4) 9 colorectal and 1 sarcoma PDO lines, 100 compounds, and 1,000 experiments. Screening technologies included multiplane high-content imaging using Rhodamine-Phalloidin, Caspase-3/7, To-Pro-3, and Hoechst staining, and ATP-based CellTiter-Glo assays. Overlapping PDO–compound experimental pairs across three of the studies enabled cross-platform correlation analyses to evaluate the reproducibility of PDO drug screening experiments. Using PDO response data, gene expressions, and drug molecular features, we evaluated six DRP algorithms (DeepTTC, UNO, GraphDRP, HiDRA, IGTD, and LightGBM) under two scenarios: (1) training models on cell-line drug screening data including 465,329 experiments and testing on the four PDO datasets; and (2) training models on cell-line data plus part of the PDO data and testing on the held-out PDO data. Both random-split and cancer-blind cross-validations were used; cancer-blind splits shared no cancer models across training, validation, and test sets.

Results: For shared experiments across studies, response measurements showed moderate agreement, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.371–0.645. In scenario 1, mean R² across the six algorithms for the four PDO datasets was 0.07, 0.25, -0.26, and 0.24 with random-split cross-validation, and 0.11, 0.25, -0.25, and 0.27 with cancer-blind cross-validation, indicating limited transferability of models trained only on cell-line data to PDOs. In scenario 2, mean R² improved to 0.73, 0.72, 0.55, and 0.71 with random splits, demonstrating a substantial benefit from incorporating PDO data in training. Under cancer-blind validation, scenario 2 achieved R² values of 0.57, 0.48, -1.40, and 0.58, improving prediction performance on three datasets compared with scenario 1.

Conclusion: We provide four AI-ready PDO drug screening datasets containing treatment responses, PDO multi-omics, and drug molecular features for the development and benchmarking of DRP models. Response measurements from different studies and technologies showed moderate consistency, supporting cross-study comparison while revealing platform variability. Across six algorithms and two validation schemes, models trained with both cell-line and PDO data generally outperformed models trained on cell-line data alone, showing the importance of including PDO data in training when predicting PDO responses. Lower and more variable performance under cancer-blind validation highlights the challenge of generalizing across cancer models. Future work will investigate transfer learning approaches that pre-train on large cell-line data and fine-tune on limited PDO data to improve generalization to new PDOs.

events.title: Moderated Panel Discussion
Type-Safe, Dynamically Defined Metadata Support for Scientific Applications
events.description:
Earlier work on offering rich metadata, such as Empress, TagIt, SoMeta, and PDC all suffer from limitations on the type and structure of the metadata they process.
The most flexible of these, Empress, hard coded the work structure of application to include run and time step, forcing this view on users.
Further, it also assumes a mesh layout, which is not conducive to simulations or experimental data layouts which do not lay on a mesh. We have a multi-language, Rust-based approach for fully flexible, type safe metadata management.

events.title: Wrap-Up and Conclusion
HOLOS: A Gradient-Descent-Based Design-Space Exploration Framework for Hierarchical AI Accelerator Systems
events.description: The rapid growth of large language models has increased demand for hierarchical accelerator systems spanning processing elements, tiles, accelerators, and clusters. Exploring these systems is challenging because hardware parameters and software mappings interact across multiple levels. We present a gradient based design space exploration framework that unifies hardware and software co design using compact tiling factors for data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism together with per accelerator PE array and tile dimensions. The minimum required hardware is inferred directly from each mapping, reducing a conventional O(hardwarexmappings) search to O(mappings). A differentiable per operation model estimates latency, area, and energy. Compared with Calculon, our model achieves 0.99 Pearson correlation and approximately 4 percent mean absolute percentage error across 13B to 540B parameter LLMs. Under realistic memory and interconnect constraints for GPU system, the search reaches within approximately 1 percent of optimal energy delay product while evaluating 27 to 64 times fewer designs.

events.title: AI Agents for Data Infrastructure: From Telemetry to Optimization
events.description: The talk will explore how AI agents could reshape the way we understand, manage, and optimize data infrastructure. Drawing on examples from telemetry preprocessing, diagnosis, and I/O optimization, I will discuss the opportunities and challenges and invite the community to help build shared benchmarks and open experimental environments.

events.title: Death by a Thousand Spreadsheets: Consolidating Infrastructure Data with NetBox
events.description:
If you work in HPC infrastructure, you know the drill: rack elevations in one spreadsheet, IPs in another, cable maps in Visio if they exist at all, and the rest living in someone's head. It works fine until that person is out sick or leaves.
This talk covers NetBox Enterprise as a replacement for that patchwork: DCIM for racks, devices, and cabling, IPAM for address space and VLANs, plus the extra tooling at the Enterprise tier. Most of the time is spent live in the tool: building out inventory, mapping topology, and showing what it looks like to consolidate scattered infrastructure data into one place instead of five.
The goal isn't to sell anyone on NetBox, but to give a realistic look at what the migration involves, what it fixes, and what it doesn't so you can decide if it's worth doing at your own site.

events.title: WHPC Newcomers Session
Instrumentor: Customizable and Generic Instrumentation for LLVM
events.description: Instrumentation-based tools are essential for developing high-performance, efficient, and correct codebases in HPC and AI domains. However, code instrumentation mechanisms remain highly fragmented across compiler infrastructures, and LLVM is no exception. Building these tools usually requires developing custom LLVM passes, a tedious and repetitive task that demands deep knowledge of compiler internals. In this paper, we introduce the LLVM Instrumentor, a generic and customizable LLVM pass that instruments IR driven by user-provided configurations. The Instrumentor, configurable through a JSON file or programmatically, simplifies the development of new instrumentation-based tools by providing a wide coverage of instrumentation features. To demonstrate its versatility and ease of use, we present several instrumentation tools built with just a few lines of JSON configuration and runtime code.

events.title: An ELF-Aware DMA Engine for Distributed-Memory Accelerators
events.description: Distributed-memory, many-core accelerators are often bottlenecked by the task of transferring data to and from the local memories. Existing solutions place much of the orchestration burden onto the host processor. Instead, we propose an ELF-aware DMA engine that parses an ELF file from host memory and uses off-the-shelf DMA and interconnect IP to transfer data with minimal host intervention. We also extend the ELF format to encode both high-fan-out load and many-to-one gather operations in one file. On our FPGA proxy modeled after a kilocore accelerator, our design is 4.8× faster than host memcpy and 39% faster than scatter-gather DMA on load, with host preprocessing reduced to two register writes. Extrapolation to the kilocore scale suggests the engine costs roughly 1.6% of PE capacity. For many-core distributed-memory accelerators, we conclude that this approach is a viable middle ground between the host manually transferring bytes and a custom NoC/DMA stack.

events.title: Watts Behind the Weights: Characterizing Energy Consumption of the AI Training Lifecycle in HPC
events.description: Modern AI training workloads have become a leading contributor to energy consumption in HPC infrastructures. Yet this consumption is treated as a monolithic block, attributed to execution alone. The training lifecycle includes preparation and post-execution stages, and execution itself comprises multiple phases whose energy consumption varies with the task, model, dataset, and infrastructure-related factors. This work closes this gap by characterizing energy consumption across the entire AI training lifecycle in HPC infrastructures, following a fine-grained approach that attributes energy to individual phases and events, rather than to training as a whole. We apply this methodology on a production supercomputer, assessing preparation and post-execution using distinct datasets and models, and characterizing execution over workloads with distinct resource requirements, namely the I/O-intensive ResNet-50 and the GPU-bound Qwen3-8B. We draw several lessons to help HPC users accurately attribute energy consumption across their workloads and make their training pipelines more energy-efficient.

events.title: Auditing drug-response transfer at scale: an HPC-parallel, IMPROVE-conformant control pipeline
events.description:
Deciding which cell-line-to-clinic drug-response transfer gains are real, rather than artifacts of a
favorable seed or an uneven cohort, is not one large computation but thousands of small independent ones: each claim must be scored one drug at a time, under leak-free cross-validation, against a matched negative control, and repeated over seeds. We present the HPC harness that makes this audit routine on a single multi-GPU node. The pipeline is IMPROVE-conformant - one data model and one central metrics module across cell lines, xenografts, organoids, and patients - and its unit of work is a (dataset, method, drug-shard, seed) tuple. Drugs are partitioned disjointly by p mod num_shards so workers never race; a flexible pinned-slot scheduler auto-detects the device count and keeps exactly one job per GPU, refilling each device the instant its job exits; and several small experiments are packed onto disjoint GPU subsets to saturate the node. The statistical nulls are the primary parallel workload-per-drug label permutations and a 5,000-resample paired bootstrap fan-out with the same sharding, and a memory-efficient attention kernel fits a genomic foundation-model probe into 16GB. The same scripts scale down to one GPU, so every result is bit-reproducible. Run at this scale with a null on every claim, the science is sobering: a feature-free base-rate predictor reproduces a published transfer model's discrimination (r=0.94 across four cohorts), the training loss beats the encoder
(0.81 vs 0.42 rank correlation).

events.title: MPI Windows as an Abstraction for CUDA Interprocess Communication
events.description: CUDA interprocess communication (IPC) allows direct pointer access to GPU allocations of peer processes. Applications are required to handle export, collective exchange, per-peer import, pointer caching, failure handling, and cleanup. We show that these operations can be managed through an MPI window instead, using existing MPI shared-window query mechanisms. We implement this approach in WinIPC, a library that intercepts MPI window operations through the MPI profiling interface. We evaluate the approach using distributed matrix transpose, five-point stencil, and CUDA-enabled LULESH. We demonstrate peer-pointer access across 32 GPUs on eight physical nodes of a GB200 NVL system. For distributed transpose with accumulation at matrix order 1024, the single-kernel direct implementation achieves 2.44x the throughput of GPU-aware MPI. At matrix order 6912 on 32 GB200 GPUs, this variant reaches 20x the GPU-aware MPI rate. Moreover, we identify an allocation-time restriction of fabric-enabled IPC that limits its use with container-managed GPU buffers.

events.title: ARC-FL: Fault-Tolerant Federated Learning via Error-bounded Lossy Compression and Unequal Error Protection
events.description: Federated Learning(FL) trains models across clients without sharing local data, but its iterative training process requires frequent transmission of model updates and introduces high communication overhead. Error-bounded lossy compression can effectively reduce this overhead. However, existing studies mainly focus on data reduction and accuracy but have limited attention to communication reliability. Compressed bitstreams are sensitive to transmission errors, and a few corruptions can cause an entire model layer to fail reconstruction. We propose ARC-FL, a framework that combines hierarchical compression with unequal error protection. ARC-FL assigns model layers to three protection levels by parameter update magnitude and uses a layer-wise fallback for partial decoding failures. At a BER of 3E-3, equal error protection(EEP) with strong protection fails to maintain model convergence in several configurations. Meanwhile, ARC-FL preserves meaningful accuracy across all tested architectures and datasets and achieves up to 7.5x the accuracy of EEP in the most affected configuration.

events.title: Novel Profiling Pipeline for Replay-Based Performance Analysis
events.description: Replay-based profilers collect hardware metrics by executing the same code multiple times with different metric groups. While this overcomes hardware-counter limits, it breaks down for multi-GPU applications: interdependent kernels in NCCL and NVSHMEM require ranks to progress together but independent replay passes are susceptible to divergence. We present a coordinated pipeline for replay-based profiling of multi-GPU applications. To preserve correctness, we introduce a profiler-side synchronization mechanism and a heuristic kernel-grouping algorithm that replays dependent kernels in lockstep across ranks. We introduce a bundling-based metric distribution algorithm that partitions metric sets across profiler instances. The pipeline merges per-process reports into a unified profile and supports report clustering for scalable exploration. We implement the profiling pipeline in NVIDIA NCU and evaluate our metric distribution implementation. Replay coordination eliminates deadlocks in interdependent workloads, while metric distribution reduces the maximum replay count by up to 3.50× versus single-GPU profiling with profiling data quality preserved.

events.title: Community Discussion and Q&A
Teaching HPC to Advanced High School Students at a Summer Program
events.description:
Since 2023, staff and students from Tennessee Tech's Information Technology Services department have participated as a research and exploration group for the Governor's School for Emerging Technologies (GSET), a 3-week summer program for Tennessee high school students. We introduce a subset of those students to a variety of topics and careers related to research computing, including having the students build small (but fully-functional) HPC clusters, both in virtual machines on their laptops, and also on recently-decommissioned desktop computers.
The students begin developing a broad set of skills including Linux systems administration, networking, benchmarking, parallel programming, and other concepts core to HPC. They also present their choice of computationally intensive applications, usually run on their own cluster, as a project presentation to other GSET students and staff.
This presentation will give an overview of our GSET experience and how it might be adapted to other institutions and audiences.

events.title: Characterizing Simulation-AI Coupled Workflows on Frontier: Benchmarks and Digital-Twin Replay
events.description: Simulation–AI workflows now consume a large share of HPC cycles, shifting usage away from traditional modeling and simulation and leaving users and facility policymakers without a clear picture of how these coupled workloads consume system resources. We present a framework that characterizes the HPC resource usage of distributed simulation–AI workflows across six machine learning architectures used for AI training and inference. The framework couples a simulation–AI benchmarking suite with a digital twin of the system, built by extending, customizing, and integrating existing components. We port the benchmarks to the OLCF Frontier supercomputer and run six 64-node experiments, one per architecture, capturing computation, I/O, and energy telemetry without instrumenting any component's source. A translator bridge makes the collected telemetry replayable by the digital twin. We further demonstrate what-if scenario evaluation—energy projections at larger scales and outcomes under alternative scheduling policies—illustrating the framework's broader utility.

events.title: GPU-Initiated Data Movement for Accelerator-Centric HPC
events.description: Accelerator applications must move data between GPUs while computation continues, yet conventional host mediation delays transfer submission until control returns from an OpenMP target region. GiOMP moves the initiation point into GPU execution, so movement begins at data readiness and overlaps independent work. Using OpenMP target offloading, GiOMP provides device callable PUT, GET, and completion operations over HPE Slingshot. Its proxy path sends dynamic requests through a CPU worker, while its GPU trigger path releases prepared network operations without later CPU submission. On Tioga, a fused pipeline on two nodes achieves up to a 1.23× speedup over GPU aware MPI, with 5.6 to 6.8 microseconds attributed to eliminating a target relaunch. Jacobi weak scaling reaches 1.87× on Tioga and 1.82× on Delta AI. Remote GPU memory is the first concrete target of a broader GPU driven data movement layer, with future investigation of storage facing staging and in transit consumers.

events.title: DPUCrumbs: Dissecting DPU Pathways
events.description:
Data processing units (DPUs) such as NVIDIA's BlueField-3 increasingly used to offload MPI collectives, compression and data movement in HPC.
Yet cost of offload is spread across every layer between the application and the card.
Existing tools observe one layer at a time, each on its own clock, so host, driver and card cannot be joined into one timeline.
A slow offload is therefore observable but not explainable.
We present DPUCrumbs, an eBPF-based tracer that extends DataCrumbs across PCIe onto the card.
It captures application calls, DOCA and ibverbs entry points, MLX5 driver and kernel's DMA and IOMMU paths.
NIC hardware timestamps then place both endpoints on one time axis.
On a DOCA RDMA ping-pong, DPUCrumbs measures PCIe crossings at 13.2 and 8.6 µs, shows the DPU responding in 0.82 µs and and and reveals that reply waits 6.1 µs at the NIC before host consumes it, at 3.6% overhead.

events.title: Wrap-up and Closing Remarks
Closing Remarks
Towards PIM-Aware Expert Decomposition and Mapping for MoE Inference
events.description: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference presents system challenges because experts receive uneven workloads and exhibit different execution characteristics. This work explores how processing-in-memory (PIM) can complement GPUs to improve MoE inference efficiency. We propose a PIM-aware approach that selectively assigns suitable expert computation to PIM while retaining other computation on the GPU. The approach also considers how experts can be decomposed and mapped to available PIM resources. This WIP talk will briefly introduce the motivation and proposed solution, highlight the main design considerations, and outline the next steps toward evaluating the feasibility and potential benefits of PIM-assisted MoE inference.
