Our results reveal that insertion is bottlenecked by per-batch consistency requirements, additional cores can reduce query throughput by up to 30.67%, and scaling from 16 to 256 workers yields a 2.67x improvement with 16 nodes before QPS begins to decline. This scaling paradox exposes the fundamental mismatch between cloud-oriented designs and HPC systems, highlighting the need for new, HPC-aware vector database designs.

events.title: Network Research Exhibition (NRE) Theater Talks
SCinet — Technical Overview
ORCA: Steerable Observability for Bulk-Synchronous Parallel Applications
events.description:
The bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) paradigm powers critical computational workloads from scientific simulations to large-scale machine learning training. Running on tens of thousands of processors, these systems are uniquely sensitive to performance variations that current observability approaches struggle to diagnose—post-hoc analysis of massive traces introduces latency and rigidity that obstructs timely diagnosis.

To address these challenges, we present ORCA, a system for always-on, steerable BSP observability. ORCA enables operators to materialize relevant views from running applications on demand and intervene in response, via a tree-based overlay providing coordinated collection, in-situ SQL analytics, and timestep-consistent control. ORCA accelerates observability workflows across the spectrum. On a real AMR code at 4,096 ranks, ORCA collects equivalent traces at ~2% overhead (vs. 56%–81%), enables up to 7275× faster analyses, and 99.999% in-situ data reduction. In an LLM-driven evaluation of steerability, a performance anomaly that took months to diagnose manually is localized in 27 minutes.

events.title: Observability and Operational Intelligence for Leadership Systems
events.description: These papers address how leadership systems can be understood, operated, and improved using steerable observability, job-centric production telemetry, reliable LLM-assisted I/O analysis, and structured application-readiness practices from the El Capitan Center of Excellence.

events.title: HieraSparse: Hierarchical Semi-Structured Sparse KV Attention
events.description: The deployment of long-context LLMs poses significant challenges due to the intense computational cost of self-attention and substantial memory overhead of the KV cache. We introduce HieraSparse, a hierarchical KV cache compression framework with acceleration kernels that leverage GPU Sparse Tensor Cores to speed up semi-structured KV cache attention for both prefill and decode phases. With hierarchical design, our method allows for flexible quality-sparsity trade-off and successfully converts sparsity into efficiency. Compared to state-of-the-art decode method that utilizes unstructured sparsity, HieraSparse achieves 1.2× KV compression ratio and 4.57× attention speedup at the same sparsity level. Furthermore, we extended semi-structured KV cache pruning to the prefill stage, which demonstrated up to 1.85× attention speedup at the highest sparsity. Lastly, we evaluate generation quality of HieraSparse with a simple magnitude-based pruning method, and the results show that 1.37× prefill speedup and 1.77× decode speedup can be achieved without significant quality drop.

events.title: Sparse and Low-Precision AI Kernels
events.description: This session advances sparse and quantized AI computation through structured attention, sparse inference, low-bit models, and data-movement-aware kernels. The papers focus on converting model sparsity into realized hardware speedup.

events.title: DeepSim: SOL-Based Explainable GPU Performance Projection with Multi-Task Learning
events.description:
Accurate kernel-level GPU performance projection is essential for early-stage architecture design when target hardware is unavailable and only high-level specifications are known. Existing methods face a trade-off: simulators reveal bottlenecks but are slow and require unavailable hardware details, while analytical and end-to-end learning models are efficient yet rely on idealized assumptions and provide limited explainability.

We present DeepSim, an explainable GPU performance projection framework for single-GPU kernels that learns unit-level speed-of-light (SOL) ratios to calibrate bottleneck pressure using multi-task learning. Given target chip specifications and kernel traffic from existing GPUs, DeepSim constructs idealized limiters, predicts per-unit SOL ratios, and maps them to practical limiters reflecting target-chip behavior. Using this representation, DeepSim infers dominant bottlenecks, classifies workloads, and estimates execution time. Across 290K samples and 284 kernels spanning NVIDIA Ampere, Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs, DeepSim achieves 12.29% mean absolute percentage error on held-out B200 and 14.78% on unseen kernels.

events.title: Explaining and Debugging GPU Performance
events.description: The papers provide explainable tools for GPU performance projection, energy optimization, stall diagnosis, and debugging. Together they move performance engineering from measurement toward actionable diagnosis.

events.title: ACM Gordon Bell Finalists Presentations
Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy
events.description: Resolving individual stars in simulations of the Milky Way (MW), where we live, is essential to understanding its formation and time evolution. Recent multi-wavelength, multi-modal observations have shown the detailed structures of the MW. Correspondingly, high-resolution simulations that resolve individual stars with multiphysics are required. Leveraging exascale systems, we present PHEASANT: star-by-star MW galaxy simulations including physics across multiple spatiotemporal scales with up to 5.4 trillion particles, ~10,000 times more particles than the state-of-the-art. On Aurora, our code processes 144 billion particles per second using 60,236 GPUs, approximately three times the throughput of a state-of-the-art N-body/smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulation, while its gravitational interaction kernel achieved 976 PFLOP/s in FP32. The code is highly portable, achieving 101 billion and 135 billion particles processed per second with 37,908 GPUs on OLCF Frontier and 20,736 GPUs on JSC JUPITER, respectively, while maintaining high kernel performance across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.

events.title: From Discovery to Patient Impact: Bridging the Translational Gap
events.description: Bringing biomedical discoveries from the research environment to the bedside requires more than technology. It requires collaboration across disciplines, institutions, and perspectives. This panel brings together participants from the Regional Technical Hub representing academia, national laboratories, industry, and clinical practice to share their experiences using AI, high performance computing, and other advanced technologies to accelerate biomedical research and translation. Panelists will explore the opportunities and challenges of cross-disciplinary collaboration, translating innovation into practice, integrating new tools into clinical workflows, and responsibly working with sensitive biomedical and clinical data. Together, we will consider how we can bridge the translational gap and harness emerging technologies to improve outcomes for patients.

events.title: From Discovery to Patient Impact: Bridging the Translational Gap
AI Supercomputers: Evolution or Revolution?
events.description: AI has had a profound impact on the supercomputing ecosystem, with dramatic advances in technology, size, and scale of supercomputers being deployed. While there is no doubt that AI software is very different from scientific computing applications, underneath the software, how different are the supercomputers powering the AI revolution? Have AI workloads fundamentally changed the technology used to build supercomputers that are the foundation of scientific computing, or have AI workloads just accelerated in time the path that scientific computing was already on? In this panel, our experts will examine this question, looking at the hardware and software that power the world’s largest supercomputers for both HPC and AI, and discuss the implications this has on organizations who rely on these systems and how this affects the next generation of professionals starting out in a supercomputing field that is changing faster than it has in its 60+ year history.

events.title: AI Supercomputers: Evolution or Revolution?
Quantum Computing I
TangleLab: A National Hybrid Computing Platform to Unlock Quantum Information Science and Engineering Research and Education
events.description: TangleLab is a hybrid quantum-classical computing platform under development by the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center in collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Rigetti Computing and funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2537076). The platform will integrate GPU-accelerated HPC resources with a superconducting quantum processor to support emerging hybrid applications while exploring architectural models for future heterogeneous cyberinfrastructure. This presentation focuses on the system's architecture and deployment strategy, including integration of classical and quantum resources, scheduling and access models, software environment design, and operational considerations for supporting both research and education. We will also discuss hybrid deployment approaches that combine local quantum hardware with cloud-accessible quantum systems to support scalable workflows as quantum technologies evolve. TangleLab will provide a practical blueprint for HPC centers seeking to integrate quantum computing into production cyberinfrastructure and prepare researchers for the next generation of heterogeneous computing environments.

events.title: Experience Meets Innovation: Intergenerational Collaboration in HPC
events.description:
Success in high performance computing (HPC) and research depends on bringing together diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to problem-solving. This panel explores the value of intergenerational collaboration in the workplace and how teams can thrive by leveraging the unique strengths of each generation.

Featuring professionals from a broad range of career stages, panelists will share their experiences working across generations, discuss common challenges and opportunities, and highlight strategies for building inclusive, high-performing teams. Attendees will gain insights into fostering mutual learning, bridging communication styles, and creating environments where institutional knowledge and fresh ideas come together to drive innovation.

Whether you are early in your career or a seasoned professional, this discussion will provide practical takeaways for strengthening collaboration and advancing success in the research and high performance computing community.

events.title: Experience Meets Innovation: Intergenerational Collaboration in HPC
AI and Data Analytics I
What Production AI Demands from Data Infrastructure
events.description: Moving AI from pilot projects into production requires more than GPUs — it requires data infrastructure designed for scale. Modern AI workloads depend on continuous access to massive volumes of unstructured data while balancing performance, cyber resilience, governance, and operational simplicity. This session examines how organizations are building AI data pipelines that support ingestion, training, inference, and long-term knowledge retention from a common architectural foundation. We'll discuss practical approaches to reducing unnecessary data movement, improving GPU utilization by bringing data closer to AI workloads, and eliminating storage silos. Attendees will gain architectural guidance drawn from production AI deployments, including proven design patterns and common pitfalls to avoid as AI environments continue to grow.

events.title: AI in Healthcare and Cancer Research
Bringing HPC to Life: The Convergence of Computing, Technologies and Communities in Health
events.description:
There is a transformation underway in medicine. Not that long ago, employing AI and HPC to address key challenges in cancer was uncommon. The uses of medical digital twins to help doctors and patients work together for better outcomes were simply flights of fantasy. Today, these are only a few of the developments that are rapidly becoming mainstream, empowered by interdisciplinary communities working together, driving hard to overcome shared challenges in compute, policy, data and many other areas to improve health, medicine and overall wellness.

How did we get here? Where are we going? What does the future hold? These are questions that commonly arise when discussing the transformation in health and life sciences that recent advances in AI and computing have enabled. The talk will deliver insights on how the past decade has created a solid foundation for healthcare innovation, share examples of how data science and AI are continuing to accelerate the pace of change in healthcare worldwide, and provide perspectives on future opportunities and challenges awaiting around the corner!

events.title: TBD — WAN
Constructing a Job-Centric Frontier Telemetry Dataset to Accelerate HPC Operations, Systems, and Energy Research
events.description: Comprehensive analysis of high-performance computing (HPC) systems requires linking workload execution to system behavior. This kind of analysis is vital for diagnosing performance issues, managing capacity, detecting anomalous workloads, and understanding how applications interact with system hardware. However, node telemetry data and job scheduler records are collected and analyzed in isolation and application identification requires a directed effort. We present a job-centric telemetry dataset that unifies scheduler job records with node-level measurements, enabling direct association between workloads and their corresponding power, thermal, and performance characteristics. This dataset, which spans two years of Frontier operations, aims to support a wide range of research and operational applications, including workload characterization, system analysis, and anomaly detection. This paper describes the dataset curation process, including data collection, normalization, and association of telemetry with individual job metadata. To enable further study, the dataset will be published alongside this paper for use by the HPC community.

events.title: FastInfer: Breaking the Low-to-Moderate Sparsity Barrier for Efficient LLM Inference
events.description: As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale, unstructured pruning has become a key technique for reducing inference cost. However, to preserve model quality, pruning is typically limited to low-to-moderate sparsity (30%–60%), where existing GPU-based sparse inference frameworks often fail to deliver consistent speedups over dense baselines. This paper proposes FastInfer, a new sparse LLM inference framework in the low-to-moderate sparsity regime. FastInfer introduces a novel thread-centric encoding paradigm that rethinks sparse computation on Tensor Core Units from the perspective of per-thread register requirements. Based on this, we design the TFBE format, which enables low-overhead operand reconstruction. FastInfer integrates an affinity-aware data-movement mechanism and a triple-stage pipeline to better exploit modern GPU features and improve pipeline utilization. Compared with the state-of-the-art SpInfer, FastInfer achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.52x (up to 2.1x) for sparse kernels and 1.27x (up to 1.42x) for end-to-end sparse inference on H100.

events.title: EMO: Energy Efficiency Modeling and Optimization for AI Workloads
events.description:
The massive energy consumption of GPU-accelerated AI workloads challenges sustainable computing. We observe that execution asynchrony (e.g., CPU-GPU, concurrent streams, and multi-GPU) creates slack, allowing non-critical kernels to run at lower frequencies to save energy with minimal performance impact. However, existing approaches struggle to achieve both workload generality and fine-grained slack discovery, while high-fidelity modeling incurs substantial overhead.

We present EMO, a lightweight framework for exploiting these opportunities. EMO constructs a low-level dependency graph capturing execution asynchrony and performs what-if timing analysis to identify slack windows. It then introduces dependency-aware kernel packing, which preserves critical paths while collapsing redundant details, enabling high-fidelity latency-energy modeling with minimal profiling cost. Finally, EMO combines graph analysis and pack-level models to formulate and solve a constrained combinatorial optimization problem for frequency policies under given latency targets. Evaluations show that EMO reduces energy consumption by 15%–28% with only 2%–5% performance loss and negligible overhead.

events.title: Exascale Multiphysics Simulations for Liquid Metal Fusion Blankets
events.description: We present pioneering multiphysics simulations of lead-lithium and water flows in the ITER WCLL fusion test blanket set using NekRS on exascale platforms, including Frontier and Aurora. Developed at Argonne, NekRS is a high-performance, open-source multiphysics solver that employs rapidly convergent high-order spectral element methods with minimal numerical dissipation and dispersion. Advanced multilevel preconditioners, high-order time-splitting schemes, and adaptive communication strategies are enabled through OCCA-based kernels, ensuring portability and scalability across emerging HPC architectures. This work presents the first complete, high-fidelity, high-resolution multiphysics model of a fusion blanket, including turbulent flow resolution, heat transfer, buoyancy, magnetohydrodynamics, tritium breeding and transport, and water activation. We also present the largest spectral element model in NekRS to date and the largest simulation of fusion systems to date.

events.title: Comfort Dogs
Building Sovereign AI: Infrastructure for Trusted AI Environments
events.description:
As governments, research institutions, and regulated enterprises accelerate AI adoption, they face a new challenge: delivering high-performance AI while maintaining sovereignty over data, models, operations, and critical infrastructure. Building sovereign AI environments requires more than governance frameworks, it demands resilient infrastructure architecture, secure operations, and specialized engineering expertise.

This session explores the technical and operational considerations for deploying production-ready sovereign AI environments, including cluster design, workload isolation, data residency, network segmentation, lifecycle management, and operational governance. Using the deployment of Haein, South Korea's national sovereign AI infrastructure, as a prime sovereign example, attendees will gain practical insights into architectural decisions, deployment strategies, and operational best practices to accelerate production while maintaining security, compliance, and trust. Participants will leave with actionable frameworks for building secure, scalable, and trusted AI infrastructure for sovereign, enterprise, and research environments.

events.title: Speed Mentoring
International Demonstration of 400 Gbps 8K Uncompressed Video Processing Using SRv6-Based In-Network Computing
events.description: nri102s1

events.title: Understanding Reliability Bottlenecks in LLM Agents for HPC I/O Telemetry Analysis
events.description: High performance computing (HPC) facilities collect extensive I/O telemetry, but turning it into operator-relevant insight remains a manual, expert-driven process. Tool-using LLM agents could help automate this workflow, but their reliability on realistic telemetry-analysis tasks remains unclear. We study this using CIODI-Bench, a benchmark of 49 expert-curated tasks built from more than two years of public production telemetry from the Polaris supercomputer. Using CIODI-Bench, we compare tool-using agents for HPC I/O telemetry analysis under controlled conditions. We find that the main reliability bottleneck depends on task structure: on constrained extraction tasks, curated semantic grounding improves performance from 73.0% to 93.5%; on data-analysis tasks, process-aware review improves performance by 13.2% over baseline; but on insight-generation tasks, the added orchestration yields no improvement while increasing output cost by nearly 3x. Our analysis results clarify the reliability limits of current agentic approaches and offer practical guidance for building more trustworthy telemetry-analysis agents.

events.title: TileFlow: Data-Movement-Centric Optimization for Irregular GEMM on Matrix-Unit CPUs
events.description: Irregular GEMM, where one or more dimensions are small, is common in workloads like LLM inference and vector search. On CPUs with matrix units (e.g., Intel AMX), irregular GEMMs are data-movement-bound: limited reuse and fragmented accesses let packing and cross-NUMA traffic dominate. State-of-the-art BLAS libraries are tuned for regular shapes, using coarse-grained, ahead-of-time packing and placement-agnostic parallelism assuming substantial reuse and contiguous access. We show that the gap stems from a mismatch in computation and data movement: how operands are packed and where they reside in NUMA systems. TileFlow addresses this via (1) a fine-grained packing–compute pipeline overlapping on-demand packing and memory access with computation at micro-kernel granularity, and (2) a placement-aware task assignment reducing cross-NUMA traffic under NUMA-local allocation and page interleaving without explicit placement control. On two AMX-enabled CPUs, TileFlow achieves speedups of 1.36×, 1.47×, and 1.39× for irregular GEMMs, Llama3-8B inference, and approximate nearest neighbor search.

events.title: LEO: Tracing GPU Stall Chains via Cross-Vendor Backward Slicing
events.description: More than half of the Top 500 supercomputers employ GPUs as accelerators. On GPU-accelerated platforms, developers face a key diagnostic gap: profilers show where stalls occur but provide limited dependency paths explaining why. Furthermore, the same kernel may have different stalls and underlying causes on different GPUs. This paper presents LEO, a root-cause analyzer for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs that performs backward slicing from stalled instructions, considering dependencies arising from registers as well as vendor-specific synchronization mechanisms. LEO attributes GPU stalls to source instructions to explain performance inefficiencies. Across 21 kernel/region evaluation units on three GPU platforms, expert-designed, LEO-informed optimizations deliver per-platform geometric-mean speedups of 1.73×–1.82×; these are not end-to-end application speedups. Our case studies show that (1) the same kernel may require different optimizations for different GPU architectures, and (2) under our LLM protocol, prompts containing LEO's structured diagnostics yield better outcomes than code-only and raw-stall-count prompts.

events.title: Crossing the 12,000-Atom Barrier with Heterogeneous Quantum-Classical Supercomputing: Quantum Chemistry of Protein-Ligand Complexes
events.description: We develop a workflow decomposing a molecule into fragments via quantum embedding and simulating them with a heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) method. We sample fragment electronic configurations on two 156-qubit quantum processors (ibm_cleveland, ibm_kobe), using up to 94 qubits, running 21,006 circuits for over 239 hours, collecting 3B measurement outcomes: the most resource-intensive HQC computation for quantum chemistry to date. We compute fragment wavefunctions via optimized subspace diagonalization on supercomputers Fugaku, Miyabi-G, and ROQUO, achieving 72.5% parallel efficiency with scalable distributed linear algebra kernels. We simulate two protein-ligand complexes spanning dispersion- and electrostatics-dominated regimes (11,608 and 12,635 atoms), demonstrate 40x increase in system size and up to 210x improvement in accuracy over previous state-of-the-art, with HQC matching coupled-cluster (CCSD) accuracy in fragment energies. We present the first HQC protein-ligand binding prediction using a mixed-basis set and an automated end-to-end workflow enabling practical HQC calculations of large protein systems.

events.title: Turning Quantum Into an HPC Resource: Automation, Virtualization, and Containerization
events.description:
As quantum computing transitions from the lab to industrial environments, HPC data centers face a fundamental integration gap between traditional automated software stacks and the low-level manual and physical control required for quantum hardware. Because quantum relies on qubits, rather than traditional integrated circuits, it requires a dedicated software architecture to make it compatible with existing compute paradigms.

This presentation outlines how applying the established compute principles of automation, virtualization, and containerization to quantum computing transforms complex quantum systems into deployable, plug-and-play HPC resources. We examine how packaging automated control and optimization software into a containerized sub-system enables quantum hardware to become a seamless compute accelerator. Featuring real-world case studies from on-premise deployments at RIKEN and hardware co-integrations with partners including QuantWare, Equal1, Anyon Systems, and the Quantum Utility Block model, attendees will learn practical design considerations for integrating turnkey quantum nodes into data center architectures.

events.title: Sparse Linear Algebra Accelerates Genotype Representation Graph Computation at Biobank Scale
events.description: Biobank-scale genomic analyses are increasingly constrained by computational costs, as hundreds of thousands to millions of samples and variants must be analyzed together. The genotype representation graph (GRG) compactly encodes population genetic variation to accelerate computation, but the current approach does not exploit modern accelerator architectures. This work introduces Mikado, a new methodology for expressing GRG-based computation using sparse linear algebra primitives. Under a reverse topological ordering of the graph nodes, the GRG adjacency matrix is strictly block-lower-triangular, and the genotype matrix-vector product becomes a sparse triangular solve that can be further decomposed into a pipelined sequence of blocked sparse matrix-vector multiplies. By decoupling computation from graph representation, our approach exposes fine-grained parallelism and enables hardware-optimized sparse primitives on GPUs. Mikado was evaluated across the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC and Google Cloud. Mikado achieves an order-of-magnitude speedup for PCA and BOLT-LMM compared with the original GRG traversal approach, including on All of Us Research Program cohorts, demonstrating that advanced computing infrastructure is now central to progress in biological research. Portability across supercomputer nodes and cloud instances makes these gains broadly accessible, providing a scalable, hardware-portable, researcher-friendly tool for population genetics at biobank scale.

events.title: Disk-to-Disk File Transfer Experiment on an End-to-End 400 Gbps Line Between Japan and the USA by MMCFTP
events.description: nri102s1,NRE109

events.title: The Operational Journey From HPC Cluster to AI Factory: Power, Cooling, Data and Operational Readiness for the AI/HPC Era
events.description:
AI infrastructure deployments are forcing HPC operators to confront challenges that extend far beyond GPU procurement. Rising rack densities, power constraints, liquid cooling adoption, storage bottlenecks, data pipelines, and evolving operational processes are reshaping how modern HPC facilities are designed and managed.

This presentation shares practical lessons from organizations transitioning from traditional HPC clusters to AI factories capable of supporting training, fine-tuning, post-training, and inference workloads. Rather than focusing on theory, we examine the operational realities of infrastructure planning, facility readiness, workload placement, data management, and day-to-day operations. Attendees will learn how power, cooling, networking, storage, and operational decisions interact, where common bottlenecks emerge, and what steps can be taken to prepare existing HPC environments for large-scale AI adoption.

events.title: The Design and Organization of the El Capitan Center of Excellence for Application Readiness
events.description:
El Capitan is the first U.S. exascale system for national security. Its Center of Excellence (COE) enabled co-design and application readiness. The COE's central goal is to prepare applications to use the AMD Instinct MI300A APU and Cray Slingshot interconnect effectively on the first day of delivery, and continuously improve after delivery. Application engagements are driven by a team of eight engineers from HPE and AMD who support approximately 20 applications from three national laboratories. Quarterly hackathons had attendances reaching upwards of 50 participants.

We describe the technical scope, engagement model, and organizational structure that supported COE activities, emphasizing the key components of a high performance computing COE. We highlight five select case studies that demonstrate technical challenges in addressing functionality and performance across many software and hardware updates, often utilizing experimental software to overcome issues. We summarize lessons learned and AI impacts that may benefit future COEs.

events.title: Pushing the Envelope of LLM Inference with Ultra-Low-Bit Quantized Models
events.description: The advent of ultra-low-bit LLM models, approaching the perplexity and task accuracy of their full-precision counterparts, is ushering in a new era of LLM inference. While these advances promise models that are cost-effective in latency, memory, throughput, and energy consumption, the runtime efficiency for deploying ultra-low-bit models remains under-explored. We take a bottom-up approach: we first implement 2-bit microkernels for modern CPUs, achieving close-to-roofline performance. We integrate these microkernels into LLM inference pipelines and present end-to-end results with 2-bit models, outperforming the state-of-the-art (SOTA) bitnet.cpp runtime by 2.2x, and deliver up to 7x speedup over 16-bit inference. We extend this work to Intel Xe2 GPUs where we implement mixed-precision 2-bit kernels, and show their performance to be close-to-optimal. Integrated into the vLLM framework, these kernels deliver up to 6.7x speedup over the 16-bit end-to-end pipeline across a range of models and Xe2 GPUs, thus pushing the envelope of LLM inference.

events.title: Interactive Debugger for Performance-Portable Python HPC Kernels
events.description: We propose pkdb, the first interactive debugger for performance-portable kernels written in Python. Python is widely used in HPC, with frameworks such as PyKokkos translating Python-embedded domain-specific languages to native code that runs across various CPUs and GPUs. pkdb enables standard interactive debugging like breakpoints, stepping, continuation, and variable inspection while preserving actual on-device execution without source modification. Beyond these fundamentals, pkdb introduces three advanced capabilities that exploit the dynamic nature of Python and PyKokkos: (1) live code evaluation, (2) hot-swap, and (3) concurrent kernel comparison. Our performance evaluations on Intel and AMD CPUs and NVIDIA and AMD GPUs show that pkdb introduces limited overhead and is practical for everyday use, and introduces critical debugging features to the Python HPC ecosystem.

events.title: Closing the FeMo-Cofactor "Quantum-Advantage'' Gap with Exascale Supercomputers
events.description: The FeMo-cofactor (FeMoco) of nitrogenase has for nearly a decade been the canonical "killer app" motivating fault-tolerant quantum computing for chemistry: the CAS(113e, 76o) active space is beyond exact diagonalization and remains challenging for every polynomial-scaling classical method. We report the first exascale classical solution of this active space. The resulting code has been tuned for two exascale supercomputers, LineShine and China's New-generation Intelligent Supercomputer (CNIS), reaching sustained performance on 20,480 LineShine nodes of 1.456 EFLOP/s in double precision (58.9% of the machine peak) and 5.626 EFLOP/s in mixed precision. These computational achievements enable the FeMoco ground-state consensus to be reached on 1,280 LineShine nodes within a measured end-to-end wall time of 105 minutes (1.75 h), approximately one-fifth of the best published 8.6-hour single-run projection for fault-tolerant quantum computing on the same active space.

events.title: UDTS-Integrated SRCNet Data Control System
events.description: nri102s1

events.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Maria Jaromin
events.description: Maria Jaromin brings a multidisciplinary background spanning computational engineering, technology transfer, research development, and compliance. She currently leads the Healthcare Innovation Program Office at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois Urbana‑Champaign. In this role, she fosters and advances cross‑disciplinary research collaborations across the university and with external partners, with a focus on integrating advanced technologies into health and biomedical research. Prior to her current position, Maria served as a Technology Manager in the Office of Technology Management at the University of Illinois System, where she managed an intellectual property portfolio in engineering and physical sciences. Her work included evaluating the patentability and commercialization potential of university innovations, negotiating legal agreements, and educating researchers on technology transfer processes and policies. Maria began her career at the Illinois Applied Research Institute as a Research Engineer, specializing in modeling and simulation to enhance the efficiency, safety, and performance of engineering systems and processes. She holds a bachelor’s and master’s degree in Power Engineering from the Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland; a Licentiate of Engineering in Energy Technology from the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, Sweden; and an MBA from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

events.title: PATH: Path-Aware Adaptive Traffic at the Host for High-Performance Data Transfers
events.description: no NRI

events.title: OpenSHMEM: Toward a Unified GPU-Aware Auxiliary Specification and 2.0
events.description: OpenSHMEM is a community-driven partitioned global address space (PGAS) API for low-overhead, one-sided asynchronous communication across diverse HPC architectures. This BoF will present progress since the 1.6 specification and discuss ongoing work toward OpenSHMEM 1.7, the proposed GPU auxiliary specification for accelerator support, and the longer-term OpenSHMEM 2.0 roadmap. As heterogeneous systems become the norm, the session will bring together users, implementers, middleware and tool developers, hardware vendors, and HPC facilities to share experiences, discuss evolving requirements, and help shape a simple, portable, and vendor-neutral future for OpenSHMEM.

events.title: Beyond the GPU: The Future of AI Acceleration in the Zettascale Era
events.description: The rapid evolution of AI is driving unprecedented innovation in computing architectures, from GPUs and AI accelerators to novel memory, networking, and system designs. This BoF brings together leaders from industry, academia, and national laboratories to discuss emerging directions in AI acceleration for future zettascale systems. Rather than focusing on specific products, participants will explore common challenges in architecture, programmability, scalability, energy efficiency, software ecosystems, and deployment at scale. The session will emphasize audience interaction, community discussion, and roadmap development, providing attendees an opportunity to help shape the future of AI acceleration and AI-enabled supercomputing.

events.title: Mixed Feelings About Mixed Precisions
events.description: What if we have been oversolving in computational science and engineering for decades? Are low-precision arithmetic formats only for AI workloads? How can HPC applications exploit mixed-precision hardware features? This BoF invites the HPC community at large interested in applying mixed precisions into their workflows and discussing the impact on time-to-solution, memory footprint, storage, data motion, and energy consumption. Experts from scientific applications/software libraries/hardware architectures will briefly provide the context on this trendy topic, share their own perspectives, and mostly engage with the audience via a set of questions, while gathering feedback to define a roadmap moving forward.

events.title: SIGHPC Annual Member Meeting
events.description: The SIGHPC Annual Member Meeting brings together ACM SIGHPC members and the broader HPC community to review the organization's activities, celebrate recent accomplishments, and discuss priorities for the coming year. The meeting provides an open forum where members can interact directly with SIGHPC leadership, learn about ongoing initiatives in education, awards, student programs, chapters, diversity and inclusion, publications, and conference activities, and help shape future directions. Whether you are a long-time member or new to the community, this session offers an opportunity to engage with SIGHPC leadership, provide feedback, ask questions, and become involved in the society's activities.

events.title: Reproducibility of Computational Research: Building a Community of Practice for the AI Era
events.description: Reproducibility remains a fundamental challenge for computational science and AI-enabled research. Building on successful BoFs at SC22, SC24, and PEARC22-PEARC25, we established the Reproducibility of Computational Research Community of Practice, which now includes an active mailing list, public website, webinar series, and emerging working groups. This interactive BoF will engage the SC26 community in shaping the next phase of this effort by sharing community progress, launching working groups, and exploring how AI can improve the capture of reproducible computational artifacts while addressing new challenges. The session welcomes researchers, research computing professionals, software developers, librarians, and cyberinfrastructure practitioners.

events.title: Workflows Community: Next-Generation Workflows for HPC — AI, Agentic Systems, and Scientific Discovery
events.description:
This BoF will convene the workflows community to discuss the challenges of next-generation scientific workflows. A central focus will be on how the role of the human changes as workflows become increasingly autonomous: where people remain in the loop, how they steer and validate agentic systems, and how our community can support workflow developers.

The session will bring together workflow users, developers, theorists, and industrial collaborators, highlighting emerging research directions and practical needs from scientific campaigns. Through interactive discussions, participants will explore collaborative strategies to enable resilient, scalable, and adaptive workflows that meet the evolving demands of scientific discovery.

events.title: The Future of Python on HPC Systems
events.description: Python is the most widely used programming language today — but on HPC systems, it’s often more pain than power. From slow module loading on shared filesystems to packaging headaches and incompatible distributions, these hurdles block new users and frustrate seasoned developers alike. Meanwhile, major changes to Python’s core — new array APIs, packaging reforms, JIT compilation, and threading primitives — are happening without HPC at the table. This BoF brings together language leaders and HPC practitioners to shape Python’s future, learn what’s coming, and connect with peers.

events.title: The Status and Future of Unified Shared Memory in the CPU+GPU Ecosystem
events.description: Originally GPU and CPU memory spaces were completely separate, with explicit data movements needed for interaction between CPU and GPU compute cores. Over time, all major GPU vendors have added hardware and software capabilities for transparent access to each other’s memory, with various levels of granularity and integration, with unified shared memory (USM) representing the most tight integration. This BoF will start by outlining the history, current state, and planned future of cross-memory technologies. We will then open the floor for discussion with conference attendees to gather their perspectives on where this technology should evolve going forward.

events.title: The Impact of GenAI on HPC Programming and Programming Models
events.description:
According to many mainstream media outlets and tech gurus, the age of computer programmers is fading away as GenAI proves itself capable of helping with programming tasks, or completing them independently. And many of us probably have positive (and negative) stories about using AI in our day-to-day lives. But what do we expect the impact of GenAI to be on programming for HPC systems and applications?

This session kicks off with opening statements from thought leaders representing various HPC programming models (MPI, OpenMP, NVIDIA, Kokkos, COMPSs, and Chapel), followed by an open session for audience opinions, Q&A, and healthy debate.

events.title: OpenCHAMI Community Birds of a Feather
events.description: HPC centers are modernizing how they provision and operate clusters as systems become more heterogeneous, security-sensitive, and composable. OpenCHAMI, an HPSF emerging project, is an operator-led open-source control plane that brings cloud-like APIs and modular services to HPC system management. This BoF will help newcomers understand what OpenCHAMI enables today, give current users a forum to compare deployments and priorities, and invite operators, vendors, and developers to shape the roadmap. We will discuss adoption paths, including but not limited to xCAT transitions, and collect community feedback on tooling, integration, documentation, and operational requirements.

events.title: HPC Procurement, Energy Efficiency, and Sustainability
events.description: Energy efficiency has evolved from an operational objective into a contractual engineering requirement for next-generation HPC systems. This BoF explores how procurement contracts shape future supercomputer design by comparing approaches from China, Japan, and Europe. Yutong Lu examines the architectural evolution from Tianhe-2A to CPU-based LineShine, highlighting CPU-based acceleration methods without relying on accelerator components. Masaaki Kondo presents Fugaku to FugakuNEXT, emphasizing procurement strategies for higher simulation performance within a power envelope. Maria Grazia Giuffreda discusses energy-to-solution requirements and software optimization clauses. An interactive forum debates how procurement clauses drive architectural choices, software portability, sustainability, and innovation in late-2020s deployments.

events.title: Open-Source Hardware Tools: Advancing Architecture Research and Chip Prototyping
events.description: As demand for specialized architectures grows in the post-Moore era, this BoF will foster a sustained community around chip prototyping using open-source hardware tools. Building on themes explored in previous editions of this BoF at SC24 and SC25, the session will focus on practical tool experiences, current gaps, domain-specific accelerators, AI-assisted design workflows, and chip prototyping as an emerging HPC workload. Invited speakers from architecture, open-source EDA, accelerator design, and HPC will seed discussion. Expected outcomes include actionable insights, stronger collaboration, and follow-up community initiatives to advance open-source chip prototyping.

events.title: Julia for HPC
events.description: The “Julia for HPC” BoF provides a place for the HPC community with interests in the Julia programming language as an LLVM front-end to close the gaps between high-productivity languages and the performance of compiled languages. We invite participants from industry, government, and academia to discuss their experiences, identify and learn about opportunities and gaps. Topics include Julia adoption for quantum computing, auto-tuning, mixed precision, and agentic AI. The fifth consecutive BoF continues the “Julia for HPC” engagement with the SC community, and complements the tutorial on Julia for HPC at SC26. Presentations will be posted here: https://github.com/JuliaParallel/julia-hpc-bof-sc26.

events.title: Ethics in HPC: With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility
events.description: The implications of HPC technology on society and the environment prompt us, as a community, to discuss and understand our direct and indirect impacts. This BoF is highly interactive and aims to facilitate discussion within the community, relating ethical behavior and societal norms to the design of HPC solutions and autonomous/intelligent systems. The BoF will feature breakout groups and then converge to a plenum discussion. By furthering this dialogue, we can ensure that the HPC community advances its commitment to technology for the benefit of humanity as a whole. We do not expect to reach conclusions, but raise ideas.

events.title: Advanced Architecture Testbeds: Community Resources for HPC-AI Research
events.description: Testbeds play a vital role in assessing the readiness of novel architectures for upcoming supercomputers for the exascale and post-exascale era. These testbeds also act as co-design hubs, enabling the collection of application operational requirements, while identifying critical gaps that need to be addressed for an architecture to become viable for HPC. Various research centers are actively deploying testbeds, and our aim is to build a community that facilitates the sharing of information, encouraging collaboration and understanding of the available evaluation resources. This BoF will facilitate the exchange of best practices, including testbed design, benchmarking, system evaluation, and availability.

events.title: Data Readiness for AI in HPC: Building a Community Around Dimensions, Metrics, and Tools
events.description: AI now drives discovery across HPC science, yet models are only as trustworthy as the data they use. Many teams still lack a shared way to judge whether their data is ready for AI. This BoF brings together the HPC and scientific communities to define data readiness for AI using seven practical dimensions: quality, understandability, fair and unbiased representation, structure and organization, feature importance, governance covering ethics, security and privacy, and AI-specific needs such as labels and distributions. Through short talks and open discussion, we will compare practices, identify gaps, and begin building shared metrics, tools, and benchmarks.

Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Bob Grossman
events.description: Robert L. Grossman, PhD, is the Frederick H. Rawson Distinguished Service Professor in Medicine and Computer Science and the Jim and Karen Frank Director of the Center for Translational Data Science at the University of Chicago. He joined the faculty in 2010 and served as the chief research informatics officer (CRIO) of the Biological Sciences Division from 2011-2024. He is also the Chief of the Section of Biomedical Data Science in the Department of Medicine. He is the principal investigator for the National Cancer Institute Genomic Data Commons (GDC), a platform for the cancer research community that manages, analyzes, integrates, and shares large-scale genomic datasets in support of precision medicine. The GDC is used by more than 150,000 researchers each month. He has also built data commons to support research in other areas, including cardiovascular diseases, infectious diseases and medical imaging. His research interests include data science, AI, and machine learning. He is the founder and a partner at Analytic Strategy Partners, which helps companies develop AI strategies, and a Director of the Open Commons Consortium (OCC), which is a not-for-profit that manages and operates data commons and data meshes to advance scientific and biomedical research. He served as a member of the NOAA Scientific Advisory Board (SAB) from 2017-2024 and as a member of the Frederick National Laboratory Advisory Committee (FNLAC) from 2014-2021. He earned his PhD in applied mathematics at Princeton University and an AB in mathematics from Harvard University.
