Nautobot
DNoF: Rearchitecting the Collaborative I/O Processing Stack Between CPU and DPU for NVMe Over Fabrics
events.description: To reduce the overhead associated with transferring large volumes of data from storage to the CPU in data-intensive applications, data centers integrate data processing units (DPUs) to manage NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) remote storage access. However, current heterogeneous DPU and CPU system architectures for NVMe-oF face challenges of limited flexibility and suboptimal utilization of bandwidth and computational resources. In this paper, we present DNoF, a collaborative I/O processing stack for DPU and CPU in NVMe-oF systems, and implement it in a real-world environment. DNoF explores collaboration strategies between the DPU and CPU, achieving near-optimal system performance for NVMe-oF remote access under various workloads and delivering more than a 2x throughput improvement compared to DPU-only NVMe-oF.

events.title: Next-Generation Scientific Storage and I/O
events.description: The papers redesign the scientific storage stack across DPUs, NVMe, all-flash systems, and query offload. Together they ask how I/O architectures can keep pace with data-intensive HPC.

events.title: Adaptive Execution for Sparse and Irregular Computation
events.description: Sparse and irregular workloads require different execution strategies across kernels, solvers, tensor contractions, and distributed systems. SPIKe adapts GPU execution to matrix structure; the distributed SpMM work co-models tasks and data to avoid communication; LCD transforms loop-carried dependencies to expose GPU parallelism in sparse solvers; and TIDES selects hardware-matched execution tiers for heterogeneous block-sparse contractions.

events.title: Loop-Carried Dependence Transformation for Parallel Sparse Solvers on GPUs
events.description: Loop-carried dependences create significant computational bottlenecks in scientific solvers, hindering the effective utilization of massive GPU parallelism. Existing libraries are typically restricted to specific numerical methods or matrix types, making them difficult to scale, while previous compiler techniques often target only fully parallel loops or multicore CPUs. We propose a loop-carried dependence parallelism (LCD) transformation that automatically enables GPU parallelism for loops within sparse solvers. LCD lowers identified loops from a broad range of sparse operations, mapping them to thread-blocks and warps while implementing efficient and correct synchronization strategies. This framework utilizes a thread-block manager and a thread manager, both orchestrated by a central scheduler. Implemented as a Python just-in-time (JIT) compiler, the code generated by LCD achieves a geometric mean speedup of 1.60x-4.56x over the cuSPARSE library on H100 GPUs across various operations.

events.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training Over 10,000 GPUs
events.description:
Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations, degrading training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under-provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur.

To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control, BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1,040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14× and 1.13× average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kwai and AdaPipe, respectively.

events.title: Scaling Complex AI Training Workloads
events.description: This session examines the system challenges of training MoEs, multimodal models, and other heterogeneous AI workloads. The papers emphasize memory variability, hierarchical communication, and pipeline orchestration.

events.title: Communication Avoidance and In-Network Reduction
events.description: This session explores reducing communication cost through sparse embeddings, in-network reduction, and SmartNIC/SmartSwitch co-design. It connects algorithmic communication avoidance with network-supported collective operations at extreme scale.

events.title: Communication Avoiding Parallel Sketching via Sparse Subspace Embeddings
events.description: This paper considers sketching via sparse subspace embeddings that are commonly employed in randomized algorithms due to their efficiency when applied to large-scale matrices. We introduce lower bounds on communication and design optimal algorithms for sketching large-scale matrices using sparse random embeddings. We consider different matrix dimensions and aspect ratios that are relevant for scientific computing and machine learning applications. We demonstrate the strong and weak scalability of these algorithms on both CPU and GPU architectures.

events.title: ACM Gordon Bell Finalists Presentations
Exascale Distillation Workflows for Protein Structure Prediction on El Capitan
events.description: Understanding the structure of proteins is critical to many biological applications. Recent deep learning approaches, such as AlphaFold, make high-quality structure predictions. However, training state-of-the-art models requires producing distillation datasets, which need several times more compute than training. We describe ElMerFold, an optimized distillation data generation workflow that scales to 11,200 nodes (44,800 APUs) on El Capitan, by leveraging a combination of inference, workflow, I/O, and resiliency innovations. We demonstrate this for the OpenFold 3 monomer protein distillation dataset, which uses a complex workflow centered on a set of pretrained OpenFold 2 models to predict structures for ~41 million proteins. ElMerFold achieves a 45.4x speedup over the state-of-the-art, predicting 6,718 structures/s, and achieving 1.99 Eflop/s peak for FP32 model inference (1.81 Eflop/s sustained including I/O). As distillation and synthetic data become more common, these workflows will help drive scientific advancement.

events.title: Exascale Biomedical Digital Twins: From Biophysical Simulation to Clinical Impact
events.description:
Biomedical digital twins represent a frontier for exascale computing and AI, offering transformative potential for proactive healthcare, precision medicine, and medical-device innovation. However, translating complex human physiology into real-world clinical workflows introduces critical HPC challenges in model fidelity, speed, data integration, regulatory validation, and deployment cost.

This panel brings together leaders across academia, medical devices, and modeling software: Dr. Amanda Randles (Duke University; computational digital twins and HPC biophysical simulations), Darrell Swenson (Medtronic; HPC integration in medical device development), and Dr. Mark Palmer (Synopsys; clinical translation, simulation, and enterprise digital twin adoption). Using cardiac digital twins as a primary high-impact case study, the panel will explore the broader roadmap for biomedical HPC. The session is structured around interactive debate and direct audience engagement to address a central question: What must the supercomputing community solve next to make high-fidelity biological digital twins routine, scalable, and impactful across clinical and industrial settings?

events.title: Exascale Biomedical Digital Twins: From Biophysical Simulation to Clinical Impact
Building and Managing Exascale HPC/AI Supercomputing Infrastructure
events.description:
Designing and operating exascale infrastructure for HPC and AI workloads is no longer a distant challenge — it is accelerating faster than ever, bringing unprecedented complexity in performance, cost, scalability, and security. National labs, hyperscalers, neo-clouds, commercial enterprises, and academic centers all face these problems, often arriving at very different solutions shaped by their workloads, regulatory contexts, supply chains, and economics.

This 90-minute panel brings together operators from across the sector to compare approaches, debate trade-offs, and surface the practical lessons most worth carrying across organizational boundaries. Topics under discussion include cost-effective scaling, exascale data movement, security and multi-tenancy, energy and power management, and operational resilience.

The panel delivers insights that benefit the broader HPC and AI ecosystem — turning isolated operational lessons into a shared, comparative view, aligned with the theme of SC26: HPC Unites.

events.title: Building and Managing Exascale HPC/AI Supercomputing Infrastructure
AI, CXL and Open Sourcing Software
Building the Future of AI Infrastructure with CXL
events.description: Discover how the Compute Express Link® (CXL®) ecosystem is helping solve the memory challenges limiting today's AI infrastructure. Recently, leading cloud service providers and GPU manufacturers have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access and enabling more efficient AI inference at scale. This Exhibitor Forum session highlights the growing momentum behind CXL adoption, featuring demonstrations from CXL Consortium members that showcase memory expansion, pooling, composable infrastructure, software enablement, validation, and production-ready solutions. Attendees will gain insight into how a diverse ecosystem of silicon providers, system manufacturers, software developers, and infrastructure companies is working together to bring CXL to market and address the memory and infrastructure challenges of modern AI workloads.

events.title: 900 Petabytes and Not a Watt More
events.description:
Bandwidth, not capacity, drives the power draw of modern storage systems, and flash has made this performance-capacity ratio a genuinely open design choice rather than one fixed by economics. Every architect must now decide how much bandwidth per petabyte to power, and those watts come out of the compute budget. Both directions are expensive: too little bandwidth costs productivity as applications contend with each other, and too much forfeits the GPUs those watts could have powered. The capacity-optimized end carries an added reliability risk, because ultra-high-capacity SSDs demand data protection techniques that scale with them.

We map this design space using two production systems built from the same architecture and components: one providing over 900 PB of usable capacity, and the other 10x less capacity but significantly higher performance. From this, we demonstrate that bandwidth requirements now warrant scrutiny proportional to the costs they impose on system design.

events.title: HPC System Hardware and Architecture
Quantum Programming and Applications
Real Science on Integrated Quantum-Classical Computers
events.description: This talk explores pioneering research work that integrates quantum computing with conventional supercomputing in two distinct domains. In one, we look at some of the complex molecular mechanisms of life by focusing on GPCR proteins which are targets for around one-third of all drug discovery projects. The second describes how the use of integrated quantum computers enhances the long time prediction of the spatio-temporal evolution of chaotic dynamical systems, such as occurs commonly in turbulent fluids, and takes us beyond that attainable using conventional machine-learning methods.

events.title: TBD — Automation
SuperSSD: Rethinking JBOF to Break the Cost-Performance Trade-Off in All-Flash Storage
events.description: Disaggregated storage offers high resource utilization but faces cost and performance challenges in large-scale all-flash storage deployments. To address these limitations, this paper proposes SuperSSD, a system-device co-designed JBOF architecture that rethinks the enclosure design along two key dimensions. First, SuperSSD unifies conventional network protocol translation and storage-side architectural support within a single framework, eliminating redundant data movement. Second, it centralizes performance optimization and reliability enhancement at the system layer, leveraging enclosure-level mechanisms to reduce complexity within individual SSDs, thereby lowering per-device design overhead and overall cost. To sustain high system-layer performance, we implement a full-stack FPGA-based solution that integrates networking and storage-side computations into a unified datapath, enabling efficient centralized data aggregation and processing. Prototyping evaluation shows that SuperSSD reduces the TCO to 53.7% of that of CPU-based JBOFs, while achieving up to 1.35x higher peak random-write IOPS and up to 59.32% lower latency at the same IOPS.

events.title: SPIKe: Generating Practical SpMV Kernels for Sparse Iterative Methods on GPUs
events.description: Sparse iterative methods with static sparse matrices form the backbone of many applications, where SpMV is the primary performance bottleneck. Conventional optimizations typically involve costly matrix-specific preprocessing, causing unamortizable overhead as algorithmic advances reduce iteration counts. We present SPIKe, a practical SpMV kernel generator targeting efficient sparse iterative methods across a wide spectrum of iteration counts. SPIKe comprises three key techniques: 1) Online Thread-Level Parallelism Adaptation policy, using a thread-computed row span proxy to enhance load balance for uniform tiles; 2) Online Warp-Level Asymmetric Scheduling policy, featuring a lightweight Warp-as-a-Sensor to route skewed tiles to asymmetric code paths; 3) Offline Architecture-Domain Co-Aware Code Generation for kernel optimization following the preceding policies. Across 2,294 matrices, SPIKe outperforms six baselines with negligible preprocessing overhead. In end-to-end evaluations spanning varying iteration counts, SPIKe achieves average speedups of 2.78x for PageRank and 4.26x for GMRES against GraphBLAS and PETSc.

events.title: HCCL: Collective Communication for Meta Training and Inference Accelerators
events.description: We present HCCL, a collective communication library co-designed with Meta's MTIA 300 accelerator, the first Meta chip to integrate backend networking directly on die. MTIA 300 includes dedicated message engines (MEs) with near-memory compute (NMC) that fully offload collective execution from the compute grid, enabling near-perfect overlap between computation and communication. HCCL uses a compiled communication model in which the host generates a complete description of each collective including dependencies. We describe the control and data path architecture, topology-aware algorithm selection across MTIA 300's asymmetric scale-up and scale-out network, and optimizations for both training and inference workloads. For training, HCCL achieves up to 940 GB/s on intra-rack collectives while introducing less than 0.5% degradation to concurrent compute throughput. For inference, we leverage one-sided communication primitives that bypass the scheduling path to minimize collective latency and describe collective designs that improve compute-communication pipelining for latency-sensitive workloads.

events.title: SmartReduce: Efficient Sparse AllReduce via Low-Latency SmartNIC-Switch Coordination
events.description: Sparse AllReduce is a promising primitive for accelerating distributed machine learning training with sparse gradients, but existing designs fail to deliver high algorithm bandwidth. The root cause is their reliance on CPU-initiated coordination, which imposes high packet-processing overhead during aggregation and creates severe load imbalance across CPU cores, limiting effective exploitation of sparsity. We observe that sustaining high-throughput sparse AllReduce requires removing the CPU from both the coordination path and the fine-grained sparsification path. Guided by this insight, we present SmartReduce, a SmartSwitch-aware, SmartNIC-centric sparse AllReduce. SmartReduce combines two key mechanisms: (1) a switch-aware, NIC-initiated aggregation mechanism that performs in-network coordination between SmartNICs and the SmartSwitch with stable sub-RTT overhead, and (2) a NIC-centric fine-grained sparsification mechanism that processes fine-grained blocks in high parallelism to exploit intra-block sparsity. Experimental results show that SmartReduce at 99% sparsity achieves up to 6.4x higher algorithm bandwidth than the state-of-the-art aggregator-server-based sparse AllReduce method.

events.title: Extreme-Scale Linear-Scaling Kohn-Sham DFT at 100 Million Atoms: Bridging Quantum Simulations and Experiments
events.description: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) remains the workhorse of ab initio materials simulation, yet cubic computational and quadratic memory scaling have confined calculations to a few hundred to thousands of atoms, spanning only nanometers, far below experimentally relevant length scales. We introduce XLSDFT, a linear-scaling DFT framework based on divide-and-conquer decomposition of the one-particle density matrix and Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration, achieving linear computational and memory scaling while retaining DFT accuracy. Deployed on the LineShine exascale supercomputer, XLSDFT reduces computational complexity by orders of magnitude, enabling unprecedented DFT scale: a 200-million-atom silicon crystal, twentyfold beyond the prior record. Our implementation achieves 96.6% weak-scaling efficiency and sustained 157.9 Pflop/s (FP64) for a 100-million-atom scaling study. We further simulate an 11-million-atom all-solid-state battery interface of unprecedented complexity, 1,000 times beyond prior DFT for such systems, revealing how lithium metal reacts with the solid electrolyte at atomic resolution, in quantitative agreement with spectroscopy experiments.

events.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Ameen Salahudeen
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Avinash Maurya
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Nicholas Chia
events.description: Nicholas Chia is a Computational Biologist at Argonne National Laboratory whose work spans artificial intelligence, cancer biology, complex systems, and translational medicine. He received a B.S. in Physics from Georgetown University and a Ph.D. in Physics from The Ohio State University, followed by postdoctoral training in biocomplexity, collective effects, and evolution at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Prior to joining Argonne, Chia spent more than a decade at Mayo Clinic, where he served as Waterman Endowed Co-Chair of the Microbiome Program, Director of the Beyond DNA Multi-omics Strategic Theme within the Center for Individualized Medicine, Associate Director of the Microbiome Program, and Associate Professor of Medicine. During that time, he helped build Mayo’s microbiome and multiomics programs and contributed to the introduction of technologies that ultimately supported 19 laboratory-developed tests reaching clinical go-live. His research has focused on colorectal cancer, cancer evolution, microbial ecology, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and the integration of multi-omic data into clinical and biological discovery. He is recognized for early work applying inverse reinforcement learning to cancer evolution, framing tumor progression as an adaptive process and developing computational approaches to infer the evolutionary pressures that shape disease trajectories. At Argonne, his work has expanded into AI for Science, scientific reasoning, biological foundation models, and large-scale computational biology. He is a contributor to BioAlchemy, a large-scale biological reasoning corpus derived from the scientific literature, and leads and collaborates on programs spanning scientific reasoning, causal inference, disease modeling, population health, biological foundation models, and AI-enabled discovery. His work leverages leadership-class computing resources to develop and evaluate AI systems for scientific research. Across national laboratories, academic medicine, and interdisciplinary research programs, Chia has worked on problems that require the integration of large-scale data, mechanistic modeling, and decision-making under uncertainty, with applications ranging from cancer and microbiome science to scientific reasoning and AI-driven discovery.

events.title: Enabling Agentic AI Serving with Disaggregated Memory Pools
events.description: Our proposed system, developed through strategic collaborations with leading CXL device providers, a major GPU vendor, and a prominent AI model company, leverages CXL shared memory to enable ultra-low latency KV cache transfer in disaggregated LLM serving. By completely eliminating traditional network bottlenecks and facilitating seamless, efficient KV cache sharing across workers, our approach significantly reduces GPU memory overhead while optimizing overall resource utilization. This innovative architecture overcomes inherent hardware limitations through advanced software mechanisms, including novel locking and coherence protocols. Consequently, the system achieves remarkable performance gains: 2.6× lower time to first token, 3.0× reduced P99 latency, and 1.9× higher throughput compared to standard RDMA baselines. These results demonstrate a highly scalable, practical path toward deploying cost-effective, high-performance AI infrastructure in modern data centers, validating the transformative potential of CXL technology for next-generation large language model services.

events.title: The Impact of Fluid Chemistry on AI Infrastructure Reliability
events.description:
Coolant chemistry is a critical but often underappreciated factor in maintaining single-phase liquid-cooled system reliability. Poor control of fluid parameters can lead to biological growth, corrosion, scale precipitation, fouling, and degradation of system materials. These problems do not merely shorten coolant service life; left unchecked, they can compromise heat transfer, force performance throttling, increase failure risk, and contribute to unplanned downtime.

These risks to system performance and reliability exist in both water-based and propylene glycol systems, though they arise through different failure mechanisms. They are best mitigated by a robust monitoring program coupled with predefined response protocols for out-of-specification coolant conditions. Through real-world examples of coolant chemistry excursions that threatened system performance and availability, this presentation will demonstrate how fluid quality directly impacts AI infrastructure reliability. Attendees will leave with practical strategies for monitoring coolant health, recognizing early warning signs, and mitigating chemistry-related risks before they affect operation.

events.title: Demonstrating Entanglement Distribution: Quantum-Classical Co-Existence on Deployed Fiber
events.description: nri101

events.title: OASIS: Object-Based Analytics Storage for Multi-Layer SQL Offloading in Scientific Tabular Workloads
events.description:
Scientific analytics on disaggregated object storage suffer from high data movement overhead, often dominating query latency. While computation-enabled object storage (COS) reduces this cost via operator offloading, existing approaches assume a fixed execution boundary and restrict execution to a single storage-side layer, leaving cross-layer data movement unoptimized. We observe that this stems from a mismatch between operator semantics and execution scope, where early reduction and globally coordinated execution require different layers. Therefore, the key challenge is not operator selection, but execution boundary placement across storage layers.

We present OASIS, the first COS system that formulates storage-side query execution as a cross-layer boundary placement problem over a multi-layer hierarchy. Its core algorithm, SODA, determines the split point to minimize intermediate data movement. Integrated with Apache Spark, OASIS reduces internal data movement by 99.998% and lowers end-to-end query latency by up to 25% compared to Skyhook, a state-of-the-art COS system.

events.title: TIDES: Tiered Block-Sparse Tensor Contraction with Streaming Transpose on GPUs
events.description: Block-sparse tensor contraction is a core kernel in symmetry-preserving many-body methods such as DMRG, where physical symmetries produce thousands of block pairs that vary widely in shape and tensor order, with element counts spanning several orders of magnitude. We present TIDES, a hybrid GPU algorithm that matches this heterogeneity with three execution tiers: a warp-level dot-product kernel for small blocks, a shared-memory direct contraction kernel for medium blocks, and, for large blocks, a streaming TTGT pipeline over grouped GEMM whose transpose workspace is bounded by the largest single block pair and whose HyperTile kernel transposes many heterogeneous high-order blocks in one grouped launch. On 2D Hubbard DMRG workloads across four symmetry regimes on an NVIDIA H100, TIDES achieves geometric-mean speedups of 2.14x (FP64) and 1.69x (FP32) over NVIDIA cuTENSOR 2.6.0, with speedups up to 5.97x and 9.86x, respectively, lower setup overhead, and portable performance on other GPUs.

events.title: X-MoE-4D: Breaking the Scaling Barrier for Trillion Parameter MoEs on Hierarchical HPC Systems
events.description: We present X-MoE-4D, a distributed training system for scaling expert-specialized Mixture-of-Experts models on hierarchical HPC platforms. We observe that existing expert-parallel approaches suffer from severe scalability limits due to cross-node all-to-all communication. To address this, X-MoE-4D adopts a pipeline-global, expert-local execution model that confines expert computation within nodes while scaling across nodes via pipeline parallelism. X-MoE-4D further introduces a Minimax Pipeline Planner that jointly optimizes pipeline partitioning and activation checkpointing to minimize bottleneck stage execution time under memory constraints. Together, these techniques eliminate cross-node expert routing and mitigate MoE pipeline skew. We evaluate X-MoE-4D on the Frontier supercomputer, demonstrating the first efficient one-trillion-parameter expert-specialized MoE training on an AMD-based HPC platform. X-MoE-4D achieves 2.24× higher aggregate throughput than X-MoE at one-trillion-parameter scale (2.4× per GPU throughput) while using fewer GPUs (960 vs. 1,024), and sustains a 3.24× speedup when strong-scaling the 173B model to 2,304 GPUs. Code available at https://github.com/Supercomputing-System-AI-Lab/X-MoE.

events.title: DistFP: Scaling Floating-Point In-Network AllReduce on In-Path Programmable Switches
events.description: Floating-point (FP) gradient aggregation can bottleneck distributed machine learning training. In-network aggregation (INA) can reduce this overhead by aggregating gradients in network switches. However, current in-path programmable switches based on the protocol-independent switch architecture (PISA) lack native FP support. Existing work emulates FP INA with integer arithmetic units, consuming substantial pipeline resources and limiting aggregation parallelism. We present DistFP, a host-switch co-designed system for high-parallelism FP AllReduce on PISA-based in-path programmable switches. Its key idea is a state-dependency decomposition: DistFP moves worker-local functions to the host while retaining cross-worker collective functions in the switch, allowing more concurrent switch aggregation instances under a fixed resource budget. On a real Tofino 1-based prototype, DistFP achieves 1.3x and 6.7x higher FP32 aggregation throughput than NCCL Ring and FPISA, respectively. In our end-to-end training evaluation, DistFP improves performance by up to 1.14x over NCCL Ring.

events.title: Quantum Gates Considered Harmful
events.description:
Quantum computing is easy once it is described for what it is. It is a probabilistic computational method with one crucial addition: interference. A computation creates multiple possible paths, manipulates their amplitudes and phases, and then recombines them. Destructive interference suppresses outcomes associated with unwanted paths. Constructive interference increases the probability of useful ones. In this view, a quantum algorithm is simply a carefully designed interferometer. However, quantum gates do not expose this simple computational model. Borrowed from reversible digital logic, they describe the operations used to construct an interferometer. A programming model should instead describe the interference pattern that the algorithm intends to produce. As a result, quantum algorithms appear more complicated than they actually are.

This talk argues that quantum gates should be considered harmful as a programming abstraction. Alternative programming models should make computational paths, phases, correlations, and interference first-class concepts, leaving gates as implementation details. Such models could not only improve programmability, but also expand the design space for quantum algorithms by drawing on fields that have long mastered interference, including beamforming, antenna theory, wave physics, and signal processing. Perhaps richer quantum algorithms will emerge when we stop programming gate sequences and begin programming interference patterns.

events.title: Publishing the Repository Is the Easy Part: Taking Research Software Public
events.description:
Research groups across the HPC industry build universally useful software all the time, but most of it is never shared with the world. Open-sourcing it can fix that, but publishing a project is much more than publishing the repository.

This talk walks through the decision the way I walk through it with the many teams who ask me: finding your real motivation, whether your institution is on board, what long-term support you can honestly commit, and what structure fits (an informal group, an umbrella foundation, fiscal sponsorship, or your own). Then the practical side: getting the code ready, getting the project ready to receive feedback, getting yourself ready for contributors, and defining what success looks like before you need it. Attendees will leave with a solid plan for how to approach this decision and what defines success. I will post the slides and a checklist gist afterward.

events.title: Increasing Liquid Cooling Capacity for AI and HPC Infrastructure Through Optimized Coolant Velocity Limits
events.description: As AI and HPC rack thermal densities rise, liquid cooling systems are being asked to deliver more capacity without proportional increases in footprint or infrastructure complexity. This presentation examines whether commonly applied coolant velocity limits remain appropriate for modern hose-based coolant distribution systems. Using analytical modeling and empirical testing of peroxide-cured EPDM hose assemblies operating with PG25 coolant, the work evaluates how elevated velocity affects heat transfer capability, pressure loss, flow-induced vibration, noise and long-term system reliability. The findings provide engineers and cooling system designers with a practical framework for assessing when higher flow rates can increase cooling capacity, and where operational or mechanical limits should define safe boundaries. Attendees will gain a data-driven perspective on using velocity as a design lever for scalable liquid cooling in next-generation AI and HPC environments.

events.title: Z-SPDK: Accelerating Lossy Compressed I/O on NVMe-SSDs
events.description: Lossy compression is widely used to reduce storage space and I/O demands. However, its benefits diminish on NVMe-SSDs, where compression and decompression runtimes can exceed raw device throughput. Leveraging the low-level Storage Performance Development Kit (SPDK) driver to bypass the kernel and filesystem overheads, we conduct the first systematic study of lossy compressed I/O on NVMe-SSDs and expose key bottlenecks in process control, pipeline utilization, and parameter tuning. To address these issues, we design Z-SPDK, a novel extension of SPDK that incorporates fixed-ratio compression control, dual-pipeline parallelism, per-chunk error-bound, and zero-copy data transfer, thereby co-optimizing lossy compression with NVMe I/O. Experiments on three high-speed lossy compressors across five scientific datasets demonstrate up to 12X runtime speedup, while satisfying user-defined error bounds and improving NVMe bandwidth utilization by up to 5.9X. In addition, we evaluate with HDF5 and observe up to 82.56% runtime reduction with Z-SPDK.

events.title: A Unified Multi-Dimensional Parallel Algorithm for Communication-Avoiding SpMM
events.description: Distributed sparse matrix–dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) is often bottlenecked by communication and performs poorly under irregular sparsity patterns. We propose a unified task–data parallel (TDP) framework that jointly models task decomposition and data distribution, enabling communication analysis across the SpMM design space. Within this framework, we identify two complementary 2D submodels, $mn\text{-}r_A r_B$ and $kn\text{-}c_A r_C$, with distinct sparsity-dependent communication costs, and develop a fused MNKN algorithm that partitions the sparse matrix into tiles and assigns each tile to the lower-cost submodel using lightweight sparsity-aware metrics. This design enables fine-grained dense-side communication avoidance without additional storage overhead while naturally overlapping communication and computation. Experiments on large-scale SuiteSparse matrices show performance gains on 68% of 135 matrices, including up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over 2D SUMMA and an average speedup of 2.4x over the sparsity-aware CRP baseline on 10 representative matrices. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in polynomial-filtering eigensolvers.

events.title: Arachne: Orchestrating Cascades for Efficient Text-to-Video Model Training
events.description:
The rising demand for AI-generated videos is fueled by advances in large-scale text-to-video (T2V) models, trained on extensive datasets of video clips spanning diverse resolutions and durations. To address this data heterogeneity, current training methods often use a bucketing strategy that groups samples into discrete buckets for efficiency. However, this approach struggles to scale with compute and data volumes under static parallelism schemes, such as data and sequence parallelism, leading to significant workload imbalances and hardware under-utilization.

In this paper, we present Arachne, a novel training framework for efficient T2V model training at scale. Arachne decomposes the training process into fine-grained computational units, called cascades, orchestrating their distributed execution and synchronization across the cluster through coordinated spatial and temporal optimization. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that Arachne reduces iteration time by up to 65% over leading frameworks, exhibiting a positive scaling trend where its performance advantages amplify as training scale grows.

events.title: Scaling Neural Network Quantum States to 8,192 GPUs: Treating Transition-Metal Clusters in Hilbert Spaces Beyond 10³¹ Dimensions
events.description: Computing ground-state energies of strongly correlated transition-metal clusters remains a central challenge due to exponentially growing Hilbert spaces. We present a scalable neural network quantum state (NNQS) framework based on a Transformer-encoder wavefunction with neural-network backflow, targeting large-scale heterogeneous supercomputers. An asynchronous CPU–GPU pipeline, mixed-precision optimization, semi-stochastic coupling for local energy evaluation, and a scalable distributed second-order optimizer collectively achieve 98.9% weak-scaling efficiency on 4,096 and 88.94% strong-scaling efficiency on 8,192 GPU accelerators. We compute ground-state energies for three metalloenzyme active sites, including the P-cluster of nitrogenase (146 spin orbitals, 114 electrons)—doubling the previous NNQS system-size frontier into Hilbert spaces beyond 10³¹ dimensions. Our results establish NNQS as a viable framework for strongly correlated quantum chemistry at unprecedented scales.

events.title: SCinet Research and NRE Talk
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Prem Kumar
events.description: Prem Kumar is the John A. Dever Professor of Information Technology at the McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science at Northwestern University. His primary research focus is on photonic devices and their applications utilizing the principles of nonlinear and quantum optics (>$30M cumulative research funding). Recent projects have included: generation, distribution, and ultrafast processing of photonic entanglement for applications in quantum information networks; novel quantum light states for precision measurements, imaging, and sensing; and novel optical amplifiers and devices for networked classical optical communications. Although Dr. Kumar’s primary appointment is in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, an affiliation with the Applied Physics program allows him to recruit multidisciplinary students into his research group, a privilege that has proven extremely beneficial for his research interests that lie at the interface of basic quantum science and applied information technology. Because of this interdisciplinary exposure, Ph.D. graduates from his research group (37 completed, 5 in progress) have gone on to build careers in academia, industry, and US national labs. His group has cumulatively published >500 research papers (Google Scholar h-index: 69), including 1 edited book, 2 book chapters, 6 patents, >200 peer-reviewed journal papers, 45 articles in hard-bound volumes, and >300 conference papers with >100 invited. From Feb’13 to Jan’17, Dr. Kumar was on leave from Northwestern to be at DARPA, where he served as a Program Manager in the Defense Sciences Office. At DARPA, Dr. Kumar created and managed a ~$20M/year portfolio of programs in basic and applied sciences, targeting a diverse range of topics that included neuroscience and engineering, ultrafast laser science and technology, precision navigation and timing, stand-off chem-bio defense, quantum effects in biological environments, and quantum information science and technology. He was also program manager for the Defense Science Study Group, which allowed him to interact with young academic faculty from universities across the US in various national defense settings. For his strong portfolio of programs in basic science and technology and his mentoring of DARPA Risers—young, noteworthy performers on DARPA programs—Dr. Kumar was selected Program Manager of the Year in 2015 and awarded the Secretary of Defense Medal for Outstanding Public Service in 2016. Prior to joining DARPA, Dr. Kumar served on the National Academies Committee that issued the 2012 landmark study: “Optics and Photonics: Essential Technologies for Our Nation,” which spawned the National Photonics Initiative (NPI). From 2018 to 2024, Dr. Kumar served on the NPI Steering Committee, lending his expertise to issues pertaining to the National Quantum Initiative. Dr. Kumar is a Fellow of Optica (formerly OSA), APS, IEEE, IoP (U.K.), AAAS, and SPIE. He has been a Distinguished Lecturer for the IEEE Photonics Society, Hermann A. Haus Lecturer at MIT, recipient of the Quantum Communication Award from Tamagawa University in Tokyo, Japan, and the Walder Research Excellence Award from the Provost’s office at Northwestern University. From 2020 to 2025, he served as the Editor-in-Chief of Optica, the flagship journal of The Optica Publishing Group (formerly OSA) for high-impact research. Currently, he co-chairs the National Academies Committee on Atomic Molecular and Optical Sciences, and was recently appointed to the External Advisory Board for NTT Basic Research Laboratories in Atsugi, Japan. Internal to Northwestern, he serves on the Executive Committee for the Institute at Northwestern for Quantum Information Research and Engineering (INQUIRE). Beginning Fall’26, he will also serve as the Interim Chair of the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department.

events.title: Improving Progressive Compression with Adaptive Interpolation and Coefficient Decomposition
events.description:
Exascale simulations generate data far faster than it can be stored or analyzed, making efficient data reduction essential. Error-controlled lossy compression offers high compression ratios under user-specified error bounds, but the target tolerance must be fixed at compression time. Progressive compression relaxes this restriction, yet existing methods still rely on fixed refactoring strategies and do not fully exploit correlations among decomposed coefficients, limiting the efficiency of progressive retrieval.

In this work, we present an adaptive progressive compression framework that improves retrieval efficiency for two common targets, namely error-bound and peak signal-to-noise ratios.

events.title: Trustworthy GPU Lossy Compression
events.description: The papers advance GPU scientific compression while preserving quantities of interest and region-specific accuracy. The session traces the shift from generic error bounds toward adaptive, application-aware data reduction.

events.title: Accelerating SpGEMM Through Lightweight Clustering and Cache-Aware Accumulation
events.description:
Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication is one of the most crucial kernels in linear algebra solvers, graph analytics, and machine learning workloads. The clustered row-row style has emerged as a favorable SpGEMM workflow because of its potentially good parallelism. However, due to frequent data movement caused by irregular memory access, existing approaches often suffer from three issues: (1) workload imbalance and prohibitive preprocessing overhead, (2) unsatisfactory data locality, and (3) inefficient accumulation strategy.

To this end, we propose LeSpGEMM, a locality-enhanced SpGEMM algorithm. LeSpGEMM introduces a lightweight row-clustering method to improve spatial locality with near-linear complexity, and a cache-aware hybrid accumulation strategy to exploit data reuse across diverse sparse patterns. It further incorporates optimized kernels, including a SIMD-accelerated dense accumulator and an efficient hash-based accumulator. Experimental results on multiple platforms show that LeSpGEMM significantly outperforms six state-of-the-art implementations while maintaining low preprocessing overhead.

events.title: Sparse Algebra, Preconditioning, and Tensor Decomposition
events.description: This session focuses on irregular numerical kernels, including sparse matrix multiplication, randomized preconditioners, tensor decomposition, and matrix powers. The unifying topic is restructuring computation and data access for scalable performance.

events.title: Observing, Modeling, and Designing Communication at Scale
events.description: The session moves from measuring communication, to redesigning it, to predicting its system-level consequences: fine-grained RDMA tracing, long-haul collective design, workload-grounded AI-network performance envelopes, and scalable rocHPL performance prediction using kernel and network simulation.

events.title: SigmaTrace: Library-Agnostic Observability for CPU/GPU-Initiated RDMA Communication
events.description:
RDMA networking enables low-latency, high-bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per-operation behavior. The gap is widest for GPU-initiated networking, whose in-kernel RDMA operations are invisible to the host.

We present SigmaTrace, a library-agnostic RDMA profiling framework providing fine-grained, per-operation visibility for CPU and GPU-initiated networking. It traces operations at the libibverbs/mlx5dv layers, the common denominator beneath communication libraries on InfiniBand and RoCE, and employs a low-overhead memory interposition technique that, to our knowledge, gives the first observability into GPU-initiated RDMA without source patching or binary instrumentation.

Host-side tracing adds 1.3% overhead on NCCL AllReduce at 128 GPUs and under 2% on RCCL at 1,024 GPUs. On a persistent-kernel BFS and Mixture-of-Experts inference, SigmaTrace exposes an in-kernel barrier spread and 2.13x inter-node traffic skew invisible to existing profilers.

events.title: Extreme-Scale Multiphysics and PDE Solvers
events.description: These papers advance large-scale simulation through parallel-in-time methods, GPU solvers, hardware abstractions, and ultra-large meshes. Together they ask how numerical methods and software design must evolve for increasingly complex multiphysics workloads.

events.title: Printing in a JIFFY: A Parallel-in-Time Heat Transfer Solver for Additive Manufacturing
events.description: Certification of mission-critical 3D-printed components can take over a year because it is sensitive to process parameters. Simulation could shorten this, but 3D printing spans vast spatial and temporal scales. We isolate one key physics challenge: predicting the temperature field. We introduce JIFFY, a parallel-in-time solver for heat transfer with a moving point source. Given the source path and an approximate Green's function, we construct a directed acyclic graph encoding space-time dependencies, decompose it into spatial path segments processed in parallel, and resolve remaining dependencies with a few iterations local in space and time. JIFFY achieves near-ideal weak scaling and good strong scaling. Our Python implementation (GPU+MPI) simulates a multilayer print on 64 GPUs in under 30 minutes at an effective uniform-grid resolution exceeding tens of billions of points and hundreds of thousands of time steps; a state-of-the-art single-GPU adaptively refined solver without temporal parallelism would need over a day.

events.title: 4D Parallelism Unlocks Exascale Bayesian Neural Networks for High-Fidelity Atmospheric Modeling
formats: ACM Gordon Bell Climate Modeling Finalist
events.description:
We present BEAST, the first-ever Bayesian Swin Transformer for atmospheric forecasting on 0.25° global resolution. To overcome the associated computational bottlenecks, we devise an orthogonal 4D-parallelization scheme that introduces a unique domain-tensor-parallelism strategy and a novel uncertainty parallel method, enabling us to fully leverage GPU capacity and efficiently scale model training. For a 2.4-billion-parameter model, we achieve a peak performance of 3.96 EFLOP/s on 20,480 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on the JUPITER supercomputer.

We train BEAST as a 700-million-parameter model with 96 random weight samples on 384 nodes on 40 years of data for nearly one million gradient updates. This model achieves predictive skill scores competitive with state-of-the-art probabilistic atmospheric AI models and numerical models, and can predict extreme events with exceptional skill, while generating large ensembles 3–4 times faster than the current-best AI model. Our contribution unlocks the potential of high-fidelity uncertainty quantification in atmospheric AI models.

events.title: Back to the Future for HPC and Cancer: The Transformative Next Decade in Cancer Research and Cancer Care
events.description: A decade ago, in 2016, the U.S. National Cancer Institute and the U.S. Department of Energy announced their truly unique collaboration to take advantage of each agency's strengths, bringing together the power of emerging exascale systems and the collective data, knowledge, and wisdom of the cancer community. With the advances of the last decade in HPC, AI, and availability of cancer clinical and research data, the opportunities ahead are tremendous to improve cancer care. Enabled by HPC, the next decade will be truly transformative as clinical opportunities and potential are realized, research connections are made, and the paths for translation of data science insights to treat patients are widened. The panel will reflect on the experiences and advances of the past decade, share insights on current challenges, and look ahead to the future as HPC unites communities to take on cancer.

events.title: Back to the Future for HPC and Cancer: The Transformative Next Decade in Cancer Research and Cancer Care
Building Gigawatt-Scale Infrastructure for AI
events.description: The explosive scale of generative AI models demands highly specialized infrastructure. This panel explores the critical challenges of building and scaling dedicated AI clusters tailored specifically to the modern model lifecycle: massive-scale pre-training, nuanced post-training, and high-throughput, capacity-demanding inference. As models scale to trillions of parameters, infrastructure must deliver unprecedented compute density, ultra-low latency interconnects, data processing, reliability requirements, parallelisms, and continuous I/O throughput. Our panelists will dissect the unique hardware and software bottlenecks inherent to each phase. We will debate the most effective strategies for mitigating hardware failures at scale, optimizing distributed storage pipelines, and tackling power constraints. This interactive 90-minute session will equip attendees with actionable insights into architecting the resilient, high-performance systems required to power the next generation of generative AI breakthroughs.

events.title: Building Gigawatt-Scale Infrastructure for AI
Beyond QPU Access: Lessons From Neutral-Atom Applications and HPC Deployments
events.description: Integrating QPUs into HPC requires more than making hardware accessible. It requires application-led co-design spanning scientific workloads, quantum and classical computation, and facility operations. This talk distills lessons from Pasqal’s development and deployment of neutral-atom QPUs in HPC environments. We examine how applications determine useful hardware capabilities, why classical computation remains essential for validation and orchestration, and what resource management must provide for shared QPU access. Two experiments ground the discussion: a 256-qubit simulation of TmMgGaO4, a frustrated magnetic material, validated against measurements of the material together with the MagLab at Los Alamos National Laboratory and classical calculations, and an end-to-end differential-equation solver implemented with logical qubits. Attendees will gain a framework for evaluating QPUs as HPC accelerators based on scientific validity, application-level performance, and operational usability.

events.title: Quantum Computing and Beyond Moore
HPC Power and Cooling
New Concept Liquid Cooling for Networking and Computing
events.description: As AI and HPC systems push optical bandwidth and silicon power density toward physical limits, liquid cooling is becoming part of the compute and optical platform itself — and heat removal, not transistors, increasingly sets deployable density. This talk presents two complementary "new concept" cooling architectures. The first is a decoupled architecture for high-density optics (1.6T OSFP and near-package optics), which keeps fluid distribution stable while letting each local thermal interface adapt independently, controlling contact pressure, Z-tolerance, warpage, and serviceability as optics move toward the switch ASIC. The second is a first-principles "point–body–point" framework that co-designs chip-level exchange (thin thermal boundary layers) with system-level transport (hierarchical branching at least pumping work). Validated on the largest AI wafer in production (17.6 kW), it cuts thermal resistance 55% and pressure drop 67%, meets the ASHRAE flow guideline, and scales to 250 W/cm². Together they offer practical design rules for cooling next-generation networks and accelerators.

events.title: Test of Time Award Presentation
Twenty Years of Sparsity on GPUs
events.description: The first CUDA-capable GPU was launched 20 years ago, and a sparse matrix-vector product (SpMV) kernel was one of the first CUDA kernels I attempted to write. The SIMT execution model of the GPU made it relatively easy to build a working implementation, but the simplest kernels suffered from several performance pitfalls. A couple of years later, Nathan Bell and I set out to design kernels that would deliver truly high throughput and utilize significant fractions of the high bandwidth that GPUs provide. The paper we published in SC09 demonstrated that this was indeed possible. It also highlighted two key ideas: selecting the right data structure that exploits known matrix structure makes high performance straightforward, and irregularity is easily managed if it is rare. Since that time, a great deal of work has been done for both sparse computations and linear algebra on the GPU. In this talk, I will look back at the lessons of our early work, some notable steps on the path since that time, and consider some of the challenges ahead of us.

events.title: DOE Genesis Mission
BlockMGARD: Accelerating Adaptive Scientific Data Reduction with Region-of-Interest Error Control on GPUs
events.description: The growing scale of scientific data makes lossy compression essential for reducing data volume under controllable error. Transformation-based compressors using multilevel decomposition, such as MGARD, achieve strong compression ratios but map poorly to GPU architectures. We propose BlockMGARD, an adaptive, region-of-interest (ROI)-supported GPU lossy compressor, with four contributions: (1) an In-cache Block decomposition leveraging GPU on-chip memory and constant lookup tables to accelerate decomposition; (2) a hybrid hierarchy combining In-cache Block and global decomposition to balance speed and compression ratio; (3) an end-to-end pipeline with fine-grained ROI error control for feature preservation; and (4) an evaluation against state-of-the-art methods on five real-world datasets. Compared to MGARD-X, BlockMGARD achieves up to 4.2x and 9.1x higher compression and decompression throughput, and up to 8.63x higher compression ratio than uniform-tolerance baselines under ROI-aware error control. Across four GPUs, BlockMGARD achieves near-ideal linear scaling and up to 1.58× I/O cost reduction over MGARD-X.

events.title: Tackling Parallelization Challenges of Randomized Preconditioners with Dependency Tracking
events.description: Incomplete Cholesky (IC) is a common memory-efficient preconditioner for large graph Laplacian systems, but classical IC can break down on irregular graphs. Approximate Cholesky (AC) addresses this with randomized dropping that is provably breakdown-free. Its stochastic fill-in pattern, however, resists static parallelization, creating a "setup bottleneck." We present ParAC, which parallelizes the AC sampling rule of Gao, Kyng, and Spielman using dynamic dependency tracking and architecture-aware memory management to execute it efficiently on CPUs and GPUs while preserving its numerical updates. Total time-to-solution speedups over deterministic IC reach 57.3× on CPU and 52.2× on GPU. Algebraic multigrid (AMG) generally remains preferable on structured PDE discretizations. On the irregular graph Laplacians tested, ParAC is up to 7.2× faster than AMG on CPUs and 6.0× faster on GPUs. On 200 heterogeneous SDDM systems, ParAC converges on every instance, whereas the AMG solvers fail on 15 and 19, on CPU and GPU, respectively.

events.title: LRCCL: Rethinking Collective Communication for Long-Haul RDMA Networks
events.description:
Long-haul RDMA links operate at millisecond-scale round-trip times that break the assumptions baked into collective communication stacks designed for microsecond-scale-datacenter networks. We rethink the collective communication stack for this regime and present LRCCL, a long-haul-RDMA-based collective communication library co-designed across three layers.

First, through the first systematic characterization of collective communication on the real-world ESnet long-haul RDMA, we identify three dimensions that govern collective performance: inter-node round count, per-round data scaling, and inter-rank timing skew induced by mixed intra/inter-node work. Second, we propose a split-plane transport design specifically for long-haul RDMA, with a software reliability combining automatic repeat request and forward error correction. Third, we identify long-haul-friendly collective algorithms guided by the three dimensions. On a real ESnet long-haul testbed, LRCCL achieves 4.2x-22.6x speedup over MPICH+UCX's default RC transport under the same collective algorithm and 2.0x-3.4x end-to-end speedup on NPB and LLM workloads, including under injected moderate and burst loss.

events.title: Fluid-Structure Interaction Simulation of Nuclear Reactors with Ultra-Large-Scale Meshes on GPU Clusters
events.description: To overcome mapping bottlenecks and resource underutilization in large-scale nuclear reactor fluid-structure interaction simulations on heterogeneous supercomputers, we propose a GPU-accelerated framework. A matrix-free treecode (MFTC)-RBF strategy is designed to address mapping bottlenecks. It mitigates network latency and synchronization overhead caused by cross-node irregular communication via asynchronous computation-communication overlap. Furthermore, it resolves GPU instruction pipeline stalls induced by transcendental functions using a spatially-decoupled mixed-precision scheme combined with Horner polynomial approximation. To maximize intra-SM resource utilization and throughput, a dual-pipeline asynchronous scheduling (DAS) strategy is adopted to concurrently execute compute-bound and memory-bound tasks on Tensor and CUDA Cores. Evaluations show that MFTC-RBF delivers a 7.08x mapping speedup with scalability across 32,768 GPUs, while DAS hides approximately one-third of DGeMM latency. MFTC-RBF supports state-of-the-art mesh mapping with over 40-billion mesh points. End-to-end benchmarks further demonstrate a ~70% reduction in total runtime. Simulation results closely align with reference data in lead-cooled reactor benchmarks.

events.title: Global Attention with Linear Complexity for Exascale Generative Data Assimilation in Earth System Prediction
formats: ACM Gordon Bell Climate Modeling Finalist
events.description: Accurate Earth system prediction requires state inference from incomplete observations, but conventional two-stage data assimilation (DA) is computationally prohibitive because repeated PDE-based ensemble forecasts, observation updates, and intermediate data movement limit ensemble size at high resolution. We introduce STORM, a one-stage generative AI framework that reformulates DA as diffusion-based posterior sampling, replacing PDE forecasts with scalable AI inference. It combines a spatiotemporal transformer with a global-attention algorithm that reduces complexity from quadratic to linear through scalable gradient propagation, enabling high-resolution, long-context Earth modeling. STORM scales to 74,400 GPUs on Frontier with 96%–99% strong-scaling efficiency and up to 6 ExaFLOPs sustained BF16 throughput, while enabling 32,768-member ensembles for uncertainty quantification in 34 seconds on 4,096 GPUs. It scales to 20 billion spatiotemporal tokens and 177,000 temporal frames. Hurricane tracking and long-term climate reanalysis demonstrate improved accuracy, including benefits from longer temporal context and recovery of temperature extremes missed by forecast-only predictions.

events.title: Science-Aware Network Operations for Research Networks (SciNet)
events.description:
The emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed.
Research networks, however, remain passive communication infrastructures that optimize packet delivery while being agnostic to the scientific workflows they support, a disconnect that creates bottlenecks in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making.
This paper presents Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a networking paradigm in which artificial intelligence (AI) embedded in the network control plane continuously observes scientific workflows, predicts future network demands, reasons about workflow dependencies, and autonomously adapts network behavior.
Unlike conventional AIOps systems that optimize utilization or reliability, SciNet optimizes for scientific productivity through workflow-aware routing, predictive resource allocation, and autonomous failure mitigation.
We describe the SciNet layered architecture and its optimization objective, characterize the network requirements of Department of Energy (DOE) science workflows through stakeholder interviews, distill these requirements into six recurring use cases with associated quality-of-service classes, and outline ongoing research directions under the Genesis Mission toward AI-driven autonomous laboratories.

events.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: John Towns
events.description: John Towns is the Deputy Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. He leads the NSF-funded ACCESS Coordination Office, as part of the overall ACCESS Program supporting researchers and educators nation-wide in the use of advanced computing systems, and plays key roles in the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot as co-Chair of the Allocations Working Group and Chair of the Coordination Team. He also serves as executive sponsor of NCSA’s Quantum Program Office, a partnership with the Illinois Quantum Information Science and Technology Center (IQUIST), to advance quantum research. With over 35 years of experience, Towns has held leadership roles in numerous national and international initiatives supporting advanced research computing. He holds M.S. degrees in Physics and Astronomy from the University of Illinois and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Missouri-Rolla.

events.title: Programming a Trapped-Ion QPU as a Heterogeneous Accelerator: CUDA-Q, QIR, and a GPU-Coupled Hybrid Workflow Platform for Helios
events.description: High-fidelity, error-corrected quantum processors are now commercially available, raising a practical question for HPC and AI teams: How do you schedule a QPU as just another heterogeneous accelerator next to your GPU pools? This talk is a hands-on account of integrating a trapped-ion processor — Quantinuum's Helios, with 48 error-corrected logical qubits and GPUs coupled into its control system — into a GPU-centric cloud environment, programming it through NVIDIA's CUDA-Q. We show how CUDA-Q kernels and QIR let one codebase target both the Helios emulator and physical hardware, and we demonstrate a browser-based research platform we built that combines GPU-accelerated simulation, an AI coding assistant, and one-click submission to either a simulator or physical Helios. Using GenQAI, quantum chemistry, and optimization workflows, attendees leave with a concrete model for evaluating hybrid quantum-classical integration — and an honest account of today's logical-qubit and wall-clock limits.

events.title: Power and Cooling Convergence: Enabling Reliable and Scalable AI Infrastructure
events.description:
AI workloads are transforming data center and HPC infrastructure, driving higher rack densities, increasing thermal loads, and placing greater demands on uptime, scalability, and energy efficiency.

This session explores how power distribution and liquid cooling are becoming increasingly interconnected across computing, infrastructure, and optical applications. It highlights four key challenges shaping next-generation AI environments: high density, service continuity, modularity, and sustainability.

Through real-world examples and industry trends, attendees will gain insights into how electrical and fluid connectivity technologies work together to support reliable, scalable, and energy-efficient infrastructures. The presentation also examines the role of open standards and industry collaboration, including initiatives such as OCP, in enabling future-ready architectures for AI and high performance computing.

events.title: SD3: The First Operationally-Proven, Fully Heterogeneous-Accelerated Global Kilometer-Scale Model with Inline Physics Architecture
formats: ACM Gordon Bell Climate Modeling Finalist
events.description: We present Super Dynamics on the Cube (SD3), the first operationally-proven, fully heterogeneous-accelerated global kilometer-scale model. Through a full-stack reconstruction in native CUDA C, SD3 introduces an "inline physics" architecture that deeply couples its non-hydrostatic cubed-sphere dynamical core with fast physical processes. This design maintains high physical consistency, ensures energy and mass conservation, and mitigates "grey zone" mismatches. Five years of continuous operational forecasting, together with validation against diverse observations, demonstrates the scientific fidelity of SD3. Recently, SD3 achieved an unprecedented 205.7 simulated days per day at global 1.5 km resolution using 24,576 GPUs. SD3 establishes a hardware-agnostic, portable, and reproducible paradigm across diverse exascale ecosystems. Beyond weather and climate research, SD3 offers a transformative paradigm for the HPC community and the next-generation Digital Twin Earth to establish a robust, high-performance blueprint for the future of Earth system modeling.

events.title: TOPIQ: Statistical Error Propagation for Quantity-of-Interest Prediction Under Lossy Compression
events.description: Lossy compression is essential for managing massive scientific data, but per-element error bounds do not translate into bounds on downstream quantities of interest (QoIs) such as regional averages, neural network predictions, or multi-field derived quantities. We present TOPIQ, a statistical error-propagation framework that predicts QoI-level bias and uncertainty from compact compression metadata (less than 0.1% of original data). TOPIQ decomposes QoIs into primitive operators with closed-form propagation rules accounting for spatial error correlation and data-error coupling; new QoIs are supported by composition at runtime with no per-QoI derivation or retraining. Across 552 evaluations spanning four datasets, three compressors, four QoI families, and eight error bounds, 93.1% of configurations achieve well-calibrated predictions. Pre-computed metadata enables post-hoc uncertainty quantification for arbitrary query regions at 56x-402x speedup over direct computation. A case study demonstrates integration into an AI-driven analysis pipeline with end-to-end confidence intervals for dynamically composed queries.

events.title: ReLATE: Accelerating Tensor Decomposition via Safe and Efficient Learning of Sparse Encodings
events.description: Tensor decomposition (TD) is essential for analyzing high-dimensional sparse data, yet its irregular computations and memory-access patterns pose major performance challenges on modern parallel processors. Prior works rely on expert-designed sparse tensor formats that fail to adapt to irregular tensor shapes and data distributions. We present the reinforcement-learned adaptive tensor encoding (ReLATE) framework, a learning-augmented method that discovers safe and efficient sparse encodings, without labeled examples, via a hybrid model-free and model-based algorithm that learns from both real and imagined actions. Moreover, ReLATE introduces elastic training, rule-driven action masking, and dynamics-informed action filtering to ensure correct encoding with bounded execution time, even during early learning. After offline training, with geometric-mean overhead of only 5.82% relative to TD workflow time, ReLATE deploys the best encoding with zero inference overhead. Across diverse real-world sparse tensors, ReLATE consistently outperforms the best expert-designed format by up to 2×, with a geometric-mean speedup of 1.38×–1.41×.

events.title: Provisioning Networks for AI Supercomputers: A Trace-Driven Study of Performance Sensitivity at Unprecedented Scale
events.description: AI workloads on supercomputers make interconnect performance a primary design constraint. Hardware specifications and microbenchmarks alone do not show how real workloads respond to latency, bandwidth, and jitter. We present a trace-driven study of network sensitivity for training and inference workloads at scales up to 4,096 GPUs. Our methodology combines signature-based trace decomposition with linear programming to make broad network-parameter sweeps feasible. It preserves the recorded NCCL schedules and program dependencies, and estimates a lower bound on runtime under the LogGP model. We validate the compositional analysis against monolithic linear programs, LogGOPSim, and hardware measurements at feasible scales. The resulting latency-bandwidth envelopes identify low-sensitivity regions and performance cliffs that vary substantially across workloads. They also show when bandwidth upgrades provide meaningful returns and when additional network performance has little effect. These results translate execution traces into practical guidance for evaluating network configurations while making the model assumptions explicit.

events.title: A Hardware Abstraction for Exascale Lattice Boltzmann Simulations: Rotor-Resolved Wind Farms on Aurora and LUMI
events.description: Developing performance-portable lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) codes for heterogeneous hardware without extensive hardware-specific duplication is challenging. We introduce a unified hardware abstraction within the open-source OpenLB framework. By expressing models against abstract cell-level concepts, this design enables compile-time binding to platform-specific data structures and common subexpression elimination across composed operators, yielding up to 2.5-fold speedups over an unoptimized baseline. We validate this approach using a rotor-resolved, wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES) of a 32-turbine wind farm, combining LBM with Brinkman penalization, moving walls and atmospheric boundary layer inflow. This complex fluid-structure interaction executes across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs from a single-source implementation without hardware-specific modifications. At extreme scale, we execute the simulation on up to 2,048 Aurora nodes, achieving 86% weak scaling efficiency against a single node. Resolving 5.9 trillion cells at 51 trillion cell updates per second, this is the largest GPU-accelerated LBM simulation reported to date.

events.title: LLM-Driven Root Cause Analysis of BGP and BFD Flap Events
Accelerating CAE Simulations via Analog Laser-Based Computing
events.description:
Predicting corrosion is critical for vehicle and aircraft design, yet numerical simulations of its complex chemical physics require prohibitive computational budgets. Bounded by billions of degrees of freedom, these partial differential equation (PDE) workloads remain unrealistic for effective design space exploration on classical hardware.

To overcome these traditional memory bottlenecks, we present a practical case study featuring joint work by Boeing and LightSolver. We introduce an analog optical approach that embeds PDEs directly onto the governing physical dynamics of a laser system, which naturally converges to the solution. LightSolver’s laser-based processor serves as a linear solver within Boeing's simulation workflow. We present benchmarks comparing this architecture against modern HPC methods, specifically the COMSOL platform utilizing the PARDISO solver. The results validate that this analog architecture delivers highly accurate solutions with superior performance and energy efficiency, enabling viable corrosion-resistant design space exploration.

events.title: Dynamic Thermal Control: The Next Critical Layer in AI Infrastructure
events.description:
This session explores how dynamic thermal control is emerging as a critical enabling technology for next-generation AI infrastructure. Attendees will learn why thermal management can no longer be viewed solely as a static facility-level service, but instead as an active, software-defined control layer that operates in concert with compute, networking, workload orchestration, and infrastructure management platforms. By integrating thermal intelligence directly into the AI stack, organizations can move from reactive cooling strategies to predictive thermal and workload optimization, unlocking gains in compute, token generation and energy efficiencies.

The discussion will also explore how thermal telemetry can be integrated into data center orchestration frameworks through standards-based interfaces, enabling workload-aware scheduling and thermal-aware resource allocation. When deployed across a facility, these capabilities form the foundation of a predictive thermal fabric that allows operators to optimize workload placement, manage thermal headroom more effectively, and balance performance, energy consumption, and asset utilization at scale.

events.title: ORBIT: An AI-Powered Assistant for NOC Operations in a Data-Intensive Science Network
events.description: ESnet shares its pragmatic journey developing AI tools that deliver measurable improvements to Network Operations Center efficiency. Rather than chasing trends, ESnet focused on AI-assisted ticket resolution. This presentation details two concrete applications — Intelligent Resolution Guidance that proactively surfaces relevant documentation, and Adaptive Incident Summarization that generates audience-tailored ticket summaries. Through systematic stakeholder engagement and incremental development, ESnet demonstrates how responsible AI implementation can genuinely augment operational capabilities. Attendees will gain practical insights on balancing AI capabilities with limitations, ensuring tools address real workflow pain points while integrating seamlessly into existing processes, and learn from both successes and challenges encountered.

events.title: From Error-Bounded to Fixed-Ratio: Efficient Sampling-Guided GPU Lossy Compression
events.description: Modern high performance computing (HPC) applications generate massive datasets, creating memory pressure and costly data movement that hinder scientific discovery and AI innovation. GPU lossy compression reduces data volume, but existing approaches face limitations. Error-bounded compression provides strict quality guarantees but produces unpredictable compressed sizes, complicating memory provisioning and system integration. Fixed-ratio compression ensures predictable memory requirements but lacks explicit error control, potentially compromising data fidelity. We introduce MILIO, a GPU lossy compression framework that combines fixed-ratio control with error-bounded compression. Built on dimension-aware sampling, fine-grained ratio profiling, and multi-stream global synchronization, MILIO achieves user-specified compression ratios with high throughput while supporting error control. Across nine real-world scientific datasets, MILIO achieves a compression throughput of 257.1 GB/s on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, delivering 3.25× the throughput of cuZFP at comparable compression ratios. It integrates seamlessly with scientific and AI workloads and demonstrates near-optimal scalability across multiple GPUs.

events.title: FastMPK: Unleashing Cache Reuse for Sparse Matrix Power Kernels on Many-Core Architectures
events.description:
Many applications rely on the sparse matrix power kernel (MPK), which evaluates a short sequence of sparse matrix-vector multiplications (SpMVs) with the same matrix. MPK is therefore dominated by the memory traffic of repeatedly streaming the sparse matrix, and cache reuse across successive SpMVs offers a major opportunity to reduce data movement. However, exploiting such reuse introduces inter-SpMV dependencies that can severely restrict parallelism and induce frequent global synchronization, especially on GPUs.

This paper presents FastMPK, a cache-aware MPK designed to run efficiently on both CPUs and GPUs. FastMPK models the matrix as a dependency graph, recursively partitions it into cache-resident subgraphs, and constructs a separator subgraph to decouple cross-subgraph dependencies and recover parallel work. A dependency-preserving runtime schedule maximizes immediate cache reuse while a multi-granularity parallelization strategy enables scalability on many-core processors. Evaluated on diverse architectures, FastMPK delivers average speedups of up to 1.84× over state-of-the-art implementations.

events.title: Faithful Prediction of the Performance of rocHPL Despite Hardware and Software Complexity
events.description: High Performance LINPACK (HPL) remains the primary benchmark for ranking supercomputers and often serves as a dimensioning design component for system constructors. Its performance depends on a wide variety of parameters and remains difficult to predict on large, modern, heterogeneous clusters. Using stochastic performance models of computational kernels and the network simulation capabilities of SimGrid, a simulation framework for parallel application performance prediction, we design a lightweight simulator of the implementation of HPL on AMD GPUs (rocHPL). Taking advantage of the structure of HPL, we reduce the simulation complexity by several orders of magnitude. We evaluate the predictive capability of our approach across four distinct accelerated platforms comprising up to 1,024 GPUs, two software releases, and a wide range of parameters, and demonstrate its accuracy (simulated and real executions differ by 4% on average), flexibility, and scalability (at this scale, simulations take less than an hour on a laptop).

events.title: TokaGLINT: A Scalable GPU-Tailored Implicit Solver for Full 3D Tokamak Electromagnetic Simulations
events.description: We introduce TokaGLINT, a GPU-accelerated implicit solver for electromagnetic field computations in full 3D tokamak simulations, aimed at efficient large-scale parallel GPU computing. Its central innovation lies in the co-design of hierarchical domain decomposition and a fast exact local solver, where hierarchical partitioning is tailored to match fine-grained intra-card subdomains and exploit the tensor-based solver dedicated to curvilinear-coordinate symplectic CN-FDTD-discretized 3D Maxwell equations. Backed by automated operator fusion and batching customized for the intra-card multi-subdomain structure, the solver decouples unknowns through discrete transformations and leverages tensor-structured computations to achieve high hardware utilization, while preserving the long-time stability characteristic of symplectic discretizations. TokaGLINT scales the electromagnetic field solve beyond 10,000 GPUs, achieving 90.1% weak and 53.9% strong scaling efficiency, while delivering a 2.67x single-node speedup over an unpreconditioned BiCGStab baseline (HIP-enabled HYPRE). It is validated in EAST tokamak simulations within the SymPIC plasma simulation code, enabling high-fidelity long-duration modeling.
