events.title: National Data Platform, National Research Platform and Open Science Data Federation: How They Collectively Enable Data-Intensive Science
events.description: Our work examines VFL through the lens of policy-aware execution across distributed infrastructure. We present communication-efficient VFL methods and evaluate their trade-offs among execution time, computational cost, model utility, and privacy considerations. This work fits well the SCinet Research Exposition because it demonstrates how advanced networking and geographically distributed research infrastructure influence the practical deployment of privacy-preserving AI workflows. Rather than simulating a distributed deployment, we execute VFL workflows on FABRIC, including the CIENA node, in an environment representative of the infrastructure that SC attendees develop and operate. Our findings support the adoption of policy-aware collaborative machine learning by identifying effective execution strategies for distributed scientific settings.

Using your registration details, we’ll generate a one-of-a-kind fractal image just for you — sent to you and showcased on displays throughout the conference. You’ll also appear on the HPC Around the World map, celebrating the global reach of high performance computing. Be sure to come back each day to generate a new image.

events.title: Wheelchairs and Scooters
2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
events.description: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

events.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
events.description:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman
Music Composition and Performance: Stephan Vankov

Produced at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, UIC, and Calit2, UCSD

events.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
events.description:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

events.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
events.description:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.

events.title: Art of HPC Exhibition
events.description:
Art of HPC

Where Creativity Meets HPC

Creativity has always been at the heart of innovation. It drives new perspectives, fuels artistic expression, and allows us to see beauty in unexpected places. By leveraging cutting-edge technology and resources, we can push the boundaries of both science and art. SC proudly presents Art of HPC, a showcase of the intersection between artistic creativity and high performance computing.

events.title: Biological Interfaces
events.description:
Water at biological interfaces contributes substantially to the mechanical behavior of membranes, yet how it responds to mechanical stress is not well characterized. This artwork was developed from molecular simulations, which examined how lateral tension influences interfacial water in lipid model membranes representative of mammalian and bacterial composition under physiological conditions.

In the resting state, interfacial water organizes into hydrogen-bonded networks, with small ring-like arrangements linking adjacent lipid. In the video, these ring-like arrangements are highlighted by the glowing planes between golden spheres. When lateral stress is applied, these arrangements persist in one mammalian membrane type, while in the other, stress-induced flattening of the membrane surface causes interfacial water to become partially decoupled from the lipid interface. This differential behavior points to a close relationship between a membrane's mechanical properties and the structural organization of its associated water network, offering insight into the mechanisms by which interfacial water contributes to membrane resilience under mechanical load. Whilst the video is mostly for aesthetical purposes, the findings of the molecular simulations suggest that interfacial water is not merely a passive boundary layer but an active participant in membrane stability that responds dynamically to stress, with implications extending across biophysics, drug design, and the study of biological adaptation.

events.title: Boiling the Ocean ... Literally
events.description:
The video shows monthly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the North Atlantic since 1980. The colors represent warming and cooling up to 2026 compared to the monthly averages from 1980 to 1995. The visualization highlights the rapid speed at which our oceans have been warming in a period of just over 45 years.

The video was made as realistic as possible with satellite imagery, realistic atmosphere thickness and density, a topography map and the use of ray-traced renders to present the data as realistically and prominently as possible.

events.title: Colourful Wind Assistance
events.description:
The video shows the flow past two wing sails arranged in tandem, representative of wind-assisted propulsion devices. The simulation was performed with x3d2, a high-order finite-difference incompressible-flow solver developed within the Xcompact3d framework (https://www.incompact3d.com). The simulation uses the immersed-boundary method to represent the foil geometry, together with non-periodic streamwise inflow/outflow boundary conditions and periodic transverse boundaries.

The calculation uses a uniform Cartesian mesh of approximately 381 million grid points. Based on the wing-sail chord and imposed inflow velocity, the Reynolds number is approximately 28,000. The case is an illustrative demonstration of the numerical methodology rather than a full-scale wing-sail prediction. Simulations were run in double precision on an NVIDIA Grace Hopper GH200 GPU using x3d2’s CUDA backend.

events.title: Entropy on the Edge of Collapse
events.description: This is a dynamical rendering of a detailed three-dimensional simulation of the explosion of the very-rapidly rotating core of a massive star that is exploding as a supernova. Rapid rotation leads to a powerful jet-like explosion along the two poles, accompanied by the generation and tangling of strong magnetic fields. This movie depicts the earliest phases of the supernova explosion that is simultaneously giving birth to a rapidly rotating radio pulsar.

events.title: Fatal Attraction
events.description:
Supermassive black holes are among the largest objects in the Universe. Their masses range from at least one hundred thousand to many billions of times that of our Sun. In a tidal disruption event, a star is captured by the black hole’s gravitational field.

This artwork illustrates the different phases of destruction of a star by the tidal field of a supermassive black hole.

The right panel combines multiple instants of times highlighting the enormous stretch incurred by the star as it is pulled back toward the black hole.

The left panel shows the star after its first orbit around the black hole. The star is then subsequently destroyed when colliding with its own accretion stream.

events.title: Flow Through a Pebble-Bed Reactor in NekRS
events.description: The pb146 case in NekRS is a benchmark computational fluid dynamics problem that simulates flow through a packed bed of 146 spherical particles, representing a simplified pebble-bed reactor geometry. It features a densely packed arrangement of spheres inside a cylindrical domain, producing complex flow behavior with tight gaps, recirculation zones, and turbulent interactions that are challenging to resolve numerically. Using NekRS’s high-order spectral element method, the case captures detailed boundary-layer physics and serves as a realistic yet standardized workload, making it widely used for testing solver accuracy, scalability, and performance on GPU-based high performance computing systems.

events.title: Fulfillment: Artistic Encounters with the Hidden Labor and Environmental Footprint of High Performance Computing
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) has become one of the defining infrastructures of contemporary society. Beyond enabling scientific discovery, HPC increasingly powers artificial intelligence, climate modeling, logistics, digital commerce, autonomous systems, and large-scale simulation. Despite its transformative role, HPC largely remains invisible to the public, obscuring the vast networks of human labor, material extraction, energy consumption, and environmental impact required to sustain computational infrastructures.

This project argues that artistic practice can make HPC visible, not only by visualizing scientific data, but by revealing the social, ecological, and political systems in which computational infrastructures are embedded. Rather than treating HPC solely as a technological achievement, the work positions it as part of a cultural-material landscape whose hidden operations shape everyday life.

Fulfillment is an interdisciplinary virtual reality artwork developed at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL), University of Illinois Chicago, in collaboration with anthropologists, designers, and computer scientists from several research institutions spanning the U.S., Europe, and Asia with support from the National Science Foundation. This proposal is for a public exhibition of the Fulfillment project as part of the Art Gallery Program at the SC26 conference. While the original work investigates global logistics and supply chain capitalism, this exhibition reframes those systems through the computational infrastructures that increasingly govern them. Warehouses, AI-driven optimization, cloud computing, data centers, predictive algorithms, and real-time simulation are presented as interconnected expressions of contemporary HPC ecosystems.

events.title: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night
events.description: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night (IOAN) is a multi-player VR experience that brings the rhythms of the cosmos to life in an endless remix instrument. Created from 758,457,209 magnitude readings for 817‚373 astronomical objects captured by the AST3 robotic telescopes in Antarctica, the experience transports players inside of a field of objects at the heart of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Within a multiplayer VR arena, and floating inside a luminous field between the Earth and the Large Magellanic Cloud, multiple players explore and collaboratively create new visual and sound remixes to perform the AST3 dataset as a soundscape for external visitors to the VR arena. The collaborative experience is inspired by communal percussion and multiplayer instruments. Real-time database queries, selections, and filtering operations enable multiple players in VR to collaboratively interact with the objects in the field to create data remixes from astronomical data. Visitors to the arena see and hear the virtual world in correct spatial relation to their real-world positions through spatialized 4K portals and spatialized ambisonic audio that align the physical space of the arena installation with the inner space of the multiplayer virtual environment.

events.title: JASMIN in July (Per Day): Brownian Bouquet
events.description:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Brownian Bouquet, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one day in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Stochastic Sea (which instead plots one spindle for one hour), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case a bouquet of flowers. The flower-like nature is encouraged by coercing the spindle centers into a sunflower-inspired pattern.

Brownian Bouquet invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

events.title: JASMIN in July (Per Hour): Stochastic Sea
events.description:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Stochastic Sea, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one hour in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Brownian Bouquet (which instead plots one spindle for one day), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case suggestive of a filamentary superstructure such as galactic super-clusters or a network of synapses. The spindle centers are randomly distributed across the composition, reinforcing this impression of a complex, interconnected structure.

Stochastic Sea invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

events.title: Ligand Dynamics Control Structure, Elasticity, and High-Pressure Behavior of Nanoparticle Superlattices
events.description: The spherical clusters in this image are a molecular dynamics simulation of lead sulfide nanocrystals, each seven nanometers wide, coated with radiating oleic acid ligands that allow such particles to self-assemble into an ordered crystal called a nanoparticle superlattice. The underlying research found that below a critical ligand coverage density, nanoparticles collapse and fuse together, while above it, the ligand layer cushions the structure enough to withstand applied pressures up to nearly 56 gigapascals while largely retaining its ordered arrangement. The image renders this simulated nanoscale structure alongside additional micrographs of nanoparticle superlattice material from the same body of research.

events.title: Morphogenesis
events.description:
Long before computers, Alan Turing asked how a smooth egg becomes a spotted, striped, branching creature. His answer, reaction-diffusion, is the chemistry of pattern itself. Here that chemistry runs as living paint: two competing substances diffuse and react across a field, blooming into coral, fingerprints, dividing cells, and restless worms, cycling endlessly through nature's vocabulary of form.

But look closely, and the field is split into three vertical territories, each a separate GPU. The luminous seams between them are the secret of large-scale simulation: the halo exchange, where neighboring processors trade their edge values every timestep so the pattern can flow seamlessly across boundaries. Gold packets pulse along the seams and communication is made visible.

This is how we simulate weather, galaxies, and combustion: cut reality into pieces, solve each in parallel, and stitch the edges back together. The pattern is the phenomenon; the seams are the high performance computing. Turing's morphogenesis is computed the way modern science actually computes it.

events.title: Oil on Canvas: Galactic Center on Palette
events.description:
My painting (Oil on Canvas) translates a radio-astronomy observation of our galaxy's heart into a dusky, nebular atmosphere, its aubergine and violet field that surrounds the Milky Way's core.

The source of my interpretation of the galactic center stemmed from discussions with Prof. Florina Ciorba from the University of Basel (UniBas), Switzerland, who is the co-founder member and PI of the UniBas node of the SKACH project — The SKA (Square Kilometre Array) of Switzerland Consortium (SKACH, https://skach.org/about-skach/). The underlying data comes from the 1.28 GHz MeerKAT galactic center mosaic created by Heywood et al. (2022), released by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO). The image that inspired me and my painting is a re-rendered version by J.C. Muñoz-Mateos and branded by SKACH (the Swiss SKA Consortium) and SKAO (the Square Kilometre Array Observatory).

https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/milky-way-center-meerkat-and-webb/

events.title: One-Sided: A Portrait of the New OpenSHMEM Standard
events.description:
In MPI, every memory transfer requires negotiation. The sender announces. The receiver posts a matching receive. Both wait. This is the contract at the heart of parallel communication — and this visualization begins there, in the weight of it: 256 processing elements, bilateral arcs crossing in every direction, a single REQUEST suspended at its target with no response coming.

Then the model changes.

OpenSHMEM eliminates the contract. Any process can write directly into any other's memory. No handshake. No prior agreement. The target is simply — a destination.

This 90-second visualization is a portrait of that principle, built entirely from real benchmark data captured on an HPE internal research cluster: four nodes, 256 processing elements, HPE Slingshot fabric.

The visual language is built around directionality. 256 PEs are arranged in four organic galaxy clusters — Realms α, β, γ, δ, 64 PEs each — with arcs cycling through one source cluster at a time so the viewer can track individual operations to their specific destinations, not interpret a global blur. Periodic spotlights isolate single PE-to-PE operations. The contrast with the MPI opening is deliberate and exact.

The data behind the animation is 500,000 real GUPS operations — Giga Updates Per Second, a standard benchmark for irregular remote atomic writes — captured live on the HPE Slingshot fabric. Each arc is a real operation. The pattern it makes is not designed; it is measured.

The closing act shows the full system in motion, with the GUPS source code, an operation counter climbing to 500,000, and the key argument: this workload cannot be handled without a global synchronization barrier in MPI — a cost that scales with every PE added. In OpenSHMEM, it just runs.

events.title: Open Polarity
events.description: This image depicts the 3D structure of the Sun's open coronal magnetic field from a snapshot of the “Live Prediction” HPC simulation developed by Predictive Science Inc. as part of their research for the August 12, 2026, total solar eclipse. See eclipse.predsci.com for more details on the simulation, which was created using the Magnetohydrodynamic Algorithm outside a Sphere Fortran code (github.com/predsci/mas) at a resolution of over 50 million cells. It ran faster than real time using 24 128-core EPYC Turin 9745 CPUs (3,072 total cores) on NASA's Athena supercomputer.

events.title: Portrait of Data Center
events.description:
A supercomputer has vital signs: a temperature, a metabolism, and a heartbeat. This piece paints them. Streaming GPU telemetry (utilization, power draw, temperature, and interconnect traffic) drives a generative flow field: thousands of particles drift and glow, each colored by heat, brightened by power, their speed set by how hard the machine is thinking. Nothing is invented; every gesture is a reading of the machine's own body.

The work is deliberately multi-dimensional. One dimension is data, which is the honest mapping of live signals to light. Another is choreography, drawn from Martha Graham's foundational language of modern dance: contraction and release. Graham built movement from the body's core, a gathering inward that coils tension, then an expansive release outward. Here the machine's heartbeat performs exactly that: on each slow breath the particles are drawn toward the core, gathering; then, on the release, they are expelled outward in a bloom of light and sparks, timed to the pulse. As load climbs from idle to peak, the breath deepens and the release becomes a throw. A supercomputer that is moving through its own register, from rest to full, dramatic exertion.

The third dimension is metaphor: the data center as a living, feeling body, its telemetry the score to which it dances. By borrowing Graham's grammar of gather-and-expel, the piece asks the audience to read a machine not as cold infrastructure but as a performer; one whose choreography is authored not by a human hand but by the physics of computation itself. High performance computing, rendered as contemporary dance.

events.title: Radiation: When Steels Fall Apart
events.description:
This visualization uses a high performance computing-based workflow to reveal the atomic-scale structure of neutron-irradiated steel. Highlighted in the image are nanoscale defects and chemical features that formed or evolved as a result of irradiation.

The specimen examined in this study was prepared from an HT-9 alloy irradiated to 0.68 displacements per atom (dpa) at 478 degrees Celsius in Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor. The visualization combines two correlative datasets collected from the same specimen: a two-dimensional image acquired using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and a three-dimensional dataset acquired using atom probe tomography (APT).

The combined datasets reveal several complex microstructural features associated with radiation damage. These include spherical clusters enriched in nickel and silicon, dislocation lines decorated with solute clusters, and a grain boundary exhibiting radiation-induced solute segregation. The dataset also captures a pre-existing vanadium nitride precipitate. Characterizing these features is important because they can influence the physical and mechanical properties of the alloy.

Using high performance computing and advanced deep-learning methods, this image-based workflow improves feature identification and enables more accurate spatial correlation of the complementary TEM and APT datasets. The multimodal computational model under development uses structural information obtained from TEM to support further analysis of the APT dataset and improve the identification and characterization of solute clusters.

This visualization is composed entirely of experimental data obtained from TEM and APT measurements. Rendering the datasets in this form allows researchers to more effectively interpret correlative measurements, identify and analyze complex radiation-induced features, validate computational methods, and communicate scientific findings.

events.title: Simulation of Tungsten Transport in the ASDEX-U Tokamak Plasma
events.description: Simulation of tungsten transport in the ASDEX-U tokamak plasma reveals critical insights for fusion reactor design. Tungsten, used for its heat resistance, ionizes during operation and can penetrate the core, radiating energy and reducing efficiency. These simulations explore the interaction of tungsten ions with rotation and light impurities like boron and helium in the complex edge region near the wall. The study highlights the role of binary collisions and asymmetries in tungsten penetration. Confidence in the model is bolstered by recent validation on a separate physics problem.

events.title: Spiral Wave: The Heart's Chaotic Dance
events.description:
A spiral of crimson, gold, mocha, and magenta moves through the heart, tracing the electrical activity that coordinates every heartbeat. Here, that rhythm has broken down. The spiral is a rotor, a self-sustaining electrical wave that drives atrial fibrillation, one of the most common and dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

Every frame is generated directly from a high-performance cardiac electrophysiology simulation. The left atrium is modeled as a large network of electrically coupled tissue, simulated in near real time using custom CUDA code running on NVIDIA GPUs. This computational framework allows researchers to investigate how atrial fibrillation begins, evolves, and responds to targeted intervention.

The colors are not arbitrary; they are the language of physiology. Crimson marks tissue at rest, ready to activate. Gold follows the wave of depolarization as it propagates through the muscle. Mocha and magenta represent the refractory period, when the tissue is recovering before it can fire again. In this simulation, the refractory period is shortened, and a precisely timed electrical stimulus initiates the spiral wave.

Spiral Wave lives at the intersection of computation, medicine, and art. Every color, every curve, and every swirl emerges from the underlying physics of cardiac tissue. Nothing in this animation was designed to be beautiful. It simply is.

events.title: The Oracle at DKRZ
events.description:
This video is a visualization of the algorithm used to generate "prophecies" from machine code — that will form part of a sculptural installation to be exhibited at the German Climate Computing Centre (DKRZ).

The work situates climate modeling in the broader, non-scientific history of humanity's attempts to grapple with the future. By reinterpreting the binary of the ICON climate model into words, and searching for where those words combine into statements about the future, ICON is reimagined as a modern-day oracle. The algorithm's lexicon comes from English translations of classical Greek texts. In these fictions, prophecies are true, and are intertwined with the distinct tragedy of not being believed or acted upon — a startling parallel to humanity's lackluster response to the climate crisis.

Inspiration for the project came through conversations with scientists at DKRZ; about the computation and storage of data, as well as the Centre's role in scientific research and weather prediction. On the computational side, the ability to abstract almost anything into a string of zeros and ones highlights a wonderful symmetry: if anything can be binary, then binary can be anything. From this perspective, binary becomes an interface between seemingly disparate media and raises questions about how the systems we use to interpret data give rise to meaning.

The connection to a history of fortune telling was developed through understanding the role DKRZ plays within the scientific landscape. The vast array of resources spent in the construction and maintenance of its supercomputers is a testament to how far humanity will go to fulfill a specific need — to know what the future will be like. From this perspective, it represents an incredibly sophisticated approach to something humans have been doing throughout history and across civilizations. The rulers of city-states in Ancient Greece would climb the steps to the Oracle at Delphi seeking counsel. Now, various clients come to DKRZ, looking to use its computing power for projections on the weather and climate.

events.title: Vortex Bubbles in Anabatic Upslope Flow During Morning Transition
events.description: Sea of bubbling vortices arising in upslope (anabatic) flow at a slope angle of eight degrees after sudden imposition of surface heat flux against a constant ambient stratification. This serves as a simplified model for the morning transition from nighttime downslope (katabatic) drainage to daytime upslope flow occurring during sunrise in valleys or mountains when solar radiation starts to heat up the sloped terrain, reversing the buoyancy and pressure gradients established during the cooler nocturnal conditions. Flow shown here is in an intermediate regime between laminar and fully turbulent.

events.title: Where Data Becomes Light: The Beauty of Scientific Visualization
events.description:
Where Data Becomes Light is a digital light projection and immersive visual experience that celebrates the beauty of science through contemporary visualization. On view nightly, Thursday through Sunday, at THE MART (artonthemart.com) September through mid-November, the large-scale imagery transforms the 2.5-acre building façade into a luminous canvas, where sweeping animations and vivid imagery inspire curiosity and wonder, and invite audiences to witness the elegance and complexity of the natural world through modern scientific computing.

Scientific discovery often begins with numbers, signals, and equations, but its deepest insights emerge when those patterns become visible. Scientific visualization transforms complex data into images that reveal structure, motion, and meaning, allowing us to see phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden. In these images, turbulence becomes choreography, molecular interactions resemble intricate architecture, and the evolution of galaxies unfolds like a vast celestial landscape.

Like Art of HPC, Where Data Becomes Light celebrates creativity and beauty in computational science. The projection includes several works from past SC Art of HPC exhibits and Scientific Visualization and Data Analytics Showcases, bringing the SC community's work to the city's skyline.

The Collaboration

For decades, researchers have used visualization to transform massive datasets into images that reveal patterns hidden in raw numbers. As high-performance computing has grown in prominence to address the biggest challenges in science and engineering, Argonne National Laboratory has played a key role in this evolution, operating world-class supercomputers and producing visualizations that illuminate everything from the structure of materials and the behavior of turbulent flows to the formation of galaxies and the dynamics of climate systems.

At the same time, the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago helped define the modern field of visualization. EVL researchers’ work contributed to the landmark National Science Foundation report on scientific visualization, which helped establish visualization as a critical component of scientific discovery. EVL’s innovations in immersive visualization environments and collaborative visual computing have expanded the ways scientists and the public experience complex data.

events.title: You Only Have Seven Seconds
events.description:
You Only Have Seven Seconds is a poetic, human–AI collaborative documentary that unfolds as both a visual archive of an internationally exhibited installation and a cinematic experiment in memory preservation. Against the backdrop of rising Alzheimer’s cases and the emergence of machine-generated false memories, the film reimagines remembrance through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Inspired by her grandmother’s cognitive decline, the artist developed a custom AI system that transforms fragmented spoken recollections into synthetic visual sequences. Presented as an interactive AI art installation, the project ReCollection has traveled worldwide, welcoming thousands of visitors to whisper their fading memories — each within seven seconds — into the artwork and generate visual memories in real time. These memories form the foundation of an evolving archive, constructed through speech recognition, text auto-completion, and text-to-image generation.

Drawing from this archive, the film incorporates emerging speech-to-video technology to weave a collective, culturally diverse montage of love and loss. The participatory datasets are curated to build dialogical relationships, forming patterns, counterpoints, and resonances that evoke a poetics of relation. Initially conceived as a personal reflection, the work has evolved into a living, breathing, shared world-building experience that reassembles the ephemeral past into a dynamic portrait of collective human selfhood.

Build on the Past … Invent the Future
events.description:
If there is any enduring lesson in computing, it is the constancy of change, some predictable and some deeply disruptive, that repeatedly reshapes the status quo. Today’s computing ecosystem is in extraordinary flux, with profound implications for research and discovery, economic competitiveness, and global security. From the geopolitics of semiconductor foundries and their exponentially rising costs through the rise of cloud hyperscalers and shifting loci of economic leverage to the profound and still uncertain effects of deep learning and AI, the future promises to be different from the past.

Navigating this uncertainty will require new technical approaches and different mindsets. Drawing on five decades of experience across high performance computing, academia, industry, and policy, this talk explores how historical technology shifts can guide our path forward. We will examine how the future is being shaped by technology — semiconductors, AI, biology, mathematics, and software — and driven by politics and economics. Overlaying these technical and economic questions are equally important issues of policy, law, and ethics.

events.title: The Green Iron Age: HPC Sustainability and the AI Energy Frontier
events.description:
More than two decades ago, Dr. Kirk Cameron created the PowerPack framework to measure and manage energy efficiency in servers, supercomputers, and data centers. Since then, energy efficiency has become a key HPC design driver, with 200-fold improvements in supercomputer efficiency (Green500) and 20-fold improvements in server efficiency (SPECpower/Energy Star). At about $1M per megawatt per year, the world’s most powerful supercomputers have historically been limited to power budgets of approximately 20–30 megawatts.

Frontier AI models are driving computing infrastructure from tens of megawatts to gigawatts. The promise of trillions in AI revenue means traditional HPC power limits no longer apply. Reminiscent of the late-20th-century Big Iron Era, a new Green Iron Age has emerged — one in which efficiency enables ever-larger machines, even as total energy consumption rises. This talk explores the challenges and opportunities of this emergent AI Energy Frontier and asks how 25 years of HPC sustainability progress can drive transformative change.

events.title: Exhibitor Lounge
Active Memory Architecture: Beyond the Frontier
events.description:
Almost exactly 30 years ago, Seymour Cray passed away after a tragic traffic accident. He was arguably the father of supercomputing. A month later, the third Beowulf commodity cluster was presented at the Caltech booth at the SC96 conference, the first to demonstrate a sustained 1 Gigaflops sustained performance on a real application at a cost of under $50K. Eight years prior to this, in 1988 in Orlando in a rare event, Seymour Cray gave the keynote address at the first Supercomputing Conference. The moment was electric for an inaugural crowd of over a thousand attendees. It was largely wrong in its many predictions. In fact, Cray never sold another machine up to his death eight years later. Although he did not know it at the time, the field of supercomputing was undergoing a major transformation to massively parallel processing with the Intel Touchstone Delta in 1991.

Now 30 years later, the field of supercomputing is again in a transformative stage with the end of Moore’s Law and the realization of nanoscale implementation technology. After many decades of von Neumann architecture and the von Neumann bottleneck, exponential performance growth no longer applies. Yet hopes for quantum computing are grossly premature and overhyped. A major gap again confronts the field and only a revolution can again launch a new future. This presentation at the SC26 conference in Chicago will present the innovative Active Memory Architecture, which is under development at the Texas Advanced Computing Center. If successful, it will once again transform the field of HPC with drastically reduced scale and cost while transitioning the exascale performance regime towards zettaflops capability. This presentation is given in honor of the memory of Seymour Cray.

events.title: SCC Connect
events.description: SCC Connect is a companion to the Student Cluster Competition (SCC) with a focus on accessibility and education. Using provided, cloud-based hardware, SCC Connect teams build and run benchmarks and a selection of real HPC workloads in a two-day nonstop competition. Teams compete remotely from all around the world, and several teams will attend SC26 and compete from booths in the Exhibit Hall. Come by to meet the teams and cheer them on!

Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Ravi Madduri
events.description: Ravi is a senior computer scientist working in the intersection of HPC/AI and biomedicine. His research interests are in building sustainable, scalable services for science, reproducible research, large-scale data management, analysis using HPC and AI. He leads the PALISADE-X project that is developing Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework to build robust, trust-worthy AI models. He co-leads the MVP-CHAMPION project, which is a collaboration between VA and DOE and develops methods to perform large-scale genetic data analysis using DOE’s high performance computing capabilities, including methods for generating PRS scores in Prostate Cancer, genome-wide PheWAS on Summit supercomputer. Additionally, Ravi served as MPI for an NHGRI R01 on creating a cloud service for large-scale genomics analysis and was one of three key contributors to the National Institutes of Health $100M Cancer Biomedical Informatics Grid (caBIG), which linked 60 NIH-funded cancer centers and clinical sites engaged in cancer research. For his efforts in project management, tool development, and collaboration, Ravi received several Outstanding Achievement Awards from NIH. For his work on “Cancer Moonshot” project, he received the Department of Energy Secretary award in 2017.

events.title: A Cloud Accessible Four-Qubit Electron Spin Quantum Processor in a 300 mm Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Process
events.description:
We present a cloud accessible electron spin qubit quantum processor manufactured using a 300 mm metal-oxide-semiconductor process. Four single-electron spin qubits form a linear array with controllable nearest-neighbor exchange coupling; the unit cell can be tiled without design modification, providing a direct path to larger processors. The system is installed at the UK's National Quantum Computing Centre, where automated calibration maintains operation with minimal human input and users submit circuits through industry-standard frameworks including Qiskit and Cirq. This deployment is a prototype for future HPC integration.

Single-qubit gates are driven by magnetic resonance; two-qubit CPhase gates use electrically modulated exchange coupling. Single-shot readout via a parallel array of charge sensors achieves fidelities above 99% in under 10 µs and supports mid-circuit measurement.

We demonstrate two applications: a variational quantum eigensolver determining the equilibrium bond length of molecular hydrogen, and stabilizer measurements demonstrating the building block of quantum error correction.

events.title: A Distributed Mixed-Precision N-Body Engine: Scaling Behavior and the Precision Limits of a Direct-Summation Kernel
events.description: We report a distributed direct-summation N-body engine used to study two coupled limits: where the single collective per step begins to limit strong scaling, and where reduced-precision arithmetic begins to corrupt the physics. At fixed N = 32768 on one 96-core node, the kernel scales almost ideally to 16 ranks and reaches 57× speedup at 96. In-core phase timers show that the loss beyond 16 ranks comes from one straggling rank, whose peers wait at the collective, rather than from data transfer, which stays under 1% of a step. A precision ladder from FP64 down to FP8 shows that the accumulator, not the individual force terms, sets the error floor: rounding the running sum costs 92×–125× more force error than rounding the terms alone.

events.title: A Fused Computation-Communication Collective for Irregular Distributed-Memory Applications
events.description:
Irregular distributed-memory applications often perform local computation and memory operations around a many-to-many communication exchange. We introduce AllScatterApply (ASAP), a fused collective communication primitive for this pattern. ASAP overlaps local and remote operations at fine granularity, scales to 32,000 CPU cores on NERSC Perlmutter, and delivers up to 74× speedup over point-to-point implementations built on the same one-sided runtime library.

We evaluate ASAP on genomic k-mer counting (KC) and connected components (CC). For KC, ASAP achieves 2×–5× speedup over bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) baselines and matches the performance of a hand-tuned asynchronous algorithm. For CC, ASAP is 1.8× faster than both optimized BSP and asynchronous baselines. By avoiding expensive graph partitioning, ASAP also achieves 8.8× faster end-to-end performance than a dedicated asynchronous graph-processing system.

events.title: A GPU-Friendly SSOR Preconditioner Based on an Approximate Inverse of Triangular Matrices
events.description: We develop a GPU-friendly variant of the symmetric successive over-relaxation (SSOR) preconditioner for efficient execution of the preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) method on GPUs. To avoid the forward and backward substitutions required by the original SSOR preconditioner, which constitute a major bottleneck on GPUs, we incorporate an approximate inverse of a triangular matrix appearing in the SSOR preconditioner, with a dropping strategy to reduce the cost of applying it. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SSOR variant against existing parallel SSOR variants on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. The proposed variant substantially reduces the cost of applying the preconditioner by replacing the forward and backward substitutions with SpMVs, while largely preserving the convergence improvement of SSOR. Consequently, despite the additional cost of constructing the approximate inverse, the total PCG execution time is reduced for most of the test matrices, demonstrating that the proposed approach provides an effective GPU-friendly SSOR variant.

events.title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Framework for Solving Computational Fluid Dynamics and Nuclear Physics Equations Using Quantum Singular Value Decomposition and Transformation
events.description: Quantum computing offers a great promise to significantly reduce the computational cost of solving multidimensional partial differential equations (PDEs). However, existing quantum linear solvers, such as the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) algorithm, exhibit limited scalability, prolonged execution times, and low accuracy. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical framework comprising two quantum PDE solvers based on quantum singular value decomposition (QSVD) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). The proposed methodology is validated on PDEs from computational fluid dynamics and nuclear engineering — potential flow past a 2D cylinder and a Joukowsky airfoil, and the neutron transport equation (NTE) — using noise-free and noisy simulators and hardware emulators from IBM-Quantum. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed methods.

events.title: A Linear-Scaling, Sparse Matrix Electronic Structure Solver on the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
events.description: We present a linear-scaling electronic structure solver for the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), a data-flow architecture integrating more than 900,000 processors on a single silicon wafer. We combine a novel, WSE-optimized sparse-matrix squaring kernel with a sparse, recursive Fermi-operator expansion to construct the density matrix on this massively parallel architecture. Our approach solves the quantum-mechanical eigenvalue problem for one self-consistent-field iteration with a computational complexity that is linear in the number of atoms. For a bulk water system described at the density-functional tight-binding level of theory, we achieve a 31x speedup for a single density-matrix solve relative to a single-GPU reference calculation running on an NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper superchip.

events.title: A Model‑Agnostic Orchestration Engine for Multi‑Stage High-Performance Scientific Workflows
events.description: Scientific workflows increasingly require the integration of independently developed models and heterogeneous data sources. We present a model-agnostic orchestration engine that represents both data sources and simulation models as producers of named variables. Given a requested target, the engine recursively resolves variable dependencies, derives an executable workflow, manages intermediate products through a shared data layer, and dispatches computation through configurable execution backends. We demonstrate the approach using an asteroid-impact wildfire scenario in which a requested fire-spread product automatically resolves the data required to execute WRF-SFIRE on high-performance computing resources. The prototype demonstrates target-driven workflow generation, dependency resolution, provenance tracking, and intermediate-product reuse, providing a foundation for multi-stage cascading-hazard workflows.

events.title: A Multi-Phase GPU Pipeline for Biconnected Components
events.description: Graph biconnectivity is a fundamental primitive for structural analysis, but classical algorithms rely on depth-first search, which is inherently sequential and does not scale to GPUs. We present a multi-phase, GPU-resident pipeline for computing biconnected components on large-scale undirected graphs. Our pipeline first removes 1-core vertices through iterative peeling, then grows depth-capped breadth-first search trees from multiple random roots in parallel, ensuring each vertex joins exactly one tree. We resolve each tree's non-tree edges into local biconnected components, then merge components across tree boundaries using the remaining cross-tree edges. We evaluate our approach on 17 real-world networks on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Our approach substantially outperforms earlier GPU and CPU baselines, including WK-17, WK-18, and CPU-based FAST-BCC, and achieves an average speedup of 2.49x over FAST-BCC-Filter, the current state-of-the-art GPU approach.

events.title: A Naive D3Q27 Lattice Boltzmann Implementation on the Cerebras CS-3: Comparison with GPUs
events.description:
The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) is a stencil-based CFD method widely used across engineering fields, in which the domain is divided into a lattice, each element is computed independently, and data is exchanged with adjacent elements. Thus, it is expected to map well onto the Cerebras CS-3, which features large distributed on-chip memory and high-bandwidth inter-PE communication.

In this work, we naively implement a three-dimensional LBM (D3Q27 Model) on the CS-3 by assigning a 1x1xn lattice to each processing element (PE). To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first attempt made to implement 3-D LBM and measure its performance.

On the largest domain, the CS-3 achieves 83.74 GLUPS — a 17.4× and 8.5× speedup over the NVIDIA A100 and GH200 — while sustaining a parallel efficiency of 1.0 under weak scaling. These results indicate that wafer-scale computing can serve as a promising platform for memory-bound stencil computations.

events.title: A Physics-Informed AI Architecture for One-Dimensional Turbulence Modeling
events.description: One-dimensional turbulence (ODT) represents turbulent flow on a one-dimensional domain through continuous molecular diffusion and stochastic triplet-map eddy events. This work examines what a deterministic machine-learning surrogate can learn from such a stochastic system. Fourier neural operators trained on individual ODT realizations converge toward ensemble-mean dynamics because future eddy events cannot be inferred uniquely from the instantaneous flow state. Training directly on ensemble averages confirms accurate interpolation across unseen jet velocities and widths, with more than 300× speedup relative to generating the corresponding ensembles. We therefore propose a hybrid physics-informed architecture that mirrors the ODT solver: a neural operator advances the continuous diffusion dynamics, while stochastic triplet-map events are applied explicitly. Using the same eddy sequence, the hybrid model reconstructs individual realizations with a final relative L2 error of 0.028 and approximately 9× faster rollout than the original solver. This decomposition provides a practical framework for learning stochastic turbulence models.

events.title: A Side-Channel Methodology for DL Model Recovery Using Power Traces
events.description: Deep learning architecture represents proprietary intellectual property and serves as a basis for model extraction and adversarial attack techniques. By analyzing only the total GPU power consumption, sampled every 20ms via standard telemetry during inference, without access to weights, inputs, activations, or the computational graph, we can reconstruct the sequence of layer types executed. Our methodology involves segmenting the power trace, matching each segment against a library of per-layer power templates using k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), and refining the classification with a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that encodes typical layer transition patterns with a Viterbi decoder. Evaluations across 21 models and 8-layer classes reveal an average layer-type sequence recovery accuracy of 60.1%, reaching up to 92% for some models.

events.title: A Taxonomy of Application Properties for Mixed-Precision Autotuning
events.description:
Modern HPC platforms increasingly rely on reduced-precision hardware for performance and energy efficiency, but many scientific applications still default to FP64. Although parts of these applications may tolerate lower precision, identifying safe and profitable precision reductions remains difficult. Tool-based mixed-precision autotuners help automate this task, yet their success varies widely across applications. Existing work focuses mainly on autotuning tools rather than application suitability.

We present a completed application-centric study of the properties that make mixed-precision autotuning feasible, costly, fragile, or beneficial. Our novel contribution is a taxonomy that organizes these properties into structural, behavioral, numerical/domain, and performance/architectural categories, maps them to autotuning workflow costs, and expresses them as decision gates for readiness assessment.

In the poster session, we will present the framework using visual summaries and examples to discuss tool assumptions, benchmark design, and practical adoption.

events.title: A Viskores-Enhanced Vision Transformer Framework for MRI-Based Cancer Image Classification on Frontier
events.description: High performance computing (HPC) enables workflows that integrate scientific visualization and artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery. This work investigates the integration of Viskores, a performance-portable visualization framework, into a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based MRI classification pipeline executed on the Frontier supercomputer. Instead of training directly on raw magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, our approach generates visualization-derived feature representations using Viskores operations, including median filtering, Sobel gradients, Laplacian filtering, texture extraction, Otsu thresholding, and morphological processing. We evaluate these representations on a four-class brain tumor MRI dataset containing 7,200 images and compare them with a conventional raw-image ViT baseline. The best-performing visualization-enhanced pipeline improves classification accuracy from 91.94% to 95.50%. The poster presents the end-to-end HPC workflow, performance comparison, and an ablation study, demonstrating the potential of integrating scientific visualization and AI within scalable, reproducible workflows for medical imaging applications.

events.title: A-OASIS: Building an AI-Coupled Atmosphere-Ocean Foundation Model
events.description: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) water-for-energy planning requires predictions of precipitation and hydroclimate variability from weeks to years, yet these horizons depend on coupled atmosphere-ocean-land feedback that are difficult to learn from observations. Established dynamical Earth system models and explicit couplers remain the scientific reference, but producing long simulations and forecast ensembles is computationally intensive. This work in progress asks a bounded question: after careful, domain-guided data harmonization, how much of the coupling workflow can a unified AI foundation model learn directly, and where does that strategy become limited? We present the Atmosphere-Ocean Artificial System for Integrated Simulation (A-OASIS), an Aurora-derived model that jointly encodes atmosphere, ocean, and land states in one latent space rather than training and coupling separate emulators. Initial experiments demonstrate stable full resolution distributed training and decreasing validation loss with increased model capacity. These results establish implementation feasibility, driving the next step of validating forecast capability.

events.title: AI for Quantum at the Quantum Science Center: Towards Building a Connective Layer Across the Quantum Computing Stack
events.description: We present the AI for Quantum efforts of the Agentic Software team at the Quantum Science Center (QSC), Oak Ridge National Laboratory, advancing a unifying thesis: that artificial intelligence can serve as the connective and accelerating substrate of the quantum computing stack. Our portfolio spans three axes. For **knowledge infrastructure**, Quantum RAG grounds frontier models in curated quantum corpora, and the Quantum Computing LLMWiki provides a machine-readable knowledge resource. For **evaluation**, the Quantum Computing Benchmark Leaderboard rigorously benchmarks frontier models on quantum code generation, coupled with a hard benchmark and shared-task problems developed for IEEE Quantum Week (QCE). For **domain reasoning and systems**, ChatQEC, FTQEC, and hardware-aware error correction lower the barrier to reasoning about codes and decoders under realistic device constraints, while a multi-agent framework decomposes quantum-HPC workflows across specialized agents. We further extend EPIC toward quantum-HPC co-execution, integrating these capabilities into a unified orchestration substrate.

events.title: APQF: Agentic Profiling-Guided Structured Pruning and Mixed-Precision Quantization with Adaptive Fine-Tuning
events.description: Deep neural networks are powerful but too large to run cheaply on edge devices. Pruning and quantization help, but deciding how and where to compress a model is still manual, or relies on algorithms that are hard to apply across architectures. We introduce APQF, an agentic profiling-guided framework that combines structured pruning, mixed-precision quantization-aware training, and accuracy recovery in one automated pipeline. A profiling agent measures cost distribution and pruning sensitivity, which then drive per-group pruning ratios, per-layer bit-widths, and the recovery strategy. Our experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 show that APQF compresses convolutional and transformer models further than a joint pruning and quantization baseline at comparable or higher accuracy, and stays stable across different planners, including free open-weight ones.

events.title: Accelerating Materials Discovery with ADAM: An AI Co-Pilot for Physical Experimentation
events.description: The rapid discovery of new materials for energy storage, advanced computing, and other technologies requires us to remake scientific experimentation beyond the limits of human cognition and manual interaction. Most existing autonomous experimentation relies on deterministic scripts or narrowly-scoped post-hoc machine learning. Large language models offer a fundamentally different capability, in the form of generalized reasoning from natural language goals, but we must still address safe LLM reasoning with real-time instrument feedback in a closed-loop workflow. Here we present ADAM, a multi-agent large language model framework integrating a retrieval augmented generation pipeline grounded in internal documentation, a validated instrument tool registry, and human-in-the-loop oversight positioned at semantic reversibility boundaries. By inferring these boundaries from natural language rather than hard-coded rules, ADAM achieves high autonomy in routine experiments and applies precise human oversight only when needed. We demonstrate this system in two materials characterization and processings examples.

events.title: Adaptive Error Quantization for Lossy Compression of Scientific Datasets
events.description: Large-scale scientific instruments and applications generate massive amounts of data, creating storage and I/O bottlenecks for analysis. Error-bounded lossy compression methods mitigate this, but certain unpredictable datasets make it difficult to obtain large compression ratios with prediction-based compressors without introducing a large error. This work introduces adaptive error quantization, a novel extension to the SZ3 compressor framework. Our implementation dynamically refines the prediction error of an unpredictable data point by allocating additional error quantization bins through continuous bisection of the error, improving data fidelity for hard-to-compress datasets while minimizing storage overhead. We present a comparison of our adaptive method against the baseline SZ3 compressor on the HACC particle simulation datasets, highlighting our algorithm's advantage when compressing high-entropy fields.

events.title: Adaptive Orchestration of Heterogeneous LLMs with Dynamic Escalation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
events.description: LLM-based multi-agent systems offer strong reasoning capabilities but often incur substantial computational and operational costs. This work presents an adaptive two-orchestrator framework for coordinating heterogeneous small and large LLMs. Orchestrator-1 (O-1) determines the initial number of expert agents and model tier using task-level risk signals. The primary adaptive component, Orchestrator-2 (O-2) evaluates multiple round-level signals using a heuristic approach and selectively escalates only when the current model configuration is deemed insufficient. After evaluation across various benchmarks using models deployed with vLLM we found that compared with the Large-only configuration, the Small + Large configuration improved accuracy by 0.51–6.67 percentage points, reduced average cost per task by 15.99%–33.65%, and decreased execution time by 8.1%–18.06%. Only 0.10%–3.60% of tasks required escalation, demonstrating the effectiveness of O-2’s signal-driven decision mechanism. These results validate that dynamic escalation can preserve or improve performance while reducing unnecessary use of Larger models.

events.title: Agentic AI Augmentation for Recursive Mixed-Precision Linear Solvers
events.description: High performance computing increasingly relies on low-precision hardware for throughput, yet scientific applications demand numerical accuracy. Recursive mixed-precision algorithms address this, but extending them to new solvers requires expert-level knowledge. This work investigates agentic AI augmentation to transfer knowledge from a recursive mixed-precision Cholesky solver to new algorithms, evaluating in-context learning (ICL) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), using implementations, documentation, and mathematical formulations as structured knowledge. We find that full-context ICL enables frontier LLMs to generate a high-performance recursive mixed-precision LU factorization achieving up to a 4.9x speedup over cuSOLVER FP32 on H200 GPUs while preserving accuracy, whereas PEFT memorizes the framework but fails to generalize, showing that expert-designed HPC implementations can serve as reusable knowledge for AI systems. At the poster, I will present our knowledge-transfer framework via figures comparing runtime and speedup across ICL prompting levels and models, fine-tuning accuracy results, and our recursive mixed-precision framework and future directions.

events.title: Agents of Intelligence: Lowering the Barrier to AI for Domain Scientists
events.description: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how science is done, yet most domain scientists face a steep barrier to adopting it. The landscape of models, platforms, and data pipelines is fragmented, and navigating it rewards tacit expertise accumulated over years of practice. We present Agents of Intelligence (AoI): a modular, composable, human-in-the-loop framework of AI agents that sense workflow context, automate routine decisions, recommend models and compute resources, and learn from usage. AoI is grounded in interviews with 11 Schmidt AI postdoctoral researchers spanning eight scientific domains, and it integrates with the National Data Platform to support the full research lifecycle from data acquisition through model deployment, making AI-assisted science accessible across domains.

events.title: Algebraic Breadth-First Search on the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
events.description: Graph traversal is memory bound on conventional hardware: irregular access defeats the cache hierarchy. The Cerebras WSE-3 gives each of its 900,000 cores its own 48 KB of SRAM, turning irregular access into local access, but leaves them coordinating over a 2D mesh and a slow host-device link. We present an algebraic BFS that runs entirely on device, avoiding the link that host-callable SpMV kernels would cross every iteration. Sweeping Graph500-specification R-MAT graphs from scale 10 to 20 across PE grids up to 750x750, we find adding cores helps only up to a point, past which larger collectives outweigh the smaller share of work per PE. At that turning point up to 89% of device time goes into collectives, while exporting results costs two orders of magnitude more than the search itself. Within the kernel, distributed on-chip memory removes the memory wall and leaves collective communication as the next target.

events.title: An MLIR Dialect for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
events.description: To achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), a compilation pipeline must address quantum error-correcting codes, syndrome extraction, magic-state distillation, and physical-gate decomposition. We introduce ftqc, an open-source dialect for MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) that treats these concerns as first-class constructs in the intermediate representation (IR). Logical qubits are type-safe static single-assignment (SSA) values parameterized by their error-correcting code and distance, letting the compiler enforce code and distance compatibility at the type level. The dialect provides operations covering the logical life-cycle: encoded initialization, transversal Clifford gates, T gates and Toffoli gates by magic-state injection, syndrome extraction, and distillation. A resource estimator derives physical-qubit counts and logical error rates directly from ECC metadata in the IR, and three validated backends emit OpenQASM 3, QIR (Quantum Intermediate Representation), and Stim. Across four benchmarking quantum circuits, end-to-end compilation completes in under 15 ms, and a full logical-error-rate sweep through Stim runs in under 4 s.

events.title: Analyzing the Impact of Architectural Design Decisions on Performance Across Generations of NVIDIA GPUs
events.description: The high performance computing (HPC) industry is moving past an era in which each new generation of devices provided uniform performance improvements across all workloads. In this work, we profile a diverse suite of applications across multiple generations of NVIDIA HPC GPUs to evaluate how architectural design decisions translate into real-world application performance, in terms of speedup and energy efficiency. The suite of applications was hand-picked to represent the modern HPC landscape; it covers scientific computing, AI inference, AI training, and targeted microbenchmarks. GPU-level performance counters, execution time, power, and energy measurements were collected and analyzed to identify which architectural improvements provide the greatest benefit, which are less impactful, and what workload characteristics determine their effectiveness. Relative to the increase in transistor count, the data exhibits significant performance gains among Tensor Core bound applications, expected gains in memory-bound applications and below-expected gains in vector throughput-bound applications.​

events.title: Automated Isolation of Vulnerable Workloads
events.description: Kubernetes and OpenShift support scientific services, data platforms, and artificial-intelligence workflows at high performance computing facilities. Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS/StackRox) identifies vulnerable images, policy violations, and risky deployments, but operators still must interpret risk and coordinate containment. That handoff is slow; immediate deny-all isolation can interrupt shared services before owners remediate. We present an automated, risk-based system that converts RHACS findings into controlled Kubernetes NetworkPolicy actions. A shared backend classifies risk, assigns configurable remediation windows, stores workload state, and applies or removes managed policies. Dashboard, CLI, operator, REST API, and Splunk integrations support manual and automated response. Namespace scoping, policy simulation, rollback, opt-out metadata, and structured audit events preserve operational control. Prototype validation demonstrates end-to-end detection, tracking, containment, and recovery for representative vulnerable workloads. Together, these mechanisms make response timing visible, repeatable, and recoverable instead of relying on ad hoc operator judgment.

events.title: BFS-FAR: Fragmented Asynchronous Breadth-First Search on UPMEM Processing-in-Memory
events.description:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is difficult to accelerate because of irregular memory access, low work per edge, and frequent synchronization. On UPMEM Processing-in-Memory systems, DPUs cannot communicate directly, so existing PIM-BFS designs rely heavily on host-mediated frontier exchange.

We present BFS-FAR, a completed fragmented BFS design that combines locally asynchronous relaxation within each DPU with host-side minimum-level reconciliation. Its key contribution is allowing improved levels to be reused within the same DPU launch, reducing repeated global frontier exchange and host coordination. Experiments using up to 2,540 DPUs cover R-MAT graphs with approximately 262K–4.2M vertices and 4.2M–67.1M directed edges, and controlled-size synthetic graphs ranging from 200K vertices and 10M edges to 13.6M vertices and 730M edges. BFS-FAR achieves 18.0×–86.5× algorithm-only speedup over UPMEM baseline, PrIM-BFS.

The poster will present the BFS-FAR workflow, performance results, timing breakdowns, DPU scaling, and the effects of locality and workload balance.

events.title: Batched GPU Execution for High-Throughput Combinatorial Search
events.description: Simplifiable strong uniquely solvable puzzles (SUSPs) connect combinatorial search to upper bounds on the matrix-multiplication exponent. The process of evaluating each candidate requires expensive parallel workloads, which have been handled efficiently using GPUs. However, the existing search sent one candidate at a time to a GPU, so allocation, data transfer, and synchronization cost all the benefits of fast evaluation on a GPU. We redesigned the search by batching same-size candidates into one kernel launch. Besides that, we also optimized the workflow by decoupling GPU work from multi-threaded search expansion on the CPU. In our experiments, the single-GPU pipeline raised end-to-end throughput by 3.09–5.75 times, while the double-GPU pipeline could achieve over 11 times. With a new, better search program, we found a new (79, 10)-SUSP, improving on the best width-10 result reported by Anderson and Le.

events.title: Benchmarking AI Vector Databases for Genesis Mission
events.description:
In support of the Genesis Mission, the U.S. government's national AI initiative, Circe is an HPC-hosted AI service environment that supports model access, custom knowledge databases, and external tool integration. A central feature of Circe is effective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which requires streamlined vector databases. This work aims to identify and recommend the best-performing vector database backend for Circe's RAG services, promoting efficient and accurate query retrieval at scale.

We benchmarked five databases—Qdrant, Redis, Weaviate, ChromaDB, and Elasticsearch—using Qdrant's vector-db-benchmark framework, comparing their scalability, query speed, latency, and retrieval accuracy across three configurations. Redis achieved the strongest baseline performance, with Weaviate following closely behind. With tuning, Weaviate reached the highest throughput (3,002.3 requests per second), while Qdrant demonstrated the largest proportional improvement (620.0 to 1,504.3 requests per second). We conclude that Weaviate is the strongest candidate for maximum query speed, while Qdrant offers the greatest flexibility for tuning.

events.title: Bigger Networks, More Trajectories: Scaling Exact Stochastic Simulation on GPUs Through Sparse Storage and a Warp-ary Propensity Tree
events.description:
Exact stochastic simulation of biochemical networks requires large trajectory ensembles for increasingly large reaction models, creating two main bottlenecks: dense model storage can exceed device memory, while serial reaction selection costs O(M) per step.

We built an exact GPU Gillespie solver in Lattice Microbes software that stores stoichiometry and the reaction dependency graph in a compressed sparse row format and selects reactions using a warp-cooperative 32-ary propensity tree in O(log₃₂M). Our major contribution combines sparse storage with warp-cooperative logarithmic selection for exact GPU SSA. The solver is implemented and validated against StochKit2; release in Lattice Microbes v3.0 is planned.

On an NVIDIA B200 across five models with 18–58,276 reactions, memory use decreases by ~800×, enabling up to 100K trajectories where other tools run out of memory. This poster presents the algorithm, sparse data layout, scaling, and comparative performance, including up to ~20× higher throughput where competing tools still fit.

events.title: Breaking the Chain: Geometry-Native State Preparation with ASPIRE
events.description: Loading data into quantum computers is a key bottleneck threatening end-to-end quantum advantage. Compilers for structured states, like matrix product states (MPS), help manage this bottleneck in quantum chemistry, finance, and many-body simulation. Approximate MPS preparation typically uses layered staircases of nearest-neighbor gates. We present Adaptive State Preparation by Iterative Removal of Entanglement (ASPIRE). ASPIRE approximately compiles state-preparation circuits by selecting gates using the state's entanglement geometry and target processor's connectivity. It scores candidate qubit pairs on entanglement removability and identifies layers of parallel long-range gates removing the most entanglement. We test ASPIRE on Hamiltonian ground states and multivariate amplitude-encoded functions, including qubit connectivity, hardware noise, NISQ, and early-fault-tolerant settings. For states with long-range entanglement, ASPIRE typically achieves higher fidelities and shallower circuits than existing methods, even including classical optimization. ASPIRE is a competitive, resource-frugal protocol, especially promising for applications tolerant to imperfect fidelity, like quantum phase estimation guide states.

events.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap in Long-Term Agent Memory Retrieval
events.description: LLM-based agents perform well across many tasks but still struggle with long-term interactions requiring coherence, continuity, and personalization. LLM-based agents often use RAG-style memory systems to retrieve past experiences, but direct query–memory similarity can fail when user queries and fine-grained memories are semantically misaligned. We address this semantic gap with an iterative, anchor-guided retrieval strategy inspired by spreading activation in associative memory.
