Starting from a small set of seed memories, the method expands through global semantic associations and local temporal neighbors, while a path-aware cross-encoder selects complementary evidence across multiple hops. Retrieved memories are accumulated and reused as anchors for further exploration.

events.title: Building an HPC User Documentation Process Via Layers of Writing Infrastructure
events.description: We are technical communication scholars working as guest faculty researchers at Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF) at Argonne National Laboratory in Lemont, IL. We research documentation processes for high performance computing (HPC). We are building an applied theory of writing infrastructure to model these processes. Building and maintaining user documentation that is responsive to changing user needs and technologies for complex computing systems, such as the exascale machine Aurora, is challenging. It is a whole-facility endeavor that depends on layers of writing infrastructure that are built incrementally over time. This poster builds on our model of the documentation process for the supercomputer Aurora. It traces the timeline of building the layers of writing infrastructure, such as cross-cutting committees, networked communication tools and diverse document types, to illustrate how the process was implemented. Takeaways include the importance of a collaborative culture for documentation and a metric-driven culture of continuous improvement.

events.title: CADI: Semi-Automatic Insertion of Host-Device Data Transfer Directives Based on Code Analysis
events.description: In heterogeneous computing using directive-based parallel programming models such as OpenACC, programmers typically need to explicitly specify host-device data transfer directives, increasing programming effort. Existing automatic approaches may introduce runtime overhead that can degrade performance. To reduce programming effort while preserving opportunities for performance optimization, we propose a semi-automatic approach that combines static code analysis with runtime memory tracking while allowing programmers to specify transfer directions. Based on this approach, we present CADI (Code Analysis-based Data-transfer directive Insertion), a foundation for semi-automatically inserting data transfer directives. CADI automatically determines the base address and transfer size required for each directive, while the programmer specifies the transfer direction to retain control over performance-related data movement. CADI achieved execution performance comparable to manually optimized implementations on the Himeno benchmark, indicating minimal runtime overhead. The poster presents the design of CADI, its code analysis and runtime mechanisms, and experimental results.

events.title: CLASP: Index Compression for Finite Element SpMV
events.description: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) in finite element methods is memory-bound, with index storage consuming a significant fraction of bandwidth. We exploit mesh connectivity to partition the assembled matrix into element-wise blocks each covering at most B = 256 nodes, enabling 8-bit column indices and 16-bit row pointers, a 4x index compression over standard CSR. We show that the encoding is provably compressive with node duplication overhead bounded by $1 + O(B^{-1/d})$ for d-dimensional meshes. We present three GPU kernels: partitioned CSR, partitioned CSR with shared-memory buffering, and a prefix-sum-based COO variant. We test our kernels on four NVIDIA GPU generations and show that the proposed encoding results in a faster SpMV operation achieving 1.4x-1.7x speedup over cuSPARSE CSR. We further show that COO-variant is more suitable for high-bandwidth-equipped GPU systems. A direct CPU implementation of partitioning CSR kernel with vectorization achieves up to 2x speedup over Intel-MKL for SpMV operation.

events.title: Cache-Driven Super-Linear Scaling in a Python Fluid Solver
events.description: Turbulent convection transports heat in stars, planets, and the Earth’s atmosphere, and simulating it demands extreme-scale computing. We present DHARA, a modular fluid solver written in Python (NumPy, CuPy, mpi4py) with compiled stencil kernels for CPUs and GPUs. On the CPU-based Shaheen III (KAUST), DHARA scales to 786,432 cores for compressible convection, and its strong scaling is super-linear: adding cores speeds up each step by more than the ratio of the core counts. Profiling explains why. As the domain is split across more cores, each subdomain’s stencil working set drops into the fast L1/L2 caches, so cache misses collapse, leading to a better than doubling of the per-core throughput. The same code carries over to the Frontier (OLCF) and Polaris (ALCF) GPU systems with near-ideal strong scaling.

events.title: Characterizing Cooperative I/O Caching for Data Loading at Scale on Aurora
events.description:
Deep-learning jobs on exascale systems begin by reading identical files: Python packages, then training data from a shared filesystem, forcing thousands of processes to issue near-identical requests at once and slowing startup for the whole machine. Cooperative caching can relieve this by serving redundant reads locally, but it adds overhead, so it is not always worthwhile. We ask when it pays off.

We characterize Copper, a cooperative read-caching filesystem, against direct Lustre reads on Aurora, measuring PyTorch startup and ResNet-50 dataset loading, cold and warm, from 2 to 2,048 nodes. We find a crossover: as scale grows, Copper's bounded coordination cost overtakes direct reads whose cost climbs with contention. At 2,048 nodes, startup through Copper is ~3× faster cold, ~11× faster warm. Import-torch results are complete; a synthetic file-size guideline is in progress.

The poster presents the crossover and its mechanism, inviting discussion of when cooperative caching should be applied.

events.title: Characterizing GPU Performance in AI Inference with Power Metrics
events.description: Large language model inference is increasingly limited not only by raw compute capability, but also by memory bandwidth, runtime behavior, and GPU power efficiency. We study how LLM inference performance and energy use vary across hardware platforms and inference frameworks. Experiments are conducted on NVIDIA's Jetson Thor, and A100 and H200 GPUs using two inference frameworks: vLLM and Hugging Face Transformers. Three open-weight LLMs are evaluated. For each hardware, framework, and model combination, inference metrics are collected. Pareto and histogram analyses are used to study the trade-off between throughput and energy efficiency. To connect inference behavior to hardware limits, BabelStream benchmark's triad kernel is used to measure host-memory and GPU-memory bandwidth. In addition, roofline analysis separates prefill and decode phases to show when performance is compute-bound or memory-bound. These measurements help explain why the Jetson Thor can be energy-efficient, while A100 and H200 provide higher throughput but consume more power.

events.title: Characterizing Scaling Performance of LLM Inference on GPU-Based Supercomputers
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly important for scientific computing and agentic coding workflows. With growing model sizes, a single node on current-generation HPC systems no longer suffices for LLM inference. Inference must span slower scale-out interconnects and combine different parallelization strategies. This combinatorial space of strategies is large, and each configuration places different demands on the hardware. Which configuration performs best at a given scale, workload, and model architecture remains unclear. To address this, we empirically sweep hundreds of parallel deployment configurations across models and workloads on two leadership-class systems. We analyze scaling trends and find optimal configurations for different workloads and performance metrics, aiming to provide actionable insights for HPC practitioners.

events.title: Cheap Plans, Costly Trades: Host-Device Tradeoffs for SpGEMM on AiM
events.description: Sparse matrix–matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) is bandwidth-bound, the kind of kernel a memory-side accelerator ought to absorb, but the processing-in-memory hardware that ships is built for AI inference. We map 𝐶 = 𝐴 · 𝐴 onto SK hynix’s Accelerator-in-Memory (AiM), whose fixed-function units multiply dense bfloat16 vectors but cannot compute an address, so the host must place every product in advance. The mapping trades host planning for device time; we measure the trade over four designs, from almost no planning to a simulator-in-the-loop search. A single packing pass cuts device time 7×–122×, every further plan buys at most 8.5× more, and on a single product each plan costs more host time than it saves.

events.title: Chemically Accurate End-to-End Classical Simulation of Qubitization-Based Quantum Phase Estimation on 1,024 GPUs
events.description: Qubitization-based quantum phase estimation (QPE) is a core algorithm for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), and molecular ground-state energies are among its most promising applications. Resource estimates predict the qubits and gates required, while end-to-end simulation directly tests whether the resulting circuits achieve the target accuracy; yet a naive chemical-accuracy H4 circuit needs 99 qubits and 1.78 billion gates. We combine established qubit- and gate-reduction techniques with distributed state-vector simulation using our prior communication optimizations for hierarchical GPU interconnects, on ABCI-Q's 1,024 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The H4 circuit shrinks to 28 qubits and 0.32 billion gates, runs in 1.5 hours, and yields a one-million-shot measurement distribution whose peak lies 0.53 milli-Hartree from the exact full configuration interaction (FCI) energy, within chemical accuracy. These runs check, at small scale, that estimated resources deliver the target accuracy. The poster also presents each reduction stage's effect, strong scaling, and remaining bottlenecks.

events.title: CoEncode: Reclaiming Idle Encoder GPUs in Multi-Tenant Multimodal LLM Serving
events.description: Disaggregated multimodal LLM serving improves stage isolation but can leave dedicated encoder GPUs substantially underutilized. We present CoEncode, a workload-aware encoder pooling approach that uses model-specific capacity profiles to provision fractional GPU resources and colocate encoder workloads while accounting for end-to-end pipeline conditions. Our evaluation shows that CoEncode maintains comparable end-to-end TTFT SLO attainment while improving SLO goodput perGPU by 19.3% and reducing encoding energy consumption by 45.9%. These results demonstrate the potential of encoder pooling to improve resource and energy efficiency without sacrificing end-to-end serving quality.

events.title: Collaborative Partitioning of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Workloads: Cost-Model-Driven Planning for Tensor-Network/QPU Execution
events.description: Quantum processors sit beside CPUs and GPUs in HPC centers, yet nothing decides, before execution, which part of a workload belongs where, and on a noisy device that decision needs two currencies at once, wall-clock time and error. We supply the missing layer for matrix-product-state simulation. A computation is partitioned at one bond: the weakly entangled side is contracted exactly, the strongly entangled fragment becomes a single ancilla-free staircase circuit driven by a seam register of fewer qubits, whose sampling cost is bounded by chi^2 /epsilon^2 and adapts to the Schmidt spectrum. A planner prices every candidate: classical time and quantum time from transpiled gate durations, against a four-term error envelope, always retaining a classical fallback, and emits a per-run receipt comparing prediction with measurement. On 64-site Ising chains the envelope covers the realized error on every executed plan, and the planner correctly declines the QPU.

events.title: Communication Strategies for Wafer-Scale Iterative Solvers
events.description: Collective communication strongly affects the performance of iterative scientific applications. Conjugate gradient repeatedly computes global dot products that require reductions across many processing elements. This work evaluates chain and hierarchical XY two-phase reductions on a Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine. We developed a reproducible workflow for compiling wavelet programs, executing them on hardware, collecting distributed timer values, and producing graph-ready data. Measurements across 262,144 processing elements show a payload-dependent crossover. XY two-phase communication performs best for small payloads, but chain communication becomes faster as the payload grows. These results motivate adaptive collective selection based on message size.

events.title: Completion-Driven, Staging-Free AlltoAllv with Local-NIC Balancing
events.description: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training workloads use imbalanced AlltoAllv collectives at bandwidth-bound message sizes. On Frontier, one-sided AlltoAll can beat RCCL and Cray-MPICH, but only with the right schedule and only as per-peer fetches shrink. Other approaches balance load across a node's NICs by explicitly copying data between GPUs, which costs GPU staging buffers and overlaps that copy with network traffic only coarsely. We introduce CURLEW, a completion-driven, GPU-staging-free RDMA AlltoAllv with dynamic local-NIC balancing. CURLEW achieves near-flat bandwidth across GPU counts and message sizes on balanced patterns, is 1.9x faster than previous work at max-to-mean skew above 8, and reduces end-to-end training time of a 201B-parameter model by 22% at a capacity factor of 1.25.

events.title: Computers as Information Channels: A Common Yardstick for the Post-Moore Hardware Zoo
events.description: We propose a novel measurement unit for computing performance that's grounded in information theory. Modern computing systems are increasingly diverse, supporting low-precision formats, hardware specialization, and emerging paradigms such as analog, quantum, and neuromorphic hardware. Traditional metrics like floating-point operation (flop) counts no longer accurately capture this complexity. Instead, we frame computation as the transformation of information through a channel and define performance in terms of the mutual information between a system’s inputs and outputs. This approach measures not just the quantity of data processed, but the amount of meaningful information encoded, manipulated, and retained through computation. Our proposal aims to provide a principled, implementation-agnostic foundation for evaluating performance.

events.title: Continental-Scale, High-Order, High Spatial-Resolution Ice Flow Modeling Based on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)
events.description: Solving time-independent stress-balance equations to predict ice velocity is the most computationally demanding part of ice-sheet simulations, both for memory and execution time. In this study, we develop numerical algorithms that use the parallel processing power of graphics processing units (GPUs) and implement them in the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM) three-dimensional (3-D) Blatter-Pattyn higher-order (HO) module. Our setups are based on the ISSM Antarctic model from the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison for CMIP6 (ISMIP6), with about 10^7 degrees of freedom (DoFs), and a higher-resolution version with about 10^8 DoFs. We compare the GPU-accelerated 3-D HO ISSM stress balance module to the standard CPU-based version. We evaluate predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness. The poster will present the science question being investigated in this study, the methodology, results, and implications of the findings, and will outline future research objectives.

events.title: Correlation-Aware Uncertainty Visualization of Multivariate Data with Many-Core Acceleration
events.description: This research addresses a fundamental limitation in state-of-the-art uncertainty visualization of multivariate data: omission of statistical correlation between underlying data fields. Existing approaches either ignore correlation, yielding overconfident or underconfident uncertainty estimates and potentially misleading visualizations, or rely on computationally expensive Monte Carlo integration that limits practical applicability. We enable efficient, scalable, and reliable correlation-aware uncertainty visualization by modeling bivariate uncertainty using correlated Gaussian distributions and multivariate uncertainty using kernel density estimation (KDE), both capturing data correlation. We develop analytical frameworks for Gaussian and KDE models to propagate uncertainty into extracted level sets, providing the first rigorous study of correlation effects on multivariate level-set uncertainty while eliminating costly numerical integration. Compared to Monte Carlo methods, our approaches achieve speedups of up to 500x on equivalent serial and parallel hardware using the Viskores library. Results on synthetic and real-world datasets underscore the criticality of correlation-aware uncertainty quantification for trustworthy data analysis.

events.title: DPGraph: Code Optimization with Dynamic Program Graphs Using Heterogeneous GNNs
events.description: Heterogeneous high-performance computing systems require selecting suitable devices (e.g., CPU or GPU) and optimization parameters such as vectorization and interleave factors. Existing LLVM-IR-based program representations mostly rely on static information and may miss runtime behavior important for performance optimization. We propose DPGraph, an execution-flow-aware program graph representation that augments fine-grained LLVM-IR-based program representations with dynamic data dependencies to better capture runtime program behavior and identify effective optimization configurations. We evaluate DPGraph on vectorization and interleave factor prediction, CPU/GPU parallelism detection, and optimal loop-order prediction tasks. Across these tasks, DPGraph achieves around 13.6%, 7.06%, and 7.05% higher performance gains than state-of-the-art approaches, respectively. DPGraph is also data- and compute-efficient: it achieves 13.6% better speedup than MIREncoder while using over 40X fewer training samples and reduces training time by about 86% for CPU/GPU configuration prediction compared to state-of-the-art method ConTraPh.

events.title: Data Layout and Differentiation for Efficient Training of Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks
events.description: Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks reduce dependence on simulation-generated training data, but their training requires higher-order spatial derivatives at many function-coordinate pairs, causing severe computational and memory costs. We reorganize PI-DeepONet training around its tensor-product structure. Our compact data layout eliminates duplicated Branch inputs and Trunk coordinates, enables GEMM-based contraction, and shares Trunk derivatives among input functions. We further compare forward-mode automatic differentiation, zero coordinate shift, and explicit derivative propagation. In a completed two-dimensional Navier–Stokes benchmark, the optimized implementation achieved a 4.87-fold speedup and a 144-fold reduction in peak GPU memory for a representative case while preserving numerical equivalence. The implementation has also enabled a three-dimensional indoor ventilation demonstration. The poster will present the data layouts and differentiation strategies using schematic diagrams, summarize the complete performance sweep, and show the three-dimensional predicted flow fields as an animation.

events.title: Data-Driven GPU Performance Model for Molecular Dynamics in Computational Drug Discovery
events.description:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations increasingly rely on GPU acceleration to meet the computational demands of large biomolecular systems. However, predicting application performance across diverse molecular systems and heterogeneous GPU architectures remains challenging due to complex heterogeneous MD kernels with varying compute and memory demands. Conventional analytical models, including Roofline analysis, provide only coarse estimates and cannot capture the heterogeneous execution characteristics of modern MD workloads.

This work presents a hierarchical, reasonably explainable surrogate model that integrates molecular descriptors, simulation parameters, GPU architectural features to learn architecture-aware representations of MD execution on GPUs. Proposed teacher-student model's knowledge distillation removes the dependence on expensive runtime profiling while maintaining strong accuracy across previously unseen GPU architectures, providing a practical foundation for architecture-aware performance modeling in computational drug discovery.

events.title: Design the Plant and the Control Together
events.description:
Exascale cooling plants are often sized and operated by convention, making it unclear how much energy can be recovered through control and how much performance is fixed by plant design. We developed and validated a digital twin of the Frontier supercomputer cooling plant using one year of operational telemetry, then optimized control settings, coolant flow, subloop topology, and life cycle cost and carbon. The novel contribution is an end-to-end co-design framework showing that implementable control recovers 27.8% of annual cooling energy, while optimized flow allocation reduces topology sensitivity by 93%, leaving embodied carbon as the main remaining design criterion.

The study has completed model validation, annual optimization, topology enumeration, and life cycle analysis. During the poster session, we will use a system diagram, validation plots, energy savings comparisons, topology results, and a life cycle decision map to show why control should be optimized before hardware redesign.

events.title: Diamond Agent: Agentic Control of Federated HPC Resources as a Service
events.description: We present Diamond Agent, an agentic system that enables intelligent execution of HPC workflows across heterogeneous clusters with typed skills as the interface. Diamond Agent provides an agent-facing workspace and skills that unify cross-site resource discovery, resource specification, data movement, task execution, and result retrieval. A centralized Diamond Agent instance can operate multiple supercomputers without being deployed separately on each login node. Diamond Agent translates high-level agent actions into valid site-specific executions, moves data through Globus Transfer, and uses live system capability and queue information to select feasible placements. Its event-driven continuation mechanism decouples agent actions from long-running batch jobs: persistent services monitor remote execution and resume the agent only when a result or decision-relevant event is available.

events.title: Digitizing the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary: Accelerating Document Analysis with VLMs and HPC Infrastructure
events.description: The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD), completed in 21-plus volumes over 90 years (1921–2011), is a foundational Akkadian lexical reference locked in print and print-derived images. Manual text generation from dictionary scanned images requires domain expertise and is time-consuming. We present a generalizable pipeline that converts dense mixed-script dictionary pages into accurate UTF-8-encoded structured data. The HPC-enabled pipeline combines image preprocessing and layout segmentation with Vision Language Model (VLM)–based Optical Character Recognition (OCR), prompt engineering, and post-processing. In few-shot experiments on the gold standard dataset, Claude Opus 4.6 achieved a 1.45% CER and 5.75% WER on the training set (for optimal prompt design and selection) and 1.49% CER and 4.73% WER on the validation set. Using the pipeline, running on CPU compute nodes, we extracted raw text in less than a week, with domain expert text verification underway to finalize the scholarly dataset for human-environment history research.

events.title: Do AI Workloads Fail Differently? A Cross-Cluster Characterization of Failure Types in AI and HPC Systems
events.description:
High performance computing studies conclude that user error causes most job failures, while large-scale AI training reports attribute most interruptions to hardware. The two literatures are rarely read together, because they publish failure evidence in incompatible forms: attributed causes, scheduler outcome labels, or bare event rates.

We surveyed 162 public datasets and operational reports, assigned every one an evidence verdict, and normalized the usable evidence into an 11-class taxonomy that tags each failure type as a cause, a symptom, or an outcome label. The resulting denominator-disciplined maps cover 38 systems across 44 matrix columns and include a GPU error-class characterization spanning five hardware generations. The work is complete: every value passed three verification passes, and the artifact is public.

events.title: Drava: An Event-Driven Runtime for Scientific Pipelines with Agentic Configuration Optimization
events.description:
Next-generation X-ray science (XRS) detectors are driving continuous, multi-stage streaming pipelines with facility-scale data rates approaching petabytes per second. These workflows require real-time reconstruction, AI inference, and feedback-driven control under strict performance and energy constraints, yet current software stacks often require manual tuning of batching, transport, and resource decisions.

We propose Drava, an event-driven runtime for scientific streaming pipelines. Developers express application stages as reusable components, while Drava manages scheduling, batching, data movement, and execution across heterogeneous resources. Integrated with ptychography and tomography applications, Drava sustains high-rate streaming at about 31 kHz. Compared with PvaPy, it handles unpaced input without dropping frames and achieves up to 2.36× higher throughput. Batching improves throughput by up to 2.44×, while agentic Bayesian optimization identifies a configuration 2.24× faster than the best manual configuration. Drava also exposes throughput-energy trade-offs for performance- and energy-aware scientific workflows.

events.title: E-dLLM: Energy-Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference via Phase-Aware DVFS
events.description: Existing diffusion LLM (dLLM) serving systems focus on optimizing latency and throughput, while their energy efficiency remains less studied. We show that dLLM decoding moves between compute-bound cache-refresh and memory-bound cache-reuse phases, and that decoding configurations create a broad accuracy–energy trade-off. We present E-dLLM, which combines configuration selection with phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). On LLaDA-8B, reactive DVFS reduces energy by 17% with less than 1% latency overhead, while preserving model outputs.

events.title: Early Lessons From Characterizing Unified CPU-GPU Memory on DGX Spark
events.description: NVIDIA DGX Spark integrates an Arm CPU and Blackwell GPU behind one coherent LPDDR5X memory pool. A roofline view captures throughput, but the shared-memory programming model can blur where CPU–GPU memory-policy costs are charged. We isolate three attribution factors: ownership state, lifecycle boundary, and timing window. Handoff tests show cold first touch reaches 35x steady reuse, with managed-family paths still 1.6x–1.7x above steady at 256 MiB. Lifecycle tests show explicit and mapped host paths spend 264 ms and 246 ms in 256 MiB setup+teardown, versus 0.22–0.24 ms for managed-family paths. In a 400 MiB-per-array vector addition, end-to-end and steady-state timing change policy ranking. Unified physical memory simplifies data visibility, but it does not remove ownership, lifecycle, or timing-window cost attribution.

events.title: Efficient Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Systems and Continual Task Adaptation
events.description:
This dissertation addresses two fundamental challenges in distributed machine learning: client heterogeneity and continual adaptation to new tasks. It develops efficient fine-tuning and representation-learning frameworks that let distributed models acquire new knowledge and align it across clients without communication bottlenecks or catastrophic forgetting.

First, we introduce a dual-distilled federated learning framework for clients with heterogeneous systems and data. Trainable global prototypes with adaptive margins align local representations and logits without requiring a shared model architecture, enabling robust knowledge transfer and stable convergence.

Next, we propose a communication-efficient federated framework for large language models (LLMs) based on representation fine-tuning. By intervening on hidden states rather than weights, and combining All-But-Me aggregation with dynamic test-time computing, it reduces communication cost while balancing local personalization and global generalization.

We then present SETA, a mixture of sparse experts for task-agnostic continual learning in LLMs. SETA resolves the plasticity–stability dilemma by structurally decomposing the parameter space into shared and task-specific experts, protecting shared knowledge from semantic drift while preserving task-specific features.

Finally, we introduce FedSEAM, which extends sparse experts to federated continual learning. Clients learn experts on private task streams, and the server merges them through subspace agreement: it combines only the update directions clients share, keeps disagreeing directions as client-private experts, and protects prior-task subspaces from being overwritten.

Together, these contributions chart a path toward scalable, resource-aware machine learning systems that bridge decentralized efficiency and continual real-world deployment, learning new tasks across privacy-constrained environments without forgetting.

events.title: Embrace the Chaos: Harnessing Variability in Accelerator-Rich Systems
events.description:
HPC and ML workload scaling have led supercomputers to deploy large, heterogeneous systems with extreme power limits. Current GPU thermal design power limits (TDPs) range from 1,400–2,000W, scaling to extreme power budgets at scale. Thus, power has displaced performance as the dominant constraint. My research addresses this challenge by co-optimizing power and performance at scale through cross-stack approaches spanning hardware, firmware, systems, and applications.

Power management (PM) causes performance variation across accelerators, making it hard for users to get repeatable performance and for administrators to balance resource utilization. I was the first to characterize GPU variability across production clusters, uncovering consistent variability. This work guided MLCommons' benchmarking effort on handling variability. To harness this variability, I developed PAL, a cluster scheduler that leverages application-specific variability during job placement to optimize latencies and resource utilization.

Further investigating PM, we found GPU power often spikes above TDP (temporarily), triggering frequency throttling that hurts performance. I investigated these power excursions, especially frequent in compute-intensive workloads, and developed solutions that reduce excursions and improve latency.

As workloads rapidly evolve, new workloads often show different excursion characteristics as well as power/performance variability. To adapt our solutions to new, unseen workloads, I developed Minos, which groups similar workloads using power and utilization characteristics while reducing profiling overheads.

Overall, my research demonstrates the critical impact of excursions and GPU variability on large-scale systems. As power constraints intensify and hardware limits are pushed, this cross-stack co-design offers essential techniques to improve power-constrained supercomputing in the future.

events.title: Energy and Carbon Footprint of the x3d2 CFD Solver on AI-First and HPC-Class GPUs
events.description:
Estimates of the energy and carbon cost of computation are almost never checked against direct measurement. We instrument x3d2, a compact, high-order finite-difference CFD solver, across three GPU architectures and a 24-core server CPU.

While an AI-first accelerator uses 1.27x–1.40x lower energy than either HPC-class GPU, hardware selection is second-order: shifting a job's start time across 12 months alters emissions by 28x. Four standard carbon-accounting tools, all correctly configured, agree within 1.3x on that accelerator while overestimating energy measured at the wall socket by 1.9x–2.9x. On an A100 node, the same tools land within 0.64x–1.11x of whole-node energy.

The measurement campaign is complete: 124 instrumented runs on two platforms, plus a 36-run arm on a third, with full per-run telemetry and a complete analysis pipeline.

During the poster session, we will guide attendees through the power telemetry, visual tool-accuracy breakdowns, and the practical realities of carbon-aware scheduling.

events.title: Energy-Efficient Coupled Simulations with Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling
events.description: Dynamic inter-solver load imbalance in coupled multiphysics simulations leaves faster solvers idle at synchronization points, wasting energy. We investigate whether dynamic voltage and frequency scaling can exploit this slack without increasing time-to-solution. Our runtime framework combines preCICE for coupling and timing with MERIC for energy monitoring and online CPU-frequency control. A controller based on the Jitter algorithm maps each solver’s active fraction to a target frequency, while an energy model estimates savings from activity, power, and frequency-induced slowdown. We evaluate the method on a partitioned, iteratively coupled 2D air-water heat transfer problem using DUNE on the Barbora and Karolina clusters. On Barbora, total energy-to-solution fell by 13% with negligible runtime overhead, while the faster air solver used 28% less energy. On Karolina, solver runtime is dominated by communication overhead, causing DVFS to unnecessarily slow the simulation and significantly increase energy-to-solution.

events.title: Evaluating All-Reduce Operations in DDP Training with FABRIC: Framework for Architecture, Backend, and Reduction Interchange Comparison
events.description: Distributed deep learning increasingly relies on large GPU systems, where distributed data parallel (DDP) training replicates models across devices and synchronizes gradients each step. As model sizes and GPU counts grow, gradient synchronization becomes a major overhead. Although many optimized all-reduce algorithms exist, they are often embedded in different communication libraries or stack layers, making controlled comparison in full training workflows difficult. We present FABRIC (Framework for Architecture, Backend, and Reduction Interchange Comparison), an open-source, portable, and extensible framework for evaluating PyTorch DDP across communication backends and collective strategies. Using DDP communication hooks, FABRIC integrates alternative all-reduce algorithms without modifying PyTorch internals or training code, enabling reproducible comparisons across models, datasets, and backends including MPI, NCCL, and RCCL, and letting researchers add and benchmark custom communication methods. Experiments on Frontier and Polaris reveal meaningful performance differences among synchronization strategies. The poster presents FABRIC's architecture, extensibility, and productivity, and current results.

events.title: Exploring Tree-Based Approaches for Collective Communications on Cerebras WSE-3
events.description:
Collective operations are a key performance factor on the Cerebras WSE-3, a wafer-scale processor with 900,000 cores on a 2D mesh. At this scale, communication distance strongly affects latency, making locality a first-order concern in the design of collective algorithms.

We develop tree-style schedules that minimize communication distances for 1D Reduce, the building block of 2D collectives and AllReduce. We port Bine trees, the locality-optimized binomial trees we recently introduced, to the WSE-3; implement balanced binary-tree reductions; and introduce unbalanced binary trees as well as two-phase variants with tree-based outer phases. Each schedule is paired with an analytical cost model and implementation-level optimizations such as fused receive-send transports. On the official cycle-accurate simulator, our schedules outperform fixed-pattern state-of-the-art algorithms by up to 1.63x.

events.title: Exploring the Performance Portability of Modern Programming Languages
events.description: This poster evaluates the performance portability of Julia, Mojo, Python, and Rust across NVIDIA and AMD accelerators using four scientific benchmarks: seven-point stencil, BabelStream, Hartree–Fock, and miniBUDE. Native CUDA and HIP implementations were ported idiomatically to KernelAbstractions.jl (Julia), Mojo, Triton (Python), and CubeCL (Rust), respectively, and assessed in single and double precision. Results highlight the tradeoffs each language makes with its programming model and compiler design. Although these languages are relatively immature, they demonstrate promising potential for productive, performance-portable high performance computing (HPC) development.

events.title: Extending I/O Observability to Explainability for Targeted Optimization
events.description: HPC I/O profilers such as Darshan report POSIX-level metrics but do not trace the kernel stack: VFS, page cache, block layer, NVMe driver, and storage media. We present PEARL, an eBPF-based cross-layer tracing plugin for DataCrumbs, that builds one causal timeline per request from syscall to disk completion. We evaluate PEARL on Chameleon Cloud with IOR workloads. Page-cache faults account for 82% to 93% of kernel I/O time, a signal Darshan cannot capture. PEARL traces the same requests at 9.0 to 15.7 microseconds where Darshan reports 0.45 to 5.88 milliseconds. Overhead is negligible and within system noise. PEARL moves profiling from reporting what happened to explaining why, enabling targeted evidence-based optimization.

events.title: FBench: A Flexible Benchmark for CFG-Based What-If Exploration of HPC I/O Patterns
events.description: The I/O performance of large-scale HPC applications depends on a complex interplay of access patterns, middleware optimizations, and file system configurations. To explore these effects without rerunning full applications, we introduce FBench, a flexible, code-transparent benchmark for what-if analysis. FBench leverages context-free grammars (CFGs) derived from Recorder traces to either generate a simplified global configuration file or replay I/O patterns on-the-fly without preprocessing. It supports POSIX and MPI-IO and injects optimization hints via JSON. FBench reproduces IOR's scaling within 6.9%, captures the irregular file-per-process pattern of HACC-IO, and reveals a 30% collective/independent gap on Lustre that striping cannot close.

events.title: FFUSE: I/O Fault Injection and Resilience Scoring for HPC and AI Workloads
events.description: As HPC and AI/ML workloads increasingly share storage, filesystem faults (errors, partial I/O, latency spikes, silent corruption) can cause crashes or undetected data loss. To our knowledge, no systematic comparison of HPC and AI responses to identical filesystem faults, or unified cross-domain metrics, exists. We present FFUSE, a FUSE-based framework injecting seven filesystem fault categories transparently at the application I/O layer, and FIORE, a metric for failures without error reporting. Across 27 runs per workload, LAMMPS (HDF5 checkpoints) had lower crash (29.6% vs. 51.9%) and failure (44.4% vs. 66.7%) rates than ResNet-50 (pickle-based checkpoints). FIORE was 0.333 (LAMMPS) and 0.222 (ResNet-50), indicating ResNet-50 reported a larger share of its failures. Checkpoint format was associated with differences in I/O-layer fault behavior; a small paired pilot holding the application fixed suggests format can alter recovery outcomes but cannot isolate its effect. These results may inform checkpoint reliability in converged HPC–AI systems.

events.title: FPGA-Accelerated Simulation of a RISC-V Vector Architecture
events.description: A profusion of RISC-V-based system-on-chip (SoC) accelerator architectures has emerged in the past few years, fueled by AI and high performance computing. In many of these architectures, the RISC-V CPU serves as a control processor to route data and instructions to specialized IP blocks. Design, implementation, optimization, and validation of such architectures requires modeling and simulation of the integrated SoC at the register transfer level (RTL) in software simulators and FPGA. In this work, we evaluate the performance of a RISC-V scalar core augmented with the ARA2, a multi-lane floating-point vector unit, on workloads that are challenging for software RTL simulation. To accelerate evaluation, we map the RTL design to a low-cost FPGA development board. Here, we implement a heterogeneous system in which an ARM CPU manages benchmark setup, execution, and result collection for the RISC-V system, enabling fast, autonomous performance evaluation of the ARA2 vector processor.

events.title: Faster Biobank-Scale Genomics Through Sparse Linear Algebra on Genotype Representation Graph
events.description: Biobank initiatives include half a million phased genomes, outpacing the tools available to analyze them. Conventional genotype formats treat variants independently and fail to exploit the shared ancestry structure underlying population genetic variation. Prior work introduced the genotype representation graph, a compact graph encoding that captures shared ancestry directly but relies on traversal algorithms that map poorly onto modern accelerators. Here, we show that this computation can be expressed exactly as sparse linear algebra: under a topological ordering, the graph’s adjacency matrix becomes strictly block triangular, so the core genotype matrix–vector product reduces to a block sparse triangular solve. Further, we decompose this solve into a pipelined sequence of blocked sparse matrix-vector multiplications, exposing fine-grained parallelism and enabling mature, hardware-optimized primitives in place of hand-tuned kernels. The result is substantial, portable speedups across accelerator hardware, from cloud deployments to supercomputers.

events.title: Field-Preserving Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Visualization of Large-Scale Cosmological Simulations
events.description: Large-scale cosmological simulations generate hundreds of millions of particles, making interactive visualization computationally expensive. Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) provide an efficient compressed representation of particle datasets, but existing GMM-based renderers incur additional computational overhead from depth-plane sampling and alpha compositing, while Gaussian splatting methods are designed for photorealistic rendering rather than scientific visualization. We present a field-preserving Gaussian splatting framework that combines GMM compression with orthographic projection and GPU tile-based rasterization to reconstruct additive particle density and continuous scalar attributes directly from compressed Gaussian representations. Built on the gsplat framework, the proposed renderer executes entirely on the GPU for interactive visualization. Experiments on the Illustris-3 (94,196,375 particles) and HACC cosmological simulations (331,644,184 particles) achieve density PSNRs of 43.27 dB and 46.07 dB, respectively, while sustaining up to 92 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

events.title: Finite-Element Methods and Exascale Algorithms for Fully Relativistic Noncollinear Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory: From Mathematical Formulations to Efficient Computational Realization and Magnetic Materials Applications
events.description:
Fully relativistic noncollinear density functional theory (DFT) is essential for simulating spintronic and topological materials but costs 12–30 times more than unpolarized DFT, largely because each electron state becomes a two-component spinor. This cost is dominated by a sparse Hermitian eigenproblem with ~10^8 unknowns and ~10^5 eigenvectors, re-solved every self-consistent-field iteration in complex arithmetic. This thesis co-designs finite-element discretizations, eigensolvers, and GPU implementations within the open-source DFT-FE code.

The central contribution is residual-based Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI), which reformulates the Chebyshev recurrence around the residual so that errors from inexact operations shrink with it. Whereas standard Chebyshev filtering stalls, R-ChFSI converges to residuals of 10^-8 with approximate overlap-matrix inverses and FP32/TF32 arithmetic, making reduced precision and compressed communication safe. On Aurora, combining TF32 filtering with 10–12-bit block-floating-point compression of point-to-point messages accelerates filtering by up to 3.5x and the full ground-state solve by 2.27x over FP64, changing the energy by 1.3x10^-10 Ha/atom.

Band parallelization sustains 94% filtering efficiency when strong-scaling an 11,468-electron system to 384 nodes, and calculations reach 78,988 electrons on 800 Aurora nodes. On CPUs, DFT-FE achieves 8x–10x lower minimum wall time than Quantum ESPRESSO at equal accuracy, and GPU runs need 40x–70x fewer node-hours than CPU runs. The thesis also derives consistent forces and stresses and introduces adaptive-coordinate meshes that reduce energy errors up to 28x at fixed degrees of freedom. These capabilities enable a novel study of how vacancies reshape magnetism in the two-dimensional magnet Fe3GeTe2.

events.title: Foundation Models for Discovery and Exploration in Chemical Space
events.description:
Accurate, rapid prediction of molecular properties remains a bottleneck in materials innovation because experiments and conventional simulations are too costly to explore vast, high-dimensional chemical spaces. Scalable and interpretable molecular foundation models can accelerate discovery across chemical space while using computational resources efficiently. We demonstrate this with MIST, a family of molecular foundation models trained with up to an order of magnitude more data and parameters than prior work. To train MIST we developed Smirk, a tokenizer which preserves nuclear, electronic, and geometric information, enabling representation learning across chemical systems.

The largest MIST model has 1.8B parameters and was trained on 2B molecules. Training such a large model is an expensive endeavor. To make model development tractable on an academic compute budget we developed hyperparameter-penalized neural scaling laws which guided identification of compute-optimal model configurations without exhaustive sweeps at every scale, reducing model-development cost by an order of magnitude.

MIST models have been fine-tuned to predict over 400 structure–property relationships spanning domains from psychophysics to electrochemistry. They demonstrate state-of-the-art benchmark performance and enable real-world applications including stereochemical reasoning for organometallics, olfactory perception mapping, and electrolyte formulation design.

Beyond raw predictive accuracy, using mechanistic-interpretability methods we determine MIST learns chemically meaningful concepts during training. Analysis of token vectors, low-dimensional embedding projections and model logits reveals concept-aligned structures not explicitly labeled during training.

Together, these contributions connect molecular representation learning, compute-optimal scaling, and broad scientific validation, establishing scientific foundation models as robust tools for materials discovery and optimization.

events.title: From Microbenchmarks to LLM Inference: An End-to-End Analysis on the Energy Efficiency of the Grace Hopper Superchip
events.description: The NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) Superchip introduces a tightly integrated CPU-GPU architecture with shared power management, enabling new opportunities for energy-efficient high performance computing and AI inference. However, the impact of its power controls across different workloads remains largely unexplored. We present an end-to-end analysis of the GH200, spanning power sensor validation, HPL and HPL-MxP benchmarking, and LLM inference using Llama-3.1-8B. Our study quantifies the interaction between module and GPU power limits, evaluates energy-performance trade-offs, and analyzes operational and total cost of ownership. We demonstrate highly accurate onboard power measurements, identify workload-dependent optimal power settings, and show that mixed precision and inference workloads respond differently to power capping. During the poster session, we will present our experimental methodology, discuss the observed trade-offs, and highlight practical guidelines for energy-efficient deployment of GH200-based HPC and AI systems.

events.title: From Millions to Billions: Scaling Explicit Red Blood Cell Modeling on Exascale Systems
events.description: Explicitly resolving deformable red blood cells (RBCs) at physiological scale remains a fundamental challenge in computational hemodynamics due to high levels of memory, communication, and initialization demands. We present the first explicit billion-scale RBC simulation using HARVEY, a massively-parallel fluid–structure interaction solver characterizing high-fidelity deformable cell simulations. By combining scalable cell packing, distributed data management, and heterogeneous CPU–GPU execution, we initialize and simulate 4.95 billion RBCs within a 1 mL blood volume using 9,400 Frontier nodes (601,600 CPU cores and 75,200 AMD GPUs). The simulation occupies 3.76 PB of CPU memory and 1.44 PB of GPU memory while maintaining approximately 75% weak-scaling efficiency near full-system scale. These results extend explicit RBC modeling from millions to billions of cells and establish the computational foundation for physiologically-scaled cell-resolved blood flow simulations.

events.title: From YAML to Insight: Interactive Visualization of hws Hardware Samples
events.description:
The hws library provides a simple, easy-to-use way to capture hardware metrics for CPUs and GPUs from various manufacturers, including NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel. Having a holistic view of how an application interacts with the underlying hardware is crucial for application developers optimizing not only for peak performance but also for other targets such as energy efficiency. Up until now, hws has exported the hardware samples as YAML files, leaving the data analysis and visualization of the results to the user.

Therefore, in this e-poster, we present a companion visualization tool for hws that generates interactive, standalone HTML reports, enabling users to quickly gain insights from hws data with minimal setup effort. Our interactive research e-poster will include a live version of the visualizer embedded as an iframe, allowing visitors to freely explore the tool with example scenarios and quiz questions on their own using the touchscreen.

events.title: Fully GPU-Accelerated Distributed Full Configuration Interaction Beyond Trillion-Determinant Scale
events.description: Full configuration interaction (FCI) provides exact reference energies for benchmarking approximate quantum chemistry methods including emerging quantum algorithms, but its applicability is severely limited by exponential computational and memory requirements. To enable practical large-scale FCI calculations, we present a fully GPU-accelerated distributed implementation that combines chunk-based determinant partitioning, a hybrid GPU–CPU memory scheme, and GPU-native communication using NVIDIA NCCL. The proposed implementation computes the fully converged ground-state energy of NH2OH/6-31G with 1.7 trillion determinants in 13.4 hours and demonstrates execution of C2H4/6-31G with 2.4 trillion determinants, representing the largest determinant space reported to date for an uncompressed FCI implementation. It scales efficiently on up to 1,024 GPUs, and achieves up to a 58× speedup over our previous CPU-based implementation. These results establish the practicality of trillion-determinant FCI calculations on modern GPU clusters and provide large-scale exact benchmark data for validating approximate quantum chemistry methods.

events.title: GIFT: Geometry-Informed Low-Precision Gradient Communication for LLM Pretraining
events.description: Gradient communication is a major scaling bottleneck in large language model (LLM) pretraining. While FP8 can substantially reduce communication cost, direct quantization in Euclidean coordinates can distort highly anisotropic gradients. We present GIFT, a geometry-informed gradient communication method that transforms gradients into more isotropic coordinates before low-precision quantization. To make this practical, GIFT uses a one-sided, low-rank geometry approximation and applies it selectively to layers most sensitive to quantization error, while leaving the optimizer, training recipe, communication collective, and FP8 format unchanged. Across Llama-style models with approximately 600M and 2B parameters, GIFT achieves downstream performance comparable to Muon training with FP32 gradients. On 64 NVIDIA GH200 Superchips, GIFT reduces end-to-end training step time by 10.87% for Llama-600M and 17.05% for Llama-2B relative to FP32 gradient communication.

events.title: GNNs Beyond HBM: Compressed, Bit-Exact Feature Streaming for Out-of-Core Training
events.description: Graph neural networks increasingly train on node-feature matrices that exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory: ogbn-papers100M's is ~57 GB, beyond a commodity 8-40 GB card. Out-of-core systems (GIDS, Ginex, MariusGNN, GraphBolt, HMGraph) already stream features from host memory past HBM, but always uncompressed. GnnPress compresses the streamed feature store: it exposes an ordinary float array to the GNN while storing features compressed and materializing only a small, double-buffered resident window. On an NVIDIA A100-40GB, GnnPress trains ogbn-papers100M (52.9 GiB), which out-of-memories an in-core layout. A lossless zstd codec is bit-identical to the in-core run every epoch (max|dloss|=|dacc|=0), including under mini-batch SGD; a GPU-native lossy codec, cuSZp, reaches 3.13x while perturbing training loss by at most 1e-6 over 30 epochs. Mini-batch SGD reaches 61% accuracy at a measured 1.7 GiB peak GPU (31x below in-core). Compressing the feature stream, not merely avoiding OOM, distinguishes GnnPress from prior uncompressed out-of-core GNN training.

events.title: GenASPEN: Agentic AI for Automatic Performance Modeling of HPC Codes
events.description: The growing heterogeneity of HPC programming models and hardware architectures has made automated performance modeling more essential and more difficult. Compiler-based frameworks such as COMPASS and MAPredict need programming model-specific integration; frontier LLMs are flexible but predict runtime poorly; custom LLMs buy accuracy at prohibitive cost. We present GenASPEN, an agentic AI framework that assigns each task to the component best equipped for it: a Code Translation Agent (a context-aware chain-of-thought pipeline over GPT-OSS 120B, or a Code Llama 7B assistant fine-tuned with ChatHPC) converts CUDA/HIP kernels into ASPEN application models, and a Performance Modeling Agent combines them with machine and analytical models to predict FLOPs, loads, stores, and execution time on modern GPUs. Across 22 benchmarks on NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI300A, GenASPEN reaches 98.5% operation-count and 94.40%/93.09% execution-time accuracy, beating four frontier LLMs on 16 of 22 kernels with zero manual annotation.

events.title: Genome Variant Representation in Genome LMs and Multi-Omic AI: Efficiency, Scalability, and Medical Actionability
events.description:
The recent rapid growth and curation of large multi-omic datasets, driven largely by high-throughput sequencing, have provided unprecedented opportunities in medical and clinical research, especially for precision medicine. This presents an opportunity for improved multi-omic deep learning implementations for oncology tasks. However, it comes with a set of challenges, namely:

1. Granularity in genomic variant representation: representing complex, arbitrary-length genomic variant data without destroying spatial context or non-coding regulatory signals in both standalone and multi-omic models

2. Scalability and efficiency: establishing efficient and domain-informed data loading strategies, hyperparameter optimization guidelines and computationally scalable architectural choices, especially for resource-intensive medical applications

3. Systematized multi-omic integration: How can we rigorously evaluate multi-omics integration strategies and assess which combinations of omics modalities yield the most informative biological representations for oncology tasks?

To address these issues, we have made the following contributions. First, we developed a feasibility study into the representation of genomic variant data, leveraging genome language models (gLMs) to capture nucleotide-level dependencies across variable-length somatic variant-associated sequences for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis. Next, we scaled our framework to combine both coding exomes and non-coding regions by implementing input load balancing and architectural changes, improving performance on chosen oncology tasks. Finally, we introduced a generalized, versatile, and modular framework that incorporates key autoencoder architectures for representation learning, enabling exploration and robust evaluation of multi-modal omics integration.

The cumulative findings bridge hardware-efficient scaling, biological representation learning, and cancer-specific multi-omics to drive medical actionability.

events.title: HARD: Leveraging FleCSI for Heterogeneous Multi-Material Hydrodynamics
events.description:
Simulating multi-material hydrodynamic systems with disparate equations of state requires maintaining sharp material interfaces without numerical diffusion, a challenge for traditional methods that compromise accuracy or computational efficiency.

In this poster we extend HARD, a multi-material hydrodynamics code built on FleCSI that employs the Ghost Fluid Method enhanced with a multi-material Riemann solver for physically consistent interface treatment. Our novel contributions include sparse data structures reducing memory footprint by 25% and FleCSI backend optimizations enabling exceptional GPU scalability. We achieve 98.3% weak scaling efficiency on 32 CPU nodes and 81.3% on 16 GPU nodes, with single GPU nodes delivering 12.2× speedup over 128-core CPU nodes.

The implementation is complete and validated against analytical solutions and experimental data through shock tube, Rayleigh-Taylor instability, and 3D shock-bubble benchmarks.

Our poster will demonstrate performance metrics, showcase high-resolution 3D simulations, and provide live comparisons between CPU and GPU execution on representative multiphysics problems.

events.title: HPC and AI Water Usage: Findings From 11 Leading Supercomputing Centers
events.description: High-density artificial intelligence (AI) and high performance computing (HPC) workloads are increasing thermal loads and making water use an important facility consideration. This study establishes an operational baseline from 11 large HPC facilities using a 35-question survey covering cooling systems, water consumption, WUE, blowdown, water quality, and conservation barriers. Facilities with hybrid/adiabatic cooling report a lower WUE, indicating higher water efficiency among surveyed sites, while evaporative facilities generally reported higher WUE. Cooling-tower blowdown accounted for approximately 15%–33% of facility water use at surveyed evaporative sites. Higher cycles of concentration (CoC) can reduce water use, but water chemistry can limit operation. The study also identified a definite water-energy trade-off, particularly during peak summer conditions. Finally, closed-loop liquid cooling does not necessarily eliminate on-site water use; water consumption depends on the outdoor heat-rejection method.

events.title: HV-Coll: Co-Designing Collective Communication with Vectorized Homomorphic Compression
events.description: Inter-node collective communication constrains large-scale scientific simulations and distributed AI. Error-bounded lossy compression can reduce data volume, but prior CPU frameworks underuse memory bandwidth with scalar packing, lose compression ratio (CR) at SIMD-friendly block sizes, and repeat decompress–operate–compress (DOC) work during reductions. We present HV-Coll, which co-designs a block-aligned representation, SIMD encoding, outlier-aware fixed-length encoding, compressed-domain addition, and MPI collective schedules. Evaluated on 3,584 CPU cores, HV-Coll's homomorphic compression is up to 8.1x faster than hZCCL's scalar DOC workflow, and its outlier-aware encoding improves CR by up to 27.2%. HV-Coll collectives reach up to 47.2x, 23.4x, 43.8x, and 67.6x speedups over native MPI for Bcast, Scatter, Allreduce, and Alltoall, respectively.

events.title: Hall Pass: Per-Action Authorization for Shared Agents
events.description:
Autonomous agents deployed across federated research infrastructure are most valuable when shared across teams, yet few frameworks provide a way to control who may invoke which of an agent's actions. An owner must choose between keeping a private copy of an expensive agent or exposing one that any caller can use, inspect, or terminate. We examine three models for authorizing calls to a shared agent and prototype the third in the Academy middleware, backing per-action permissions with Globus Groups and enforcing them on the message path. We demonstrate with a shared SAM3 agent on Purdue Anvil.

At the poster we will walk through the three models and where each enforces access, then present overhead measurements and a larger shared-agent deployment on Anvil with results collected after initial submission.

events.title: Hardware-Aware Matrix-Free Algorithms for Accelerating Large-Scale Finite-Element Simulations on Distributed CPU and GPU Architectures
events.description:
Large-scale simulations governed by partial differential equations reduce, after finite-element (FE) discretization, to two kernels: operator action on large blocks of vectors inside eigensolvers, and the solution of Poisson or Helmholtz systems inside linear solvers. Both are limited by data movement rather than floating-point throughput, and the traditional assembled sparse-matrix and cell-matrix strategies scale poorly at high polynomial order, the first bound by memory traffic, the second by an operation count that grows as the sixth power of the order.

This dissertation develops hardware-aware matrix-free algorithms that evaluate operator actions on the fly through sum factorization, batched over the multivector dimension. The contributions are batched FE Helmholtz matrix-multivector products, using even-odd decomposition and SIMD vectorization on CPUs and fused register-blocked kernels on GPUs, a matrix-free Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonian action covering nonlocal projectors, real and complex arithmetic and inline constraint handling on AVX2/AVX-512/SVE CPUs and on GPUs with tensor cores and reduced-precision ghost exchange, a distributed-memory GPU fast-diagonalization solver that inverts the FE Laplacian exactly at O(N^(4/3)) FLOPs, and a device-native fused conjugate-gradient solver with a Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner.

Measured inside DFT-FE against existing baselines on Summit, Frontier, Fugaku, Polaris, Pravega and Aurora, the operator actions run 2.6x–5.8x faster than cell-matrix. The fused solve runs 5.86x faster than deal.II on 384 Aurora GPUs, and p-multigrid holds it at 5–7 iterations across polynomial orders. On tensor-product meshes one exact solve is 34x–3,186x faster than p-multigrid. The algorithms assume nothing specific to DFT and carry over to higher-order FE applications.

events.title: Helios: A Disaggregated MySQL Database That Scales Without Replication
events.description: Modern in-memory transaction engines can outpace a single SQL query processor, but scaling through replicas or shards adds propagation or coordination. Helios is a disaggregated MySQL database that scales query processing without read-serving replicas. Multiple read/write-capable MySQL nodes share one in-memory LineairDB engine, which validates consumed point and range reads and orders commits to provide external consistency. To avoid row-at-a-time RPCs, Helios compiles MySQL's chosen execution plan into a dependent read plan. Embedded DuckDB executes consistent analytical queries over the same PAX layout using epoch cuts and before-images. Our prototype achieves 40.5k transactions/s with four MySQL nodes at 1,024 TPC-C sessions, 3.24x the one-node throughput. On TPC-H SF=10, Helios is 2.20x faster than TiDB with TiFlash and 62.4x faster than MySQL with InnoDB. We present the architecture, consistency mechanisms, and performance results through diagrams and benchmark figures.

events.title: High-Performance Star-M SVD for Big Data Compression
events.description: In the era of big data, effectively compressing large datasets while performing complex mathematical operations is crucial. Tensor-based decomposition methods have shown superior compression capabilities with minimal loss of accuracy compared to traditional matrix methods. Under the star-M tensor framework, tensors can be decomposed in a matrix-mimetic way, including using the star-M SVD. This tensor SVD has optimality guarantees and has shown exceptional performance on specific types of data, but software implementations have been mostly limited to productivity-oriented languages. In this work, we present our development of a shared-memory parallel, high-performance solution designed to efficiently implement the underlying algorithms. This software will enable optimal compression of extensive scientific datasets, paving the way for enhanced data analysis and insights.

events.title: How the NERSC User Community Connects
events.description: High performance computing centers, such as NERSC, serve thousands of projects and users across many science domains and funding offices, yet staff have few systematic ways to see how these communities form, persist, and connect for planning and outreach. As an exploratory step toward surfacing actionable insights from allocation data, 2020–2026 Perlmutter allocation records are turned into yearly project and user networks, and community detection, weighted betweenness bridge detection, and liaison ranking. Null-model and matched-popularity tests confirm the structure is real and actionable: communities stay above the 95% null modularity band every year; about 10% of projects carry 66%–74% of cross-office connectivity; and the top 200 liaison candidates reach 69% of active users. To our knowledge, this is the first network analysis of an HPC facility’s community.

events.title: Impact of GPU Multistreaming on Task-Based DAG Execution in Dagger.jl
events.description:
Task-graph runtimes like Dagger.jl can now run independent tasks across multiple concurrent GPU streams, raising two questions: how should tasks be assigned to streams, and do more streams improve performance regardless of placement?

We benchmark four policies (round-robin, random, SDQ, and locality-aware) across four DAG topologies (linear, diamond, chainlink, tangled) and four stream counts (1, 2, 8, 32) on an NVIDIA H200 and an AMD MI300A. Every policy speeds up with more streams, but placement matters. At 32 streams, round-robin is fastest, averaging 4.5x speedup on H200 and 2.5x on MI300A, with SDQ close behind on H200 (4.0x). Locality-aware assignment issues 1.6x to 8x fewer synchronization events but reaches only 2.5x and 1.5x, so policy choice alone changes wall-clock time by up to 2.2x.

At the poster, we will walk attendees through the DAG-topology taxonomy and policy comparisons, and discuss which policy suits each workload and hardware backend.

events.title: Informing Probabilistic Tsunami Forecasting with Massive Earthquake Ensembles: FFT-Based Multi-GPU Source-to-Waveform Generation and Posterior-Start Flow Matching
events.description:
Cascadia tsunamis can reach nearby coastlines within minutes, demanding rapid probabilistic forecasts from early seafloor-pressure observations. Gaussian Bayesian inference is fast but cannot capture non-Gaussian earthquake variability, while generating large simulation ensembles is expensive.

We developed a distributed FFT-based source-to-waveform pipeline that reuses precomputed physical responses, generating full-scale Cascadia waveforms in 24 ms per rupture on 64 GB200 GPUs after setup. Our contribution couples this scalable generator with posterior-start flow matching, which transports the pressure-conditioned Gaussian posterior into an earthquake-informed, non-Gaussian distribution. Trained on one million stochastic ruptures, the model reduces RMSE by 79% and CRPS by 86% relative to the Gaussian baseline across 4,096 held-out events.

events.title: Interactive Knowledge Graph Supporting Self-Directed and Personalized High Performance Computing Education
events.description: Across universities, compute centers, and industry partners, significant resources are put into developing educational materials for researchers and developers in high performance computing (HPC). It is important to acknowledge that the range of research backgrounds in HPC is beneficial for the community in many ways but poses challenges for education. In particular, many HPC users and developers would benefit from foundational knowledge that may seem obvious to computer scientists. We propose an interactive knowledge graph of fundamental concepts of HPC, allowing learners to choose their own starting point and navigate forwards or backwards through related topics. This content is delivered through accessible, short lecture videos featuring animations that are delivered by HPC specialists. These videos are supplemented with formative assessments, and all of the concepts are structured into an interactive knowledge graph which specifies dependencies between concepts so that the learner can find their own pathways through the learning journey.

events.title: JUNIQ Benchmark Suite: A Decade of Application Benchmarks on Quantum Computers
events.description:
As quantum computing hardware rapidly evolves, traditional metrics like gate fidelity and Quantum Volume are insufficient for predicting real-world utility. Researchers and industry users need objective, application-centric benchmarks to gauge when quantum processors will be ready for practical tasks. However, the lack of standardized infrastructure often leads to non-reproducible performance claims and makes it difficult to track progress across different hardware generations and technologies.

We present the JUNIQ Benchmark Suite (JBS), a large collection of benchmark problems and a vendor-agnostic, open-source initiative designed to track quantum technology readiness over decades. Unlike suites focused on synthetic benchmarks, JBS (https://go.fzj.de/juniq-benchmark-suite-page) emphasizes application-domains including computational biology, logistics, and hardware-diagnostics.

JBS hosts an extensive repository of empirical performance data collected over more than a decade (2016–2026) across over 30 analog and digital quantum processing units, tracking quantum technology readiness over successive hardware generations.

events.title: K2S-Gate: A Secure Kubernetes-to-Slurm Gateway with Unified Service Catalogs for Web-Based AI and HPC Applications
events.description: The rapid growth of AI and high performance computing (HPC) applications demands seamless integration of cloud-native and HPC environments, yet heterogeneous software stacks keep these systems isolated, limiting unified deployment of and access to web-based applications. This work presents K2S-Gate, a secure Kubernetes-to-Slurm gateway that bridges cloud-native and HPC infrastructures through a unified web platform. K2S-Gate introduces a job-to-service transformation paradigm that converts Slurm batch jobs into dynamically accessible web services, enabling one-click execution on HPC compute nodes without SSH tunneling or port forwarding. It also provides a template-based Unified Service Catalog for deployment across heterogeneous environments. For secure, scalable access, K2S-Gate integrates a Secure Access Layer combining single sign-on (SSO), an OAuth2-based identity provider (IdP), and an Istio ingress gateway. Validated on the KISTI-5 supercomputer and integrated into the MyKSC portal, K2S-Gate demonstrates its practicality in real-world HPC environments.

events.title: Kamo: Bringing Many-Core Scalability to MySQL
events.description:
MySQL’s SQL ecosystem is widely used, but its default InnoDB storage engine does not scale well under high concurrency. Kamo is a prototype DBMS built on MySQL that substantially extends the initial LineairDB storage-engine integration. Our contributions include named tables, relational insert/update/delete semantics, secondary and composite indexes, ordered scans, and broader MySQL handler coverage sufficient to execute all five BenchBase TPC-C transaction classes. The current prototype has been implemented and evaluated on single-node and semi-synchronously replicated configurations, reaching up to 18.7× the request throughput of MySQL/InnoDB under the evaluated settings.

In the poster session, we will present Kamo’s system architecture, the key relational and MySQL-integration extensions, and end-to-end TPC-C and YCSB-A results. We will also discuss the observed scaling behavior, current bottlenecks, and limitations of the prototype.

events.title: Large-Scale Distributed State-Vector Simulation of IQPE for Early-FTQC
events.description:
Iterative quantum phase estimation (IQPE) is promising for Early-FTQC because it recycles one ancilla, but classically validating molecular workloads requires distributed state-vector simulation, where qubit reordering and GPU-to-GPU data movement limit scalability.

We present a communication-aware IQPE implementation in chemqulacs-gpu. Building on published Lazy Qubit Reordering for topology-aware mapping reuse, our IQPE-specific contributions are rank-global Z folding that avoids unnecessary reordering, rank-MSB probability evaluation without amplitude gathering, and their integration for systems-scale execution. All components are implemented and evaluated on ABCI-Q. A 32-qubit chlorine workload retains 90.2% parallel efficiency from 2 to 1,024 H100 GPUs, and the widest completed run uses a 41-qubit, 32-TiB complex-FP64 state vector across 1,024 GPUs.

At the poster, circuit and data-movement diagrams will explain the techniques, while scaling plots and a large-run table will support discussion of communication costs, memory limits, and practical IQPE simulation.

events.title: Learning Within the Laws of the Hardware: Rethinking Multi-GPU Performance Modeling and Workload Characterization
events.description: Performance modeling enables runtime estimation, scalability analysis, and bottleneck identification without committing large-scale compute resources. However, existing methods rely on either analytical or empirical models: the former are interpretable and generalize by construction but are limited in accuracy by architectural assumptions, while the latter are accurate only where training data exists and offer no insight into performance-limiting factors. Addressing these concerns, we propose hardware-informed neural networks (HINN), applying the physics-informed neural network (PINN) methodology to multi-GPU performance modeling, where the governing "physics" consists of hardware-derived architectural laws. HINN retains established analytical models as differentiable priors and learns residual corrections subject to hardware-derived constraints enforced via automatic differentiation across the domain. Evaluated on five HPC applications on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, HINN achieves 7.6% and 9.9% median relative estimation error for kernel and communication predictions, while enabling extrapolation to unseen configurations and automated bottleneck classification.

events.title: Leveraging Sparsity for LLM Inference in a Commercial Processing-in-Memory Prototype
events.description: LM decoding is bounded by the memory wall: weights and KV cache move every token, and the low-arithmetic-intensity matrix–vector products of decode leave throughput set by bandwidth rather than compute. Bank-level PIM attacks this by keeping weights resident and computing in place, but its lockstep execution cannot skip zeros. We present the first end-to-end sparsity-aware inference framework for bank-level PIM. A column-union cost model shows that lockstep cost is set by the union of columns (or KV tokens) a bank-group must visit, not the nonzero count. Activation-aware weight pruning aligns surviving columns across rows and matrices, while a group-aligned adaptation of query-aware KV selection collapses the attention scan. Against a measured NVIDIA H200 at batch-1, this work cuts per-token latency by 4–7× and, beyond moderate context, undercuts the GPU’s most energy-efficient batched configuration (crossing near 10K, around 6× lower at 128K), while preserving accuracy and extending on-board context.

events.title: Load Balancing and Communication Bottlenecks in SpMV on the Cerebras WSE-3
events.description:
SpMV is a fundamental kernel in scientific computing, but irregular memory access limits its scalability on conventional parallel systems. The Cerebras CS-3 distributes all data across on-chip SRAM on a two-dimensional PE mesh, so accessing non-local data becomes inter-PE communication rather than a memory-hierarchy traversal. Whether this low-latency advantage is sustained at scale remains unclear.

We present the first execution-time breakdown of SpMV on the CS-3. Our novel contribution is identifying, under load balancing, which component dominates among computation, inter-PE communication, reduction, and synchronization wait. Load balancing achieved a 3.40x speedup for Poisson3Da, while inter-PE communication reached 71.2% of execution time for F1. We evaluate five matrices from the SuiteSparse collection.

At the poster session, we will walk visitors through our execution-time breakdown charts, explain the bottleneck transition using a simple broadcast-round model, and discuss implications for communication-aware SpMV on wafer-scale processors.

events.title: MATCH: Multimodal Alignment Through Contrastive Learning of Heterogeneous Sensor Streams at Static Nodes
events.description:
Multimodal environmental sensing networks routinely capture temporally co-occurring conditions across incompatible representations: an RGB frame, a thermal frame, an audio clip, and environmental readings share no common feature space.
