We present MATCH, a contrastive learning framework that combines frozen, domain-matched pretrained backbones with lightweight trainable projection heads to align real-world node data across all four modalities in a shared 512-dimensional embedding space without task-specific labels. A multi-view InfoNCE loss aligns all six modality pairs. Evaluated on a 195-observation held-out test set from a single deployed node, retrieval improves over random across all six pairs, with RGB↔Thermal strongest — notably, 73.3% of its incorrect top-5 retrievals fall within ±2 hours of the correct time of day, versus a 20.4% chance baseline, indicating the learned space captures coarse diurnal structure.

At the poster we'll present our architecture, cross-modal retrieval examples, quantitative alignment results, and discuss next steps toward node-specific adaptation.

events.title: Machine Learning-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for HPC Workload Scheduling
events.description: As high-performance computing (HPC) systems reach exascale, schedulers that optimize a single objective, typically throughput, prove inadequate for facilities that must simultaneously manage performance, energy consumption, and resilience under substantial workload uncertainty. This dissertation develops and empirically validates a three-component multi-objective scheduling framework built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), testing the hypothesis that graph-structured representations of jobs and system state, combined with adaptive multi-objective learning, outperform traditional and single-objective learned schedulers in production HPC environments. The framework comprises (1) GNN-RL, a graph attention network and PPO-based scheduler encoding job dependencies and resource contention; (2) HARMONIC, a Bayesian uncertainty-aware optimizer that separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and balances performance, energy, and resilience via a multi-objective DDPG agent with Pareto-front guarantees; and (3) EA-GATSched, a GATv2-based scheduler driven by a GEOPM-calibrated physics power model and a state-conditioned Pareto-weighting network. GNN-RL and HARMONIC evaluations are complete: GNN-RL improves utilization by 13.8%–20.2% and throughput by 15.0%–50.0% over EASY-backfilling across 377,234 production jobs on three ALCF systems; HARMONIC reduces energy by 10%–19%, improves throughput by 16%–25%, and cuts performance variability by 18%–32% across simulation and a 64-node testbed. EA-GATSched, the framework's in-progress third component, has achieved 27.3%–56.6% energy reduction and up to 95.8% utilization across 389,604 jobs on the same three systems, with cross-architecture GEOPM validation remaining as future work. These two studies draw on overlapping, not additive, job sets from the same ALCF systems and together establish relational, uncertainty-aware, and physics-grounded learning as jointly necessary for sustainable exascale HPC scheduling.

events.title: Magellan: A Carbon-Aware Task Scheduler for Geo-Distributed Systems
events.description:
Magellan is a decentralized carbon-aware task scheduler that reduces the carbon footprint of long-running, stateful workloads through checkpoint-restart migration across geo-distributed infrastructure. Prior carbon-aware systems have largely relied on simulation and targeted stateless or batch jobs while overlooking the real overheads of wide-area migration.

Magellan addresses these gaps through three primary contributions: a decision engine that jointly balances computational progress, carbon emissions, migration overhead, and monetary cost under an explicit budget cap; a decentralized bidding and destination-arbitration protocol with a checkpoint-restart runtime using CRIU for unmodified processes and native checkpoints for ML and HPC workloads; and validation on CloudLab and Google Cloud under real WAN conditions and measured destination capacity constraints. Across 72 annual scenarios and three workload classes, Magellan reduces lifecycle carbon by up to 92.8% (13×) with 11.6% lower makespan at approximately neutral cost. The poster presents the architecture, migration workflow, decision model, testbeds, and key carbon-cost-performance tradeoffs.

events.title: Malleable OpenFOAM: Communication-Efficient Dynamic Reconfiguration for CFD
events.description:
We introduce the first malleable implementation of OpenFOAM, the most widely used open-source CFD solver, allowing it to dynamically change its node allocation mid-run instead of staying fixed for the job's duration. The system uses communication efficiency (CE), measured live by TALP/DLB, to trigger resizing via the DMR framework, which handles checkpoint-restart at a new node count. The key technical contribution is identifying which runtime objects must be redistributed at reconfiguration using OpenFOAM's AUTO_WRITE flag to isolate true solver state, while discarding stale cached objects that otherwise cause deadlocks at scale.

Tested on a 92M-cell automotive CFD benchmark on the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer, the controller successfully converges from both under- and over-provisioned starting points to the target CE band. This malleable implementation of OpenFOAM automatically selects resources so users only pay for the efficient run and do not waste resources or wait longer for results.

events.title: Mallet: An Open-Source Formal Verification Flow for Agile Domain-Specific Accelerator Development
events.description: Custom domain-specific accelerators are gaining attention for the significant performance gains they deliver on specialized workloads: scientific instruments utilize custom accelerators to sustain extreme data rates, and molecular dynamics accelerators can achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups over general-purpose supercomputing systems. However, their increasing complexity and specialization make verification challenging, allowing design flaws to escape detection and leading to incorrect results. Formal verification can fill this gap, but accelerator designs shift quickly, formal properties are hard to write, and LLM-generated designs often mirror bugs in the very properties meant to catch them. We present Mallet, an open-source formal verification flow for the Chisel stack. Mallet renders properties from human-specified AXI memory-map annotations, so design-spec drift is caught at compile time, and issues them to multiple model-checking engines, producing an adjudication matrix that ranks proof strength and flags vacuous passes. We demonstrate Mallet across five AXI4-Lite DUTs and a fault-injection suite.

events.title: Measurement Error for CPU Performance Counters
events.description: Understanding supercomputers’ performance and behavior is critical for their optimization and acquisition. Performance counters, which count the number of various types of CPU events, are the primary means of profiling CPUs. However, they may be inaccurate due to measurement errors. We can identify measurement error if we can calculate the true event count, but the true count is obscured by hardware and software unknowns. We handle hardware unknowns by measuring events that do not depend on the hardware implementation, and we handle software unknowns by carefully configuring standardized benchmarks. While we find measuring errors up to 0.45% of the true count, the measuring errors we find are typically much less than 0.01%.

events.title: Measuring Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Dependability via Wide Area Network Fault Injection
events.description: Hybrid high-performance computing and quantum computing (HPC-QC) systems rely on quantum networks for secure communication, yet their dependability under real-world conditions has not been systematically studied. This work presents a fault injection study of BB84 QKD using QFabric, a quantum-network emulation platform built on the FABRIC testbed. Unlike simulators, QFabric routes classical sifting traffic over a real WAN link, enabling cross-layer fault injection. We find that polarization fidelity, rather than packet loss, determines QBER, with no significant interaction between the two; detector efficiency similarly affects key rate independently of packet loss. However, individual runs at marginal fidelity still exceed the security failure threshold from ordinary variance alone, despite a mean QBER that appears safely below it, while no such failures occur at higher fidelity. This shows that aggregate QBER statistics can mask real per-session security risk, and that cross-layer fault interaction in BB84 depends on the specific physical mechanism involved.

events.title: Megabytes in Murmuration: From 8-MB X-Ray Projections to Interpretable TB-Scale Structure Through Automated HPC
events.description: Synchrotron tomography beamlines routinely produce large sequences of two-dimensional X-ray projection images as their primary experimental output. Individually, these images often provide limited scientific value: the features of interest in biological samples typically emerge only after transformation into three-dimensional reconstructed volumes. This transformation is computationally demanding, requiring sustained high-throughput data transfers, and multiple processing steps — even more so for samples larger than the field of view. We describe the automated data acquisition and processing system implemented at the EMBL P14 beamline at PETRA III, Hamburg, Germany, and the underlying computing architecture that enables the beamline users to inspect interpretable three-dimensional representations of their samples shortly after X-ray exposure.

events.title: ND-Locate: Localizing Non-Determinism in MPI Applications
events.description: Large-scale MPI applications can yield different scientific results from identical inputs due to non-deterministic execution, yet current tools offer little help in pinpointing its source. We present ND-LOCATE, a framework that localizes execution-level non-determinism to application functions, achieving Pearson correlations up to 0.97 on benchmark applications and identifying the code regions responsible for output variability in the production cosmological simulator Enzo.

events.title: Near-Real-Time Performance Visualization of MPI Applications: Integrating Performance Analysis Into HPC Education
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) has become an essential capability in both industrial practice and scientific research, making the acquisition of practical HPC skills an increasingly important objective in higher education. Parallel programming with models such as MPI and OpenMP is central to this training, and students should gain experience on real HPC clusters rather than on local machines. However, universities often have access only to limited, partitioned, or decommissioned cluster resources, while learners must also master operational concepts such as SSH, SCP, and batch-based job management with systems such as SLURM. In addition, efficient MPI programs require performance analysis, yet established tools are designed for experts and assume prior knowledge of instrumentation, measurement, and interpretation.

EduMPI Suite addresses this gap by providing an educational environment for executing and analyzing MPI programs on HPC clusters in near-real-time. It automatically delivers visual feedback on MPI communication events during execution, enabling students to observe program behavior and understand the performance characteristics. A distinctive feature is the visualization of internal algorithmic communication patterns of collective operations, which are often hidden in professional tools but are crucial for understanding the performance implications of collective communication.

Usability evaluations over multiple semesters show that EduMPI Suite lowers the barriers to practical HPC performance analysis, is recommended by students, and improves the success rate of identifying and explaining performance problems to 96%, compared with 60% for professional analysis tools. Its near-real-time performance analysis is enabled by low measurement overhead <3.8% and low query latency <0.09 s.

events.title: Nexus: Malleable Physical Infrastructure for Dynamic Workload Convergence
events.description: Contemporary research environments demand the integration of heterogeneous computing paradigms. This poster introduces Nexus, an incubator research project and empirical testbed designed to deploy complex, dynamic bare-metal infrastructure. Nexus bridges bare-metal immutability with cloud-native orchestration to enable the automated convergence of disjoint computational paradigms onto unified, reproducible hardware.

events.title: One Page, Two DMAs: Writing 400 GbE TCP Streams to NVMe Without Touching the Data
events.description: Data transfer nodes write wide-area TCP streams to storage. On a 400GbE testbed, the buffered-write path delivers only 138Gbps on a server whose SSDs sustain 453Gbps: cores saturate copying, dirty-page throttling stalls the application, and stalls leak into TCP as window collapse and spurious retransmissions. We present zcp_ingest, which establishes an end-to-end alignment invariant that lets a NIC RX page serve unmodified as a storage write buffer, using only mainline mechanisms. Header-data split plus one TCP_MAXSEG option makes virtually all payload bytes arrive page-aligned; TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE maps NIC-written pages into userspace; io_uring writes them to NVMe via O_DIRECT — virtually all payload bytes reach storage without CPU copying. With deterministic sender-side placement (SRAP), 16 flows sustain 373.4Gbps — 2.7x the buffered baseline and 97.4% of the path ceiling — with bit-exact terabyte-scale transfers and 4.4x lower CPU cost. Controlled violations establish one-flow-per-queue placement as a prerequisite for fair, drop-free, reproducible operation.

events.title: Online Load Balancing of High-Order Mixed-Element Simulations on Heterogeneous Architectures
events.description: Scale-resolving simulations performed on clusters can be expensive, spanning hours to months. Efficient use of shared HPC resources increasingly involves allocations combining devices with different throughputs, requiring effective load partitioning across heterogeneous architectures. This work develops an online, distributed, diffusion-based repartitioning strategy driven by observed MPI wait-time statistics at runtime. The method infers cost imbalance to derive a target load distribution, then incrementally relocates interface-adjacent elements across ranks while preserving the existing partition structure. Integrated into the open-source compressible Navier–Stokes solver PyFR, the method is evaluated for flow around a circular cylinder at Re = 3900. Online load balancing achieves 101%, 116%, and 119% of homogeneous sum-of-parts performance targets across three heterogeneous configurations. Completed RK45 simulations achieve 2.4x, 2.8x, and 7.7x time-to-solution speedups.

events.title: OpenCCL: A Proposed Open Standard and Reference Implementation Unifying *CCLs for Performance, Portability, and Productivity
events.description: NVIDIA's NCCL is the de-facto GPU communication API for distributed AI, but it is a toolkit rather than a specification: its semantics are thin, it is tied to one vendor's stack, and other *CCLs re-implement or fork it. OpenCCL proposes an open standard and reference implementation: a normative specification with an ABI-stable header over pluggable transports and collective engines, so one library spans vendors and fabrics without application changes. OpenCCL runs unmodified NCCL codes and addresses all 33 entry points of NCCL 2.23.4. On Slingshot-11 it builds on RAPIDS Cascade APIs: kernel-initiated transfers behind a stream-triggered interface that fits NCCL semantics. Preliminary results on LLNL's Tuolumne, an El Capitan-class system, outperform RCCL and Cray MPICH for Allreduce from 256 bytes to 16 KiB, and Cascade outperforms Cray MPICH and our earlier stream-triggered MPI for small messages. MSCCL's AllToNext is implemented. The poster invites participation in standardization, implementation, and AI adoption.

events.title: OpenCosmo Visualization: In-Browser Exploration of Cosmological Particle Data
events.description: Querying a cosmological simulation and seeing it are usually separated by a dedicated tool, a preprocessing step, and a broken workflow. The OpenCosmo Visualization Application (OVA) closes that gap inside the OpenCosmo Portal: a completed query opens directly into an interactive 3D view of the queried particles, in the same browser tab, with no export, installation, or preprocessing. Built on WebGL2 and Babylon.js, OVA adds per-type controls, dynamic filtering by scalar range, a 3D clipping plane, screen-space selection statistics, and one-click immersive WebXR on top of point rendering. Even on integrated laptop graphics, OVA ingests and renders 5M points of a HACC halo end-to-end in about 6.7 seconds, sustains 114.8 FPS, and records zero blocking main-thread tasks.

events.title: OpenEvolve-Driven Selection and Tuning of Ozaki-Scheme GPU Matrix Multiplication
events.description: Ozaki-Scheme is an established numerical method for emulating high-precision GEMM on low-precision GPU hardware. Using it means navigating a costly accuracy/performance tradeoff across algorithm variants and their tuning parameters. This work automates that process with a multi-stage pipeline combining rule-based variant selection with an LLM-driven evolutionary tuner (OpenEvolve). New features include a monotonicity-constrained XGBoost classifier predicting whether an accuracy target is reachable before spending GPU time and a throughput-priority mode trading bounded accuracy for up to 106.6% higher GFLOPS. A per-island-search fix stabilizes OpenEvolve convergence, widening the best-valid range from about 45-50K to 61-108K GFLOPS. In the Quantum ESPRESSO AUSURF112 workload, native cuBLAS remains 1.21x faster than the tuned complex-GEMM configuration, and the pipeline reaches 20.6x native cuBLAS on GB10 versus 1.42x on GH200. At the poster session, we will talk through the pipeline, presenting five result panels: throughput mode, feasibility classifier, OE-search convergence, AUSURF benchmark, and GH200/GB10 hardware comparison.

events.title: OptimasX: An Agentic End-to-End GPU Performance Optimization Workflow in the Code Editor
events.description: Optimizing a GPU kernel costs 30 manual steps before code changes: pick a profiler, reach a remote system, submit a job, read the report. Domain scientists hold the most GPU hours and the least profiling expertise, so no one tunes the code with the most to gain. OPTIMAS removes two steps by guiding a language model with runtime evidence, but assumes the user can produce it. We transformed OPTIMAS into OPTIMASX, a multi-agentic system that produces the evidence and removes all 32 steps. From a VS Code extension, OPTIMASX profiles code, reads evidence, proposes changes, checks correctness, and measures runtime. The extension holds workflow state, so a queued job or backend restart cannot end the session. On an A100, OPTIMASX reached 4.80× on XSBench and 1.19× on Sobol with bit-identical output, and extends to Cholla and eight HeCBench apps. The speedups are OPTIMAS’s, and the end-to-end automation is ours.

events.title: Optimizing HPC Performance for CDC-Based Storage and Reconstruction of High-Resolution Imagery
events.description: High-resolution imagery is increasingly used for community asset management, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. These missions preserve details needed for inspection, but they can generate hundreds of gigabytes of data, creating long-term storage and transfer burdens. To reduce this burden, this study evaluates conditional diffusion compression (CDC) for storing and reconstructing high-resolution imagery on GPU supercomputers. We do not propose a new compression model. Instead, we study how CDC should be configured to make better use of HPC resources. Using 100 RGB images from Galveston, Texas, on NCSA DeltaAI GH200, we compare checkpoint and tiling settings by measuring compression ratio, runtime, throughput, peak GPU memory, image quality, artifacts, object detection, and segmentation stability. The balanced b00064 checkpoint with 256 × 256 tiling reduces peak GPU memory to 1.57 GB, reaches 45.4 images per hour, and keeps a 79.98× compression ratio.

events.title: PERNIX: High-Throughput SIMD Floating-Point Compression
events.description: Scientific applications increasingly spend time and energy moving floating-point data between CPUs, memory, and accelerators. PERNIX is an open-source C++ library for block-wise floating-point compression and decompression on CPUs, motivated by the transfer and storage of electron repulsion integrals in CP2K. It combines established quantization with novel SIMD bit-packing and unpacking kernels for AVX2, AVX2+BMI2, and AVX-512-VBMI. Table-driven permutations, shifts, and sign extension enable efficient processing of non-byte-aligned widths. ARM NEON and SVE2 backends are under development. We evaluate in-core throughput, cache and DRAM behavior, and end-to-end host-to-device and device-to-host PCIe pipelines. The poster presents the 512-bit format, SIMD design, measured-versus-modeled throughput, and end-to-end transfer results.

events.title: ParslBox: Computational Materials Workflow Executor for AI Agents on High Performance Computing Systems
events.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can autonomously construct large computational materials workflows, but executing these adaptive, fine-grained workloads efficiently across diverse high performance computing (HPC) systems remains challenging. We present ParslBox (PBX), a lightweight workflow execution toolkit for computational materials applications on HPC systems. PBX provides a local job database, fine-grained CPU/GPU resource management, portable execution across heterogeneous HPC systems, and command-line, Python, and Model Context Protocol interfaces for both users and AI agents. Scalability was demonstrated on up to 2,000 nodes and 24,000 concurrent workers while maintaining low orchestration overhead. Strong-scaling studies using LAMMPS with MACE models and VASP demonstrated transparent execution of production scientific applications. Agentic benchmarks showed reliable workflow construction across multiple closed-weight and open-weight language models. End-to-end agent-driven generation of machine-learned force fields for molten LiCl-NaCl and LiCl-KCl systems further demonstrated autonomous orchestration of complex multi-stage HPC workflows.

events.title: Performance Analysis of Inline Compression on Sparse Matrix Vector Multiplication ​
events.description: Sparse matrix vector multiplication (SPMV) plays a critical role in scientific computing. From computational fluid dynamics, to artificial intelligence, to economics problems, the use cases are vast. Additionally, the data required for high performance computing (HPC) jobs is quickly outgrowing available memory storage. In-line compression aims to mitigate this memory bottleneck by keeping data compressed in storage and only decompressing as needed. We analyze the effects of performing this in-line compression with SPMV and apply various optimizations to examine their effects on execution time and the overall memory footprint.

events.title: Performance Analysis of Phaseless Auxiliary Field Quantum Monte Carlo
events.description: Predicting molecular behavior requires knowing a molecule's ground-state energy, a calculation whose exact cost grows exponentially with system size. Phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC) approximates this energy via guided random walks, where accuracy and cost depend heavily on the quality of the trial wavefunction used to steer the walk. We compare two quantum methods for preparing this trial wavefunction, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and the Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE), benchmarked on NERSC Perlmutter using linear hydrogen chains. At H8 (16 qubits), GQE reduces end-to-end pipeline wall-time by roughly 5x relative to ADAPT-UCCSD, while matching VQE-family accuracy near equilibrium bond length. These results motivate extending the study to H10 chains and multi-node scaling to determine whether GQE's cost advantage persists at larger, more strongly correlated systems.

events.title: Performance Evaluation of a Heterogeneous CPU-GPU Framework for Real-Time ECG Analytics
events.description: Real-time cardiac digital twins require analytics pipelines that are both computationally efficient and diagnostically accurate. This paper presents a heterogeneous high performance computing framework integrating OpenMP parallelized CPU preprocessing with a CUDA-accelerated convolutional neural network for ECG beat classification using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. The preprocessing pipeline achieved a 4.85× speedup and 79% runtime reduction using eight CPU threads. The GPU classifier achieved 78.17% accuracy, a macro-ROC–AUC of 0.773, and throughput of 175,712 beats/s, representing an 11.2× improvement over CPU batch inference. A Digital Twin Readiness Assessment Framework evaluated predictive performance, computational efficiency, scalability, and deployment feasibility. Results indicate that preprocessing and inference satisfy real-time requirements, while classification of minority arrhythmia classes remains the primary limitation. Future work will focus on optimizing the classification model to improve minority-class performance and overall digital twin readiness.

events.title: Performance-Portable GPU Acceleration of the Hybrid PIC Code dHybridR
events.description: Hybrid particle-in-cell simulations are widely used to study kinetic processes in collisionless astrophysical and space plasmas, yet the high cost of large-scale three-dimensional runs has largely confined production studies to two dimensions or restricted domains. To address this challenge, we present a performance-portable GPU implementation of the hybrid particle-in-cell code dHybridR. It combines OpenMP target offloading with specialized SYCL kernels for the most expensive operations in a unified CPU-GPU codebase for Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs. On the exascale supercomputers Aurora and Frontier, dHybridR achieves weak scaling efficiencies of 86%–97% at 49,152 accelerators on each machine, and at 256 particles per cell, its full-node GPU throughput is up to 32x that of the vectorized CPU implementation at approximately 90% less energy per particle-update. To our knowledge, no other hybrid particle-in-cell code has reported GPU performance at this scale. These advances lower the barrier to large-scale three-dimensional hybrid-kinetic simulations.

events.title: Plexus-v2: Extreme-Scale GNN Training with Communication-Free Sampling and 4D Hybrid Parallelism
events.description: GNNs are widely used for learning on graph datasets derived from various real-world scenarios. Learning from extremely large graphs requires distributed training, and mini-batch training is a popular approach for parallelizing GNN training. Existing distributed mini-batch approaches have significant performance bottlenecks due to expensive sampling methods and limited scaling when using data parallelism. We present Plexus-v2, a four-dimensional hybrid parallel framework for scalable mini-batch GNN training that combines communication-free distributed sampling, three-dimensional parallel matrix multiplication, and data parallelism. Plexus-v2 introduces a uniform vertex sampling algorithm, enabling each process to construct its local shard of subgraph without any inter-process communication. Combining 3D PMM with data parallelism enables Plexus-v2 to scale to much larger GPU counts than vanilla data parallelism with significantly lower communication overheads. We evaluate Plexus-v2 on five graph datasets and scale to 2,048 GPUs/GCDs. On Perlmutter, Plexus-v2 achieves 3.5x end-to-end training speedup over the best-performing SOTA frameworks on ogbn-products.

events.title: Posters Display (Research Posters, Interactive Research e-Posters, ACM SRC, Doctoral Showcase)
Predictive Modeling of Effective Peak Throughput for Regional In-Network Caching
events.description:
Large-scale scientific experiments, particularly in high-energy physics, generate massive datasets repeatedly accessed worldwide. Regional in-network caching reduces redundant long-distance transfers through efficient local data sharing. To optimally allocate bandwidth, we must understand and predict peak cache throughput behavior.

We analyzed three years of cache hit and miss throughputs from the Southern California Petabyte-Scale Cache and built a machine learning model to forecast daily peak throughput. We examined three peak metrics: maximum, 99th percentile, and 95th percentile. Each distinctly guides resource allocation, as maximum captures all traffic but wastes capacity, while percentiles cover most traffic at lower bandwidth.

Results show one-day-ahead forecasts closely following demand, but accuracy degrades at longer horizons. Future work includes enhanced long-horizon models and more granular hourly models.

In the poster session, I’ll explain caching, describe peak throughput trends, and discuss results, limitations, and future work from forecasting.

events.title: Proposal of a Transparent Dynamic Core Allocation Method for MPI/OpenMP Hybrid Parallelization
events.description:
Load balancing is essential for maximizing performance and energy efficiency in MPI/OpenMP hybrid applications on supercomputers. While dynamic core binding (DCB) mitigates process-level imbalances by dynamically binding CPU cores, conventional methods require manual source code modifications. We propose a fully transparent DCB method eliminating user-level code alterations. By leveraging OpenMP Tools (OMPT) and Profiling MPI (PMPI) via a dynamically linked shared library, our method automatically intercepts computation phases and calculates load parameters from actual computation time by subtracting MPI wait time from the execution time of OpenMP parallel regions.

Evaluations on the Miyabi-C supercomputer using a Lattice H-matrix application demonstrate up to a 1.54x speedup and 32.0% energy reduction on a single node. Furthermore, 16-node tests demonstrate performance and energy benefits at scale.

Our poster will feature architectural diagrams of the OMPT/PMPI integration and performance graphs comparing static mapping, conventional DCB, and our transparent approach.

events.title: Pumped Two-Phase Cooling for the Next-Gen Chips with Heat Flux Over 4 W/mm2
events.description: Pumped two-phase cooling is a promising solution for the increasing heat flux of next-generation GPUs. This study presents a pumped two-phase cooling distribution unit (CDU) and loop architecture and compares the thermal performance of a two-phase cold plate with the same design operating with PG25 coolant. Test results show that the two-phase cold plate can dissipate over 3500 W, while both refrigerant and PG25 cooling can meet the projected thermal requirements of future GPUs with average heat flux above 1 W/mm² and hotspot heat flux above 3 W/mm². Although cooling performance is ultimately limited by fluid thermophysical properties and flow conditions, the thermal challenges of upcoming GPU generations remain manageable. Future work will investigate alternative cold plate materials and thermal conductivity optimization to further enhance cooling performance.

events.title: QR-Omega: Communication Avoiding 2.5D Householder QR
events.description: Orthogonalization is a key step in Krylov methods, tensor-network algorithms, least-squares solvers, and emerging machine-learning methods. Householder QR is numerically robust for orthogonalization, but on GPUs its performance is often limited by data movement and synchronization. We present QR-Ω, a hierarchical 2.5D Householder QR formulation that extends hierarchical QR with four execution operations: Split, Replicate, Combine, and Pipeline. These operations control how data is partitioned, replicated, reduced, and overlapped across the GPU memory hierarchy while preserving the Householder elimination order. On an NVIDIA H200, we compare QR-Ω with tuned cuSOLVER, MAGMA, and SLATE implementations in FP64, FP32, TF32, and 3×TF32. Across matrix sizes up to n = 131,072, QR-Ω approaches matrix-multiplication throughput while maintaining small numerical errors in FP64, FP32. Our implementation surpasses the state-of-the-art libraries cited above in performance by up to two times without loss of accuracy, while maintaining advantage in all tested sizes and precisions.

events.title: Qdislib: Implementation and Evaluation of Circuit Cutting and Sampling Techniques for Quantum Circuits
events.description: Circuit cutting enables quantum circuits to exceed the qubit limits of current quantum hardware and simulators by partitioning circuits into independently executable fragments. However, different cutting strategies introduce distinct trade-offs in computational overhead, sampling complexity, and reconstruction accuracy. We present a systematic evaluation of the four circuit-cutting techniques implemented in Qdislib, an open-source framework for scalable hybrid quantum–classical execution across CPUs, GPUs, simulators, and QPUs. Our study compares theoretical complexity, reconstruction accuracy, execution time, and distributed scalability, highlighting an optimized wire-cutting implementation that reduces fragment scaling from 8^k to 3^k+4^k and a Hadamard-based gate-cutting method that eliminates mid-circuit measurements while preserving accuracy. The poster will present the Qdislib workflow, implementation details, and experimental results, providing practical guidelines for selecting circuit-cutting strategies on HPC systems and quantum hardware.

events.title: QoS Coverage Maps for Placement and Readiness in Urgent Digital Twins
events.description: Urgent continuum workflows may miss deadlines because of poor task placement, delayed artifact readiness, insufficient compute capacity, or excessive full-fidelity execution time. We isolate placement and readiness while holding capacity and fidelity fixed. We introduce QoS coverage maps, which vary offered load and readiness delay, and classify whether the primary diagnostic target (tau) of 50% on-time completion is met by the best-performing of three non-learning baselines, learned placement, advance artifact staging, or neither. The threshold separates operating regions. For wildfire, learned placement improves on-time completion by up to 85.5 percentage points, while increasing readiness delay from 0 to 10 s at 1.0 fps reduces completion from 87.7% to 0.4%. For earthquake-tsunami, learned placement adds no coverage relative to the primary baseline because 96.4% of critical-path computation is fixed to HPC. At tau = 50%, 10 of 30 tested conditions remain uncovered in each workflow, motivating capacity scaling or bounded approximation.

events.title: Query-Driven Visualization Over Compressed Scientific Data via Data–Index Co-Compression
events.description:
Large-scale scientific simulations routinely produce petabyte-scale datasets, making error-bounded lossy compression indispensable for alleviating storage and I/O bottlenecks. However, most visualization pipelines still reconstruct the entire compressed dataset before analysis, even when a visualization query accesses only a small subset of the volume, resulting in substantial computational overhead and limited interactive responsiveness.

We apply data–index co-compression to enable efficient query-driven visualization, jointly compressing block-level index with scientific data to support selective decompression while minimizing index overhead. During visualization, only the compressed blocks satisfying the query predicate are decompressed, avoiding unnecessary data access and reducing end-to-end visualization cost.

Experimental evaluation on three representative scientific applications demonstrates substantial end-to-end acceleration, achieving up to 50.1× speedup over conventional full-decompression workflows while preserving comparable visualization quality.

events.title: Real-Time High-Fidelity Bayesian Inference and Forecasting of Tsunamis: A Digital Twin for Tsunami Early Warning Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
events.description:
Tsunamis resulting from megathrust earthquakes are rare events that can cause devastating socioeconomic damage and loss of life. State-of-the-art early-warning systems rely on simplified physics models that can be inaccurate for near-field predictions, leading to delayed, missed, or false warnings. Tsunami propagation codes typically use shallow-water equations, which omit coupled ocean-acoustic and surface-gravity wave dynamics, while high-fidelity hydrodynamics codes are too computationally expensive for real-time use. My doctoral research develops a digital twin framework for tsunami early warning that incorporates high-fidelity physics, uses Bayesian data assimilation, and leverages GPU-oriented algorithms to enable accurate, real-time forecasts with rigorously quantified uncertainties for the Cascadia Subduction Zone.

The computational advance is an offline–online decomposition exploiting time-shift invariance in the parameter-to-observable and parameter-to-prediction maps. Their block-triangular Toeplitz structure enables fast Fourier transform-based matrix-vector products, delivering approximately one-hundred-thousand-fold speedups over repeated partial differential equation solves. The Bayesian inverse problem is reformulated in the smaller observation space using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, enabling offline factorization and real-time inference.

For a margin-wide Cascadia rupture with 600 hypothetical pressure sensors, the method infers more than one billion parameters and predicts wave heights at 21 locations in under 0.2 seconds on 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, a ten-billion-fold speedup over state-of-the-art methods—a breakthrough recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The framework also enables scalable Bayesian optimal experimental design by recasting sensor placement as dense matrix subset selection to minimize uncertainty in inferred seafloor motion or wave-height forecasts. This digital twin paves the way toward accurate, uncertainty-aware tsunami forecasts worldwide.

events.title: Refuse To Guess: A Declared Precondition in a UXarray MCP Server Caught What No Model Checked
events.description: We wrapped UXarray, a Python library for unstructured earth meshes, in a Model Context Protocol server so that language models call the library rather than reimplement it. Beyond schema validation, the server declares scientific preconditions that must hold before it computes. We tested what that buys across 480 runs: six mesh-analysis tasks, four interfaces, four models, five trials. One task was rigged to have no honest answer, asking for a remap onto a target grid with zero overlap with the source data. All 60 server-backed runs reported the server’s structured refusal. Writing their own code against the same library, models produced a confident number in 10 of 20 runs and, in all 20, never noted that the target lay outside the data. Across the other five tasks, interface changes were mostly within noise. This is one server and one library, but it isolates a mechanism model capability did not supply.

events.title: Reliable Numeric Fault Detection During Edge TPU Inference
events.description: Detecting floating-point exceptions during Edge TPU inference is structurally hard: the accelerator has no floating-point unit, and attaching it fuses the mapped partition into one opaque operation whose values never leave the chip, so tensor inspection is impossible there. We instead read the host CPU's floating-point status register before and after each inference, which every floating-point operation in the pipeline sets because all of them execute on the host. Across five stock models, register polling detected 100% of exception-raising faults, tensor scanning 98.8%, and output inspection 24.6%. Polling adds under 1% to latency; the optional tensor scan costs 7% to 58%. Detection holds on the accelerator, where 90% to 99% of tensors become unobservable. The tool also counts int8 saturation, targeting the 72% of output-corrupting faults that raise no exception.

events.title: Resource Adaptivity in the GPTune Autotuning Framework
events.description:
Autotuning frameworks often consist of various phases, such as sampling, modeling, and search, each with different resource requirements. Hence, traditional, static resource management for such frameworks often leads to wasted resources since not all allocated resources are used throughout all phases of the tuning process.

To address this inefficiency, we demonstrate the use of dynamic resource management for autotuning frameworks, building on the well-known GPTune framework. The original GPTune implementation uses MPI Spawn to launch processes for each phase within a static allocation. We adapt the implementation to use MPI Sessions and Dynamic Processes with PSets (DPP), expressing resource needs of each phase using DPP's generic, graph-based abstraction. This allows resource managers to adapt allocation to current resource needs.

Our evaluation shows that dynamic resource management can reduce the resource usage of GPTune by 46% compared to the static GPTune version.

events.title: Revisiting Distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering on Fugaku and Beyond
events.description: Large-scale simulations produce substantial data, making data output and interactive visualization costly. We implement and evaluate a distributed particle-based volume rendering (PBVR) workflow on Fugaku that separates CPU-based particle generation from interactive rendering on a GPU-equipped local PC. Building on JAEA's PBVR framework, we integrate in-situ particle generation into OpenFOAM using VTK and KVS. Experiments demonstrate scalability to 110,592 CPU cores (2,304 MPI processes with 48 OpenMP threads each). Separate evaluations on a smaller model show output data reductions of approximately 55%–90%. Although particle generation adds computation, reduced output can offset this overhead by lowering I/O costs. This architecture also offers a model for utilizing available CPUs during GPU-dominated simulations. At the poster session, we will present the system architecture, integration workflow, scalability results, and opacity-dependent data reduction.

events.title: Runtime Power Feasibility for Small Modular Nuclear Reactor-Powered Datacenters
events.description: Datacenters are exploring on-site small modular reactors (SMRs) for low-carbon power, but reactor power carries multi-hour state that conventional power scheduling does not capture. A power maneuver that is feasible when requested can become infeasible hours later as iodine–xenon dynamics evolve. We expose reactor feasibility through a runtime layer that checks the projected reactor state before the workload scheduler commits to a maneuver. Using eight Google Borg workload traces and PJM grid data, we evaluate reactor- and workload-aware policies at one-minute resolution. At low reactor margin, workload-aware scheduling without reactor state leaves 172 MWh unserved and averages 7.4 reactor shutdowns, while adding projected reactor feasibility reduces unserved work to 169 kWh with no shutdowns. Fixed recovery delays do not reproduce this behavior, and sensitivity experiments examine lookahead, enforcement margin, and reactor-model mismatch.

events.title: SHARD-DB: Scalable Hash-Based Retrieval for High-Throughput Reference Database Construction
events.description: Reference databases tailored to metabarcoding loci are essential for environmental-DNA analysis, but constructing them can require thousands of searches against multi-terabyte nucleotide collections. CRUX-style workflows commonly expand primer-derived sequences using BLAST. SHARD-DB instead performs broad approximate retrieval with densified one-permutation MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), followed by targeted locus localization. On a full NCBI NT MiFish workload of 10,292 queries, SHARD-DB completed retrieval and localization in 73:38 using 28.6 GiB peak RSS, while CRUX-style Merged BLAST completed in 52:16 using approximately 407 GB peak RSS. SHARD-DB retrieved 1,606,861 unique candidate accessions versus 133,387 for BLAST, providing a substantially broader reference pool for database construction. Historical matched-subset experiments also showed large SHARD-DB runtime advantages for MarVer3 16S and PR2 18S, demonstrating strong workload-dependent performance.

events.title: STORM: Scalable One-Sided Communication for Distributed Monte Carlo Particle Transport
events.description:
Domain-decomposed Monte Carlo transport moves particles between MPI ranks as they cross spatial subdomains. Transfers are irregular, bursty, and unpredictable. Existing asynchronous algorithms commonly use matched MPI messages, requiring receiver participation and progress polling.

STORM converts OFI/libfabric one-sided operations into a receiver-passive migration protocol with ordered publication, dynamic buffer growth, and termination accounting. On 2,240–13,440 ranks of Leonardo, STORM retains 88.3% constant global workload scaling efficiency under constant global transport work and more than 97% weak-scaling efficiency, with up to 1.27× speedup over optimized point-to-point MPI. In one three-dimensional Implicit Monte Carlo Hohlraum run, it is 1.41× faster at 4,480 ranks.

events.title: Scalable OpenCHAMI Node Infrastructure Collection (SONIC)
events.description: Reliable hardware telemetry is foundational to HPC cluster operations, enabling proactive thermal management, power optimization, and failure prediction. HPC monitoring systems often struggle with data loss, service interruptions, and scalability limitations. This work presents a BMC telemetry system deployed on Los Alamos National Laboratory's SI research cluster that achieves high availability through event-driven architecture combining intelligent polling, triple-redundant data paths, and fault-isolated services. Intelligent polling reduces network overhead by 81% while maintaining sub-second latency. A centralized consumer with batched writes achieves 82% reduction in database CPU utilization. Load testing collected over 77,000 samples across multiple load levels, demonstrating counterintuitive inverse scaling where consumer performance improves as cluster load increases. The poster will present the hybrid architecture pipeline, performance metrics under realistic workloads, and Grafana visualization dashboards demonstrating operational deployment on a nine-node production testbed.

events.title: Scalable Performance Diagnostics on Leadership Computing Platforms
events.description: Exascale supercomputers Frontier and Aurora provide infrastructure for executing applications across thousands of compute nodes, with massive MPI tasks, intensive CPU multi-threading, and heavy computation offloaded to GPUs. These heterogeneous workloads pose significant challenges for performance measurement and analysis tools. We refined the hpcanalysis framework as a multi-layered infrastructure consisting of a C++ ingestion engine for high-throughput, selective access to performance measurement slices, a query interface for extracting slices via specialized queries, and a Python API for high-level analytical tasks. This provides a scalable, efficient, interactive interface that ingests measurements for an execution across 100K MPI ranks on Aurora in under 10 seconds. We also designed HpcDataFrame, a GPU-accelerated substitute for the Pandas library, offloading heavy computations to NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, achieving speedups of up to 314x over Pandas processing. Collectively, our contributions provide a scalable substrate for performance diagnostics at the absolute limit of modern supercomputing.

events.title: Segments: A Reusable Sparse-Data Abstraction for Multicore CPUs and GPUs
events.description: Sparse matrices, graphs, numerical meshes, and particle methods differ in semantics, yet repeatedly process collections of variable-length groups such as matrix rows, adjacency lists, incidence relations, and particle neighborhoods. Implementations commonly bind these groups to a particular storage format and hardware-specific execution strategy, forcing traversal, reduction, and scheduling logic to be duplicated across data structures and backends. We present TNL Segments, a reusable C++ abstraction that separates irregular-data semantics from physical representation and parallel execution. Segments provide the mapping (segmentIdx, localIdx) → globalIdx, while application-specific values, column indices, edge weights, and mesh data remain in independent arrays. The same interface supports multicore CPUs, CUDA GPUs, and HIP GPUs.

events.title: Skyway My Way! InfiniBand to Ethernet Optimization and Benchmarking
events.description: Modern high performance computing and AI/ML workloads increasingly require efficient bridges between InfiniBand compute fabrics and Ethernet storage systems to enable large data transfer capabilities. The NVIDIA Skyway is a gateway device designed to translate IPoIB (Internet Protocol over InfiniBand) for external Ethernet services. This work seeks to evaluate and optimize the Skyway by benchmarking bandwidth performance, validating multi-tenant partition security boundaries, and identifying optimal deployment strategies for HPC workloads. Testing is performed on a nine-node cluster with an InfiniBand, Ethernet, and Skyway switch. A modified version of GPCNeT is used to measure cluster bandwidth under congestion. NFS performance is benchmarked within both the Ethernet network and across the Skyway. Finally, the network is partitioned to separate traffic of two controller nodes, emulating a secure user compute system. Our experimentation paves the way for Skyway implementation on production clusters, providing insight on hashing and storage I/O improvements for future work.

events.title: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication on Cerebras WSE-3
events.description: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is bounded by data movement rather than arithmetic, since every nonzero fetches from an unpredictable address. We present a general tile-wise SpMV kernel for the Cerebras WSE-3, whose ~893,000 processing elements (PE) hold the working set in on-chip SRAM. The kernel partitions the matrix with a deterministic host-side balancing algorithm and sums per-PE partials eastward along each grid row. Sweeping to the full wafer, the local compute scales linearly and a two-parameter model predicts it exactly across 17 configurations; the eastward reduction, parallel along one axis only, is the sole limit on total scaling, and a standalone chain-latency model underpredicts it by up to 26% once it overlaps compute. On a biobank-scale genotype matrix of 5.28 billion nonzeros the kernel sustains 64,700 GFLOP/s; on a matched smaller instance it completes in 59.6 μs against 5.46 ms for four A100 GPUs.

events.title: StageOnce: Speculative Cross-Job Data Staging for LLM Agent Fleets
events.description: Scientific workflows increasingly run as fleets of LLM agents analyzing the same large immutable datasets. On a shared compute node, independent staging repeats source reads and creates storage contention, while each job discovers its inputs during reasoning. StageOnce coordinates these speculative path predictions through a node-local daemon, coalescing concurrent misses into one immutable copy while preserving dataset versions and private outputs. Tools read staged inputs directly from the filesystem, without per-read coordination. Recorded-session replays in genomics and astronomy on SSD and HDD backends reduce fleet makespan by 31%–51% at 12 concurrent jobs against independent staging. Logical staging remains one copy across every tested fleet size. An ablation isolates speculation, which reduces makespan by 8%–49% against reactive shared caching.

events.title: StrataVR: A Unity-Based Out-of-Core Pipeline for Interactive Exploration of Multi-Terabyte Volumes in Virtual Reality
events.description:
Large volumetric datasets often exceed GPU memory, making responsive exploration in virtual reality (VR) difficult. StrataVR is a Unity-based out-of-core volume renderer that stores datasets externally and loads a small multi-resolution working set as the view changes. To our knowledge, it is the first Unity-based out-of-core VR volume renderer demonstrated on a multi-terabyte dataset. A C++ tool prepares bricks and metadata, while view-aware planning and asynchronous streaming keep relevant data in a fixed GPU pool. Coarser resident bricks remain visible until finer data arrives, providing continuous feedback and progressive refinement. The working system supports multichannel visualization, empty-region skipping, channel controls, cross sections and cutouts.

The interactive e-poster will show how StrataVR turns a multi-teratbye dataset into a responsive VR experience. Animations will explain how StrataVR works, while Unity and headset footage will show it in use.

events.title: Streaming Nuclear Physics at Scale
events.description: Nuclear physics experiments have long challenged the limits of high-rate and low-latency logic. Presently, streaming readout can move decision making from fixed detector electronics to software, allowing raw detector data to be processed continuously as they are produced. We highlight the state of Jefferson Lab and ESnet collaborative work with example workflows. First, existing data from the CLAS12 detector were replayed across ESnet through the EJFAT network load balancer to the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC, reaching 100 Gb/s as jobs dynamically scaled the workflow. Second, live data direct from the CLAS12 electromagnetic calorimeter were streamed, showing end-to-end capabilities and real-time cosmic ray identification. These demonstrations go beyond earlier transport benchmarks to physics-based streaming workflows, thus combining high-rate data transport with online scientific processing. We also discuss applying this approach to Jefferson Lab’s development of streaming-readout modules for positron emission tomography (PET) processing, enabling future whole-area, whole-body scanning otherwise considered impractical.

events.title: Structure-Aware Linear Solvers for Matrix-Free High-Order Finite-Element Simulations on GPUs
events.description: Higher-order finite-element simulations solve the same Poisson and shifted-Helmholtz systems repeatedly, and preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) needs iterations that climb with polynomial order and mesh grading, each ending in a latency-bound global reduction. We present two GPU solvers selected from the structure the mesh and the operator retain. On tensor-product meshes, an exact fast-diagonalization inverse needs one apply and no iterations. It is 138 to 4,570 times faster than converged Chebyshev-Jacobi PCG and 14 to 140 times faster than our own p-multigrid solve on uniform meshes. Where that structure is gone, a device-resident Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner converges in five to seven iterations against 106 to 668 for Jacobi PCG. Both are measured in DFT-FE on up to 128 A100 GPUs and 1,024 MI250X GCDs. This is unpublished work in preparation. The poster walks from the problem through the choice of solver to the measured gains and limits of each.

events.title: Subgraph Counting: Methods, Frameworks, and Applications
events.description:
Subgraph counting and matching are core primitives in network analysis, underpinning applications from computational biology to fraud detection to performance analysis in HPC. Existing methods assume static, small networks, rely on hardware-specific kernels that do not scale across the accelerator ecosystem, and emphasize counting over the harder problem of locating pattern instances. This dissertation addresses all three.

We develop ParaDyMS, a parallel method for counting all motifs of size k ≤ 5 on fully dynamic networks under batched edge insertions and deletions. Rather than recomputing from scratch, ParaDyMS updates motif counts incrementally using only the delta induced by a batch of changes. Implemented in the Kokkos C++ Performance Portability ecosystem, ParaDyMS targets both OpenMP and CUDA from one source, achieving up to 124× speedup over the state-of-the-art static method and outperforming 112 CPU cores with a single GPU.

To address hardware portability, we present PyGB-LAPIS, a compilation pipeline lowering graph algorithms written in Python-GraphBLAS through MLIR and the LAPIS backend into Kokkos-flavored C++. PyGB-LAPIS generates kernels across five sparse storage formats and multiple hardware backends from one source, matching hand-written Kokkos performance while eliminating per-backend engineering effort.

Finally, we develop an exact subgraph matching method that decomposes query and host graphs into size-4 graphlets and searches a compressed graphlet-overlap representation. This supports arbitrary-size queries and, uniquely, resolves multiple simultaneous queries in one pass through a shared search tree rather than restarting per query, with the union graph traversed on the fly and pruned by graphlet frequency to control its size.

events.title: TEIR: A Tiled Execution IR for Tensor Contractions
events.description: Tensor contractions are core kernels in scientific computing and machine learning. Efficient execution requires hardware-aware tiling and a schedule across cores and over time that depends on the contraction and the microarchitecture. Existing systems search this space with auto-tuning (TVM), optimize it with library heuristics (BLIS, TBLIS), or transpose whole tensors around a GEMM (TTGT). Recent systems expose tiles explicitly, from programming environments (cuTile, Triton-CPU) to tile-based primitives (KleidiAI, CUTLASS, LIBXSMM). We introduce the Tiled Execution Intermediate Representation (TEIR), which explicitly represents what runs (kernels on tiles), when it runs (an execution schedule), and how data is laid out (per-tensor strides and offsets). We implement TEIR as an MLIR dialect whose optimization passes schedule a contraction and lower it to LIBXSMM kernels. Across 24 TCCG contractions on AVX-512, NEON, and SME, TEIR achieves 1.5×–1.9× the geometric-mean throughput of the next-best backends and leads in 54 of 72 cases.

events.title: Tensor Compilers for AI and HPC
events.description: The recent developments in AI have prompted an interest in tensor compilers, but their use is not universal and often they are coupled with hand optimized kernels in real deployments. In this work, we dive deep into tensor compilers and adjacent systems to build a holistic systems understanding of tensor program optimization. We define our own tensor operator taxonomy. Using a modern GPU as an example, we condense GPU kernel optimization into two principles, from which many optimization techniques emerge. Using the PyTorch 2.0 compiler backend, TorchInductor, and the Triton compiler as examples, we explain in detail what intermediate representations and optimization techniques are used during the compilation process. We find that kernel fusion is the most consequential optimization. In the end, we are able to understand the value proposition of tensor compilers, the type of optimizations they apply, their limitations and how they can be used effectively and augmented.

events.title: Tensor Contractions on AWS Trainium
events.description:
Tensor contractions are fundamental across computational science and machine learning, yet reaching high performance on domain-specific accelerators with large systolic arrays, such as AWS Trainium, remains challenging.

We present a compiler that optimizes a binary tensor contraction, given as an einsum equation with axis sizes, and lowers it into a Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) kernel. The core contribution of the poster is the automatic search: the contraction is lowered to an intermediate representation, and candidate kernel and SBUF tilings are ranked by a measurement-based model of Trainium2's engines. The compiler is evaluated on Trainium2, where the generated kernels reach 155 of 157 TFLOPS on square matrix multiplication and run 2.3 to 2.9 times faster than torch.einsum on four contractions from the TCCG benchmark.

In the poster session we walk visitors through the pipeline, from einsum equation to emitted NKI code, and discuss the tiling decisions behind the results.

events.title: Tessera: User-Defined Compiler Optimizations for High-Performance Scientific Computing
events.description: Despite the extensive capabilities of today's compilers, general-purpose compilers cannot exploit domain-specific properties for optimization in scientific software because the semantic meaning of the code is lost as it is transformed from the application and library layers down to the compiler and hardware. To solve this problem, we present Tessera, an MLIR-based framework that allows domain experts to annotate scientific code with high-level mathematical and structural properties — including symmetries, matrix properties, and algebraic identities — which are automatically compiled into performance optimizations. This enables scientists to benefit from domain-specific optimizations without needing to restructure their code or have deep compiler expertise. To demonstrate Tessera's generality, we show that our framework achieves performance improvements on benchmarks built on both linear algebra and arbitrary-precision floating-point libraries.

events.title: The Cost of Parallelism: A Measured Comparison of Sequential and Systolic INT8 GEMM on an FPGA
events.description: Matrix multiplication dominates neural-network inference, and hardware designers choose between reusing one multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit over time and instantiating many that run concurrently. That exchange rate is usually assumed rather than measured, and is least favorable at small problem sizes. This work measures it. Two INT8 architectures, a single-MAC baseline and a 4x4 output-stationary systolic array, were implemented in SystemVerilog behind one shared interface and compared on an Intel Cyclone 10 GX FPGA under identical operands, device, tools, and constraint. The array is 7.4x faster in cycles for 16x the DSP blocks and 1.62x the ALMs, with no loss of clock frequency. Per-cycle occupancy explains the sublinear return: the array peaks at 12 of 16 active elements and never fills. The work is complete and validated on silicon. The poster walks through both architectures, the measured tradeoff, and the occupancy analysis, with QR-linked RTL.

events.title: The Unassessed Attack Surface: Channel-Based Provenance in HPC and Quantum-Computing Open-Source Software
events.description: Software trust is negotiated in communication channels such as the README, the registry listing, or the maintainer's account. AI agents now consume these channels directly, and attackers enter through them: the XZ Utils backdoor arrived through a mailing list, the Shai-Hulud worms phished maintainers to compromise 1,000+ npm packages, and in 2026, AI agents repeatedly installed a hallucinated package that never existed. Existing tools assess repositories, builds, and artifacts, but not this layer. We present channel-based provenance, to our knowledge, the first assessment framework for this layer: 18 signals spanning identity and access, communication channels, knowledge infrastructure, and distribution metadata, measured on 87 HPC and quantum-computing projects with a hand-verified 30-project panel. We find near-total provenance blindness; no missing signal requires new infrastructure, so the gap is adoption. The poster walks viewers from attack timeline to framework to per-project results, closing with concrete calls for maintainers, software stacks, and facilities.

events.title: ToolFuse: Provenance-Aware In-Flight Coalescing of Redundant Agent Tool Calls
events.description: Scientific workflows increasingly run as fleets of LLM agents analyzing immutable datasets. Independent agents can issue equivalent expensive read-only tool calls simultaneously, before a completed-result cache has anything to reuse. ToolFuse addresses this cold-wave gap by coalescing active calls at a gateway between agents and tool handlers. Its contribution is a provenance-aware execution identity that establishes equivalence from versioned dependencies and execution context, rather than arguments alone. Under contention on an exclusive HPC node, 16 equivalent requests become one execution, reducing CPU time by 11.79× and makespan by 2.36×. Peak memory growth falls from 6.44 GiB to 0.53 GiB. Trace replay shows that sharing depends on call duration and arrival timing. For cheap calls, coalescing remains inactive with negligible overhead.

events.title: Toward HEPScore4GPU: Scaling and Power of Real HEP GPU Applications on the A100 and H100
events.description: The HEPiX Benchmarking Working Group is developing HEPScore4GPU, a GPU benchmark for high-energy physics (HEP) built from real HEP applications for the High Lumi-LHC program. A key question is how efficiently GPUs can be used for HEP today. We take three candidate applications under development, a Monte Carlo Generator, a detector full simulation and an AI-based end-to-end simulation application, and run them on NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs, measuring how throughput scales from one to four GPUs and how much power they use. In this contribution we will describe the measurement process and the understanding of the different behaviors, with the objective of providing input to the application developers to further improve the software and exploit the maximum power of the GPUs.

events.title: Towards Resource-Efficient Parallel Concept Drift Detection in Data Streams
events.description:
Modern data science increasingly outpaces the efficient use of parallel hardware, creating a need for computational performance engineering. Because HPC tools are not embedded in exploratory data science environments, data scientists lack support for such investigations. This PhD project therefore bridges HPC and data science, using concept drift detection as a case study.

Concept drift—the change in data distributions after ML model deployment—must be detected to ensure robust streaming ML systems. However, the computational overhead of drift detectors (DDs) remains underexplored, even though directly affecting latency, energy consumption, and deployability. This gap motivates the thesis contributions.

First, a framework is introduced for systematically investigating the computational performance of DDs, including complexity analysis, benchmarking and performance analysis. Second, building on this framework, a survey and benchmark evaluate DDs bi-objectively, measuring both runtime and accuracy. The results reveal that computational performance is treated as secondary in the literature, no single detector dominates across scenarios, and higher accuracy consistently requires longer runtimes. Simultaneously, timely drift detection can reduce pipeline runtime by avoiding unnecessary model updates. Third, performance analysis identifies bottlenecks in state-of-the-art DD implementations, particularly inefficient BLAS and OpenMP usage in streaming scenarios. Consequently, the thesis presents MoPEDDs, a modular parallel ensemble of DDs that exploits unused parallel resources improving detection with negligible runtime overhead.

Finally, because performance engineering remains complex for most data scientists, the thesis introduces JUmPER (Jupyter meets Performance). It embeds performance engineering into Jupyter through coarse- and fine-grained monitoring, making HPC expertise accessible where data science happens.

events.title: Towards Scalable and Efficient Deep Learning: Structured Optimization Across Training and Fine-Tuning
events.description:
Modern deep learning systems must balance optimization quality against computation, memory, communication, and reliability constraints, whose relative importance varies across supercomputing architectures. This dissertation develops controlled relaxation as a structured optimization strategy: preserve information essential to learning while relaxing costly requirements in synchronization, curvature representation, and parameterization.

The thesis develops this principle through three contributions. AD-KFAC relaxes global synchronization in distributed second-order optimization while retaining curvature information in asynchronous, versioned, and recoverable state. BD-KFAC replaces dense curvature representations with block-diagonal structure, exposing a controllable trade-off between statistical fidelity and resource cost. RRLoRA relaxes the requirement for an uninterrupted low-rank optimization trajectory by periodically refactorizing the learned update and restarting the learning-rate schedule, allowing the parameterization to evolve without discarding accumulated information.

Together, these methods address complementary bottlenecks in distributed second-order training, resource-efficient curvature estimation, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning while preserving the optimization structure that makes each approach effective. The results support controlled relaxation as a systems-aware design principle: preserve signal-carrying structure, relax constraints that impose disproportionate system cost, and keep the resulting approximation or asynchronous state observable and recoverable. This principle offers a practical framework for designing efficient and reliable machine-learning systems on large-scale supercomputing platforms.

events.title: Towards Verifying OpenMP Target Offloading
events.description:
With the rise of LLM-generated and translated codes alongside the rise of heterogeneous computing, verification of concurrent programming dialects is becoming a necessity. OpenMP is one of those many concurrency dialects with support for heterogeneous computing using their target offloading feature. There is little work formalizing and verifying this feature. Existing work in OpenMP verification does not handle the added complexities that target offloading brings, such as host-device execution semantics and data mapping semantics.

We help address this by developing a formal model for target offloading using an existing verification tool that supports base OpenMP, CIVL. With this formal model, we simulate multiple simple bugs in OpenMP and show that our model can be used to catch these bugs.

The poster presents how the formal model represents OpenMP target offloading semantics and how some simple bugs were simulated and tested.

events.title: Towards a Distributed QHPC Workflow for Gadget-Aware Circuit Cutting and Pulse Synthesis
events.description: Pulse-level synthesis of compound gadgets (repetitive macroscopic gate blocks) compresses quantum control footprints. However, classically optimizing these schedules via optimal control algorithms creates severe compute bottlenecks, while scaling deep algorithms exhausts classical memory. These constraints demand distributed quantum high-performance computing (QHPC) workflows, but current tools use gate- or wire-level cutting that destroy data boundaries required for compound pulse gadget synthesis. We introduce Kodoki, a pulse gadget optimization framework that enables gadget-aware circuit cutting. Coupled with Qdislib and PyCOMPSs, Kodoki provides a decoupled distributed workflow. PyCOMPSs orchestrates pulse synthesis offline. Online, workers are given subcircuits and query a lookup table (LUT) of pre-computed pulses to execute subcircuits. Evaluations show Kodoki's compound synthesis achieves a 4.38x reduction in pulse execution time (from > 1000𝜇s to 240𝜇s). Shifting synthesis offline replaces an 865.5s compute bottleneck with a 2.326ms online query (𝑃₉₉ = 3.35ms). Ongoing evaluations will quantify scaling behavior across variational ansatzes.

events.title: Training-Free Mixture-of-Agents for CUDA Kernel Translation and Optimization
events.description: This poster presents a kernel-aware multi-agent framework for CUDA optimization that analyzes both performance gains and optimization cost. We compare Fixed, Adaptive, and Collaborative optimization modes across two kernels: Lattice-Boltzmann Method (LBM) and SYMM. Fixed applies a predefined sequence of coalescing, tiling, and atomic-focused transformations, while Adaptive uses routing to stop when additional layers are unnecessary. Collaborative uses multi-model proposals with GPT-OSS aggregation. Our layer-influence analysis measures how strongly each intermediate optimization layer shapes the final kernel using similarity-based scores. Results show that LBM benefits from deeper staged refinement, with later layers contributing most to the final output, whereas SYMM converges earlier after coalescing and tiling. Cost analysis further shows that Adaptive optimization can reduce tokens, energy, and optimization time by avoiding unnecessary transformations. Overall, the results highlight the importance of kernel-aware routing and layer-aware stopping for practical LLM-driven GPU optimization.

events.title: Transit-Layer Tensor Representation for Serverless Inference
events.description: The scale of frontier machine learning systems has led to an increasing need to efficiently store and transfer model weights. Existing methods for serverless inference employ scheduling policies to reduce cold start and model swapping latency, but have largely reached the limitations of hardware. In this paper, we introduce Condense, an ultra-fast method of compressing tensor weights across applications. We implement Condense in a serverless runtime as a transit-layer representation and evaluate the latency reduction. Across Llama models from 1B to 13B parameters, Condense reduces stored weight sizes by 2.27x-2.38x and improves cold-start loading time by 1.92x-2.17x over ServerlessLLM while retaining competitive downstream accuracy. We demonstrate that compact tensor representations can be generated quickly to provide significant runtime reductions across machine learning applications.

events.title: Trustworthy Agentic AI for HPC Operational and Predictive Data Analytics and Forecasting
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer promising pathways for automating high performance computing (HPC) operations, yet their real-world deployment is severely constrained by silent operational failures, uncalibrated confidence, and brittle central control. In this work, we chart a new vision for reliable, agentic AI across supercomputing facilities. We explore the architectural paradigm shift from centralized orchestration to decentralized, peer-to-peer agent topologies, illustrating how typed dialogue and bounded knowledge limits ensure defensible, transparent operational guidance. Furthermore, we examine the critical challenge of stance fidelity, demonstrating how verbalized confidence must be audited as dynamic system telemetry rather than taken at face value. Based on these insights, we advocate for a fundamental re-architecting of facility AI: prioritizing honest refusal over raw recall, establishing auditable ground-truth benchmarks, and transitioning AI tools from passive historical log lookups to active, pre-submission job steering.

events.title: Understanding AllReduce Performance Through Hardware Telemetry
events.description: Inter-GPU AllReduce operations traverse several tightly coupled hardware components, including the GPU, PCIe interface, NIC, and network. Each component exposes hardware telemetry for its local behavior, and no single telemetry source observes the complete communication path. A combined view is therefore needed to narrow where performance is limited and to guide optimization. We combine selected NVIDIA A100 GPU counters with Cassini NIC counters on HPE Slingshot-11 to analyze a 1 GiB inter-node AllReduce across NCCL protocols, NCCL channel counts, and GPU-aware MPI versus NCCL. Across the three studies, the joint telemetry associates performance differences with distinct behaviors: work amplification for NCCL LL, increased synchronization and reduced transfer progress at high channel counts, and slow transfer progress with additional rank imbalance for MPI. Joint GPU–NIC telemetry therefore helps distinguish different sources of AllReduce slowdown and narrows where optimization effort should be focused.

events.title: Understanding and Improving Multi-Rack Symmetric-Memory AllGather in NCCL
events.description: Rack-scale GPU systems such as the GB200 NVL72 extend the NVLink scale-up domain from four or eight GPUs per server to 72 GPUs per rack. Large language model (LLM) training still scales across many racks, with all-gathers spanning heterogeneous NVLink and InfiniBand fabrics. These all-gathers operate in a message-size regime where both latency and bandwidth matter. In this work, we characterize NCCL's symmetric-memory and legacy all-gather performance for this regime. We derive a closed-form topology-aware bandwidth bound and extend it with a latency term for comparison with empirical measurements. Based on observed trends and model insights, we design two new GPU-initiated symmetric-memory all-gather implementations that outperform NCCL's symmetric-memory all-gathers by up to 2.6x for 32-512MB messages.

events.title: Understanding the NERSC User Community Through Network Analysis
events.description: NERSC users collaborate, forming a network. Which users occupy the most structurally influential positions in the NERSC user community? Using 2020–2026 NERSC allocation records, a proxy collaboration graph was analyzed to reveal the user community’s dynamics. Two definitions of user connectivity were compared using available data on project allocation size: unweighted degree and repository-size-adjusted (RSA) strength. Degree distributions, program-office affiliation, and user roles were analyzed. Results show that RSA strength is a more accurate measurement of user connectivity than unweighted degree. The strongest connectors in the network are career scientists and users associated with high-energy physics. These findings suggest that in HPC network data, unweighted connectivity is not a reliable measurement of network influence or cross-disciplinary reach. Findings also suggest that allocation networks reflect certain field-specific collaboration patterns, implying that allocation networks may provide a useful proxy for co-authorship networks in the same field.

events.title: Union of Containers: Layered Software Stacks with Cross-Container Dependency Reuse for HPC
events.description: HPC software stacks are typically distributed as one container image per accelerator target, and every image duplicates the CPU-generic majority of the stack. This work splits the stack across containers. A shared provider holds the architecture-generic dependencies; thin specialized layers hold only GPU-compiled packages and reuse the provider's builds instead of recompiling them. The layers compose at run time through absolute RPATH entries under fixed paths, with no search-path configuration.
