Published kernel-level optimizations target older architectures, while no prior work investigates how Hopper's Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), warpgroup execution, expanded shared memory, and asynchronous pipelines reshape the design space. We present an analytical model that captures roofline bounds, L2 reuse, pipeline overlap, and wave quantization for Hopper sparse GEMM. It serves as a guardrail for configuration search. Guided by the model, we develop an auto-tuned kernel combining warp-specialized TMA pipelining, metadata prepacking, barrier-decomposed overlap, and per-operand swizzles. On an H800 PCIe GPU, it outperforms cuSPARSELt on 80 of 95 shapes (84%) under identical problem configurations, with mean speedup of +16.7% and up to 1.4x. The model identifies memory bottlenecks and narrows the configuration space before compilation, reducing tuning cost while retaining high-performance configurations. This paper bridges both gaps.

events.title: CoCoDiff: Optimizing Collective Communications for Distributed Diffusion Transformer Inference Under Ulysses Sequence Parallelism
events.description:
Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are increasingly adopted in scientific computing, yet growing model sizes and resolutions make distributed multi-GPU inference essential. Ulysses sequence parallelism scales DiT inference but introduces frequent all-to-all collectives that dominate latency. Overlapping these with computation is difficult due to tight data dependencies, large messages, and asymmetric interconnect bandwidths.

We introduce CoCoDiff, a distributed DiT inference engine exploiting two observations: (1) V requires only linear projection while Q/K need additional normalization and RoPE, enabling overlap of V's communication with Q/K computation; (2) adjacent denoising steps produce similar tensors, yielding temporal redundancy. CoCoDiff introduces three mechanisms: Tile-Aware Parallel All-to-all (TAPA) decomposes collectives into topology-aligned phases; V-First scheduling hides V's communication behind Q/K computation; and V-Major selective communication transmits only active projections on slow interconnects. On Aurora with four DiT models across 1–8 nodes (up to 96 Intel GPU tiles), CoCoDiff achieves an average speedup of 3.6×, peaking at 8.4×.

events.title: ZOCheck: CPU-Shadow Checkpointing for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
events.description: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization is an attractive option for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning, but its fault tolerance remains underexplored. Unlike first-order training, ZO progress can be represented by lightweight seed-and-scalar step logs, yet naive log-only recovery still incurs replay cost that grows with training progress, and shortcut replay does not preserve the executed floating-point trajectory. We present ZOCheck, a fault-tolerant ZO training system that exploits this replayable structure through a CPU shadow process that continuously replays logged updates, materializes consistent recovery images off the GPU critical path, and persists them asynchronously. ZOCheck combines non-blocking checkpointing with fast recovery from a near-current state. We also develop a cost model for choosing the snapshot policy under realistic failure rates. Experiments show that ZOCheck reduces checkpoint overhead by up to 219.7× and recovery latency by 1.55× on average over asynchronous full-state checkpointing, yielding up to 21.3× lower end-to-end wasted time while preserving exact recovery behavior.

events.title: NCCLZ: Compression-Enabled GPU Collectives with Decoupled Quantization and Entropy Coding
events.description: Collective communication is a major bottleneck for multi-node GPU workloads in scientific computing and distributed deep learning, especially when inter-node bandwidth is limited. Although NCCL provides optimized GPU-centric collectives, large messages can still dominate end-to-end performance. Existing compression-enabled collective libraries either rely on MPI-based stacks that cannot fully exploit NCCL, omit entropy coding, or tightly couple full compressors with communication primitives, limiting compression ratio, flexibility, and communication-computation overlap. This paper presents NCCLZ, a compression-enabled GPU collective that decouples quantization and entropy coding and integrates them at different layers of the stack. NCCLZ places quantization at the interface, embeds entropy coding into NCCL primitives, uses a lightweight device-side selector to choose coding strategies, and overlaps compression with communication to reduce exposed overhead. Experiments on scientific datasets, training gradients, and synthetic workloads show up to 9.65x speedup over NCCL and up to 3.34x improvement over prior compression-assisted collective libraries.

events.title: From Image to Action: Using AI-Based Pathology Biomarkers To Guide Treatment
events.description: In his talk, Dr. Pearson will discuss how AI-based pathology biomarkers can extract clinically meaningful information from tissue images and help guide treatment selection. He will explore how AI-based computational methods development can move pathology beyond diagnosis toward making more trustworthy, personalized, and actionable treatment decisions.

events.title: StarLight Agentic AIDTN for High-Performance Data/Process Transport with Research Platforms
events.description: NRI103

events.title: Where Quantum and HPC Join Hands
events.description: Quantum computation offers significant potential to enhance scientific discovery in fields including chemistry, optimization and artificial intelligence. However, due to the limitations of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, integration of quantum systems with high performance computing (HPC) systems may be critical for near-term useful hybrid quantum algorithms. Recently welcomed as an Internet2 member, this talk from IQM Quantum Computers and Internet2 underscores how industry and the research and education community can join together in support of HPC/Quantum hybrid solutions. IQM Quantum Computers discusses its superconducting qubit platform, focusing on its suitability for hybrid quantum-classical computation. We briefly review hardware characteristics before examining how integration with high performance computing systems enables efficient execution of these workflows.

events.title: Towards Exascale Fully Relativistic Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory Calculations with Mixed-Precision Computation and Compressed Communication Using Residual-Based Subspace Iteration
events.description: Materials exhibiting noncollinear magnetism or strong spin-orbit-coupling underpin many spintronic and topological applications, but their simulations require complex two-component spinors and costs substantially more than scalar density functional theory (DFT). We present a GPU-centric exascale finite-element DFT framework with noncollinear magnetism and spin-orbit-coupling, combining (1) adaptive higher-order finite-element discretization; (2) a matrix-free Poisson solver; (3) residual-based Chebyshev filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI) for sparse generalized eigenproblems; (4) R-ChFSI-enabled mixed-precision computation with block floating-point compressed MPI communication; and (5) communication-efficient band partitioning. R-ChFSI permits inexact matrix-multivector products and 4x–6.4x compression of communicated data relative to FP64 while preserving double-precision robustness and reducing computation and data movement. Results demonstrate strong scaling on Aurora and Frontier, with up to 3.4x faster Chebyshev filtering. On Aurora, total self-consistent-field (SCF) solve wall time reduces by 2x. An 800-node (9,600-GPU) calculation demonstrates fully relativistic pseudopotential DFT for ~80,000 electrons in under seven minutes per SCF iteration.

events.title: SpCCL: A Sparsity-Aware Collective Communication Library for GPU Platforms
events.description: Collective communication is essential to high performance computing and machine learning workloads, yet libraries such as NCCL do not exploit sparsity in message payloads. Sending only nonzero values can reduce network traffic, but explicitly handling sparsity introduces challenges such as compression and decompression overheads. We address these challenges with sparsity-exploiting versions of all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-reduce collectives. Our implementations use a new bitvector-based format, Pici, designed for low space overhead and fast GPU-based compression and decompression. Further, our collective algorithms adapt to the degree of sparsity in data, modifying data representations during the course of the collective. At 99% input sparsity, our collectives achieve up to 5.25×, 2.5×, and 2.66× speedups over NCCL for all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-reduce, respectively. Integrating our collectives into a representative deep learning application, we achieve a 26% end-to-end speedup.

events.title: Maze: A Distributed Framework for Large Language Model Agents
events.description:
LLM agents are transitioning from single-node to large-scale, multi-tenant services. A user request no longer corresponds to a single inference call, but to a long-running workflow interleaving heterogeneous tasks. Existing agent systems struggle with these workloads due to resource-blind, coarse-grained placement or ignore agentic workload awareness.

We present Maze, a distributed agent framework bridging the abstraction gap from agentic logic to fine-grained task-level deployment. At its core, Maze anchors task resource semantics and introduces Heterogeneity-Aware Criticality Scheduler, a scheduler leveraging agentic workload features and value-density scoring to prioritize valuable agentic workflows and critical tasks while eliminating cross-resource head-of-line blocking. Coupled with elastic inference engine scaling, zero-VRAM optimizations, and closed-loop fault tolerance, Maze ensures a robust, performant runtime. Evaluation on diverse workloads demonstrates that Maze achieves up to 2.9x higher throughput, reduces P95 latency by 54.2%, and increases GPU utilization by 50% compared to state-of-the-art frameworks.

events.title: Papers in Conversation
events.description: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

events.title: Science-Aware Network Operations for Research Networks (SciNet)
events.description:
The emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed.
Research networks, however, remain passive communication infrastructures that optimize packet delivery while being agnostic to the scientific workflows they support, a disconnect that creates bottlenecks in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making.
This paper presents Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a networking paradigm in which artificial intelligence (AI) embedded in the network control plane continuously observes scientific workflows, predicts future network demands, reasons about workflow dependencies, and autonomously adapts network behavior.
Unlike conventional AIOps systems that optimize utilization or reliability, SciNet optimizes for scientific productivity through workflow-aware routing, predictive resource allocation, and autonomous failure mitigation.
We describe the SciNet layered architecture and its optimization objective, characterize the network requirements of Department of Energy (DOE) science workflows through stakeholder interviews, distill these requirements into six recurring use cases with associated quality-of-service classes, and outline ongoing research directions under the Genesis Mission toward AI-driven autonomous laboratories.

events.title: QuLore: An Adaptive Security Framework To Extend Quantum-Safe Communications
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Jordan Fauser
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Michelle Hoffmann
events.description:
Michelle Hoffmann, Ph.D. has been serving since August of 2021 as the Executive Director of the Chicago Biomedical Consortium (CBC), a consortium of biomedical researchers across Northwestern, the University of Illinois at Chicago, the University of Chicago, and six other Chicagoland institutions, that is generously supported by the Searle Funds at The Chicago Community Trust (CCT), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and The Walder Foundation. The CBC's mission is to find and fund research that will most likely become commercial biomedical applications driving Illinois's economic development.

In her time as Executive Director, Dr. Hoffmann has reorganized the CBC, developed a process to scout and build biopharma applications of Illinois's academic researchers, organized the greater entrepreneurial community and market it to coastal investors and biotech, and trained local PhD talent in the business of early science commercialization. Before this role, from 2019-2021, Dr. Hoffmann was the Senior Vice President of Deep Tech at P33, a privately funded nonprofit charged with elevating Chicagoland's innovation economy and driving inclusive economic growth.

Before P33, Hoffmann spent 15 years helping life sciences companies grow, most recently as a senior vice president at Boston-based Back Bay Life Science Advisors, an integrated strategy and investment firm for global life science companies, venture-backed startups and their investors. During her nine years at Back Bay, Hoffmann led projects for large, publicly traded companies and small, private, venture-backed health care and life sciences companies.

events.title: Family Day on the Exhibits Floor
events.room: Exhibit Hall F, Skyline Ballroom A-C

events.title: Demonstrating FPGA-Accelerated Packet Processing for Network Anomaly Detection and Pre-Trade Risk Management
events.description: NRI103

events.title: Accelerating Graph Analytics on GPUs
events.description: These papers accelerate graph analytics through tensor cores, hierarchical traversal, and specialized dependency handling. The session highlights the growing convergence of graph algorithms and dense accelerator hardware.

events.title: TempGNN: An Efficient Real-Time TGNN Inference Accelerator via Target-Centric Dependency Packets
events.description: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) effectively model dynamic graphs, but inference suffers from limited useful parallelism and irregular memory accesses because strict temporal dependencies require timestamp-ordered vertex updates. We present TempGNN, a target-centric accelerator for high-performance real-time TGNN inference. TempGNN reorganizes sampled temporal computation into target dependency packets (TDPs), each capturing the minimal temporally valid dependency states required to update a target vertex. By decoupling dependency preparation from ordered target-state commitment, TempGNN preserves temporal correctness while exposing branch-level parallelism across partially overlapping targets. To realize this execution model, TempGNN integrates a dependency-driven TDP construction and data-loading scheme together with an overlap-aware synchronization strategy that eliminates redundant dependency processing and supports efficient on-chip execution. Implemented on a Xilinx Alveo U280 FPGA, TempGNN achieves 28.2× speedup and 33.5× energy savings over an A100 GPU, and further delivers 3.8×–7.6× speedups with 6.5×–10.2× energy savings over prior TGNN accelerators.

events.title: Adaptive Scheduling for Distributed AI
events.description: This session examines scheduling decisions across heterogeneous AI training, dynamic graphs, multi-job execution, and adaptive networks. It asks how runtimes can respond to changing workload and system conditions.

events.title: OctoPipe: Reducing Pipeline Bubbles for Heterogeneous Models via Co-Optimizing Partitioning, Placement, and Scheduling
events.description:
Pipeline parallelism is widely used to train large language models (LLMs). However, increasing heterogeneity in model architectures exacerbates pipeline bubbles. Prior approaches typically optimize a single phase of the pipeline schedule (i.e., partitioning, placement, or scheduling), leaving substantial bubbles. While promising, co-optimization poses three key challenges: (1) complex performance modeling, (2) a combinatorial search space, and (3) irregular execution orders.

We propose OctoPipe, a pipeline parallelism system to co-optimize partitioning, placement, and scheduling. First, we build a graph-based pipeline simulator to model heterogeneous pipeline execution for co-optimization. Second, we develop an iterative bubble-aware tuner to efficiently explore the combinatorial search space. Third, we implement a unified pipeline executor that dynamically orchestrates computation and communication to support irregular execution orders without deadlocks while maximizing communication-computation overlap.

Experiments show that OctoPipe achieves 1.09x-1.49x throughput improvement over the state-of-the-art pipeline parallelism approaches across various heterogeneous model configurations and GPU cluster scales.

events.title: Best Papers: Algorithms for Adaptive HPC Decisions
events.description: This session spans automatic pipeline construction, causal diagnosis, and large-scale experimental design. The common thread is using structure and inference to make difficult computational decisions efficiently.

events.title: Format-Driven Automatic Pipeline Construction and Load Balancing for SpMM on GPUs
events.description: Sparse matrix-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) is critical for graph neural networks, yet GPU optimization faces challenges from irregular sparsity and thread-block load imbalance. Existing hand-tuned solutions tightly couple format design with kernel implementation, requiring reimplementation when the format changes. We present Sparsene, a format-driven automated framework that derives all kernel-level optimizations from a single sparse format specification. A hierarchical DSL decouples format structure from implementation via declarative blocking primitives and dynamic lowering transformations. The frontend compiles the DSL into a pGraph of pTasks, whose granularity and dependencies are determined by the format. This format-derived pGraph drives both automatic pipeline construction, where a hardware-aware simulator and two-stage hybrid search identify high-quality pipeline plans, and format-aware load balancing, which selects among binding strategies through per-input profiling to mitigate thread-block load imbalance. Experiments on NVIDIA A100, H100, and RTX 4090 demonstrate up to 8x speedup over state-of-the-art solutions with performance portability.

events.title: DiffSpec: Accelerating Long Sequence Generation with Differential Speculative Decoding
events.description:
Long sequence generation is a critical workload for large language model (LLM) inference, but its high computational cost limits scalable deployment. Existing speculative decoding methods accelerate inference by verifying multiple draft tokens per step, yet uniform speculation concentrates failures in late decoding stages, where marginal payoff is highest, reducing overall speedup.

We propose DiffSpec, a differential speculative decoding framework that adapts speculation to position-specific utility. At the algorithmic level, DiffSpec employs utility-guided draft construction with relevance-aware key-value (KV) selection and adaptive draft tree construction, improving candidate quality in high-impact regions. At the system level, a differential speculative execution engine supports utility-adaptive speculation via reuse-aware KV residency and topology-aware fused verification, handling irregular KV cache accesses and heterogeneous workloads. Experiments on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs with sequences up to 128K tokens show end-to-end speedups of 7.72×, 3.45×, and 2.36× over EAGLE-3, TriForce, and MagicDec, respectively.

events.title: Speculative and Observable LLM Inference
events.description: This session examines how speculative generation and performance diagnosis can reduce latency in modern LLM inference. The papers connect adaptive resource decisions, draft-model design, and top-down profiling into a common systems story.

events.title: MatterScale: Scaling Foundation Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Billion-Atom Molecular Dynamics on the Next-Generation Supercomputer
events.description: Machine learning interatomic potentials have enabled molecular dynamics with ab initio accuracy at greatly reduced cost and at large scale. The field is now shifting toward foundation machine learning interatomic potentials with broader transferability, but these models are harder to scale because message-passing layers complicate distributed communication and two-body and three-body features increase graph-construction cost and memory footprint. We present MatterScale, an end-to-end framework for deploying foundation MLIPs on massively parallel molecular dynamics workloads on a next-generation supercomputer. MatterScale combines a Halo operator for nearest-neighbor inter-layer feature exchange, an ML-based multiple-time-step scheme for higher throughput, layer-wise activation checkpointing for higher per-node capacity, and a parallel graph-construction algorithm. With MatterSim, MatterScale scales to 32,768 GPGPUs with 94% weak scaling efficiency and simulates up to 1.13 billion atoms.

events.title: Papers in Conversation: Scientific AI at Extreme Scale
events.description: The papers use foundation models and autonomous agents to scale molecular dynamics, materials workflows, and simulation monitoring. The panel can explore where scientific judgment should remain human and where AI can safely steer computation.

events.title: The Future of the HPC Workforce: Skills, Scale, and Sustainability
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) is undergoing rapid transformation with the convergence of simulation, AI, data-intensive science, and emerging quantum computing. This evolution is reshaping the skills required to effectively use and advance these systems, creating urgent challenges in workforce development. This panel brings together perspectives from national laboratories, academia, and industry to discuss how to build a sustainable, inclusive, and future-ready HPC workforce.

Key questions include: What will the HPC workforce need to look like in the next 5–10 years? Where are the most critical gaps in skills, training pathways, and access? What skills are currently missing or undervalued in existing curricula? Which collaboration models across institutions have proven effective? How can we broaden participation and lower barriers to entry?

The session will include interactive audience engagement, with opportunities to submit and prioritize questions in real time, ensuring a dynamic and relevant discussion.

events.title: The Future of the HPC Workforce: Skills, Scale, and Sustainability
The Computational and Economic Breakeven of Hybrid HPC/ML
events.description: High performance computing is rapidly integrating machine learning with traditional numerical solvers, creating hybrid workflows and digital twins. This panel audits the "total energy to solution" for hybrid HPC workloads, quantifying their operational power demands from silicon hardware to total cost of ownership. Panelists will address the following core questions: What is the energy required to generate large-scale, ground-truth training datasets versus the direct computational cost of ML training? What, if any, is the energy overhead of running traditional physics engines alongside ML for active validation? At what computational breakeven point does deploying an ML surrogate yield a net reduction in total energy use? Finally, how do these physical energy ledgers translate into real-world budgets and sustainability goals for scientific deployment? Bringing together perspectives from materials science, weather forecasting, hyperscale computing, and computing economics, this panel evaluates the physical and financial energy realities of ML integration in HPC.

events.title: The Computational and Economic Breakeven of Hybrid HPC/ML
Best Poster Finalist Presentations (ACM SRC Grads)
HPC Fault Tolerance
What It Takes to Adopt Live Migration for GPU Training: Lessons from Orchestrators, Neoclouds, and Enterprises
events.description:
At scale, distributed training jobs can fail every few hours due to component failures, wasting GPU-hours as resources sit idle during recovery and repeat the work lost since the last checkpoint. Live migration, paired with proactive health checks, can avoid these costly restarts by moving a running job from a degraded or draining node to a spare node before job disruption and restart, we enable the job to resume from the exact interrupted step after migration. Clockwork’s fault tolerance solution (TorchPass) supports this through model-transparent CRIU snapshots or model-aware hooks, preserving training progress while enabling GPU resilience.

We share lessons from deploying GPU live migration across Kubernetes, Slinky, Slurm, and orchestration platforms that use versioned blueprints, spanning neocloud and enterprise on-premises environments. We present measured results on job performance and migration overhead, alongside a live demo showing training continuity during a node drain. We also examine the integration challenges that determine whether migration works reliably in practice: scheduler failure semantics, environment restoration, and control-plane resilience. Attendees leave with a practical checklist for evaluating live migration on their own clusters, including its operational requirements, resiliency tradeoffs, and role alongside checkpoint-based recovery.

events.title: HPC Software and Tools
Parallel Python Debugging in HPC: Challenges, Approaches, and Real-World Lessons From DOE Labs
events.description:
Python is now a first-class language in HPC, powering simulations, AI/ML pipelines, and data-intensive workflows at national laboratories and research institutions. Yet the debugging toolchain has not kept pace: traditional single-process debuggers were not designed for jobs spanning thousands of MPI ranks, GPU accelerators, or hybrid Python/C++ architectures.

Based on collaboration with various teams at DOE labs, this session presents core requirements for parallel Python debugging in HPC environments. We will examine what breaks when traditional debugging is applied to distributed Python workloads, what capabilities a parallel debugger must provide, and how those needs are being addressed in practice. Real-world DOE lab use cases, including ML data pipeline debugging, ground the discussion.

Informal audience polling and Q&A will connect the material to attendees’ own Python technologies, AI/ML frameworks, and debugging challenges.

events.title: perfSONAR in the Cook County Community
events.description: NRI106, NRI107

events.title: BTC-TC: Exact GPU Triangle Counting with Hybrid Bit Tensor Cores and CUDA Cores
events.description: Triangle counting is fundamental to graph analytics, yet GPUs face a tension between exact, irregular adjacency-list intersection and regular, inaccurate FP16 Tensor Core execution. ToT's FP16 pipeline is incorrect on 12 of 36 inputs and requires pre-kernel symbolic matching. We observe that semantic alignment alone is insufficient under heterogeneous mask density. We present BTC-TC, an exact system built around binary MMA. AND-popcount implements common-neighbor counting with 32-bit accumulation and enables online block matching. Because mask density varies, BTC-TC combines multi-granularity Bit-BSR with two-level adaptivity: it selects block geometry per graph, dispatches dense blocks to Bit Tensor Cores, and routes sparse blocks to CUDA cores. Across 36 inputs and 12 baselines on RTX PRO 6000, BTC-TC achieves the lowest post-clean end-to-end time on every input, with 1.92x geometric-mean kernel and 8.0x end-to-end speedups over ToT. It matches CPU ground truth on every input and maintains the gains on H100 and A800.

events.title: REAL: Efficient Distributed Training of Dynamic GNNs with Reuse-Aware Load Balancing Scheduling
events.description:
Dynamic graph neural networks (DGNNs) enable learning from evolving graphs by capturing both structural and temporal dependencies. However, scaling DGNN training remains challenging due to three conflicting objectives: maximizing resource utilization, minimizing data movement, and maximizing data reuse. Existing systems typically optimize one objective at the expense of the others, leading to communication bottlenecks, load imbalance, or redundant computation.

We present REAL, an efficient distributed system for DGNN training that jointly addresses these challenges. REAL minimizes data transfers through snapshot-group scheduling and introduces an incremental aggregation mechanism that decouples computation from structural updates, enabling snapshot- and group-level reuse to eliminate redundant I/O and FLOPs. We further design two complementary schedulers: Real-L, an ILP-based optimizer for globally optimal planning, and Real-G, a scalable greedy heuristic. Experiments on six dynamic graph datasets and four DGNN models show that Real-L and Real-G achieve up to 3.26× and 3.16× speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

events.title: From Alert Fatigue to Root Cause: Causal Failure Cascade Discovery in HPC Systems
events.description: Production HPC systems generate massive volumes of heterogeneous logs that encode rich signals about failure propagation across hardware and software layers. In this paper, we present a framework for causal discovery in HPC logs that combines three complementary methods: transformer-based counterfactual intervention, PCMCI+, and transfer-entropy. Because production environments lack labeled ground truth, our framework uses cross-method triangulation to assign confidence to discovered causal relationships. We further introduce an architecture-aware AI-agent that evaluates the physical plausibility of these relationships and enriches them with mechanism-level explanations, diagnostic commands, and severity assessments grounded in Frontier system documentation. We apply the framework to 18.4 billion log events from the Frontier supercomputer and construct a structured taxonomy of 87 event types spanning diverse hardware and software subsystems. Our results reveal causal relationships across HPC-subsystems, including rare failure pathways and multi-hop cascade chains. This work provides a scalable path toward architecture-grounded root-cause diagnosis in production HPC-systems.

events.title: Spec-K: Adaptive Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview for Efficient MoE Inference
events.description:
Inference serving for large language models (LLMs) often relies on static resource allocation—such as fixed Top-k routing in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models—despite substantial token-level heterogeneity. This mismatch causes systematic over-provisioning, magnified in long reasoning and batched speculative decoding.

We introduce Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview (RASP), a framework that leverages predictive signals from a draft model to guide token-level allocation before target-model verification, enabling fine-grained adjustment of compute budgets to match instantaneous demand. As an instantiation, Spec-K applies RASP to MoE routing: it uses speculative preview to estimate token uncertainty and reallocates the Top-k budget dynamically via a minimalist policy, reducing expert computation, communication traffic, and activated expert count in batched verification—thereby improving throughput and even speculative acceptance.

Experiments on distributed MoE inference show that Spec-K achieves up to 1.72× end-to-end throughput improvement over a strong baseline, with negligible accuracy loss on complex reasoning and instruction-following tasks.

events.title: Star-LAFT: An Agent-Driven Adaptive Framework for Fault-Tolerant High-Throughput Materials Informatics
events.description: High-throughput computational materials science workflows execute millions of simulations on HPC clusters to build materials genome databases for data-driven discovery. However, these workflows face critical challenges: complex task dependencies reduce scheduling efficiency, load imbalances waste resources, and parameter-sensitive simulations suffer poor fault resilience. We present Star-LAFT, an agent-driven framework integrating large language models (LLMs) for automated workflow construction, dynamic resource optimization, and multi-level fault recovery. Key innovations include: (1) LLM-based automatic inference of computational parameters from material specifications; (2) chain-of-thought-driven dynamic resource allocation; and (3) a hybrid fault-tolerance agent that pairs an LLM diagnoser with a reward-guided recovery-action selector. Benchmarks show Star-LAFT achieves a 2.12× wall-time speedup and 10.08% higher task completion with only 2.76% additional cost. At production scale (~300k materials), it generated a million-entry database in 10 weeks at 94.3% completion rate, enabling effective downstream AI model training.

events.title: High Value, Petabyte-scale Data at JHU
Regional Tech Hub Wednesday Meet and Greet: Volodymyr Kindratenko
events.description: Volodymyr Kindratenko serves as the Assistant Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he also holds the position of Director for the Center for Artificial Intelligence Innovation (CAII). He is an Adjunct Associate Professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and a Research Associate Professor in the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. Prior to his current role, Dr. Kindratenko led NCSA's Innovative Systems Laboratory, a center-wide research initiative focused on evaluating emerging computing technologies for high-performance computing applications. Dr. Kindratenko earned his D.Sc. degree from the University of Antwerp, Belgium, in 1997. His research interests encompass high-performance computing, special-purpose computing architectures, cloud computing, and machine learning systems and applications. His work has received funding from NSF, NASA, ONR, DOE, and industry. Dr. Kindratenko has published over 140 papers in refereed scientific journals and conference proceedings and holds five US patents.

events.title: Self-Healing GPU Clusters: Fault Tolerance and Straggler Remediation for AI Workloads
events.description: GPU scarcity is a fact of life across industry, universities, research organizations, and government agencies. Worse, these scarce resources are routinely wasted since distributed training runs only as fast as its slowest worker, and a single failure can crash a thousand-GPU job. This talk, joint work between Hyperstack and Clockwork.io, presents an architecture and demonstration for self-healing training on Kubernetes clusters. We stand up an on-demand GPU Kubernetes cluster, launch a multi-node PyTorch training job with a deliberately degraded worker, rapidly detect the straggler using fine-grained collective-timing analysis, and live-migrate it to a healthy node so training returns to full speed. We then inject a hard failure and show the workload seamlessly migrate and proceed with forward progress preserved, without restarting from the most recent checkpoint. Attendees will leave with practical techniques for dealing with stragglers and failures and an architectural understanding of live GPU migration.

events.title: Bull’s Evaluation and Prediction Performance Tools for Large Modern Multipartition Computing Facilities, the Grand Cru Project
events.description:
Modern supercomputers increasingly combine CPU clusters, GPU partitions, AI systems, and multiple hardware generations under a unified scheduler, making them particularly hard to design. Also, benchmark implementations still assume homogeneous systems, forcing computing centers to evaluate each computing partition independently.

High-Performance Linpack (HPL) and its mixed-precision extension HPL-MxP remain among the most widely used reference benchmarks for assessing the performance of large-scale HPC systems, notably in the context of TOP500 submissions. However, the most performant implementations are often tightly coupled to vendor-specific software stacks, which limits portability and complicates early-stage performance evaluation for heterogeneous platforms.

In this presentation, we address three complementary objectives: first, the development of a portable HPL/HPL-MxP implementation for Bull; second, the execution of the HPL and/or HPL-MxP benchmark across an entire heterogeneous supercomputer; and third, the ability to predict performance at scale to support cluster designing. Results will be presented according to each objective.

events.title: Sensor Placement for Tsunami Early Warning via Large-Scale Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design
events.description: Real-time tsunami early warning relies on distributed sensor networks to infer seismic sources and seafloor motion. Optimizing these networks via Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) is exceptionally challenging for systems governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations, which lack the spectral decay required by standard low-rank approximations. We present a scalable Bayesian OED framework for linear time-invariant systems. By reformulating the inverse problem in the data space, we transform OED into dense matrix subset selection. We propose a multi-GPU, Schur-complement-update-based, greedy algorithm that solves the OED problem using a pipelined approach that fully overlaps I/O with GPU computations. Our framework achieves near-perfect weak and strong scaling across hundreds of GPUs on Perlmutter and Frontier. Applied to the 2025 Gordon Bell Prize-winning digital twin for tsunami forecasting in the Cascadia Subduction Zone, we optimize a 175-sensor network, minimizing the uncertainty of a parameter field with over one billion degrees of freedom.

events.title: Parallel k-Clique Counting via Hierarchical Breadth-First Search
events.description: We propose a new parallel algorithm for k-clique counting, a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. The state-of-the-art algorithm combinatorially counts k-cliques within maximal cliques to reduce the search tree size. However, its parallel performance degrades rapidly with clique size, due to (1) wasted work exploring subproblems that contain no k-cliques, and (2) load imbalance from highly irregular subproblem sizes. We introduce a hierarchical BFS-based algorithm, Calico, that restricts the search to a reduced edge set. To mitigate load imbalance, Calico also limits search tree depth by reformulating dense subproblems as counting independent sets on their corresponding complement graphs. Calico achieves up to 16,631× speedup over parallel baselines with scaling up to 192 cores on large real-world graphs. Calico is the first to count k-cliques of any specified size on the previously intractable com-LiveJournal graph, reducing the reported runtime from approximately 62 hours (k ≤ 13) to under 14 seconds.

events.title: BatchFlow: Benefit-Aware Data Pipeline Allocation and Batch Reuse for Multi-Job Training
events.description: Deep learning training is often limited by data pipeline throughput, reducing accelerator utilization and increasing training time and cost. This is particularly challenging in multi-tenant environments, where jobs compete for storage and CPU resources. We present BatchFlow, a data pipeline service that improves aggregate training throughput by dynamically allocating data pipeline workers across jobs. BatchFlow uses online profiling to estimate how quickly each job consumes mini-batches and how quickly workers can prepare them, then allocates workers to jobs where data supply is most likely to fall behind training demand. BatchFlow also caches prepared mini-batches for reuse across jobs, reducing repeated reads from slow storage and redundant CPU preprocessing. When cache capacity is limited, a benefit-aware policy determines which mini-batches to prefetch and retain. Across multi-job workloads, BatchFlow increases aggregate training throughput by up to 3.8× and cost efficiency by up to 2.1× relative to prior systems.

events.title: TIDE: Temporal Incremental Draft Engine for Self-Improving LLM Inference
events.description: Speculative decoding can substantially accelerate LLM inference, but realizing its benefits in practice is challenging due to evolving workloads. We present TIDE (Temporal Incremental Draft Engine), a serving-engine-native framework that integrates online draft adaptation directly into high-performance LLM inference systems. TIDE reuses target model's intermediate hidden states generated during inference as training signals for draft adaptation, thereby avoiding additional target model computation and serving-time overhead. It employs adaptive runtime control to activate speculation and draft model training only when beneficial. TIDE exploits heterogeneous clusters by mapping inference and training to appropriate GPU classes. Across diverse real-world workloads, TIDE achieves up to 1.66× throughput over no-speculation baselines while recovering performance on misaligned workloads where static draft models degrade throughput. TIDE also reduces training time by up to 3.02× and storage requirements by 24× compared to existing draft training approaches, and improves system throughput by up to 1.22× on heterogeneous GPU clusters.

events.title: Trigger, Render, Reason: Multimodal LLM Agents for Science-Aware Scientific Simulation Monitoring
events.description: Scientific simulations on leadership-class HPC systems routinely waste millions of core-hours producing invalid results, yet no tool monitors whether a running simulation computes valid science. We call this blind spot dark waste. Detecting it requires physics-aware judgment at every timestep, which neither humans nor system-level monitors supply. Multimodal LLM agents could, but they cannot ingest scientific data: no field fits in a context window. What an agent can ingest is a rendering, a lossy encoding that discards precision, preserves structure, and stays a fixed size regardless of the field behind it. Because a fixed rendering answers only the question it was made for, we give the agent control of the visualization. Vigil instantiates this as a trigger-render-reason pipeline: cheap deterministic triggers watch every timestep, and only flagged states are rendered and reasoned over. Across four codes, Vigil detects every parameter-induced failure and dismisses a trigger fired on a healthy run.

events.title: ACSC Student Presentations
events.description: The University of Texas at Austin will host this event.

events.title: Students@SC Alumni Reception
events.description:
Join us at McCormick Place in the South Lobby of the Grand Ballroom for the SC Students and Alumni Reception, an evening of HPC, machine learning, and quantum computing mysteries. Compare theories, trade debugging stories, and meet someone new.

Participants will have the opportunity to meet each other and VIP guests, hear about their career paths, and ask questions or exchange advice one-on-one. Throughout the evening, we will solve riddles inspired by the real pitfalls of advanced computing. Hors d’oeuvres will be served, and SC swag raffles will take place at 5:00, 5:30, and 6:00 p.m. We want to bring together all registered students, Early Career Program participants, alumni, and VIPs to create as many opportunities for networking and engagement as possible.

Here is your first mystery:

The case of the simulation that refused to finish

A simulation must count twenty million events before it stops. On the workstation, it finishes. On the accelerator, it runs indefinitely. The accelerator is still processing events. No error is reported. Its counter has reached 16,777,216 and will not move, although the program keeps adding one.

What has the machine run out of?

Come prepared to solve more mysteries and make connections.

events.title: File-System-Aware Incremental Backup at Billion-File Scale: Lessons From GPFS, Lustre, and ZFS
events.description: Backing up persistent research data presents a different challenge from managing HPC scratch and archive tiers. When few files change, repeatedly scanning an entire filesystem can consume the backup window and compete with research workloads. This presentation explores how IBM Storage Scale (GPFS), ZFS, and Lustre help backup applications identify changes more efficiently. We present comparative results across all three filesystems, including preliminary ZFS and Lustre findings, and discuss reliability and integration challenges. Production experience includes a ZFS deployment at MIT with 140 million files, where scanning was 14 times faster. Attendees will gain a practical framework for evaluating filesystem-aware incremental backup, understanding its limitations, and balancing performance with reliable recovery in large research environments.

events.title: Making RAG Count: Ground-Truth-Validated Aggregation Over 3,052 HPC Outcome Reports
events.description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbots often fail on aggregation queries because conventional retrieval returns the most relevant chunks instead of the complete set of records required for accurate aggregation. We extend an existing RAG pipeline with two components. A Schema-directed Extractor converts documents into typed SQL tables at ingestion, while a Query-time Aggregation Agent identifies schema-defined objects in user queries, executes aggregation over the structured tables, and cites the supporting evidence. We applied the method to a public RAG chatbot for outcome reports on shared HPC resources in Japan. Against manually constructed ground truth for all 3,052 reports, the Extractor achieved 99.9% resource-row recall and 99.9% exact agreement for both allocated and used node-hours. In an end-to-end evaluation of 13 queries, nine of ten SQL-routed queries exactly matched the ground truth, one differed in the population aggregated, and three out-of-schema queries were correctly routed away from SQL to the text-retrieval path.

events.title: TriBIT: Triangle Counting Using Binary Tensor Core Operations
events.description:
The graph triangle counting (TC) problem appears frequently in scientific computing domains such as large-scale graph processing, bioinformatics or social network analysis, motivating the need for efficient TC techniques on HPC platforms. However, existing approaches deliver suboptimal end-to-end performance due to (1) high memory consumption; (2) expensive graph preprocessing overheads; and (3) substantial data movement across heterogeneous CPU-GPU platforms.

To overcome these problems, we propose TriBIT, the first TC algorithm for GPUs that (1) leverages bitmap-based compressed data structures particularly tailored to the TC problem, significantly reducing memory footprint; and (2) exploits bitwise operations in GPU Tensor Core Units (TCUs). On single-GPU scenarios, using 810 sparse graphs from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection, TriBIT achieves geometric mean speedups ranging from 4.63× to 213.61× over state-of-the-art approaches. In multi-GPU scenarios, TriBIT processes graphs with more than 128 billion edges, achieving a throughput of 381 billion triangles per second on 32 GPUs.

events.title: Ordered Chaos: Towards Adaptive Multipath Load Balancing with Precise, Fast Loss Detection
events.description: Load balancing in best-effort datacenter fabrics faces a trade-off. Order-preserving schemes such as equal-cost multipath (ECMP) retain loss semantics but use path diversity coarsely, while packet spraying balances load well but removes the ordering signals needed for fast, precise loss detection. We present Ordered Chaos, an end-host design that preserves enough structure for reliable loss detection without giving up fine-grained multipath routing. Reactive subflow spraying (RSS) divides each flow into ordered, dynamically routed subflows. Precise fast loss detection (PFLD) combines this ordering with probes to distinguish reordering from congestion, corruption, tail, and retransmission losses within one RTT. Across simulations, AI and HPC workloads, and a DPU prototype, RSS+PFLD improves tail flow completion time by up to 3x, eliminates up to 99% of timeout-based recoveries, and accelerates collective and training communication by up to 35%.

events.title: LLMProf: Identifying Performance Bottlenecks in LLM Serving Systems with Top-Down Profiling
events.description: Large language model (LLM) serving systems have become critical cloud workloads, yet their performance diagnosis remains challenging due to rapid software-hardware evolution, dynamic request patterns, and the limitations of existing profiling tools. These gaps force developers to rely on manual heuristics for performance optimization, leading to slow progress and error-prone code. We present LLMProf, a low-overhead profiling framework tailored for various LLM serving systems. LLMProf employs a top-down, multi-level analysis approach that captures only the most relevant metrics at each profiling level to balance detail with minimal performance impact while remaining agnostic to frameworks and hardware. We present case studies that leverage LLMProf to optimize real-world LLM serving workloads, from which we derive a performance diagnosis taxonomy that provides actionable guidance and enables automated postmortem analysis. Our case studies demonstrate that by applying simple optimizations uncovered by LLMProf, we can achieve up to 2.09× throughput improvement.

events.title: Papers in Conversation
events.description: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

events.title: The International Post-Exascale (InPEx) Project
events.description:
Several (trans-)national initiatives have recognized the crucial importance of co-design between hardware, software, and application stakeholders in the path to exascale and beyond. However, these regional efforts are somehow disconnected while the community would benefit by sharing return of experience, common know-how, and advancing on the new problems arising as exascale machines become more and more available.

The International Post-Exascale (InPEx) Project will bring together researchers and engineers, companies, funding bodies, and policy organizations to contribute to the implementation of an international, shared, high-quality computing environment based on the principles and practices of co-design.

events.title: MLPerf: A Benchmark for Machine Learning
events.description: As AI workloads scale exponentially, evaluating machine learning infrastructure requires rigorous, standardized benchmarking. This Birds of a Feather session brings together HPC researchers, hardware architects, and software engineers to discuss the future of the MLPerf benchmark suite. The discussion will address critical scaling challenges, heterogeneous accelerator evaluation, and performance metrics for disaggregated infrastructure. Participants will collaborate on driving reproducibility and expanding benchmarks to encompass emerging, complex AI workloads. Join us to share deployment insights and directly shape the benchmarking roadmaps guiding the next generation of supercomputing systems.

events.title: Analog Computing for Science: From Emerging Technologies to a Shared Research Agenda
events.description: Analog computing is re-emerging as a broad approach to scientific computation, offering opportunities beyond energy efficiency, including low-latency physical dynamics, reduced data movement, computation integrated with sensing, and new methods for simulation, optimization, and artificial intelligence. Yet progress remains fragmented across physical substrates, applications, architectures, mathematics, and software. This highly interactive BoF will bring the SC community together to identify challenges, promising workloads, shared infrastructure, and opportunities for collaboration. Building on the DOE ASCR report Basic Research Needs for Analog Computing for Science, participants will prioritize research directions and help shape a community agenda for analog and hybrid analog-digital computing.

events.title: AI and ML for HPC Workload Analysis: From Isolation to Reproducibility — Building Common Benchmarks
events.description: HPC facilities each build operational data analytics in isolation, with no shared benchmarks to compare methods or reproduce results across sites. This seventh-edition BoF convenes the community around a common goal: shared standards, open benchmarks, and cross-facility collaboration for HPC workload analysis. Using the HPC ODA Commons, introduced to the community at ISC 2026, as a working exemplar, we examine how standardized schemas and benchmark recipes enable reproducible comparison across systems. We present an emerging multi-facility study, invite sites to contribute data, schemas, or models, and work together to prioritize analyses and plan a community report.

events.title: Inference Services and Agents on HPC: Scaling Scientific AI for Academic Community
events.description: Initiated at SC25 to explore AI inference services in the academic HPC community, this BoF returns to address the fast-evolving landscape of inference services, agentic AI, tool services, and AI4Science. This practitioner forum brings centers and researchers together to share practical insights and experiences spanning infrastructure, software, and use cases. This session aims to cultivate collaborative solutions for AI developments. The goal remains to foster a sustained, cross-institutional "community of practice" bridging academic and governmental HPC centers and the user community to foster collaborations in this area.

events.title: Open Source and Sovereign Infrastructure for HPC and AI
events.description:
Open source has long been at the heart of HPC infrastructure management. Traditional HPC platforms have been well served by software stacks designed to meet this specific purpose.

A new era brings new demands for HPC and AI. Open source infrastructure management faces new challenges on many fronts.

This session features leading practitioners of a new generation of software-defined open HPC-AI infrastructure. The session will present a diverse range of open source solutions for current use cases, including advantages and disadvantages. Common problems will be identified and solutions shared. Attendees will be invited to share their experiences.

events.title: Ultra Ethernet: Next-Generation Networking for HPC Supercomputers and AI Factories
events.description: Ultra Ethernet has emerged as a major effort to create a scalable, open networking architecture for both AI factories and high-performance computing systems. As AI clusters continue to grow while HPC workloads demand ever-higher communication performance and efficiency, many networking requirements are beginning to converge. This BoF provides a forum for researchers, system architects, operators, application developers, and network vendors to discuss experiences, emerging requirements, unresolved challenges, and future directions for large-scale networking. The discussion aims to identify common needs across HPC and AI and foster collaboration toward open, interoperable networking solutions for next-generation computing systems.

events.title: Quantum Jumps: From NISQ to FTQC to Hybrid HPC
events.description: Quantum computing is experiencing accelerating transitions, from noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices to fault-tolerant quantum computers, and from quantum computers being objects of research to their becoming scientific computation tools. Quantum programming habits and assumptions must be revisited, and for the HPC community, this is more than an incremental hardware upgrade; it affects entire stacks. This session will explore how compilation workflows, execution models, and algorithmic strategies are expected to change to incorporate error correction and integrate with production HPC workflows. Thought leaders from the quantum industry, HPC, and academic research will exchange perspectives and engage the audience in discussion.

events.title: The Green500: Trends in Energy-Efficient Supercomputing
events.description: With power being a first-order design constraint on par with performance, it is important to measure and analyze energy-efficiency trends in supercomputing. To raise the awareness of greenness as a first-order design constraint, the Green500 seeks to characterize the energy efficiency of supercomputers for different metrics, workloads, and methodologies. This BoF discusses trends across the Green500 and highlights from the current Green500 list. In addition, the Green500, Top500, and Energy Efficient HPC Working Group have been working together on improving power-measurement methodology, and this BoF presents updates that will improve ease of submission without compromising accuracy.

events.title: Procurements Under Pressure: Adaptive Strategies for HPC Centers in an Uncertain World
events.description: HPC computing centers face mounting procurement risks driven by geopolitical tensions, semiconductor supply constraints, and AI-driven demand for GPUs. Leading-edge fabrication is concentrated among a small number of fabs worldwide, leaving centers exposed when disruptions strike. What was once a predictable multi-year planning cycle has become a landscape of uncertainty. This BoF brings together center directors, vendors, and system integrators from across the international HPC community to develop shared adaptive strategies — from flexible RFPs to extended machine lifetimes. Community participation is central: the goal is not to deliver answers, but to build them together.

events.title: Key Features Coming to OpenMP API Version 6.1
events.description: The OpenMP Architecture Review Board releases new versions of OpenMP every 2-3 years. This year, we will release OpenMP API version 6.1 just before SC26. Feature champions from the OpenMP Language committee will highlight key features in the OpenMP API version 6.1 through short lightning talks with rounds of discussion to give participants ample opportunity to interact with OpenMP experts, ask questions, and provide feedback. We will also include talks from vendors supporting compilers to discuss timelines for support of OpenMP API features.

events.title: Numerical Linear Algebra in the Age of Coding Agents
events.description: Since SC25, a revolution has taken hold: coding agents have moved from curiosity into nearly every institution's pipeline, and "vibe coding" is now how much software, numerical included, gets written. That matters for numerical linear algebra (NLA), whose libraries underpin modern science and whose trustworthiness was built over 50 years of human expert engineering. Now, when a plausible NLA kernel is nearly free to generate, what holds that trust together? This BoF gathers established leaders and younger NLA scientists from academia and industry to open a discussion, so our community shapes this shift rather than being swept along.

events.title: Who Shapes the Future of Public HPC? Planning, Priorities, and Investment in the Age of AI and Quantum Computing
events.description:
HPC infrastructures are being reshaped by rapid hardware innovation, pressure for greater energy efficiency, and the rise of AI and data-intensive workloads. Simultaneously, future directions are influenced not only by scientific communities and public research agendas, but also by industry roadmaps and emerging QC ambitions.

This BoF will examine how different countries plan future public HPC investments, how priorities are set, and who has influence in that process. The aim is to better understand whether public HPC remains community-driven or is increasingly shaped by industrial and market forces, and what this means for the future of research infrastructures.

events.title: Hands-On Outreach: Bridging AI, Supercomputing, and the Public
events.description: As AI rapidly reshapes public interest in computing, the HPC community has a unique opportunity to demystify these technologies and introduce foundational computational concepts. This interactive Birds of a Feather (BoF) session brings together HPC educators, trainers, and outreach practitioners to explore, facilitate, and evaluate hands-on AI outreach activities. Participants will test proven activities, discuss engagement best practices, and collaborate to design new resources using both human-led and AI-assisted frameworks. Attendees will walk away with a toolkit of reusable activities, insights into AI-driven content generation, and a collaborative network to strengthen HPC outreach community-wide.

events.title: Scientific Software and the People Who Make It Happen: Building Our Communities and Practices
events.description:
Software has become central to all aspects of modern science and technology. Especially in high performance computing (HPC) and computational science and engineering (CSE), it is becoming ever larger and more complex while computer platforms evolve and become more diverse. Simultaneously, the teams behind the software are becoming larger, more technically diverse, and more geographically distributed. AI tools add both great potential and significant caution.

This BoF will address these issues and more, sharing experiences and best practices, and building community around software topics. Presentations and discussion notes will be made available at the BoF series website (http://bit.ly/swe-cse-bof).

events.title: MPICH: A High-Performance Open-Source MPI Implementation
events.description: MPICH is one of the most widely used open-source implementations of the MPI standard and the foundation for many vendor MPI libraries powering today's HPC systems. This BoF brings together MPICH developers, industry partners, and HPC users to share the latest project developments, discuss support for emerging architectures and MPI features, and explore future directions for the MPI ecosystem. This year's session will also discuss opportunities for community engagement and contributions to MPICH. Attendees are encouraged to participate in an interactive format, ask questions, share experiences, and help shape the future of one of HPC's core software infrastructures.

Art of HPC & HPC Around the World: Fractal Image Generator
events.room: Central Concourse - HPC Around the World
events.description: Join this interactive, community-building experience by scanning your badge at the interactive kiosk, located in the Central Concourse, across from Registration. Using your registration details, we’ll generate a one-of-a-kind fractal image just for you — sent to you and showcased on displays throughout the conference. You’ll also appear on the HPC Around the World map, celebrating the global reach of high performance computing. Be sure to come back each day to generate a new image.

events.title: Wheelchairs and Scooters
2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
events.description: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

events.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
events.description:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman
Music Composition and Performance: Stephan Vankov

Produced at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, UIC, and Calit2, UCSD

events.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
events.description:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

events.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
events.description:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.

events.title: Art of HPC Exhibition
events.description:
Art of HPC

Where Creativity Meets HPC

Creativity has always been at the heart of innovation. It drives new perspectives, fuels artistic expression, and allows us to see beauty in unexpected places. By leveraging cutting-edge technology and resources, we can push the boundaries of both science and art. SC proudly presents Art of HPC, a showcase of the intersection between artistic creativity and high performance computing.
