events.title: Trustworthy Agentic AI for HPC Operational and Predictive Data Analytics and Forecasting
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer promising pathways for automating high performance computing (HPC) operations, yet their real-world deployment is severely constrained by silent operational failures, uncalibrated confidence, and brittle central control. In this work, we chart a new vision for reliable, agentic AI across supercomputing facilities. We explore the architectural paradigm shift from centralized orchestration to decentralized, peer-to-peer agent topologies, illustrating how typed dialogue and bounded knowledge limits ensure defensible, transparent operational guidance. Furthermore, we examine the critical challenge of stance fidelity, demonstrating how verbalized confidence must be audited as dynamic system telemetry rather than taken at face value. Based on these insights, we advocate for a fundamental re-architecting of facility AI: prioritizing honest refusal over raw recall, establishing auditable ground-truth benchmarks, and transitioning AI tools from passive historical log lookups to active, pre-submission job steering.

events.title: Understanding AllReduce Performance Through Hardware Telemetry
events.description: Inter-GPU AllReduce operations traverse several tightly coupled hardware components, including the GPU, PCIe interface, NIC, and network. Each component exposes hardware telemetry for its local behavior, and no single telemetry source observes the complete communication path. A combined view is therefore needed to narrow where performance is limited and to guide optimization. We combine selected NVIDIA A100 GPU counters with Cassini NIC counters on HPE Slingshot-11 to analyze a 1 GiB inter-node AllReduce across NCCL protocols, NCCL channel counts, and GPU-aware MPI versus NCCL. Across the three studies, the joint telemetry associates performance differences with distinct behaviors: work amplification for NCCL LL, increased synchronization and reduced transfer progress at high channel counts, and slow transfer progress with additional rank imbalance for MPI. Joint GPU–NIC telemetry therefore helps distinguish different sources of AllReduce slowdown and narrows where optimization effort should be focused.

events.title: Understanding and Improving Multi-Rack Symmetric-Memory AllGather in NCCL
events.description: Rack-scale GPU systems such as the GB200 NVL72 extend the NVLink scale-up domain from four or eight GPUs per server to 72 GPUs per rack. Large language model (LLM) training still scales across many racks, with all-gathers spanning heterogeneous NVLink and InfiniBand fabrics. These all-gathers operate in a message-size regime where both latency and bandwidth matter. In this work, we characterize NCCL's symmetric-memory and legacy all-gather performance for this regime. We derive a closed-form topology-aware bandwidth bound and extend it with a latency term for comparison with empirical measurements. Based on observed trends and model insights, we design two new GPU-initiated symmetric-memory all-gather implementations that outperform NCCL's symmetric-memory all-gathers by up to 2.6x for 32-512MB messages.

events.title: Understanding the NERSC User Community Through Network Analysis
events.description: NERSC users collaborate, forming a network. Which users occupy the most structurally influential positions in the NERSC user community? Using 2020–2026 NERSC allocation records, a proxy collaboration graph was analyzed to reveal the user community’s dynamics. Two definitions of user connectivity were compared using available data on project allocation size: unweighted degree and repository-size-adjusted (RSA) strength. Degree distributions, program-office affiliation, and user roles were analyzed. Results show that RSA strength is a more accurate measurement of user connectivity than unweighted degree. The strongest connectors in the network are career scientists and users associated with high-energy physics. These findings suggest that in HPC network data, unweighted connectivity is not a reliable measurement of network influence or cross-disciplinary reach. Findings also suggest that allocation networks reflect certain field-specific collaboration patterns, implying that allocation networks may provide a useful proxy for co-authorship networks in the same field.

events.title: Union of Containers: Layered Software Stacks with Cross-Container Dependency Reuse for HPC
events.description: HPC software stacks are typically distributed as one container image per accelerator target, and every image duplicates the CPU-generic majority of the stack. This work splits the stack across containers. A shared provider holds the architecture-generic dependencies; thin specialized layers hold only GPU-compiled packages and reuse the provider's builds instead of recompiling them. The layers compose at run time through absolute RPATH entries under fixed paths, with no search-path configuration. With Spack and E4S recipes, each specialized layer compiled 1 of 20 buildable packages at two facilities, Midway3 and NSF ACCESS Anvil. On Anvil, each further GPU target adds 1,412 files where a monolithic build adds 10,772, rebuilding a layer is 1.8 to 2.8 times faster, and application performance is unchanged on A100 and H100 GPUs. The same install trees run unmodified under Apptainer and Charliecloud. The poster also reports four constraints on where reuse holds.

events.title: Useful Data, Not Just More Data: Cost-Aware Floating Car Data Generation in Large-Scale Traffic Simulation
events.description: Large-scale traffic simulations can generate millions of floating car data (FCD) records, but more output does not necessarily provide more useful information. Using Ruth on LUMI, we study a Chicago scenario with 6.9 million input vehicle trips and 748,509 road-network nodes. We compare output size, road-edge coverage, temporal coverage, and speed similarity against a high-detail simulation reference. With vehicle updates fixed at 20 seconds, increasing the FCD sampling period from 5 to 20 seconds halves output while retaining 97.1% road-edge coverage and 88.9% temporal coverage. Tests on 1–16 nodes show sublinear gains in the traffic-time interval recorded within a fixed wall-time budget. Reducing rerouting participation from 80% to 50% extends this interval by 18%–22% and lowers wall time per second of recorded traffic time by 15%–18%. We recommend selecting the smallest output meeting task-specific coverage and speed-error requirements; rerouting changes still require validation of traffic outcomes.

events.title: VLIW Scheduling: Timing Is All You Need
events.description:
AMD's XDNA2 NPU packs 32 six-issue VLIW cores where the schedule must resolve nearly all pipeline hazards. Each core achieves 1,843 GFLOPS by always issuing a VMAC.F operation, an 8×8×8 block-floating-point (BFP16) matrix multiply-accumulate. This corresponds to an array-wide performance of 59 TFLOPS. One obstacle is register pressure: a standard double-buffered 2×2 output block needs eight accumulator registers, whereas a core has only five.

We present a hand-scheduled VLIW BFP16 tensor-contraction kernel that time-multiplexes the output block's four accumulation chains onto two registers and issues a VMAC.F in every steady-state cycle.

On one core with L1-resident data, our kernel achieves 96.4% of theoretical peak (5.0× faster than the compiled mm_bfp.cc kernel). With the operands streamed from DRAM, a pre-tiled M3840×N3840×K8192 matrix multiplication reaches 21.4 TFLOPS on the whole NPU.

At the poster, we will walk visitors through the VLIW scheduling diagrams and the scannable artifact reproducing every measurement.

events.title: VisKnacks: Agentic ParaView Visualization on HPC
events.description: Artificial intelligence can assist in prototyping scientific visualizations. To assist visualization experts, we introduce VisKnacks, an autonomous ParaView visualization agent enabled by large language models (LLMs). VisKnacks integrates multi-agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and containerized rendering services for high performance computing (HPC) systems while remaining compatible with existing agent harnesses. The system supports hybrid workflows in which ParaView rendering is distributed to HPC resources while pipeline creation and iterative refinement remain local. We present the system overview, initial benchmarks, visualization quality benchmarks, and lessons learned from deploying this system.

events.title: VisionHPC: AI Generation of Expert-Level HPC Codes From High-Level Mathematical Abstractions
events.description: We present VisionHPC, an agentic AI framework that generates expert-level high performance computing (HPC) code directly from high-level mathematical abstractions. Following extensive expert-guided training, it produces HPC implementations for multicore CPUs and GPUs using widely adopted parallel programming models, including OpenMP, OpenACC, and CUDA/HIP. The framework accepts images of mathematical formulations from three representative scientific domains — linear algebra, partial differential equations, and computational fluid dynamics — and translates them into efficient parallel code. Compared with state-of-the-art multimodal models, including ChatGPT, MathGPT, and Claude, VisionHPC achieves up to 12× higher correctness than the strongest baseline, reaching an average correctness exceeding 95%. These results demonstrate that AI can reliably bridge high-level mathematical descriptions and expert-quality HPC software, substantially improving productivity for scientific software development.

events.title: When More Cores Hurts: The Vector Database Scaling Paradox in HPC
events.description: Vector databases have been designed and optimized for cloud environments; however, emerging scientific AI workloads (e.g., molecular search, meteorological trajectory detection, and literature-driven hypothesis generation) demand efficient, scalable execution on HPC systems. We present a large-scale evaluation of three state-of-the-art vector databases — Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate — on two production supercomputers, scaling to 256 distributed workers across 64 compute nodes. We evaluate VDBs using Yandex-T2I, a multimodal embedding dataset, and Pes2o-VE, a novel real-world scientific dataset. Our results reveal that insertion is bottlenecked by per-batch consistency requirements, additional cores can reduce query throughput by up to 30.67%, and scaling from 16 to 256 workers yields a 2.67x improvement with 16 nodes before QPS begins to decline. This scaling paradox exposes the fundamental mismatch between cloud-oriented designs and HPC systems, highlighting the need for new, HPC-aware vector database designs.

events.title: Lowering the Barrier to HPC/AI: Open OnDemand at Recod.ai
Network Research Exhibition (NRE) Theater Talks
TBD
Detecting and Containing Silent Errors
events.description: These papers study silent errors across GPUs, DRAM, and large-model workloads. They combine characterization, predictive modeling, error correction, and low-overhead detection to improve trust in long-running HPC computations.

events.title: LLM-PRISM: Characterizing Silent Data Corruption from Permanent GPU Faults in LLM Training
events.description: Large-scale LLM training is increasingly susceptible to hardware defects stemming from manufacturing escapes and silicon aging. These defects manifest as silent data corruption (SDC) that perturbs gradients and parameters throughout the training process. We present LLM-PRISM, a methodology to characterize LLM pre-training resilience to hardware faults. LLM-PRISM couples RTL-level GPU fault simulation with a stochastic injection engine embedded in Megatron-LM. Through 7,664 training runs across FP16, BF16, and FP8 regimes, we analyze how fault type, rate, and numeric format govern resilience. We find that while LLMs resist low-frequency faults, impact is highly non-uniform; critical datapaths and specific precision formats can induce catastrophic divergence even at moderate fault rates. This study provides the first hardware-grounded, pre-training characterization of SDC resilience.

events.title: Mapping and Programming Emerging Spatial and Wafer-Scale Systems
events.description: Emerging spatial and wafer-scale systems require new approaches to topology, mapping, and programming. The papers span wafer-scale interconnect architecture, scalable mapping of tensor-network DAGs, geometric multigrid on WSE-3, and a high-level spatial-dataflow language and compiler.

events.title: Wafer-Net: A Flexible Hierarchical Interconnection Architecture Based on Wafer-Scale Integration
events.description: High-performance interconnection networks are typically built upon high-radix routers. As system scale continues to grow, the conventional switch-centric scaling paradigm faces severe challenges in latency, deployment cost, and scalability. This paper proposes Wafer-Net, a flexible hierarchical interconnection architecture enabled by wafer-scale integration. Wafer-Net abstracts distributed on-wafer compute and switch resources into two composable building blocks—the Compute Chiplet Group (CCG) and the Switch Chiplet Group (SCG)—and thereby recasts conventional interconnection networks as a hierarchical structure that combines local high-bandwidth domains with global low-latency switching. We further propose a formal mapping framework based on hierarchical compression transformations and dynamic programming. Using this framework, we instantiate three representative Wafer-Net topologies, which significantly reduce network diameter and cabling overhead while supporting concise and efficient minimal/non-minimal and adaptive routing algorithms. Simulation results show that these Wafer-Net topologies consistently outperform both their conventional counterparts and the wafer-scale baseline in throughput and latency.

events.title: Energy and Contention in Large-Scale AI Training
events.description: The papers examine energy, scale, and interference in large AI training systems. They connect phase-aware power control, simulation, cross-layer measurement, and multi-tenant performance.

events.title: PHANTOM: Phase-Aware Power Management for Energy-Efficient LLM Training
events.description: GPUs enable large-scale LLM training, but high energy consumption and sharp power transients hurt efficiency and reliability. Existing GPU power-management methods are largely reactive and do not exploit the phase structure of training iterations. We present PHANTOM, a predictive, phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) framework for sustainable and reliable multi-GPU LLM training. We show that iteration-level power traces exhibit repeatable, fine-grained phase patterns. PHANTOM uses a lightweight temporal convolutional network (TCN) to predict short-horizon GPU power from synchronized hardware events and phase signals, then applies a Pareto-based multi-objective optimizer to choose frequencies ahead of phase transitions, balancing energy efficiency and power stability under real-time constraints. This design is lightweight enough for online deployment without intrusive changes to the training workflow. On multi-GPU LLM workloads, PHANTOM reduces energy by 15%–16%, normalized power-slew rate (NPSR) by 9%–15%, and energy–delay product (EDP) by 10%–11% compared with the default hardware DVFS policy.

events.title: Quantum and Tensor Methods on Emerging Accelerators
events.description: Three papers center on quantum-classical computation for linear systems, electronic structure, and peptide structure prediction; SpG-Attention provides a complementary example of algorithm–accelerator co-design by mapping irregular sparse graph attention onto dense Tensor Cores.

events.title: Towards High-Performance Sparse Graph Attention on Dense Tensor Core Units
events.description: Sparse graph attention (SGA) is a critical building block of attention-based graph neural networks (GNNs). Existing approaches either optimize individual primitives (e.g., SDDMM or SpMM) in isolation or rely on block-sparse representations, which fail to map graph-sparse workloads efficiently onto dense TCUs. We propose SpG-Attention, a unified framework that bridges sparse graph attention with dense TCU computation. Specifically, SpG-Attention introduces: (1) memory-efficient SGA (ME-SGA) parallel strategies that classify attention multiplications by their reduction characteristics and choose row/column-wise parallelization accordingly; (2) a TCU-friendly condensed-sparse format and customized fused kernels with MMA-aligned tiled execution, discrete-to-contiguous tiled loading, metadata prefetch pipelining, and register-fragment alignment; and (3) input-aware runtime optimizations based on graph statistics and refined by bounded online profiling to handle structural diversity and long-tail degree distributions. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate that SpG-Attention achieves average speedups of 2.45x over Fused3S for inference and 2.15x over FlashSparse for end-to-end training.

events.title: OCEAN: Open-Source CXL Emulation for Hyperscale Architecture and Networking
events.description: Compute Express Link (CXL) 3.0 introduces fabric-level memory pooling, yet the absence of production CXL 3.0 hardware and the complexity of multi-host configurations pose significant barriers to the research community. This paper presents OCEAN, a high-fidelity, open-source emulation framework that reproduces the fabric-level feature set that distinguishes CXL 3.0—including multi-host memory sharing, dynamic capacity management, and coherent pooling across hosts—using QEMU virtualization and custom Linux kernel modules. OCEAN makes two central technical contributions: active latency injection and a software cache coherence layer implementing MESI-state management with distributed snoop filters to maintain correctness across up to 16 hosts. We validate OCEAN against a real CXL Type-3 device. In addition, case studies on Tigon database workloads quantify the throughput impact of hardware cache coherence—an 11× improvement at full coverage—while a design-space sweep of 12 memory-placement policies on GROMACS demonstrates up to 7% performance variation from policy choice alone.

events.title: Papers in Conversation: Memory-Centric HPC: CXL, Tiering, and Shared Memory
events.description: This session addresses CXL from three complementary angles: open emulation, transparent tiered-memory management, and the cost of software-managed synchronization. It provides a focused forum on how pooled memory will change HPC architecture and programming.

events.title: My Coauthors Don’t Sleep: Agentic AI and Trust in Computational Science
events.description: This panel will discuss the role of agentic AI and ML in the predictive science setting, with a focus on impacts to computational science and HPC. In particular, questions related to trustworthy agentic AI for science will form the core theme, as enabled by explainability and interpretability methods, as well as robust treatment of uncertainty in models and data. What are the particular challenges and opportunities for agentic workflows for modSim at exascale? How can uncertainty quantification be a scaffold for scientific AI/ML, and what are the pitfalls? This discussion will lay the foundation for future work in HPC co-design at the interface of theory, software, and hardware optimization as we prepare for new paradigms of predictive modeling and simulation in the era of agentic AI.

events.title: My Coauthors Don’t Sleep: Agentic AI and Trust in Computational Science
HPC–Quantum Integration: Software, Systems, and Hybrid Workflows
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing are coming together to enable hybrid workflows that combine classical and quantum resources within a single computing environment. As quantum technologies evolve at different paces, integrating them into HPC systems introduces challenges for software, hardware, and scientific applications.

This panel brings together perspectives from HPC centers, quantum hardware development, and academic research to examine how HPC–quantum integration is approached in practice. Panelists will discuss software and systems layers enabling hybrid execution, including programming models, workflow orchestration, and middleware connecting HPC environments to quantum resources.

Drawing on early integration efforts, the discussion will highlight how communities are engaging with hybrid workflows — from deploying and evaluating quantum resources within HPC facilities to developing hardware and exploring algorithms and use cases. Panelists will share insights into challenges such as latency, resource management, as well as differing expectations around performance, usability, and readiness across quantum paradigms.

events.title: HPC–Quantum Integration: Software, Systems, and Hybrid Workflows
Doctoral Showcase I Presentations
Near-Real-Time Performance Visualization of MPI Applications: Integrating Performance Analysis Into HPC Education
events.description:
High performance computing (HPC) has become an essential capability in both industrial practice and scientific research, making the acquisition of practical HPC skills an increasingly important objective in higher education. Parallel programming with models such as MPI and OpenMP is central to this training, and students should gain experience on real HPC clusters rather than on local machines. However, universities often have access only to limited, partitioned, or decommissioned cluster resources, while learners must also master operational concepts such as SSH, SCP, and batch-based job management with systems such as SLURM. In addition, efficient MPI programs require performance analysis, yet established tools are designed for experts and assume prior knowledge of instrumentation, measurement, and interpretation.

EduMPI Suite addresses this gap by providing an educational environment for executing and analyzing MPI programs on HPC clusters in near-real-time. It automatically delivers visual feedback on MPI communication events during execution, enabling students to observe program behavior and understand the performance characteristics. A distinctive feature is the visualization of internal algorithmic communication patterns of collective operations, which are often hidden in professional tools but are crucial for understanding the performance implications of collective communication.

Usability evaluations over multiple semesters show that EduMPI Suite lowers the barriers to practical HPC performance analysis, is recommended by students, and improves the success rate of identifying and explaining performance problems to 96%, compared with 60% for professional analysis tools. Its near-real-time performance analysis is enabled by low measurement overhead <3.8% and low query latency <0.09 s.

events.title: Advancing HPC Research and Development Workflows with High-Speed Data Transfer and Data Provenance for AI-Driven Science
events.description:
The rapid adoption of AI in scientific research is increasing the importance of data-centric computing infrastructures that support large-scale data movement, management, and reproducibility. While HPC systems provide the computational foundation for scientific discovery, challenges related to efficient data utilization frequently limit research productivity.

This talk presents research information infrastructure (RII) that integrates data management, high-speed data transfer, and provenance-aware computing for AI-driven scientific workflows. The infrastructure incorporates ultra-high-speed data transfer system (UDTS), which enables efficient disk-to-disk transfer of large datasets across high-bandwidth networks, and data provenance system for HPC (DPS4H), which automatically captures execution histories, file dependencies, and workflow metadata without requiring modifications to existing applications. Proof-of-concept evaluations demonstrated effective utilization of available network resources and practical applicability to data-intensive research environments. By combining scalable data movement and automated provenance collection, RII provides a foundation for reproducible, collaborative, and data-centric scientific computing in the AI and exascale era.

events.title: HPC Networks
Conversations on Neurodiversity
events.description: This fireside chat explores neurodiversity within the HPC community. Join speakers from Microsoft and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory as they discuss workplace interactions, mentorship, and vital resources for neurodiverse individuals.

events.title: Conversations on Neurodiversity
AI Applications in the Real World
Bits to Bites: Securing the Future of Agricultural Production Using AI
events.description:
Tackling the grand challenges of 21st-century agriculture requires a fundamental shift in the way we envision the role of data science and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, and in the way we build agricultural AI systems. Farmers and policy makers face variable profitability, major crop loss and poor crop quality owing to a number of challenges including labor shortage, weather and production uncertainties, and water scarcity. While there is certainly a growing interest in AI-based solutions because of a rapid adoption of precision agriculture technologies, traditional approaches to developing digital solutions do not necessarily work well in this landscape. A deeply embedded model toward development, that engages AI and data engineers directly with extension scientists and growers, is likely to be more fruitful.

In this talk, Ananth Kalyanaraman will present ongoing developments of scalable AI solutions and tools for the U.S. specialty crop agricultural systems. In particular, he will cover machine learning models and tools for two classes of agricultural applications: 1) farm intelligence: delivering decision support at the farm scale, toward mitigation of weather-induced risks and providing farmers with forecasting capabilities; and 2) water intelligence: delivering decision support at a regional scale, toward seasonal planning of water allocation and reservoir management in snow-dominant watersheds. Through these experiential reports, he aims to provide the audience an idea about the kind of AI solutions and tools that he likes to call “Agricultural AI” that are needed for agricultural ecosystems, and share the lessons learned about the limitations and associated challenges, along with areas where new breakthroughs and investments are needed, to scale AI development and use for enhanced agricultural productivity.

events.title: Data Centers and Water: Socioenvironmental Risks in Times of Digital Expansion
Towards Resource-Efficient Parallel Concept Drift Detection in Data Streams
events.description:
Modern data science increasingly outpaces the efficient use of parallel hardware, creating a need for computational performance engineering. Because HPC tools are not embedded in exploratory data science environments, data scientists lack support for such investigations. This PhD project therefore bridges HPC and data science, using concept drift detection as a case study.

Concept drift—the change in data distributions after ML model deployment—must be detected to ensure robust streaming ML systems. However, the computational overhead of drift detectors (DDs) remains underexplored, even though directly affecting latency, energy consumption, and deployability. This gap motivates the thesis contributions.

First, a framework is introduced for systematically investigating the computational performance of DDs, including complexity analysis, benchmarking and performance analysis. Second, building on this framework, a survey and benchmark evaluate DDs bi-objectively, measuring both runtime and accuracy. The results reveal that computational performance is treated as secondary in the literature, no single detector dominates across scenarios, and higher accuracy consistently requires longer runtimes. Simultaneously, timely drift detection can reduce pipeline runtime by avoiding unnecessary model updates. Third, performance analysis identifies bottlenecks in state-of-the-art DD implementations, particularly inefficient BLAS and OpenMP usage in streaming scenarios. Consequently, the thesis presents MoPEDDs, a modular parallel ensemble of DDs that exploits unused parallel resources improving detection with negligible runtime overhead.

Finally, because performance engineering remains complex for most data scientists, the thesis introduces JUmPER (Jupyter meets Performance). It embeds performance engineering into Jupyter through coarse- and fine-grained monitoring, making HPC expertise accessible where data science happens.

events.title: COPPER: Improving DRAM Reliability with Low Overheads via Cooperative Parallelized Error-Correcting Codes
events.description: DRAM scaling increases fault rates, motivating stronger and more efficient error correction. However, the transparency between on-die ECC (OD-ECC) in DRAM and rank-level ECC (RL-ECC) in the memory controller introduces substantial storage, reliability, and performance overheads. We propose COPPER, a cooperative ECC mechanism that improves reliability with low performance and area overheads. COPPER exploits the fixed mapping between DRAM data arrays and interface pins to convey a crafted error-location hint from OD-ECC to the memory controller, enabling parallel rank-level cross-checking and decoding without stalling memory transfers. We further propose POD-RMW, which provably parallelizes OD-ECC operations during read-modify-write. Our evaluations show that COPPER incurs only 0.007% DRAM-chip area and at most 0.001% CPU area. With 19.5% storage overhead, COPPER reduces DUE and SDC rates by up to 15x and 430x, respectively, while improving performance by up to 2.1x over prior cooperative ECC approaches under high fault rates.

events.title: Scalable Generation of Distributed-Memory Mappings for Large Tensor Networks
events.description:
Large-scale tensor networks are a critical class of computations widely used in domains such as computational chemistry, machine learning, and others. Owing to their memory footprint and complexity, their execution requires distributed-memory clusters and deeply efficient communication.

This work proposes an enhanced non-linear formulation that unifies previously proposed modeling and optimization schemes for DAGs of tensor operators. Our new modeling and formulation finds high-performing mappings for large tensor networks. Our key scientific contribution is a novel representation of the hyper-dimensional grid of processing elements. The new abstraction exponentially expands the search space, yielding higher performance and enhanced scalability. Furthermore, we reformulate the mapping to exploit optimization procedures in Google CP-SAT, leading to over 50x scalability improvement relative to prior work.

We evaluate our approach on various DAGs targeting CPU and multi-GPU clusters. Our approach achieves average speedups of 4.01x and 1.73x over the Cyclops Tensor Framework and NVIDIA cuTensorNet, respectively.

events.title: Scalable and Efficient Simulation of LLM Training
events.description: Simulation offers unique values for both enumeration and extrapolation purposes, and is becoming increasingly important for managing the massive machine learning (ML) clusters and large-scale distributed training jobs. In this paper, we build Echo to tackle three key challenges in large-scale training simulation: (1) tracing the runtime training workloads at each device in an ex-situ fashion so we can use a single device to obtain the actual execution graphs of 1K-GPU training; (2) accurately estimating the collective communication without high overheads of discrete-event-based network simulation; and (3) accounting for the interference-induced computation slowdown from overlapping communication and computation kernels on the same device. Echo supports both dense and MoE workloads with high fidelity and further enables GPU memory-aware ex-situ simulation. Echo delivers on average 8% error in training step (~3x lower than state-of-the-art simulators) for GPT-175B on a 256-GPU H800 cluster with 3D parallelism on Megatron-LM under three minutes.

events.title: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver
events.description: VQLS is a promising hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving linear systems Ax=b, but its practical deployment is hindered by the massive circuit execution overhead required when encoding arbitrary matrices via linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition. Evaluating the VQLS cost function requires quadratic scaling requirement with the LCU terms, resulting in tens of thousands of circuits per iteration and millions of executions across a full optimization trajectory. To address this, we present a scalable, distributed implementation of VQLS that exploits the embarrassingly parallel structure of the gradient-free-based cost function using NVIDIA CUDA-Q conjunction with multi-node distribution for HPC system. Benchmarking on the Perlmutter supercomputer, we validated the VQLS algorithm with a sample tridiagonal Toeplitz and a canonical Hele-Shaw fluid flow problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate near ideal strong scaling and high efficiency weak scaling performance. We also used Nsight to benchmark the distributed framework to explore ideal concurrency.

events.title: TPage: Transparent Page Management for CXL-Based Tiered Memory Systems
events.description: The emerging Compute Express Link (CXL) technique introduces critical management challenges in tiered memory systems, particularly the trade‑off between data migration overhead and memory space efficiency. A 4KB‑based page unit enables fine‑grained memory management but incurs high migration latency and high page table scan overhead. 2MB‑based transparent huge page (THP) improves the migration efficiency but often wastes significant memory space due to the underutilized page space. To resolve the problem, we propose TPage, a transparent page management framework for CXL‑based tiered memory systems. TPage enables four key innovations: (1) PMU‑assisted memory imbalance monitor, (2) two‑phase page table scan, (3) hybrid page hotness tracking, and (4) huge-page‑aware page placement. TPage dynamically monitors inter‑node memory access pressure imbalance and proactively migrates pages to mitigate it. These mechanisms collectively reduce memory bloat and accelerate page migration, speeding up the performance by 3.6× over Transparent Page Placement (TPP).

events.title: Passport to Prizes Card Drop-Off
Powering Africa’s AI Future: Affordable Renewable Energy Pathways for Sustainable HPC and Datacenters
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: John Towns
events.description: John Towns is the Deputy Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. He leads the NSF-funded ACCESS Coordination Office, as part of the overall ACCESS Program supporting researchers and educators nation-wide in the use of advanced computing systems, and plays key roles in the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot as co-Chair of the Allocations Working Group and Chair of the Coordination Team. He also serves as executive sponsor of NCSA’s Quantum Program Office, a partnership with the Illinois Quantum Information Science and Technology Center (IQUIST), to advance quantum research. With over 35 years of experience, Towns has held leadership roles in numerous national and international initiatives supporting advanced research computing. He holds M.S. degrees in Physics and Astronomy from the University of Illinois and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Missouri-Rolla.

events.title: Comfort Dogs
Towards Scalable and Efficient Deep Learning: Structured Optimization Across Training and Fine-Tuning
events.description:
Modern deep learning systems must balance optimization quality against computation, memory, communication, and reliability constraints, whose relative importance varies across supercomputing architectures. This dissertation develops controlled relaxation as a structured optimization strategy: preserve information essential to learning while relaxing costly requirements in synchronization, curvature representation, and parameterization.

The thesis develops this principle through three contributions. AD-KFAC relaxes global synchronization in distributed second-order optimization while retaining curvature information in asynchronous, versioned, and recoverable state. BD-KFAC replaces dense curvature representations with block-diagonal structure, exposing a controllable trade-off between statistical fidelity and resource cost. RRLoRA relaxes the requirement for an uninterrupted low-rank optimization trajectory by periodically refactorizing the learned update and restarting the learning-rate schedule, allowing the parameterization to evolve without discarding accumulated information.

Together, these methods address complementary bottlenecks in distributed second-order training, resource-efficient curvature estimation, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning while preserving the optimization structure that makes each approach effective. The results support controlled relaxation as a systems-aware design principle: preserve signal-carrying structure, relax constraints that impose disproportionate system cost, and keep the resulting approximation or asynchronous state observable and recoverable. This principle offers a practical framework for designing efficient and reliable machine-learning systems on large-scale supercomputing platforms.

events.title: When Fiber Becomes a Sensor: New Applications for Research and Education Networks
events.description: Research and education networks are built to move massive volumes of scientific data, but the same optical fiber that carries that data can also become a distributed sensor. This session explores how fiber sensing can transform deployed fiber routes into real-time sources of operational and environmental intelligence. By detecting subtle changes caused by vibration, strain, temperature shifts, construction activity, cable movement or seismic events, fiber sensing can help networks identify risks earlier, improve fault isolation and support more resilient high-capacity infrastructure. The talk will introduce key sensing approaches, including distributed acoustic sensing, polarization-based sensing and reflectometry, and explain how AI-driven analysis can turn raw optical signals into actionable insights. Attendees will learn how research and education networks can use fiber sensing to protect critical backbones, reduce maintenance effort and enable new science applications across terrestrial and subsea network environments.

events.title: Extending the Life of HPC Systems in Resource Constrained Environments
Temporal Modeling of Soft Error Propagation Using Dynamic Bayesian Networks
events.description: With the ever-shrinking size of transistors, modern devices have become increasingly susceptible to soft errors that can lead to silent data corruption (SDC), seriously compromising system reliability. Understanding how these corruptions propagate through a program's execution is essential for accurate resilience analysis, yet existing analytical models rely on static assumptions that miss temporal behavior, while fault-injection studies reveal only final outcomes without exposing the intermediate propagation paths. This paper introduces Hydra, a temporal error-propagation framework that constructs a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) from the program execution trace to model how corrupted values traverse dataflow, control-flow, and memory-dependency transitions. Hydra captures masking, reactivation, multi-step propagation, and long-range dependencies, enabling estimation of program-level SDC probabilities without repeated injections and revealing interpretable propagation pathways. Across a diverse benchmark suite, Hydra's predicted SDC probabilities closely match fault-injection results, achieving a mean absolute error of 2.2 percentage points, while substantially reducing computational cost.

events.title: GLOW: Accelerating Geometric Multigrid Layers on Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
events.description: This paper describes the mapping of geometric multigrid (GMG) onto the Cerebras Wafer Scale Engine (WSE-3). The WSE wafer integrates almost a million cores along with a low-latency 2D mesh network, providing unprecedented on-chip bandwidth and fine-grained communication. Although the architecture is predominantly used for deep learning, we explore the suitability of WSE for accelerating GMG. GMG solves sparse linear systems efficiently by recursively coarsening the grid, which leads to more rapid convergence with less computation. As compared to prior implementations of stencils on WSE, this demonstration highlights the challenges of mapping a layered algorithm – and the full set of operators – onto a dataflow architecture. We compare the performance of this implementation to that of the HPGMG benchmark on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU. Across different GMG configurations and problem sizes, we observe a speedup of up to 25× as compared to a single GH200 node.

events.title: Cross-Layer Energy Analysis of Multimodal Training on Grace Hopper Superchips
events.description: Multimodal deep learning jointly processes text, images, and video, but scaling models and sequences shifts training bottlenecks from computation toward memory capacity and data movement. DeepSpeed addresses these limits through CPU offloading, activation checkpointing, and sequence parallelism, yet these techniques add communication and system activity that can alter energy efficiency. We present a cross-layer study of multimodal training on NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) systems, characterizing interactions among the application, runtime, and hardware layers. Using controlled experiments across multiple model scales, we evaluate power, energy, runtime, and throughput under offloading and parallelism strategies. Results show that energy efficiency depends primarily on data movement and compute-communication overlap rather than raw accelerator utilization; consequently, runtime-optimal configurations are not always energy-optimal. We derive practical guidelines for selecting offloading modes, sequence-parallelism degrees, and hardware-aware schedules that balance memory pressure, communication cost, time-to-solution, and energy on tightly coupled heterogeneous systems.

events.title: ZenKO: Guided and Iterative Quantum-Classical Method for Molecular Electronic Structure Using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
events.description: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement; however, determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across H₂O, H₁₀, and N₂ molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.

events.title: Quantifying the Cost of Software-Managed Synchronization on Multi-Host CXL Memory
events.description:
Current multi-host CXL platforms provide shared, byte-addressable memory, but no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations. As a result, the main challenge is not remote-memory latency itself, but the software overhead required to ensure visibility and synchronization.

We quantify this overhead on a real four-host CXL shared-memory system, covering raw memory performance, software-managed publish/observe visibility, and synchronization built from explicit flushes and polling. On our platform, one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs, and each lock acquisition costs 3–5 µs, roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks. These overheads dominate synchronization-heavy workloads: BFS gains nothing from adding a second host; it requires frequent barriers and cross-host exchange. In contrast, triangle counting, which is read-dominated with little synchronization, does speed up when scaling from 32 to 32+32 threads across two hosts. Overall, suitability depends on remote-write intensity, synchronization frequency, and whether hot metadata stays in local DRAM.

events.title: Embrace the Chaos: Harnessing Variability in Accelerator-Rich Systems
events.description:
HPC and ML workload scaling have led supercomputers to deploy large, heterogeneous systems with extreme power limits. Current GPU thermal design power limits (TDPs) range from 1,400–2,000W, scaling to extreme power budgets at scale. Thus, power has displaced performance as the dominant constraint. My research addresses this challenge by co-optimizing power and performance at scale through cross-stack approaches spanning hardware, firmware, systems, and applications.

Power management (PM) causes performance variation across accelerators, making it hard for users to get repeatable performance and for administrators to balance resource utilization. I was the first to characterize GPU variability across production clusters, uncovering consistent variability. This work guided MLCommons' benchmarking effort on handling variability. To harness this variability, I developed PAL, a cluster scheduler that leverages application-specific variability during job placement to optimize latencies and resource utilization.

Further investigating PM, we found GPU power often spikes above TDP (temporarily), triggering frequency throttling that hurts performance. I investigated these power excursions, especially frequent in compute-intensive workloads, and developed solutions that reduce excursions and improve latency.

As workloads rapidly evolve, new workloads often show different excursion characteristics as well as power/performance variability. To adapt our solutions to new, unseen workloads, I developed Minos, which groups similar workloads using power and utilization characteristics while reducing profiling overheads.

Overall, my research demonstrates the critical impact of excursions and GPU variability on large-scale systems. As power constraints intensify and hardware limits are pushed, this cross-stack co-design offers essential techniques to improve power-constrained supercomputing in the future.

events.title: Building Intelligent Systems for STEAM: From Physics to Arts
events.description:
As HPC systems reach exascale, a single simulation run can generate petabytes of data, and the parallel file system, the traditional path for reading and writing simulation data, has become the bottleneck that limits what can actually be learned from that data. Now imagine multiple simulation runs. Ongoing work with plasma physicists explores integrating high-performance simulation(s) and machine learning so tightly that data never has to touch disk. An in-transit workflow is presented in which one to many simulations are streamed directly into an ML framework, transformed asynchronously in flight, and used to train a model while the simulation is still running. The system and software challenges of porting and coupling such a workflow are many, but the right orchestration among the moving parts can open doors to scientific questions that could never even be posed before. At exascale, the data ecosystem is the experiment, and scientific discovery is determined by how the system manages flow of information. This proof-of-concept points toward a larger vision, one in which supercomputers, AI reasoning, surrogate modeling, autonomous workflows, software infrastructure and human-in-the-loop are integrated into a single, unified ecosystem.

Not every science needs an exascale-sized effort, yet the lessons learned at scale can be applied far more broadly, democratizing the convergence of HPC and AI for science across domains as varied as physics, sports analytics, and cultural-heritage conservation. This talk will conclude with some stories from the humanities. Applying computing across disciplines depends on consistent communication between computer scientists and domain scientists, which is only possible when the two communities work together, made possible via the research software engineering (RSE) workforce.

events.title: Strategies for Sustaining HPC Systems under Resource Constraints
Machine Learning-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for HPC Workload Scheduling
events.description: As high-performance computing (HPC) systems reach exascale, schedulers that optimize a single objective, typically throughput, prove inadequate for facilities that must simultaneously manage performance, energy consumption, and resilience under substantial workload uncertainty. This dissertation develops and empirically validates a three-component multi-objective scheduling framework built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), testing the hypothesis that graph-structured representations of jobs and system state, combined with adaptive multi-objective learning, outperform traditional and single-objective learned schedulers in production HPC environments. The framework comprises (1) GNN-RL, a graph attention network and PPO-based scheduler encoding job dependencies and resource contention; (2) HARMONIC, a Bayesian uncertainty-aware optimizer that separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and balances performance, energy, and resilience via a multi-objective DDPG agent with Pareto-front guarantees; and (3) EA-GATSched, a GATv2-based scheduler driven by a GEOPM-calibrated physics power model and a state-conditioned Pareto-weighting network. GNN-RL and HARMONIC evaluations are complete: GNN-RL improves utilization by 13.8%–20.2% and throughput by 15.0%–50.0% over EASY-backfilling across 377,234 production jobs on three ALCF systems; HARMONIC reduces energy by 10%–19%, improves throughput by 16%–25%, and cuts performance variability by 18%–32% across simulation and a 64-node testbed. EA-GATSched, the framework's in-progress third component, has achieved 27.3%–56.6% energy reduction and up to 95.8% utilization across 389,604 jobs on the same three systems, with cross-architecture GEOPM validation remaining as future work. These two studies draw on overlapping, not additive, job sets from the same ALCF systems and together establish relational, uncertainty-aware, and physics-grounded learning as jointly necessary for sustainable exascale HPC scheduling.

events.title: The Global Network Advancement Group: A Next-Generation Multi-Tbps Campus and Global Network System for Data-Intensive Sciences
events.description:
The Global Network Advancement Group (GNA‑G), through its Data‑Intensive Sciences (DIS) and SENSE/AutoGOLE Working Groups, is developing a next‑generation, multi‑terabit/sec global system to support the rapidly escalating demands of data‑intensive science. Scientific programs such as the LHC, Rubin Observatory LSST, SKA, Cryo‑EM, genomics, and distributed AI/ML workflows now generate unprecedented data volumes, requiring coordinated global infrastructure capable of predictable, high‑throughput, multi‑domain operation.

Building on the progress of previous SC conferences, especially SC25, and state-of-the-art technology and AI/ML developments since then, partner teams from the U.S., Europe, Latin America, Asia and Africa will field more than a dozen Network Research Exhibitions to demonstrate this architecture at scale, while showcasing multi‑domain orchestration, programmable data planes, AI‑driven optimization, digital twin simulation, and multi‑Tbps global data movement. The system supports progressive deployment spanning R&D → advanced production → full production, ensuring coexistence with general R&E traffic while enabling scientific discoveries.

events.title: Low-Overhead Silent Error Detection for Large Language Model Inference at Scale
events.description: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed across large-scale computing systems, where soft errors can silently corrupt computations and degrade output quality. Existing protection techniques often rely on broad monitoring or expensive checking mechanisms, incurring non-negligible runtime overhead and limiting scalability across architectures and workloads. In this work, we propose TRACE, a lightweight fault-detection technique for generative LLMs. TRACE identifies a small set of critical layers that are most informative under fault conditions, places lightweight activation-based symptom monitors on these layers during inference, and uses a trained model to determine whether a fault has corrupted the generated output. Across 15 LLMs and three datasets, TRACE achieves 95.3% average fault-detection coverage with only 0.56% runtime overhead, a 6.1× reduction relative to prior LLM fault-tolerance techniques. TRACE further remains effective under multi-bit faults and multi-dataset profiling, demonstrating robust detection across diverse fault conditions and workloads.

events.title: SpaDA: A Spatial Dataflow Architecture Programming Language
events.description: Spatial dataflow architectures like the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine deliver exceptional performance in AI and scientific computing by distributing scratchpad memory across hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs). Yet programming these architectures remains difficult: with no shared memory, data movement requires explicit configuration, and asynchronous task management introduces substantial complexity. We present SpaDA, a programming language that offers precise control over data placement, dataflow patterns, and asynchronous operations while abstracting low-level architectural details. We design and implement a compiler targeting Cerebras CSL through multi-level lowering and unique optimization passes. SpaDA functions as a high-level programming interface and an intermediate representation for domain-specific languages (DSLs), demonstrated here with the GT4Py stencil DSL. SpaDA enables concise expression of operations with complex parallel patterns — including collective operations, multi-dimensional stencils, dense and sparse linear algebra — in 7.49× fewer lines than CSL, achieving over 260 TFlop/s across 730,000 PEs on a single device.

events.title: Characterizing the Scalability and Performance of Large-Scale AI Training Under Multi-Tenancy
events.description: Characterizing AI workload performance on modern HPC systems requires understanding both their scalability in isolation and their behavior under concurrent execution. However, the interplay among parallelization strategies, network congestion, compute capability, and interconnect technologies remains poorly understood. This work investigates the performance and scalability of AI models up to 2,400 GPUs. We quantify the communication overheads and their impact across different interconnects by evaluating scale-up, scale-out, and rack-scale configurations under multiple allocation schemes. Finally, we study how multiple concurrent training jobs interfere with each other by designing a realistic noise model. We design a benchmark suite of AI models to evaluate the performance of five distinct parallelization strategies across different supercomputing clusters, including Alps, Leonardo, LUMI, JUPITER, NVL72 GB300, and DGX A100. Our work provides a systematic characterization of the scalability and execution efficiency of distributed AI training, while offering key insights into performance behavior under realistic multi-tenant scenarios.

events.title: Quantum Sampling Architecture for Protein Structure Reconstruction on Utility-Scale Hardware
events.description: Predicting the structure of short peptides in protein binding pockets remains difficult: the regime requires physics-based conformational search, yet no existing method performs that search practically on current hardware. We present QSAD, a quantum-classical framework that reformulates peptide structure prediction as amino-acid-level Hamiltonian sampling and replaces iterative optimization with non-iterative Hamiltonian evolution. Executed entirely on IBM Heron R2 across 101 binding-pocket peptides (5-18 residues), QSAD improves prediction accuracy by 27%-71% over all evaluated AI and quantum baselines, with the lowest variance across tested lengths. QSAD also tolerates noise levels 3x-5x beyond typical hardware error rates, where iterative methods fail, and achieves a mean per-case speedup of 27x in quantum execution time relative to VQE. The sampled ensemble further supports approximate reconstruction of protein energy landscapes. These results establish coarse-grained quantum sampling as a practical path for structure prediction where data-driven methods lack sufficient signal.

events.title: Papers in Conversation
events.description: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

events.title: Building Skills and Community Through HPC in South Africa

Finite-Element Methods and Exascale Algorithms for Fully Relativistic Noncollinear Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory: From Mathematical Formulations to Efficient Computational Realization and Magnetic Materials Applications
events.description:
Fully relativistic noncollinear density functional theory (DFT) is essential for simulating spintronic and topological materials but costs 12–30 times more than unpolarized DFT, largely because each electron state becomes a two-component spinor. This cost is dominated by a sparse Hermitian eigenproblem with ~10^8 unknowns and ~10^5 eigenvectors, re-solved every self-consistent-field iteration in complex arithmetic. This thesis co-designs finite-element discretizations, eigensolvers, and GPU implementations within the open-source DFT-FE code.

The central contribution is residual-based Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI), which reformulates the Chebyshev recurrence around the residual so that errors from inexact operations shrink with it. Whereas standard Chebyshev filtering stalls, R-ChFSI converges to residuals of 10^-8 with approximate overlap-matrix inverses and FP32/TF32 arithmetic, making reduced precision and compressed communication safe. On Aurora, combining TF32 filtering with 10–12-bit block-floating-point compression of point-to-point messages accelerates filtering by up to 3.5x and the full ground-state solve by 2.27x over FP64, changing the energy by 1.3x10^-10 Ha/atom.

Band parallelization sustains 94% filtering efficiency when strong-scaling an 11,468-electron system to 384 nodes, and calculations reach 78,988 electrons on 800 Aurora nodes. On CPUs, DFT-FE achieves 8x–10x lower minimum wall time than Quantum ESPRESSO at equal accuracy, and GPU runs need 40x–70x fewer node-hours than CPU runs. The thesis also derives consistent forces and stresses and introduces adaptive-coordinate meshes that reduce energy errors up to 28x at fixed degrees of freedom. These capabilities enable a novel study of how vacancies reshape magnetism in the two-dimensional magnet Fe3GeTe2.

events.title: IDIA: A review of over a decade of data-intensive computing and a look at the future
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Matt Zajac
A Reflection on a Decade of Grassroots HPC: From Repurposing Decommissioned Racks to Building a Continent-Wide Movement
Watts, FLOPs, and Impact: Rethinking Energy in the Exascale Era
events.description: Energy consumption has become a key constraint in high performance computing (HPC), shaping system design, procurement, software, and scientific workflows in the exascale era. As large-scale simulations and AI-driven workloads increase power demand, the community must reconsider how performance is measured, optimized, and reported beyond FLOPs alone. This BoF session will convene researchers, facility operators, vendors, and application scientists to discuss energy measurement, performance-per-watt metrics, efficient algorithms and runtimes, workload scheduling, and carbon-aware computing. The session will identify practical gaps, share lessons from production systems, and define community priorities for sustainable, energy-efficient HPC at scale.

events.title: Real-Time Scientific Data Streaming to HPC Nodes: Challenges and Innovations VI
events.description:
Emerging scientific needs are driving a new class of workflows that require near real-time processing, urgent computing, and time-sensitive decision-making. The traditional "compute-store-analyze" paradigm, which relies on dumping massive datasets to file systems for post-processing, has become an unsustainable bottleneck. It introduces unacceptable latency, and often renders high-frequency data analysis practically impossible.

This BoF discusses this challenge by exploring the architectural shift from file-based workflows to high-performance streaming. In this new paradigm, storage is treated not as a buffer for post-processing, but as a sink for final scientific results, while analysis, visualization, and reduction occur in-transit or in-situ.

events.title: Open MPI State of the Union 2026
events.description:
Open MPI continues to advance portable, high-performance communication for increasingly heterogeneous, accelerator-rich systems and workloads. Over the past year, the community has advanced MPI-5.0 conformance, expanded accelerator support, improved collective performance, and worked with partners across the HPC ecosystem. We'll discuss what Open MPI has accomplished over the past year and present a roadmap for the next year.

One of Open MPI's strengths lies in its diversity: we represent many different viewpoints across the HPC community. To that end, many developers from the community will be present to discuss and answer your questions both during and after the BoF.

events.title: Continuum Computing: Agentic AI for Intelligent Orchestration
events.description: Continuum computing (digital continuum) is a distributed ecosystem spanning edge devices, scientific instruments, cloud platforms, data centers, supercomputers, and quantum systems. As these infrastructures become increasingly complex, agentic AI offers new opportunities for intelligent orchestration of computation, data, workflows, and heterogeneous resources. This BoF will explore how collaborative AI agents can enable autonomous scientific computing while ensuring trust, resilience, and human oversight. Topics include multi-agent coordination, AI-driven resource management, autonomous workflows, foundation models for scientific computing, and new programming models. The session will identify key research challenges and foster cross-disciplinary collaboration to advance the next generation of intelligent continuum computing.

events.title: HPC User Support in the AI and Exascale Era
events.description:
As HPC enters an era of extreme heterogeneity and AI integration, user support is a critical strategic enabler. However, rising system complexity and finite staffing strain traditional models. To thrive in the AI and exascale era, a collaborative community approach is essential.

This BoF session invites practitioners, providers, and users to collaboratively reshape HPC support. Featuring insights from facility leaders on managing rapid AI adoption, an interactive live survey, and open group discussions, participants will share experiences regarding scaling, AI automation, and knowledge transfer. Outcomes will form a post-conference report dedicated to fostering a sustainable, community-driven support ecosystem.

events.title: Bringing Quantum Computing to the HPC Datacenter
events.description: As quantum computing matures, challenges with the adoption of this technology shift from theoretical feasibility to practical deployment within established supercomputing infrastructures. This BoF examines the holistic framework required to operationalize quantum systems, from the physical datacenter floor requirements to the high-level application layer. We dive into the complex interplay between infrastructure installation, platform requirements, security protocols, and the necessary evolution of the software stack to support quantum algorithms and hybrid QC-HPC workflows. As such, this BoF outlines a strategic blueprint for building resilient, high-performance quantum-classical hybrid computing environments suitable for next-generation scientific discovery.

events.title: The State of Open-Source Computer Architecture Simulators: Shared Problems and Community Action
events.description: Computer architecture simulators are central to exploring the design space of modern high-performance hardware and analyzing its performance. Many open-source simulators exist, targeting different hardware scopes, granularities, and metrics, yet none is perfect: issues with speed, accuracy, and usability limit their effectiveness for architecture researchers, accelerator designers, hardware-software co-designers, and performance engineers, among others. This BoF convenes an expert panel of users and developers from academia and industry to discuss these tools' shortcomings and possible responses. We invite all who build, use, or depend on these simulators to join the discussion and identify impactful community efforts, with outcomes shared publicly.

events.title: HPC Next: Reflections and Progress on the RISC-V Ecosystem
events.description:
RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) enabling the open development of CPUs and a shared software ecosystem. There are already over 30 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has enjoyed, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads.

This BoF aims to connect the RISC-V and HPC communities. We will explore how the technology is progressing and identify lessons learnt from previous years' predictions.

events.title: Democratizing AI Accelerators for HPC Applications: Challenges, Success, and Support
events.description: A recent surge in novel AI accelerator hardware has sparked intense interest in running HPC applications and driven algorithmic research on these architectures. However, the maturity levels of associated tooling and software stacks vary significantly, with gaps in documentation and support. This BoF aims to explore trends in AI accelerators for HPC, ideal programming models, software stack support, code portability, training resources, and common challenges. We hope to foster a community of users interested or experienced in using AI accelerators for HPC applications.

events.title: Three Axes for Scientific AI on HPC: Energy Efficiency, Uncertainty, and Verifiable Trust
events.description: Scientific AI on leadership-class HPC sits at the intersection of three concerns the community usually addresses separately: energy efficiency, uncertainty quantification (UQ), and verifiable trust. Compression and quantization change model behavior in ways that matter for scientific validity. Energy optimizations can quietly erode privacy and safety properties. And the HPC, UQ, and AI-safety communities rarely meet in one room. This BoF session brings them together to identify shared challenges, gaps in current practice, and concrete next steps toward AI systems for science that are simultaneously efficient, uncertainty-aware, and verifiably trustworthy on the world’s largest computing systems.

events.title: The Future of Dynamic Resource Utilization in HPC: Chances and Challenges
events.description:
The increasing computational demands are driving the deployment of ever-larger HPC and AI infrastructures. While these systems deliver unprecedented performance, they also pose critical challenges to their efficient use, particularly in terms of energy consumption.

This BoF will explore dynamic resource management as a key enabler of higher utilization and reduced energy consumption. Instead of traditional batch scheduling, dynamic resource control at the start or during a job’s runtime enables better allocation of compute capacity, memory, network availability, and storage. This BoF will address the two major key challenges of novel scheduling and its integration across the software stack.

events.title: Trustworthy Data at Scale: HDF5 in the Age of AI-Driven Science
events.description: HDF5 has anchored HPC I/O for 25 years, and AI-driven science is redefining what "trustworthy data at scale" demands: verifiable provenance, concurrent I/O, and cloud-native interoperability. Short talks from domain scientists launch interactive segments where an opt-in agentic survey captures attendee priorities, pain points, and open questions in real time, with aggregate results used to steer the discussion. This session is for seasoned HDF5 developers and domain scientists, and anyone just starting out or wondering what HDF5 is about: bring the problems you'd like to solve, and help steer the discussion and provide input to future HDF5 roadmap planning.

events.title: AI-Assisted Engineering in HPC
events.description: Software engineering is changing rapidly as AI-assisted programming becomes accepted. Tools and approaches have matured rapidly from “vibe-coding” to using complex and highly productive agentic harnesses. In this session, we will discuss the implications for the scientific programming community, with a particular focus on HPC software. This includes systemware, middleware, and tools used to operate, manage, and maintain HPC systems, as well as parallel simulation and modelling software used in HPC settings. Topics include trustworthiness and validation for AI-generated software, career futures and professional implications for systems engineers and research software engineers, security implications, and emerging current "best performance practices."

events.title: Trusted Research Environments for AI and Integrated Science: Launching the Genesis Mission
events.description: This BoF aims to build on the successful launch at SC25 of a multi-national community of practice. This year we focus on the Genesis Mission and DOE’s American Science Cloud and AI Models Consortium projects, to include establishing best practices for multi-facility or multi-institutional workflows, lessons learned from international contexts, sharing and accessing resources, developing mixed public/private partnerships, and protecting sensitive data privacy and security. Our goal is to advance progress in developing secure and trustworthy infrastructures for AI and integrated science. We seek to understand trustworthiness in supercomputing environments from both technical and socio-technical perspectives.

events.title: Designing Open, Heterogeneous System Monitoring Around OpenCHAMI
events.description: While modern management platforms like OpenCHAMI streamline cluster orchestration, they do not inherently provide the comprehensive monitoring and data collection required to observe every facet of a next-generation data center. Operating heterogeneous, large-scale systems requires a unified, open-source observability framework capable of aggregating distributed logs, metrics, and traces across thousands of bleeding-edge compute nodes. This BoF session brings together HPC systems engineers, data center architects, and site reliability engineers to discuss the architecture, integration challenges, and best practices for building robust telemetry pipelines around OpenCHAMI, ensuring operational visibility, rapid fault isolation, and open-source compliance in next-generation supercomputing environments.

events.title: The Future of NSF-Supported Advanced Cyberinfrastructure
events.description: The U.S. National Science Foundation's vision and investment plans for cyberinfrastructure (CI) are designed to address the evolving needs of the science and engineering research community. Senior leadership and program staff from NSF’s Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure (OAC) will discuss OAC's vision, strategic and national priorities, as well as highlights from the latest funding opportunities across all aspects of the research cyberinfrastructure ecosystem. Substantial time will be devoted to audience Q&A between attendees and NSF staff and unstructured time to meet informally with NSF staff.
