events.title: HSTUFuse: Training-Compatible Efficient Fusion for Long-Sequence Recommenders
events.description: Generative recommenders improve the modeling of long-range behavioral dependencies through unified causal sequence modeling, where the hierarchical sequential transduction unit (HSTU) serves as a core sequence encoder. However, the original HSTU implementation incurs fragmented operator execution, cross-feature reductions in LayerNorm, padding overhead from dense materialization, and redundant spatial aggregation. We present HSTUFuse, a training-compatible CUDA optimization that decomposes HSTU into three stages—pointwise projection, spatial aggregation, and pointwise transformation—with fused forward and backward implementations. It further replaces LayerNorm with Dynamic Tanh, internalizes jagged-tensor addressing, and combines valid-position computation with causal lower-triangular pruning. ML-1M training runs show stable convergence while retaining recommendation quality close to the PyTorch HSTU. On ML-20M, it achieves per-batch HSTU execution speedups of 19.53× on RTX 4090 and 22.46× on H800, measured using the sum of forward- and backward-pass times.

events.title: Restructuring Data and Computation for Accelerator Performance
events.description: The papers improve accelerator performance by changing how data and computation are represented and mapped to hardware: fused long-sequence recommender kernels, configurable-precision GPU arrays, adaptive SRAM allocation for sparse computation, and tensor reformulation of Viterbi decoding for massive parallelism.

events.title: PIMCQG: Co-Designing Billion-Scale Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for Processing-in-Memory
events.description: Graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) delivers superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for large-scale AI applications, but remains fundamentally bottlenecked by the ”memory wall” on CPUs and GPUs. Processing-in-memory (PIM) offers massive internal bandwidth by co-locating computation with data, making it a natural fit for irregular, memory-bound workloads. However, directly mapping graph-based ANNS onto PIM exposes severe algorithm–architecture mismatches: restricted per-PU memory, costly inter-PU communication, heavy coordination overhead, and weak compute capability, forcing existing PIM-based ANNS to rely on cluster-based algorithms that plateau at low recall. We propose PIMCQG, an algorithm–hardware co-design framework through three optimizations: (1) a compact index reducing PIM-resident footprint by 14.5×; (2) an asynchronous pipelined scheduler fully utilizing host–PIM bandwidth; (3) a multiplication-free distance kernel with <0.08% recall loss. Evaluations on three billion-scale datasets show up to 20×/17.1× throughput over CPU/GPU baselines, 129× over prior PIM accelerators at high recall, and scale across multi-node and emerging PIM architectures.

events.title: Specialized Acceleration and Services for Emerging HPC Workloads
events.description: These papers redesign systems around emerging workloads that do not fit conventional HPC execution models: processing-in-memory graph search, GPU zero-knowledge proof generation, secure MPC-based collectives, and eBPF-based serverless HPC.

events.title: BatchMine: Accelerating Approximate Graph Pattern Mining via Batch Processing
events.description:
Approximate graph pattern mining, as a fundamental technique in graph analysis, has been widely applied in machine learning, biomedical research, and social network analysis. However, existing solutions still face significant challenges in efficiency and scalability when dealing with complex pattern graphs or giant data graphs. To address these limitations, we introduce BatchMine, an out-of-core system for approximate graph pattern mining. BatchMine leverages three key techniques: (1) a partition-based estimation method to accelerate convergence; (2) a batch-processing framework with adaptive refinement to enhance external-memory access locality and improve convergence efficiency; and (3) a hybrid data layout that balances sampling efficiency and storage overhead.

To the best of our knowledge, BatchMine is the first graph pattern mining system capable of handling graphs exceeding main memory capacity, enabling mining on graphs with nearly 100 billion edges on a single machine within 1,000 seconds. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of BatchMine.

events.title: GPU Graph Search and Pattern Mining
events.description: The papers address irregular graph search and pattern discovery on GPUs, spanning subgraph matching, approximate mining, and shortest-path computation. The session focuses on how batching, scheduling, and memory management unlock performance.

events.title: Reengineering Scientific Simulation for Modern Accelerators
events.description: The papers redesign scientific simulation around modern and emerging platforms: exascale GPU agent-based ecology, neuromorphic stochastic turbulence, accelerator-friendly DFT, and scalable GPU FMM for molecular dynamics. The common thread is algorithmic restructuring to make difficult scientific workloads practical on new architectures.

events.title: Toward Continental Forest Dynamics Modeling at Individual-Tree Resolution on Exascale Systems
events.description: Modeling continental-to-global forest dynamics at individual-tree resolution is essential for Earth system prediction but has remained computationally impractical because of cross-scale interactions among billions of trees in heterogeneous atmospheric and soil environments. We present GGap, an agent-based forest model designed for exascale systems. GGap employs a Site–Gap–Tree hierarchy that co-locates each site's ensemble on a single GPU to maximize data locality. It leverages two-level parallelism: site partitions run concurrently across MPI ranks, while GPU threads update agents within each rank. To avoid CPU–GPU synchronization, a multi-priority kernel pipeline executes sequential ecological phases entirely on-device, using grid barriers to enforce their order. On Frontier, the largest weak-scaling configuration simulates 10.25 billion agents on 2,048 GPUs at 96.2% parallel efficiency. A 1,000-year contiguous United States simulation across 1,424 sites and 235 species reproduces regional patterns of species composition, forest structure, productivity, and biomass, demonstrating ecologically meaningful continental-scale forest simulation.

events.title: Papers in Conversation: Quantum–HPC Integration Moves to Real Systems
events.description: The papers demonstrate real-hardware integration, trace-driven hybrid-system modeling, and GPU-enabled quantum-classical workflows. The panel can discuss the software and facility requirements for quantum resources to become routine components of HPC.

events.title: Practical HPCQC Integration with QDMI: A Real-Hardware Case Study with IQM Systems
events.description:
Quantum computers are entering HPC centers, shifting the main challenge from hardware access to integration. Many software paths still rely on vendor-specific adapter chains between user SDKs, schedulers, and backend APIs, which complicates operations and slows the move from pilots to production. We present a practical integration path built on the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI). Using IQM superconducting systems as a hardware case study, we implement an IQM-backed QDMI layer and connect it to two software layers HPC centers already care about: Slurm-based job execution and Qiskit-facing user workflows. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/iqm-finland/QDMI-on-IQM.

The message is that integrating quantum hardware into HPC need not be a bespoke effort per backend. Once the software–hardware boundary is standardized, large parts of the stack become reusable across providers and deployment styles. We do not claim that this removes all HPCQC challenges, but that this boundary can be standardized today.

events.title: From Access to Impact: Designing HPC–Quantum–AI Workflows for Scientific Productivity
events.description:
Quantum computing is increasingly being integrated into HPC environments, yet its impact on scientific discovery, especially in combination with AI workflows, remains limited by a more fundamental challenge: usability. Today’s hybrid quantum–HPC–AI workflows are fragmented, manually assembled, and difficult to reproduce, requiring users to navigate multiple abstraction layers, toolchains, and system constraints. At the same time, the user base is expanding beyond quantum experts to domain scientists who require intuitive, reliable, and scalable workflows.

This panel examines how to move from access to impact by focusing on the design of user-centered quantum–HPC–AI workflows. Drawing on perspectives from scientific computing, data workflows, system design, and applied research, panelists will explore workflow bottlenecks, abstraction strategies, orchestration challenges, and the role of AI. The discussion will focus on what is required to make hybrid systems usable in practice and how to translate emerging capabilities into measurable scientific productivity.

events.title: From Access to Impact: Designing HPC–Quantum–AI Workflows for Scientific Productivity
Orchestrating the Future: Heterogeneous Disaggregation at Scale for Agentic AI Workloads
events.description:
As agentic AI and dynamic dataflow models increasingly dominate modern compute landscapes, monolithic architectures struggle to maintain optimal cost-performance ratios. This panel explores the heterogeneous disaggregation of AI workloads, addressing the critical systems-level challenges of orchestrating complex models across diverse, next-generation accelerators.

Panelists will discuss the evolution of software infrastructure, alongside advanced scheduling strategies required to manage dynamic execution and cost-aware SLAs. By decoupling memory, compute, and networking, we can achieve highly efficient, scalable execution in fragmented environments. Join experts as they debate the future of hardware-software co-design, evaluate marginal cost-efficiency trade-offs across contemporary AI hardware, and outline the system software innovations necessary to fully realize the potential of disaggregated infrastructure at scale.

events.title: Orchestrating the Future: Heterogeneous Disaggregation at Scale for Agentic AI Workloads
Doctoral Showcase II Presentations
Real-Time High-Fidelity Bayesian Inference and Forecasting of Tsunamis: A Digital Twin for Tsunami Early Warning Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
events.description:
Tsunamis resulting from megathrust earthquakes are rare events that can cause devastating socioeconomic damage and loss of life. State-of-the-art early-warning systems rely on simplified physics models that can be inaccurate for near-field predictions, leading to delayed, missed, or false warnings. Tsunami propagation codes typically use shallow-water equations, which omit coupled ocean-acoustic and surface-gravity wave dynamics, while high-fidelity hydrodynamics codes are too computationally expensive for real-time use. My doctoral research develops a digital twin framework for tsunami early warning that incorporates high-fidelity physics, uses Bayesian data assimilation, and leverages GPU-oriented algorithms to enable accurate, real-time forecasts with rigorously quantified uncertainties for the Cascadia Subduction Zone.

The computational advance is an offline–online decomposition exploiting time-shift invariance in the parameter-to-observable and parameter-to-prediction maps. Their block-triangular Toeplitz structure enables fast Fourier transform-based matrix-vector products, delivering approximately one-hundred-thousand-fold speedups over repeated partial differential equation solves. The Bayesian inverse problem is reformulated in the smaller observation space using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, enabling offline factorization and real-time inference.

For a margin-wide Cascadia rupture with 600 hypothetical pressure sensors, the method infers more than one billion parameters and predicts wave heights at 21 locations in under 0.2 seconds on 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, a ten-billion-fold speedup over state-of-the-art methods—a breakthrough recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The framework also enables scalable Bayesian optimal experimental design by recasting sensor placement as dense matrix subset selection to minimize uncertainty in inferred seafloor motion or wave-height forecasts. This digital twin paves the way toward accurate, uncertainty-aware tsunami forecasts worldwide.

events.title: Building Multi-Tenant AI Infrastructure at Scale
events.description:
Every large AI cluster begins with the same goal: deliver GPU infrastructure that can scale reliably. The challenge is that networking quickly becomes far more complex than simply connecting switches and servers. As clusters grow, operators must coordinate edge networking, Ethernet fabrics, InfiniBand, NVLink, and host/DPU networking while continually provisioning, resizing, and maintaining tenant environments.

Drawing on lessons from 60+ GPU clusters and 500,000 GPUs under management, this session explores how networking for AI has evolved beyond traditional data center operations. It examines why organizations outgrow manual configuration and DIY automation, why hardware-enforced multi-tenancy has become a foundational operational requirement, and how experience gained across many deployments helps reduce operational risk.

Attendees will gain practical architectural and operational guidance for designing networking that can support the scale, security, and lifecycle demands of modern AI infrastructure.

events.title: HPC Networks II
Subgraph Counting: Methods, Frameworks, and Applications
events.description:
Subgraph counting and matching are core primitives in network analysis, underpinning applications from computational biology to fraud detection to performance analysis in HPC. Existing methods assume static, small networks, rely on hardware-specific kernels that do not scale across the accelerator ecosystem, and emphasize counting over the harder problem of locating pattern instances. This dissertation addresses all three.

We develop ParaDyMS, a parallel method for counting all motifs of size k ≤ 5 on fully dynamic networks under batched edge insertions and deletions. Rather than recomputing from scratch, ParaDyMS updates motif counts incrementally using only the delta induced by a batch of changes. Implemented in the Kokkos C++ Performance Portability ecosystem, ParaDyMS targets both OpenMP and CUDA from one source, achieving up to 124× speedup over the state-of-the-art static method and outperforming 112 CPU cores with a single GPU.

To address hardware portability, we present PyGB-LAPIS, a compilation pipeline lowering graph algorithms written in Python-GraphBLAS through MLIR and the LAPIS backend into Kokkos-flavored C++. PyGB-LAPIS generates kernels across five sparse storage formats and multiple hardware backends from one source, matching hand-written Kokkos performance while eliminating per-backend engineering effort.

Finally, we develop an exact subgraph matching method that decomposes query and host graphs into size-4 graphlets and searches a compressed graphlet-overlap representation. This supports arbitrary-size queries and, uniquely, resolves multiple simultaneous queries in one pass through a shared search tree rather than restarting per query, with the union graph traversed on the fly and pruned by graphlet frequency to control its size.

events.title: FitFloat: Read/Write Random-Access Compressed Floating-Point Arrays for GPUs
events.description: In many floating-point applications that use GPUs, device memory is a bottleneck limiting the maximum problem size. One solution is to use Unified Virtual Memory, but the limited physical GPU memory likely causes page evictions, incurring potentially large performance penalties. We present FitFloat, a drop-in floating-point array replacement supporting user-specified precision on GPUs with the goal of reducing storage requirements of scientific applications while maximizing performance over unified memory. FitFloat targets applications limited by the GPU's memory capacity, allowing larger problem sizes to be efficiently processed. We evaluate the storage savings and performance improvement of our approach relative to using native arrays on 11 single-precision and three double-precision codes from the HeCBench suite on two different GPUs. In the best case, FitFloat yields a speedup of 739 and provides a geometric-mean speedup of 16.1 for the float codes and 20.1 for the double codes on an RTX 4090.

events.title: FluxZK: Scalable and Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proof Computation via GPU Acceleration
events.description:
Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols enable privacy-preserving verification but face critical performance bottlenecks at the proof generation stage, particularly when handling large-scale computations that exceed GPU memory capacity. We present FluxZK, a framework that addresses scalability and efficiency challenges through ZKP-specific GPU-based optimizations. Our framework introduces FluxMSM, an efficient multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) implementation that leverages fine-grained parallelism and overlapped data transfer with computation. Additionally, we develop FluxNTT, a high-performance number theoretic transform (NTT) solution supporting both out-of-core and on-GPU computation paradigms. Extensive evaluations on data center GPUs demonstrate that FluxZK scales well to large input sizes of up to 2³⁰ elements, delivering an estimated performance improvement of up to 2.16x over existing solutions in real-world ZKP applications.

Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/SJTU-Liquid/FluxZK.

events.title: KSPine: Fast Parallel K-Shortest Path Computation via Block-Cut+ Tree Decomposition and Dynamic Caching
events.description: Efficiently computing K-shortest path (KSP) on graphs is critical for many real-world applications. Existing solutions suffer from query-dependent pruning, limited parallelism, and redundant computation across repeated queries. To address such challenges, this paper presents KSPine, a fast parallel KSP framework. KSPine is built on block-cut+ tree (BC+ tree), a structural decomposition that identifies a compact, query-independent skeleton of the graph using biconnected components and articulation points. This skeleton allows KSPine to prune each query to a small structural subgraph and solve independent sub-KSP problems within each BiCC block in parallel. To combine local sub-KSP results into global top-K paths, we design a merging-based method with early stopping that reduces unnecessary computation. KSPine also introduces a hierarchical dynamic caching mechanism that reuses sub-KSP results across queries, avoiding redundant computation under continuous workloads. On six real-world graphs across various domains, KSPine achieves an average speedup of 1.5× over state-of-the-art methods.

events.title: Demonstrating the Neuromorphic Advantage on Stochastic Dynamics in Turbulent Flows
events.description:
Graphics processing units (GPUs) excel at workloads dependent on linear algebra, covering a wide range of topics like artificial intelligence and quantum mechanics. However, in workloads that are not well captured by linear algebra, such as probabilistic systems, GPUs may not provide optimal performance.

In this work, we demonstrate a neuromorphic advantage in energy efficiency for simulating turbulent flows with stochastic methods. We observe energy savings across the board and runtime speed-up for some methods when comparing a neuromorphic platform to equivalent workloads on GPU and CPU. Specifically, our neuromorphic implementation achieves 1.52x speed-up and 37.46x less energy consumption, compared to a GPU running the same 1.5 million random walks over discretized space. For 100,000 walks in continuous space, GPU outperforms neuromorphic in execution time but consumes 2.37x more energy. As the technological landscape for neuromorphic systems rapidly evolves, their performance relative to current hardware is likely to significantly improve.

events.title: End-to-End Modeling and Trace-Driven Replay for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Supercomputing
events.description: Hybrid quantum-classical applications increasingly execute as multi-stage workflows spanning HPC nodes, simulators, workflow runtimes, network services, and remote quantum backends. Evaluating such applications is difficult because their end-to-end critical path crosses heterogeneous components with incompatible observability and control interfaces, making reported results hard to reproduce, compare, and extrapolate. We present QTrace, an end-to-end methodology for performance analysis of hybrid quantum-classical workloads. QTrace combines a unified cross-layer tracing schema with a dependency-aware, trace-driven replay engine that preserves workflow causality while enabling controlled perturbation of backend latency, scheduling policy, and reliability-related effects. This supports both faithful reproduction of observed executions and systematic "what-if" studies for future quantum-accelerated systems. We evaluate QTrace on representative iterative and adaptive workloads across simulator-backed and remote-backend settings. The results show that QTrace reconstructs workflow behavior with high fidelity, reproduces observed executions with low replay error, and exposes bottlenecks that are often hidden by backend-centric metrics alone.

events.title: NAAIR
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Avinash Maurya
Efficient Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Systems and Continual Task Adaptation
events.description:
This dissertation addresses two fundamental challenges in distributed machine learning: client heterogeneity and continual adaptation to new tasks. It develops efficient fine-tuning and representation-learning frameworks that let distributed models acquire new knowledge and align it across clients without communication bottlenecks or catastrophic forgetting.

First, we introduce a dual-distilled federated learning framework for clients with heterogeneous systems and data. Trainable global prototypes with adaptive margins align local representations and logits without requiring a shared model architecture, enabling robust knowledge transfer and stable convergence.

Next, we propose a communication-efficient federated framework for large language models (LLMs) based on representation fine-tuning. By intervening on hidden states rather than weights, and combining All-But-Me aggregation with dynamic test-time computing, it reduces communication cost while balancing local personalization and global generalization.

We then present SETA, a mixture of sparse experts for task-agnostic continual learning in LLMs. SETA resolves the plasticity–stability dilemma by structurally decomposing the parameter space into shared and task-specific experts, protecting shared knowledge from semantic drift while preserving task-specific features.

Finally, we introduce FedSEAM, which extends sparse experts to federated continual learning. Clients learn experts on private task streams, and the server merges them through subspace agreement: it combines only the update directions clients share, keeps disagreeing directions as client-private experts, and protects prior-task subspaces from being overwritten.

Together, these contributions chart a path toward scalable, resource-aware machine learning systems that bridge decentralized efficiency and continual real-world deployment, learning new tasks across privacy-constrained environments without forgetting.

events.title: Accelerated Services Framework: Programmable Services Using DPUs
events.description:
Modern data centers, enterprise networks, and AI infrastructure require network services such as security, encryption, traffic management, and segmentation to scale across hybrid cloud and edge environments. In the post-Mythos era lateral movement turns one compromised workload into a breach, hence DC east-west traffic monitoring becomes increasingly critical. Today, these services often rely on dedicated appliances or server software, increasing cost, complexity, power consumption, and operational overhead.

This paper presents an accelerated services framework (ASF) which combines an open-source software abstraction layer for network services and couples it with an open-source composable DPU hardware form factor. This allows for a flexible software front-end that is coupled with scalable hardware. We envision ASF delivering accelerated services and security in multiple form factors such as SmartSwitches, dense Rack-scale nodes, and AI clusters.

ASF calls for vendor neutrality to simplify operations, reduce infrastructure costs, and free server resources for enterprise and AI factories.

events.title: Students@SC Wrap-Up
Chisa: Dynamic Logical Way Partitioning for Efficient Caching in Sparse Accelerators
events.description:
Sparse tensor computations are memory-bound, making on-chip data reuse critical to sparse accelerator performance. Guided cache replacement derives lookahead information from structural relationships between operand tensors, but its effectiveness hinges on the prefetch observation window in SRAM. Under constrained SRAM, the window is inevitably small and guidance becomes noisy or misleading—precisely when caching matters most.

We propose Chisa, a dynamic logical way partitioning scheme for sparse accelerator caches. Inspired by victim caches, Chisa integrates buffer semantics into cache sets: a single role bit lets each way dynamically serve as a logical cache or buffer way without data migration, so mistakenly evicted blocks can be rescued upon reuse. Chisa further incorporates Jaccard similarity-based initialization and rescue rate-based runtime adaptation. On real-world sparse matrices, Chisa achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.23x and 1.27x over the state of the art on SpMSpM and SpMM, respectively, peaking at 4.46x and 4.64x.

events.title: MPCAR: Scalable and Secure Multi-Party Computation-Based AllReduce
events.description: Scalable and secure collective communication is critical in modern HPC and AI workloads, especially AllReduce. State-of-the-art (SOTA) solutions use homomorphic encryption (HE) to ensure data privacy, but incur complex key management and overheads, and weak integration with collective algorithms. We present MPCAR, the first multi-party computation-based AllReduce framework, which decouples AllReduce into two phases, data reduction and distribution, and applies tailored secure methods to each. MPCAR employs secret sharing MPC schemes for the data reduction phase and asymmetric one-time-padding-based protection for the distribution phase, while also allowing user-defined secure communication protocols. We co-design these schemes with multiple AllReduce algorithms and implement several system-level optimizations. Evaluated across five platforms spanning AWS and HPC clusters at scale, including two exascale supercomputers and scaling to 8,192 ranks, MPCAR improves latency/throughput by up to 30.5%/41.2%. MPCAR also outperforms SOTA by up to 21.3% on real-world workloads, including DNN applications and three DeepSeek-distilled models.

events.title: PUMatch: Bandwidth-Efficient DFS-Based Subgraph Matching Under GPU Memory Oversubscription
events.description: Subgraph matching on massive graphs is hindered by GPU memory oversubscription, where frequent CPU-GPU data transfers create severe performance bottlenecks. Existing unified memory solutions suffer from bandwidth waste due to coarse-grained page transfers, while BFS-based approaches often fail due to intermediate result explosion. To address these challenges, we present PUMatch, a bandwidth-efficient, DFS-based CPU-GPU collaborative framework. PUMatch introduces four key innovations: (1) dual-scale packaging that reorganizes missing neighborhoods into compact CSR units to maximize bandwidth efficiency; (2) a synchronization-free asynchronous coordination protocol for DFS execution; (3) orthogonal warp scheduling with trie-based resumption that operates independently of the SM’s built-in scheduler; and (4) an adaptive hybrid data access scheme that dynamically optimizes data movement via a lightweight learning controller. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs with billions of edges demonstrate that PUMatch achieves up to 10.49× speedup over state-of-the-art BFS baselines and 3.45× over DFS baselines, while reducing PCIe traffic by 73%.

events.title: MakoXC: Rearchitecting DFT Exchange–Correlation with Matrix-Aligned and Knowledge-Organized Sparsity
events.description: Density functional theory (DFT) is essential to materials science and drug discovery, yet exchange–correlation (XC) evaluation remains a major bottleneck. Linear-scaling methods exploit electronic nearsightedness but introduce irregular sparse workloads that underutilize modern AI accelerators. We present MakoXC, a matrix-aligned XC engine that restructures nearsightedness-induced sparsity into regular accelerator-friendly computation. MakoXC combines matrix-aligned cells to organize interactions into dense clusters, sparsity-guided activation to expose implicit sparsity for practical linear scaling, and a kernel-fused pipeline to consolidate fragmented workloads into a compute-intensive execution path. MakoXC achieves average speedups of 67.8x over standard XC evaluation and 4.7x over state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods. Integrated into a production-grade commercial DFT package, MakoXC scales to ubiquitin (1,231 atoms, def2-SVP) on 64 GPUs, completing end-to-end DFT in under five minutes. MakoXC demonstrates how scientific workloads can achieve genuine low complexity while maximizing parallel efficiency on AI accelerators.

events.title: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q
events.description: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly potential-energy-surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3% and wall-time by up to 74.8% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.

events.title: Genome Variant Representation in Genome LMs and Multi-Omic AI: Efficiency, Scalability, and Medical Actionability
events.description:
The recent rapid growth and curation of large multi-omic datasets, driven largely by high-throughput sequencing, have provided unprecedented opportunities in medical and clinical research, especially for precision medicine. This presents an opportunity for improved multi-omic deep learning implementations for oncology tasks. However, it comes with a set of challenges, namely:

1. Granularity in genomic variant representation: representing complex, arbitrary-length genomic variant data without destroying spatial context or non-coding regulatory signals in both standalone and multi-omic models

2. Scalability and efficiency: establishing efficient and domain-informed data loading strategies, hyperparameter optimization guidelines and computationally scalable architectural choices, especially for resource-intensive medical applications

3. Systematized multi-omic integration: How can we rigorously evaluate multi-omics integration strategies and assess which combinations of omics modalities yield the most informative biological representations for oncology tasks?

To address these issues, we have made the following contributions. First, we developed a feasibility study into the representation of genomic variant data, leveraging genome language models (gLMs) to capture nucleotide-level dependencies across variable-length somatic variant-associated sequences for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis. Next, we scaled our framework to combine both coding exomes and non-coding regions by implementing input load balancing and architectural changes, improving performance on chosen oncology tasks. Finally, we introduced a generalized, versatile, and modular framework that incorporates key autoencoder architectures for representation learning, enabling exploration and robust evaluation of multi-modal omics integration.

The cumulative findings bridge hardware-efficient scaling, biological representation learning, and cancer-specific multi-omics to drive medical actionability.

events.title: SCinet Network Overview
events.description: This session provides a technical overview of SCinet’s architecture for both the Conference/Exhibitor network and the Science Connector Network.

events.title: Foundation Models for Discovery and Exploration in Chemical Space
events.description:
Accurate, rapid prediction of molecular properties remains a bottleneck in materials innovation because experiments and conventional simulations are too costly to explore vast, high-dimensional chemical spaces. Scalable and interpretable molecular foundation models can accelerate discovery across chemical space while using computational resources efficiently. We demonstrate this with MIST, a family of molecular foundation models trained with up to an order of magnitude more data and parameters than prior work. To train MIST we developed Smirk, a tokenizer which preserves nuclear, electronic, and geometric information, enabling representation learning across chemical systems.

The largest MIST model has 1.8B parameters and was trained on 2B molecules. Training such a large model is an expensive endeavor. To make model development tractable on an academic compute budget we developed hyperparameter-penalized neural scaling laws which guided identification of compute-optimal model configurations without exhaustive sweeps at every scale, reducing model-development cost by an order of magnitude.

MIST models have been fine-tuned to predict over 400 structure–property relationships spanning domains from psychophysics to electrochemistry. They demonstrate state-of-the-art benchmark performance and enable real-world applications including stereochemical reasoning for organometallics, olfactory perception mapping, and electrolyte formulation design.

Beyond raw predictive accuracy, using mechanistic-interpretability methods we determine MIST learns chemically meaningful concepts during training. Analysis of token vectors, low-dimensional embedding projections and model logits reveals concept-aligned structures not explicitly labeled during training.

Together, these contributions connect molecular representation learning, compute-optimal scaling, and broad scientific validation, establishing scientific foundation models as robust tools for materials discovery and optimization.

events.title: From Hero Run to Fleet Proof: Reproducible AI Training Across 512 GPUs
events.description:
One fast benchmark run does not prove that a large AI cluster will perform consistently in production. This presentation explains how Nscale moved from a single “hero run” to repeatable fleet-level validation across a 64-rack NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 deployment.

We will show how 14 workload configurations, each using 512 GPUs, were repeated across independent allocations to test whether performance held across different racks, NVLink domains, NCCL paths and InfiniBand fabric. The session covers topology-aware placement, firmware consistency, health validation, workload comparability and the preservation of evidence needed to distinguish a genuine fleet capability from an isolated peak result.

Attendees will learn a practical methodology for designing reproducible large-scale training tests, identifying infrastructure variance and deciding when benchmark evidence is strong enough to support production-readiness claims.

events.title: High-Performance Tensor Formulation of the Viterbi Algorithm for Hidden Semi-Markov Models
events.description: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) are fundamental probabilistic models widely adopted across diverse domains, from computational biology to finance and signal processing. The Viterbi algorithm decodes the most likely state sequence given an HSMM and can be applied iteratively for ab initio model learning. However, existing Viterbi implementations remain sequential, and GPU-accelerated solutions are entirely absent, making HSMM decoding impractical for large-scale workloads. We present a tensor-based formulation of the Viterbi algorithm for HSMMs, restructuring the inner loops into tensor operations that naturally map onto SIMD units and massively parallel architectures. Building on this formulation, we provide optimized implementations spanning single- and multi-core CPUs, and, for the first time, GPU. Experimental evaluation demonstrates speedups of up to 14× on a single core, over 200× with multi-core, and over 570× on GPU over the state-of-the-art sequential baseline, establishing a new performance baseline for large-scale HSMM decoding.

events.title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
events.description:
HPC workflows are growing in scale and complexity, demanding elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained parallel execution. While serverless computing is conceptually well-suited due to its on-demand model, existing frameworks are primarily designed for lightweight, event-driven workloads, leading to fundamental mismatches in highly concurrent HPC scenarios.

In such workloads, large numbers of function instances must be created simultaneously, introducing significant startup and communication overhead. Kernel-dependent mechanisms—such as cgroups, namespaces, and the network stack—become bottlenecks: instance initialization triggers heavy lock contention, while cross-node communication incurs additional costs from data copying, serialization, and context switching.

To address these issues, we propose eFaaS, a serverless architecture tailored for HPC. By leveraging eBPF, eFaaS enables lock-free isolation and zero-copy communication, minimizing kernel overhead. Experimental results show that eFaaS maintains stable performance under extreme concurrency, significantly reduces long-tail latency, and achieves end-to-end speedups of 1.27×–3.74× across representative HPC workflows.

events.title: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling
events.description: Batched matching is widely used in drug discovery, software analysis, and social network analysis. Its core operation, subgraph matching, is an NP-complete graph algorithm that has been optimized in the HPC field for decades. As for batching scenario, we find that current subgraph matching systems are unable to leverage the common structure patterns of real-world graphs, thereby missing potential optimization opportunities. In this paper, we propose BMS2, a batched matching system with structure-aware scheduling. BMS2 incorporates these intrinsic properties into previous general filter-join strategy: (1) in the filter phase, BMS2 utilizes the presence information of special structure for early termination; (2) in the join phase, we exploit the similarity of batched queries to reuse matching results of common structure. Experiments demonstrate that BMS2 can achieve an order of magnitude performance improvement on GPUs compared to the state-of-the-art with the ability to process two orders of magnitude larger dataset.

events.title: From PME to FMM: A Modern Approach to Long-Range Force Calculation in GROMACS
events.description:
The fast multipole method (FMM) is a potentially scalable method for long-range electrostatics in molecular dynamics (MD) codes such as GROMACS. Most MD codes have relied for decades on the highly optimized particle mesh Ewald (PME) method, but its reliance on fast Fourier transforms introduces all-to-all communication that ultimately limits strong scaling, whereas FMM uses a hierarchical communication pattern in which farther nodes exchange less information.

In this study, we tightly integrate a highly-scalable and GPU-accelerated FMM into GROMACS, which for the first time shows an actual advantage over PME in time-to-solution. We compared both FMM and PME on the ALPS cluster across one to 128 Grace Hopper compute nodes, each equipped with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs, over multiple MD test systems. Across these systems, including a 44-million-atom simulation, our FMM implementation shows markedly better scalability than GROMACS' highly optimized PME implementation and achieves up to 2.57× speedup at scale.

events.title: Papers in Conversation
events.description: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

events.title: Hardware-Aware Matrix-Free Algorithms for Accelerating Large-Scale Finite-Element Simulations on Distributed CPU and GPU Architectures
events.description:
Large-scale simulations governed by partial differential equations reduce, after finite-element (FE) discretization, to two kernels: operator action on large blocks of vectors inside eigensolvers, and the solution of Poisson or Helmholtz systems inside linear solvers. Both are limited by data movement rather than floating-point throughput, and the traditional assembled sparse-matrix and cell-matrix strategies scale poorly at high polynomial order, the first bound by memory traffic, the second by an operation count that grows as the sixth power of the order.

This dissertation develops hardware-aware matrix-free algorithms that evaluate operator actions on the fly through sum factorization, batched over the multivector dimension. The contributions are batched FE Helmholtz matrix-multivector products, using even-odd decomposition and SIMD vectorization on CPUs and fused register-blocked kernels on GPUs, a matrix-free Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonian action covering nonlocal projectors, real and complex arithmetic and inline constraint handling on AVX2/AVX-512/SVE CPUs and on GPUs with tensor cores and reduced-precision ghost exchange, a distributed-memory GPU fast-diagonalization solver that inverts the FE Laplacian exactly at O(N^(4/3)) FLOPs, and a device-native fused conjugate-gradient solver with a Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner.

Measured inside DFT-FE against existing baselines on Summit, Frontier, Fugaku, Polaris, Pravega and Aurora, the operator actions run 2.6x–5.8x faster than cell-matrix. The fused solve runs 5.86x faster than deal.II on 384 Aurora GPUs, and p-multigrid holds it at 5–7 iterations across polynomial orders. On tensor-product meshes one exact solve is 34x–3,186x faster than p-multigrid. The algorithms assume nothing specific to DFT and carry over to higher-order FE applications.

events.title: Beyond the Add-On: Absorbing Quantum Into the HPC Ecosystem
events.description:
Quantum computing has often been integrated with HPC systems as an add-on: scheduled through custom adapters, monitored through bespoke hooks, bolted onto facilities as parallel infrastructure. This reflects how most sites operate today, but it stops short of deep integration and does not provide the right foundation for the decade ahead.

The alternative view holds that quantum and HPC should be designed as one holistic system from the start, with quantum resources running through the same schedulers, workflow engines, and observability systems already in place. SC26 arrives at an inflection point: nine DOE national laboratories are actively deploying quantum systems, IBM has published its Quantum-Centric Supercomputing reference architecture, and DOE has launched the $293 million Genesis Mission targeting quantum-AI-HPC convergence. The systems are going in. This panel asks how to design that integration correctly from day one rather than assembling it as a series of bolt-ons.

events.title: Beyond the Add-On: Absorbing Quantum Into the HPC Ecosystem
Can Regional Collaborations Save HPC?
events.description: AI-driven workloads are outpacing what any single institution can afford, power and cooling constraints are tightening, and the workforce required to support next-generation HPC is in short supply. Regional collaboration is increasingly proposed as the answer — but does it actually work? This panel directly confronts that question. Drawing on operational experience from national HPC centers, regional networks, and campus research computing programs, panelists will debate the economics of cost-sharing, the governance challenges of federated infrastructure, and the realities of shared staffing and data management. Informed by the March 2026 NSF-CASC Workshop on NAIRR regional hubs and PEARC community discussions, the panel is structured as a moderated debate designed to surface genuine divergence/agreement and drive toward actionable insight for institutions making long-term infrastructure decisions right now.

events.title: Can Regional Collaborations Save HPC?
HPC Architecture and Networks
The Maverick Architecture: A Runtime-Adaptive Dataflow Paradigm for Exascale Computing
events.description:
AI is rebuilding compute — and it is exposing the limits of today's infrastructure.

For years, the industry believed the answer was simple: more GPUs, larger clusters, and specialized hardware for every new workload. But as multimodal AI, agentic systems, and increasingly heterogeneous architectures become the norm, the bottleneck is no longer the accelerator. It's the system itself.

The next generation of HPC and AI won't be won by fixed architectures optimized for today's models. It will be won by infrastructure that adapts as workloads evolve.

This session explores why maximizing FLOPS is no longer enough. Using the successful deployment of the Spectra supercomputer at Sandia National Laboratories as a real-world example, we'll examine how adaptive computing is redefining system efficiency, eliminating infrastructure bottlenecks, and preparing HPC for an era where software changes faster than hardware can be built.

events.title: Awards Ceremony and SC27 Launch
SC26 Awards Ceremony and SC27 Launch
Three Ways a Filesystem Panics When a Data Center Goes Dark — and How MooseFS 5 Avoids Them
events.description:
Distributed filesystems are mostly engineered around disk and server failures. A site outage is a different kind of event: many servers vanish at once, correlated, sometimes deliberately. Systems that treat it as many simultaneous disk failures tend to develop three concrete pathologies: leader election can deadlock because the survivors are no longer a majority; the repair machinery starts re-replicating everything the lost site held, saturating the inter-site link; and there is often no way to tell the system, "This site is down on purpose."

This talk describes how MooseFS 5 addresses each. Election counts sites, not servers — a site votes if a majority of its servers respond. Repair stays inside a site whenever surviving copies or EC parts allow, crossing the WAN only as last resort. Sites carry an explicit three-state lifecycle, so maintenance is not an emergency. Illustrated by MooseFS in production at IMGW-PIB across Warsaw and Kraków.

events.title: SMB and NFS behaviors for AI training
events.description:
Everyone knows NFS is the ideal remote file protocol for Linux and AI; after all, it’s the one everyone uses. So … what if they’re wrong?

In this Exhibitor Forum presentation, we will contrast SMB and NFS behaviors for AI training, showing real results and case studies of a modern SMB server stacked up against its Linux kernel-mode NFSD alternative, all on Linux, to debunk the myth of NFS being the only correct remote file system for Linux. Using tools like MLPerf, VDBench, IOR, and FIO, we will show the specific ways that SMB can be a superior fabric for AI training, checkpointing, and multi-platform data aggregation. You will leave this presentation with a clear understanding of the protocol impacts on AI workloads, the caveats of specific file systems and security measures, and how you can better optimize your AI training and checkpointing regardless of chosen protocol.

events.title: Wheelchairs and Scooters
2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
events.description: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

events.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
events.description:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman
Music Composition and Performance: Stephan Vankov

Produced at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, UIC, and Calit2, UCSD

events.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
events.description:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

events.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
events.description:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.
