events.title: Welcome
Invited talk: High RISC, High Reward: The Journey from Ratified Specs to RVA23 Superclusters
Featured Talk: The Amazing World of Programming for Accelerators: From GPUs to SmartNICs and QPUs (Among Many Others)
events.description: Hardware heterogeneity is not anecdotal anymore, but rather the norm. Furthermore, it is not any longer limited to the now-customary CPU+GPU system architectures. These days we haveSmartNICs, processing-in-memory (and its variants), quantum accelerators, FPGAs, vector processors, and a plethora of domain-specific accelerators, to name only a few, admittedly indifferent degrees of maturity and adoption. Application developers always struggle to figure out the right programming model(s), language(s), strategies (…) to make their codes future-proof.While AI-programming has quickly become the norm, we still want to understand AI-generated code (at least for the time being). In this talk, I will go over the current landscape of hardwareheterogeneity and its programming, my expectations for the upcoming future, and some solutions that my group has been working on for a variety of accelerator technologies.

events.title: Invited Talk
HPC Education and Training: Emerging Opportunities and Challenges
JUPITER: From Consistent Imaging to Continuous Benchmarking
events.description: This invited talk presents the full JUPITER installation journey — from an empty data center to consistently maintaining 6000 nodes. We describe how we envisioned the JUPITER Management Stack during procurement and system design, the benchmarks selected to assess system performance, and the lessons learned during installation. We cover how reference databases are rendered into configuration and compute node images, and how continuous benchmarking during operations detects system degradation over time. We close with lessons from what went wrong and how we plan to evolve this process for future systems in the era of AI-enhanced operation at exascale.

events.title: Invited Talk - Full stack sustainability: Looking at opportunities from Data Centres through to Applications, Adrian Jackson, EPCC
events.description: In this talk Adrian Jackson will outline some of the research activities underway at EPCC to improve the sustainability of computational research in the UK and global. As EPCC operates it's own data centre, has hardware and software researchers, and works closely with application developers and users, we are well position to impact efficiency and therefore sustainability across the whole computing stack. We will cover data centre optimisations, computing hardware innovations, storage and application efficiency improvements, and emerging workload performance in the AI inference space as well aim to explore where best to apply innovation to enable sustainable HPC.

events.title: Scale to See: From Extreme-Scale Computing and Scalable AI to New Scientific Discovery
events.description: Modern scientific problems increasingly demand more than faster computation—they require fundamentally new computational capabilities. This talk explores how the convergence of AI, mathematical modeling, and extreme-scale computing can transform scientific computing from solving known problems faster to enabling questions that were previously computationally inaccessible.Through examples in computational imaging, inverse problems, and Earth-system science, I will discuss how scaling AI to unprecedented model sizes, spatial and temporal resolutions, and ensemble sizes can reveal structure, quantify uncertainty, and enable scientific inference that is difficult or impossible at conventional scales. I will highlight how advances in AI algorithms, architectures, and HPC systems work together to create these new capabilities, and discuss opportunities and challenges for the next generation of scientific discovery.

events.title: Pre-Training AuroraGPT on Intel XPUs
events.description: AuroraGPT pre-trains open foundation models for science on Aurora, an HPE Cray EX system of ~127,000 Intel Max-series XPUs and one of the largest non-NVIDIA GPU systems in production. Training at this scale on a SYCL/oneCCL stack, rather than CUDA/NCCL, surfaces portability and reliability problems the usual toolchain does not address. We present an open, portable stack: ezpz, a launcher that runs the same unmodified PyTorch script across Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, and an experiments/ezpz fork of TorchTitan. The completed AuroraGPT-2B run reached 7.77T tokens; on the migrated stack, an in-flight 20B run matches that fully-trained 2B's peak evaluation scores at comparable compute while consuming ~17x fewer tokens. We detail the failures behind these numbers: a silent loss-reporting bug caught only by bit-exact regression, an 80B instability that NaN'd three optimizers, and a launcher-native auto-retry protocol that eliminated a silent-failure mode responsible for nine lost runs in two weeks.

events.title: A case study on the resource utilisation and queue dynamics of an institutional HPC system
events.description: HPC systems are often evaluated using aggregate metrics that implicitly assume a uniform user population. Using a year-long trace from an institutional HPC system, spanning 4.2 million jobs and 596 users, we show this assumption fails for demand-concentrated workloads: a small cohort drives most computational demand, energy consumption, and the mismatch between requested and actually-used resources. This concentration produces severe queue unfairness governed by job shape: small, backfill-compatible jobs dispatch instantly regardless of priority, while larger jobs do not, so the users best served by the scheduler are not those with the least demand, but those whose jobs fit available capacity. Counterfactual simulation shows targeted interventions recover most of the achievable benefit: resizing resource requests cuts mean queue wait by 67%, and pacing the heaviest 5% of submitters cuts mean wait by 82%. Both the waste and the queue risk are predictable from submission-time metadata alone, enabling proactive management.

events.title: Invited talk: From Streaming Data to Timely Decisions: Infrastructure for Urgent Science
events.description: Urgent science describes time-critical, data-driven scientific workflows that can leverage distributed data sources in a timely way to facilitate important decision-making. Despite the exponential growth of available digital data sources and the ubiquity of non-trivial computational power to process this data, realizing urgent science workflows remains challenging. This talk will explore application use cases, the requirements and challenges of urgent computing, and how the National Data Platform (NDP) can support AI-enabled urgent science workflows.

events.title: How the Paradigm of Scientific Computing Evolves Through the Genesis Mission
Can LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code?
events.description: Large Language Models are increasingly integrated into software development, yet HPC remains demanding for them. Their performance has been measured for low-level, kernel-based parallel programming paradigms, but task-based and workflow orchestration paradigms, despite growing importance, have seen less rigorous evaluation. We extend the ParEval benchmark, originally demonstrated on C++ kernel-level models, to task-based paradigms and demonstrate it on PyCOMPSs, asking whether LLMs generate correct and efficient task-based parallel code. We further propose a multi-tier prompting scheme, from programming-model knowledge to infrastructure-aware coding, and evaluate the first two levels. Across 21 models, correctness and efficiency decouple: the most correct model is among the least efficient, and only one frontier model is strong in both. Open-weight models close the gap to the previous commercial generation with framework-specific guidance. The main barrier is framework knowledge, not the parallel algorithm, and correct code still achieves limited efficiency at the studied problem size.

events.title: On preprocessing heterogeneous HPC telemetry for use in foundation models and digital twins
events.description: HPC facilities publish telemetry supporting foundation-model training and digital-twin replay but lack common fields, units, and privacy conventions. We extend REDI and AIDRIN to HPC telemetry via a new domain processor and agentic telemetry skill, and apply SetGo, forming an end-to-end pipeline that transforms heterogeneous telemetry into AI-ready and digital-twin-ready datasets. For digital twins, we demonstrate cross-facility replay fidelity: naively replaying Marconi100 telemetry through a Frontier twin violates its physical power envelope on 10.23% of samples; renormalization reduces this to 0.0042%. The pipeline supports representative replay and targeted emulation. For foundation models, we find static scheduler metadata alone gives no signal for predicting job-level details; however, ExaFM predicts job runtime with R2 = 0.960 when conditioned on a pre-anonymization identity embedding; without it, transferring that head to Marconi100, unseen during pretraining, reaches R2 = 0.716. We close with actionable recommendations for publishing AI- and digital-twin-ready telemetry toward future pretraining corpora.

events.title: HPC Education Across Institutional Boundaries: Leveraging NCShare's Statewide Cyberinfrastructure
events.description:
Most introductory HPC training assumes a local cluster, local staff, and a local allocation process-resources many institutions lack. NCShare, an NSF-funded coalition of North Carolina institutions, operates shared statewide cyberinfrastructure, including NVIDIA H200 GPUs, open to all member campuses.
We describe the design and operation of the NCShare HPC Workshops, a free series taking participants from no prior HPC experience to a completed scientific job. Co-taught by NCShare staff and instructors across member institutions, the curriculum covers access, storage and data movement, containers, CPU-parallel and GPU-accelerated applications, and scientific visualization.
Two design decisions follow from the shared infrastructure. With no environment-module system, containers are the primary route to scientific software making a participant's first environment portable and reproducible. Because allocation latency is the main barrier to participation, workshops run on a dedicated scheduler partition.
We report workshop assessment, post-workshop usage, and release all materials for reuse.

events.title: Exploring the Exascale Universe
events.description: Recent exascale cosmology simulations are producing multi-petabyte datasets with unprecedented volume, resolution, and physical fidelity in support of next-generation observational surveys. These datasets allow us to visualize the evolution of cosmic structure across enormous spatial and temporal scales and to generate synthetic observations for direct comparison with survey data. They also provide powerful inputs for AI, including emulators and digital twins, as well as agent-based approaches that can streamline complex, multi-step scientific queries and analyses across datasets whose scale and complexity make traditional exploration increasingly difficult.

events.title: A JIT framework for Implicit GEMM and FlashAttention Micro-Kernels in RISC-V
events.description: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) is a credible CPU deep-learning inference target, but its software stack lags the silicon: optimized kernels are scarce, and prior co-design studies of RVV convolution use compile-time intrinsic kernels built on the memory-hungry im2col+GEMM formulation, evaluated almost entirely in simulation. We present a lightweight just-in-time (JIT) framework that generates register-blocked, vector-length-agnostic Implicit GEMM micro-kernels for RVV at runtime, once the true vector length and layer shape are known, and integrates them into Intel oneDNN, eliminating the im2col buffer. We characterize six vector widths (VLEN 128-8192 bits) in cycle-accurate gem5 and validate on a BananaPi-F3 board, then extend the infrastructure to JIT FlashAttention. Implicit GEMM reaches 3.28x over scalar in gem5 and 3.08x on silicon; for FlashAttention, runtime generation is fastest up to VLEN=512, the range of every shipping RVV core. An autotuner separates portable tuning knobs (tile height MR) from ISA-specific ones (LMUL, NR).

events.title: Proper Rewards: Post-Training Time Series Foundation Models with Scoring-Rule GRPO
events.description: Temporal data are central to science, yet post-training methods that drive major advances in language modeling remain underexplored for time series foundation models (TSFMs). Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve model capabilities but tends to narrow the model's output distribution, causing overconfident probabilistic forecasts. We resolve this tension by combining group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with rewards based on proper scoring rules. Scoring-rule GRPO elicits calibrated predictive distributions: trajectory-level rewards improve general-purpose forecasting, whereas functional-level rewards specialize the predictive distribution for a task-specific quantity. Across diverse dynamical systems data, post-training with the energy-score reward reduces RMSE by 54% and in-distribution functional forecast error by 57% relative to the pre-trained model. These results show that proper scoring rules are promising rewards for temporal reasoning. Because the prediction quality of this post-training strategy transfers across tasks, it moves TSFMs closer to being truly foundational for scientific applications.

events.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and AI for Science
events.description: Many valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized because they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or subject to data-sovereignty restrictions. Federated AI therefore provides essential infrastructure for training models across institutions while keeping data local. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community on moving federated AI from pilots to dependable multi-site production. The analysis uses a five-domain readiness framework and two frontier-scale deployments: federated large language model training across three U.S. National Nuclear Security Administration laboratories using heterogeneous NVIDIA and AMD accelerators, and cross-facility fine-tuning spanning Aurora, Polaris, Frontier, and Perlmutter across Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD systems. We highlight systems challenges in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; summarize best practices for privacy, security, and decentralized trust; and identify open problems in asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts that motivate an international open-science working group.

events.title: Measuring the Impact of the Better Scientific Software Fellowship Program
events.description:
The Better Scientific Software Fellowship (BSSwF) Program was launched in 2018 in the U.S. to recognize, develop, and support leaders advancing practices, processes, and tools for better scientific software. Over eight years, the program has supported 43 Fellows and 43 Honorable Mentions across institutions and career stages to advance developer productivity and software sustainability and strengthen the scientific software community. A 2025 impact assessment
examined program reach, contributions to developer productivity and software sustainability, and effects on careers, mentorship, and community engagement. Based on a landscape analysis, review of Fellow projects, and interviews with Fellows, findings indicate that the program expanded professional networks and visibility and created opportunities for collaboration, mentoring, and career advancement. Program elements include community-facing projects, professional engagement, mentoring, and dissemination of Fellows’ work. BSSwF provides a model and insights for training, professional engagement, networking, and workforce-development programs supporting individual careers and the broader scientific
software ecosystem.

events.title: Perlmutter-Agent: Design and Early Deployment of a Local, Tool-Grounded LLM Assistant for HPC Incident Investigation
events.description: HPC incident investigation requires system administrators to correlate metrics, logs, and ticket history across heterogeneous data sources. We present Perlmutter-Agent, a locally deployed, tool-grounded large language model (LLM) assistant for incident investigation on NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer. An orchestrator converts Slack messages into structured requests and dispatches them to specialized metrics, logs, and ticket sub-agents. Guided by site-specific agent skills, the sub-agents query operational data through MCP servers and return evidence that the orchestrator summarizes into likely causes. All agents use an open-weight Qwen3.8-27B model served locally by vLLM, keeping operational data from external model providers. In a restricted beta, 339 of 380 user requests (89.2\%) completed successfully; diagnostic accuracy and operator usefulness remain to be evaluated.

events.title: Evaluating Fused Weight-Decompression General Matrix Multiplication for Quantized LLM Inference in SYCL
events.description: General matrix multiplication (GEMM) constitutes major computation load in Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Although weight quantization is the de facto standard of modern LLM inference, the GEMMs are often sub-optimized for non-CUDA backends, such as SYCL. A fused weight-decompression GEMM could potentially raise throughput via removing intermediate VRAM traffic. This paper evaluates the efficacy of the fused kernel for INT8 weight-quantized LLM inference in SYCL: We conduct standalone microbenchmarks to isolate the GEMM throughput and accuracy, followed by an inference-engine integration of the fused path that demonstrates its end-to-end gain. At the kernel level, the fused path is 1.20–1.36× faster than the baseline in GEMM. In LLM inference, the fused path raises prefill throughput by 20–57%. It closes the prefill gap against a CUDA backend from over 40% to within 7–26% where the model fits both devices, and surpasses CUDA where the Intel GPU's larger memory avoids layer-offloading.

events.title: ClusterBench: A Framework for Cluster-Wide Continuous Benchmarking and Regression Testing
events.description: Data centers need tooling that validates an entire installation rather than individual nodes, at acceptance and at regular intervals thereafter. This requires dispatching identical benchmarks to every node in a single submission, and therefore cluster-aware scheduling. This paper presents ClusterBench, a framework for cluster-wide continuous benchmarking. It ships with a benchmark collection targeting each component: CPU, GPU, memory, interconnect, and I/O. Because measurements are repeated throughout the cluster's lifetime, ClusterBench collects data across space and time. Comparison against earlier runs detects performance regressions introduced by software changes, such as kernel updates or new library versions. The measurements also form a dataset for research on hardware variability. On the NHR@FAU clusters Helma, Alex, and Fritz, variation within a single component stays within 1%. Variation across specimens reaches 5%, despite nodes identical by specification. Correlating performance with power draw, frequency, and temperature shows that this relationship differs between air- and liquid-cooled nodes.

events.title: Fast and Accurate ML Surrogates from Simulation: An HPC Liquid-Cooling Models Case Study
events.description: ExaDigiT is an open-source state-of-the-art digital twin framework for liquid-cooled HPC facilities. This framework models cooling systems using Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU)-based thermo-fluid simulators, which are computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale and real-time applications. This paper develops deep learning surrogates from a baseline LSTM through Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) variants to a Deep Multi-scale \& Multi-physics Network (DeepM\&Mnet) architecture. The paper builds on comprehensive data analysis that revealed structural properties of the cooling system: primary-secondary loop dynamic decoupling, spatial independence among Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs), and variable-dependent thermal time constants. Because most of these outputs are strongly persistent, we score against a persistence baseline in addition to $R^2$. Evaluated across 2,827 outputs (11 $\times$ 257 CDUs), the model beats persistence on 1,541 of the 1,799 outputs that carry learnable structure (85.7\%); the remaining 1,028 are shown to be persistence-locked, in particular, one group at a measured sensor noise floor. The mean $R^2$ is 0.926 (median 0.999), and at the 60\,s evaluation window, one forward for all 257 CDUs costs 4.1\,ms against 79.3\,s of FMU wall clock, a 19{,}514$\times$ speedup, turning a 10{,}000-member uncertainty ensemble run from 220 hours into 41 seconds. Architectures agree on aggregate $R^2$ to within 0.0002.

events.title: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
events.description:
The Ainekko (formerly Esperanto) ET-SoC-1 is a massively parallel RISC-V accelerator. Its compute array comprises 1024 dual-threaded in-order ET-Minion cores (2048
harts) operating at 600 MHz, each core providing an eight-lane 256-bit packed-single (PS) SIMD datapath shared by its two harts, with access to LPDDR4X memory at a nominal 133 GiB/s. This paper presents a performance investigation using single-precision general matrix multiplication (sGEMM) as the benchmark kernel. Two device kernels are implemented and
evaluated on the ET-SoC-1, these are a register-blocked packed-single (PS) SIMD baseline with two-step software pipelining, and a TensorFMA32 kernel that drives the same FMA datapath
through the per-core tensor micro-operation sequencer, with double-buffered A scratchpad loading. Because both kernels are bounded by the same arithmetic peak, the comparison isolates
the effect of operand delivery from that of arithmetic width. Performance is compared against four CPUs references and two GPUs.

events.title: SORT: Slurm-Orchestrated ROCm Telemetry for Facility-wide GPU Observability on HPC Systems
events.description:
Nearly 300 projects use Frontier at the Oak Ridge
Leadership Computing Facility each year, with approximately
30% turnover in the project population. These projects execute
heterogeneous applications across CPUs and GPUs, and their
computational requirements evolve as new workloads enter the
facility. Planning next-generation systems requires OLCF lead-
ership to better understand accelerator usage across the facility
workload population.
We present SORT, a Slurm-Orchestrated ROCm Telemetry
framework that uses traditional prologue and epilogue hooks
to control a ROCprofiler-SDK-based telemetry collector over the
lifetime of a Slurm allocation. SORT integrates ROCprofiler-SDK
counter collection with the Slurm allocation lifecycle and joins
compact counter artifacts with scheduler metadata for offline
analysis. Deployed on Borg, SORT collected 88,269 valid counter files associated
with 67,373 jobs. The resulting telemetry supports population-
level characterization of instruction, memory-request, and FP64
activity and can help identify candidate jobs for deeper profiling.

events.title: How Much Can We Compress Field Images for Smart Agriculture?
events.description: Camera-based smart-agriculture systems capture visual evidence of weeds, diseases, and pests, but multi-megapixel images are costly to transmit over low-power field networks. Many systems therefore perform on-device analysis and transmit only compact summaries, preventing remote visual verification. Image compression can reduce this burden, but must preserve information needed for downstream analysis. We present a preliminary task-level study using four annotated sugar-beet field images compressed with JPEG and JPEG~2000 over a 2--16$\times$ range, rerunning the same species-level weed detector on each reconstruction. Results show that lossy compression can substantially reduce image size while retaining useful detection performance, with JPEG~2000 consistently outperforming JPEG at the task level. We also find that similar PSNR values do not necessarily imply similar detection utility. However, payloads remain costly even at compression ratios that preserve detection quality, motivating agriculture-specific compression methods that more aggressively reduce data while protecting task-relevant visual information.

events.title: ArchAgent: Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains
events.description: The design space for modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures (GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators), memory technologies (HBM, GDDR, and SRAM), and interconnects (NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet). No single architecture is optimal for LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present \textbf{ArchAgent}, a hierarchical multi-agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems handled by specialist agents. A deterministic analytical evaluator closes the loop, ensuring all performance estimates come from analytical models rather than the LLM. On a mixed AI+HPC workload under a 1 MW power budget, ArchAgent discovers heterogeneous designs delivering a 1.93× weighted geometric mean speedup over a homogeneous GPU baseline, outperforming 100-evaluation hill climbing (1.65×) after only 18 evaluations.

events.title: Sustaining Early-Career Talent Through an HPC Bootcamp Pipeline
events.description: The Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) user facility, hosts an annual Intro to HPC Bootcamp that introduces students to foundational high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) skills through a one-week, hands-on, project-based program. To retain early-career talent in HPC and DOE laboratories, the bootcamp has developed a workforce pipeline with progressively deeper opportunities for participant re-engagement. Approximately 25% of each cohort return as peer mentors, and two former peer mentors return as summer interns to further develop their skills while innovating the program. Evaluation data demonstrates increased participant-reported confidence in technical skills and interest in HPC and DOE careers following the bootcamp. Participants and peer mentors also pursue internships at DOE laboratories through connections made during the program. Together, these pathways provide continued access to HPC resources, mentorship, professional development, and community to support early-career professionals in pursuing HPC careers.

events.title: Scaling Computation, Expanding Discovery: From Medical Imaging to Continental-Scale Archaeology
events.description: Scientific discovery is increasingly limited not by the availability of data, but by our ability to analyze and interpret complex information across spatial and temporal scales. Advances in AI, scalable computational methods, and high-performance computing (HPC) are transforming these limits, enabling scientists to see, infer, and understand phenomena previously beyond reach. Drawing on examples from medical imaging to continental-scale archaeology, this talk explores how radical collaboration among domain scientists, AI researchers, and HPC experts unlocks new scientific insights from massive, heterogeneous imaging and spatiotemporal datasets. Beyond accelerating existing workflows, these collaborations demonstrate how scaling computation can fundamentally expand the boundaries of scientific discovery.

events.title: From Idle to Urgent: A Resource-Harvested HPC Workflow for High-Fidelity Seismic Estimation
events.description: We propose an Urgent Interactive HPC workflow that dynamically integrates high-fidelity 3D nonlinear analysis with surrogate neural networks (NNs) to enable rapid decision-making during large-scale earthquakes. This approach achieves both "Resource Harvesting", which utilizes idle computing capacity during non-emergency periods, and immediate response during crises. By developing two specialized HPC kernels, the proposed method reduces energy-to-solution by 76% and improves throughput by 3.7-fold during normal operations to efficiently construct training datasets, while during emergencies, it couples NN-based inverse analysis with physics-based simulations and dynamic refinement to reduce conventional computational costs by over 97.9%, enabling the generation of highly reliable spatial time-history ground motion distributions within 30 minutes post-earthquake.

events.title: Towards Performance-Portable GPU Acceleration of MOM6 with Standard Fortran and OpenMP
events.description:
We describe a performance-portable GPU implementation strategy for the MOM6 ocean model, where portability is realized through a single codebase built on language standards while maintaining competitive performance on target CPU and GPU platforms. The implementation uses standard Fortran ``do concurrent`` as the kernel-level expression of parallelism, with OpenMP support for device-data residency and GPU-aware MPI communication.

Performance results show GPU acceleration of the dynamic core up to 3x relative to a single-socket CPU baseline while preserving bitwise-identical CPU and GPU results. Fixed-domain tests show scaling across multiple H100 GPUs. Module-level timings show that solver taxonomy guides the porting strategy but does not by itself predict realized speedup.

events.title: PerfDecode: Accelerating LLM Decoding on Systolic Arrays via Performance Modeling
events.description:
The autoregressive nature of large language model
(LLM) decoding results in matrix multiplications with small
token dimensions, which underutilize systolic arrays and exhibit
low arithmetic intensity. Efficient execution of these workloads
requires jointly improving processing-element utilization and
coordinating data movement with computation under limited
on-chip memory. We present PerfDecode, a performance-model-
guided approach to accelerating LLM decoding on systolic
arrays. PerfDecode reorganizes matrix multiplication execution
to exploit idle processing elements and pipeline data movement
with computation. At its core, an analytical performance model
captures DMA transfer and launch overhead, systolic-array com-
putation, reduction and write-back costs, and on-chip memory
constraints to automatically determine blocking configurations
for different matrix shapes. On AWS Trainium2, PerfDecode
consistently outperforms tiled matmul across diverse decode
operators in Llama-3-8B and Llama-3-70B, achieving geometric-
mean speedups of 2.73× and 2.85×, respectively.

events.title: Tracking HPC Software Stack Drift and Performance with Benchpark
events.description: As HPC systems grow in architectural complexity, system software stacks undergo continuous, autonomous development separate from HPC applications. Existing benchmarking frameworks do not fully automate evaluation of the changing software stacks, and a binary pass/fail result provides insufficient information to root cause test failures or performance changes. We present a continuous integration (CI) methodology that tracks changes in the software stack, tests functionality and performance, and identifies software and configuration changes that may explain failures or performance regressions. We demonstrate our methodology on HPC systems in two different compute centers, and attribute performance regressions to updates in the ROCm runtime library. By associating experiment results with software changes, our methodology provides a basis for diagnosing and reviewing evolving HPC environments.

events.title: EcoShift: Performance-Aware Power Management for Power-Constrained Heterogeneous Systems
events.description: Power constrained HPC systems increasingly execute heterogeneous CPU–GPU applications under strict cluster wide power limits. Existing power management policies typically rely on fair sharing or utilization based heuristics, overlooking application specific sensitivity to CPU and GPU power caps and therefore allocating reclaimed power inefficiently. We present EcoShift, a performance aware framework for cluster wide power management. EcoShift combines online performance prediction with a dynamic programming allocator that distributes reclaimed power among CPU–GPU applications to maximize average performance improvement. We evaluate EcoShift through emulation on two heterogeneous platforms equipped with Intel CPUs and NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPUs across diverse CPU–GPU workloads. EcoShift consistently outperforms state of the art policies, delivering up to 6% higher average performance while strictly maintaining the cluster wide power constraint.

events.title: A Tale of Two Teams: Scientists Versus the Multi-Agent System
events.description: We introduce a multi-agent cosmology system designed to access and analyze the largest cosmological simulations in the world. The system is designed as an interactive, end-to-end analysis suite with the goal of accelerating and streamlining complex analysis of cosmological simulations. Instead of benchmarking, in this work we compare the workflow of a real scientific team, reflecting a typical academic researcher group, to one scientist operating the MACosmo system. Both the scientific team and the agentic team found meaningful new information: the agentic system team isolated a distinct population of cool-core clusters residing in dynamically disturbed halos that a dark-matter-only classification would misclassify, while the scientific team derived new observables that aid robust classification through observational data. This work suggests that carefully designed multi-agent systems, used as collaborators, can accelerate and broaden the analysis of cosmological simulations while reaching conclusions that supplement an expert team.

events.title: Machine Learning-Based Performance Prediction for RISC-V Vector (RVV) Processors
events.description: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) offers rich architectural flexibility for data-parallel HPC workloads, but its vast microarchitectural design space is expensive to explore by cycle-accurate simulation, so machine-learned surrogates have become the standard substitute. Two questions that decide whether such a surrogate is useful are rarely examined: where its features come from, and how its generalization is measured. We study both on a gem5 model of the Ara vector unit, sweeping vector and memory-system parameters across TSVC2 kernels and training regression models on static, dynamic, and interaction features. We find that hardware configuration alone predicts CPI poorly, at 52.6% error under leave-one-kernel-out validation, while program features recovered from the compiled binary reduce this to 25.4%. More consequentially, the validation protocol dominates the reported accuracy: on identical data, features, and models, a random split reports 0.28% error against 23.2% when whole kernels are held out.

events.title: What is Your Cluster Actually Doing? Understanding Users, Utilization, and Performance Through Extensive Slurm Job Data Analysis
events.description:
Most HPC clusters collect and save job accounting data that can offer insights into how the cluster is used. Many others have looked at this and other data, with particular results and insights. This study adds a novel approach, looking at job data through a four-way job classification, and then analyzing cluster utilization through this lens. Additionally, we infer some amount of application usage data, and infer parallel configurations being utilized by users.

Some important results, among others, of our analysis are: a large fraction of HPC usage is from single-node jobs; user provided job walltime limits are largely unrelated to actual job walltime; and parallelism configurations (inferred) seem to be a place for significant user training and improvement.

events.title: Lowering the Barrier: Leveraging JupyterHub for K–12 AI and Data Science Outreach
events.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) and data literacy are becoming increasingly important for a competent STEM workforce, yet infrastructure barriers present a significant bottleneck for access, especially in the K-12 space. High-performance hardware such as GPUs requires significant funding to procure and host, which puts them out of reach for most school systems. Meanwhile, institutions of higher education possess the requisite hardware and often have underutilized compute capacity, but these resources are typically homed within a secure research ecosystem that creates friction for students unfamiliar with cluster computing concepts. To bridge this gap, we present our implementation of JupyterHub for a series of high school AI summer camps, highlighting the key design choices that contributed to the nearly 100% engagement of participating students.

events.title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
events.description:
Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance.
GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends.
We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs.
The new SYCL backend comes within \qty{3}{\percent} of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to $1.75\times$ and $2.17\times$ on the A30 and up to $1.79\times$ and $4.62\times$ on an AMD Instinct MI210.
On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPU's, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend.
Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.

events.title: SPEAR: Semantic Partitioning and Edge-Adapted Routing for Distributed LLM Serving
events.description: Edge deployment of LLMs requires multiple devices working together, since no single device matches a cloud server's range. Existing edge routers treat each query as one unit and use fixed, offline-trained policies that break down as workloads change. We present SPEAR (Semantic Partitioning and Edge-Adapted Routing), which routes work at the subtask level and keeps adapting after deployment. We split each query into subtasks, send each to an edge device by capability score and risk threshold, and fall back to a cloud model only when confidence is too low. We also update each device's LoRA parameters from cloud feedback, so edge models and the router keep improving without cloud-side retraining. On a testbed of Raspberry Pi 4s, Jetson Orins, and an RTX 4090 server, SPEAR reaches 94.7% routing accuracy, beating baselines like RouteLLM, with only 32.4 ms overhead; local adaptation raises Banking77 accuracy from 31.0% to 56.5% over five rounds.

events.title: Hitting the Memory Wall: Why Cache Miss Tolerance Defines CPU Performance Now
events.description: The memory wall is the defining bottleneck in today's AI, automotive, data center, and HPC SoCs. CPUs operate at GHz frequencies with single-digit nanosecond cycle times, yet DRAM latency remains stubbornly at 60–100 ns, and MMIO accesses across complex Networks-on-Chip can take even longer. No single architectural feature can solve this alone — it demands a multi-dimensional defense. This article shares our experience using Google's FlatBuffers library as a memory subsystem stress test on the Andes 46-series RISC-V core. Our evaluation found outstanding transaction capability delivers up to 39% architectural benefit when memory accesses are independent, but only 6% under pointer-chasing patterns. The 46-series attacks this problem from every angle: outstanding transactions to exploit memory-level parallelism, hardware prefetching to anticipate access patterns, and software prefetch to give programmers direct control.

Faster Scientific Multi-dimensional data analytics with NVIDIA cuPhoton
events.description: Observatories and telescopes, lasers and X-ray light sources, and other high-throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU-bound pipelines can process it to support timely decisions. The computational bottleneck is rarely one slow kernel, but rather an end-to-end workflow that spans from the sensor/simulation to a decision: load, read, HPC processing and analysis, AI-signal detection. Modern facilities routinely accumulate petabytes of multidimensional data across a single survey or experiment campaign. With CPU-first implementations, it can take hours to months—sometimes a year or more—to obtain scientifically useful results from data the instrument produced in seconds. These delays make it harder for scientists and engineers to extract insights to make informed decision and advance their research. What is missing is a GPU-native path that covers every stage from the sensor to the decision, not a faster version of any one step. I will talk about how NVIDIA cuPhoton provide open-source NVIDIA CUDA-X toolkit of GPU-accelerated building blocks for that path, spanning use cases from spectral and optical astronomy to time-domain laser/X-ray analysis. By keeping image data on the GPU from sensor read through classification—on either single to hundreds of GPUs—cuPhoton collapses the wait to as low as microseconds, resulting in a tight loop that researchers can run interactively, shortening time to insight and letting facilities keep pace with the data their instruments are producing.

events.title: Empowering K-12 Education through HPC-enabled AI and Computational Thinking: A Living Lab Case Study
events.description:
As High Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) become ubiquitous, there
is a critical need to bridge the gap between advanced computational research centers and K-12
educational environments. This lightning talk and demo present a case study of a piloted
collaboration between Penn State University, Cornell University, and the Milton Hershey School
(MHS). By establishing a “Living Lab” ecosystem, this initiative provided hands-on AI and
computational training for K-12 teachers while simultaneously developing the conversation for
applied AI solutions for complex school administration challenges. We demonstrate how
open-ended “lessons learned” conversations can demystify advanced technologies for non-
traditional disciplines and outline future directions for K-12 and HPC center partnerships. This
work has led to a state-wide “Listening Tour” funded by the Pennsylvania Department of
Education for additional conversations with K12 school districts across the state, that
may continue to build and further develop this andragogical workforce training approach.

events.title: Accelerated Genetic Programming Hyper-Heuristics for Simulation-Based Scheduling via Agentic AI
events.description: Python is widely used in scientific research because it enables rapid development and provides rich ecosystems for data analysis, AI and machine learning. However, customised research code can become prohibitively slow as experiments scale. This challenge is particularly acute in discrete-event project-scheduling simulations, where sequential state updates, nested loops, conditional evaluations, and object-oriented structures limit the benefits of compiled numerical and GPU-accelerated libraries. Addressing these bottlenecks typically requires iterative profiling, refactoring, testing, and validation, yet researchers may lack the time or specialised software-engineering expertise for low-level optimisation. This paper presents a systematic refactoring approach using Claude agentic AI on real-world project-scheduling workloads in a high-performance computing environment. Guided by representative benchmarks and correctness checks, the agent identifies bottlenecks, implements targeted optimisations, and evaluates their effects, while the researcher retains final control. Testing runtime reduced from 1,298 seconds to under 200 seconds without changing outputs, saving four million core-hours (NZ$320,000) annually.

events.title: The Shape of Speed: Impacts of Partition Geometry and Rank Density in Distributed Quantum Circuit Simulations
events.description: In distributed quantum circuit simulation, a poorly shaped partition can halve performance before computation begins. Evaluation on Fugaku across 764 validated configurations (twelve algorithms, thirteen torus partition geometries, and six rank densities for 39-qubit simulations on 1,024 nodes) shows that partition geometry dominates runtime. All twelve algorithms run 1.73–2.31x slower on flat partitions than on near-cubic ones despite identical data transfer, proving the slowdown stems from network delivery rather than communication volume. This penalty scales with the 3D torus partition aspect ratio (runtime ∝ α^0.39, r = 0.72). Rank density is secondary, cutting runtime by 11% at 16 ranks per node only on compact geometries. Ultimately, requesting a near-cubic partition with 16 ranks per node roughly halves time-to-solution relative to flat partitions, which also consume 1.82x more energy. A simulator-free all-to-all microbenchmark confirms a similar geometry penalty for collective-dominated workloads.

events.title: Compositional Energy Modeling of Layer-Resolved GPU Training
events.description: We present a compositional energy model for layer-resolved GPU training on AMD MI300X and NVIDIA H100 datacenter GPUs. Instead of fitting whole-run energy, the model assigns energy coefficients to hardware work classes, including matrix-engine convolutions, GEMM kernels, bandwidth-bound layers, gradient all-reduce, and static device power. Coefficients are calibrated in situ from steady-state replays of production ResNet-50 training kernels, then composed over full runs whose classes interleave, overlap, and contend for shared resources. On MI300X, coefficients calibrated on a native HIP implementation transfer to unmodified PyTorch without refitting, predicting energy to -7.3% at one GPU and +8.5% at sixteen GPUs. On H100, a frequency-dependent active-state term scoped by matrix-pipe utilization gives 9.0% mean absolute error over 42 operating points and 6.4% where the architecture took part in no modeling decision. Residuals identify missing vector work, state power, and operating-point effects. Power-cap sweeps show that per-operation energy falls by 20-41% from 750 W to 450 W on MI300X, so coefficients must be remeasured or corrected when the operating point changes.

events.title: Governed Agents: An Evidence-Based Architecture for the Computing Continuum
events.description: Agents can automate model selection, data curation, placement, retraining, and recovery across edge, cloud, and HPC resources, but this autonomy can turn uncertain model outputs into costly, privacy-sensitive, or irreversible actions. We define a governed agent as one whose proposed actions pass machine-checkable gates for context validity, decision uncertainty, policy compliance, execution feasibility, and auditability. Drawing on results from the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and related work, we present an architecture that integrates semantic typicality, runtime anomaly detection, neuro-symbolic verification, uncertainty-aware evaluation, lossless model compression, and modular agentic data curation. These mechanisms form a governance plane that mediates a sense-decide-act-learn loop across the computing continuum. Because current evidence remains component-level, we specify a falsifiable integration protocol, evaluation metrics, and failure tests to determine whether governed autonomy improves utility without obscuring risk or shifting excessive burden to human operators.

events.title: Porting and Benchmarking Chapel on Emerging RISC-V Hardware: An HPC Viability Study
events.description:
The Chapel programming language recently added support for the RISC-V architecture.
Here we discuss what changes were needed for Chapel to work on RISC-V as well as lessons learned from the porting process.
We use some of Chapel's extensive benchmark suite to gain further insight into the suitability of the RISC-V architecture for future HPC use.
We compare performance on SiFive P550 and Unmatched boards and a Sophon SG2042 with a variety of other recent HPC CPU platforms.
Various portability and performance anomalies arose on different architectures and are discussed.
While the RISC-V machines represent smaller preliminary offerings and not HPC-class hardware, these results still provide hope that RISC-V hardware can become viable for HPC in the near future.

events.title: The Empty Shelf: Vertical Market Failure in Data Storage for HPC and AI
events.description: For decades, computing drew on a shelf of demonstrated, but undeployed, technology, stocked largely by government-funded research. HAMR, the technology now carrying the HDD roadmap, came off that shelf: a 2001 federal cooperative agreement co-funded its early development; volume shipment arrived two decades later. The government funding instrument retired in 2007 on the premise that industry would restock the shelf. In magnetic data storage, where few suppliers face few hyperscale buyers, that premise collapsed into a vertical market failure, with suppliers rationally declining to fund breakthrough R&D. Buyers feel the consequences in shortages, rising prices, year-long lead times, and missed technology roadmaps. Demonstrated technologies sit unfunded, and the market still lacks a tier combining tape's low cost with quick access. The panel debates whether this stall threatens other computing technologies and closes on two ways to restock the shelf: pooled and matched pre-competitive investment, and AI demand for near-storage processing.

events.title: The Empty Shelf: Vertical Market Failure in Data Storage for HPC and AI
Interactive Visualization of Data Center Monitoring Data on a 3D Cluster Model
events.description: Modern data centers generate large volumes of heterogeneous monitoring data. While conventional two-dimensional visualization tools are effective for many analytical tasks, they provide limited spatial context at system and facility scales, particularly for cooling and network infrastructures. This paper presents a framework for spatially contextualized visualization of monitoring data using a realistic 3D cluster model. The approach maps multi-layer monitoring data onto a 3D representation, enabling both system-level overviews and detailed node-level inspection. Metrics are encoded using color-based textures and chart-based visualizations. Blender serves as the visualization platform, providing extensibility, high-quality rendering, and support for interactive and immersive exploration. The framework is demonstrated using a realistic model of the Karolina cluster. A generalized pipeline for parametric model creation is also introduced. It transforms tabular input data into a structured JSON representation and subsequently into Universal Scene Description (USD) format, enabling reusable and extensible 3D model generation.
