events.title: VERA: Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Memory Scaling of HPC Workloads in Kubernetes
events.description: Memory over-provisioning results in resource underutilization when HPC workloads run on Kubernetes. The default Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) cannot anticipate phase-driven memory spikes for first-run HPC jobs. In this work, we present a reinforcement learning recommender called VERA that formulates vertical memory scaling as a Markov Decision Process and trains an agent on 3,353 real Prometheus traces. Evaluated on a live Google Kubernetes Engine cluster using LAMMPS, graph analytics, in-memory analytics, and MLPerf 3D-UNet, the RL agent reclaims 31.6% of the available memory headroom and incurs at most one OOM event while VPA reclaims -7.9% over the same runs, raising memory provisioning, and its recommendation would have been insufficient to avoid OOM in 30 runs. The results demonstrate that an observation-driven RL recommender could outperform retrospective heuristics for dynamic memory scaling.

events.title: The Cornell Virtual Workshop: Looking Back, Looking Forward
events.description: The Cornell Virtual Workshop (CVW), developed to deliver asynchronous training for high-performance computing (HPC), has served for more than three decades as an innovative platform for collecting and delivering training for HPC users and computational scientists. Created by the Cornell Center for Advanced Computing, the CVW service has followed the development of both HPC systems and generations of programming languages. We describe the evolution of the CVW over time across a series of experiments and innovations, through use by more than 300,000 visitors per year, and describe challenges in maintaining a long-standing training environment. Finally we offer some ideas for future innovations and tracking the direction of computational science research.

events.title: A community developed simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix architecture
events.description:
Tenstorrent's RISC-V based accelerators have become popular not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Whilst Tenstorrent document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present a community developed simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack.

Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, it is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.

events.title: PRISM: Task-aware Slimming for Edge-Cloud LLMs
events.description: While LLM compression techniques for cloud and HPC environments often assume diverse, unpredictable workloads, edge deployments typically serve fixed, single-task objectives. We identify two important distinctions in edge-based serving: first, unlike cloud inference which is bound by attention and KV-cache transfers, edge inference is primarily bottlenecked by MLP layers; second, layer and weight importance exhibit strong, task-specific sensitivity signatures. Building on these insights, we present PRISM, a task-aware compression framework for edge-cloud LLM serving. In cloud, PRISM profiles per-task sensitivity using causal ablation and AWQ-style quantization error, generating an execution layer mask and a precision weight mask to form a task-specialized inference DAG. On the edge, a novel sliding-chunk scheduler minimizes the resident memory footprint by streaming weights and overlapping I/O with computation. Evaluated on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5 across four tasks, PRISM reduces peak memory by up to 2.9x and end-to-end latency by up to 26% compared to dense baselines.

events.title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
events.description: LLM agents can make expert scientific workflows accessible through natural language, but a plausible response does not establish that the requested computation ran. This matters at synchrotron facilities, where calibration and integration are multi-step operations over terabyte-scale datasets. We present APEXA, a deployed framework coordinating 61 tools for synchrotron data reduction. A deterministic execution-integrity guard prevents it from returning results for tool calls that did not execute, and the same tool layer enforces motor safety: across 50 adversarial scenarios and four models, it produced 0/200 violations against a simulated EPICS controller, versus 15/200 for a prompt-only baseline. We also introduce APEXA-Bench, 58 facility tasks organized by scientific correctness and physical consequence. On real APS beamline data, one prompt recovered detector geometry and integrated a full attenuation and exposure sweep. Trustworthy scientific agents need deterministic validation of execution, not model-side assurances. We release the framework, benchmark, and traces.

events.title: Annotation-Driven Migration of CUDA Programs to Tenstorrent Blackhole
events.description: Tenstorrent Blackhole combines distributed local memories, explicit inter-core communication, and Tensix cores decoupling data movement from computation. CUDA offers a substantial HPC software base but leaves physical data placement and scheduling largely implicit. Migrating CUDA HPC kernels to Blackhole requires spatial mapping across cores and per-core coordination of compute and data-movement kernels. We present an MLIR-based compiler deriving data placement, inter-core communication, and tile computation from a statically shaped affine CUDA subset. Declarative annotations express choices not fixed by the source, including compute/DM operation placement and streaming granularity. We evaluate it on Gaussian elimination, five-point stencil, and symmetric rank-k update. Relative to our compiler's default realizations, the best measured configurations achieve a 4.2× speedup for BF16 Gaussian and 2.1–2.2× for FP32 Gaussian and Jacobi. A choice's performance impact can reverse with surrounding policies, precision, and loop schedule, motivating comparison of alternative per-core realizations rather than independent policy selection.

events.title: Diagnosing and delivering repairs for Fortran GPU offload compiler defects
events.description: Many production simulation codes reach GPUs through directive-based Fortran offload, where compiler support is immature. Compiler suites are built largely from single-construct tests, leaving the clause combinations applications write thinly covered. We use a production flow solver as a compiler-validation instrument: golden files and grindtime detect a defect, metamorphic probes confirm it, and a C-to-Fortran differential and bisection localize it. Three months yielded 45 defects across the AMD, Cray, and Intel toolchains and 18 patches. About a dozen sit below any directive, in Fortran lowering, the back end, or the linker; several reproduce only under OpenACC. Fifteen give wrong answers with no diagnostic, so 42\% of what we found passes a compile-and-run suite. Delivery, not repair, delays users: Cray CCE 21.0.2 ships two defects whose upstream repairs predate its declared base by three and four months, and five merged fixes await a vendor build absent for 109 days.

events.title: From GPU-Accelerated Systems to Modern NVIDIA and AMD Superchips: Analyzing Energy and Power of a Heterogeneous SYCL Application
events.description:
Recently, the landscape of heterogeneous HPC systems has changed drastically once more, from classic GPU acceleration to tightly coupled systems such as the NVIDIA Grace Hopper superchip and the AMD MI300A APU.
Since energy consumption is a critical factor for the sustainable operation of HPC facilities, we analyze a heterogeneous SYCL application capable of CPU-GPU co-execution to investigate how power draw, energy consumption, and performance evolve in this ongoing transition.
Comparing heterogeneous and GPU-only scenarios, we find that the trade-off between maximum performance and minimum energy consumption observed in a conventional system persists even in modern superchips.
Furthermore, we observed significant energy savings in GPU-only settings on NVIDIA's GH200 platform compared to a classic GPU-accelerated system, driven by an over 140W lower CPU idle power draw. In a GPU-only scenario, AMD's MI300A APU achieves almost 19 percent lower runtimes than the NVIDIA GH200, while consuming only 1.03 times the energy.

events.title: AC-STRR: Training-Aware Visual Token Reduction for Scalable High-Resolution Medical Vision-Language Models
events.description:
High-resolution chest radiographs produce long visual-token sequences that increase large vision-language model (LVLM) fine-tuning cost and inference prefill latency.
We present \textbf{A}nchor-\textbf{C}ontext \textbf{S}implified \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}etention and \textbf{R}eduction (AC-STRR), a training-aware framework that filters background tokens, preserves locally distinctive anchors, and merges redundant context before the language decoder.
AC-STRR applies the same reduction path during fine-tuning and inference while retaining the original position indices used by Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding.
On VinDr-CXR with Qwen3-VL-8B and Low-Rank Adaptation, AC-STRR reduces fine-tuning time on one L40S by 24.9\% and achieves a 9.07$\times$ combined speedup on eight L40S GPUs over the single-GPU full-token baseline.
It also reaches up to 63.5\% token reduction on native-resolution MIMIC-CXR.
Tuned AC-STRR keeps report quality close to the full-token baseline while lowering prefill latency.
These results suggest that domain-aware token reduction can improve fine-tuning and inference prefill efficiency for high-resolution medical LVLMs.

events.title: TULCA-Based Visual Analytics of HPC Operational Data: A Case Study of Fugaku Rack's Power Data
events.description: In this paper, we apply Tensor Unified Linear Comparative Analysis (TULCA) to rack-level power consumption data from the supercomputer Fugaku. The data are represented as a third-order tensor with temporal, spatial, and variable axes, with each time point labeled by its operational period. TULCA generates low-dimensional representations that emphasize differences among labeled groups while preserving the tensor structure. Based on this representation, we construct an analysis workflow that provides an overview of temporal behavior and traces differences between analyst-selected temporal clusters back to the contributing compute racks. We applied the workflow to power consumption data from Fugaku's 432 compute racks across two operational periods. In case studies, the racks contributing most strongly to the observed separation exhibited sharp, short-term power fluctuations. These results demonstrate the potential of the workflow for interactive comparative analysis of HPC operational data.

events.title: Placing the Control Plane: Cloud-Native Federated Learning Across Batch-Scheduled HPC
events.description: The United Kingdom's AI Research Resource (AIRR) opens national supercomputers to a community familiar with always-reachable cloud services. With batch-scheduled HPC, a user requests a time-bounded allocation that is then reclaimed. Federated Learning (FL) exposes this tension, pairing a long-lived control plane with short-lived training. We characterize the resulting placement asymmetry: the coordination server sees only model updates and control metadata, so it can sit on neutral infrastructure, whereas the client control process is bound to the participating site's data and must remain within its trust boundary. The outbound-only connection this implies is also how edge clients connect, though the batch-scheduler mismatch is specific to HPC. We demonstrate a cross-silo federation spanning three independently administered systems (Isambard-AI, Isambard 3, and Zenith) using unmodified production FL frameworks (FLARE-wrapped Flower), measure the cost the client placement incurs, and propose Kubernetes-as-a-service as the in-boundary home for the persistent process.

events.title: From dispersed training materials to a centralized learning solution: The conceptualization of the SDSC Learning Hub
events.description:
HPC centers accumulate decades of training materials — slides,
documents, videos, code, and repositories — but as these collections
grow, so does the challenge of helping users find what’s relevant to
them under FAIR principles. We present the SDSC HPC Learning
Hub, a user-centered prototype connecting learners with training
resources drawn from a corpus spanning 2018 to the present (500+
cataloged materials). A novel feature is the use of learning paths
that can be customized to user activities. In this paper, we report on
the current public prototype, evaluation methodology, and lessons
learned for organizations transforming fragmented educational
collections into coherent learning environments.

events.title: AI Agents for Nuclear Science: Evaluation of Vaults, Skills, and Multi-Agent Verification
events.description: Scientific AI agents increasingly assist researchers in software development, workflow orchestration, data analysis, and simulation-driven discovery. However, scientific environments impose requirements beyond those of general-purpose assistants, including domain-specific knowledge integration, reproducibility, correctness verification, and continuous adaptation to evolving software ecosystems. In this paper, we present a design of scientific agents evaluated across four nuclear-fuel specialists spanning open-ended research to deterministic workflow execution. We evaluate the impact of structured knowledge vaults and reusable skills on agent performance, execution cost, and reliability and find that across five foundation models, the answer quality improves by roughly 1.2x-1.5x more than they raise execution cost. We describe a correctness-verification agent that traces cited references to validate outputs, reducing relative grading error against manual evaluation and discuss a path toward collaborative multi-agent systems combining agents that follow our design. The study provides practical guidance for building scalable, trustworthy scientific AI agents.

events.title: Dependency-Preserving GPU Work Decomposition for Earthquake Rupture Simulation Using the Fast Domain Partitioning Method
events.description: The Fast Domain Partitioning Method (FDPM) reduces the time and memory complexity of boundary-integral-equation simulations of earthquake rupture. Its matrix-generation phase exposes independent element pairs, but each pair's three slip-direction series produce hundreds of coefficients reused by closed-form evaluations throughout a time window. A one-thread-per-pair mapping exceeds register capacity, whereas distributing only the evaluation across threads routes coefficients through device memory. GPU-kernel and thread boundaries therefore cannot be chosen independently. We propose dependency-preserving work decomposition that jointly selects both boundaries from producer–consumer dependencies and GPU resource and execution constraints. For FDPM, one fused kernel handles each series and one warp lane owns each term-specific coefficient–evaluation chain, keeping coefficients on chip and exchanging only low-volume scalars. On an NVIDIA H100, matrix generation runs about 12× faster than a direct OpenACC port on the same GPU. With additional time-evolution optimizations, the whole simulation runs 45× faster than the production A64FX baseline.

events.title: Scalable In-Domain Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Dense Representation Transfer in High-Resolution Plant Imaging
events.description:
High-resolution plant imaging enables detailed characterization of plant
morphology, but dense scientific imaging analysis remains limited by costly pixel-level
annotations, large image dimensions, and variable imaging conditions. This
work proposes a scalable in-domain self-supervised foundation model for
high-resolution poplar imagery. A masked autoencoder with a ViT backbone is
pretrained on more than 10 million multi-species plant image tiles using distributed
training. The learned representations are benchmarked for fine-grained dense
prediction and coarse global retrieval under limited supervision and realistic
downstream conditions. Across limited annotations, cross-view variation, and
resolution degradation, the in-domain FM achieves a Mean Dice of 0.8686 and a
Pooled Dice of 0.8959, outperforming an ImageNet-pretrained MAE by 0.0694 and
0.0613, respectively. Increasing pretraining scale further
improves dense feature transfer, suggesting that scalable in-domain pretraining
can reduce domain gaps in high-pixel-dimension scientific imaging.

events.title: Scale Up Platform Enabled by RISC – SUPER
events.description:
Scale Up Platform Enabled by RISC-V (SUPER)
is an open source firmware extension that provides a remote
memory model implementation for RISC-V, mapping physical
memory operations, e.g., loads, stores, and atomics, to operations
over unmodified networks such as Slingshot, UAL or UEC. Unlike other remote memory, memory expansion, or scaleup
implementations, SUPER requires no hardware
beyond a packet-based network. Instead, SUPER uses unique
capabilities of the RISC-V architecture to intercept physical
memory accesses and convert them to remote memory accesses.
The overhead for this interception is less than 10 nanoseconds
on the new NextSilicon Arbel CPUs. Unlike previous systems,
SUPER requires no globally coherent address space map.
This paper describes

• what SUPER provides

• how it uses the unique properties of RISC-V

• its performance

events.title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
events.description: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet the data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab for what-if exploration. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies, revealing how the same workload would have unfolded under different decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, supporting real-time decision-making. The dashboard covers the complete workflow---workload characterization, experiment configuration, and multidimensional comparison---letting users see which policies suit a workload and at what trade-offs. We validate CQTwin on Argonne Leadership Computing Facility production traces spanning 2016--2023.

events.title: A Scalable and Sustainable Online Environment for HPC Education: Integrating projectEUREKA! with Local Kubernetes Infrastructure
events.description: Academic institutions need scalable approaches for providing students and faculty access to high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence without requiring infrastructure expertise. This paper presents an online environment built on the CAMSA cluster at Texas A&M University–San Antonio using K3s, KubeVirt, Ansible automation, and projectEUREKA! to provide browser-based access to local computational resources. Standardized application environments and automated provisioning reduce repetitive configuration and infrastructure-management burdens for learners, instructors, and support staff. Traditional HPC resources remain available alongside Kubernetes, allowing backend complexity to be introduced progressively when appropriate. The approach is evaluated through deployment reproducibility and access-complexity analysis, comparing the skills, dependencies, and actions required to reach a functional computing environment. The resulting architecture provides a transferable, sustainable model for institutions using HPC to support education and training without making HPC expertise itself the educational objective.

events.title: SplitFT: An Edge-Cloud Collaborative Federated Split Learning System for LLM Fine-Tuning
events.description:
Federated Split Learning (FSL) has emerged as an effective paradigm for mitigating the computational burden of edge clients in classical federated learning while preserving data privacy. However, applying FSL to large language model (LLM) fine-tuning introduces several critical challenges. In particular, cut-layer selection must be adaptively configured across clients to accommodate heterogeneous data distributions and device capabilities, which can significantly affect system performance. Moreover, reducing communication overhead during fine-tuning remains an important yet underexplored problem.

We propose SplitFT, an edge-cloud collaborative federated split learning system for LLM fine-tuning. SplitFT allows clients to select different cut layers according to their computational resources and model performance. It further reduces communication costs by decreasing the LoRA rank at the cut layer. To better emulate real-world data heterogeneity, we introduce a length-based Dirichlet partitioning strategy. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks demonstrate that SplitFT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both fine-tuning efficiency and model performance.

events.title: From Candidate to Confirmed: A Verification-First Agenda for Open Autonomous Science
events.description: Automation, robotics, and LLMs are reshaping scientific discovery, generating hypotheses, designs, and analyses faster than humans can review them. Over the past year, multi-agent systems have produced laboratory-validated hypotheses, and interface standards like MCP and A2A have begun connecting agents to scientific tools and to one another. Progress on generation has outrun the infrastructure needed to trust it. Agents nearing expert performance on closed-ended questions complete only a small fraction of open-ended research tasks, no system has self-validated a novel discovery end to end, and a widely cited autonomous-discovery result was corrected after its novelty claims were contested. Verification, not generation, is now the binding constraint on autonomous science, and the open-model community is well positioned to address it. We propose a verification-first agenda of open, reproducible evaluation, end-to-end provenance for agentic workflows, and interoperable, accountable agent interfaces, artifacts that belong in shared open infrastructure alongside the models themselves.

events.title: Mechanism-Aware Analysis of Cross-Platform GPU Fault-Injection Outcomes
events.description:
HPC test practitioners frequently compare fault injection results across GPU platforms, software stack versions, and computing facilities. Standard outcome categories such as masked faults, silent data corruptions (SDCs), and detected unrecoverable errors (DUEs) provide useful campaign summaries, but matching labels or distributions do not necessarily indicate comparable behavior. We present a mechanism aware method for interpreting cross platform GPU fault injection results and apply it to six reproducible cases on production NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPU systems. The cases show that bit position can determine whether a test completes with SDC or causes device failure, that aligned injections can become different effective faults after backend lowering, and that faults reaching control or address logic may remain masked. We recommend
retaining lightweight runtime evidence for all tests and performing targeted propagation analysis on key cases before declaring cross-platform results equivalent.

events.title: Does New Hardware Improve Carbon Impact of HPC systems?
events.description: The carbon footprint of computing systems is growing rapidly, driven by exponential AI growth. Many studies have suggested approaches such as fast hardware upgrades, using renewable power, and extending system lifetime to improve overall carbon efficiency and reduce carbon footprint. We analyzed carbon efficiency of the top 500 high performance computing (HPC) systems. It shows that a combination of key factors affects carbon efficiency. We propose tempered hardware upgrade, where hardware upgrades are performed while considering carbon optimization, accounting for both new and old hardware's embodied carbon. We evaluate several approaches and find that optimizing for just one factor: performance, operational carbon, or embodied carbon fails to improve carbon efficiency, sometimes worsening it or yielding negligible gains. For example, a fast hardware upgrade worsens embodied carbon efficiency by 0.9x but slightly improves operational carbon efficiency by 1.1x, however increasing embodied and operational carbon emissions by 125.5% and 47.2%, respectively. In contrast, tempered hardware upgrade improves embodied carbon efficiency by 1.7x and operational carbon efficiency by 19x, while increasing embodied carbon emissions by only 12.7% and reducing operational carbon emissions by 86.2%. We conclude that a balanced approach is required to improve carbon efficiency and reduce carbon footprint of systems.

events.title: SkyMatch.jl: Fast, Differentiable Modeling for Millimeter-Sky Inference
events.description:
Generating realistic millimeter/sub-millimeter (mm/sub-mm) sky simulations is essential for de-blending sources and understanding cosmic dust-obscured star formation, but remains computationally expensive. While the previous tools could simulate only a small fraction (<0.25%) of the mm-sky, the next-generation telescopes are now mapping nearly 25% of the sky at high sensitivity, probing the faintest and farthest populations of galaxies. Interpreting this data and de-blending sources effectively requires accelerating forward modeling and inverse problem-solving techniques.

In this paper, we present SkyMatch.jl, a fast and differentiable framework for computing mock mm-sky maps and catalogs. Leveraging the Reactant.jl compiler, SkyMatch.jl automatically optimizes the simulation's tensor computations to run efficiently on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Overall, SkyMatch.jl achieves speedups of up to 90× on CPUs and 3300× on GPUs, enabling us to realistically simulate data from state-of-the-art mm-wave telescopes and interpret the resulting source populations.

events.title: Panel: Security of Interactive and Urgent sessions in the era of hacking AIs
events.description: The panel session will be a curated discussion about the featured talk, paper presentations, and lightning talks. Topics for the discussion are likely to include challenges with scheduling and running urgent streaming HPC jobs, tools for interactive HPC, use of agentic agents for interactive and urgent HPC, and security challenges with running interactive and streaming HPC systems.

events.title: JACC.Async: Performance-Portable Asynchronous Multi-GPU Programming with Just-in-Time Compilation
events.description:
We present JACC.Async, a new feature of Julia for ACCelerators (JACC), the performance-portable metaprogramming framework built on the just-in-time (JIT) and LLVM compiled
Julia language. JACC.Async enables scientific applications to exploit asynchronous executions across multiple GPUs through a high-level, portable, and easy-to-use interface. Despite the fact that asynchronous multi-GPU execution is essential for achieving high performance on modern systems, existing solutions often rely on low-level, vendor-specific programming models and complex synchronization mechanisms. JACC.Async addresses this reliance by providing the first JIT-based solution for asynchronous multi-GPU computing, offering a unified abstraction that overlaps computation, communication, and data movement across diverse accelerator architectures. JACC.Async supports the two major GPU vendors (NVIDIA and AMD). Scientific workloads based on the conjugate gradient algorithm were used to evaluate JACC.Async on modern multi-GPU platforms featuring NVIDIA A100 GPUs and AMD MI250X GPUs. The results demonstrate that JACC.Async achieves scalable performance with minimal modifications to existing applications.

events.title: The Art of the Hack: Deconstruct--Reconstruct--Apply as a Constructionist Framework for AI-Enabled Gateway Development
events.description: Hackathons are widely used for technical workforce development, yet their effectiveness is attributed to informal learning rather than grounded in learning theory. We present Deconstruct–Reconstruct–Apply (DRA), a constructionist framework for training in the era of LLM coding assistants, and report its first formalized instantiation: the SGX3 Virtual Coding Institute (June 1–19, 2026) and HackHPC@ADMI26 (June 22–26, 2026). Instruction taught students to dismantle AI systems before rebuilding them; the hackathon required teams to redeploy that toolchain in untaught domains and ship user-facing science gateways.

events.title: Automated Task Placement for Hybrid HPC-Serverless Workflows
events.description: Serverless computing offers HPC workflows elastic capacity, but only some tasks fit its runtime and memory limits, and finding them has required manual placement. We separate two questions that manual placement conflates: deployment-independent candidacy, which combines platform limits with task-level heuristics and is settled before execution, and deployment-dependent placement, which turns on how much workflow parallelism the local allocation absorbs. Our framework combines static DAG analysis with one bounded profiling run per task type to assign each a candidacy class, then splits candidates across local and serverless backends without per-task input. In a single-run campaign on Epigenomics, Seismology, and Cycles, hybrid execution reaches the lowest observed makespan of three strategies, but the margin tracks how capacity-constrained each workflow is: 65.0% on Seismology against 4.9% and 9.0%. Withholding the task types the analysis rejects lowers observed makespan a further 9.8–39.9%, and dispatch costs a median of 221 µs.

events.title: Predicting the Energy-Optimal GPU Clock for Production VASP Jobs Before They Run
events.description: VASP is a dominant HPC workload, and while many users are migrating their workflows to GPUs, not every job uses the hardware efficiently. Lowering the GPU clock for these jobs can reduce their energy consumption with limited impact on performance. However, the right clock differs from job to job. We present a model for per-job energy optimization, one that chooses each job’s clock from its input files alone, before the job runs. Every job’s slowdown follows the same machine-wide curve as the clock drops, scaled by a per-job sensitivity, and this shared curve carries 99.72% of the variance across jobs. Hence choosing the clock needs only the sensitivity, predicted from the submitted files. Under a 5% slowdown budget the selection saves 14.25% of GPU-board energy on 310 production GH200 jobs at 5.45% mean slowdown, and the median job lands on budget at 4.92%. The error concentrates in the most clock-sensitive jobs, whose sensitivity is underpredicted, but it falls as the corpus grows, so the remedy is more training data. Finally, the model transfers. We show sensitivity carries across machines, so a single calibration job maps the model onto an A100, and a handful of jobs settles the delivered clocks.

events.title: Characterizing Low-bit Deployment of 3D Medical Image Analysis on Portable AI Supercomputer
events.description: The sensitivity of patient data limits the direct deployment of web-based generative AI and other cloud-hosted models in clinical environments, motivating secure, on-premise inference. However, local deployment is constrained by computational resources, memory capacity, and hardware portability, particularly for demanding tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation. In this work, we investigate low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) for efficient offline deployment on the NVIDIA DGX Spark, a compact system with a Grace-Blackwell accelerator and 128 GB of unified memory. Using a unified TensorRT quantization workflow, we deploy nine representative 3D segmentation models spanning CNN- and transformer-based architectures, from 5.7M to 1.46B parameters, and evaluate them on the BTCV abdominal CT benchmark. Eight of nine models can be quantized to 8-bit weights and activations (W8A8) without meaningful accuracy degradation. Compared with full-precision inference, W8A8 achieves 3.9x-7.2x higher inference speed while substantially reducing memory consumption, enabling efficient, portable, privacy-preserving 3D medical image inference.

events.title: TSVC-RVV: A Diagnostic Extension of TSVC for Evaluating RISC-V Auto-Vectorization
events.description:
RISC-V is attracting growing interest in high-performance computing (HPC), with the RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) providing a vector-length-agnostic architecture for accelerating data-parallel workloads. Realizing this potential requires compiler toolchains that reliably generate efficient RVV code. Assessing and improving RVV auto-vectorization is therefore important to the RISC-V HPC software ecosystem.

The Test Suite for Vectorizing Compilers (TSVC) is widely used to evaluate auto-vectorization. It contains 151 loops, each designed to exercise a specific vectorization pattern. However, effective TSVC evaluation requires substantial manual effort, as the suite provides no reference vector implementations and each loop may admit multiple valid vectorization strategies.

We extend TSVC with two complementary RVV-focused references: (1) RVV intrinsic implementations for all 151 loops, providing vectorization strategies; and (2) source-code variants that expose limitations in RISC-V compiler toolchains. Together, these references enable more informative TSVC evaluation and provide actionable guidance for improving RVV support for HPC workloads.

events.title: Emerging Personas and Tools for Hybrid Quantum-HPC Systems
events.description: Quantum computing is entering an era where quantum processing units (QPUs) with tens to hundreds of qubits are increasingly integrated with high-performance computing (HPC) systems to support hybrid quantum-classical workloads. This paradigm, often referred to as Quantum-Centric SuperComputing (QCSC), introduces new operational, software, and infrastructure challenges. In this paper, we identify and characterize six distinct personas involved in QCSC environments. Particular attention is given to emerging roles that arise at the interface between quantum and HPC systems. We analyze the responsibilities and tools associated with each persona and examine their differing requirements for operational data. Consistent data representations and analytics frameworks will be required to support diverse users across the quantum-HPC ecosystem. By defining personas and their data needs, we provide a foundation for future discussions in this critical area.

events.title: Invited Talk: Victor Fung (Georgia Tech & Lila Sciences)
events.description: Victor Fung will discuss autonomous science and the emerging integration of AI reasoning, scientific tools, and automated experimentation to accelerate scientific discovery.

events.title: JForce: Fortran on AI Hardware via OpenMP Offloading and XLA JIT Compilation
events.description:
Modern accelerator increasingly rely on tensor-oriented execution units and compiler stacks originally developed for AI workloads, yet Fortran HPC applications cannot readily exploit them through existing toolchains.
The OpenMP \verb|workdistribute| construct defines a restricted class of Fortran array computations whose semantics closely resemble tensor computation graphs.
However, executing such regions on domain-specific accelerators still requires bridging the semantic gap between Fortran/OpenMP and tensor compiler infrastructures.
We present JForce, a Just-In-Time compilation and execution framework that intercepts the high-level MLIR representation of an OpenMP region, translates it into StableHLO, and compiles it using XLA.
JForce delegates tensor computation to XLA while retaining the standard OpenMP runtime for host--device data mapping and integration with the remaining OpenMP code.
We evaluate JForce on CPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and Google TPUs, demonstrating portable execution across heterogeneous backends and competitive performance for sufficiently large or repeatedly executed workloads.

events.title: Beyond the helpdesk: a lightweight, reproducible model for just-in-time HPC learning and support
events.description:
Formal HPC courses and individual helpdesk interactions address different user needs, but leave a gap for users who need timely guidance on practical problems without requiring a full course or a one-to-one support case. JSC HPC Support Corner, a monthly one-hour online session designed to make HPC expertise more accessible. It has the following structure: a 10-15 minute expert presentation, topic-specific Q&A, open discussion, and live troubleshooting. Participants can submit questions in advance in a shared document, and Zoom breakout rooms can be used for dedicated discussions. The sessions also serve as an orientation and awareness-raising channel, helping users discover services and workflows that are not necessarily covered in formal courses or encountered through individual support requests.

This work describes the educational rationale, distributed organisation, lessons learned, evaluation, and a reproducible workflow that other HPC centres can adapt as a complement to formal training and ticket-based support.

events.title: HPCTESTS Panel 2026
events.description: The HPCTESTS panel hosts all five presenters for a final discussion on the workshop's topics and presented work.

events.title: Out-of-View Depth and Motion Prediction in Robotic Endoscopy
events.description: The endoscope can observe only a narrow cone of the surgical field. Tissue leaving this cone deforms, which can lead to injuries if unnoticed. The hidden region has no visible pixels, so depth and motion must be predicted rather than measured. Reusing the last observed depth is a strong baseline over short intervals, but its error grows as tissue deforms, reaching 9.05 mm at the longest interval. We adopted a pretrained V-JEPA2-AC encoder with low-rank adaptation, where two decoders predict depth and optical flow for the hidden region from a reference RGB-D frame and a later view showing 16% of the frame. Under leave-one-organ-out cross-validation on four ex vivo DRENDS organs, with CRCD in every training fold, the adapted model reduces hidden-region depth RMSE from 6.852 to 6.197 mm, and endpoint error against RAFT pseudo-flow from 3.285 to 3.004 px relative to assuming zero motion.

events.title: Data-Driven Static MIG Planning for an H200 Research Cluster
events.description:
Research computing clusters support GPU workloads ranging from small interactive jobs to large full-device training runs. Exposing each GPU as a monolithic resource wastes capacity because many jobs require only a fraction of a GPU. Modern GPUs, such as the NVIDIA H200, support Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitioning, but real-time reconfiguration is impractical for heterogeneous, continuously arriving HPC workloads.

We frame MIG planning as an operational data analytics problem, using long-term production telemetry to make a one-time provisioning decision. We construct a slot-level demand matrix and formulate layout selection as an exact mixed-integer linear program (MILP), evaluating planners by weighted fulfillment. Our optimal layout improves in-sample fulfillment from 66.8% to 98.1%, reaches 97.6% on held-out data, and 99.7% on raw demand. A simple greedy planner achieves the same optimum due to a near-zero LP integrality gap (<0.001%). The layout is robust to demand inflation, and deploys directly with Slurm GRES.

events.title: Panel Discussion
Beyond Job Submission: Developing System Literacy through Productive Struggle
events.description: High-performance computing training reliably teaches users how to submit jobs. It rarely equips them to reason about why their work behaves as it does on a shared system. At a PEARC26 Birds-of-a-Feather session on system literacy, practitioners nearly all agreed that users should hold a working mental model of system behavior, and nearly all reported that users do not. We argue that this gap persists because system literacy is formed incidentally rather than taught: users assemble their own models from documentation, experience, and chance interactions, producing models that vary widely in accuracy and surface as uneven productivity on shared infrastructure. We locate the mechanism by which such models are revised in productive struggle, the calibrated difficulty skilled facilitators already sustain when they diagnose the misconception behind an error rather than only correcting it. Whether that practice can be scaled is the question we pose.

events.title: Load-Balanced Communication Overlap for Lattice H-Matrix–Vector Multiplication on GPU Clusters
events.description:
Lattice hierarchical H-matrices provide a structured low-rank representation for parallel boundary element method solvers, but the concentration of dense and poorly compressible submatrices near the matrix diagonal causes load imbalance under conventional process-grid mappings.
We develop a lattice-H-matrix-specific design for load-balanced communication overlap on GPU clusters.
The design combines a one-dimensional column-cyclic task assignment with a coarse-grained diagonal/off-diagonal decomposition.
The assignment distributes the expensive diagonal-block workload across processes, while the decomposition allows the collective reduction of off-diagonal contributions to proceed concurrently with diagonal-block GPU kernels.
An MPI+OpenACC implementation was evaluated on NVIDIA GH200 nodes using the HBI earthquake simulation application.
The proposed design distributes the dominant diagonal-region workload more evenly and achieves up to a 3.08x speedup over the conventional two-dimensional process-grid implementation.

events.title: The Economic Value of Heat Reuse
events.description: Due to the AI frenzy, the energy demand of data centers continues to grow dramatically, and AI factories that consume hundreds of Megawatts have become the new normal. The heat that those data centers generate from their electricity consumption is typically rejected as waste heat to ambient air, although it has potential value for other industries to be reused. This paper proposes an economic model to assess the value of such heat. We describe a demand function tailored to data center waste heat, use it in combination with demand curves to determine the heat’s value, and validate it with cooling data from the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Garching, Germany. We also present industrial use cases for heat at varying temperatures and discuss the potential economic advantages of heat reuse. Finally, we consider infrastructure costs and provide supply equations that outline the return on investment and payback periods.

events.title: Toward a Foundation Plug-and-Play Prior for Computed Tomography Reconstruction via a Multimodal Diffusion Model
events.description: Computed tomography (CT) throughput is limited by scan time, which grows with both the number of projections acquired and the detector integration time for each. Reconstructing high-quality volumes from sparse-view or low-dose measurements therefore depends on an informative prior, typically a neural network trained for one specific scan setting and retrained whenever the modality, geometry, or material changes. We investigate whether a single diffusion model trained across several imaging domains can instead serve as a prior for many CT problems simultaneously. We evaluate the proposed method using the same frozen model on three datasets that differ in modality, beam geometry, material, and degradation type, spanning flaw analysis in additively manufactured metal parts imaged with cone-beam X-ray CT and concrete microstructure imaged with parallel-beam neutron CT. Our proposed method out-performs analytic reconstructions in all three cases, providing a step toward a reusable foundation prior for heterogeneous CT reconstruction problems.

events.title: Accelerating Fast Fourier Transforms with the RISC-V Vector Extension
events.description: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) enables greater flexibility for Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) and vector processing compared to established extensions like AVX for x86. For Fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) in particular, variable vector lengths, segmented loads and stores, and permutation instructions allow for novel vectorization strategies previously not feasible with traditional SIMD. In this work, different vectorization schemes for FFTs are derived by systematically matching unique RVV features to complex data flows and arithmetic operations. The resulting FFT algorithms are then evaluated on a wide range of RVV 1.0 hardware, including the SpacemiT K1 and K3, the Sophon SG2044, and the SiFive X280. The results demonstrate that achieving high performance across diverse platforms requires four distinct vectorization paths, as the optimal strategy depends heavily on the hardware. Ultimately, these results highlight the necessity of dynamic, run-time kernel selection to sustain optimal performance in FFT across the heterogeneous RISC-V ecosystem.

events.title: Closing Remarks
Q/A and Closing Remarks
SuperSAM: Crafting a SAM Supernetwork via Structured Pruning and Unstructured Parameter Prioritization
events.description: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates the design of efficient networks, with one-shot NAS enabling greater efficiency by training a single weight-sharing supernetwork that contains many subnetworks. Designing such search spaces is challenging due to considerations involving architectural space, scoring methods, and computational cost. We present SuperSAM, a one-shot NAS search space derived from the Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our proposed NAS approach involves automated search space design via layer-wise structured pruning and activations-based MLP parameter prioritization. The SAM supernetwork is trained with the sandwich rule, while deployment uses a program autotuner to discover efficient subnetworks. Discovered models are 30–70% smaller than the original SAM ViT-B, with some outperforming the pre-trained model.

events.title: Towards MPI Communication Modeling From Passive Network Telemetry
events.description: The distribution of MPI message sizes issued by an application is a first-order determinant of its communication behavior, yet recovering this distribution typically requires application-level instrumentation and/or a priori knowledge of the communication pattern. We present an application-agnostic model of MPI communication that reconstructs the MPI message-size distribution from passive network telemetry: packet-level counters that modern NICs expose and that facility operators already collect continuously, system-wide, at negligible cost. The model requires no knowledge of the network topology, the communication peers, or the MPI operations in use, and can be applied retroactively to archived telemetry. Instantiated on the Cassini counters of NERSC's Perlmutter, the model estimates OSU Micro-Benchmark message counts within 0.5% and the dominant LAMMPS size classes within 10%, which is a first step toward instrumentation-free prediction of communication time.
